en: Adhyāya 3, Pāda 1:
Now begins the first quarter of the third chapter in the illustrious Nyāyasudhā.
One should worship that beloved of Śrī, whose state the wise resort to, considering it a pleasure no different from the shade of the hoods of a provoked serpent.
This chapter concerns the investigation of the means of attainment (*sādhana*).

The fact that the first quarter (*pāda*) establishes the states of transition and so forth for the sake of dispassion (*vairāgya*) is clear from the Commentary (*Bhāṣya*) itself regarding what each chapter and quarter propounds.
However, with the intention of stating the internal connection (*saṅgati*) by unifying them for the sake of brevity, [the author] will explain it later; thus begins the third chapter.
He states, in brief, the arguments for the prima facie view and the established conclusion regarding the locus of the feet: "svābhāviketi" (it is inherent).
Intrinsic nature, alteration, non-existence, co-existence, and what has been otherwise stated;
non-distinction, distinctions, concomitance, and mixture. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.1.1)

Contradictory speech, coexistence, futility, and a different interpretation—these are the arguments for the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa), intended for the purpose of demonstrating a superior quality [of the final conclusion]. Mānava 3.1.2.

Arising, twofold nature, superiority, conformity, fitness, strength, classification, absence of cause, postulation, and lack of another recourse— these are the proofs for a philosophical tenet (siddhānta). (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.1.3)
The term "sādhakāḥ" (proving factors) is connected here as well with the phrase "of the pūrvapakṣa" which is to be mentioned later.
In the expression "pūrvapakṣasya siddhāntasya," the singular number is used in the sense of a class (*jātāvekavacanam*). The form "sādhakāḥ" is a Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).
Alternatively, in the phrase "reasons for the prima facie position" (*pūrvapakṣasya yuktayaḥ*), the word "provers" (*sādhakāḥ*) is understood as being implied;
thus, the meaning is simply "reasons related to the prima facie position.
However, in the phrase "provers of the established conclusion" (*siddhāntasyaiva sādhakāḥ*), the word "principles" (*nyāyāḥ*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. *9,10*
Regarding this, the Sūtra states: "The body [arises] from the womb.
This has been explained in the Bhāṣya:
the living being (jīva), having descended from heaven, enters into the seeds of rice and other grains by way of rain, and then [into semen].

It is well known that, having entered the *kṛtaka-puruṣa* (the created person) along with the semen, it enters the womb through the mother’s birth canal and attains a body produced through the sequence of the *kalala*, *budbuda*, and so forth.
Regarding this, there is a doubt: is it real or is it unreal?
The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that it is not real.
Why?
Because of such statements as: "Having departed from heaven, he might enter some body situated within a womb."
Furthermore, in the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, we observe the birth of Māndhātṛ, Droṇa, Drupada, Kṛpa, and others even without a connection to seeds and so forth;
and when a matter can be established otherwise, it is not proper to resort to many assumptions.
Therefore, these [stories] serve solely to produce dispassion (*vairāgya*).
"The doctrines of those who know the inner self are precisely this";
such is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). Why? Because it is the truth.
“Having become a cloud, it rains;
then here rice, barley, medicinal herbs, trees, grasses, sesame, and beans are produced.”
For whoever eats food,
or whoever pours forth semen, becomes again of that very form. Thus, those here whose conduct has been pleasant will, for the most part, attain a pleasant womb.

This is because of such scriptural passages as these. Furthermore, when the meaning is not perceived through other means, the possibility of an alternative explanation (anyathāsiddhi) has no scope. Nor is there any contradiction with the indications found in other scriptural statements.
Because in some cases there is also the absence of a connection with seeds and so forth, it has that as its object;
as it has been said:
"He goes from heaven to the stationary beings."
"Having reached the heavens, he becomes stationary"—
this is [the meaning] according to the Śruti and Smṛti.
This interpretation, however, is incorrect.
Because it deviates from the sūtra.
Although the word *yoni* here could be explained as indicating seeds (*bīja*) and so forth, nevertheless, it is the very necessity of its connection that is understood in the sūtra;
there is no mention anywhere of its absence.
And if there were an absence of connection with seeds and so forth in some cases, then there would be the consequence of their being accidental; therefore, he says: "The seed... etc.

The body arises from the womb. The Blessed One spoke with the word "atha" regarding the abandonment of the fixed rule concerning the union of the seed, the person, and the womb. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.1.4a-c) *9,11*

By the word "seed" (*bīja*), rice and the like, as well as semen, are meant. "Absence of restriction regarding connection" (*saṅgatiniyama*) refers to the lack of a fixed rule concerning relationships.
This is the meaning.

Regarding the phrase "the union with semen" (*retaḥsig-yoga*), the word *atha* from the preceding sūtra is also carried over here; and it signifies a transition to a different topic from the one previously under discussion.
Thus, [the soul] enters the body through the womb.

The Blessed One, the author of the Sūtra, has indicated by the word "atha" that there is no fixed necessity regarding the connection with seeds and so forth, even in the absence of those [causes] in certain cases; therefore, the objection that this contradicts the Sūtra is not tenable. He refutes the argument previously stated—that if this were so, it would follow that [the arising of sprouts] is causeless—by saying: "And because of the cause."
...and [he should know] her by reason of her cause. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.1.4d)
And he states that the restriction regarding the connection with seeds and so forth is due to a cause;
this is what is meant:
the general rule is that a living being, drawn by the unseen force (adṛṣṭa) which is the cause of birth, attains a body through its connection with seeds and so forth.
And that [rebirth] is sometimes set aside by a specific cause characterized by excellence in knowledge, austerity, yoga, and so forth;
for example, as there is an exception regarding the production of a body for the torment of small creatures.
And thus it has been said:
“From a specific cause alone is a specific birth desired;
and the common birth of humans likewise arises from a common cause.
Therefore, this interpretation is correct.

Thus ends the first quarter of the third chapter in this commentary on the *Anuvyākhyāna*— the work of the venerable Pūrṇaprajña Bhagavatpāda— composed by the ascetic named Praguṇajayatīrtha, which provides an explanation of the meanings of difficult words and sentences. *** Adhyāya 3, Pāda 2, Sūtra 9.16 ***
"Bhakti is what is taught in this section;
for it is for the sake of bhakti that the greatness of the Blessed One is described"— thus, what is to be established in this section is made clear in the Bhāṣya itself.

Intending to explain the connection later on, he states the arguments for the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) in this section of the chapter in brief, beginning with the words "paścāt" (later).

Subsequently, there are: the non-perception [of the cause], the time of consciousness, suffering, distinctness, difference of location, contradiction, similarity of reasoning, and arising from itself. (MAnu 3.2.1)

The equilibrium of the qualities (guṇasāmya), non-union (ayoga), subversion by reasoning (tarkabādha), contrariety (vilomatā), manifoldness (nānābhāva), and seduction (pralobha) belong to the prima facie arguments (pūrvapakṣa).

The incapacity for agency, powerlessness, innate ignorance, and that very state [of ignorance]; the postulation of non-means of knowledge, the establishment of valid means of knowledge, extreme deficiency, and non-existence.
And in the statement regarding inference from specific observation (*viśeṣadṛṣṭi*), the power of the person (*puṃśakti*) is a clear illustration;
[the characteristics of such a person are] its non-worldliness, its superiority, its independence, and its definitive cognitions.
"Belonging to the prima facie position" (*pūrvapakṣagāḥ*) means connected with the prima facie position.
"Means of valid cognition for the final determination" (*nirṇayapramāḥ*) refers to the instruments of knowledge intended for the purpose of establishing the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).
[======= JNys_3,2.I: The Section on the Twilight Devotions (Saṃdhyādhikaraṇam) =======]
The creation occurs in the intermediate state, for so the scripture says.
Oṃ, the creation occurs in the intermediate state, for so the scripture says. Oṃ.
From the aphorisms beginning with "The body from the womb," the birth of the individual soul (jīva) is understood;
and for one thus born, the connection with states such as sleeping and so forth is well known.
In this particular section (adhikaraṇa), the majesty of the Blessed Lord, characterized by His being the instigator of the state of dreaming, is determined.
For instance:
a dream consists of objects and cognition.
In that regard, it is first of all untenable for the objects of a dream—such as elephants, horses, and so forth—to be dependent upon a Supreme Lord.

Because they are unreal, these [elements] are certainly not eternal and beginningless; for otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of perceiving them prior to and after the state of dreaming.

For it is not possible that they exist yet are not perceived while the means of perception, such as the eyes and so forth, remain unceased; rather, they are perceived because of their logical possibility,
nor have they gone elsewhere.
Because they are not perceived by others either, and because these [entities] are seen to have no fixed measure; nor is anything of such a nature— beginningless and eternal— ever observed.
Nor do they possess arising and destruction;
for if that were the case, it would follow that they would be perceived both before and after [their supposed moment].
Nor should it be argued that their arising and destruction occur at that very same moment, as is the case with lightning and the like.
Because there is no means of valid cognition for such a state [of existence],
and because it would entail the perception of the prior clay and so forth, as well as the potsherds and so forth, subsequently;
nor is there [any proof] for these [being simultaneous].
We observe both the material cause and the efficient cause within that very birth;
furthermore, the individual soul (*jīvātman*) cannot be the agent,
because the seer is devoid of activity.
Nor is it God, because another [creator] is not observed and because there is a lack of valid evidence.
And their nature as error is established by the statements:
"having the form of dreams and illusions," and "just like a dream or a mental fantasy."
This is made known by such scriptural and traditional texts (*śruti-smṛti*).
We shall discuss the student’s erroneous explanation and restatement later.
Thus, in this way, dream-objects do not have their existence dependent upon the Lord (*īśvara*).
Nor does it belong to the cognition of that [object],
because that too, due to the absence of a causal sign (*nimitta*), is not ultimately real.
First of all, the eyes and so forth are not [the cause] therein...
It is not objectless,
because those [senses] have ceased;
nor is it [objectless] in relation to the mind.
Because it lacks the capacity (due to a lack of independence) with respect to an object possessing form and other qualities,
it is for this very reason not a witness.
When the sense organs do not function, there is likewise no scope for inferential signs or verbal testimony.

Since this state appears in a non-mediated form, it follows that the dream state—consisting of the cognition of objects—is not dependent on Īśvara; having reached this conclusion, he provides an introductory statement (*upodghāta*) for its refutation: "Latent impressions" (*vāsanā*).
There is creation in the intermediate state, for so the scripture declares;
and some say there is a creator, as well as sons and other such beings;
but it is mere illusion, because its true nature is not manifested in its entirety.
The latent impressions (vāsanās) of all things, acquired through beginningless experience,
truly exist within the minds of all living beings from time immemorial.
The formative forces (saṃskāra) are synonymous with cultivation (bhāvanā).
The purpose of including the term "all" will become clear later.
Now, is it not the case that the formative force called cultivation is produced by experience?
Furthermore, it is not the case that all living beings experience all things;
how then can it be said that the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of all things exist for all living beings without exception? To this it is replied: "beginningless" (*anādi*).
They are produced from a beginningless stream of experience.
The Vaiśeṣikas and others maintain that latent impressions (vāsanās) are inherent in the self;
in order to refute this, it is said that they "reside in the mind."
The singular number is used to denote the class (*jātāvekavacanam*).
To the question, "How can the mind have a connection with beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*)?", it is said: "beginningless" (*anādi*).
He elaborates on this very point by stating: "consisting of the three qualities" (*triguṇātmaka*).
The mind, consisting of the three qualities, exists indeed until liberation as a constant entity;
it is precisely therein that all latent impressions are perpetually accumulated.

In order to indicate the reasoning for why the mind alone—and not the self—is the substratum of the latent impressions (saṃskāras), it is described as "consisting of the three qualities" (triguṇātmaka).
If it were merely stated that it "consists of qualities" (guṇātmaka), there might arise the understanding that it consists of qualities such as dimension (parimāṇa) and so forth;
since this would apply equally to the self, the term "three" (tri) is included.

And thus, the individual soul (jīvātman) is not the substratum of mental cultivation (bhāvanā), because it does not consist of the qualities such as *sattva* and the rest, just like the Lord (Īśvara).

Alternatively, mental cultivation must have as its substratum a substance consisting of the qualities such as *sattva* and the rest, because it is a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), like velocity (*vega*) and so forth.
And by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), it follows that this [substratum] is indeed the mind (*manas*). This is what has been stated.
However, for one who does not accept qualities such as *sattva*, the term "insentient" (*acetana*) should be used in its place;
and the mention of being "composed of the three qualities" (*triguṇātmaka*) is a statement of its essential nature.
The word "asti" (exists) is indeed [the subject], with "always" being the understood remainder.

If that were so, then because of its existence even in liberation, there would be the consequence of falling into states such as dreaming; therefore, he explains this by saying "as long as" (*yāvat*).

Although the mind (*manas*) is indeed eternal by its very nature, its connection with the individual soul (*jīva*) lasts until liberation; therefore, this was stated. Furthermore, since it is heard in the *Sūkta* that "that divine [mind] is indeed the mental faculty of the individual soul by which one becomes blissful," and given the question of how it can be said to last "until liberation" when the soul's connection with the mind is thus established, it is therefore described as being composed of the three qualities (*triguṇātmaka*).
Even though the mind in its essential nature as the self (*ātman*) is liberated when it exists [as pure consciousness], this limit is stated with reference to the insentient mind (*jaḍamana*).
The word "ca" (and) has the sense of "therefore" (*tasmāt*).
It refers to that very [insentient mind] and not to the self (*ātman*). (9.23)

Since it is heard in scripture that "from this [Being] is born the vital breath, the mind, and all the senses," how can its beginninglessness be asserted? To this he says: "By virtue of its subtlety" (*sūkṣmatvena*).
Even though it exists during dissolution, it is augmented by the material elements (*prākṛta*) due to its subtlety.
If that [unmanifest] does not exist at the time of creation, how can there be the persistence of the cycle of existence?
The word "ca" (and) has the sense of "eva" (only).
[The term] "prākṛtaiḥ" means by those consisting of egoity and so forth.
The word "manas" (mind) is understood to carry over.
The intention is that even though [the world] exists during the dissolution (*pralaya*), there is scriptural mention of its "birth" in view of its subsequent accumulation.
Why is this conceptualization made?
He says—beginning with "yadā"—because there exists a sublation of the primary meaning.
If the mind were indeed born [of itself] in the primary sense, then it would not exist at the time of dissolution (pralaya).
And if it did not exist at the time of dissolution, then the persistence of the self in the state of transmigratory existence (saṃsāra) would be impossible.
Nor is it tenable to say that its persistence in the state of transmigratory existence during dissolution should simply not occur.
Furthermore, because those who are liberated do not undergo rebirth in saṃsāra, it would follow that creation itself is impossible.
If it is argued that saṃsāra is dependent on ignorance, desire, karma, and so forth, we say no;
for ignorance and the rest are themselves nothing other than saṃsāra.
Furthermore, this contradicts such Smṛti passages as, "They declare the mind to be the supreme cause.
And so too says the Śruti:
"Because the mind is eternal due to its beginninglessness, a person does not exist without a mind";
this means that the person is one who transmigrates (*saṃsārī*).

What follows from this, if such is the case—that there exists the presence of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) deposited by the experience of all objects? To this he says: "By means of latent impressions. (*9,25*)
Having created the manifold world through his formative forces (*saṃskāra*), the Blessed One himself displays it during the state of dream... MAnu 3.2.8a-c.
In this context, by the word "having created" (*sṛṣṭvā*), the faults pertaining to the position that [the world] is beginningless and eternal are refuted simply by not accepting them.
By the phrase "having created at the very time of dreaming," the consequence of perceiving [the creation] both before and after [the dream] is set aside;
for "creation" here serves as an indication of "dissolution" as well.
The mention of "formative forces" (*saṃskāra*) is a reference to their being the material cause (*upādāna*).
Nor is it untenable for them to be the material cause by virtue of being qualities (*guṇa*),
because they are substances (*dravya*) insofar as they are mental modifications (*manovṛtti*).

Since conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are beyond the reach of the senses, their non-perception prior to and after their birth and destruction—just as in the case of the arising and perishing of a triad (*tryaṇuka*)—is not a fault.
The term "the Blessed One" (*bhagavān*) is an indication of the agent.

Since it might be considered impossible for him to perform creation and dissolution at that very moment, the word "Blessed One" is used to indicate his capacity as an agent capable of what is otherwise difficult to accomplish.
And this being so, the fact that [objects] have such causes as "truth" and so forth is indeed well-established.

This shows that it has been stated not only that the reality of objects depends upon the Blessed One by virtue of their possibility of being real, but also that his knowledge [of them] does so as well.
The word "jīvāya" (for the sake of living) is the ellipsis [to be supplied].
And he will state that the mind alone is the instrument of perception; furthermore, by "perception," direct experience is intended.
By this, the view that "this is merely recollection" is refuted.

Indeed, its status as recollection must be postulated either because of the presence of that sign (the object) with the mental apprehension "that," or because its object is not present [to the senses], or because it arises from a latent impression (*saṃskāra*).
Not the first,
because that [object] is absent from the mental imprint "this.
Therefore, if it is argued that this is merely a misconception of memory, we say no.
The first [alternative] is not tenable because recollectiveness itself is unestablished;
nor is the second,
because the proximity of the object has already been demonstrated.
Not the third [alternative], because the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is exhausted at the moment the object arises and thus cannot be established [as the cause].
Therefore, just as one experiences objects born of latent impressions through the mind in a daydream or in meditation, so too in a dream; what is there that is illogical?
However, this is the distinction:
in the case of mental desires and the like, the creation of objects is preceded by effort;
in dreams, moreover, it is [dependent on] the will of the Lord.
"It is certainly dependent [on that]" (*rādhīnaiva*).
Others, however, maintain that this experience indeed exists,
but they consider it to be merely an object to be remembered from what was experienced during a waking state.
That too is incorrect;
for instance, is this experience (anubhava) consistent with reality or inconsistent with reality?
The first [option] is not tenable,
because external objects are inaccessible due to being separated by space and time;
as for the second, it must be stated whether this [cognition] is erroneous because it presents an elephant where there is no elephant.
Or, is it that the elephant itself, though not proximate, is apprehended as being proximate, such that [the cognition] is erroneous?
In the first case, there would arise a sublation [in the form]: "This is not an elephant, but rather a gavaya.
In the second case, there would be a sublation [in the form]: "This is not proximate; on the contrary, it is distant."
But this is not the case;
therefore, it is logical that this is simply a valid cognition of an object that is a truth closely approximated by the impressions (*saṃskāra*).
If so, why is it stated in the *Śruti* and *Smṛti* that dream-cognition is an error? To this he says: "It is an error."
... for even the waking state is indeed an illusion.
The term "state of waking" (*jāgrattva*) indicates the cognition thereof;
the word "only" (*eva*) excludes the intrinsic nature of the objects themselves.
The state of waking is the identity [of the dreamer] with the objects experienced during the waking state.
For in a dream, one indeed identifies sons and other such things—which have never been seen before—as having been seen before, due to their being perceived at that moment.
Alternatively, "wakingness" refers to the eternality of space and so forth;
it should be understood as the fact that jars and the like have clay and so forth as their material causes, and their capacity for external causal efficiency, and so on.
The point is that because the perception of being awake is an error, the Śruti and other scriptures have that [perception] as their object.
This might be argued:

since there certainly exists a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) for the state of being awake as well, and thus the possibility of it having a material cause (*upādāna*) exists, how can that perception be called an error?
"Otherwise, even the cognition of an object would be an error, as there is no distinction [between them].
Not so;
for we do not maintain the reality of objects merely on the basis of the occurrence of the causal complex.

However, we shall state that [the world is real] because there is no sublation. But against one who asserts its unreality due to the absence of causal totality (*sāmagrī*), its very non-establishment has already been indicated.
Moreover, there is a sublation of the cognition of being awake,
because [cognitions] such as "this is merely a dream, not an experience of the waking state" arise.
This is indeed expressed by the word "hi" (*for*).
It is incorrect to say that the perception of things while dreaming is itself an error,
because since some objects are non-existent, the perception of them is likewise an error.
Even in dreams, things such as the cutting off of one's own head are perceived;
yet there is no material cause (*upādāna*) for their arising,
because since they have not been previously experienced, the arising of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is impossible.

If one were to admit the arising of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) even with respect to what has not been experienced, there would be a contradiction with such scriptural and traditional texts as, "What is unseen is not heard," and so forth;
furthermore, it would follow that there could sometimes be a recollection of an object never before experienced.

Therefore, even though there is no direct contradiction regarding such things as the cutting off of one's own head, nevertheless, non-existence must be admitted due to the impossibility of its cause; thus he says: "And if it is not seen... and so forth.
When an entity has neither been seen nor heard, no [new] entity arises;
because an entity has not been seen or heard, no entity arises.
Thus, the statement found in the Śrutis and Purāṇas is appropriate because [the Veda] is beginningless.
"In the sense of 'bhāva' means in the sense of an entity (padārtha). Alternatively, 'bhāva' means latent predisposition (vāsanā). The fifth case ending is used in the sense of the seventh."
The word "tu" (but) following the word "uktiḥ" (statement) is to be understood as follows:
the ellipsis is "because saṃsāra is beginningless.

Since saṃsāra is beginningless, it is possible for the experience of even such things as the cutting off of one's own head to occur in some birth; thus, the existence of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) is established.
Even if [the recollection] is true, the statement found in the Śruti and Purāṇas is indeed logical and not contradicted;
for it would only be contradicted if one were to accept the arising of a latent impression (saṃskāra) even without experience.
Here, by the mention of "not having heard," it is indicated that even in this present birth, the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by hearing is possible.
However, where there is not even hearing and so forth, there the state of being beginningless (*anāditva*) is established.
By this, the utility of all that was previously stated regarding the universal [nature of the self] is explained through the succession of beginningless experiences. *9,32*
But [one might ask]: how is it in the case of the cognition of a rabbit’s horn and the like?
For even in another birth, such an experience is not possible, since it is heard that all kalpas are of one kind, being "just as before."
Not so;
for even in the absence of a valid cognition of a rabbit’s horn and the like, a latent impression (saṃskāra) is possible through the occurrence of error via words and other means.
But how [could it be] for one who has not apprehended a rabbit’s horn and so forth even through error?
For there is no rule that everyone wanders everywhere,
nor can it be restricted that one does not see such things in a dream.
It is said:
In this context, is non-existence asserted because of the impossibility of finding a material cause for the hare and so forth, or for their horns and so forth;
or rather, because of the lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between "hare-ness" and "horn-ness," and so on?
He refutes the first [position] with the words: "Sometimes."
Sometimes it may be unfit for inspection; even in that case, [one should examine it] by means of division.

"...is seen" (dṛṣṭam) ... [Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.2.11a] // *9,33* The ellipsis is "that which is seen in a dream. It is seen in the waking state without the common substratum (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) that exists through differentiation (*vibhāgataḥ*).

Although the coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of "hare-ness" and "horn-ness," or the specific relation between a hare and a horn, is not experienced during the waking state, nevertheless, "hare-ness" and so forth are indeed experienced in their distinctness;
thus, it cannot be said that hares and the like are non-existent.
Regarding the second [alternative], he states the answer in agreement: "samam" (equally).
And it is observed as being in grammatical apposition [with the self], yet that is an error.
This is an expression in which the abstract state (bhāva) is predominant;
furthermore, this is an illustration.
In the phrase "it is seen" (*dṛśyate*), the pronoun *sa* refers back to the meaning of the verbal root.
The word "yat" (which) is understood here;
the meaning is that in this dream, there is not only the state of being awake [as in the waking state],
but also that for which material cause is possible and sublation does not exist.
The meaning is that this very [dream object] has already been excluded by the word "previously" (*prāk*).
All this would be so if dream objects lacked, like those perceived while awake, clarity characterized by the capacity for external causal efficiency;
otherwise, they would possess it—this is the sense.
That which is seen is observed as being in a state of grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*), yet that is an illusion.
This is the underlying intention:
objects such as jars in a dream are certainly not non-existent, because there is no sublation (*bādha*) of them.
Nor are they eternal from beginningless time,
because no prior or subsequent [state] is perceived;
nor is an arising without a causal basis tenable.
Therefore, since a material cause (*upādāna*) must necessarily be pursued,
it cannot first be external things such as clay and the like.
Because it lacks the capacity for external causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).

The argument is formulated as follows: "The jar under dispute is not produced from external material causes such as clay, because it is devoid of the causal efficiency that results from external material causes such as clay, like a cloth."
Otherwise, that [absurdity] would follow;
yet there is no other material cause (upādāna).
Therefore, by process of elimination, they must have mental impressions (vāsanā) as their material cause.

By the word "ca" (and), he collects as corroborating evidence the scriptural passages concerning the Lord as the agent, the fact of [the dream state] being subject to origination and destruction at that very moment, and the remainder [of the arguments], such as: "He who is awake among those who sleep," "For from Him alone is a son born," and "There are no chariots there," etc.
Thus, by this entire sequence [of reasoning], it is established that there is creation in the intermediate state (sandhye), for so the scripture declares.
Some [hold that the world] has a creator, as well as sons and so forth;
however, it is merely an illusion because its true nature is entirely unmanifested—thus is the triad of sūtras explained.
Others, however, explain these sūtras in another way.
For it is heard in scripture: "There are no chariots there, no draft animals, and no roads; yet he creates chariots, draft animals, and roads," and so forth.
In this regard, there is a doubt:
Is the creation in the dream state as real as that in the waking state, or is it composed of illusion (*māyā*)?
On this point, they first set forth [the following].
There is creation in the intermediate state, for so the scripture says;
[it refers to] the state of deep sleep (*saṃprasāda*) as the place of awakening from sleep.
At the junction of the two states,
that which occurs is the intermediate state, namely the dream state;
therein, creation takes on exactly such a form.
Why?
Because the authoritative Śruti declares thus:
"Then he creates chariots, horses for the chariots, and paths," and so forth.
And some [maintain] that it is the creator, as well as sons and so forth;
moreover, certain followers of particular Vedic branches (śākhins) recognize the Self as the creator of desires during the intermediate state (saṃdhye), according to the text:
"This Person who remains awake among those who sleep, creating each and every desire."
In this context, "desires" (kāmāḥ) refers to sons and so forth, as they are what is desired;
it does not, however, refer to specific types of longing.
[As it is said: "Choose sons and grandsons who shall live for a hundred years."

Thus, since the word "desire" (kāma) is employed in the context of the sons and others under discussion with the words, "I make you a partaker of desires," we understand from both the context and the remainder of the passage that this creator is the Wise One (the Supreme Self).
"This is indeed a section concerning the wise man, beginning with the words, 'Other than dharma, other than adharma'; moreover,
the supplementary passage is also, 'That alone is the pure, that is Brahman,' and so forth."
And the creation [in the intermediate state] is produced by an intelligent agent and is of such a nature as it appears; such is the creation in the twilight state (*sandhya*).
This being the position reached, he replies: "But it is mere illusion (*māyāmātram*), because its true nature is not manifested in its entirety."
The word "tu" (but) sets aside the previous position.
By "māyā," beginningless and indefinable ignorance (avidyā) is meant.
The creation in the intermediate state (sandhye) is indeed māyā; there is not even a trace of ultimate reality (paramārtha) therein.
Why? "Māyā" refers to beginningless, inexpressible ignorance (*avidyā*).
This creation in the intermediate state is merely *māyā*; it does not possess even a scent of ultimate reality.
Why?
Because its essential nature is not manifested in its entirety.

"In its entirety" (*kārtsnyena*) refers to the perfection of place, time, and causal conditions, as well as non-obstruction; since its essential nature lacks manifestation through these, it is not fully revealed.
For instance: first of all, a suitable location for chariots and the like does not exist in a dream;
for within the confined space of the body, chariots and such could find no room.

Nor should it be argued that one perceives dreams outside the body because of the Vedic text, "Having moved about outside the nest as an immortal," and because of the distinction between the notions of staying and moving;
for a sleeping person can traverse and return from a place separated by hundreds of yojanas in a mere moment.
Because it is impossible for [the dreamer] to possess such capacity [to travel],
and because in some cases a dream occurs that is devoid of returning— such as when one thinks,
"While lying here today in the Kuru country, I reached the Pañcāla country in a dream," and upon waking, [finds oneself back where he was].
If it were to depart from the body, one would awaken among the Pañcālas; however, one awakens precisely in the Kurus. Furthermore, by means of this very body, one perceives other regions in a dream.
Those [objects] do not exist in that very way [as they appear].
If one were to see while running about, one would perceive the object as it actually is, like one who is awake.
And the Śruti shows the dream to be within oneself: "In his own body, he moves about according to his desire."
Therefore, because it contradicts both scripture and logical reasoning, the external scripture must be interpreted figuratively, as it shares the same quality of being unhelpful [to the soul].
Furthermore, the distinction between the cognitions of staying and moving must be accepted as an illusion;
even a discrepancy in time occurs during a dream.
For those who sleep during the night, they consider it to be day in the land of Bhārata;
likewise, even a mere moment is considered a year.
And there are also [other] signs.
In a dream, those [objects] do not exist for the purpose of cognition or action;
furthermore, these chariots and so forth seen in a dream are sublated upon waking.
Moreover, these very [objects] are easily sublated even within a dream,
because deviation is observed at both the beginning and the end;
for indeed, what is determined in a dream as "this is a chariot" becomes in an instant a human being.
A tree determined to be "this is a human being" in an instant [is seen];
moreover, the scripture clearly teaches the non-existence of chariots and so forth in a dream, stating:
"There are no chariots there, no yoked chariots, and no roads," and so on.
Therefore, the vision in sleep is merely an illusion. Another says: because its nature is not fully manifested, it cannot be defined by the seers as "existent" or by other such terms. For instance:
Regarding the chariots and other objects in a dream, there must be either a difference, a non-difference, or both difference and non-difference between them and their perceiver.
First of all, they are not different;
for if they were, it would follow that even those standing nearby would perceive them.
Furthermore, internality is not established;
nor is there non-difference,
because it is impossible for a single, undifferentiated entity to possess a manifold and multiple nature without the presence of illusion.
And because it contradicts the cognition of difference;
nor can there be both difference and non-difference, due to contradiction.
Therefore, this is merely the manifestation of indeterminable ignorance (*anirvācyāvidyā*).
For the scripture indicates it, and those who know that declare it.
For the scripture indicates it, and those who know that declare it.
If it is argued that because [the dream] is mere illusion, there is not even a trace of ultimate reality in a dream, we say: no.
For a dream is indeed indicative of future good and evil.
Why?
This is because of scriptural passages such as "when [one performs] actions," and so forth;
and those who are experts in the study of dreams also declare this. In that case, let there be truthfulness for what is being indicated therein.
The sense is that for the indicator, however, there is only falsity;
as it was said: "For [the scripture] says.
This being the case, it must be explained as being figurative.
For during sleep, one is called the "maker" of chariots and so forth because of being the agent of good and evil deeds which are the causes for seeing dreams;
thus, even the scriptural passage regarding "creation" (nirmāṇa) must be explained as figurative.
As for what was said—that the scriptures declare this conscious self (prājña) to be the creator—that too is incorrect.

In another Śruti passage, because the activity of the individual soul (jīva) is heard in the words, "having himself wandered about, having himself created," another [teacher] has explained the Sūtra as "and the other [the dreamer] is a pointer for this very purpose."
For a dream indicates what is auspicious or inauspicious;
indeed, it is not possible for a wise person to be joined with the auspicious or the inauspicious.

Thus, in the concluding statement "that very [self] is white," having set aside the state of being a *jīva*, the state of being Brahman is taught—just as in "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) and other such passages—and therefore the context of Brahman is not contradicted.
Or let there be the practical usage of the wise even regarding dreams;
yet, by that much alone, the dream does not possess reality like space and so forth,
because the difference between them has already been stated.
It has also been established in the *Ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa* that the manifold expansion (*prapañca*) beginning with space is likewise unreal.
The manifold expansion beginning with space is sublated by the realization of Brahman as the Self;
however, because the [dream] state occurs daily, this specific illusory nature (*māyāmātratva*) of the intermediate state (*sandhya*) has been demonstrated. (9.45)

"But it is concealed by the meditation on another; for from that [concealment] come its bondage and its opposite. This is the response to the objection: "Just as a spark, which is a portion of fire, possesses the powers of burning and illuminating, so too the individual soul (jīva), being a portion of the Lord, must possess the powers of knowledge and sovereignty; and consequently, creation should be accomplished by mere volition. The meaning is as follows: although the individual soul is indeed a part of the Lord, its powers of knowledge and sovereignty are not manifest, because they are obscured by the meditation upon another—that is, by the influence of *māyā* and *avidyā*. For it is due to this concealment that the soul experiences both bondage and liberation. It is not the case that a part must necessarily share all the specific powers of the whole; for instance, while a single ray of light from a lamp does not perform the functions of the entire lamp, such as lighting a house or dispelling darkness, the same cannot be said of a spark. Therefore, the individual soul, though a part of the Lord, does not possess the power of creating the universe through mere volition. Thus, the objection is refuted.
It is indeed true that the individual soul possesses similarity to the Lord, yet it is concealed;
however, that [similarity] becomes manifest solely through meditation upon the Supreme Lord.
Why is this so?
Therefore, from that cause, namely Īśvara, the bondage and liberation of this individual soul (jīva) occur;
or rather, they occur through its connection with a body.
Why, then, does the suppression of the soul's knowledge and sovereignty take place?
To the objection that "it is indeed logical that there should be no concealment [of the Self], just as there is none for sparks," this is the reply:
even that concealment of the individual soul (jīva) arises from its connection with a body;

it is produced by the error of non-discrimination resulting from the association with limiting adjuncts (upādhis) such as the body, senses, mind, intellect, objects, and sensations, which are fashioned by name-and-form (nāmarūpa) presented by ignorance (avidyā).
Just as fire arises from the application of the fire-drill, what is the use of this conceptualization?
Or rather, let the individual soul (jīva) be entirely different from the Supreme Lord; this is the alternative indicated by the word "or" (vā).
[The opponent] says: "It excludes [the identity].
[The author] replies: "Not so;
because that would contradict such scriptural passages as 'That thou art' (*tattvamasi*). (9.47)
This interpretation is untenable;
for instance,

we understand that the two sūtras which establish the ultimate reality of the creation in dreams are intended as a restatement of a previous position only if there were a formal proposition (*pratijñā*) stating that it is "mere illusion" (*māyāmātra*), implying its indeterminability (*anirvācyatva*).
But this is not the case,

because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish it. Now, was it not stated that [the Self] has its nature unmanifest in its entirety, and thus lacks the absence of contradiction regarding the perfection of place, time, and causes, as well as the impossibility of being defined by such attributes as difference and so forth?
Not so;
for that [position] is untenable,
since it has been demonstrated therein that the absence of location and so forth is logically inconsistent.

Intending to show that [the truth] will become manifest simply by clarifying the meaning of that sūtra, he says "Difference," etc., [pointing out] that regarding the refutation stated by means of questions concerning conceptual constructions such as difference, the question itself is untenable, let alone the statement of a refutation.
The question of whether there is difference, non-difference, or a pair [of both] is not applicable to the dreamer... // MĀnuv 3.2.12a-c //

Having raised the alternative (vikalpa)—whether there is a difference, or non-difference, or both difference and non-difference (dvandva), i.e., both difference and non-difference—between the dreamer Devadatta and the dream-objects such as chariots perceived in the dream, the question is not tenable.
Why? To this he says: "Because it is seen" (dṛṣṭatvāt).
...because difference alone is perceived by all people. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 3.2.12cd)
The phrase "of the dreamer" is understood to carry over [from the previous context].
For a question based on conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is rooted in doubt;
however, no such doubt is possible in the present case.
This is because the distinction between the dream and its perceiver is perceived by all people, and thus there is no disagreement [regarding this].
It might be argued:
"Let it be that this doubt is not rooted in disagreement."
However, a doubt arising from the perception of common characteristics will occur:
"Is this object different from the perceiver, or not different, or both different and not different?
From this, a doubt may arise as to whether the object is different from that [perceiver] or not different, and so forth.
Not so;
for does doubt arise from the mere perception of a common property, or rather from that [perception] conjoined with the absence of a decisive factor?
Not the first,
because it would follow that doubt would arise everywhere;
for indeed, there is some degree of similarity in every case.
Furthermore, it would follow that [the property] could never cease;
for a common property never ceases to exist.
As for the second [alternative], how could there be any doubt in this case?
Since difference itself is perceived by all people, the absence of any means of determination [of non-difference] is unestablished.
Now, if it is thought:
"Indeed, some kind of difference is seen as ultimate reality, as in the case of a pillar and a jar."
Furthermore, there is some ultimate reality regarding the two moons;
yet this difference is perceived, and therefore doubt must indeed arise.
This also is not the case;

for if that were so, since a question involving conceptualization must be made according to one's doubt, [you might argue] that this very [doubt] is being produced by this turn of phrase. If you say this, we reply: no.
For even mere cognition does not become a cause for doubt,
because it would follow that doubt would arise in all cases, and because it would follow that such doubt could never be removed.
For its cessation is to be sought through the cognition of its specific [opposite];
yet even there, doubt certainly persists,
though it is merely defiled by misconception and the like.
And it has already been stated that this [error] does not exist here;
for the rule for cognitions is to correspond with reality,
while deviation from it is an exception.
Thus, since its object is already established, this very question is untenable.
But surely, by accepting the position of difference (*bheda-pakṣa*), the fault stated therein can indeed be avoided;
for, being produced from the mind (*mano-yoni*), it is possible that pleasure and so forth are not perceived by those standing nearby, just as they are not perceived by others.
So what is the purpose of this section of questions?
True;
nevertheless, this is intended to instruct the disciples that a respondent must not overlook any deficiency in their own position.

And so he will state [later]: "In order to explain, by way of incidental discussion, the remainder of the principles established in the *Yuktipāda*, and we shall here show briefly the utility of that explanation. (9.56)
When an object is established, doubt regarding it is not tenable; therefore, it has been stated that a question based on conceptual construction is likewise not tenable.
In this context, what is the meaning of "is not tenable"?
It is not the case that it does not arise at all,
because its arising as a question involving doubt and conceptualization is established by valid cognition;
nor is it the case that even when arisen, it is without cause.
Because the arising of an effect without a cause contradicts valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
nor does it arise from what is not its cause;
for that from which it arises is precisely what is defined as its cause, and [to claim otherwise] would be a contradiction.
And since there is no other lack of logical consistency, he says: "By the question," etc.

The faults of conceptual objections and contradictions with valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) have already been explained; since [the objection] that the meaning is already established is not distinct from these, it is not mentioned separately. An example of self-contradiction (*svavyāhati*) is as follows:
Is a barren woman possessed of sons or not? An example of an irrelevant connection (*asaṅgati*) is as follows:

when it is said that "the Lord is happy," [one might ask] regarding the momentariness of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), is perception (*pratyakṣa*) the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or is it inference (*anumiti*)?
But for one who has achieved their goal, it is simply natural; its fruitlessness is, for example, like saying "a crow has ten teeth."
The word "iti" (thus) is to be supplied after "vaiphalyam" (futility).
This is the intended meaning:
first of all, these three—self-contradiction and so forth—constitute a refutation of the question itself.
Since authorities have enumerated contradictions with one's own thesis (*pratijñāvirodha*), shifting to another subject (*arthāntara*), and so forth as points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*),
it must be stated what kind of irrationality exists in that [position] by which it could function as a refutation.
Now, one might think:
"The absence of contradiction and so forth is a factor for the communication of meaning."
Furthermore, it is inferred that one who utters such [statements] as "contradictory" (vyāhata) neither understands that [meaning] nor understands its opposite;
therefore, because they serve as signs of non-comprehension and misconception, [the statement] is untenable.
If that is the case, then the same would apply to the fact that [the Veda] has an established meaning (siddhārthatā); how then is this not a fault?
For a question based on doubt is rooted in uncertainty;
and uncertainty arises from the perception of common characteristics and so forth, assisted by the absence of a decisive factor.
Or, even in the absence of common characteristics and the like, or even when a decisive factor is present, one who remains in doubt and asks alternative questions [is the subject].
It is inferred that he has indeed apprehended what is non-existent— such as common characteristics and so forth— and has not apprehended the existence of a definitive proof;
for an effect cannot exist without a cause,
yet it is observed that effects such as fear and trembling arise even from the delusion of a snake.
Now, one might object: these treatises proceed by way of the method of formal debate (*vādakathā*),
and in debate there is no point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), because debate culminates in the ascertainment of truth.
For when either the proponent or the opponent has been defeated by means of such faults as the abandonment of the thesis (*pratijñāhāni*), the determination of the other side is not established;
this is because it is possible for them to re-establish their position and counter-argue once again.
As for what is stated in the *Vāda-sūtra*: “It is not contradictory to one's own tenet and is endowed with the five members [of a syllogism]”;
Thus, it has been indicated that points such as *apasiddhānta* (contradiction of one's own tenets) constitute grounds for defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
However, even that is untenable because it contradicts the fact that a formal debate (*vāda*) must conclude with the determination of one of the two opposing positions.
Furthermore, if certain grounds for defeat such as *apasiddhānta* were to exist in a formal debate, then why would other [grounds for defeat] not also exist?
Because the contradiction consisting in the fact that [the opponent's position] ends with the determination of reality is equal in both cases;
for if one were defeated by [charges such as] "abandoning the thesis" (*pratijñāhāni*), there would be an abandonment of the state of being free from passion (*vītarāgatva*).
If it is argued that [the fault] would not arise, [we reply] that this applies equally in the case of an "unestablished tenet" (*apasiddhānta*) and so forth.
Therefore, since there is no ground for defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) in a formal debate (*vāda*), how can one point out the defects of a question? To this, he says: "Not by those... (*na tair...*).
... by them there would be no determination of the truth. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.2.13d)
By these questions that are self-contradictory and so forth;
the meaning is that such questions, being self-contradictory and the like, are opposed to the determination of reality (*tattvanirṇaya*).
For even if a matter were already established, one who remains in doubt cannot be made to understand the truth even by a hundred means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Because doubt is not thereby dispelled even in that case.
To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "Regarding reality... (tattve).
For even in a formal debate (vāda), there is defeat if one acts contrary to the determination of reality.
The existence of points of defeat (nigrahasthāna) occurs not only in mere talk (jalpa) and cavil (vitaṇḍā), but also in formal debate (vāda).
For "defeat" (nigraha) is that by which one is defeated, and it would certainly constitute a point of defeat.
However, there is this distinction:

It is not like the case of frivolous talk (*jalpa*) and cavil (*vitaṇḍā*), where everything [is prohibited]; rather, only that which is contrary to the determination of reality (*tattvanirṇaya*) is prohibited.
And it has been stated that questions regarding what is already established (*siddhapraśna*) and so forth are contrary to the determination of reality.

How, then, could there not be a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) in debate? For how could one who acts contrary to the very purpose for which he has engaged [in the debate] not be at fault? This is the meaning of the word "hi" (for). The abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) in "vailomya" (contrariety) is used for the purpose of extracting the cause of defeat. *9,63*

[Objection: "In that case, would it not contradict the fact that debate has the determination of truth as its purpose? Furthermore, there would be no distinction between [this] and *jalpa* and so forth, since they too have victory as their purpose. Likewise, there would be the presence of the same points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) as well. To this, he says: "[The fault] must indeed be pointed out."
Only what is to be pointed out would remain; there would be no conclusion to the discussion.
But in a debate for victory, the cause for bringing the discussion to an end is as follows.

The term "debate" (*vāda*) follows from the phrase "contrary to the determination of reality. *Avasiti* means that by which one causes [the opponent] to settle [on a conclusion]. This refers to the discourse of those seeking victory, characterized as *jalpa* and *vitaṇḍā*.
The remainder [of the argument] is that every cause for the cessation of the discussion is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
What is meant by this is that even in a formal debate (*vāda*), there is nothing whatsoever that is not possible.
Just as in the case of distraction and so forth,
because that [instruction] is intended for the purpose of concealing ignorance and the like,
and because one who desires to ascertain reality has no interest therein.
Even that which is somewhat plausible should not be pointed out,
such as non-reproduction (*ananubhāṣaṇa*) and so forth;
for since it is not in contradiction with the determination of what is desired by both parties, its pointing out would be useless.

When something merely to be pointed out— such as the contradiction of the thesis (*pratijñāvirodha*) and so forth— is relevant to the matter at hand, its pointing out serves as a factor for determining the truth (*tattvanirṇaya*), because by causing that [contradiction] to be abandoned, it acts as an auxiliary to the determination of truth. However,
the conclusion of the debate occurs when one of the two [parties] has established either the proof (*sādhana*) or the refutation (*dūṣaṇa*).
And when there is no failure in the refutation,
that itself constitutes the determination of truth.
However, in the case of *jalpa* and *vitaṇḍā*, every possible point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) must both be considered possible and be brought forth.
And it brings the discussion to a conclusion,
because both serve the purpose of victory,
as they are the means for achieving victory in every case.
"Therefore, there is no fault whatsoever.

Having thus established that the objection concerns the question's having an already-accomplished object (*siddhārtha-viṣayatva*) as its refutation, he says—"Even in the case of the answer"—in order to indicate the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) that would follow if one does not accept that it is indeed a refutation.
Even if [the opponent] offers a rebuttal, the proof remains established; this constitutes a refutation of the proponent's thesis... // MAnu 3.2.15c-e //
The fact that the subject matter is already established is not merely a fault in the question; rather, it is a fault in both the avoidance [of the question] and the answer as well.
However, there is this distinction:
in the case of a question, the fault lies in the fact that the matter being asked is already established for the questioner.
However, it is indeed logical that the counter-positive (pratiyogin) must be established;
otherwise, its status as a probans would be untenable.
Therefore, does this mean that the establishment of the entire meaning of the respondent's statement by the opponent constitutes a flaw?
We say: no.

Rather, the connection is as follows: even when the meaning of the proposition itself is refuted, the fact that the meaning of the proposition has been established for the opponent constitutes a "refutation" (dūṣaṇa).
This is what is meant:
if the posing of a question regarding one's own established position were not a fault, [then this objection would hold].
In that case, even a thesis (*pratijñā*) consisting of a matter established for the opponent would not constitute a fault, as there is no distinction [between them].
Now, is it not the case that a thesis is the statement of a position (*pakṣavacana*) for the purpose of proving [something] to another? And that which is already established does not require proof.
Therefore, because it would contradict one's own thesis,
the fact that the meaning is already established for the opponent is indeed a flaw.
If that is so, then a statement preceded by a desire to know is a question.
Furthermore, the desire to know (*jñīpsā*) is not possible regarding what is already known;
therefore, since this contradicts its status as a question, why would having a subject matter that is already established for oneself not be a flaw?
To the question, "Then for what purpose is it stated [in the definition] 'in the proposition' (*pratijñāyām*)?", he says: "of that which is other than that" (*tadanyasya*).

... for it is precisely the established nature of that which is other than this [the probandum] that serves as the means of proof. The meaning of the thesis (*pratijñārtha*) consists in the connection of the pervading property (*vyāpaka-dharma*) with the subject of the probandum (*sādhyadharmin*), and the purpose obtainable from the non-termination of that [connection].
Indeed, it is the established nature of the meaning of the reason (*hetu*) and so forth—being other than that [thesis]—that becomes the prover of the probandum.
Because there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) if an unestablished logical mark (*liṅga*) and so forth were to prove the probandum (*sādhya*),
it was stated [in the rule] "in the thesis" (*pratijñāyām*).

By this, it is understood that since only the meaning of the subsequent statement— which is distinct from the matter of the thesis— is established, its lack of establishment constitutes a flaw (*dūṣaṇa*).
And that [unestablished reason] is of many kinds; for instance,
the non-establishment of the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*) is the unestablished reason regarding the locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*).
For example: "A human horn exists, because it is a horn, like a cow's horn.
This is the non-establishment of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma-asiddhi*), which has another designation: "unestablished qualification" (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatā*).

For example, [the argument] that "mother-of-pearl-silver and the like are distinct from both the existent and the non-existent because they are sublatable" involves the unestablished nature of the logical mark (*liṅgāsiddhi*). Likewise, [the argument] that "the subject of dispute is insentient because it is distinct from both the existent and the non-existent" [is similarly flawed].
The non-establishment of the reason's presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) is as follows:
for example, "Sound is eternal because it is visible.
This is the non-establishment due to a lack of common locus (*vyadhikaraṇāsiddhi*).
For example: "Sound is impermanent because it is produced, like a pot.
This is a case of unestablished pervasion (*vyāptyasiddhi*).
For example: "Whatever exists is momentary, like a lamp."
"Existence and conceptual proliferation"—in this way, other fallacies such as the "unestablished qualification" (viśeṣaṇāsiddhi) and so forth are also to be understood.
Since all these types of unestablished reasons would otherwise result in being mere defects [of the argument], he states the exception: "The basis... (*āśraya...*).
For some, the refutation consists of the non-establishment of the locus, the non-establishment of the locus-possessor, and the non-establishment of the probandum. MAnu 3.2.16a-c.

Although the fallacies of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*), the unestablished due to a different substratum (*vyadhikaraṇāsiddhi*), and the unestablished probandum (*sādhyāsiddhi*) are considered defects by some, such as the Naiyāyikas,
they are nevertheless not actual defects in reality.
The unestablished locus is of many kinds.

[The opponent might argue that there are] five faults: having a non-existent locus, having a locus of non-existence, having an unperceived locus, being non-existent in the form of the subject under discussion (*pakṣa*), and proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatva*).
Regarding these, he asserts that the first two are not faults with the words "And not... (*na ca*).
And those faults do not apply in any way when there is pervasion (vyāpti).
Because the status of being a fault—such as having an unestablished substratum (*apratītāśrayatva*) and so forth—is already proven;
for this very reason, it has been stated elsewhere: "of that which has a non-existent substratum," and so on, as well as:
"nor even an absolute non-existence."
The same should be understood for what follows as well.
By the term "unestablished basis" (āśrayāsiddhi), the deficiency of the example regarding its basis is also included. If it is asked, "Why are these not faults? [the answer follows].
Is the status of being a defect due to the failure of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth, or is it due to some other manner even when pervasion and so forth exist?
It is not the first,
because pervasion and so forth exist even in cases such as the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*).
In the second [case], however, this applies:
"When pervasion exists, there is no fault whatsoever, by any means.
The mention of the apprehension of pervasion is an indication of [the other conditions], such as the non-sublated nature of the object.
In reality, since its utility lies precisely in pervasion (*vyāpti*), it was not mentioned separately;
the subsequent section is for the purpose of elaborating upon this very point.

In that regard, the fact that even the non-existence of the Blessed One is established by valid cognition (*prāmāṇika*) and possesses common characteristics (*sadharman*) has already been proven previously.
However, it must be stated: how can that which has a non-existent locus be defective?
For otherwise, there would be the unwanted consequence that even such arguments as "the horn of a kiṃnara exists, because it is a horn" would constitute valid proof.

Or rather, because a non-existent thing lacks properties (*nirdharmaka*), it is impossible for it to serve as the locus of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*); thus, the argument would have a sublated object (*bādhitaviṣayatva*).

Now, [the reason is fallacious] either because its subsistence in the locus of the property to be proven is untenable due to being unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*); or else, because that which is non-existent cannot be the object of any conventional usage; or finally, because that which lacks epistemic warrant cannot possibly be a constituent of valid cognition.
Alternatively, [the objection was raised] that pervasion is untenable for that which has a non-existent locus.
He refutes the first [position] with the words: "The fault."
In the proof of the existence of a human horn, there is indeed the fault of contradiction.
Contradiction (*vyāhati*) is opposition to a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For the word "horn" (*śṛṅga*) is intended to be a denoter of a specific part that is large, connected to a head, and possessed of color;
or else, it might denote something beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*).

In the first case, because its non-existence is determined by perception, there is no over-extension, since "horns-ness" is not a probans precisely because it is sublated by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). In the second case, however, this is merely the presentation of something that is already accepted. *9,79*
This might be the case:
it is undisputed that "horns-ness" (*śṛṅgatva*) is not a valid probans;
furthermore, in that instance, there is both a sublated object (*bādhitaviṣayatva*) and an unreal locus (*asadāśrayatva*).

In this regard, since it is precisely the fact that the object [of the reason] is sublated that is the determinant for its lack of probative power—and not the fact that its locus is non-existent—how can it be restricted [otherwise]? To this, he says: "Where... (yatreti).
Since there is no contradiction therein, what excessive attachment could there be to its proof?
In a case where there is no contradiction— that is, no sublation by valid cognition (pramāṇa)—
what over-extension (atiprasaṅga) could there be even when proving that [thesis] by means of a reason based on a non-existent locus?
There is no fault whatsoever.
"Contradiction" (*vyāhata*) is an elliptical expression; it should also be understood as including "inconstancy" (*vyabhicāra*) and so forth.
This is what is meant:

There exists, first of all, the proof of the coldness of fire and so forth through [the reason] "because it is produced" (*kṛtakatva*) as an example of a reason whose object is sublated (*bādhitaviṣaya*), unmixed with other defects.
By means of that,
we ascertain its status as a defect.
Furthermore, there is no uncontaminated example where having an unreal locus (*asadāśrayatva*) is a defect while [the reason] possesses an uncontradicted object (*abādhitaviṣayatva*) and so forth,
by means of which we might recognize its status as a defect;
for when other defects such as having a contradicted object are absent, there is no subverting argument against an unreal locus alone functioning as a logical reason.
And such a thing is seen to function as a reason, for example:
"The son of a barren woman is not a speaker because he is insentient, like a stone.
Therefore, it is determined that the property of being a horn is not a non-probative reason solely because its object is sublated, and not because its locus is non-existent. *9,80*
Now, if it is thought: "The son of a barren woman is a speaker because he is a son, like an agreed-upon [speaker]"—why would this not be a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣa*)?
For you yourself have abandoned the fear of having an unreal locus (*asadāśrayatā*).
Not so;
for since the effect of that person's authorship has never been perceived by anyone at any time, it is weak because its object is sublated, and thus it cannot serve as a counter-argument.
Indeed, a fawn is no match for a hyena.
If it is argued that non-speech also consists in being an agent of actions other than speaking—and therefore, even the lack of consciousness has its object sublated—this is not so;
for what is to be proven is merely the absence of the state of being a speaker.
But [one might ask]: how can there even be an absence when the thing itself does not exist?
If it is argued that this is because of the absence of properties (dharma) in that [substratum], we say no; for properties are of many kinds,
some of which indeed inhere in the substratum (dharmī).
Just as color-form and so forth;
some things, even when inherent in one thing, may color another,
such as cognition and so forth in relation to jars and the like.
Some do not even require inherence in a substratum, but are defined by something alone,
such as non-existence (*abhāva*).
Nor should it be said that non-existence must also be defined by means of two existing things.
Because it would follow that antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and the other [types of non-existence] could not be defined.
If it is argued that this is not so because a jar or the like exists at some time, we say no; for such an entity is of no use at the very moment when its definition is being formulated.
If it is argued that [the son of a barren woman] is perceived through dependence [on conceptual construction], this applies equally to the case at hand as well;
for even the son of a barren woman can be perceived through the appearance of a word and so forth. (9.83)
Furthermore, the sonship of the son of a barren woman is unestablished;
yet this does not constitute a contradiction of one's own words,
because a real state is negated by means of a reference to a conceptual construct.
If it is asked, "How can that which is conceptual (kālpanika) possess the status of a thesis (pakṣatva)?", we say no;
for there is no obstacle to its being a thesis with respect to a negation,
otherwise it would be impossible to refute the positions of others.
If it is argued that its lack of consciousness is also unestablished because its nature is distinct from consciousness, we say no;
for the reason consists merely in the exclusion of consciousness.
It has been stated that even for a non-existent absence, a definition is logically possible; furthermore,
the reason "existence" (*sattva*) is inconclusive with respect to a mute person.

If it were qualified by "not being mute," then because that [quality] is not distinct from "being a speaker," there would be the fallacy of the subject being non-different from the probandum (*sādhyaviśiṣṭatā*).

By this, all the alternative positions (*vikalpitāḥ pakṣāḥ*) have been refuted; let this suffice for the details. [This concludes the section on] sublation by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇabādha*).
It has been stated that the reason "being a horn" (*śṛṅgatva*) is a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) because of contradiction.

Now, why is contradiction with a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇavirodha*) also a defect? Because when all the necessary factors such as pervasion (*vyāpti*) are complete, the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) is inevitable.
In the absence of that [external object], its status as a mere appearance follows from that very fact;
what need is there for sublation by a means of valid cognition? To this, he says: "by perception," and so forth.
For all principles of reasoning are indeed rooted in perception and scripture;
those that lack such roots are mere fallacies of reasoning.
The word *tu* is used for emphasis; the word *hi* indicates what is well-known (*prasiddhi*) and also signifies "because.

Although it has been stated that the subject (*dharmin*) of the example, even if unestablished (*aprāmāṇika*), can sometimes serve as the locus (*āśraya*) for a probans (*hetu*) that consists of a negation, since its nature is negative; [nevertheless...]
Nevertheless, in the case of prescriptive [means of knowledge] and those whose nature is positive, there must necessarily be a basis grasped through perception or scripture;
likewise, in the case of a negation— whether it be the negation of a negator or when that which is to be proven is of a negative nature— [the same applies].
In some cases, the counter-positive must be apprehended through perception or other means;
furthermore, a logical mark (liṅga) is not capable of producing the cognition of the probandum (sādhya) by its own nature alone,
but rather by having its essential nature and pervasion (vyāpti) ascertained through perception and scripture.
Thus, it is well established that all principles (*nyāya*) are in various ways rooted in perception (*pratyakṣa*) and scripture (*āgama*).
For this reason, those principles which are baseless—that is, those which contradict the perception and scripture that constitute their own roots—are merely fallacious principles (*nyāyābhāsa*).
For example:

Even an axe, though perfected with a sharp edge and other qualities, does not produce a cut in that which is not its proper object, such as the sky; likewise, even inferences, being sublated by perception and scripture—which are stronger due to their being foundational—cannot produce valid cognition regarding what is not their proper object, and thus they are merely fallacious (*ābhāsa*).
Now, it may be argued that there is indeed a system (*nyāya*) rooted in inference.

Since it has been stated that [the means of knowledge] proceed by taking the eye and so forth as their basis, how then can they have perception and scripture as their roots? To this, he says: "Of the method" (nyāyasya).
... those two, moreover, [are the means] for another principle. (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 3.2.18d)
For any other reasoning (*nyāya*) besides those rooted in direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and scripture (*āgama*), those two—direct perception and scripture—are themselves the root.
How so?

Because even for any other reasoning that serves as a foundation, those two are once again the root; thus, since in the final analysis it never transcends direct perception and scripture in any way, it is stated accordingly.
Although scripture (*āgama*) is also rooted in perception (*pratyakṣa*), it sometimes serves as the root for perception itself; therefore, both are mentioned.
Although inference (*anumāna*) is also occasionally rooted in that [perception], it is not so when it is independent; therefore, it is excluded.
Thus, it has been established that what is sublated by functioning outside its proper domain is defective, even without depending on the violation of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth.
He states another variety as well: "unseen" (adṛṣṭa).
But when no deviation has been observed, it is clearly known through the witness alone that this [evidence] is probative. ... // MĀnuv 3.2.19a-c //
The word "tu" (but) is used for emphasis.

That mark, such as smoke and so forth, is a prover of fire and the like only when it is indeed entirely unobserved (*addhā*) to deviate from the probandum; it is not [a prover] when deviation is observed. This much is clearly known by the witness (*sākṣin*) himself. (9,90)

If it is argued that the capacity of a probans (*liṅga*) to establish the probandum (*sādhya*) is established by direct perception only when there is no observed deviation, he says: "māna... [and so forth].
... that would not exist when pride is destroyed. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 2.19d)
That the validity of means of knowledge is determined by the witness alone.
If there were sublation by a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇabādha*), there would be no deviation from that very example;

for when coldness and so forth are removed from fire and the like by sublation through a valid means of cognition, one observes the deviation of the probans—such as "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*)—from the probandum in that very instance.
Thus, it is stated that sublation constitutes a flaw because it causes the breakdown of pervasion (*vyāpti*).
In this regard, the distinction is as follows:
after the application for the sake of another, it is precisely the occurrence in a non-subject that must be pointed out,
not the failure of pervasion.

For the purpose of establishing the failure of pervasion (*vyāptibhaṅga*), since the inference is already defective by virtue of its functioning outside its proper domain (*aviṣayavṛttitva*)— upon which [the inference] depends— it is improper to resort to the failure of pervasion, which is a secondary mode of apprehension; whereas at the time of grasping the pervasion, it functions precisely as the cause for that failure,
because at that time the object has not yet ascended into the intellect.

And because the very breakdown of pervasion (vyāpti) is what first manifests, it was said "by the witness alone" (sākṣiṇaiva). In connection with that, he establishes [the point] with the words "That which... (yad iti).
Since the validity of all means of knowledge (*māna*) and cognitions (*jñāna*) is determined by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) alone—
because otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of infinite regress (*anavasthā*) and so forth—
it has already been stated that the validity of inference (*anumāna*) as well is known by that very same [witness]. *9,91*

If, then, validity were cognizable by the witness-consciousness (sākṣin), the previously established rule of the witness's necessity for truthfulness would be violated; for sometimes even that which is not valid is apprehended as being valid. Otherwise, there would be no activity prompted by the suspicion of error and the like.
And since its lack of correspondence with reality is known through sublation, he says: "of that which is not a means of valid cognition."
But for one who is free from pride, the state of being an authority would be unstable due to the presence of pride.
Invalidity and the apprehension of invalidity are unstable and sublated;
however, the validity that is apprehended in what is [otherwise] invalid is apprehended by the mind alone, not by the witness-consciousness.
Therefore, its sublation does not entail any defect;
this is the process here:
the Witness perceives every cognition whatsoever.

If there will be a sublation of this [cognition], then it is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*); if not, it is indeed a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and thus one also apprehends its validity.

When there is a purpose and a desire to know validity and so forth, one establishes either validity or invalidity by following an investigation (*parīkṣā*).
