However, if no such investigation is obtained, one remains indifferent due to the lack of a definitive determination of the specific [characteristics]. (9.92)
In this state, the mind, defiled by passion and other afflictions, determines validity and so forth with the aid of a semblance of investigation;
and that [determination] is sometimes sublated and sometimes not.

If it is asked, "From where does this conceptualization arise? [the answer is: because the rule of the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) regarding its conformity to reality has already been established.
And this will be stated [later]:

"In the case of the unperceived, there is deviation"; thus it has been said that a mark which deviates from the probandum is not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*). In that context, it follows that a mark whose deviation has been observed is also not a means of valid cognition.
Regarding this, he states the distinction: "even by way of general rule."

Even that which is obtained by way of a general rule (*utsarga*), provided it is devoid of exceptions (*apavāda*), shall indeed be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), as long as it does not deviate due to an exception. That mark (*liṅga*) which, by its very nature as a general rule, is established and determined to be free from exceptions— that is, free from deviation from the probandum— becomes a valid means of knowledge only when it is not rendered deviant by an exception, namely, by a specific cause.
It will be so.
This is what is meant:
just as the mere concomitance of the probans with the probandum is not useful for establishing validity.
But [the relation] must be unconditional;

otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that even "being the son of Maitrī" and the like— which have a conditional connection with the probandum— would become a means of proving dark complexion.
Likewise, even deviation (vyabhicāra) is a reason for non-probative-ness only when it is unconditional (nirupādhika),
as in the case of "knowability" (prameyatva) with respect to "eternality" (nityatva).

We do not perceive any restrictive rule to the effect that "knowability (*prameyatva*) does not deviate from eternality by its very nature, whereas it does deviate due to another cause," while we do perceive such a rule for that which "does not deviate from eternality by its very nature, whereas it does deviate due to another cause. Furthermore, when a probans (*sādhana*) deviates from the probandum (*sādhya*) by its very nature, yet its deviation is merely adventitious (*aupādhika*) due to some other condition, that [adventitious deviation] is not a cause for invalidity.
To the question "Why is this so?", he says: "For from this... (ato hi).

"For this reason, the inference that food and such things are means for achieving a desired end is always the authority in worldly practice... (*Manusmṛti* 3.2.22a–c). The word "eva" (only/precisely) is to be supplied here.

For it is precisely because a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) that is conditional (*sopādhika*) lacks the status of being a cause for invalidity that there can be an inference of the means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatā*) regarding future meals and the like. If even a conditional deviation were a cause of invalidity,
then the inference— "The meal under dispute is a means to what is desired, because it is a meal, like yesterday's meal"— would result in being invalid.
To the objection that "let it simply be invalid," he says: "In practical activity" (vyavahṛtau).
The word "reason" (*kāraṇam*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.

If this [cognition] were non-authoritative due to deviation (*vyabhicāra*), then it would likewise be determined by practitioners (*vyavahartṛbhiḥ*) to be non-authoritative, just like [the cognition of] "knowability" (*prameyatva*).
And in that case, there would be no engagement in eating on the part of prudent people (*prekṣāvatām*) based upon it.
But surely, a proof that is inconclusive brings about doubt;
and doubt, too, is a cause for engagement.
True.
Doubt produces an activity that is hesitant, not one that is unrestrained;
yet this [activity] is unrestrained and is established by the experience of everyone.
This is what was meant by saying "eternal."
The connection is with what precedes. [Objection:
This inference is indeed a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), but it is so precisely because there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*). To this, he says: "For deviation... (*vyabhicāro hi*).
... for in that case, there is indeed deviation [from the rule]. (Manu Smṛti 3.22)

In that regard, when "being food" and so forth are employed as the reason (*sādhana*) to prove [the property of] being undesirable (*aniṣṭa*), the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) from the probandum (*sādhya*)—namely, not being a means to what is undesirable—is quite evident; for in some cases, even that which is not a means to what is undesirable is observed.
However, this is based solely on the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of being unwholesome (*apathya*) and so forth.

Nor should it be argued that the property of being food qualified by wholesomeness and so forth is itself the means (sādhana); for such a qualification is established only after the activity has occurred,
since it is to be inferred from the result and is therefore unestablished prior [to that activity].
Indeed, it is not possible for people like us to ascertain that fruits, roots, and so forth have not been affected by poisonous leaves and the like.
Therefore, the deviation [of the reason] is indeed unconditional; thus, the reason "not being a means of proof" is a fallacy.

Consequently, since there are possible ways in which sublation by a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇabādha*) constitutes a flaw, it is not appropriate to employ the counter-argument (*pratibandī*) that "having a non-existent locus" (*asadāśrayatva*) is not a flaw.

Having thus refuted the status of "having a non-existent locus" as a flaw in a reason (*hetudoṣa*), [the author], while also refuting "residing in a different locus" (*vyadhikaraṇatva*) as such, considers the following alternatives: whether the status of "residing in a different locus" must be accepted as a flaw in a reason because it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)—such that if even a reason residing in a different locus were valid, then "the self is non-eternal because of the blackness of a crow" would also be a valid reason—or because of a lack of pervasion (*vyāptyabhāva*), or because of a lack of the property of being a predicate of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*). Keeping these options in mind, he refutes the first by stating: "In the case of pervasion... (*vyāptatve*) // 9.99 //
But if [the self] is all-pervading, how indeed can its having multiple substrates be a fault? (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.2.23ab)

Since the means of proof (sādhana) is pervaded by that which is to be proven (sādhya), how indeed could it be a defect for them to have different loci? It is not a defect in any way. This is what is meant: * *sādhanasya sādhyena vyāptatve sati tena vibhinnāśrayatvaṃ kathameva hi dūṣaṇam / na kathañcit / idamuktaṃ bhavati /* * Since the means of proof is pervaded by that which is to be proven, how indeed could it be a defect for them to have different loci? It is not a defect in any way. This is what is meant: The point is this: when the reason (*hetu*) is necessarily concomitant with the property to be proved (*sādhya*), the fact that they reside in different substrata (*vibhinnāśrayatva*) does not invalidate the inference. For example, when one infers fire on a mountain from smoke on a lake, the reason (smoke) and the probandum (fire) do not share the same locus; nevertheless, because the smoke is pervaded by fire, the inference remains valid. Thus, a difference in locus is not a logical fault in such cases.
Indeed, the blackness of a crow does not prove its eternity precisely because it lacks pervasion (*vyāpti*), and not because it is a reason residing in a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇa*).
Therefore, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Why is this so?

Because nowhere has it been observed that a reason is non-probative merely by virtue of being in a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇatva*) when all its constituent factors, such as pervasion (*vyāpti*), are complete.
If it is argued that this is seen in cases such as "Sound is impermanent because a jar is produced," [we reply:
is the phrase "of a jar" a qualification of the reason (*hetu*) or not?
In the first case, there is futility;
in the second, how could it be non-probative?
If it is argued that "even though 'being produced' is pervaded by impermanence, its occurrence in a jar does not prove impermanence in sound," we say no.
Because there is no pervasion (*vyāpti*), as we shall explain later [in verses 9.102]. Thus,
it is not only when the members such as pervasion are complete that a fault is observed merely by virtue of being in a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇatva*).

However, since it is observed that even a reason residing in a different locus (vyadhikaraṇa) can be a prover when it possesses the necessary conditions such as pervasion (vyāpti), he says: "Rohiṇī... etc.
"Since Rohiṇī is near its rising because Kṛttikā has already risen," when this was said, what means of proof did they have? ... MAnu 3.2.23c-e.

Having raised the objection that the inference of rain in the upper region from the sight of a river in flood, and the inference of the presence of a potter from seeing the revolving wheel of a fresh clay pot, are invalid, someone has stated: "In this case, the upper region is not the subject (*pakṣa*); rather, it is the river itself.
By means of its very property—the flood—"
The property to be proven (*sādhya*) is that very property [of the cloud], namely its connection with a northern region characterized by rain.
Likewise, from the two properties of the saucer and the wheel—freshness and rotation—one infers that very same property, which is the potter's presence.
Therefore, this other example has been stated.
For it is not possible here to establish two properties for either Rohiṇī or Kṛttikā.
But surely, even in this case, one should employ the argument by taking time as the subject?
"The time under dispute possesses proximity to the rising of Rohiṇī, because it is time, like the time of the rising of Kṛttikā. (Not so.

If this were the case, since co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) exists everywhere by taking either space or time as the locus, there would never be a case of "unestablished due to being in a different locus" (*vyadhikaraṇāsiddha*); thus, the exclusion of that [fallacy] would be useless.
If it is argued that in such an application, the state of being in a different locus still finds its scope, we say no.
For if that were so, it would follow that there is no fault in the statement because the truth [of the thesis] is established;
nor is there even the fault of the statement itself,
since we experience that even a statement with a different locus (vyadhikaraṇa) serves as a factor for the establishment of the probandum (sādhya).
In this very way, the expressions of worldly people are used;
for even investigators employ such statements as, "Its validity is due to its initial appearance of validity," and so forth.

This has been stated: even though this statement was made with a different grammatical subject (*vyadhikaraṇatayā*), does the means of proof (*sādhana*) not indeed become a constituent part for the establishment of the probandum (*sādhyasidhyaṅga*)?
Furthermore, regarding the point that one should effect a modification of the formulation (*prayogavipariṇāma*) by taking time (*kāla*) and so forth into account—what [is the purpose of this]?
Is the doctrine of the Naiyāyikas and others the regulator, or is there some other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) here?
He refutes the first alternative with the words "for not" (na hi).
For in this matter, mere command alone is not the means of accomplishment.
In this context, when the matter to be established is one already proven by reasoning,
the command itself is merely a conventional agreement.
If that were the case, everything would have to be taught by mere word alone,
and no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would ever need to be stated;
for the meaning of the words is that there would be a state of counter-thesis (*satpratipakṣatā*) due to a contrary instruction.

Indeed, authoritative command (ājñā) regarding objects beyond one's own sensory range, such as dharma and so forth, arises only for those who have understood the status of the person as trustworthy; nor is the second alternative [the case].
Because that [pervasion] is not apprehended.
This might be argued: pervasion is indeed a constituent factor of inference.
And pervasion (*vyāpti*) is a specific kind of relation;
moreover, a relation between two things that have different substrata (*vyāśraya*) is not tenable.
Therefore, because having different substrata is a defect, [the relation] is impossible.
That "transformation in the object" [is the pervasion]—
do not say so;
for pervasion consists merely in inseparable connection (avinābhāva).
And inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*) occurs in some cases by being included within a single substratum (*ekāśrayatā*),
as for example, that between "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and "impermanence" (*anityatva*).
For this very reason, impermanence is not established in one place by means of that [property] residing in another.
In some cases, they indeed have distinct substrata,
as for example smoke with fire;
for smoke and fire do not share a common substratum through the relation of inherence (*samavāya*).
Nor does it exist by way of conjunction (*saṃyoga*),
because [the smoke] is conjoined with both upper and lower regions (since the conjunction of smoke with the lower region is established).
If it is argued that even so, both [fire and smoke] possess the property of being conjoined with the same mountain, we say no;
for if that were the case, it would be impossible for one seeking fire to act with necessity toward a specific location.
If it is argued that it is smoke itself, as smoke, that proves the presence of fire at the base [of the mountain], [we reply:]...
Is this a worldly convention,
or is a modification made for the sake of establishing a technical term?
It is not the first.
For ordinary people, upon observing a place above to be possessed of smoke, understand the place below to be possessed of fire;
the second [alternative] is not [the case],
because it lacks any foundation.
Furthermore, since the opponent accepts the momentariness of the body and so forth,
it would be difficult to establish the inference of gravity from the act of falling;
for there can be no temporal co-location between those two.
Nor is it [established] by way of location,
because they reside in different substances.

Therefore, for some [reasons], there is an inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) precisely by virtue of having different loci (*vibhinnāśraya*). If it is objected that a property residing in a different locus cannot possess the character of being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), we reply: let it not be so; for that restriction lacks any basis.
If it is asked how, that being the case, the necessary localization of the probandum (*sādhya*) could be established, we reply: "Because of the very nature of pervasion (*vyāpti*).
For instance:

In the case of the pervasion "whatever is produced is impermanent," by including the co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the state of being produced causes impermanence to be understood precisely within its own locus.

Likewise, the rising of Kṛttikā is pervaded by the proximity of the rising of Rohiṇī, even though they are in different loci (*vyadhikaraṇa*); thus, it causes that [proximity] to be understood in exactly that way.
And just as there is a restriction of place and so forth even when there is co-referentiality, so too is there such a restriction when there is non-co-referentiality; what fault is there in this?

Therefore, because pervasion (*vyāpti*) is possible— just as in the cases of "wherever this is, there that is," "whenever this is, then that is," "whatever is thus, that is thus," and "if this is, then that is"—

and because the establishment of the reason (*hetu*) necessarily depends upon that very pervasion, while the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) is not necessary, it is logical that even a reason residing in a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇa*) can serve as a valid reason.
This remains true even when the qualifier of the probandum (*sādhyaviśeṣaṇa*) is unestablished.
For instance: since the qualification of the probandum (*sādhyaviśeṣaṇa*) is unestablished, how could it constitute a refutation?

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even such arguments as "the universe is distinct from both the existent and the non-existent because it is sublatable" would be valid.

Furthermore, if the qualification of the probandum (*sādhyaviśeṣaṇa*) were unestablished, doubt regarding it would be impossible; and since the status of being a subject (*pakṣatva*) would be untenable, it would follow that the reason lacks the property of being a predicate of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*). Alternatively, if the qualification of the probandum were unestablished, it would follow that the cognition of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the means of proof and that [probandum] could not occur.
Or else, because the words of the thesis-statement (*pratijñāvākya*) would have meanings not previously understood, it would result in the statement being unintelligible.
He refutes the first [position] with the words "anyat" (something else).
And because of the contradiction in saying "the universe is other than both being and non-being," [this view] is not valid.

If it is said that "it does not exist," then non-existence would be asserted, because non-existence consists in the negation of existence. Furthermore, if it is then said that "it does not exist [as non-existent]," there is a contradiction with one's own words.
By stating "it does not exist as such," two negations convey the original meaning with a degree of emphasis, whereby existence (*sattva*) is obtained.
When it is further stated "it does not exist as existent," there is simply a self-contradiction.
Thus, the proposition that the universe is other than both the existent and the non-existent—that it is neither existent nor non-existent—is itself invalid due to self-contradiction.
It is not because the qualification—
characterized by the distinction between existence and non-existence— is unestablished;
for what reason?
For self-contradiction, as in the case of "my mother is barren," is universally accepted as a defect;

because only that statement which is not obstructed by one's own words, logic, one's own conduct, one's own tenets, or other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) constitutes a limb of proof or refutation.
Indeed, a female serpent stunned by its own venom does not bite another.

Furthermore, we do not see any example of the non-establishment of a qualification of the probandum (*sādhyaviśeṣaṇāsiddhi*) that is unmixed with other defects, by which we might recognize its status as a fault.
If it is argued, "Why should the proof of someone's possession of a rabbit's horn and the like by means of a unique property (*asādhāraṇadharma*) not also be valid cognition?", we say no;
because even in that case, there exists the sublation (*bādha*) consisting in the non-perception of the perceptible.
If it is argued that there is no fault whatsoever in establishing contact with a supersensible being, we say no;
for by means of contact with God (Īśvara) and others, one would be proving what is already established (siddhasādhanatva).
Likewise, in other cases as well, another fault must be sought in regard to that which is universally accepted as invalid.
This is what is expressed by the word "and" (ca).
For this very reason, "because of the contradiction" (*vyāhati*) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*).
He states the second [reason]: "unestablished" (*asiddha*).
What fault is there in proving what is already established, if pervasion exists?

Where it is said that the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) is unestablished because the probandum (*sādhya*) is unestablished, does the reason possess all its other constituent parts, such as pervasion (*vyāpti*), or not?
If it does not, then the inference is already defective for that very reason; what is the use of the probandum’s qualification being unestablished?
If pervasion and so forth exist, then what fault is there in proving what is already established? None at all.
This is the intended meaning.
For the reason's property-of-the-subject (pakṣadharmatva) would be unestablished at that time if either the subject did not exist or the reason did not possess that property. Furthermore,
the property-of-the-subject would be unestablished at that time due to the absence of doubt.
If either the subject (*dharmin*) or its being a property of that [subject] (*taddharmatva*) were not present in the reason (*hetu*), then,

due to the absence of doubt, the status of being a thesis (*pakṣatva*) would be untenable; and if the state of being a property of the thesis (*pakṣadharmatva*) were thus absent, there would be the total destruction of the specific nature of inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*).
For when one who has grasped the pervasion— that whatever possesses smoke possesses fire— sees smoke on a mountain peak and recollects that pervasion,
then an inference indeed arises for him;
and there is no doubt regarding fire for him.
And when one who has ascertained the connection between fire and the mountain through the word of a reliable person observes smoke while approaching the mountain,
even then his inference of fire occurs indeed without doubt;
for the causal complex (sāmagrī) is not itself intelligent.
Having reflected that "whatever was to be done by me has been done by another," one should remain indifferent.

Furthermore, it is illogical (and impossible to assert) that once something has been delimited, another delimitation could arise, just as there cannot be a further act of cutting once the cutting is finished.
Nor is there any rule of doubt regarding inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*).
Because even one who is mistaken can logically function as a respondent (*prativādin*),
for this very reason it was stated that [an argument] which proves what is already established is indeed irrelevant, and not "unestablished in its locus" (*āśrayāsiddha*).
Furthermore, even when one who has realized the truth engages for the sake of examining another...
In that case, one asks for the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*):
at that time, the inference employed would be invalid,
because there is an absence of doubt.
Therefore, the statements of the ancients that "the subject (pakṣa) is that in which the probandum is doubtful" and so forth, are intended in the sense of a mere possibility (*sambhāvanā*).
In ultimate reality, however, the subject is precisely the object of the inference.

Consequently, since there is no impossibility of being a subject when doubt is absent, there is no defect consisting in the failure to establish the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) in the case of proving what is not already established.
He refutes the third [point] with the words: "And pervasion..."
And in that case, pervasion is understood through negative concomitance (vyatireka) by means of those very [examples].
In this regard, there are instances of purely negative (kevalavyatirekin) means of proof, such as: "The body produced from a living being possesses a self because it possesses breath and so forth";
"Earth is distinct from the other [elements] because it possesses odor";
and "God is omniscient because He is the creator of all. In these cases, the collection of proofs consists of purely negative reasons.
There is pervasion (vyāpti) even with those unestablished probanda such as "possessing a self" (sātmakatva),
and not merely the property of being a predicate of the subject (pakṣadharmatā).

And that [pervasion] is also understood through the mark (liṅga) consisting in the fact that the absence of the probandum is pervaded by the absence of the probans by way of negative concomitance (vyatireka).
This is what is meant:
for one who implies the non-apprehension of the cognition of pervasion due to the non-establishment of the qualification of the probandum, there is an absence of pervasion.
For instance:
Is purely negative inference (kevalavyatirekī anumāna) a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) or not? We shall address the position that it is not.
In the first case, the existence of its pervasion (vyāpti) and the cognition of that pervasion must necessarily be admitted;
otherwise, there would be a contradiction of its being an inference.
Furthermore, in a purely negative inference (kevalavyatirekin), the probandum is not established [prior to the inference].

If it were established in the subject (pakṣa), it would result in proving what is already proven (siddhasādhanatva). If it were established elsewhere, then the probandum would indeed be established in the purely negative inference.

If it is already established in the subject (*pakṣa*), there is the fallacy of proving what is already proven (*siddhasādhanatva*). If it is established elsewhere, then in the case of a purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekin*), the probandum (*sādhya*) would already be established.
If it is established in the subject, there is the fallacy of proving what is already proven.
If [the reason] were established elsewhere, it could not be a purely negative (*kevalavyatirekin*) reason because it would occur there;
if it did not occur there, it would follow that it is over-exclusive (*asādhāraṇya*).
Therefore, the reductio (*prasaṅga*) has a shaky foundation. If it is asked: "Where is the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of a purely negative reason, and by what is it apprehended?"
We say that it is understood through exclusion (*vyatireka*) precisely within the subject (*pakṣa*).
Because it cannot be demonstrated through contradiction (*vipratipatti*) prior to the differentiation of the subject and so forth, it is established by means of exclusion.
By the plural number in the word "by them" (*taiḥ*), he indicates the extreme well-known nature of the refutation of the pervasion in the reductio (*prasaṅga*).

It is not only we who accept that for a purely negative (kevalavyatireki) proof, there is a pervasion with the probandum and its comprehension through the negative concomitance; rather, even by some who maintain that "unestablished qualification" (aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva) is a flaw in such arguments, this is likewise accepted. Thus he says: "And by them."
It is understood; it is accepted.
As they have said:

"If there were no concomitance (*anvaya*) of this [reason] with the probandum (*sādhya*) anywhere, then one might suspect that this is indeed contradictory (*viruddha*); however, we do not deny the possibility of concomitance, but rather we accept it."
"Since you [assert this], etc.
Furthermore, just as the establishment of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is achieved through the force of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), so too must it be demonstrated by the Vaiśeṣikas;
otherwise, if there were no pervasion (*avyāpti*) between the probandum and the probans, the capacity of the negative-only inference (*vyatirekin*) to produce knowledge would collapse, and so forth.

The sense is this: how is it not contradictory that, for a *kevalavyatirekin* (purely negative inference) whose qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is unestablished, there is both the demonstration of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and the consequence that pervasion cannot be cognized due to the unestablished nature of the qualifier? As it has been stated: "Since the cognition of pervasion in a *kevalavyatirekin* is accepted by others, there is no lack of cognition of pervasion even when the qualifier is unestablished."
That is incorrect;
for there is a distinct approach regarding purely negative (kevalavyatirekin) reasons.

Indeed, in those cases where purely negative reasons are accepted as having the status of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it is precisely a general positive concomitance (*anvayavyāpti*) that must be stated.

For instance: when it is to be proven that a living body possesses a self (*sātmaka*) by virtue of its possession of breath and so forth, [the argument is]: "Whatever possesses an effect possesses a cause, just as the earth possesses sprouts because it contains seeds.

Likewise, when proving the distinction of the earth from other things by virtue of its possession of odor, [the argument is]: "Whatever possesses a unique property (*asādhāraṇadharma*) is distinct from that [to which it does not belong], just as water and so forth [are distinct from the earth]."
Thus, in establishing the omniscience of God through His status as the creator of all, [the argument is]: whoever is the creator of something knows its cause and its purpose, just as a potter does.
Likewise, sound must reside in a substance distinct from the eight substances such as earth and the rest, because there are valid arguments that refute its subsistence in earth and the others.

In arguments such as "because it is a quality" (*guṇatvāt*), a general pervasion (*sāmānyato vyāpti*) must be stated in a form such as: "Whatever is a quality when there is a sublation [of its existence] in the occurrence of x, that occurs in a substance other than x, just like odor.
Alternatively, having established the presence of the qualifier in a general sense, one should employ a purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekin*).

Just as the degree of knowledge must rest upon some ultimate limit because it is a gradation—thereby establishing omniscience in general, whose connection with God is then proven by a *kevalavyatirekin* (purely negative inference)—so too, desire and the like must reside in some substratum because they are qualities, like color;
and that which is the substratum of desire and the like is the Self. Thus, once the Self is established in a general sense, its connection with the living body is proven by a *kevalavyatirekin*.
In this manner, other cases should also be inferred according to what is possible.
In some instances, a purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekin*) proceeds by relying on the establishment of a qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*) within only one part of the subject (*pakṣaikadeśa*).

For example, in the case: "Earth is distinct from others because it possesses earth-ness (*pṛthivītva*); for whatever is not so [distinct] is not so [possessing earth-ness], as in the case of water and so forth," the qualification is established precisely in the jar (*ghaṭa*) and such things; therefore, there is no fallacy of an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatā*).
Nor does the possibility of a similar instance (sapakṣa) in this way destroy the status of the reason as being purely negative (kevalavyatirekin),
because a jar and the like constitute only a part of the subject (pakṣa);
nor is there the fallacy of proving what is already established (siddhasādhanatā) with respect to that part.
Even if [the reason] were well-known in each individual case, it would not be established from the smallest atom up to the entire terrestrial globe.

Alternatively, non-existence (*abhāva*) must be proven by a purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekin*). For if existence (*bhāva*) were to be established, then in the case of negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*), there would be a requirement for the establishment of the qualifier, since the cognition of that non-existence depends upon the cognition of its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*).
But when non-existence (abhāva) is the probandum (sādhya), this fault does not apply;
for since the non-existence of a non-existence is a positive entity (bhāva), it is independent of a counter-correlate (pratiyogin).
In this way, other specific modes of expression should also be understood.

In the absence of even one of these [three], the fault of having an unestablished qualifier (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatā*) remains a valid objection. Therefore, one cannot dispel the charge of having an unestablished qualifier by relying on the validity of purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekin*). To this end, he says: "Of that which is unestablished" (*aprasiddhasya*).
"If it is maintained that [the reason] establishes a probandum (*sādhya*) that is itself unestablished," [then the fault remains].
By what means of knowledge is this specific distinction regarding the statement of gender understood?

In the phrase "of the probandum" (*sādhyasya*), the genitive case denotes the object (*karman*); in "of the mark" (*liṅgasya*), it denotes the agent (*kartṛ*). The word "this" (*ayam*) refers back to that which is present in the mind.
This would be the case if there were a restrictive rule stating that this particular formulation must be employed in the case of a purely negative (*kevalavyatirekin*) inference.
And this is not the case;
for it must be stated: by this particular mode of expression, is the purely negative probandum (kevalavyatireki-sādhya) brought to possess positive concomitance (anvayitā), or not?
Not the first [alternative],
because it is impossible for a statement to alter the actual nature of its object;
for even with a thousand statements, a man cannot be turned into a monkey.
Or, if it were possible [to establish the probandum through perception], the validity of the purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekin*) would have to be abandoned.
This was stated regarding the second case:
when the probans, being itself unestablished, is desired to be the means of proving the probandum.

The point is this: even if it is accepted that a probans (*liṅga*) qualified by a predicate that is [otherwise] unestablished (*aprasiddha-viśeṣaṇa*) is indeed a prover of a purely negative (*kevala-vyatirekin*) probandum and does not attain the status of a positive concomitant (*anvayin*), then by what means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is this distinction known as something that must be established? By none at all.

Therefore, since a purely negative probans is a prover precisely when its qualification is unestablished, the fault of having an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddha-viśeṣaṇatva*) cannot be a defect.
There certainly exists a restrictive factor regarding the necessity of employing a specific mode of expression;
for instance,
although a specific mode of expression does not produce either a negative (vyatirekin) or a positive (anvayin) concomitance.

Nevertheless, the pervasion of the logical mark (*liṅga*) by the probandum (*sādhya*) must necessarily exist; however, that pervasion cannot be directly demonstrated in the case of a purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekin*),
because the locus for apprehending positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is obstructed by conflicting opinions.

Therefore, having demonstrated the pervasion of the absence of the probandum by the absence of the probans in the counter-example (vipakṣa), it must be established. Alternatively, even if the pervasion of the negative concomitance alone is a constituent factor for the proof of the probandum,
nevertheless, the apprehension of that [pervasion] is necessarily required.
Furthermore, negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is necessarily cognized only through the cognition of its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*);
and the two counter-correlates are the probans (*liṅga*) and the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*). Among these, the probans is already cognized in the subject (*pakṣa*).
Furthermore, the property to be proven (sādhyadharma) is neither perceived in the subject (pakṣa) nor elsewhere;
how then could the pervasion (vyāpti) even of the two negative instances (vyatireka) be grasped?
However, through these specific modes of expression, if the property to be proven—the counter-correlative—is somehow brought to mind, the apprehension of pervasion would be easily accomplished.
Furthermore, a statement of the proposition (*pratijñāvākya*) would not result in having its constituent terms unknown; therefore, he says: "the means of proof" (*sādhana*).
When the proof of something unestablished, such as atoms and so forth, is sought, why then should this [proof] not be accepted exactly according to experience? (MAnu 3.2.26)

The Vaiśeṣikas and others, who accept that atoms are the makers of effects, establish the existence of atoms; likewise, the Sāṅkhyas, who assert that the Pradhāna is the material cause, establish the existence of the Pradhāna. In the same way, other principles such as inherence (samavāya) are established by those who accept them.

In this regard, we ask: is the existence of those [atoms] being proven against one who accepts atoms and so forth, or is it being proven against one who accepts their non-existence, thinking that "atoms do not exist"?
Not the first, because it is illogical to attempt to prove what is already established.

As for the second [alternative], how could a proponent exert effort to prove something like an atom that has not ascended to the level of cognition, and how could an opponent believe in its non-existence?
Because the counter-positive is not known.

Now, you might think that by means of the instruction of Kaṇāda and others, or through inference for oneself based on what is generally observed (sāmānyato dṛṣṭa), the proponent is indeed able to establish atoms and so forth, which have been understood by himself.

Furthermore, when the opponent’s counter-correlate, such as an atom, is understood through the statement of the proponent, it is entirely appropriate for the respondent to intend the non-existence of that [correlate].

For there is no rule that a counter-correlate must be known solely by means of a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), since otherwise the cognition of the absence of things such as a rabbit's horn would result in being untenable.

If this is so, and you maintain that even something like an atom—which is absolutely unestablished [prior to inference]—is proven without overstepping the path of experience, then why not likewise accept this "negative-only" (vyatirekin) proof of the probandum as being based solely on the conformity of experience? For instance: [The argument: Whatever is not perceived despite the presence of all other conditions for perception is non-existent, just like a second head. And the subject under dispute (the mountain, etc. is not perceived despite the presence of all other conditions for perception. Therefore, it is non-existent. In this case, since the absence of the probandum (non-existence) is established by the very nature of things (*vastubalapravṛtta*), there is no need for a positive example (*anvaya-dṛṣṭānta*). Thus, the negative-only inference is established. Furthermore, if one were to say that the probans is not established because its counter-positive (existence) is not perceived, that would be a fallacy; for the non-perception of the counter-positive is itself the probans. Moreover, if one were to argue that the probans is unestablished because its locus (the subject) is unestablished, that too is a fallacy; for the non-perception of the subject is itself the probans. Consequently, the negative-only inference is established. Thus, the probans is indeed established. Therefore, the negative-only inference is valid. For the proponent (*vādin*), once he has perceived two properties in a single locus that possesses the uncommon property (*asādhāraṇadharmi*)— either through direct perception or through instruction— it is indeed easy for him to grasp the negative pervasion (*vyatirekavyāpti*), since it is possible for him to perceive the absence of those [two properties] everywhere else.

For the opponent (*prativādin*) as well, since he has understood the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) from the proponent’s statement, it is possible for him to understand the absence of that [counter-positive].
The apprehension of negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*) is indeed possible.

Thus, since the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) can be established by the method previously mentioned, it is possible to prove an unestablished probandum (*sādhya*); what is the use of these laborious conceptualizations?
And in this way, there is no consequence of the thesis statement (*pratijñāvākya*) having its meaning unknown.
"Because the meaning of that has been explained by the proponent.
He concludes with the words "wherein."
Where there is no over-extension and where the means of knowledge are not subverted,
it is extremely difficult to maintain that what is to be proven here is established by afflicted conceptualization alone.
Regarding the subject matter of a purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekin*),
there is no restrictive rule or authority that mandates that the proof must be established by means of stating a general positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and so forth.

Because the cognition of pervasion and so forth is established through other means; for it is improper to establish an object that is already proven by a direct path following immediate experience through a circuitous route that lacks such experience. This applies when one fails to provide proof in the case of the contrary.
Furthermore, there is no over-extension [of the argument],
because the status of another [position] as a fallacy follows precisely from its own internal contradiction and so forth.
In this regard, the statement that "the proof of the probandum must be carried out solely through the conceptualization of the opponent's affliction" is an extremely flawed position.
By this, it should be understood that the crooked method of the *mahāvidyā* and similar arguments, which relies upon a qualified negative concomitance (*viśiṣṭavyatireka*), is also refuted;
for that would be the case only if there were such a thing as purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekyanumāna*),
and yet it is not so.

Inference is indeed that which is endowed with five characteristics: presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), presence in the similar class (*sapakṣe sattva*), absence from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣād vyāvṛtti*), non-contradiction of the object (*abādhitaviṣayatva*), and lack of a counter-balancing argument (*asatpratipakṣatva*).
However, these do not exist for the purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekin*), because, due to the absence of a similar class, there is no presence in the similar class.

Nor should it be argued that, in this way, even a purely positive (kevalānvayin) inference would result in the fallacy of not being a valid inference because of the absence of exclusion from the counter-example (vipakṣa), due to the non-existence of a counter-example; for we do not maintain that only that which possesses both positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) constitutes an inference. Anticipating this second objection, he says: "By elimination" (pariśeṣa).
The remaining [fallacies], such as mutual dependence (*mithaḥsiddhi*), circularity (*cakraka*), and self-dependence (*svāśraya*),
must all be accepted by everyone as means of proving what is unestablished, even without the five-membered syllogism.
*Pariśeṣa* (residual method) is the cognition that remains when all other possibilities have been excluded.
*Mithaḥsiddhi* (mutual establishment) is the arising or the cognition of two things in dependence upon one another.
*Cakraka* (vicious circle) is the arising and so forth of many things in mutual dependence, like a wheel.
Its own arising and so forth depend upon itself; its locus is itself.
By the word "and so forth" (ādi), infinite regress (anavasthā) is implied.
And that infinite regress consists in a dependence on a succession of producers and so forth that is never established.
By means of the reason that it establishes what has not yet been established,
all disputants must accept the five-membered structure and the possession of the five characteristics as being inference.
Indeed, no proponent whatsoever has engaged in an investigation while disregarding methods such as *pariśeṣa* (elimination by exhaustion).
What is meant by this is that *pariśeṣa* and the others are, first of all, forms of inference (*anumāna*).

Because it is characterized by the rule that "from the knowledge of the pervaded (vyāpya) comes the knowledge of the pervader (vyāpaka)," and because even those who delight in the proliferation of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) do not accept its validity as being outside the scope of inference (*anumāna*);
furthermore, these [means] serve to establish only that which is yet unestablished (*asiddha*).

For when the connection of sound with the eight substances beginning with earth has been negated, its subsistence in a substance other than those is established by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*).
However, prior to the establishment of space (*ākāśa*), no substance distinct from earth and the others is established,
such that its subsistence therein could be known anywhere.

When an effect is established for one party by another—either through valid cognition (*pramita*) or accepted (*aṅgīkṛta*)—then for the one who accepts that it is indeed an effect of that [cause], "mutual establishment" (*mithaḥsiddhi*) is said to occur. However, such [establishment] is never actually found to exist;
for in both cases, priority (*pūrvabhāvitva*) is mutually dependent.
The same applies to the other alternative as well;
by this, the circular reasoning (*cakraka*) is explained.
[This is] because this very pot possesses the status of being the effect of this [cause].
With respect to that which is moving, its own status as a substratum is asserted;
yet, for that very thing [to be] prior or posterior in relation to itself is simply unestablished.
Against one who asserts the causality of something that is itself unestablished, an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) is stated.
Furthermore, a causal series consisting of unestablished causes is never established with respect to any effect.

As for establishment by way of generality, that is common even to the *kevalavyatirekin* (inference based solely on negative concomitance). Moreover, because these [causes] function as means of proving what is unestablished, they do not possess the five required characteristics (*pañcarūpa*).
And likewise, because these inferences also lack the possession of the five characteristics [of a valid reason],
the statement that "negative-only inference (*vyatirekin*) is not an inference due to the deficiency of the possession of the five characteristics" is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
He states another refutation: "The restriction of that," etc.
...what is the basis for that restriction? Mānava 3.2.28f.

Since there is no basis for the restriction that an inference must necessarily possess five characteristics (*pañcarūpa*), and since there is no subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against something lacking these being an inference, this fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) is not a valid probans (*aprayojaka*). [Objection: But how can it be said that there is no basis [for such a restriction], given that these characteristics serve as the means for establishing pervasion (*vyāpti*) and subsistence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), and are intended to exclude the five types of fallacious reasons such as the unestablished (*asiddha*)? [Response: [This is so because] the restriction to five characteristics lacks any logical foundation. Furthermore, even if one were to accept that an inference could consist of fewer than five characteristics, there would be no subverting argument against its status as an inference. Therefore, the claim that this is a non-probative fallacy is untenable. As for the objection regarding the necessity of these characteristics to establish pervasion and subsistence in the subject, and their role in excluding the five fallacies like the unestablished: while these functions are indeed served by the five characteristics, they do not constitute a logically necessary or foundational requirement for the definition of an inference. Thus, the restriction remains without a firm basis.
And how is there an absence of a subverting argument against the contrary case (*vipakṣa*)?
Because the very failure to establish the stated purpose serves as that subversion.

If it is argued that if something were an inference even without presence in the similar class (*sapakṣa*), then even an "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) reason—such as "the earth is eternal because it possesses odor"—would be an inference, we say no.
"Because the distinction [of the reason] is established through its presence or absence in the similar class (*sapakṣa*).

Having thus demonstrated that [objections such as] the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) and so forth are not genuine defects, it is argued that the statement, "Even if [the locus] is set aside, the fact that [the reason] is established [elsewhere] remains a defect," is incorrect.
He dispels the doubt that "in debate, there has been stated an absence of points of defeat" by saying: "siddha" (established).
And if there were the fallacy of proving what is already established, there would be no conclusion to the discussion.

Just as in the case of inquiries regarding established facts (*siddhapraśna*) and so forth, there is no conclusion to the debate; rather, because it contradicts the determination of reality (*tattvanirṇaya*), [the objection] must be raised and discarded—so too is the meaning in the case of "proving what is already established" (*siddhasādhanatā*).
For it is only the establishment of something other than that which serves as the proof.

By this, it is indicated that the refutation consists of the non-establishment of the pervasion (*vyāptyasiddhi*) and the non-establishment of the essential nature (*svarūpāsiddhi*) of the reason. Regarding this, some say that the absence of pervasion and so forth are of two kinds.
[The fallacy occurs] either by the opinion of one of the two parties— the proponent or the opponent— or by the opinion of both.
Others, however,
think that there is no such thing as "non-pervasion of one [party]" and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "because conceptual construction of an entity is impossible," he says—
anticipating the question of what the reality is in that case— "it is deviation."
"Inconstancy and the unestablished nature of the reason are defects even in the case of one party.
Here, "inconstancy" (vyabhicāra) is an indicator for non-pervasion (avyāpti) alone.

It is not only in the case of both parties, but inconstancy and the unestablished nature of the reason are indeed defects of the reason even when they belong to the position of only one of the two—the proponent or the opponent.

Although, in reality, the deviation of one or the other and so forth is impossible, nevertheless, prior to the ascertainment of the true nature of things, such [deviation] certainly occurs through mere conceit (*ābhimānika*).
Thus, even when there is doubt regarding the capacity of the reason (*hetu*), its status as a non-reason (*ahetu*) is inevitable;
for only that which is ascertained by means of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and other criteria possesses the status of a reason.

By the phrase "of that other," it is indicated that the example (dṛṣṭānta) is also unestablished (*asiddhi*) because it possesses the property to be proven (*sādhyavat*) and so forth; this constitutes a fault (*dūṣaṇa*).
Some, however, declare:
"There are no such things as faults of the example, for they are included within the faults of the reason (*hetudoṣa*) as appropriate."
He replies to them: "The probandum," etc.
The deficiency of the example regarding the probandum and the probans... // MAnu 3.2.30ab //
The term "defect" (dūṣaṇam) carries over [from the previous context].

Although [defects] such as the deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) are included within the fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*), they are classified as defects of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadoṣa*) because they appear clearly by virtue of being based on the example; because they must be pointed out precisely according to how they appear; and because the purpose of the exposition is for the sake of pointing them out. This is the intended meaning.
Some state eight faults of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*):

deficiency in the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*), deficiency in the probans (*sādhanavaikalya*), deficiency in both, and lack of a substratum (*āśrayahīnatva*)—these are the four faults of the similar example (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).

Non-exclusion of the probandum (*sādhyāvyāvṛtti*), non-exclusion of the probans (*sādhanāvyāvṛtti*), non-exclusion of both, and lack of a substratum (*āśrayahīnatva*)—these are the four faults of the dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).
He says "no" to that, [stating] "sādhyā... (the probandum, etc.).
Since [the point] is already established, this undertaking is for the purpose of restriction;
that is to say, the meaning is that the deficiency of either the probandum (*sādhya*) or the probans (*sādhana*) alone constitutes the refutation of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), and nothing else.
For instance:
To begin with, the deficiency of both [factors] need not be stated separately;
for since the example is already flawed by the deficiency of each one individually, the conception of them combined is redundant.
Otherwise, it would result in the abandonment of the position that the deficiency of each one individually constitutes a fault.

If it were stated as a separate [fallacy] merely by virtue of its occurrence, then another fallacious reason (hetvābhāsa) called "indefiniteness due to being past" (anaikāntika-kālātītatva) would have to be mentioned;
furthermore, "lack of a locus" (āśrayahīnatva) is equivalent to "unestablished locus" (āśrayāsiddhi).
It has already been explained in detail that there is no such thing as a "dissimilar instance" (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta).

Alternatively, one should understand that the deficiency of a corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*) regarding either the probandum (*sādhya*) or the probans (*sādhana*)—just like deviation (*vyabhicāra*)—is of two kinds according to either mode [of deficiency], and not of only one kind; for both types of deficiency are possible through misconception (*abhimāna*). Thus he says: "the probandum," etc.
The phrase "there is a fault even in one case" carries over [from the previous verse].
Some maintain that the presence of a redundant qualification (*vyarthaviśeṣaṇatva*) or a redundant qualificand (*vyarthaviśeṣyatva*) in a reason (*hetu*) is not a fault,
because it does not obstruct either the pervasion (*vyāpti*) or the property-of-the-subject (*pakṣadharmatā*).
He replies to them: "By means of a qualification."
When a qualification has been provided, the futility of either the qualificand or the qualification is indeed a defect of the reason (*hetu*).
For a qualification is introduced in a reason for the sake of its utility in establishing pervasion (*vyāpti*);
however, in the case of futility, since the qualified [subject] lacks pervasion, it is correct [to regard that as a defect].
Regarding "the state of being a fault of the reason" (*hetudoṣatva*):

alternatively, since it will be stated later that this includes "questions about what is already established" (*siddhapraśnādi*) and so forth, this is included within the category of "excess" (*ādhikya*).
In any case, the state of being a fault of the reason is established.

One should understand that useless qualification (*vyarthaviśeṣaṇatva*) and so forth are also of two kinds, according to either the [proponent's] or the [opponent's] way; they are not of only one kind. Thus he says: "In the case of a qualification... (*viśeṣaṇe*).
...in the case of a qualification, there would be futility... // Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.2.30bc //
The phrase "there is a refutation even in one case" carries over.

Some maintain that the non-establishment of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the non-establishment of the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) do not constitute a fault of the reason (*hetu*). For it is not the case that the reason consists of the qualifier alone or the qualificand alone, such that their non-establishment would be a refutation of the reason.
He replies to them with the words: "And when one [of the two] is established..."
And when one [of the two] is unestablished, there is indeed the non-establishment of the qualified [proposition]. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 3.2.30cd)
For a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*) is indeed the reason, not merely the qualifier and so forth.
It is well established that even if one of the two—the qualifier or the qualificand—is unestablished, the qualified entity itself remains unestablished;
for we observe the absence of a "man with a staff" when either the staff alone is absent or the man alone is absent.

Therefore, since the non-establishment of the qualified probans (*viśiṣṭahetvasiddhi*) is unavoidable even in cases such as the non-establishment of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇāsiddhi*), it is correct that this constitutes a defect of the probans.
Furthermore, that [non-establishment] is of two kinds according to either of the two ways [of qualification], as is already established from the previous discussion.

By stating "and when one [of the two] is absent" instead of "and when one is unestablished," the author intends to indicate that non-establishment (*asiddhi*) is twofold: by way of its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*) and by way of non-cognition (*ajñānataḥ*).

Thus, since it has been established that fallacies such as the "futile qualification" (*vyartha-viśeṣaṇa*) and the "unestablished" (*asiddha*) are indeed defects of the reason (*hetu-doṣa*), it is incorrect to state that among the varieties of *asiddha* enumerated by others, only the triad beginning with the "unestablished locus" (*āśrayāsiddha*) is not a defect. Furthermore, regarding the claim that there are four defects of the question (*praśna-doṣa*), it is improper to consider "futility" (*vaiphalya*) and "irrelevance" (*asaṅgati*) as defects, because they cannot be pointed out [as such].

For instance, when one employs the argument "Sound is impermanent because it is perceptible by the external sense organs of persons such as ourselves," the opponent asks, "Is the universal (sāmānya) permanent or impermanent?

In that case, if [the proponent] merely points out the futility [of the question], the opponent would defeat him through the fallacy of "reproaching what is not to be reproached" (*niranuyojyānuyoga*).

This is because, having accepted the permanence of the universal as being agreed upon by both parties, it is appropriate for the opponent to intend to point out the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) of the reason with respect to that [universal].
In that very context of the formal argument (*prayoga*), the opponent asks: "Is this [reason] a universal (*sāmānya*) that is inclusive (*anugata*), or not?

In that case, if one were to point out a lack of connection (*asaṅgati*), it would constitute an improper objection (*niranuyojyānuyoga*). For it is appropriate for the opponent to intend a connection characterized as an *upodghāta* (introduction), thinking: "Having established its permanence by means of its inclusiveness, I shall then state its inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) therein. Thus, even a connection in the form of an introduction is intended by the opponent as being suitable.
And since it is not the case that a refutation can be called such if it cannot be pointed out, he says: "uselessness" (aprayojanatā).
The lack of purpose [in that case] is the refutation of the first question.
In that regard, although the lack of purpose among the defects of a question may be difficult to ascertain in successive questions,
nevertheless, it can certainly be brought forward as a potential defect in the first question.
For such a question is not possible at the commencement of a discussion if it sets aside the inquiry into the primary subject matter (*prameya*).
By this very principle, it should be understood that even "inconsistency" (*asaṅgati*) must be pointed out only as the total non-perception of consistency.
[Objection: But if this were the case, the rule that there are only six points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) would be violated.

Even though self-contradiction (*svavyāhati*) and inconsistency (*asaṅgati*) are included within contradiction (*virodha*) and inconsistency (*asaṅgati*) respectively, [the faults of] having an established object (*siddhārthatā*) and being purposeless (*vaiphalya*) are distinct; therefore, he says: "siddha... [and so forth].
Whatever results from questions regarding the attainment of perfection and so forth, that shall fall within the range between the maximum and the minimum.

In the context of explaining how [other means of knowledge] are subsumed within [the three], in order to establish the previously stated restriction that there are exactly three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he states the subsumption of *arthāpatti* and the others—which are accepted by opponents as separate means of valid cognition—within those already mentioned:
"Presumption (*arthāpatti*), comparison (*upamā*), and non-existence (*abhāva*) are included within inference (*anumāna*)... (MAnu 3.2.32ab).
Presumption (*arthāpatti*) is the cognition of that which makes something possible, arising from the observation of what is otherwise impossible.
For example, from observing the absence of a living person from their home, there arises the cognition of their being outside.

In this case, what is meant by the "impossibility" of a living person's absence from home? Is it an absolute non-existence, or is it the impossibility of remaining [in the house] without being outside?
In the first case, would the perception of even coldness in fire— which arises from a fallacious inference— not cause one to understand some object at all?
If you say that such a perception is an error (*bhrānti*),
then how could the perception of the absence of a house, which is in every way impossible [in that location], not also be an error?
If it is argued that there is no proof for the coexistence of burning and coldness, we say no;
for even the absence of a house, which is in every way impossible [without its occupant], would likewise be unestablished.

In the second case, that very [absence] is the pervasion (vyāpti); thus, the cognition of the pervader arising from the perception of the pervaded is presumptive testimony (arthāpatti), which is nothing other than inference (anumāna).
If it is argued that there is an inconsistency because of a contradiction between two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), we say no; for such a contradiction does not exist in the present example.
Indeed, a contradiction would only arise if the statement "he lives" were to mean "he is in the house."
Alternatively, the statement "he is not in the house" would mean "he does not live," but that is not the case;
for no change of state is observed in the person himself.

For one who has been well-guarded and instructed by his parents and never goes out from his home, thinking others are likewise, concludes that the only purpose for the duration of life is the existence of beings within the house;
in that case, he would remain in doubt and would not ascertain the existence of anything outside.
Otherwise, one might even determine something by means of the "equal to the subject" (*prakaraṇasama*);
by this, the following [objection] is also refuted: as they have said—

Regarding the position that this is an inference (*anumāna*), is the probans (*liṅga*) merely being alive while outside, or merely the absence from the house, or rather the two combined as a qualified [probans]?
Neither the first nor the second [options] are tenable,
because of their deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
Not the third [alternative],
because the relationship of qualifier and qualified (viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva) between two contradictory things is untenable;
and because the cognition of non-contradiction occurs only after the conceptualization of external existence, which would result in the fallacy of mutual dependence (itaretarāśraya).
Because there is no contradiction between existence and non-existence, or because even if such a contradiction existed, presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) would still be untenable;
therefore, since it causes the cognition of an object by the force of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), presumptive testimony is nothing other than inference (*anumāna*). *9,153*

By this, the views that the purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekin*) and the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*) are merely presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) and not inference are also refuted.
Comparison (*upamāna*) is the cognition of similarity in a remembered object based on the observation of similarity in a perceived object whose counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is remembered.
For example, having experienced a cow and then gone to the forest, one perceives the similarity of a gavaya to a cow, and thereby cognizes the similarity of a cow to a gavaya.
Even if this were not a case of recollection, it is because the similarity residing in the cow has never been experienced— since its counter-correlate, the gavaya, was not previously perceived.
For an experience cannot be admitted to occur merely through the presence of a fit sensory contact when the causal totality (*sāmagrī*) is absent.
Through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is already established that the cognition of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is the cause for the perception of similarity.
Furthermore, the acceptance of an indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpaka-pratīti*) is simply without scriptural authority.
Nevertheless, because it functions as a means of knowledge by virtue of the pervasion (*vyāpti*)—"whatever is similar to X is similar to Y"—it is indeed an inference (*anumāna*).

If it is argued that this is not so because of a difference in substrata (*vyadhikaraṇatva*), we reply that this is not a fault, as has already been established; moreover, a common substratum (*ekādhikaraṇatā*) can easily be brought about.
Therefore, like the perception of dissimilarity, the perception of similarity is also not a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). (9.159)

Others, however, maintain that analogy (*upamāna*) is the recognition of the meaning of a previously heard analogical statement (*atideśavākya*) associated with the object currently perceived—this recognition being aided by the recollection of the name whose connection [to the object] was not previously understood.

Furthermore, the meaning of the analogical statement is threefold: in some cases it is similarity (*sādharmya*), in some cases dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), and in some cases mere common properties (*dharmamātra*).

For example, for one who has not yet learned the referent of the word "gavaya," there occurs through perception the recognition of the meaning experienced from the analogical statement, "A gavaya is similar to a cow."
Recalling the word "gavaya" upon perceiving a gavaya, one understands the connection of the word "gavaya" with that gavaya;
this is comparison based on similarity (*sādharmyopamāna*).

Comparison based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmyopamāna*), however, is the grasping of the connection of the word "horse" with the horse, resulting from the recognition of the meaning of the sentence: "A horse does not have two hooves, like a cow and so forth."

They maintain that the acquisition of the word-meaning occurs through the recognition of the sentence-meaning, such as "the animal possessing qualities like a long neck is a gavaya," even when the comparison is based solely on its properties (*dharmamātropamāna*).

In this regard, although the comprehension of the relationship between the name and the named cannot occur prior to the sight of the *gavaya* through the application of the analogical statement (*atideśavākya*) or by means of an indicative mark (*liṅga*) such as usage,
it is because the relationship cannot be understood so long as the related term (*sambandhin*) itself is not apprehended.
Nevertheless, it will occur through the very mark (*liṅga*) of similarity and so forth at a time subsequent to the perception of a gavaya and the like.
In this state, the sentence of instruction (*atideśavākya*) serves as the means for grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*).

For instance, just as it is accepted that for one who has heard that "earth is to be designated as such because of its connection with earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*), and who then perceives the connection with earth-ness in some substance, the comprehension of the relationship between the name and the named occurs through inference alone.
Likewise, since this is also the case here, how could this be a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?

Non-existence (*abhāva*) is the means of cognition that establishes the perception of an absence whose counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is an object suitable for the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of a jar or the like.
And since that has non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) as its defining characteristic, it is nothing other than an inferential mark (*liṅga*); thus, non-existence does not differ from inference.
Therefore, it is logical that there are only three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
To the question, "Is non-existence (*abhāva*) necessarily included within inference (*anumāna*? he says: "In some cases" (*kvacid*).
... in some cases, non-existence is included within direct perception ... // MAnu 3.2.32bc //
The meaning is that sometimes even perception (pratyakṣa) apprehends the absence of jars and so forth.
Why then [is it said that] the absence of all objects capable of being perceived is known through two means of valid cognition? To this he says: "of pleasure and so forth."
...and because of the necessity [of the experience] of pleasure and so forth. (MAnu 3.2.32d)
The meaning is as follows:
the non-existence of internal pleasure and so forth, which are cognizable by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*), must necessarily be grasped by the perception of the witness itself;
or rather, the term "non-existence" refers to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) itself.
The connection with "of that pleasure, etc. is through a mediated sequence.
The connection is with "is necessarily included within perception.
By this, it is stated that the non-existence of external objects such as jars, which are otherwise perceptible, is known through both perception and inference.
That is incorrect;

for it is impossible for a single cognition to be produced by two independent causes, and because it would result in the simultaneous acquisition of two mutually contradictory forms characterized as being both indirect (*parokṣa*) and direct (*aparokṣa*). Therefore, it is said: "in some cases" (*kvacit*).
Nevertheless, this remains untenable because there is no room for inference regarding an object that is apprehended by direct perception; therefore, he says: "Elsewhere."
Otherwise, he incurs the guilt of a Khaṭi offense... // MĀnuv 3.2.33a //

When there is a counter-positive such as a jar, distinct from pleasure and so forth, that absence which is immediately apprehended by the means of knowledge known as non-existence (abhāvapramāṇa) is perception (pratyakṣa).
As for the claim that "that which arises after a delay is inference," what is meant by this is as follows:

the Mīmāṃsakas maintain that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consisting of the non-perception of the perceptible (*yogyānupalabdhi*), which apprehends the absence of jars and the like, is indeed distinct [from perception].
The followers of the Sugata (Buddhists) maintain that this is indeed an inference based on the mark of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi-liṅgaka*).
However, both of these [positions] are untenable;
for one who possesses the recollection of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), the absence of a jar or the like in the ground before them is apprehended by perception itself.
Because it is being cognized;
because it is impossible for a cognition of absence—which conforms to the presence and absence of the sense organs—to be a result that is not perceptual;
and because its character as a direct manifestation is established by experience.
Furthermore, because there is no subverting evidence (bādhaka), it is illogical to assume that [the sense-faculty] is exhausted elsewhere;
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of having to postulate another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) even for the cognition of color and so forth.

This is because it would be impossible for something arising instantaneously—without the delay of perceiving a logical mark (liṅga) or recollecting its pervasion (vyāpti)—to be the fruit of inference.

Since a logical mark (*liṅga*) functions as a means of knowledge only when it is itself known, and since non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), being itself an absence, would lead to an infinite regress if it required another non-apprehension for its own cognition, [non-apprehension cannot be a separate means of knowledge].

[Objection: But surely, one who has gone elsewhere after not perceiving the absence of an elephant at a crossroads in the morning—due to the lack of recollection of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*)—and who later possesses the memory of the elephant, realizes, "There was no elephant at the crossroads this morning.
Since there is no scope for perception (*pratyakṣa*) in that case, one must admit that non-apprehension, characterized by such a definition, is a distinct means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Not so;
for even though non-existence (*abhāva*) is not perceptible there, it is accepted as being cognizable through inference based on the mark (*liṅga*) of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*),
and non-apprehension itself is inferable from the mark of the absence of memory.
Therefore, having meditated there for a moment, one realizes that "the elephant was not in the courtyard.
Nor is there an infinite regress, because even the absence of memory is inferable from another non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*).
Furthermore, regarding cognitions such as pleasure and so forth, which are grasped by the witness (*sākṣin*), their absence is invariably [known] through the witness-perception (*sākṣipratyakṣa*).

Regarding the phrase "because it is an object of knowledge" (*vedyatvāt*), one might ask: even so, since there exist means of valid cognition such as the introduction (*upakrama*), the conclusion (*upasaṃhāra*), repetition (*abhyāsa*), novelty (*apūrva*), result (*phala*), and explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), how can there be a restriction to those three [means]? To this he says: "The beginning and so forth... (*prārambhādyāśca*).
...and the methods beginning with the commencement [of the work]. // Manu 3.2.33b //
The "reasons" (*yuktayaḥ*) are the inferences (*anumānāni*).
To the question "Why?", he says: "Scriptural authority" (*āgama*).
All [inferences] have as their purpose the ascertainment of the meaning of scripture; they possess necessary pervasion.

The meaning is that all [cognitions], beginning with those arising from an undertaking, necessarily possess a pervasion (vyāpti)—such as the pervasion that "whatever is undertaken in a certain context must be established therein"—and they serve to determine the meaning of scripture only by depending upon such a pervasion; therefore, they are indeed *yukti*s (reasonings).
By this, their inclusion within *āgama* (scriptural authority) is also refuted.

The grammatical split (*yogavibhāga*) is as follows: "Upakrama" and the others are exclusively objects of verbal testimony (*āgama*), and are not [objects of] presumption (*arthāpatti*), analogy (*upamā*), or non-existence (*abhāva*).
He states that even for other means of knowledge such as the sentence (*vākya*), they are included within inference (*anumāna*), beginning with the word "sentence" (*vākyam*).
Sentence, context, position, and likewise title—these are the [criteria for determining meaning].

The meaning is that since even sentences (*vākya*) and so forth, being of such a nature, determine the meaning of scripture only by depending on pervasion (*vyāpti*), they are therefore nothing other than such forms of reasoning (*yukti*).

The division of the rules (*yogavibhāga*) is intended to indicate that among the *upakrama* and so forth, each subsequent one is stronger, whereas among the *vākya* and so forth, each preceding one is stronger.

[Objection: If the *upakrama* and so forth, as well as the *vākya* and so forth, are included within inference (*anumāna*), then how [is it said]: "The beginning (*upakrama*), the conclusion (*upasaṃhāra*), repetition (*abhyāsa*), novelty (*apūrvatā*), the fruit (*phala*),..."?

The separate mention of *arthavāda* and *upapatti* [alongside *liṅga*] in the statement, "And *liṅga*— consisting of *arthavāda* and *upapatti*— is for the determination of the intended meaning," is because these [the six criteria beginning with *upakrama*] are distinct from *upapatti*, which is synonymous with inference (*anumāna*).

Likewise, regarding the statement, "Direct assertion (śruti), indicative mark (liṅga), name (samākhyā), syntactical connection (vākya), and context (prakaraṇa) [are the means of proof]," since syntactical connection and the others are subordinate to the indicative mark (liṅga), he says: "like the Kurus and the Pāṇḍavas."
They are mentioned separately because they arise [as distinct groups], just like the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas;
for although the Pāṇḍavas are a subset of the Kurus, the expression “the seed of the lineage of the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas” is used in consideration of both the general and the particular.

The meaning is that, in such cases as "separate from the Kurus," a separate mention is appropriate because their [the six means of knowledge's] commencement and so forth, as well as sentences and so forth, are justified even when they function as inference (*anumāna*), due to the presence of inferential marks (*liṅga*).

Now, if it is argued that even so, the omen of birds (*śākuna*), script (*lipi*), letters (*akṣara*), gestures (*ceṣṭā*), probability (*sambhava*), tradition (*aitihya*), and elimination (*pariśeṣa*) exist as separate means of knowledge—[we reply:
no, for the inclusion of omens of birds, scripts, letters, and gestures has already been indicated in the *Vilakṣaṇādhikaraṇa*.
This is because all disputants agree that possibility (*sambhava*) and tradition (*aitihya*) are included within inference (*anumāna*) and scripture (*āgama*), respectively;
and because the status of remainder (*pariśeṣa*) as inference is established by the very statement: "Remainder is mutual proof" (*pariśeṣo mithaḥ siddhiḥ*). *9,168*
But even so, do not the Jains assert that *tarka* (reasoning) is a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?
True;
however, it has already been indicated by such statements as "establishment through mutual dependence" (*mithas-siddhi*) that this too is included within inference (*anumāna*).
Here an objection is raised: reasoning (*tarka*) is not indeed a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). How, then, can there be inference (*anumāna*)?
For it is as follows:
Tarka is the adducing of an undesirable consequence.
And the undesirable is twofold:
