for it has been stated that once one accepts liberation characterized by abiding in the non-dual Brahman, the loss of its validity is equal whether it concerns the non-sublation of the authority of scripture by the authority of perception, or [the non-sublation of the authority of scripture itself].
Now, however, intending to show that this very [position] is untenable, he asks: "Is it a cognition of falsity?"
Tell me, why is there pride regarding false views, yet no pride even regarding liberation? MĀnuv 3.2.58ab

The meaning is that the means of knowledge—whether it be scripture (*āgama*) or inference (*anumāna*)—which establishes the falsity of the entire universe, remains a means of knowledge even regarding liberation (*mokṣa*); thus, its validity is of a nature that is uncontradicted even at the time of liberation. "Not so" means that its validity is of a nature that is contradicted.
The interrogative particle *kiṃ* is connected both with what precedes and with what follows.
Alternatively, this question—"Is it by intonation alone that there is authority?"—is to be understood as follows.
This is the answer to what was asked: "Let it be stated.
He states the fault in the first case: "In the state of being authoritative... (*mānatve*) // 9.256 //
If it were a state of being honored, there would be a loss of non-duality... // MAnu 3.2.58c //

In the view that validity consists in having an uncontradicted nature, there would be a loss of non-duality because [the scripture] would have a second entity (itself); thus, liberation characterized as previously described would not be established. Regarding the second case, he states the refutation: "Even if it were invalid," etc.
... even in the state of being honored, there is no liberation.
The phrase "non-liberation" refers to the intended state [of bondage];
even under the view that the cognition of the falsity of the universe and its validity are themselves sublated, liberation is not established.
To the question "How so?", he says: "Of the universe... [and so forth].
When false pride no longer exists, there is the re-attainment of the universe.
When the cognition of the falsity of the universe does not possess a validity whose nature is sublated, then the universe would necessarily reappear;
for the sublation by a valid cognition of non-existence is invariably concomitant with existence.
And if the universe were to exist, how could there be liberation characterized as previously described?
First of all, the universe is apprehended through direct perception;
that is then temporarily set aside by means of scripture (*āgama*) and so forth.
When scripture and the like are sublated, it falls back into view once more; thus, the word "again" (*punar*) is used with reference to this cognition.
If it is argued that both the universe and its sublater are themselves sublated, we say no,
because this will be refuted later.
Furthermore, is liberation existent or non-existent?
In neither of the two positions is liberation, as defined above, established.
How so?
Regarding the first position, he says: "If it exists..."
If there were a state of liberation, it would entail the consequence of duality... // MAnu 3.2.59cd //
Liberation is indeed the very nature of the self;
as it has been said:
"The self itself is the destruction of ignorance."
And it is said: "Liberation is the subsiding of ignorance.
How, then, could there be the consequence of duality? To this, it is stated: "the state of liberation.
This is merely a state of the Self; it is not the Self itself.
For if that were the case, since it would already be established beforehand, effort would be futile.
Nor can the Self be something to be accomplished by knowledge, because it is beginningless.
If it is argued that [liberation] is not established beforehand but is to be accomplished by knowledge as characterized by the destruction of ignorance (*avidyā*), then is that itself liberation?
If you say "it exists," then, because there is no sentient being to be liberated, it would be illogical to say that liberation exists.
Furthermore, liberation is a phenomenon (dharma).
"How could he be the self itself?"—thus [the author] refutes the second [position] by stating: "and other than this" (*ato 'nyaśca*). ... "otherwise than this" (*ato 'nyathā*).
...the state of being unreleased.
From one state of being a sentient being to another state:
if liberation were non-existent, then the self would be in a state of non-liberation;
for when horns are absent, a rabbit is indeed seen to be hornless.
And if that were so, how could it possess the previously stated definition?
Now, suppose it is thought: liberation is neither existent nor non-existent, but rather indeterminable (anirvacanīya).
Even then, it remains indeed unliberated (or rather, it is simply illogical).
For even within saṃsāra, being accompanied by a second [entity] occurs only through that which is inexpressible.
If that [inexpressible state] were to persist even after that [liberation], how could there not be a lack of liberation?
By this, even the fifth alternative is refuted,
because it does not avoid the problem of indefinability (*anirvacanīyatva*).
For the state of being situated in a fourth alternative is not itself indefinability.
If that were the case, it would result in the predicament of being indefinable (*anirvacanīyatā*).
If you ask, "How could the cessation of indefinable ignorance (*avidyā*) itself be indefinable?
know that it is just like the destruction of a jar (*ghaṭapradhvaṃsa*).
To summarize this, it was stated as "otherwise" (*anyathā*).
Had it not been so, he would have said "if it were otherwise" (*anyathā satī cet*).

In this very manner, in order to refute the view that liberation consists in abiding in the non-dual state of Brahman, he states—after having also considered the alternative regarding time—that a fault must be pointed out: "likewise, [if] time."
... likewise at the proper time ... // Mānava-dharmaśāstra 3.2.60a //
Now, one might object: let there be the criticism that, having raised the dilemma of whether time exists or not in the state of liberation, "if it exists, there is the consequence of duality";
therefore, liberation must be otherwise.
To the question, "In what way, then, is there an extension [of the rule]? he says: "For [the results] are dependent on time."
For liberation indeed depends upon time.

The meaning of the word "hi" (for) is that liberation is necessarily dependent on time and has time as its locus, because of the pervasion (vyāpti) that whatever is a real entity must be connected with time. Not only is this rule regarding liberation having time as its locus established by inference, but it is also stated in scripture: "Then the wise one... and "...having seen Him alone, he is liberated."
He says "it is established by scripture as well" and states: "time alone."

"Time alone also declares liberation... (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.2.60cd). [Question: What follows from this, if liberation is thus pervaded by both the legal case (*adhikaraṇa*) and time? To this, he says: "Time," etc.
...in the cessation of time, there would also be the cessation of liberation... // Mānava-dharmaśāstra 3.2.60cd //
If time were non-existent, liberation would also be non-existent,
because when the pervader is absent, the absence of the pervaded is necessary;
thus, the extension [of this principle] is logical.
This is what is meant:
if liberation were not related to time, it would follow that it is non-existent, like the horn of a hare and so forth.
But is it not said: "Neither one desiring liberation nor one liberated—this is the ultimate reality"?
Thus, since the non-existence of liberation is accepted, the undesirable consequence [of liberation being a mere negation] does not arise; therefore, he says: "the state of being in saṃsāra."
... therefore, there would be the state of being subject to saṃsāra.

If liberation, characterized by the absence of bondage, does not exist for that which is sentient, then even one considered liberated—like Devadatta—would still be subject to transmigratory existence (*saṃsāritva*).

If it is argued that because bondage is false, neither *saṃsāra* nor liberation exist at all, we reply: no; what constitutes an "undesirable" position is not merely its non-acceptance, but rather its lack of scriptural authority (*aprāmāṇikatva*) and so forth.
Furthermore, it has already been stated previously that the falsity of bondage is not supported by valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*).
Thus, by refuting the weakness of perception from the standpoint of scripture and so forth, its strength has been demonstrated under that very pretext;

for it has been indicated that perception as witness is the basis upon which the validity of scripture and other means of knowledge depends, while the validity of everything else is determined by the witness-perception.

Therefore, it is logical that the scripture and other means of knowledge which contradict it are themselves invalid. Intending to show that perception is not only stronger than others due to qualities such as being self-sustaining (*upajīvyatva*), but is also stronger by its very nature, he says: "And where... (*kva ca*) [verse 9.264].
And where [is there] that which is obtained through direct perception and remains uncontradicted by inference or scripture? (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 2.61ab)
"Obtained through direct perception" means established by immediate realization (*sākṣātkāra*).
The terms "inference" (*anumāna*) and "scripture" (*āgama*) denote the inferential mark (*liṅga*) and the verbal expression (*vacana*), respectively,
because the determination of their validity is being undertaken at this point.
The word "seen" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].

For if we had observed that something established by direct perception (pratyakṣa) was sublated in some instance by inference (anumāna) or scripture (āgama), then we would understand the weakness of direct perception relative to inference and the rest.
But it is not so.

If it is argued that the perception apprehending defects in God is seen to be sublated by scripture (*āgama*) and other means of knowledge, this is true; however, we shall explain later that in such cases, scripture and the like possess the power of sublation because they are the very basis upon which perception depends.
"There is an inherent superiority of scripture alone among those three [means of knowledge],"—

since this statement refers to Vedic matters and since the phenomenal world consisting of earth and so forth is the subject under discussion here, there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the inference of coldness in fire is observed [to be sublated].

And because a statement such as "an elephant is trumpeting, having entered my ear" is sublated by perception (*pratyakṣabādhitatvāt*). If it is argued that even in that case, perception is the sublater because it is that upon which [the inference] depends, and not by its own nature, we say no; for the perception that apprehends the heat of fire and so forth lacks the capacity to grasp the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between a pervader and a pervaded that resides in the subject (*dharmin*).
If it is argued that "non-heat" is the absence of heat,

and that its cognition is dependent upon the cognition of its counter-positive (pratiyogin)— and since that counter-positive, heat, must be perceived directly in fire alone, [fire] possesses the status of being the necessary basis (upajīvyatva) for such an absence— this is not so, because the answer to this has already been stated.
This [objection] has been established as a refutation in the case of proving "non-heat";
however, there is no room for it when coldness is being proved by some reason. And when the non-heat of the entire mass of fire is what is to be proved, then let this demonstration stand.
However, if one takes "fire" alone as the subject of the proposition (*pakṣa*), this [inference] is not applicable;

for after perceiving heat through touch in solar and other forms of light, and then perceiving fire with the eye, the attempt to prove the absence of heat in that fire is sublated by perception itself, which is powerful by its very nature—this is the general direction [of the argument]. Although the body's status as the self is established by perception, it is negated by such inferences as "the body is not the self because it is composed of the elements (*bhūta*) and is an effect, like a pot," and by the scriptural injunction: "one should draw him out from one's own body."
Thus, [the view that the body is the self] is seen to be contradicted by scripture;
otherwise, in the absence of any other sublater, it would follow that the identity of the body with the self is real.
To the question "How is this so?", he says: "The identity of the body with the self..."
If the body were the self...
If one were to say that the identity of the body with the self, though established by perception, is seen to be sublated by inference and scripture, then we reply: "That is not so.
The phrase "that is not so" is connected both with what precedes and with what follows.
To the question "Why is it not so?", he says: "That is not so."
...that has never been attained through direct perception anywhere.
The identity of the body with the self is not something established by perception;
therefore, this is not an example for the claim that what is established by perception can be sublated by inference and other means.
This is the intended meaning.

There is no cognition whatsoever of the body as the self that is sublated by inference and other means; nor is such a cognition produced by the senses even for those nihilists and others who hold that it exists.
However, it arises only from fallacious inference and scripture;
let there be no such cognition of the body as the self for those who possess the appearance of scholars,
yet it certainly exists for common folk.
Thinking that "this very [instance] will serve as our example," he says "somewhere" (*kvacit*).
He establishes that point with the words "mine" (*mama*).
For the cognition "this is my body" is indeed valid, whereas the cognition "I am the body" is not.
For every living being, there is indeed the valid cognition and perception that "this is my body," but never the thought "I am the body.
Alternatively, because for everyone the valid cognition and correct perception that "this is my body" persists at all times, the notion "I am the body" finds no opportunity to arise.

Even in the absence of the cognition that the body is the self, there certainly exists the cognition that the attributes of the body, such as blackness and so forth, reside in the self; for we observe the common usage, "I am black," and so on. And since this [cognition], arising without depending on an inferential mark (liṅga) or the like, is produced by perception alone and is subsequently sublated by inference and other means, it will serve as the illustrative example. Therefore, he says: "And [it is] figurative" (upacāraśca).
And the metaphorical designation "I am Kṛṣṇa" ... // MAnu 3.2.62ab //
The phrase "the cognition 'I am black' does not exist" continues [from the previous context].
How, then, is there linguistic usage?
The construction is that linguistic usage such as "I am black" is merely a metaphorical designation (*upacāra*).

Anticipating that one who, by the force of conventional usage, might even infer such a cognition [of reality] for this [world] would fall into the fault of inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatva), he states an example regarding the point already explained: "kardama... (mud...).
...as in the case of a garment smeared with mud, so it would be [in this case]. (Manu 3.2.62ab) ... (Manu 3.2.62c) *9,272*
Just as when mud is smeared upon a cloth, there occurs the conventional usage of the expression "the black cloth," so too it would be in the present case.
This is the underlying intention:
for one who correctly understands both the whiteness of the cloth and the smearing of mud, there is no perception of blackness in the cloth itself.
And one employs the conventional expression "black cloth.
Therefore, the inference of such a cognition from the conventional usage "I am black" is fallacious.
If it is argued that this is merely a figurative usage (*upacāra*), [we reply:]...
"Why should it not be the same in the case of the primary meaning (*prakṛta*) as well? [Objection:

"But surely 'the black cloth' is not a metaphorical usage (*upacāra*), because even though the cloth is white by its own nature, the cognition [of blackness] is possible due to the presence of blackness caused by the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of mud. [Response: This is not so.
What is this so-called "conditionality" (aupādhikatva)?

If it is argued that it is something superimposed—due to the proximity of mud, for instance—upon what is intended as the probans (sādhana), just like the pervasion (vyāpti) [is superimposed], we say no; for it has already been stated that such a superimposition is impossible.
If it is argued that redness is reflected in the crystal due to the proximity of a hibiscus flower, we say no;
for the cloth is not transparent,
unlike the scent of saffron [which is perceived] through ghee and the like.
If it is argued that [the cloth] is manifested by the mud, we say no;
for there is no evidence that blackness existed in the cloth prior [to its contact with the mud].

Alternatively, if it is thought that [the blackness] was produced by the adjunct of the mud—just as color and other qualities are produced in an earthy substance through contact with fire—[we respond as follows:]
In this regard, we ask: does the mud, having set aside the whiteness, produce blackness in the cloth, or without setting it aside?
Not the first.
For if the blackness were removed, it would follow that whiteness could not be perceived;
yet whiteness does not arise anew,
because its cause is absent.

Not the second [alternative], because it is contradictory for two forms to occupy the same locus simultaneously; furthermore, since even that which is adventitious is real, it is no different from that which is intrinsic. *9,274*
Or, let it be granted that the blackness in a cloth is somehow adventitious; nevertheless, what is sought by adducing that example?

Nor is the aforementioned fallacy of deviation (vyabhicāra) avoided, because even if one instance of deviation is refuted, many other examples of deviation remain possible, such as "the beds are crying out" (mañcāḥ krośanti).

Now, if it is intended to suggest the possibility of such a perception—that there exists a blackness produced in the self by the limiting adjunct of the body, just as dirt on a cloth—he says: "If... (yadīti).
...if it is produced by limiting conditions (upādhi), then...

If it is possible to conceive of the perception that there is blackness in the self caused by the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the body—just as [blackness] exists in a cloth—then this is not an example for the principle that what is perceived through direct perception (pratyakṣa) can be sublated by inference (anumāna) and so forth;
such is the remainder [of the argument].
To the question "How so?", he says: "By itself" (svataḥ).
Just as whiteness exists inherently [in a conch], so too is blackness perceived as "not mine."
In this case, by the mention of a single part of both the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*), other points are also implied.
Thus, the meaning is as follows:
indeed, the blackness in a cloth is caused by an external condition (*aupādhika*), namely mud.
It should be understood in this way as it is being perceived:
"This cloth is indeed white, not black;
its blackness is produced by an adventitious condition."
Likewise, here too, one must accept that I am inherently formless; blackness, however, does not belong to me by nature,
but is perceived as being produced by the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the body.
And thus, because this cognition is in accordance with reality (*yathārtha*), it cannot be sublated by inference (*anumāna*) or other means of knowledge.
As for what was stated—that there is no cognition of the body as the self because one does not experience the cognition "I am the body"—that is incorrect;
for the very cognition "I" is itself that cognition [of the body as the self].
For the *ahaṅkāra* has as its core this very thing, which possesses such-and-such a form.
As for what was said— that because the perception of difference persists in the thought "my body," the appearance of the body as the self is untenable— [that is incorrect].
That is incorrect, because there is no recognition of a difference [between them];
for the conventional usage "this is my body" is appropriately understood as figurative, just like the expression "this is my own nature."
Indeed, the cognition of selfhood does not pertain to the body alone;
rather, it pertains to the aggregate consisting of the body, the sense organs, the internal organ, and so forth.
In that case, with respect to the aggregate, even the cognition of a connection with the body alone does not constitute a sublation.
It is like the pillar of a temple or the branch of a tree.

Furthermore, there is no clear means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the manifestation of a difference between the body, the sense organs, and so forth, on one hand, and the self (*ātman*), on the other.
By this, the notion of the body and so forth as the self would be contradicted.
As for what was also stated— that there is no cognition of attributes belonging to the body and so forth, such as "I am dark," as residing in the self because of a lack of proof—
that is not correct.
Because we observe the conventional usage "I am Kṛṣṇa," it is established as a general rule that such usage is rooted in knowledge; however,
when that [rootedness in knowledge] is untenable, one must assume it is figurative.
Furthermore, there is no cognition in the form "I am not Kṛṣṇa" and so forth,
out of fear of which we might postulate that [the former] is merely figurative.
Therefore, since there is an absence of any cognition of difference and the like, both types of cognition indeed exist.
As he said:
"Having superimposed upon one another the nature of each other and the attributes of each other.
(*9,278*) Since this cognition is born of perception, how could there be a sublation by inference or other means of what is established by perception? To this, he says: "And how? (*kathaṃ ca*).
And how is it that the distinction between the body and so forth and the self is not perceived?
By the word "distinction" (bheda), non-association is also included;
by the words "body and so forth," the aggregate and its attributes are meant.
When the ablative case is used in "from the body and so forth" (dehādeḥ), then the genitive case is used in "of the self" (ātmanaḥ).
And when "ātmanaḥ" is used in the ablative (pañcamī), then "dehādeḥ" is used in the genitive (ṣaṣṭhī);
for the opponent has stated that there is mutual superimposition.
The meaning is that the mutual difference between the aggregate of the body and so forth and the self, as well as the non-connection between their respective attributes, is indeed perceived.
To the question "How so?", he says: "As soon as they were born."
As soon as they are born, deer, cattle, elephants, birds,
and wild beasts recognize the causes of fear, safety, their own sustenance, and so forth.
They were simply born; they did not perform any other activity.
"Enjoyment" (*bhoga*) refers to pleasure (*sukha*);
by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), suffering (*duḥkha*) is included.
Lions, tigers, and the like are causes of fear;
mothers and the like are causes of fearlessness; and suckling at the breast and the like are causes of pleasure.
They recognize that scratching inside the eyes with a fingernail and so forth are causes of suffering;
for this very reason, they flee at the mere sound of a lion or similar creature,
and they approach their mother and others.
They engage in activities such as suckling at the breast and avoid actions such as scratching with their fingernails.
To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "In the absence of memory. (*9,279*)
In the absence of memory of one's previous body, how could that consciousness possibly exist?
That cognition is the cognition that "this is the cause of fear and so forth.
To the question, "If there is no recollection of a previous body, how could that cognition not exist? he says: "By way of positive concomitance" (*anvaya*).
"In the case of the forgetting of the investigation of positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*), etc."—
by the word "etc.," the inclusion of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the subject (*dharmī*) is intended; alternatively, by the mention of "etc.," oral instruction (*upadeśa*) is included.
The connection is with "in the case of forgetting the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) and so forth.
It is not merely this much;
rather, the connection is with the thought, "If there is also forgetting of the synthesis (*anusandhāna*) that 'this is thus,' how could that cognition arise?"
This is what is meant:
there is indeed the engagement of deer and other animals in activities such as suckling at the udder, and their withdrawal from activities such as scratching with their horns;
therefore, it is inferred that desire and aversion exist in them in those instances.
This is because, in cases such as our own, attachment and aversion have been determined to be the very causes of activity;
furthermore, from attachment and aversion arises the cognition that something is a means to what is desired or undesired,
since it is precisely that [cognition] which is established as the cause of attachment and the rest.
Moreover, that knowledge is not to be established by perception,
because the relationship between cause and effect is beyond the reach of the senses;
rather, it is to be established solely through inference and authoritative instruction.
Furthermore, instruction is not possible for deer and the like,
because they lack the requisite capacity;
therefore, it must be said that such instruction occurred in a previous life.
Nor can it be that he [the infant] does not remember this, for its cause [is memory]; therefore, the existence of such memory must be admitted.
Or else, there is inference:
whatever is the drinking of breast-milk is a means for achieving a desired end.
Whatever is not a means for achieving what is desired is not breast-feeding,
as in the case of a mouth; yet this [act] is breast-feeding, even without the recollection of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and so forth.
Furthermore, memory does not arise with respect to what has not been experienced,
and in this present life there is no experience of [past] continuity and so forth,
because it has already been stated that [beings] are born [with such memories] immediately upon birth.
Therefore, one must accept the recollection of the lineage and so forth experienced in other births.
Since the recollection of the instructions and the lineage from a previous existence [is possible], the recollection of the previous body must also be admitted,
as they share the same logical status.
If deer and other animals did not possess the memory of previous bodies, then, being no different from them, they would likewise lack the memory of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and so forth.
In the absence of that [memory], due to the non-existence of inference and other means of knowledge, the cognition of the cause of what is desired and what is undesired would not arise.
And if that [cognition] does not arise, because of the non-arising of passion and the like, there would be no arising of purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*) and so forth.
Because the absence of an effect is easily established when there is an absence of its cause.
If it is argued that activity and so forth occur by the power of the unseen (adṛṣṭa), we say no; for that would entail the fault of overriding what is directly perceived.
The utility of the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) is precisely this: that one remembers all that was experienced in other births, yet remembers only this much.
If it is argued that activities and so forth may occur by chance (*yādṛcchika*), we say no;
for such a thing is impossible given the infinity [of past experiences].
For this very reason, there is the plural number in "deer" (*mṛgāḥ*) and so forth.
Let it be that this is the inherent nature of the genus (*jāti*). No;
for they are perceived even when belonging to different genera.
For this very reason, it was stated that "deer, cows," and so forth;
moreover, the fault of contradicting what is observed cannot be avoided.
Therefore, deer and others do possess the recollection of their previous bodies.
In the same way, it is established that this applies to humans and others as well.
Nevertheless, to the question "What is the subject at hand? he says: "When... (*yadā*).
When there is knowledge of another body, how can there be the conviction that it is one and the same body?

When, in this manner, one who dwells in this body realizes that not only is there this present body, but that another existed prior to it— such recollection of other bodies being established through valid cognition (pramāṇa)—
then how could there be the determination of identity between oneself and this current body?

However, for one who perceives the Self as threaded through many bodies—just as a single thread is woven through many gems—it is logical that there is an ascertainment of its absolute difference from them.
And thus, the cognition of the non-connection of blackness and other qualities [with the Self] is also well-established;
for the opponent admits that such superimposition is based on the superimposition of the body and so forth upon the Self.
It has already been stated that the notion of "I" (ahaṃpratyaya) is not a superimposition;
therefore, the notion "this body is mine" is not to be subverted, and expressions such as "I am dark" must be accepted as figurative usages.
This might be so.
Metaphorical usage is not obtained merely from the impossibility of the primary meaning;
rather, it occurs when there is similarity, a relationship, or a purpose.
And here, no such similarity or the like exists.
How then is this a mere figurative expression?

Furthermore, if animals such as deer, commoners, and even humans possessed the knowledge that the body and the self are distinct, how could ancient usages found in the Purāṇas and other texts— such as "This [body] is not 'mine' or 'I', but food for dogs and jackals"— be consistent?
And how would the teachings intended for the discrimination between the body and the self not be rendered purposeless?
When there is knowledge of the distinction between the body and the self, attachment and aversion toward objects that are respectively favorable or unfavorable to the body would no longer arise;
consequently, transmigration would not occur. Therefore, he says: "Because of its pervasiveness. (9.285)
Because the self pervades the body, yet lacks proficiency in worldly activities, [it is not the agent]. (Manu 3.2.65cd)
And even when there is knowledge of their distinction, as in the case of charcoal and fire, worldly transactions proceed as if they were not distinct from themselves... [MAnu 3.2.66a-c]
In the phrase "even when there is ignorance of difference," the word "ca" (and) is connected with "and because of lack of proficiency in worldly transactions.
The expression "like charcoal and fire" means "as in the case of fire pervaded by charcoal."
The meaning is: "just as [it is] with that which is not distinct from itself, that which is non-different from itself, and that which is conjoined with itself.
The word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and conventional usages" (*vyavahārāśca*) has the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned.
[This refers to] the self (in the body).

By the statement, "Because [the one] is pervaded [by the other], worldly transactions (*vyavahāra*) occur as if [the object] were not distinct from itself," the relationship characterized by similarity—namely, being a part of the same whole—is also expressed. To the question, "Even when there is cognition of difference, what is the purpose of acting as if there were no difference? the answer is that even when there is cognition of difference, because people are unskilled in their worldly transactions, they act as if [the object] were not distinct from itself. To the question, "Even when there is cognition of difference, what is the purpose of acting as if [the object] were not distinct from itself? the answer is that even when there is cognition of difference... [the answer is that] in the cognitions of worldly people, because they are unskilled in their transactions, [they act as if there were no difference]. (Note: The final sentence fragment appears to repeat the previous point regarding the lack of skill in transactional usage.)

Even so, because people lack proficiency in worldly transactions, their dealings appear as if they were non-distinct from their own [true nature]. People do not conduct themselves in that way for the sake of some specific purpose;
rather, it is simply due to a lack of proficiency in distinct transactions.
The reason for the lack of proficiency [in discerning the Self] is that the Self pervades the body;
and with the intention that these conventional usages are so firmly established (*rūḍhatva*) that they do not depend on a specific purpose, it is said: "like charcoal and fire.

Even though there is knowledge of their difference, because the Self pervades the body—just like fire in charcoal—and because people lack proficiency in worldly transactions due to an inability to perceive them as utterly distinct, the conventions of the Purāṇas and other texts appear as if inseparable from themselves.
The intention is that those worldly transactions occur precisely because of a desire to express the absence of clear discernment (*viveka*).
For this very reason, the meaningfulness of the teachings intended for the sake of discernment is established;
indeed, it is clear discernment that serves the purpose of human life, not innate [ignorance].

Because the self pervades the body and is the ultimate object of affection, it is indeed logical that attachment and other such emotions arise. Now, one might object: "Surely knowledge alone is the cause of worldly activity; if that [knowledge] exists, how then can there be incompetence in worldly affairs? To this, he says: "Not so" (*na hi*).
For people in the world are not capable of explaining objects— even those perceived through direct perception— exactly as they are experienced. (3.66d–67c)
"According to experience" means in accordance with one's own experience, for the purpose of explaining or communicating [to others].

It is established by experience that even though parents and others perceive the absolute distinction between twins, when asked, "How are these two to be understood as distinct?", they are unable to explain it to others in this way based on their own direct perception and experience.

What indeed is the point of this inquiry? If it is argued that extreme similarity (*atyantasādṛśya*) is the obstacle there, then in this case as well, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the self throughout the body—like charcoal and fire—is already stated to be the obstacle.

With the intention of showing that the sublation (*bādha*) of perceptions such as silver in a mother-of-pearl shell by means of inference and so forth does not exist, he says: “And where is [the object] obtained through perception? (*kva ca pratyakṣataḥ prāptam*).
He concludes what was stated in the passage beginning with "ityādi" by saying: "tato hi" (for from that).
For that is established by direct perception, and not by anything else.
It is possible to restrain [them] anywhere...

The meaning is as follows: in some cases there is simply an absence of cognition; in some cases, although cognition exists, it is not produced by perception; in some cases, although there is perceptual cognition, it is not true to reality; and in some cases, even if it is not true to reality, it is sublated by a more powerful perception. It is for this very reason that the word "kvāpi" (in some cases) was used.
"By another" means by something other than scripture (*āgama*) and so forth that does not serve as a basis for reliance.
Thus, in this way, the fallacious forms of inference and scripture are indeed contradicted by perception (*pratyakṣa*), which is inherently powerful. *9,289*
Let it be that direct perception is more powerful than scripture and so forth, or let it not; nevertheless, there is no contradiction between them,
because their objects are distinct.
For instance,
scripture and the like indeed establish the sublation of future [cognitions], but not those of the present;
and it is precisely that [future cognition] which is to be understood by the term "false" and so forth.
And there would be a contradiction with perception for that [proposition] only if perception were to reject the sublation of the universe even in the future;
but it is not so.
Since that [perception] grasps only the present, it would exclude even the future sublation of the universe;
yet this is not the case,
because, by grasping only the present, it lacks the capacity to apprehend the absence of future sublation.
As it has been said:

"That which is connected [with the senses] and present is apprehended by the eye and the other [faculties]. Even when there is the apprehension of the absence of sublation at the present time, there is no contradiction.
Furthermore, there is no contradiction between two cognitions that have different objects;

for if that were the case, there would be a contradiction between the perception grasping the absence of a jar at this moment and the scriptural testimony (āgama) stating "the jar will exist. To this, it is replied:
First of all, it is a point of agreement even for the opponent that perception reveals the absence of sublation (bādhābhāva) pertaining to the present time.

Furthermore, since scriptural authority (*āgama*)—in forms such as "here there is no diversity"—establishes the sublation of the universe as occurring precisely in the present, how could it not be contradicted by perception?
Or, even if scripture and the like were to indicate sublation in the future, sublation nonetheless consists in the negation of existence across the three periods of time.

And since that [non-existence] is indeed contradicted by perception, which grasps existence at the present time, how could there not be a contradiction with perception for the scripture or other means of knowledge that propound it?
By this, the claim that "our own perception is capable of refuting sublation only when it pertains to ourselves, but not when it pertains to another person" is rejected;
for a sublation consisting in the negation of the existence of a jar or the like must necessarily be in contradiction with the perception that grasps its existence. (9.293)
Thus, even if perception grasps only the present, the contradiction between that [perception] and scripture and so forth is indeed difficult to avoid.

Nevertheless, with the intention that the actual state of things must be stated when such a contingency arises, the author begins the subsequent section to refute the restriction that perception grasps only the present; first, he refutes that restriction regarding the perception of a witness, stating: "If that... and so on.
If that [object] does not fall within the range of the subsequent cognition,
how can it be understood that the subsequent time and liberation belong to its domain?
"It is understood" is to be connected with what is about to be said.

By the word "that," the venerable author of the Bhāṣya refers specifically to the witness of the particular object of perception; since the word "if" (cet) is heard, the word "then" (tarhi) must be supplied.
[The phrase] "not within the scope of a subsequent [cognition]" means:
The meaning is that its object is exclusively the present;
the sense is that other means of valid cognition have already been refuted.
In the word "subsequent" (*uttara*), the past is also implied.
Even for those who maintain that time is entirely indivisible, they must necessarily admit a distinction based on limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*);
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that all verbal suffixes would have a single identical meaning.
Therefore, there exists a subsequent time, whether it be intrinsic (*svābhāvika*) or adventitious (*aupādhika*).
"Do not enter [into this] now; the later time has come. To the question "What is lost? What is destroyed? he says: "That which belongs to it" (tadga).

The phrase "how indeed" (kathameva) continues [from the previous context], and its meaning is "when not understood at a later time. It is "comprehended" (gamyate), that is, it is understood (avagamyate).
The reason the past is not explicitly mentioned here is that some do not accept the existence of liberation in the past;
since liberation is not understood as being connected to it when the subsequent time is not understood, liberation itself is likewise not understood,
for it is well known that when a qualifier is not understood, that which is qualified by it cannot be understood.
Furthermore, in the absence of the understanding that "liberation will come to pass," there would be no effort for its sake;
nor would there be the thought, "In liberation, the sublation of everything will occur. [Objection:
The realization that Śuka, Vāmadeva, and others were liberated through knowledge, and that "I too shall be liberated," will arise from scripture (*āgama*) alone.
To the question, "Why [is this so] here, given that witnesses have as their object things past and future? he says: "Scripture (āgama) also..."
For even scripture, once the general principle has been established through perception, can indeed lead to the understanding of a specific detail... Mānava-dharmaśāstra 3.2.69a-c.
This indeed is the established position regarding scripture:
that [the relationship] in a generality— that is, in a collection of objects possessing a common nature—
is [established] through perception or by another means of valid cognition.
Once [the general meaning] has been established,
it subsequently causes one to understand that very same collection of word-meanings as possessing a specific qualification— that is, as having a particular positive concomitance—
but it does not cause one to understand the individual word-meanings themselves.
The meaning of the word "hi" (for) is that such is seen in cases such as, "There are five fruits on the bank of the river.
To the question, "What [is established] prior to the establishment of the referents (*padārtha*)?", he says: "How? (*katham*).
... otherwise, how could there be the apprehension of the word's power? (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 3.2.69d)
If word-meanings were not already established prior [to the use of words], then there could be no apprehension of the expressive power (*vācakatva-śakti*) of words with respect to them;
for it is impossible to apprehend a power whose object is unknown.
Indeed, one who does not know wood cannot know the axe’s power to cut it. (9.296)

Granted that the knowledge of word-meanings is necessary for the apprehension of the power (śakti) of words; but for what purpose, then, is the apprehension of power itself? To this, he says: "atīta... [and so forth].

Once the apprehension of the word's capacity has arisen regarding past and future objects, a sentence may convey every particularity; it cannot do so for one who has not yet apprehended that capacity.
Here, the mention of the past and the future refers to what is under discussion.

Indeed, even an entire sentence can convey a specific syntactic relation (*anvaya*) only when the expressive power (*vācaka-śakti*) of the words toward their respective word-meanings has already been apprehended.

It is not the case that such a sentence could convey a specific relation while the expressive power of the collection of words toward those word-meanings remains unknown; this is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
It is understood that when the comprehension of a sentence-meaning is to be achieved, the apprehension of the word-potency (*śaktigraha*) is an auxiliary factor; therefore, it must be sought.

And since the sentences under discussion convey the connection of meanings belonging to the past and the future, the meaning is that the potency of words ending in the *luṅ*, *laṅ*, and other such suffixes must be known with respect to those past and future meanings. (9.297)

Granted that the apprehension of word-potency (śakti) is necessary, yet it applies only to objects that are presently existing and not to those past or future, because [potency] would be useless [in their case]; to this he says: "If potency... and so forth.
If the capacity were restricted to the present, one could not speak of the past and the future.

If the capacity of words were grasped only with respect to a present object, then a sentence would not speak of, nor convey, a past or future connection between past or future objects, due to the absence of auxiliary factors.
The term "ekavadbhāva" (singular treatment) follows the rule: "Every dvandva compound optionally takes a singular form."
This is the explanation of the intended meaning of what was stated [in the verse]: "regarding past and future objects.
It may be granted that there is a grasp of the word-potency (*śakti*) even for past and future objects;
to the question "What follows from that?", he says: "If... (*yadīti*).
If the apprehension of the word's power occurs elsewhere, how could it occur if that [power] were not apprehended?

If it is admitted that the apprehension of a word’s power occurs even for the past and the future, apart from the present, then how could there be an apprehension of a word’s power regarding past and future objects if there is no apprehension [of those objects themselves]? It could not be in any way.
Because a power devoid of an object cannot be known,
the knowledge of past and future objects must therefore also be admitted.
This is the collective meaning here.
A sentence, which is characterized by a specific relation between word-meanings, brings about the understanding of the sentence-meaning itself, and not merely the individual word-meanings.
This [understanding] requires the apprehension of the denotative power (*vācakatva-śakti*) of words with respect to their respective word-meanings;
and the apprehension of that power is the apprehension of the word-meanings themselves.
Furthermore, the apprehension of word-meanings depends upon other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and is not produced by words or sentences alone,

because that would entail fallacies such as mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). Moreover, in cases where the sentence-meaning consists of a connection with past or future objects, the apprehension of those past or future objects is indispensable.
[The opponent argues: "Śuka, Vāmadeva, and others have been liberated, and I too shall be liberated"—such statements likewise [serve as evidence].

Therefore, even by another who desires to understand the meaning taught by scripture, it must be accepted that there is a perception of past and future times and the objects related to them, which are expressed by words ending in the conditional (*luṅ*) and periphrastic future (*lṛṭ*) suffixes.
And since this does not occur without a witness (*sākṣin*), how can that [witness] have as its object only the present, when it perceives past and future objects? *9,300*
Following the view of the Mīmāṃsakas, he raises an objection: "The universal," etc.
"If this [inference] were to lead to something else based solely on what is observed in common (*sāmānyadṛṣṭa*),"—
the word "this" (*asau*) refers back to the term that constitutes part of the subject sentence under discussion.
Every object, moreover, consists of both the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*).
In this regard, it has already been established that only the universal form (sāmānyākāra) is denoted by the word, whereas the particular (viśeṣa) is merely indicated (lakṣya).
Furthermore, the universal is one and the same across past and future particulars;
and that [universal], when perceived through the eyes and other senses as being present, is indeed understood as the object of the word’s expressive power.
Furthermore, even at another time,
the word brings about cognition;
in that case, what is the use of knowledge of past and future objects?

For if particulars were the denotata of words, then because they exist in forms such as the past and so forth, the knowledge of the past and so forth would be required for the apprehension of the word's power (*śakti*).
Nor should it be argued that, for the apprehension of the power of the *luṅ* (aorist), *lṛṅ* (conditional), and other suffixes, the apprehension of past, future, and other times is unavoidable;
for even there, it is only the universal (*jāti*) of "time-ness" (*kālatva*) itself that is the denotatum.

For the Mīmāṃsakas, unlike the Vaiśeṣikas and others, there is nothing whatsoever that is devoid of a universal (*sāmānya*). Therefore, there is no dependence on the apprehension of past objects and so forth for the grasping of word-potency (*śakti*). To this, he provides the answer: "The universal," etc. (*sāmānyeti*).
How could it convey the true nature of a thing if it were devoid of universals?

Let it be granted, for now, that the eternal universal such as "cowness" (*gotva*), which pervades all particular instances, is indeed the denotation of words like "cow," while the particulars possessing dewlaps and so forth are merely indicated (*lakṣya*).
Even so, this must be addressed:
Does the word "own-form" (svarūpa) convey the own-forms of things or not?
If the position is that it does not, there is a contradiction with experience.
If the first [position] is held, it must be stated by what mode of operation (vṛtti) this occurs.
It cannot be by means of indication (lakṣaṇā),
because indication is impossible [in this case] except through the door of the primary meaning (vācyārtha).
Since it is only the universal (sāmānya) that is denotable,
and since individual forms (svarūpa) are devoid of universals,
one must therefore accept that the word "own-form" (svarūpa-śabda) denotes the own-forms of real entities (vastu). *9,303*
Now, since all universals (sāmānya) are not external to the essential nature of the thing, how can it be said that the essential nature of the thing is "devoid of universals"? To this, he says: "No."
Nowhere has the universal "essence-ness" (svarūpatva) been accepted by anyone at all.
It is true that there are universals within the individual essences (*svarūpa*),
yet these are not denotable by words expressing the individual essence.
For instance, the "cowness" residing in an individual body possessing a dewlap and so forth is not denotable by the word "cow."
But it is simply "cowness.

Therefore, in this case as well, one who accepts that the universal is the denotation of the word "essential nature" (svarūpa) must admit that it is indeed "the state of being essential nature" (svarūpatva);
yet that does not exist.
Because it has not been accepted by any investigator anywhere;
nor has the generality of "being an intrinsic nature" (svarūpatva-sāmānya) been accepted by anyone.
"I shall accept it;

for there is no rule that whatever is accepted by everyone must necessarily be accepted. To one who speaks thus out of audacity—arguing that if such were the case, differences of philosophical view (darśana-bheda) would be impossible—he replies: "If [you mean] the essential nature... (svarūpaṃ cet).
If the intrinsic nature were both inclusive and exclusive, what would that be?
The term *svarūpam* (own-nature) is an indication where the abstract state (*bhāva*) is the primary meaning.
In that regard, concerning the entity (*vastu*),
the word *kim* (what) expresses an inquiry.
The sense is that, such being the case, the question regarding reality would remain unanswered.
To the question "How so?", he says: "sarva... [Verse 9.304].
For it is held that at the end of all pervasive properties, there exists self-nature (*svatva*).
To the question "What is excluded?", the answer would simply be "the essential nature" (svarūpa). ... MAnu 3.2.74a-e.

Since the Mīmāṃsaka maintains that at the end—the final limit—of all inclusive properties (anugatadharma), their own-being (svatva) or essential nature (svarūpatva) is what is intended, therefore, when the question "What is excluded there? is asked, the only answer that could be given would be "essential nature.
This is what is meant.
The Vaiśeṣikas maintain that "ultimate particulars" (*antyaviśeṣa*) are properties that are absolutely distinct from substances.
However, if one were to accept further particulars even within those ultimate particulars, it would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
In that case, just as their own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) is itself distinct, let that very nature suffice for substances as well; what then is the use of separate ultimate particulars?
When the Mīmāṃsaka— who, by not disregarding particulars, consecrates their very nature as being "thatness" (tatsthāne)— is asked what it is that has been excluded [by his doctrine],
he simply cannot say that "it is the ultimate particulars," for that would entail the fallacy of contradicting one's own tenets (apasiddhānta).

However, although qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth are distinct, they are accepted as being inclusive by virtue of their being an inclusive substratum; thus, they are indeed to be considered as "inclusive" (*anugata*).
Therefore, one must simply state that they are the very nature (*svarūpa*) [of the substance].
If it is now accepted that this [exclusion] is pervasive, how could this question not remain unanswered? [Objection:

"Surely it will be the difference itself that is excluded, because there is neither pervasion of that nor the state of being a substratum for what is pervasive. To this, he says: "Therefore... (*tataḥ*).
If it were something other than that, then it would be nothing but that very thing for us.
The meaning is: "then [it would apply] to the single word alone.

Therefore, if it is accepted that there is another characteristic of difference, distinct from its own nature (*svarūpa*), then that very thing is our own *svayaṃ-svarūpa* (intrinsic nature), for the sake of which the object is [designated].
The meaning is that while the essential nature (*svarūpa*) has been illustrated there, the example will be the distinction (*bheda*) itself. This is what is being said:

since the specific example is not to be insisted upon, one must admit that distinction—even though it is devoid of a universal (*sāmānya*)—is cognizable by words through the function of direct denotation (*vacanavṛtti*) alone.
Furthermore, since a denotative word does not convey its meaning without the apprehension of its expressive power (śakti), the apprehension of that power must also be accepted in that case.
To the question, "What follows from this for the subject at hand?", he says: "In this way... (evam).
In this way, even when the understanding of the word's power occurs with respect to a form that has been excluded, for that [person]...

When it is accepted that the capacity of words such as "essential nature" (*svarūpa*) or "difference" (*bheda*) to denote either an essential nature or a difference—which, according to the manner described, is devoid of generality (*sāmānya*)—then from what could that apprehension of capacity arise without knowledge of that essential nature and so forth?
Since there is a rule that the knowledge of a relation must be preceded by the knowledge of the relata, [the capacity] would certainly not arise; therefore, that knowledge must be admitted.
Since it would follow that omniscience is attained through the knowledge of all individual natures and their distinctions, he says: "in a general way."
...and how could that [knowledge] exist without general knowledge? (Manu 3.2.75cd)

The meaning is that the establishment of linguistic usage occurs through knowledge of things in their general form (*sāmānyataḥ*), and because there is an absence of knowledge of them in their specific form (*viśeṣataḥ*), there is no consequence of [the Buddha] being omniscient.
Now, one might ask: "How can there be knowledge in a general sense of an intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) and so forth that is devoid of generality? To this, he says: "Therefore" (*ataḥ*).
Therefore, everything is accepted as having both a specific and a general form.
We maintain that every entity possesses both specific and general forms—the form of exclusion (vyāvṛtti) and the form of generality; therefore, there is no inconsistency whatsoever.
Why is this maintained?
Because of the reasoning established previously.

If it were exclusively exclusion (*vyāvṛtta*), then, according to the manner previously stated, it would result in omniscience or else there would be an absence of the apprehension of capacity (*śaktigraha*).
And if it were exclusively of the nature of a universal (*sāmānya*), then the cognition of exclusion would simply be untenable.
[Objection: But is this not being said in contradiction to what was stated previously?

Since it was previously established that the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) and so forth are indeed devoid of universals (*sāmānya*), and since it is now stated that everything is accepted as having the nature of both particularity (*viśeṣa*) and universality, he says: "Excluded" (*vyāvṛtta*).
And that universal which is differentiated would itself become the particular.
And for that reason, there is no single nature among these entities with respect to one another.

That very nature which is excluded [from others] is itself the universal by virtue of its specific power; for that reason, there is no single common property among the objects of reality (padārtha) in relation to one another.
This is what is meant:

previously, when it was stated that there is no universal in the difference of intrinsic natures and so forth, that was intended to mean that there is no mutually recurring single property among the intrinsic natures of the objects of reality.

Even in the absence of that [external object], if one accepts a specific universal form that is excluded from others and non-different from its own nature, then it has been stated that everything is accepted as having both particular and universal forms; thus, there is no contradiction between what precedes and what follows.
Nor is this [position] untenable.

The nature of both the particular (*viśeṣa*) and the universal (*sāmānya*) is established because a single entity, by virtue of its specific qualities, generates both exclusive and inclusive cognitions.

Thus, having accepted that universals such as "cowness" (*gotva*) are inclusive, it was stated that since there is no universal such as "being its own nature" (*svarūpatva*), knowledge of that [individual] nature is required in order to grasp the word-potency (*śabdaśakti*) with respect to it. Now, he says "of properties" (*dharmāṇām*) to show that even cowness and the like are not inclusive.
... solely through the perception of difference among phenomena. // MAnu 3.2.77c //
It is merely reiterated that there is no single common property (*ekadharmatā*) among objects in their mutual relationship.

Since properties such as whiteness, which are distinct from the aggregate [of parts], are seen to be excluded from each individual substratum (*dharmin*) through the perception of their difference, one should infer— by means of that same example— that even for objects such as cows, there is no single common property, namely the possession of a recurring property like "cowness" (*gotva*), in their mutual relationship.
The formal argument here is as follows:
"Cowness and the like are excluded from each individual [cow], because they are properties distinct from the aggregate [of individuals], just like whiteness and so forth.
The word "eva" (only/indeed) is connected with the proposition (*pratijñā*).
He refutes [the objection] that there is a sublation of the inclusive cognition (*anugatabuddhi*) because it has been demonstrated that the inclusive cognition is established in quite another way.
Alternatively, let the relationship belong to other [cognitions] just as it is.
The Prābhākaras hold that even properties such as color and so forth are indeed pervasive and do not differ from one individual instance to another;
therefore, [the example] lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalatā*).
To refute that [objection], it is said: "by the perception of difference itself" (*bhedadṛṣṭayaiva*).
Otherwise, he would have simply said "from difference" (*bhedāt*).
He says "that" (*tat*) because, if whiteness and so forth were excluded [from the universal], the cognition of persistence (*anuvṛttapratyaya*) would be contradicted.
... because of the perception of similarity to that. (Manu 3.2.77d)

In the cognition "this is whiteness, this is whiteness," it is only the similarity to the whiteness of snow that is perceived in the whiteness of the moon, and not its identity with it; therefore, there is no contradiction. [The opponent asks:
"Let there be no recurring universal (sāmānya); what of it for the subject at hand? To this, he says: "Therefore" (ataḥ).
Therefore, all objects of experience become the domain of the witness through their commonality.

The meaning is as follows: since there is no such thing as a "concomitant universal" (*anugatasāmānya*), only the individual instances (*vyakti*) of the past, future, and present could be the denotata; yet words whose expressive power (*śakti*) has not been grasped cannot convey meaning, and the grasping of that power is impossible without knowledge of the word-meanings; thus, if they were known in their specific particulars, it would entail the consequence of omniscience (*sārvajñya*).
"All" refers to those that are present, past, and future.
Let it be granted that the apprehension of capacity depends upon the cognition of the past and so forth.
And as to why that [is known] by the witness, he says: "all."
"How else could there be the cognition 'all' for all [beings]?"—
the word "eva" (only/just) is for the purpose of excluding any specific form;
the sense is that there is no other means of valid cognition [for it].
This is the response to the claim that "all general knowledge regarding the past and so forth will come about through inference":
inference indeed depends upon the knowledge that every mark—whether past, future, or present—is pervaded by the probandum;
and this knowledge is not possible without a witness (*sākṣin*).
Alternatively, by stating that the witness (sākṣin) has as its object all common forms such as the past and so forth, he is actually asserting another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
For inference is indeed preceded by the knowledge that "all things such as smoke are pervaded by corresponding things such as fire.
Thus, if the witness did not have the past and so forth as its object, and no other such [means] existed, there would be the total abolition of inference alone.
Furthermore, there must indeed be for everyone an apprehension of the power of all words;
otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the collapse of linguistic usage such as, "All this, verily, is Brahman."

Since the apprehension of the word’s expressive power (*śaktigraha*) depends upon the apprehension of its referent (*arthagraha*), it must be admitted that everyone possesses a general cognition of "everything" as "everything.
For if the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) did not have all things—past and so forth—as its object, that [general cognition] would not occur.

Objection: In the absence of a recurring universal (*anugatasāmānya*), the apprehension of the word’s expressive power itself is untenable, because individual instances (*vyakti*) are infinite and because there is the fault of deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
To the question, "How can the witness's capacity to have the past and so forth as its object be established through the impossibility of [the experience] otherwise?", he says: "Something... (kiñcit).
"Through the cognition of even a slight similarity, there may be the apprehension of the word's power with respect to the entire object... (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 3.2.79a-c).
This has been largely explained in the examination of the Vaiśeṣika school.
If this were so, one might apprehend the denotative power (*śakti*) of the word "cow" even in the case of a *gavaya*, because of the existence of similarity; therefore, he says: "that and that," etc.
... by virtue of their respective similarity [to the original].
The connection is with what precedes.
Not every cognition of similarity is the cause for grasping the power of a word;
rather, it must be free from over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
The meaning is that just as the quality of possessing a dewlap and so forth resides in the word "cow," so too does another [quality] reside in another [word].
By this, the previous term “something” (*kiñcit*) is explained. *9,312*

Having thus refuted the view that witness-perception (sākṣipratyakṣa) apprehends only the present, he now refutes that same [view] regarding mental perception (mānasapratyakṣa) as well, with the words: "Perception... (pratyakṣam).
Perception is both sensory and mental, when it has as its object a thing that has passed away.
"Mental perception has as its object only that which has already passed, and it is the cause of memory.
This connects with the subsequent sentence beginning with "when" (*yadā*).

Since it is difficult to establish the validity of memory—which has no object beyond that of the prior experience—how could it possibly be born from mental perception? To this, he says: "When... then... (*yadā... tadā*).
Then, memory has the status of a means of valid cognition when it is qualified by its having occurred in the past.

Since memory takes as its object an entity qualified by pastness—this is the remainder [of the sentence]—therefore, for that reason, the validity of memory as a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is established. To the question, "Even though its object is an entity qualified by pastness, how can memory possess validity? he says: "Excellence" (*ādhikya*).
But when something is held to have passed away after being experienced, how could it not be considered a valid means of knowledge for memory? (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 3.2.81)

Since it is accepted by everyone that the state of being past, which is made an object of memory, is something additional to the object previously experienced as present, how could memory not possess the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? And if it possesses the status of a means of valid cognition, how could it not be born from mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*)? This is the meaning.

Furthermore, this demonstration that memory has an object exceeding that of the original experience was established by accepting the definition of a means of valid cognition as "that which apprehends an object not yet apprehended."
In reality, however, this is not the definition;
rather, it is simply being in accordance with reality (yathārthatva).
And that quality exists in memory, as established by experience.
For if there were a subverting cognition (bādhakapratyaya), that [cognition] would not exist; yet such a subversion does not exist here, as he says: "And there is no subversion."
...and there is no contradiction here. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.2.81d)

With the intention that even in the case of sensory perception such as visual perception, there is no rule that it apprehends only the present, he says: "the status of being a means of valid cognition" (mānatvam).
The status of being a means of valid cognition belongs to recognition as well, as is known from all experience.
For all investigators indeed establish the permanence of the self and so forth by means of that [consciousness].
To the question, "What follows from this for the present topic?", he says: "Past... and so on.
And that [action] is seen as having the past and present as its substrata.
The meaning is that it has as its object a thing qualified by the properties of pastness and presentness; this is perceived by the witness-consciousness (sākṣin),
for the form of recognition is experienced as "this is that very same [thing]."
And the point is that it arises through the eye and so forth alone.
Now, it may be thought that four positions are possible regarding recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).

Or [the opponent might argue that] it is either experience alone, or memory alone, or a pair of cognitions consisting of memory and experience, or a single cognition such that it is memory in one part and experience in another.
Among these, the first is not tenable;
for if that were the case, there would be only "I," and not "he."
Nor is the second [alternative] tenable;
for if that were the case, it would be "that" alone and not "this," as will be explained.
Otherwise, there would be a logical fault. Therefore, one must accept the latter two positions alone.

And since that [cognition] would then be of the nature of memory due to the element "that," visual perception and the like would not have a past object as their domain; to this he says: "And not... (na ca).
And that [practice] does not consist of mere mindfulness... // MĀnuv 3.2.83a //

"Smṛtimātrā" means that which has "mere memory" (*smṛti-mātrā*) as its measure; it is so called because it consists of a collection of parts whose nature is the experience of memory, and likewise, it is not of the nature of a single cognition consisting of the experience of memory. Why is it not so? To this, he states the reason for the first proposition: "tadidantve... (*9.315*).
... but this [is] due to the grasping of the "this" as being one with that.
Because there is an experience of oneness between the apprehension of "that-ness" (tattva) and "this-ness" (idantva),
the term "apprehension" (graha) indicates that it is an experience.
He states the reason for the second proposition with the words "tadidantva."
Because the apprehension of "that-ness" and "this-ness" is a single [cognition] and partless.
This is what is meant:
it has been stated by the opponent as well that recognition is not merely memory.
Nor is it of the nature of two cognitions;
for that would entail the absence of any proof for the identity [of the object], resulting in the failure to establish the refutation of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*).
Furthermore, there is no single cognition that consists of both memory and direct experience.

Because duality is contradictory with oneness, consciousness—which is essentially of the nature of experience—is indeed one; yet, because it is produced by the eye and other faculties in conjunction with mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), it takes the form "this is that.
Just as white, green, yellow, and other colors give rise to a variegated color (*citrarūpa*).

Just as the sense faculties, when accompanied by defects, become causes of error, so too will the sense faculties, when assisted by mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), become causes of recognition; what fault is there in this? Furthermore, a mental impression does not function as a cause of cognition independently.
Because it is accepted that memory is born from mental perception,
[the author] concludes the point already stated in the passage beginning with "If that [perception] does not have a subsequent object," etc., by saying "Therefore" (ataḥ).
Therefore, there would be no restriction to the present tense alone in the case of perception produced by the senses.

The "restriction to the present alone" (*vartamānaikaniyamaḥ*) is a restriction of the form that [cognition] takes as its object only the present. Regarding what was stated—that the entire universe, consisting of the distinction between the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the object of knowledge (*prameya*), and the knower (*pramātṛ*), is unsublated—the author now offers a rebuttal to the objection: "How can the universe be threefold, given that there exists a fourth kind of cognition called 'cognizedness' (*pramiti*), which is synonymous with 'manifestness' (*prākaṭya*) or 'thatness-manifestness' (*tattā-prākaṭya*) residing in the object? He begins by saying: "And not... (*na ca*).

And there can never be a so-called "result of valid cognition" (pramiti) other than the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) itself; since there is no evidence for its existence and because such a postulation would be unnecessarily complex, what is the use of it?

That which is called "cognition" (pramiti) does not exist as a real entity at all, because there is no means of valid cognition (māna) for it. But how can there be an absence of a means of valid cognition?
[Because of the teaching: "The cognizer, the object of cognition, the means of cognition, and likewise cognition."
Because such scriptural authority exists, it was said: "Other than through valid cognition."
Valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is twofold: the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the result (*phala*).
In this context, by the word "valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*), the instrument is denoted; and by the word "cognition" (*pramiti*), that very valid cognition in the form of the result is expressed.
There is no cognition other than that.

There exists, first of all, a fixed relation of object and subject between the thing and its cognition; yet this relation is not established by mere existence or by causality, as those definitions would be over-extended.
Nor is it established by identity or by similarity.
Because it is impossible:
in the statement "that object which appears in a cognition is its object," the meaning of the locative case is untenable.
Therefore, one must accept that whatever excellence (*atiśaya*) arises in something, that thing is its object.

And so, for the sake of establishing the objecthood (*viṣayatva*) of an external thing, an excellence residing in the object produced by cognition must be accepted in every respect; how then can there be an absence of proof?
Do not say so.
If that were so, it would follow that the past and the future could not be objects of cognition;
for it is not possible for a property (dharma) to arise in the absence of a substratum (dharmin).

If it is argued that they possess object-status because the operation [of cognition] is possible there, then since such possibility exists for the present as well, "cognizedness" (jñātatā) need not be postulated.
This is what was stated by the phrase "in some cases":
the meaning is that [the object] does not exist even in the present, just as it did not exist in the past and so forth.
Furthermore, does cognition produce the state of being known (*jñātatā*) in its own object, or somewhere else?
In the second case, there is an over-extension;
in the first case, since the object's status as an object is established even before the knowledge arises, the postulation of that [knowledge] is useless—thus he says: "What is the use of this?"
Furthermore, regarding the state of being known (*jñātatā*), is the production of another state of being known admitted or not?
If the latter position is taken, it would follow that there is no objectivity for the cognition.

Regarding the first position, he says, "and because of the complexity of the conceptualization," meaning that for one who admits a continuous stream of states of being known that are never established in experience, there would be an excessive burden of conceptual construction (*kalpanā-gaurava*).
Now, if it is postulated that "cognizedness" (jñātatā) is the object even without another instance of cognizedness,
then too there is merely the fault of conceptual over-elaboration (kalpanā-gaurava).
By this, the inference— "knowledge produces some effect upon its own object because it is an action, like the act of going"— is also refuted.
If one takes cognition alone as the subject of the argument, there is sublation in the case of cognitions regarding the "cognizedness" of past and future objects;

otherwise, there would be a deviation (vyabhicāra) in those very cases. To this, he says: "By me," [in response to the objection]: "But surely, in such instances as 'the jar is known' or 'the jar is manifest,' cognizedness is perceived through direct perception (pratyakṣa) as a qualifier of the object. Thus he says: "by me."
"But the thought 'this has been known by me' refers to the object of knowledge as it appears to the witness-consciousness;
it is indeed knowledge itself... MAnu 3.2.85a-c.
"This very cognition has been known by me"—this is the objective domain of cognition.
For action resides in the agent; when it is expressed with the agent as the primary factor, it is then perceived as a property of the agent.
For example: "Devadatta desires a jar," or "he hates [it]."

But when [the object] is predominant by way of its action (*karman*), then it is so by virtue of being that [action's] property (*dharmatā*), as in "he desires" or "he hates. However, when it is predominant by way of itself, then it is independent (*svatantrā*).
"Just as desire and aversion [are known through inference]," so too,
why is it untenable that knowledge, though residing solely within the self, appears as if it were a property of the object?
But surely, knowledge itself is not perceptible.
For instance, a cognition cannot be the object of a preceding cognition;
if that were the case, [one would have the thought] "I shall know" [only in that manner].
But it would not be "I do not know," nor [would it refer] to one who has come later;
for if that were the case, there would only be "I knew."
Furthermore, there is no other cognition that arises simultaneously [with the object];

therefore, since it must be inferred solely by means of the effect characterized as "cognizedness" (*jñātatā*), why is this [cognizedness] not accepted? To this, it is said: "[It is known] by the witness" (*sākṣiṇam*).
Because the witness (sākṣin) is eternal, the aforementioned defect does not apply;
moreover, it is self-luminous.
Furthermore, he states that "cognizedness" (jñātatā) is sublated by non-perception, saying: "other than that" (tato 'nyā).
... beyond that, no other thing called "valid cognition" is observed.
For in the first cognition, only the object itself is known, not as qualified by "cognizedness" (*jñātatā*),
because at that time [the latter] has not yet arisen.

On the alternative view that [the cognition] produces that [cognizedness] and subsequently takes the object as qualified by it as its object, there would follow the consequence of a cessation and subsequent renewed activity (*viramyavyāpāra*).
Furthermore, no object greater than that which was made the object of the first cognition appears in subsequent cognitions;
as for the expression "it is known," it has already been stated that the cognition itself is the object.
(*9,324*) Now, he concludes the point previously stated in the verse beginning with "the Lord and His cognition" (īśatajjñāna): "māna... [etc.].
There is no destruction whatsoever of the means of knowledge, the objects of knowledge, and the objects of cognition.
