Therefore, the meaning is that the universe, which is threefold according to the distinctions of [the means of knowledge] such as perception and so forth, has no destruction or sublation anywhere at all; thus it truly exists.
[This concludes the discussion of] the subject at hand.
Concluding [the previous argument], he refutes the falsity of dreams by means of another reason:
"And of these things in dreams as well, no sublation is ever observed. (Manu 3.2.86cd)
What is the reason?

Because these very dreams—consisting of the means of cognition, the cognizer, and the objects of cognition—are never seen to be sublated at any time; therefore, the connection is that a dream is by no means false.
The word "api" (also) means that it is not only external manifoldness [that is negated].

To the question, "How can this be so, given that sublation is observed for one who has awakened from a dream through such [thoughts] as 'there was no elephant here'? he says: "It is merely the state of being awake."
In this case, the state of waking alone is real; otherwise, it would clearly appear as something different. Therefore, the dream is false, and not [the waking state]. // MAnuv_3.2.87a-c //
Otherwise, [it would exist] by way of non-existence;
this has already been largely explained.
As for what was said, beginning with "this is a chariot," etc., [it is as follows:]
This indicates that it has been transformed;
it will be stated that "there is no obstruction," as in:
"There are no chariots there."
Such scriptural passages [refer to] the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of that [dream].
Now, if the waking-state nature of dream-objects is established by error and sublated, then their falsity (*mithyātva*) is unavoidable.

If it is argued that dream-elephants and the like are false because they are objects of error and objects of sublation, like a shell-silver, [we ask: what is this "being an object of error"? Is it by way of being the superimposed (*āropya*), or by way of being the substratum of superimposition (*āropādhiṣṭhāna*)?
Or is it common [to both]?

Likewise, as for being the object of sublation (*bādhaviṣayatva*), is it so by way of being that which is negated, or by way of being the locus of negation, or is it common? In both cases, he states the fault regarding the second and third [alternatives] with the words "as in the waking state" (*jāgradvat*).
... as when awake ... // Mānava-dharmaśāstra 3.2.87d //
The meaning is: "just as [an object] such as mother-of-pearl is seen by one who is awake.

The point is that there is an inconclusive reason (*anaikāntya*): just as mother-of-pearl and the like are not false even though they serve as the substrata for superimposition and sublation, so too it is with dream objects.

To the objection—"But we intend to prove the falsity of mother-of-pearl and other things perceived in the waking state by this very same reason; how then can there be an inconclusive reason in that case?"—he says: "jāgrad... (waking...).
And even while awake. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.2.87d)
... as one's own self. // Manu 3.2.88a //
In that case, the meaning is that waking and dreaming are not false at all, just like the Self.
He explains this with the words "in some cases" (*kvacid*).
In some cases, the self may indeed be the object of an error;
yet for that reason alone, it is not false, whether in a dream or likewise in the waking state.
[The notion] "I am momentary" and so forth is the object of such an error.
And this is an illustration; it should also be understood that "I am not momentary, but rather permanent" is likewise an object of sublation,
both in the dream state and in the waking state.
The meaning is that even the objects perceived therein are not false;
for even when an inference is formulated by adopting both positions,
the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in respect to the self (*ātman*) remains unavoidable.
If it is argued: "But since the self, too, is understood [by some] to be momentary and so forth, it is false; how then can there be a deviation (vyabhicāra) in that case?
[We reply: Is this said because of the falsity of the superimposed momentariness and so forth, or because of the falsity of the very nature of the self?
In the second case, the contradiction with one's own established tenets (apasiddhānta) is quite evident.
Having raised the first objection, he refutes it with the words "yadi" (if).
If that which is seen as otherwise in the self were to be so here as well, it would be an error.
In that case, it would have to be stated that what is to be proven is the falsity of the superimposed form (*āropitākāra*).

And thus, there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatva*), because we also accept the falsity of superimposed forms regarding objects perceived in the waking state and in dreams.

Regarding the first position—that the reason is "being the object of error and sublation, whether by way of being superimposed or by way of being negated"—he states the defect: "unsublated" (*abādhiteti*).
But since they continue to persist uncontradicted, how can dreams and the like be considered erroneous?

Since the state of being awake (*jāgrattva*) and so forth, as well as "silver-ness" (*rajatatva*) and so forth, persist even after sublation (*bādha*), while elephants and mother-of-pearl continue to exist uncontradicted, how could dreams and the like possess the aforementioned nature of error and sublation?
Thus, there is a lack of essential proof (*svarūpāsiddhi*).
For indeed, just as the Self (*ātman*), which persists even after the time of sublation, is neither superimposed (*āropya*) nor subject to sublation (*bādhya*).

The same applies to dreaming and waking as well, because in both cases there is the persistence of such recollections as "I indeed saw an elephant. He states that the inference of the falsity of waking and dreaming—based on reasons such as being objects of error due to the absence of favorable evidence and the presence of contrary evidence—is untenable, saying: "And not... (na ca).

If everything were erroneous, there would be no valid cognition at all; and if everything were non-erroneous, how could that [very same thing] be erroneous? How, indeed, could it be both a means of valid cognition and yet possess error?
The term "the universe" (*viśva*) is intended here in both its senses [as the world and as cognition]. "Error" (*bhrāntatva*) means falsity (*mithyātva*).
Alternatively, this statement is intended to establish, by another method, the non-establishment (*asiddhi*) of the two reasons, namely "being an object of error" and so forth.
The term "of the deluded" (*bhrāntasya*) is also an elliptical indication for "that which is sublated" (*bādhyatvasya*);
therefore, the word "because of that" (*yataḥ tasmāt*) should be supplied.
"The illusoriness of that" means that both kinds of the universe are objects of illusion.

To dispel the objection—"How can there be a lack of proof [of the thesis], since the illusoriness of both dreaming and waking states is established by reasons such as 'being visible'?"—the author refutes the notion of illusoriness in another way, beginning with "Furthermore" (*kiñca*).
Furthermore, that proponent of illusoriness [must also admit] the illusoriness of his own position.
He certainly accepts... // MAnu 3.91a-c //

The proponent of error, establishing that both types of the universe are erroneous by means of such reasons as "being perceptible," [states] "of his own doctrine," meaning the property of his own thesis.
The word "certainly" (*niyatam*) is used because, otherwise, there would be the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) in that case; this is the intended meaning.
Not only must the opponent accept the erroneous nature and so forth of their own proposed thesis in order to establish their own pervasion (*vyāpti*), [but the same applies to the proponent].
But he says, "In that case," [meaning] that we also accept that.
... therein, the proponent's adherence to the truth. // MĀnuv 3.2.91d-e //
Because the object asserted by the opponent is erroneous for both the proponent and the opponent—that is, for the *vādin* and the *prativādin*.
And this should be understood as being for the purpose of refuting the "unestablished for either party" (*anyatarāsiddhi*) of the inference that is about to be stated.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "And by that... (*tena ca*).
And by that, the entire universe will indeed become free from delusion.

Not only by the aforementioned proofs, but also because the world's being erroneous and so forth would themselves be erroneous, the entire universe will necessarily be non-erroneous and likewise un-sublatable.
He indicates the pervasion (vyāpti) therein with the words: "bhrāntatva... (due to being erroneous).
If there were both the state of being an error and the state of non-error, how could there not be the truth of non-error?
Thus, these two formal arguments (prayoga) are as follows:
"The universe is non-erroneous, because it is not the object of error, like the self; likewise, the universe is non-sublatable, because it is not the object of sublation, like the self."
He states the commencement of the refutation of the erroneous interpretation with the words "aśeṣa... (beginning with "without remainder").
That doctrine, corrupted by every defect, should be rejected by those who desire their own welfare.
"His view" refers to the view that establishes the falsity of the manifold world of both dreams and waking states.
It might be argued as follows:
"Since the world is illusory, why should its non-illusoriness and so forth not also be false?

Nor is this impossible, for the 'impossibility' (durghaṭatva) of such a thing is an ornament [to our position]. Anticipating this objection, he replies with a touch of irony—stating that this [position of ours] is dull because there is no occasion to demonstrate the reasons for rejecting their view—with the words "by which...
(*yeneti*).
By which [reasoning] he has always himself accepted that his own doctrine is to be abandoned,
because its difficulty is merely a result of error and because it is actually an ornament.
How could even a madman wish to accept his doctrine? This is because it is accepted as being the object of delusion due to its very nature of delusion,
and because its inherent difficulty is accepted as its very ornament.
He is merely insane, or even directly insane, but he is not one who has become insane due to the seeds of madness and the like.
For an insane person does not himself think, "My own view is deluded and impossible.
If so, how did it come to be current in the world? To this, he says: "By the Lord," etc.
Because the power of the Lord is inconceivable, this has been set in motion by those who are greatly intoxicated.
The phrase "by those who are greatly intoxicated" provides another reason.

Since it would be irrelevant to begin the explanation of a sūtra only to demonstrate that a false interpretation is to be rejected, [the author], intending to strengthen his own exposition, first explains the meaning of the word *māyā* while elucidating the sense of the sūtra, saying: "Therefore... (ataḥ).
Therefore, wisdom is here called "māyā" by the Jaina... // MAnuv_3.2.95ab //

The word "ataḥ" (therefore) is used because an alternative explanation would be faulty; the intended meaning is that [the term *māyā*] is listed among the names for wisdom (*prajñā*) in the passage: "Māyā is insight (*vayuna*), it is vision (*abhikhyā*)."
It will be stated that Māyā is the causal ground of the intermediate state (sandhyakāraṇatva).
In that regard, as to what kind of cause the individual intellect (jaivī prajñā) is, he says: "It is indeed the material cause (upādāna)."
... that very thing is clinging itself.
The word "of the intermediate state" (sandhyasya) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
Here, it is not only the individual intellect (jaivī prajñā) that is māyā,
but the divine intellect (aiśvarī) as well.
And she says that this [state] is indeed the cause of the intermediate state: "the cause," it is said.
The sign of the Sovereign Goddess is the primary [sign]. ... // MAnu 3.2.95c //
And he will state that here the word "prajñā" is used figuratively (lākṣaṇika) in the sense of latent impression (vāsanā).
With the intention that such an interpretation is not common to both [the Lord and the individual soul], it is said "primary" (mukhyā):
the wisdom of the Lord (īśvara-prajñā) is indeed primary, whereas the wisdom of the individual soul (jīva-prajñā) is figurative. *9,333*
He explains the term "mere illusion" as follows: "that which is conjured."
... as well as that which is emanated and protected. MĀn 3.2.95d.
Together with those two, and also separately, it is called "mere illusion" (māyāmātra).
From both together, and then from each separately, [the world] is measured by the power of the Lord and protected.
The connection is with those two very [terms].
By this, the word "tu" (but/however) is explained.
To avoid the fault of [applying the terms] according to their respective order (*yathāsaṅkhyam*), it was said: "together" and "separately."

The word "ca" (and) has the sense of "tasmāt" (therefore); the words "it is moved as the intermediate state" are to be supplied. He explains what was stated as "together" and "separately" with the words "by both."

Because it is measured by the wisdom of both the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara), and protected by the sovereign wisdom (aiśvaryaprajñā), it is therefore said to be "both together and separate.
The suffix *ka* is applied according to the rule *āto ’nupasarge kaḥ* from the verbal root *āp* (to obtain), as in the word *adibhūmi* (the ground of attainment). It is like the word *hutaji*.
Although it would have been possible to form the suffix *tra* from the single verbal root alone,
it was nevertheless done in this way for the sake of obtaining an additional meaning;
because the grammatical instruction is based on the Sūtra, the suffix denotes the object (*karman*).
Or, it may be that the suffix *ka* is prescribed in the sense of "that which is similar" (*ghañ-arthe*).
But is this not contradictory to what was stated previously?
For previously it was said that the intermediate state (*sandhya*) has the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the living being as its material cause (*upādāna*).
But now, [if you say] it consists of wisdom and means (*prajñopādanaka*),
do not say so; for even the word "wisdom" (*prajñā*)...
Because it serves as the indicator (upalakṣaṇa) of that latent impression (*vāsanā*).
Now, what is the relationship between wisdom (*prajñā*) and the latent impression such that there could be an indication? To this he says: "consisting of wisdom" (*prajñātmaka*).
The mind consists of wisdom, by which the latent impressions take the form of mental objects.

For the reason that the mind (*manas*) has wisdom (*prajñā*) as its essence and takes wisdom as its material cause (*upādāna*), while the latent impressions (*vāsanās*) have the mind as their form and take the mind as their material cause, the definition [of their relationship] is established through the connection characterized by having a single cause; this is the remainder [of the argument]. To the question, "From what [source] is it known that the mind is the material cause of both wisdom and the latent impressions? he says: "Wisdom" (*dhī*).
And the Śruti directly states that *dhīḥ* and *bhīḥ* are indeed the mind itself.
In the passage from the *Śruti*, the word "iti" has the sense of "and so forth.
By this, it is understood that latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are also modifications of the mind.
The connection [of the words] is thus: "iti tu" (but it is so).

Thus, scripture— and by the word "and" (ca), other [scriptures] as well— clearly and directly states that cognition and the rest are modifications of the mind. By this, those who assert that they are effects of the Self are refuted.

Since at that time there is no cognition of external objects, and it is impossible for what is non-existent to serve as a material cause (*upādāna*), the primary meaning [of "mere"] must be set aside.

Furthermore, if the term were used in its primary sense as "merely latent impressions" (*vāsanāmātra*), then the wisdom of the Lord (*īśvara*) would not be included; yet, if both were mentioned separately, there would be prolixity (*gaurava*).
Therefore, with the intention of including both the primary and secondary senses, the term "mere illusion" (*māyāmātra*) was stated in order to encompass both with brevity.

For this very reason, it is not explained as "illusion alone" (*māyāmātra*), because there is no identity between the Lord (*īśvara*)—who is the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) of the intermediate state (*sandhya*)—and primordial wisdom (*prajñā*). [Objection:
But surely there exists a relationship of cause and effect between wisdom and its latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Let that alone be the seed of the characteristic; what is the use of describing both as being effects of the mind? To this, he says: "Consciousness" (cit).
As long as transmigratory existence lasts, this mind is indeed a mixture of consciousness and the unconscious;
therefore, the individual soul always perceives all these states.
Not only in dreams, but the living being perceives all these worldly states at all times by means of the mind alone.
Therefore, because of its primacy, the connection [between the self and objects] must be understood as occurring through that [mind] alone, and not otherwise.
Furthermore, some consider the mind to be indeed insentient (*jaḍa*).
Others, however, [hold that it is] only the insentient upon which consciousness is superimposed.
He states its true nature by refuting that view: "It is indeed a mixture of consciousness and the insentient."
The word "yat" (which) must be supplied [to the beginning of the sentence].

Since it is impossible for that which is purely insentient—such as a jar or similar objects—to possess such a state, and since the superimposition of consciousness upon it has already been refuted, one must accept that [the Self] is indeed a mixture of consciousness and the insentient. And there are scriptural authorities on this point:
If it were the case that all states are attained by means of the mind, then even in liberation those very states would exist because of its presence;
therefore, it is said that "as long as there is saṃsāra, so long does [the mind] effect benefit and harm for the individual soul (*jīva*).
He explains this by saying "because its true nature is not manifested in its entirety," namely: "the modifications of the mind. (9.341)
Objects in dreams are modifications of the mind; they do not exist as external things.
Therefore, they do not become gross, and thus their clarity is never like that [of waking objects].

Since dream-objects are modifications of mental impressions (*manojanya-vāsanā-vikāra*), for that very reason they do not exist as gross like external things; nor do they fail to find space even in a confined location.
Thus, they lack the clarity found in some cases of external objects, as well as the capacity for external causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).

Alternatively, the construction is as follows: because they do not exist as gross like external things, they lack clarity in certain instances; therefore, dream-objects are merely modifications of the mind.

How this is so has been explained previously (*9,343*). Now, one might object that because the enjoyment of a woman in a dream and the like are seen to produce external causal efficacy—such as the emission of the final element (*caramadhātu*)—the reason is "partially unestablished" (*bhāgāsiddhi*). To this, he says: "In some cases" (*kvacit*).
In some cases, they may even be clearly visible... // MDh 3.2.100a //
Those dream-objects might indeed be clear in some instances;
nevertheless, the point is that there is no fault because they are included within the category of "other than that" (i.e., other than the objects of waking experience).
If this were so, then that portion would not consist of latent impressions (*vāsanā*); to this he says: "latent impression."
... and that mental impression is called *vāsanā*. (Manu Smṛti 3.2.100b)
And that mental impression (*mānasī vāsanā*) is established;
the point is that non-materiality (*asthūlatva*) exists even in the absence of clarity.
For this very reason, the reason stated in the Sūtra has been explained in two ways.
Thus, by this statement regarding the nature of latent impressions (vāsanā), what was said—that there is no perfection of place, time, or causal conditions in a dream—is refuted.
For this very reason, the characterization of the scriptural accounts of creation as merely figurative is discarded;
furthermore, the status of the Supreme Consciousness (prājña) as the creator is not rendered futile.
The passage beginning with "having himself destroyed [the world]" and so forth has already been explained elsewhere as referring to the Lord (Īśvara). Furthermore,
the claim that there is an occurrence of connection with the auspicious and inauspicious in the creation of dreams is irrelevant,
because there is no pervasion (vyāpti) [between the two].

Furthermore, the teaching that the individual soul (jīva) possesses the nature of Brahman is untenable because it contradicts the establishment of omniscience and other attributes as being ultimately real.
Moreover, the assertion that the phenomenal world (prapañca), beginning with space, is illusory is refuted by the demonstration of its reality.
Thus concludes the section on the "Twilight" (sandhyā) in the illustrious Nyāyasudhā.
[======= JNys_3,2.II: Parābhidhyānādhikaraṇam =======] Now begins the section concerning "the meditation upon the Supreme" (*parābhidhyāna*) in the illustrious *Nyāyasudhā*.
But [the Self] is concealed by meditation on the Supreme; for from that arise its bondage and its opposite.
3.2.5. Oṃ, but [the Self] is concealed by meditation on the Supreme; for from that arise its bondage and its opposite. Oṃ.
In order to demonstrate that the [doctrine] composed by others is a misinterpretation, he states the purport of the sūtra "parābhidhyānāt" as follows: "īśa... [and so on].
"By the will of the Lord, he disappears... (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.2.100c).
The word "at twilight" (*sandhyam*) is to be understood as the remainder of the sense.
This means that not only sleep, but this disappearance as well, is dependent upon the will of the Lord; it is this very meaning that is expressed by this aphorism, and no other.
For it was stated in the second [chapter] that the soul's status as a portion of the Lord lacks scriptural authority;
furthermore, the opponent does not admit that the powers of knowledge and sovereignty belong to Brahman in a real sense.
Moreover, the phrase "concealed due to connection with a body" is sufficient [to refute the objection].
Anything else would be entirely inconsistent.
Furthermore, if conjunction with the body were the cause of concealment, then manifestation would occur during deep sleep and cosmic dissolution.

If it is argued that this is merely an illustration of ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth, then why was it not stated exactly in that way? Let this elaboration suffice. If the dream disappears, how then can its subsequent cognition be maintained? To this he says: "And it is manifested."
And furthermore, it is manifested by her.
By this, the objection raised by others is refuted.
Furthermore, because the concealment of the individual manifestation is not perceived, he concludes the meaning of the two sections with the words: "Having indeed created... (sṛṣṭvaiva).
Having created the manifold world from his own latent impressions (*vāsanā*) as if it were a dream, the unborn Lord causes it to vanish by reducing it to the state of mere impression alone.
The word *eva* (only) excludes superimposition (*āropa*).
It should also be understood as "having shown.
And [this is done] by reducing it to mere habitual tendency (*vāsanāmātratā*) and having so established it.
Otherwise, it would be a second [case]. "He causes to disappear" means he causes to go out of sight; or, it means "by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of that living being."
Or rather, it means "it causes that [state] to disappear.
Thus ends the section on "Contemplation by Another" (*parābhidhyāna*) in the illustrious *Nyāyasudhā*. [End of Section 3.2.II] [======= JNys_3,2.III:
Section on Deep Sleep, Awakening, and Delusion =======]
Now, in the illustrious *Nyāyasudhā*, the sections concerning awakening and delusion.
The absence [of that dream experience] occurs in the channels and in the Self, because of scriptural statements concerning them;
therefore, awakening arises from this [Self].
In the state of fainting, there is a partial attainment [of death], by process of elimination.
Oṃ, its absence [of movement] is in the channels; its presence is in the self due to its capacity there. Oṃ.
Oṃ, therefore awakening arises from this; Oṃ.
Oṃ! O bewildered one, [this is] due to the remainder of the half-attainment; oṃ!

In this context, in order to indicate that the identity of the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman described by the opponent is not evident from the words of the sūtras, is contrary to them, and must indeed be disregarded, he states the purport of the three sections [of the commentary] beginning with "suṣupti": "Suṣupti... etc.

The Lord of the living soul (jīveśa) always leads the individual soul (jīva)— which is itself subject to that [Lord]— into the states of deep sleep, delusion, and awakening, while remaining ever in control of them.
To the question, "How can this be so, given that other causes for deep sleep, awakening, and so forth are observed? it is said: "He is self-dependent, yet under His control.

The meaning is that although the Lord is independent, He assumes those causes as a sport (*līlā*), brings the individual soul (*jīva*) under their influence, and thereby causes it to attain states such as deep sleep;
this is clearly stated in the Commentary (*Bhāṣya*) and other works.
Thus ends the section on deep sleep, awakening, and delusion. *9,355* [======= JNys_3,2.IV:
Section on Action and Remembrance =======] Now begins the section on action and remembrance.
Oṃ, and that very [Self] exists because of the recollection of actions, the scriptures, and injunctions. Oṃ.
Some explain it as follows:

When there arises a doubt—whether it is that very same individual soul (*jīva*) who, having attained union with Brahman during deep sleep, rises again, or whether it might be another—the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that there is no fixed rule, because, like a drop of water cast into a great ocean, once it has become one with Brahman, its extraction is impossible. To this, the following resolution is offered:
It is that very same person who was asleep who arises.
Why?
Because of the completion of the remainder of one's karma, because of recognition, and because of scriptural texts and injunctions.

Because liberation would result for one who is asleep, the injunction [of meditation] would be untenable; thus, in order to indicate that this is a misinterpretation, he states the purport of the section: "Not another."
And that very [self] [is the agent], because of the recollection of actions, the word [of scripture], and the injunctions;
there is no other agent whatsoever for this.

When it has been stated that dreams and so forth are created by the Supreme Lord, a doubt arises as to whether there is another creator in other places and times, or whether the Lord alone is the creator. Since worldly lords are seen to possess sovereignty only within the limitations of specific places and times, one might conclude that this [Supreme Lord] is likewise limited.

In response, it is established here that the Lord alone is the creator of these dreams and so forth, and that there is no other creator whatsoever in any other place or time; this is precisely the meaning intended to be conveyed.
No one has any doubt as to whether it is the very same person who was asleep who rises, or someone else;
nor is it the case that the identity of the sleeper with Brahman is perceived by any means of valid cognition or accepted by the opponent—this [objection] is therefore trivial.
It should be understood that the explanation proceeds by skipping the sequence for the sake of brevity.
And the author of the Sūtras introduced an interruption in order to make it known that delusion, like a dream and so forth, is not an independent state.
Thus ends the section on the recollection of karma (*karmānusmṛtyadhikaraṇa*).
[======= JNys_3,2.V: sthāna(to 'pya)]
The Section on Non-Difference [of Place] ======= Now begins the Section on the Non-Difference of Place (sthāna).
Oṃ. Even from the standpoint of location, the Supreme possesses both characteristics, for it is so everywhere; Oṃ.
Some explain this as follows:

Brahman is heard to be of two forms—qualified (saviśeṣa) in passages such as "possessing all works, possessing all desires," and so forth; and unqualified (nirviśeṣa) in passages such as "neither gross nor subtle," and so forth.
In that regard, is Brahman to be understood as having both forms, or as having one form or the other?

Even when [Brahman] possesses one of these two forms, a doubt arises as to whether it is with attributes (*saviśeṣa*) or without attributes (*nirviśeṣa*); since both types of scriptural testimony exist, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that Brahman must possess both forms. To this, the following is said:
first of all, it is not possible for the supreme Brahman to possess both forms by its very nature, because of the contradiction involved.
"Let it be, then, that [the Self appears as different] due to its location, through connection with limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as earth and so forth.
Not so;
for a limiting adjunct does not transform one thing into another, but rather, the limiting adjuncts such as earth and so forth, presented by ignorance (avidyā), produce an error.
Therefore, even when adopting either [of the two views], Brahman must be understood as that from which all distinctions have been entirely removed;
for in all such scriptural passages as "soundless, touchless," and so forth, it is precisely Brahman of such a nature that is taught.
If it is argued that this is not so because of the existence of difference, we say no, because each [text] speaks of it as being otherwise than that.
If it is argued that Brahman is not indeed devoid of distinctions because it is taught as being distinct in such passages as "Brahman has four quarters" and "Brahman has sixteen parts," we say no;
for in passages such as "He who is here in this earth," the absence of distinction with respect to each limiting adjunct (upādhi) is expressly stated.
Moreover, some [hold] thus:
"In passages such as 'There is no diversity whatsoever here,' certain followers of particular Vedic branches (śākhins) record non-duality preceded by a censure of the perception of difference.
Anticipating that this interpretation will be set aside by the correct explanation itself—without even needing further effort—he begins the explanation.
It has been stated that the Supreme Person, residing within all bodies and in each individual body in locations such as the right eye and so forth, brings about the states of sleep and the rest.

In this regard, when there arises a doubt as to whether that which exists everywhere is indeed one or mutually distinct— since it is observed that whatever occupies different locations simultaneously is distinct,
as in the case of a jar and other such objects—
and since this [space] occupies different locations, it must therefore be distinct.

Since it is observed that among distinct things there exists a gradation and a relationship between the benefactor and the beneficiary, the objection arises as to how it can be said that "it is the very same [Brahman] which is the object of cognition. To this, the author of the Sūtras has provided the rebuttal:
"Not even from the standpoint of location" (*na sthānato ’pi*). He explains this with the word "no" (*na*).
The Supreme possesses both characteristics everywhere, even from the standpoint of location;
for there is no difference whatsoever in this Supreme Ruler due to a difference in location.
In this context, it is stated that the word "place" (*sthāna*) is an indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) of its various subdivisions.
The suffix *-tasi* is used in the sense of the locative case (*saptamī*), according to the supplementary rule (*upasaṅkhyāna*) beginning with "ādyādibhyaḥ" (Pāṇini 5.4.44). *9,360*
By stating "difference" (*bheda*), the phrase "possessing both genders" (*ubhayaliṅgam*) is explained as having a distinct nature (*bhinnasvarūpatva*).

Even though there is a difference among the locations— the bodies of gods, humans, and so forth— and even within those, among specific parts such as the right eye and others, there exists for that Supreme Lord who resides in each of those places no [quality] characterized by mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) in the form of inferiority or superiority.
Or, there is no distinction consisting of the nature of the benefactor and the beneficiary.
Why is this so? He explains the statement "for everywhere" (*sarvatra hi*) as follows: "everywhere" (*sarvatra*).
"In all respects, he possesses the qualities of a pure consciousness filled with auspiciousness, and is entirely devoid of every defect.
This should also be understood to mean that he is undifferentiated in all states.
The analysis of the compound is: "he who is a vessel for every defect" (*aśeṣadoṣoḍkha*) and "he who possesses the qualities of a full and auspicious consciousness" (*pūrṇakalyāṇacidguṇa*).
"Wholesome" (*kalyāṇā*) means free from destruction and so forth;

alternatively, since the word "quality" (*guṇa*) can also apply to suffering and the like, the term "wholesome" was stated [to exclude those]. After the word *cit*, the phrase "and so forth" (*ādi*) should be supplied.
Alternatively, the meaning is that [the Self] is of the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*), not insentient.

This is because the Supreme Self is heard [in scripture] in such passages as, "In all beings, they call this very one Brahman," and so forth; the word "since" is to be understood as the ellipsis. (9.362)
Om. If it is argued that [the whole] does not exist because of the non-existence of its parts, we say no; for it is stated that [the whole exists] in each part individually. Om.
Having raised an objection against the stated point, the Sūtra provides a resolution with the words "not because of difference" (*na bhedāt*).
It is not tenable that Brahman is undifferentiated, always free from all defects, and complete in all qualities, [if one holds otherwise], for it is said:
"Those two are bound by cause and effect."

The meaning of the objection is that such defects as difference, being subject to blemish, and possessing limited qualities—indicated by the word "difference" (bheda)—have been stated in scriptural passages from the Śruti and Purāṇas, etc.
He explains the portion of the refutation, "No," with the words: "But that is contradictory."
If it is argued that [the whole] does not [arise] from the parts, we say no, because each part is not spoken of as being that [the whole].
Furthermore, whatever is contradictory to that [whole] could never be a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) regarding it.

As for that sentence which is perceived as contradictory to the stated meaning, it cannot serve as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding that specific contradictory sense; rather, some other meaning must be understood for it.
Why? Because it has been stated that "each [word] does not express that [contradictory sense]. This appears to be untenable.

Since it would be redundant to again present that same [limited] measure when there has already been a statement that "it is everywhere," and when an objection regarding its counter-position has been raised, he states the intended meaning:
"By way of the great purport... [Mānava-dharmaśāstra 3.2.104cd]:
"But how can that be authoritative here, given that it contradicts the great purport? (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 3.2.104cd)

Since the supreme purport of all the Smṛtis, Itihāsas, and Purāṇas is that the Supreme Lord is entirely free from all defects and is replete with all auspicious qualities, how could that statement serve as a means of valid knowledge regarding the Lord’s possession of defects and so forth here, given its contradiction [with that purport]? The word "tu" (but) is intended to indicate the distinction between being a major statement (*mahāvākya*) and being a subordinate statement (*avāntaravākya*).
For it is observed that a subordinate sentence which contradicts the meaning of the principal great sentence (*mahāvākya*) lacks authority in that context.

For example, the subordinate sentence, "Whether he exists in that world or not," lacks authority because it contradicts the meaning of the principal great sentence regarding the Agnihotra sacrifice, whose purpose is heaven;
this is because [the subordinate sentence] is not a cause for the comprehension of that [principal] meaning. (9.364)
It might be argued as follows:

if the great purport of the Vedas and other scriptures were that the Supreme Lord is replete with all auspicious qualities and entirely free from all defects, then this meaning would possess valid proof.
However, we do not perceive that very point; therefore, he says: "Suffering," etc.
The Vedic word would be a means of valid cognition precisely because it is the cause for the cessation of suffering and the attainment of happiness...
[Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.2.105a–c].

Although it should have been stated "by way of being the cause of liberation," the expression beginning with "cessation of suffering" is intended to define the nature of liberation due to the conflicting views of various disputants; [liberation] consists of the absolute cessation of suffering and the manifestation of unsurpassed bliss.
Regarding the term "liberation" (mukti):
alternatively, this is intended to include heaven and other such primary goals;
the instrumental case here is used in the sense of a characteristic mark of a particular state.

The Vedic word— this being an elliptical expression for the Smṛtis and other scriptures— must be the means of establishing some object only in such a way that its status as a cause is fulfilled precisely by its being the cause of the attainment of happiness and the exhaustion of suffering. It must thus be a communicator of some meaningful reality.
This is what is meant:
a treatise must indeed possess both a subject matter and a purpose,
because it is a means of valid cognition and because it is intended for the benefit of others.
In that case, when the subject matter is doubtful but the purpose is certain,
the uncertain subject matter must be ascertained by means of the certain purpose;
for a treatise is not the direct producer of the purpose.
However, [the subject matter is determined] solely by means of the presentation of the purpose.
And thus, that very thing in which the purpose is realized once it has been made known is determined to be the subject matter;
otherwise, because the subject matter and the purpose would be unrelated, the treatise would result in being unworthy of acceptance.

Furthermore, the primary purpose of the Vedas and so forth is indeed liberation (*mokṣa*), as indicated by such passages as: "This scripture proceeds for the sake of abandoning suffering. Heaven and the like, however, are not the primary purpose.
Therefore, that very object must be postulated in which, once known, liberation and so forth are attained; thus it should be understood.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "That" (tad).
... from that very gracious Īśāna, and not otherwise.
That liberation (kaivalya), which consists of the dissolution of suffering and so forth,
can arise only from Īśāna, that is, Viṣṇu himself, and not from anyone else;
for he alone is its dispenser, and no other.

Let it be that this alone is the object; why then is it not [attained] through "perfection in qualities" and so forth? To this it is said: "only from clarity, and not otherwise, nor merely from being known.
If one asks what follows from that, he says: "clarity."
For clarity of mind arises solely from the knowledge of the excellence of virtues, and also from the thorough knowledge of their faultlessness; it does not arise through any other means whatsoever.
The grace of Viṣṇu arises solely from the knowledge of His excellence of attributes and from the thorough understanding of His faultlessness;
the word "hi" (for) indicates that this is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*),
and that will be explained later.
The word *kevala* (exclusive) has the sense of exclusion;
it means "not by anything else," that is, not by such a corresponding cognition of having few virtues and so forth, nor by ritual action (*karman*) and the like.

And thus, by means of the scripture whose purpose is liberation and so forth, there is only the knowledge of the excellence of the Lord's qualities and His faultlessness, which serves as the means for that [liberation].

Since [the Lord] is that which must be produced for the sake of living beings, it is determined that the great purport of the entire scripture lies in Nārāyaṇa alone, who is replete with all qualities and from whom every defect has been dispelled.

One might object: "This would be so if what was stated in the passages beginning with 'That Lord' and 'Āditya' were authoritative. To this, he cites scriptural statements from that context: "He who [knows] me... and so forth.
To him who knows me as one whose mass of defects is entirely exhausted and who is augmented by the totality of all virtues— to him, being well-pleased, I shall grant liberation, and not otherwise.
He who knows me as being without exception and supreme—he alone knows me;
to him I grant all desires and the highest state.
He who, being thus undeluded, reflects: "Why do my enemies revile me? [Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.2.109ab]
By the word *bṛṃhita*, he expresses that each of the qualities is also limitless.
He alone knows me— who am unsurpassed by all others in my qualities and who am the most excellent among all beings through the absence of defects.
Because knowledge of anything else is not caused by my grace.
By the words "He who [knows Me] thus," he summarizes the Lord's speech beginning with "And he has accomplished all that was to be done, O Bhārata" and ending with those words.
Thus, by means of all the qualities and the absence of defects,

the state of being pleased is illuminated through praises such as "He is the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), for He is superior to both the perishable and the imperishable, and He is the All-Knowing One."
In every way and by means of all his being;
otherwise, there would be a contradiction. Having accomplished what was to be done, he is liberated.
By the words “What [is it] to me? [the following is meant]: “I alone am the one who has overcome; what do these two do? What do these three do?
I strike down many hosts in battle; why do my enemies, being godless, revile me? (Ṛgveda 10.48.7).
Thus he cites the Śruti:
"I alone am the one who overcomes this entire universe; I alone am the *niṣpāṭ*, meaning I utterly subdue (*nitarāṃ sahate*) it. Regarding the two worlds, I alone am the *niṣpāṭ*.
Even as for the three worlds, what can they do to me? They are not able to effect anything undesirable for me.

But I alone, like a threshing-floor, strike down those many, very numerous, or most excellent harsh revilers, just as one strikes down grains situated on a threshing-floor; therefore, those powerless enemies can do nothing to me by way of reviling—
this is the meaning of the Blessed One’s words.
In this regard, it is heard that toward those who revile [the Buddha], the Blessed One feels displeasure and that they incur misfortune;
furthermore, it is well known that reviling consists in the recognition of faults and so forth. *9,369*
He states the purpose of the example of the sentence with the words "ityādi" (and so forth).
This is determined by such scriptural and traditional statements as these.
By means of the restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa*), he indicates its preeminence.
The statement to be made later, "Liberation [comes] through serene faith from the realization of the qualities," is also connected here.
Regarding this, he also states an inference: "And from common worldly experience."
And liberation from the world comes through faith, by virtue of recognizing those qualities.

The word "iti" is to be supplied; it continues from the sense of "is determined. Liberation from saṃsāra occurs through the grace of the Blessed One. That grace of the Blessed One arises from the perception of the excellence of His qualities and the perception of the absence of faults; this meaning is determined—both from common worldly experience and from inference supported by worldly examples—and thus the formal argument (prayoga) is as follows:
Liberation from saṃsāra is achievable through the grace of the supremely capable Person, because it is liberation, like the release from shackles;
for indeed, there is no one other than the Blessed One who is capable in that regard.
The devotion to the Blessed One under discussion is accomplished through the knowledge of the excellence of his qualities, because it is a form of great devotion, like the devotion of a king.
Since this is analogous to the subject of the thesis (*pakṣa*), no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) should be urged.

Concluding what was stated in the passage beginning with "by obstructing the great purport" (*mahātātparyavirodhena*), he extends the same reasoning to the refutation of the misinterpretations made by others, stating: "by the great purport," etc.
For this very reason, because it would contradict the primary great purport [of the scripture]. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 3.2.110cd)
In no way can the meaning of the Śruti, Purāṇas, and other scriptures be that [the Brahmin] is defective, devoid of qualities, or possesses only meager qualities. (Manu Smṛti 3.2.111a–c)
The mention of "being devoid of qualities" (nirguṇatva) is for the purpose of refuting erroneous explanations.
The phrase "in any way whatsoever" means "not through connection with limiting adjuncts (upādhi) and so forth."

Not only is there inferential evidence that all the Vedas and other scriptures have their primary purport (*mahātātparya*) toward the excellence of the Lord's qualities and so forth, but there is also scriptural testimony; thus he says: "That which contradicts it... [tadviruddha].
...and its opposite; and the entire meaning has been determined by Vāsudeva himself with due respect. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.2.111d–f)
Because it possesses defects and so forth, it is contradictory to the entire scripture. He recites that statement: "Thus, this is the most secret."
Thus, O sinless one, this most secret teaching has been declared by me;
having understood this, O Bhārata, one becomes wise and has fulfilled his duty.
Thus... [Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.2.113a]

Thus, that which has been stated by me regarding my own status as the Supreme Person (*puruṣottama*) and so forth—this most secret scripture is the meaning to be established through the essential purport of all scriptures. By the praise "having understood this," reverence is implied. Furthermore, it was indicated by the phrase "of the Supreme Ruler" (*pareśituḥ*) that the inference based on the distinction of locations is otherwise established (*anyathāsiddha*).
As it has been said:
"Due to its sovereignty, its form is one, yet it can manifest as many like the sun.
And he says that [this scripture] is not superseded by time (kālātīta) with the words "Therefore" (ataḥ).
Therefore, because it contradicts all authentic treatises, no inference applies to that matter... // MAnu 3.2.113a-c //
In that regard, concerning the distinction between the Supreme Lord and so forth (*parameśvara-bhedādi*),
he concludes the meaning of the section with the words "by that" (*tena*).
...by him the Lord, possessed of all excellent qualities, was discerned.
The word *sat* has the sense of "without distinction.
While it should have been concluded with the phrase "without distinction," this conclusion regarding its result is intended also to conclude the refutation of erroneous explanations.
Thus [the section on] the locus (sthāna).
The Section on Difference.
[9.373] Now begins the Section on Analogy (Upamā).
// Oṃ And for this very reason, there is a simile [of the reflection] like that of the sun and so forth. Oṃ //
Here, for the sake of establishing the absolute devotion of the individual soul (jīva) toward the Supreme Lord, the doctrine of difference-and-non-difference (bhedābheda) is refuted. To explain:
the distinction between the individual soul and Brahman is indeed accepted by the proponents of our own school (siddhāntin).
Non-difference, however, is established through inference:
the individual soul is non-different from Brahman because it is conscious, like Brahman itself,
and because it is a part of Brahman.
Whatever is a part is non-different from that [whole], just as the fish and other [manifestations] which are parts of the Lord are non-different from Him.

Thus, when it has been established that the individual soul (jīva) is both different and non-different from Brahman, the author of the Sūtras provides a rebuttal with the fragment of the Sūtra: "Like the sun and so forth" (*sūryakādivat*).

Since this statement of an illustration alone neither proves nor refutes any point, he demonstrates the thesis and the reason by first negating the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), beginning with the words: "And not... (*na ca*).
For this very reason, the analogy is like that of the sun's reflection and so forth.
Nor can the non-difference of the individual soul (jīva) from [the Lord] be established on the grounds of its being consciousness, as if it were identical to the Lord;
for scripture sufficiently declares that this soul is merely a reflection.
The phrase "because of being sentient" (cittvāt) is also an elliptical indication of [the reason] "because of being a part. The remainder [of the sense] is that [it is] non-different from Brahman.
This is like [the case of] Īśa, like Brahman, and like the incarnations of the Lord (īśvara).
It is attained and joined;
that is, the state of being a reflection of this living soul within this Brahman.
"Thus" (evam) means clearly and without contradiction.
This is what is being said:
it is not tenable to establish the non-difference of the individual soul (jīva) from Brahman through an inference based on its sentience and other such qualities.

The individual soul (jīva) is not non-different from Brahman, because it is a reflection thereof; for whatever is a reflection of something is not non-different from that thing, just as the sun's reflection and the like are not non-different from the sun and so forth—thus, there is a contradiction with this inference.
Nor is the reason unestablished, because it is clearly established by scripture.
To the question "What is that scripture?", he cites it: "Just as... (*yathā*).
Just as this shadow exists in a person, so is this [universe] spread out within Him.
Just as a shadow is spread out, so too this entire multitude of living beings is spread out—that is, dependent—upon this Supreme Self.
He demonstrates this very point through two clear scriptural citations: "Shadow," etc.
Just as a shadow resembles a person and is dependent upon that person,
even so all beings, beginning with Brahmā, have the Supreme Self as their essence.
Just as in matters concerning existence, cognition, and actions, the individual is understood to be dependent on the Person (puruṣa),
so too are the liberated souls merely manifestations of the Supreme Self;
they are essentially of the nature of the Self, yet possess limited consciousness.
Individual souls (*puruṣas*) are transmigrators.
He will state that their very nature as "reflections" (*ābhāsa*) consists precisely in their being dependent upon Him [the Supreme Lord] and so forth.
This reflection-nature of the Supreme Lord does not belong to all [souls].
And [the text] reads two scriptural passages—“The shadow of Viṣṇu” and so forth—to state its essential nature, namely that it is not direct, but rather traditional (pāramparyeṇa).
Chāyā is the wife of Viṣṇu, and Dhātṛ is the husband of Ramā; these two are the preeminent ones.
From them came Indra and Kāma, and from those two, all the others as well.
Of Hara, Brahmā, and Viṣṇu, Indra is the specific presiding deity;
and Māra is the presiding deity of all these [other] luminaries, because they are dependent upon them.

All others have only limited power, while the supreme Hari possesses full power; even though they share the quality of consciousness, they are distinct from him, and therefore [are always subordinate] to him.
Like one shadow to another;
the two distinct ones are Garuḍa and Śeṣa.
The shadow of his relics is upon those two, Garuḍa and Śeṣa.
Furthermore, for those two, Indra and Kāma,
Brahmā [is the source] of Hari;
the word "emanation" (abhāsa) is to be connected everywhere.
The explanation of "being a manifestation" is "dependence upon that.
By the word "all," he establishes that all things are manifestations of the Supreme Lord. The word "ca" (and) has the sense of the particle "tu" (but/rather), as in "Haris tu" (But Hari...).
To the question "Why [is it so] even if it is an appearance?", it is said: "even though it is conscious."
Here too, that [term] is an indication of being a part of that;
therefore, because it is a manifestation.
By the word "always" (sarvada), he indicates the restriction that [these] are indeed distinct.
He states the result of the scriptural citations mentioned above with the words "and so forth" (ityādi).
For from such scriptural passages as these, it is indeed known that there is only difference.
The meaning is that by this [scriptural statement], the soul's nature as a reflection of the Supreme Lord is known, and through that, its absolute difference [from Him] is also known.
It is not said that our two inferences are counter-balanced (*satpratipakṣa*);
rather, the intention is that our inference is sublated because it possesses greater force due to its being based on scripture (*śrauta*). *9,378*

Now, in order to explain the portion of the aphorism beginning with “And for this very reason, the comparison [is justified],” he states the doubt that must be dispelled: “For [if it were otherwise], there would be the status of being a mere semblance,” and so forth.
For it has been determined that the individual soul (jīva) is a manifestation of the Supreme Self (paramātman);
therefore, that [other view] is not tenable... 3.2.120a-c.
That the individual soul (*jīva*) is determined by the authority of scripture to be a reflection (*ābhāsa*) of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is contradicted by reasoning;
for a matter contradicted by unassailable reasoning cannot be established even by scripture.
If it were so, it would follow that the section concerning the "possessor of conceit" (*abhimāny-adhikaraṇa*) need not have been commenced at all.
Therefore, it must be construed in some way or another.
To the question "Why is it not logical? he says: "That which... (yad iti).
... that which appears depends upon the teacher. (Manu 3.2.120cd)
The meaning is as follows: since a reflection, such as that of the sun and so forth, is known to be dependent upon limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as water;
and since this dependence on a limiting adjunct for the state of being a reflection is ascertained everywhere by way of pervasion (vyāpaka).
Nevertheless, why is it not logical? To this he says: "upādhi... [and so forth].
Because of the absence of the status of a preceptor... // MĀnuv 3.2.121a //

The word "of living beings" (*jīvānām*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. Since the state of being dependent on a teacher—which is the pervader—is absent in living beings, its pervaded counterpart, the state of being a mere appearance (*ābhāsatvam*), is also not tenable. Therefore, because the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddhi*), the inference is flawed.
For this reason as well, he states that it is "defective," beginning with the words "because of being a mere semblance."
... because of the contradiction with its being a mere appearance.
Inference is also flawed because of the contradiction arising from the distinctness of the appearance (*ābhāsa*). To explain:
the ocular rays, having come into contact with a mirror or similar object, are reflected back; thus, being in contact with the face, they take that very face as their object.
But there is no appearance other than that [object itself];

therein, the exclusion, the externality, the transposition of left and right, and so forth, are perceived solely through error (*bhrānti*). And since this is an error conditioned by limiting adjuncts (*sopādhika*), it does not cease as long as those adjuncts persist.
And thus, because the state of being an appearance is pervaded by non-difference, [the reason] is contradictory (*viruddha*) when proving difference.
This is also an illustration;
one should also observe that it is "mistimed" (*kālātīta*), as it contradicts such scriptural texts as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*).

If it is asked why the inference based on the nature of appearance (*ābhāsatva*) is faulty, [the author] replies that its identity with the two previously stated uncontradicted inferences is established:
"Because of being conscious and because of being a part, the identity of the aggregate would follow" (MAnu 3.2.121cd).
The logical connection is that [the world] is a part [of Brahman].
Furthermore, it has been stated that the unity being established is not like that of the proponents of Māyā; this is indicated by the word "samudāya" (aggregate).
For the proponents of Māyā indeed accept the absolute non-difference of each individual soul from Brahman;
however, this is not our view,
because even when there is oneness of the aggregate, difference also exists.
To the question, "Why is the unity of the aggregate accepted while absolute non-difference is abandoned? he says: "Therefore" (*ataḥ*).
"Therefore, there would be a distinctness between the aggregate and its parts. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.2.122ab)

Because the oneness of the aggregate is accepted, that separateness which was stated regarding the "Lord" (Śat) and so forth would belong to the aggregate and its constituent part, the individual soul (jīva);
or rather, it would belong to both the individual soul and the Lord, who are the two parts of that aggregate.
This is what is meant.
If the absolute non-difference of the individual soul from Brahman were established, then the scriptural texts concerning difference would be contradicted;
[this difference is merely] illusory (māyika).
And if they were to designate [the self] as being other [than the body], they would fall into the state of lacking valid cognition.
Nor is this a fault on our part,

because the existence of a distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman, as well as between the individual soul and the Lord (īśvara), makes it logically possible for [the objection] to have that as its object.
By this, the refutation of the fallacious nature of the inference based on "consciousness" and so forth is accomplished.
It has been stated that there is unity of the aggregate;
he elaborates on that slightly with the words "called Īśa."
The name "Lord" (Īśa) may apply to the collection... // MAnu 3.2.122c //
The word "Īśa" refers to Brahman,
[the Lord] of the collection of conscious beings;
this is what is meant.
The reality that is established by its very nature as the oneness of Brahman is the ultimate truth; through connection with *māyā*, it attains the state of Īśvara.
He is omniscient, the Lord of all, and the agent of the creation and other processes of the universe.

The individual souls (*jīvas*), however, are portions of Brahman, having consciousness as their nature, like sparks from a fire; for this reason, they are both different from and non-different from Brahman.
The individual selves are indeed distinct from one another and from the Lord;
however, Brahman is the totality of all conscious beings and is something transcendent. Regarding this, he provides an illustration: "The Lord," etc.
... as if arisen from the forms of the Lord. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.2.122d)
Just as it was stated by the Siddhāntin that the designation "Lord" does not apply to the collection of forms such as the Fish and others even in terms of their location (*sthāna*), so it is here.

By this, having set aside absolute non-difference (*atyantābheda*) and accepted both difference and non-difference (*bhedābheda*), the two-fold scriptural testimony as well as the inference based on being a part (*aṃśatva*) has been stated.

If the individual souls (*jīvas*) were parts of Brahman in the same way that the Fish and others are parts of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), then the souls would possess freedom from suffering and other qualities just as the Fish and others possess sovereignty and other attributes.
Because the similarity between a part and the whole is never absent.

Furthermore, if the non-difference of the individual soul (jīva) from Brahman were also the ultimate reality (paramārtha), then the liberation described as "becoming Brahman itself" would be untenable; therefore, he says: "Hence... (*ataḥ*).
Therefore, upon the removal of the limiting adjuncts such as the body, there arises equanimity with those who possess the form of the Lord...
[he refers to] "that" as his own established doctrine present in the intellect.
Neither difference nor non-difference between individual souls (*jīvas*) and Brahman is inherent;

rather, non-difference is inherent while difference is adventitious (*aupādhika*). This is just as the parts of the Lord, such as the Fish-incarnation and others, are related to the Lord; however, there is this distinction: [the former is eternal, whereas the latter is not].

The Fish-form and others, for the sake of favoring the world, possess unobscured sovereignty and other attributes, being differentiated only by the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of their playful incarnations (*līlā-vigraha*).

The individual souls (*jīvas*), however, are differentiated by the limiting adjuncts of the body, senses, and so forth, which are bound by beginningless ignorance, desire, and karma; thus, their true nature as Brahman is obscured, and they experience suffering and other states conditioned by those adjuncts.

Since difference is therefore purely adventitious (*aupādhika*), when there is the absolute cessation of the adjuncts such as the body through knowledge and action, the equality of the individual souls with the forms of the Lord (*īśvara-rūpa*) occurs.

Just as the forms of the Lord, at the conclusion of their activity, attain the state of lordship by voluntarily discarding their playful bodies (*līlā-vigraha*), so too the individual souls (*jīva*), having accumulated a combination of knowledge and action (*jñāna-karma-samuccaya*), become completely liberated from limiting adjuncts such as the body at the conclusion of their *prārabdha* karma and attain their innate Brahmanhood. Thus, there is no fault whatsoever; and as for what was stated—that [Brahmanhood] would be dependent on limiting adjuncts—that is unproven.

He raises an objection with the words "Now" (atha), with the intention that there is no contradiction in accepting that even individual souls (jīvas) are mere appearances, like the reflection of the sun and so forth.
... whereas appearances are primarily like those of the sun and so forth. MĀnuv 3.2.123cd.
When ... // Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.2.124a //
The word "atha" (now/then) indicates either the commencement of a doubt or an alternative position.
The term "appearances" (ābhāsāḥ) refers to individual souls (jīvas).
The phrase "in the primary sense" means by virtue of being dependent upon limiting adjuncts (upādhi).
"It is like the sun-crystal and so forth" means it exists similarly to the sun-crystal and so forth;
this connects with the subsequent sentence. He provides the rebuttal: "In that case... (tadā).
...then the destruction of the forms of the preceptors would occur. (Manu 3.124ab)
If the souls were dependent upon limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), then upon the destruction of those adjuncts, they would be subject to destruction, just like reflections of the sun and so forth.

Alternatively, if the adjuncts were indestructible, there would be a contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge, and there would be perpetual transmigratory existence; thus, in either case, the scripture on liberation (*mokṣa-śāstra*) would be rendered useless.
Therefore, since it is impossible to accept dependence upon adjuncts, the non-establishment of their being mere appearances (*abhāsatva*) remains firmly intact. (9.384)
He introduces a portion of the Sūtra as a means to dispel this doubt, saying: "Thus, having raised the doubt..."
To dispel such a doubt, the Lord, the Master of the Vedas, said:
"Therefore, it is indeed a comparison... (Manu 3.2.124c–e).
The word "ca" (and) is placed out of its logical order [after "upamā"], as in the phrase "ata eva ca upamā" (and therefore it is a simile).
Or rather, this much alone constitutes the sentence for the purpose of dispelling that doubt; the word "eva" (only/just) indicates that this is not a citation (*pratīkagrahaṇa*) of the sūtra.
For otherwise, one might suspect a repetition of the phrase "sūryakādivat" (like the reflection of the sun, etc.).
Alternatively, by rejecting the interpretation as a single coherent statement, he declares that the explanation offered by others is a false exposition:

"Precisely because this Self is of the nature of consciousness, devoid of distinctions, transcending speech and mind, and teachable only through the negation of the other, it is for this very reason that the scriptures on liberation employ similes such as the sun in water— intending thereby its non-ultimate possession of distinctions caused by limiting adjuncts."
Even though a syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) is thus achieved, there remains a fault in the meaning which has been demonstrated in various places; furthermore, the particle *vati* is redundant,
since the sense is complete with the mere expression "sūryakādi" (beginning with Sūryaka).
He states the purport of this fragment of the sūtra— namely, that the word "iti" should not be supplied [to the preceding]— with the words "anyā" (others).
... distinguished by the appearance of something else.
By this portion of the Sūtra, the author of the Sūtras declares the specific distinction— that is, the difference— of living beings from other luminous bodies such as the sun.
Since this intended meaning is obtained through the very words of the Sūtra,
he first demonstrates the referent pointed out by the word "this" (idam) with the phrase "that which was stated."
As for what was stated— that the soul's dependence [on the Supreme] in all states without exception,
as well as its similarity [to Him], consists merely in being consciousness (*cittva*) and nothing else—
this "dependence on Him" means dependence on the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
In all activities without exception,
and in the passage beginning with "The creation during the intermediate state [is real],
for so it is said," there is similarity with the Supreme Self.
Regarding what was stated in the passage beginning with "like masculinity and so forth," what is that similarity?
It is merely the nature of being a mind (cittva),
and not anything else such as independence (svātantrya) and so on.
The intention is that [if it were so], there would be a contradiction of the reason (*hetu*).
Now, he applies the statement "and by this very fact, there is a simile" with the words "by that much alone."
And by that much alone, manifestation constitutes the form of these conscious selves.

The meaning is as follows: because they are dependent on that [the Supreme Self] and merely resemble it, we have stated that the form (*rūpa*)—that is, the essential nature (*svarūpa*)—of these conscious selves (*cidātman*) is "appearance" (*ābhāsa*).
Furthermore, the comparison to the sun's reflection and so forth is justified by that much alone.

While one might simply say "the individual soul" (*jīva*), the expression "the form of these conscious selves" is used to show that both of these [dependence and resemblance] exist even in the case of liberated beings.

By this very fact—namely, by those two qualities already under discussion, namely dependence upon that [the original] and similarity to that—it is stated that there is the nature of being a reflection (*ābhāsatva*) and the comparison with the sun’s reflection and so forth; thus, it is said that the intention of the author is revealed and the meaning of the Sūtra is established.
He shows what is excluded by the word "only" (*eva*) with the word "not" (*na*).
Nor [is it dependent] on the authority of a preceptor and so forth... // MAnu 3.2.126c //
The meaning is that [the self] is not [subject to change] even by virtue of its dependence on adjuncts (*upādhi*), its destruction when they are destroyed, or its increase when they increase.
Here, because of the use of the plural number, it should be understood that the logical consequence (*āpādana*) that "it would be perishable" is also implied as an illustration.
[Objection: But if this were the case, there would be no relationship between the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the subject of the argument (*dārṣṭāntika*).
For that [similarity] occurs only when there is absolute equality;

otherwise, since a mere similarity such as being an object of cognition (*prameyatva*) is possible everywhere, even a mosquito would become an illustration for an elephant. Therefore, he says: "not excessive similarity."
... there is no excessive similarity in the illustration.
For an example (*nidarśana*) is that in which the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the probans by the probandum is demonstrated; therefore,
only the similarity between the properties of the probandum and the probans should be sought there through the corroborative instance (*dārṣṭāntika*),
but not absolute identity.
If that were the case, it would follow that all inference would be abolished;
for even a mosquito, provided it possesses the intended property, must be accepted as an example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
[Objection: But is it not the case that "mere consciousness" (*cittvamātra*) is untenable?
Because this would contradict the acceptance of happiness and other qualities in liberation, he says: "Something... (kiñcit).
Even a slight resemblance to pleasure and so forth belongs to the gods and not to mortals.
The sense is this: apart from the asuras, even among other living beings there is indeed some degree of similarity in terms of pleasure and so forth with the Lord;
however, although such similarity in pleasure and so forth exists, it was not mentioned because it does not extend everywhere.
But the similarity in sentience (*cittva*) was mentioned because it extends everywhere.
The term "something" (*kiñcit*) is stated in order to exclude [the possibility of] infinite pleasure and so forth;
otherwise, the reason would be contradictory (*viruddha*).
This is the meaning of the whole.

The meaning of the reason "because it is a manifestation of Brahman" is that it is dependent on Brahman and resembles it, but not because it is a reflection like the sun's image in water and so forth.
Nor is this meaning unestablished,
as it has been demonstrated more thoroughly above.

Nor is it pervaded by dependence on an adjunct (upādhi), such that it would be excluded by the exclusion of that [adjunct]; for it exists even in cases devoid of dependence on an adjunct. Furthermore, there is no partial unestablishedness (bhāgāsiddhi).
This is because it has been established as having the nature of the conscious self (cidātman);
nor is it contradictory,
since it exists even among distinct entities.

Even so, if it is argued that because the original object (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*) are identical, the analogy of the sun and so forth is deficient in both the probandum and the probans, we say no;
for there is a lack of valid evidence (*pramāṇa*).
First of all, it is not perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Because that [cognition] grasps difference through such qualities as being internal or external,
recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is indeed unestablished;
nor is there inference, due to the absence of a probans (*liṅga*).
Because absolute similarity is shown to be fallacious by the case of the left and right hands and so forth; because the absence of dissimilarity is unestablished;
and because equality of action is inconclusive due to its presence in shadows and the like.
Because the absence of a separate cause is inconclusive with respect to eternal things;
because it is doubtful whether [the reflection] is produced solely by the cause that is the original object (*bimba*);
for indeed, even an unperceived separate cause is postulated in accordance with an observed effect that appears distinct.
However, one does not deny an observed effect simply because its cause is not perceived;
for if that were the case, many contradictions would arise.
Therefore, it is precisely an *upādhi* (limiting condition) that is postulated as the cause.
Scriptural traditions, however, must have only figurative meanings because they contradict perception and other means of valid cognition.
Furthermore, if visual rays, being obstructed by water and the like, were to perceive a face, then they should likewise perceive it when obstructed by stone and such.
Furthermore, there is no utility whatsoever for "transparency" (*svacchatā*) in this process; enough said on that point.
As for the contradiction with such scriptural texts as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), that will be refuted later.
Therefore, the inference regarding its being a mere appearance (*ābhāsatva*) is indeed free from fault. *9,395*
Now, by what function does the term *brahmābhāsa* (reflection of Brahman) express the soul's dependence on Brahman and its similarity to Brahman?
If you say it is by a figurative (*gauṇī*) function,
then since the employment of words rests with us, you must state the purpose for which we would employ a word that is not expressive [of the primary sense].
"Not so;
because it relies upon yoga," he says: "from that."
Therefore, it shines eternally, and in that same way, it also appears.

"Since manifestation and existence likewise proceed from it on all sides, the individual soul (jīva) is always designated as a mere reflection (ābhāsa) of the Supreme Self (paramātman). By that Supreme Self acting as the cause, it shines forth—that is, it becomes perceived; thus, its dependence upon that [Self] is stated in relation to its perception."
By the phrase "it appears like Brahman," its similarity [to Brahman] is indicated.
Furthermore, the word "api" (also/furthermore) serves to combine the explanations.
"Appearance" (bhāna) means knowledge (jñāna).
Existence (*astitva*) is being (*sattva*). The word *asti* is an indeclinable (*avyaya*), according to its inclusion in the list beginning with "asti, svati."
The word "api" (also/even) serves to conjoin existence and non-existence;
the word "ca" (and) serves to conjoin the explanation;
and the word "eva" (only/just) is connected with "tata eva" (from that very [cause]).
By the restatement "ā," the explanation is "samantāt" (from all sides).
Because [the soul] arises from the Supreme Self alone, the phrase "tataḥ kāraṇāt" (for that reason) should be applied by repetition as "tataḥ paramātmana eva jīvasya bhavataḥ tataḥ kāraṇāt.
Furthermore, *bhā* and *āmā* together form *bhā'se*.

The two manifestations (*ābhāse*) exist throughout all time; he whose manifestations are dependent upon the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is "one whose manifestation is the Supreme Self" (*paramātmābhāsaḥ*).
Regarding the rule for vowel-sandhi (*svara-saṃdhi*): "In some cases, [an element] behaves like what precedes it, while in others it behaves like what follows it."

In considering the caesura (*yati*), one should observe that because of the rule stating "the substitution of *yaṇ* is treated as if it were the beginning of the subsequent [element]," no violation of the caesura is to be feared. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.2.129ab) This is not so, because [the self] is like the reflection of the sun and other objects dependent upon water.

"Not because it is like a reflection of the sun and so forth dependent on water" means that just as reflections of the sun and so forth are dependent on conditions such as water, there is no such appearance here due to dependence on conditions.
[Objection: But surely this point has already been stated by the phrase "not because of dependence on conditions and so forth."
True.

There is no fault, for the very meaning that was stated in the passage beginning with "as has been said" and so forth, is further elaborated upon by the passage beginning with "therefore it appears as such" and so forth.
To explain:
The intended meaning of the statement, "Form belongs to these conscious selves," has been explained as being always so.
This may be the case.
The author of the Sūtra has stated merely an illustration; on the strength of that, some logical reason must be supplied. Nor is there any rule that it must necessarily be a fallacious one.
Nor is there any restrictive rule for the inclusion of the term "appearance" (*ābhāsa*);
therefore, this [objection] is inconsistent.
It is not so.
Since the author of the Sūtras intends "being a manifestation of Brahman" (*brahmābhāsatva*)— as stated in the phrase "and it is merely an appearance"— to serve as the reason here,

and since that very point already established in the relevant section of the work is brought to mind by implication through its being a part of Brahman, this discussion is appropriately carried out here; thus, there is no fault whatsoever.
Is it not the established doctrine that the individual soul (jīva) is a reflection of the Lord precisely because it possesses an adjunct (upādhi)?
Furthermore, since the adjunct itself is eternally conscious, the objection is avoided.
As it has been said:
"Furthermore, because the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is eternal, the individual soul (*jīva*) does not perish;
and since the limiting adjunct is its very nature, there can be no conception of it as having a distinct limiting adjunct.
How is this so?
Thus,
the adjunct (upādhi) of the individual soul (jīva) is indeed twofold:
internal and external.
In this context, the internal cause is that which brings about the manifestation of the thing's own nature (*svarūpa*);
the external cause, such as the internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*), is that which brings about a manifestation contrary to its true nature.
This was stated with the intention that consciousness does not possess dependence on that [body] and so forth;
as it has been said:
"The adjunct (upādhi) of the individual soul (jīva) is declared to be twofold: its own nature (svarūpa) and the external."
"The external adjunct dissolves, but for the other, there remains stability in liberation.
