Even the expression "reflection without an adjunct" (nirupādhi-pratibimba) is to be understood as intending that it does not depend upon an external adjunct.
Furthermore, the word "and" (ca) in the Sūtra has been explained as having the sense of a conjunction with the state of being a manifestation (ābhāsatva).
Alternatively, it should be understood as having the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*).
If that were so, however, there would be the fault of redundancy (*punarukta*), because the word "eva" also has the sense of restriction; therefore, he says: "dependence upon that" (*tadadhīnatva*).
"...the two [terms] occurring in the Sūtra indicate both dependence upon that very [person] and a certain degree of similarity. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 3.2.129c–f)

The word *eva* signifies "dependence upon that" (*tadadhīnatvam eva*), and the word *ca* signifies "some degree of similarity" (*kiñcit-sādṛśyam eva*); thus, it should be construed by repetition that both words together illuminate these two meanings.
Alternatively, the word *eva* signifies dependence upon that.
The particle *ca* illuminates two meanings—“some slight similarity” and “both”—which should be understood as "ascertaining.
This is what is meant:
the two meanings of the word *ataḥ* (therefore) have been stated as the reason.
Furthermore, each [of these reasons], such as "being dependent on a limiting adjunct" (upādhi), must be excluded [as a valid reason].
This is because [the opponent's reason] is based precisely on that dependence and on that similarity.
Therefore, both [reasons] are meaningful.
With the word *eva*, he negates the restriction of both [meanings] by means of a single *eva*.
One might object: "Since two meanings have already been expressed by each individual *eva*, is it not sufficient to have only one restriction?
Do not say so.
Because it is connected with two distinct objects through the intellect;
or rather, why is it not determined by unifying those two objects?
There is a meaning here that must be indicated.

If only "yata eva" were stated, then this would be a reference to only one object and not a reference to both; even when there is a reference to a second [object], it would be understood that the cause consists of the two combined. However, when the two restrictive particles (*avadhāraṇa*) are employed, by the impossibility of [the meaning] being otherwise, it is understood as a reference to two distinct objects each serving as a cause. And thus, since the subverting factor (*bādhaka*) is manifold, its strength is established, and the effort required to investigate the function of the qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*) is also dispensed with.
And the elixir of mercury would be obtained;
this is what was stated by the phrase "situated in the thread."
Thus, the inference of fallaciousness has been established as a sublater of the inference [of God] based on sentience and so forth.
Intending to show that this [inference] is indicative of other means of valid cognition as well, he says: "In all... (akhila...).
... from every kind of pride. (Manu 3.129f)
If there is indeed a perception of difference between the individual soul and the Lord, how can there be unity of the aggregate?
It is not only by means of the inference based on the nature of appearance that this is established, but rather by all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
If it were stated simply as "by the perception of difference," there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*),
because even the opponent accepts the existence of difference.
Therefore, the word "even" (api) is used;
and it is connected by the intellect with the word "difference" (bheda), even though that word is subordinate within the compound, because difference is shown through the exclusion of non-difference.
From what means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) would this be established?
In this regard, the perception that sublates [the claim of] oneness is indeed well-established,
because of such experiences as "I am not omniscient" and "I am not faultless."

For just as the absence of identity between a pillar and a jar is established by perception, so too the absence of identity with Brahman—characterized by omniscience and other attributes—is indeed established regarding the self by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*).
Furthermore, the non-erroneous nature of that [witness-consciousness] has already been demonstrated. The scriptural authorities (*āgama*) cited in various places should be consulted there. *9,407*
And he states another inference:
"Without remainder," etc.
Hari is free from all defects because of his possession of all powers.
Since it is stated that she is "endowed with all [auspicious qualities]," where could there be any fault in this unity? (MDh 3.2.131ab)
This is what is meant:
the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman do not possess non-difference, because they are the substrata of contradictory attributes,
like shadow and sunlight.
Nor is the reason unestablished;
for by the reason "and it is endowed with all [powers], because that is seen," Brahman's freedom from all defects has been established through its possession of all powers,
whereas the defects such as suffering are established by experience in the case of the individual soul (jīva).
If there were identity even between two things that possess contradictory attributes, then a pillar and a jar would also be identical.

[Objection: Let it be granted that the Supreme Self is omnipotent and free from all defects; nevertheless, its portion—the individual soul (jīva)—will be distinct due to limiting adjuncts (upādhi) and will possess defects caused by them. What contradiction is there in this?

Because the distinction of modes is the cause for the pacification of contradiction, he says: "If [He] is endowed with all powers... (Manu 3.2.131cd): "If [He] is endowed with all powers, how could He be possessed of faults due to His sovereignty?"*9,408*

If the Supreme Self is accepted as being endowed with all powers without exception, then how could He, by virtue of His sovereignty over both the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) and its cause, be possessed of defects caused by that [adjunct]?
This is the intended meaning:
whether this contradiction is resolved through such a distinction of modes or not, let it be so.
This very distinction of modes is untenable;

for it is not logical that the limiting adjuncts (upādhis), such as the internal organ and so forth, which have ignorance as their cause, should— by their own power— separate the Supreme Self and thereby produce defects such as suffering in the individual soul (jīva), who is a portion of that Self.
Because it would entail the consequence of the Supreme Self losing its omnipotence and sovereignty;

therefore, one must consider that the Supreme Self alone, being all-powerful, having divided itself by means of those [powers] which are under its own control, makes its own part—the individual soul (jīva)—subject to defects such as suffering.
And that is even more untenable.
For it would follow that [the Creator] lacks foresight;
indeed, no one possessing foresight is ever observed to make himself subject to non-human goals—such as snakes, thorns, and the like—by means of things dependent upon himself.
Nor is there any purpose for the Supreme Self in causing suffering to itself, as might be the case with an ascetic.
Because it is complete;
nor is beginninglessness a solution here for ignorance and the rest,
because even that beginningless stream is dependent upon them.
Nor is it correct to say that this is merely a sport (*līlā*), because those who act with foresight do not undertake a sport for the sake of their own personal ends.
Therefore, in no way is it logical for the Supreme Person to be associated with any defect; thus, it is not fitting for Him to be identical with the defective individual soul (*jīva*). (9.409)

Even though there is identity between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman, the aforementioned defect does not arise because Brahman lacks the experience of the suffering and so forth residing in the individual soul.

With the thought that, in this way, the contradiction will be resolved through the aforementioned distinction of modes, he raises an objection with the words: "anusandhāna... (regarding the lack of experience).
"If there were unity devoid of connection... (MAnu 3.2.132ab).
"Connection" (*anusandhāna*) is intended here as the direct experience of suffering and so forth as one's own, which is designated by the term "enjoyment" (*bhoga*). [The author] refutes this:
"Unity"—that is not unity. MĀnuv 3.2.132b.
In that case, it is undisputed that the individual soul (*jīva*), for its part, does not experience the nature of Brahman, such as its freedom from suffering and so forth.

If Brahman also did not experience the suffering and so forth residing in the individual soul, then it would effectively have been stated that there is no identity between the two. To the question "How so?", he says: "The conscious [soul]... and so on.
When there is unity of volition, this continuity of purpose is the sole authority, and nothing else.
What is the meaning of "cause"?
Let it be that the synthesis [of cognitions] is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
What follows from that?
Because there is no exclusion of the object of cognition (*prameya*) when a single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is excluded;
for let it not be the case that the absence of smoke implies the absence of fire—therefore it is said: "not another."
Now, one might ask: "Is there not identity between the pot and the pot itself, rather than a unifying awareness? How then can this be so? To this it is said: "conscious" (cetanā).
This is what is meant:
the identity delimited by consciousness has as its sole means of proof the recognition [of it as one];
whereas scripture and the like function as corroborative evidence once such recognition has occurred.

For this very reason, the statement "my self is Bhadrasena" is sublated by the absence of such recollection; likewise, a statement such as "this is not he" is sublated by the presence of recollection. Nor should one suspect a fallacy on the grounds that while there is no recollection of the suffering and so forth from a previous birth at present, there is nonetheless identity [between the two].
We do not say that there must be constant recollection;
rather, when a conscious being recollects a certain nature at any time, he is non-different from it, whereas he who does not recollect it is not non-different from it.
For that which has that [recollection] as its sole means of proof necessarily ceases upon the cessation of that [recollection].
Just as the eye ceases when the apprehension of form ceases,
consciousness cannot be made to cease,
because its existence is established for both disputants.
Therefore, it is only oneness that is excluded.
By this, it is also stated that the inference [of a single agent] from consciousness and so forth is characterized by a limiting condition (*sopādhika*).
For indeed, in the case of Devadatta and others, coordination (*anusandhāna*) is observed to be pervaded by oneness as delimited by consciousness.
Furthermore, [the reason] "consciousness" (cetanatva) and so forth is non-pervasive (avyāpaka),
because that [reason] is absent in the subject (pakṣa) itself;
thus, the formal argument (prayoga) is easily established.

The individual soul (jīva) and Brahman, being conscious, do not possess mutual identity because they lack mutual reflection of their essential natures, just like two [distinct] objects of common agreement.
Nor is the qualification in the proposition (pratijñā) redundant.
This is because, as in the case of the argument "sound is not a specific quality of that which possesses touch," [the term] is intended to avoid a deviation of the reason (*hetu*).
He raises an objection: "[It is] by means of recollection... (*anusandhāna*).

If it is argued that there is only a unity of the collection, devoid of investigation, among sentient beings... [Mānava-dharmaśāstra 3.2.133a-c] ...since I am speaking only of the unity of the collection and not of absolute identity.
Therefore, even in the case of sentient beings, it is appropriate that they lack such continuity.
This is the intended meaning:
for one who asserts the unity of the aggregate must accept both difference and non-difference between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman.
In that case, the absence of synthesis—which is the cause of the perception of difference—fulfills its purpose merely by making that difference known; it does not negate non-difference.

For in cases such as threads and cloth, where there is a unity of the aggregate, the superimposition of contradictory attributes fulfills its function simply by making the difference known, without subverting non-difference.
Otherwise, even in those instances, the acceptance of non-difference would be difficult to establish.
"Therefore, oneness is not untenable.
With a hidden intention, he offers an assenting reply: "Let it be so."
... let that be so ... // Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.2.133c //
The meaning is: "May there be oneness between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman, entirely devoid of any mutual consideration of their respective natures.
Fearing that the acceptance of a contradictory matter would constitute the point of defeat known as *pratijñāhāni* (abandonment of the proposition), he says: "It is merely a name (*nāmamātra*)."
... because it is therefore merely a name.
Since that identity is merely nominal and not real, its acceptance does not constitute a flaw.
This is the underlying intention:
the non-difference between the threads and the cloth is not established by the single means of proof consisting in the absence of the superimposition of contradictory properties.
Because that non-difference is established by perception and other means of knowledge;

and thus, the attribution of contradictory properties (viruddhadharmādhyāsa), fearing the fallacy of being "mistimed" (kālātyayāpadiṣṭa) due to its failure to sublate non-difference, ceases to function and becomes satisfied merely by establishing difference. Likewise, if the identity of the conscious [self] were accessible through another means of knowledge that leaves no room for doubt, then the absence of recollection (anusandhānābhāva), without subverting non-difference, would have its purpose fulfilled by demonstrating mere difference.
But this is not the case;
for it has been stated that the unity of consciousness is pervaded by recollection (*anusandhāna*).
Since the absence of the pervader necessarily entails the cessation of the pervaded, the statement [of unity] would be utterly meaningless in the absence of such unity. *9,415*
Let it be that the unity of the conscious self is established solely by means of recollection (*anusandhāna*);
and since even occasional recollection establishes unity,
and such recollection exists in the state of liberation (*mukti*), the proof of unity is established.
Since the liberated self, by virtue of being far removed from defects such as suffering, is free from the aforementioned faults, he says: "In liberation... [Mānava-dharmaśāstra 3.2.134ab]:
"In liberation, there would be a continuity of consciousness; this too would be extremely difficult to maintain."
Even such a statement would be extremely difficult to maintain;
the point is that it would be doubtful due to the absence of any valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, one who asserts that there will be a continuity [of consciousness] in liberation must explain why such continuity does not exist at present.
Now, if he should say that it is because of the existence of obstacles such as ignorance, desire, and karma,
then it must be said in reply:
"How do you determine that the current absence of recognition is based solely on the presence of an obstacle, and not rather on the absence of identity?
We, however, say:
this current absence of recognition is based precisely on the absence of identity, and is not caused by ignorance or other such factors."
To the question "From where does this certainty arise?", he says: "He is omniscient."
The Omniscient One does not pursue oneness, because that [oneness] simply does not exist.
The connection is as follows: since the Omniscient One does not effect a synthesis [of past and future], that synthesis does not exist at all.
What is meant is this:
if this absence of synthesis were caused by ignorance and so forth, [then it would be possible for the Omniscient One to possess it].
In that case, it would belong to the individual souls (jīvas) alone,
because they alone possess the connection with ignorance and so forth;
the Supreme Self (paramātman), however, would certainly be aware of it.
Because he lacks ignorance and so forth due to his omniscience,
he does not engage in such reflection; for,
as in the statement "I have transcended the perishable," his words reveal only the experience of non-duality.

Therefore, we conclude that the absence of mental synthesis (*anusandhāna*) is not caused by an obstacle such as ignorance (*ajñāna*), but rather has its cause solely in the absence of identity (*aikyābhāva*).
If it is argued that this [absence of synthesis] is simply due to [the lack of] God (*īśvara*), [we reply: no.
What other supreme self (*paramātman*) could there be besides that [individual soul], given the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?
Furthermore, since even the Lord (*īśvara*) is omniscient, what is the use of this [separate supreme self]?

Moreover, if oneness were established by a means of valid cognition, then the absence of recollection (*anusandhāna*) would have to be attributed to the presence of an obstructing factor; thus, such a conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) would be tenable.
And it has already been stated that such [a self] does not exist.
Now, one might object: suffering and so forth do not inhere in the very nature of consciousness of the living being;
rather, they belong specifically to its particularized forms.

Therefore, it has been stated—"oneness"—that since the Lord would otherwise not experience [the results of actions], he must at least experience oneness even in the absence of experiencing suffering and so forth; for how could the Lord fail to experience [the consequences] if there were no such connection?
For this very reason, statements such as, "When the ignorance that produces differentiation has gone to absolute destruction,
who will bring about the non-existent difference between the Self and Brahman? are to be interpreted accordingly.
For the word *vibheda* denotes opposition, as in the expression "the breach of friendship. Likewise,
the soul's state of having a contrary understanding [regarding the Supreme Self] is based upon ignorance (*ajñāna*).

The meaning is that it does not exist when that [connection] is absent. The absence of the contemplation of identity with the Supreme Self is unestablished; for although one does not contemplate this now, one will contemplate it in a future time.
He raises the following objection—namely, that "subsequent" [recollection]—on the grounds that continuous recollection throughout all times is not a pervader of unity.
If, however, there should be a subsequent investigation... // MĀnuv 3.2.135ab //
The ellipsis is to be supplied as "of the identity of the individual soul (jīva) with the supreme self (paramātman).
The clear rebuttal is that there is no evidence for this.
With a hidden intention, he states another rebuttal: "It is false."

...there would be false knowledge regarding the Supreme Self; this is the ellipsis. For if the Omniscient One were not now to perceive the identity with the individual soul (*jīva*), then that [identity] would be non-existent, like a seventh taste and so forth.
The underlying intention is this: if one were to subsequently connect [the self] in a future time in such a manner, it would follow that one is a possessor of false knowledge (*mithyājñānin*).
Now, one who connects what is non-existent as being existent becomes a possessor of false knowledge;
yet, oneness (*aikya*) is not non-existent.

How then can the Supreme Self be subject to false knowledge? Anticipating this doubt from one who has not grasped the intended meaning, he provides the rebuttal by revealing that very intention with the words: "vidyamāna... (while existing).
If there were no investigation into what exists, ignorance would result.
If oneness were actually present, then one who does not currently exercise that synthesis would be non-omniscient;
yet that is not tenable.
Therefore, it must be said that such oneness simply does not exist.
And thus, how could one who intends to reconnect with that [past state] not be possessed of false knowledge?
By this, the claim that the Lord lacks such reconnection because of the current existence of a body is also refuted,
as it cannot avoid the consequence of abandoning His omniscience.
Since the Lord’s possession of form is eternal, there is no hope for a subsequent connection even with respect to what is yet to come.
Whether that unity is non-existent or indeed existent, the two aforementioned faults would ensue;
and such is not the case.

But now, one might object: "That [object] may indeed be non-existent at present, but it comes into being later, after the time of cognition. In that case, since it is non-existent at present, there is no loss of omniscience on the part of the Supreme Self due to not cognizing it; and since it exists later, there is no state of false knowledge upon its subsequent cognition. Thus, he raises the doubt regarding a certain person's view or a remaining position, beginning with the word "asat" (non-existent).
If there were a seventh taste, then there might subsequently be a unity of the non-existent.
He refutes [this] with the words: "It might be."
The word "then" (*tarhi*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
For in beginningless *saṃsāra*, it has never been observed that something which is not identical with another becomes one with it;
nor is there any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to prove that such a thing will ever come to pass.
"‘In the supreme immutable, all become one’; ‘As long as there is liberation, there may be distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme;

beyond that, there is no distinction, due to the absence of any cause for distinction’—since such scriptural and traditional texts have scope [for application] regarding matters such as the identity of location."
Therefore, the sense is that this hope—expressed as "therefore there will be a seventh rasa"—has an object that is utterly impossible.

By extending the defects of the two views of difference-and-non-difference (*bhedābheda*)—namely, that for the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman there is both difference and non-difference in *saṃsāra*, but only non-difference in liberation—he refutes the third view, which holds that there is both difference and non-difference in both states, by stating: "samudāya... [and so forth].
Therefore, the oneness of the aggregate has always been refuted from afar.
The connection is that there is always a unity of the collection;
this is because [the opponent's position] lacks any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and because it contradicts such means of valid cognition as the fact of being a mere appearance (*ābhāsa*).
However, there is this much distinction.

The hope held by the two previous views was that difference is an obstacle to the unification that constitutes non-differentiation; once that obstacle has departed, unification will occur in liberation. But here, even that hope is absent.
Because difference is eternal,
and it has been stated that the act of recollection is pervaded by the unity of consciousness;
this is what is meant by the phrase "from afar."
If it is argued that the body and so forth are the obstacles to such recollection (*anusandhāna*), we say no;
for it will be stated later that there exists recollection even among yogins who possess bodies.

If this is so, and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is not the entire aggregate of conscious beings, then what is the limit of the status of being the Supreme Self? To this, he says: "Therefore" (*ataḥ*).
Therefore, as long as he is indeed endowed with all virtues and free from defects, for that long alone is he called "Īśvara" (the Lord).

The meaning is that, whereas in other cases there is an absence of a proving factor (*sādhaka*) throughout and the presence of a subverting factor (*bādhaka*) such as fallaciousness, here, however, it is due to both the presence and absence of those [factors].
The state of being "bound by all excellences" (*aśeṣaguṇonnaddhatva*) and "freedom from defects" (*nirdoṣatva*) are each stated as a reason for the definitive determination.
The expression "the Lord everywhere" and so forth is used to indicate that, according to our own system, there is no Brahman distinct from the Lord (*īśvara*).
The word "hi" (for/indeed) indicates that this definition of Brahman is established by the Śruti and other authorities.
When it is stated that "the reality is called Īśvara," a sense of a collective unity is perceived; he refutes that with the word "tatra" (in that regard).
...in that regard, there is no distinction anywhere. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 3.2.137d)
"In some cases" means [the relationship] between each other and with the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
By this, the following [objection] is also refuted: "The Lord (*īśvara*)..."
Regarding what was stated by the opponent— that [the Self] has arisen as if among forms—
he says "not here" to explain why that is so.
"Here there is no diversity whatsoever; this is He, and that is He"—according to such scriptural authority... [Mānava-dharmaśāstra 3.2.138a-c]
By this [verse], he cites the Vedic scripture: "There is no diversity whatsoever here," and the word "harayaḥ."
The passage beginning with "This indeed is the tawny one" and "For this is that" means "This very one is that which is this Self";
the connection is with what precedes.

The phrase "by means of the authority" (*mānena*) is stated in order to dispel the doubt that these scriptural passages lack authority regarding the intended meaning because they are devoted to non-duality (*abheda*).

Since the refutation of difference among the forms of the Lord is explicit in the first passage, and since the word *eva* is heard in the third, it follows that—in accordance with that—the word *vai* in the second passage is also understood to have the same sense. Thus, the intention is that these scriptural passages do indeed attain the status of authority regarding the intended meaning. *9,424*
If it is asked, "It has been stated that the synthesis of a single volition (cetanā) is pervasive; where is this observed? we say:
it is observed in the case of pleasure and so forth belonging to Devadatta, which are synthesized by Devadatta himself.
If it is argued, "It is not observed when there is a difference in limiting adjuncts (upādhi)," we say no.

Since [the self] is seen even when it is divided by limiting adjuncts such as hands and feet, one might object: "It is not seen when separated from the divided adjuncts. To this, he says: "The portions of the living soul (jīvāṃśāḥ)."
...and all [beings] are indeed portions of the living soul.
...who are necessarily possessed of continuous reflection. // MĀnuv 3.2.139a //
Arjuna and others are portions (aṃśa) of the individual souls (jīva), such as Indra and the rest;
this point will be established by the sūtra beginning with “one [is not the self], because of its existence in the body” (Brahmasūtra 3.3.53).

By the word "ca" (and), the portions of the Lord are included. Now, one might object: since there is a statement such as "The self indeed became the son by name," even though there is identity between father and son, there is no [mutual] recognition; how then can that [recognition] be its pervader? To this, he says: "If... (yadi).
...if oneness [of the self] exists by its own nature. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.2.139b)
In that case, the connection is "those who possess [the recognition of] continuity.
This is the intended meaning:
the recognition of a real identity is accepted as the pervading factor, but not that of a figurative one.
Furthermore, there is no deviation (vyabhicāra) regarding that which is intended;
for the identity of father and son is merely metaphorical, and thus deviation does not constitute a fault in that case. This is established by its own nature as a reality. *9,427*
Alternatively, he states that the reason—that they are portions of the Supreme Lord—is unestablished: "They are portions of the individual soul (jīva)."
This is what is meant:
the recollection of being a part delimited by consciousness is observed to be pervasive among those such as Arjuna;
however, it has been demonstrated that this does not exist between the Supreme Lord and the individual soul (jīva).
And in the absence of the pervader, the absence of the pervaded is necessarily entailed.
Since the exclusion of consciousness itself is not tenable, it is only its partiality that is excluded.
And thus is the formal argument:
The individual soul and the Lord are not part and whole, despite both being conscious,
because they lack mutual awareness of one another,
just like a jar and a cloth.
Regarding the phrase "as in the case of Indra and Arjuna":

[an objection is raised]—surely, even though there is a relationship of part and whole between father and son, there is no such recognition [of identity]; how then can that [recognition] be its pervader? To this, he says: "If..."

The meaning is that oneness consists in being in the same place and having the nature of parts; the relationship of part and whole between father and son does not consist in being in the same place and so forth.
[Objection: But if the status of being a part is excluded due to the absence of recollection (anusandhāna), would there not be a contradiction regarding the locus of the part?
[Response: There would not.
For the word *aṃśa* (part) signifies both "a portion of that" and "something similar to that. In this context,
the second sense of being a part— that which is established in the *Aṃśādhikaraṇa*— is not refuted.

Because the opponent cannot employ it as a reason (*hetu*) due to the consequence of its being inconclusive (*anaikāntya*), there is no fault whatsoever in demonstrating the non-establishment (*asiddhi*) of the first [reason]. [Objection:

But if there is indeed a continuity of consciousness (*anusandhāna*) among Indra and the others, how is it that Arjuna performed acts such as the burning of the Khāṇḍava forest, which were not desired by Indra?
And how is it that Indra [performed] acts such as burning and pacifying which were not intended by Arjuna?
For this is not observed when there is a connection with the hand and so forth; therefore, he says: "of the possessors of parts" (aṃśinaḥ).
The complete integration of even the smallest part of the whole is possible.
Whatever portion of him is born on earth experiences the pleasure, pain, and so forth belonging to that state; however, there may be some distinction made by the Lord.
Even for a part that is extremely small, there certainly exists a complete awareness of all its constituent parts.

Nevertheless, a certain distinction—such as the performance of what is not desired by the part—is brought about by the whole (the *aṃśin*) impelled by the Lord (*īśvara*), who acts through the merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*) residing in the part. This is the meaning.
The phrase "even of the small" is a mention of its essential nature.
Even by a portion born on earth, only the pleasure, pain, and so forth residing in the whole (the *aṃśin*) are experienced, but not everything.
Even though there is identity, some particularity consisting in the non-connection with all [experiences] must be due to the action of the Lord (*īśa*).
The Lord acts by taking as his causal conditions such factors as a lowly location like the earth, states such as dwelling in a womb, and the consumption of human food;
therefore, it is logical that the Lord brings about for a part [of himself] what is not desired for that very part.
For we have not stated that complete coordination [of interests] is pervaded by the oneness of consciousness and so forth.
However, the sense is that it is merely a matter of continuity (*anusandhāna*).

Now, one might ask: how can even the Lord (*īśvara*) cause [beings] to perform what is not desired by themselves, and how does he obstruct continuity when there is no difference [between them]? To this, he says: "Of the Lord" (*īśasya*).
Because the Lord possesses inconceivable power, there is nothing anywhere that is impossible for him to accomplish.

The intention is as follows: indeed, it is observed that those who are impelled by the power of the Lord, yet remain under the sway of desire, anger, and so forth, commit sins such as cutting off their own heads—which are causes of suffering in this world and the next—even though they are performing what was not previously intended.
Now, if this is so, then I too am able to say: just as, even though Arjuna’s [self] is one, his complete recollection pertaining to Indra is obstructed by the inconceivable power of the Lord.
Likewise, even though there is non-difference between the individual soul (jīva) and the supreme self (paramātman), that very [non-apprehension] will constitute an obstruction to the unification;
the limiting adjuncts (upādhis), such as the body and so forth, will function as the cause—just as a remote location and so forth do.
Thus, it is untenable to claim that because there is an absence of unification, there is an absence of oneness.
And since it is postulated that the pervasion of the investigation by unity holds only when there is no obstacle, he says: "That [is the case]."
For if his oneness with the individual soul were indeed [the case], then the state of having a Lord would be logically untenable.
That [creation] consists in the bringing about of what was not previously brought about.
This would be possible for this Supreme Self if, in your view, the Lordship of the Supreme Self were of the nature of possessing inconceivable power.
For one who is non-different from the individual soul (jīva), the state of being a Lord (īśatā) is itself untenable;
how much less, then, can there be the postulation of obstacles to his omniscience and so forth?

By the word "hi" (for/indeed), [the author] indicates the logical pervasion (vyāpti): that which is non-different from the individual soul is not endowed with the nature of a Lord whose power is inconceivable, just as, for example, Devadatta.
Even though the Supreme Self has become one with the individual soul (jīva), it remains endowed with lordship (īśatā).
To the question, "What is the subverting argument (bādhaka) against the contrary view? he says: "Of the non-lord" (anīśasya).
To claim lordship over that which is not one's own is entirely contradictory to all means of valid cognition.
It is established by experience that the individual soul (jīva) is indeed not the Lord;
since it is non-different from Him, it has already been stated that the Supreme Self (paramātman) would likewise not be the Lord.
And thus, the doubt might arise: "How can there be lordship for one who is not the Lord?"
And this [position] is contradicted by all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and is self-contradictory.
Furthermore, one who is not insane would never entertain such a doubt;
since no doubt arises at all, what occasion is there for the presentation of a subverting argument? Such is the meaning of the word "eva" (indeed).
It might be argued that the impossibility of [the world] having a creator is either a logical argument (*tarka*) or an inference (*anumāna*).
It cannot be the first.
Because oneness is established by scripture, it is impossible for it to result in its opposite;
nor is the second [alternative] tenable,
because the oneness of the individual soul (*jīva*) is not admitted by you.
If it is argued that [the word is] redundant,
it is not so;
for one for whom the identity with the individual soul (*jīva*) is already established...
Since it is accepted that [the opponent] intends to establish an inference regarding the object of the Lord's lack of sovereignty, there is no fault even in the case of *tarka* (logical reasoning).
With the intention that the scriptures do not have unity as their primary purport, he says: "By way of being the Lord alone... etc.

If the Śruti teaches that what was known as the Lord is actually not the Lord, or conversely, that what was known as not the Lord is the Lord; [then it would be sublated]. (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 3.2.142)
It will not attain the status of an authoritative means of knowledge if it contradicts that which is to be relied upon for subsistence.
Indeed, three possibilities arise here:

some scriptural passage might, with reference to the Supreme Self—who is already known through other means of knowledge as the Lord—teach that He exists in the state of a non-lord, namely as the individual soul (jīva) who is cognized as not being the Lord; or some [passage] might, with reference to the individual soul who is cognized as not being the Lord, teach that he exists in the state of the Lord, namely as the Supreme Self who is cognized as the Lord.
Someone might suggest that, having thus cognized both [the individual soul and Brahman], one should teach their identity;
however, in any case, because this would entail a contradiction with the basis upon which they depend, identity does not attain the status of being an object of valid cognition.
What must be said in this regard is: "How is Brahman to be known?"
This will be explained by the passage beginning with "ityādinā.
The term "cecchati" should be understood as applying to the second half-verse as well,
and "ādiśet" should be understood as applying to the first half-verse as well.
A third alternative must also be supplied, by prefixing the word "tarhi" (*then*) before the phrase "upajīvya" (*having depended upon*). [Objection:

Is it not the case that the Lordship and Non-Lordship (even though they are contradictory) belong to the Supreme Self through its very power (*śakti*), which has the nature of making possible what was previously impossible?
There will be a convergence in one place; how then can there be a contradiction with that which is being relied upon? To this, he says: "For this very reason."
Therefore, since his lordship is not established, nothing can be done by him.
The meaning is: "precisely because of the identity of the individual soul (jīva).
"Lordship" (īśatā) is power in the form described above.
"Something" (kiñcit) refers to the coexistence of lordship and non-lordship in a single locus.

Furthermore, it is impossible to infer the absence of lordship for this Supreme Self on the grounds of its identity with the individual soul (jīva), because its lordship is established by the scriptural statement: "Its supreme power... (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.8).
This is because it is established by such scriptural passages as these.

Furthermore, anticipating the objection that "even if the individual soul (jīva) is one with Brahman, since difference still exists, lordship (īśatva) is possible," he says— thereby dispelling that doubt— "Lordship" (īśatve), in response to the inquiry of the dull-witted as to what the limit is of the conception of the Supreme Self's power effecting the impossible.
When sovereignty has been correctly revealed by the Śruti through the distinction between the Lord and the non-Lord,
even that which is otherwise improper becomes proper by virtue of its power.

Therefore, whatever else is seen elsewhere is also to be understood as created by the Lord alone; for even that which is obtained through fallacious revelation does not contradict his status as the Lord.

By asserting that the Lordship (*aiśvarya*) is perfectly revealed by the Scripture precisely through the acceptance of the distinction of being non-Lord (*anīśa*), the contradiction with Scripture is resolved.

For instance, if the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) were ontological (*tāttvika*), then the Scripture—being contradicted by an inference that leaves no room for alternative [explanations]—would have to be taken in a figurative sense (*upacaritārtha*) and could not establish Lordship; thus, the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the inference establishing its own [contradictory] object would remain firmly intact.
Thus [it is said].
This means "by a correct distinction from the non-Lord," and not merely by distinction;
for in this way, lordship will be established through distinction.
This is rejected because non-sovereignty results from the existence of non-difference;
for the doubt remains unresolved as to whether non-sovereignty arises through non-difference or, conversely, does not arise through difference.
Except for Īśvara;
even that which exists through mutual exclusion is logical,
provided it is with respect to Īśvara— this is the implied sense.
"By that power," meaning by the power of lordship;
the word "seen" is also connected here.
"From this," meaning from the Supreme Lord.
The term "by Īśa" is a designation where the abstract state (bhāva) is the primary meaning;
the ellipsis is "it is conceived as being logical.
The phrase "in the Śruti" is an exception to what was previously stated.
And "appearance-ness" (ābhāsatva) is [so called] in relation to the actual state of things (*vastuvṛtta*); the word "hi" indicates the logical justification for this. This is the meaning.

Whatever appears to be contradictory in some respect— whether with respect to the Lord or anything else— is not established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) as being contrary to the sovereignty of the Lord;
for example, the coexistence of atomicity and magnitude, or the absence of complete omniscience in Arjuna and others.
All of that must be accepted as being possible through the power of the Lord's sovereignty;
it is not to be rejected.
However, that which is unestablished by any means of valid cognition should not be postulated, even if it were not in contradiction with the Lord's sovereignty.

Otherwise, it would result in the conceptualization of things such as a rabbit's horn; and that which, even when established by valid cognition, contradicts the sovereignty of God, must certainly not be conceptualized,
because it would destroy the very basis for such conceptualization.
However, the fallacious nature of that means of valid cognition must be described according to the specific case, as in the present instance.
As it has been stated:
"To claim lordship for one who is not a lord is entirely contradictory to every means of valid cognition. (*9,438*)
To establish that, he cites the very traditional authority (smṛti): "The Lord," etc.
"The Lord is powerless, the world is illusory, the one who suffers is liberated, and there is no duality"—
this contradiction of one's own proposition is the greatest of all faults.
For thus says the statement of the Brahmatarka... [Mānava Dharmaśāstra 3.2.147a]
For contradiction of a thesis is of two kinds,
distinguished as contradiction with means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and contradiction with one's own words (*svavākya*).
Among these, "the Lord is not the Lord," and "one who is suffering is liberated" are two examples of contradiction with one's own words.

In the example of contradiction with one's own statement—namely, "The world is false, for there is no distinction; [the Lord] is powerless, miserable, and liberated"—the phrase "the world is false" illustrates contradiction with one's own system (*svanyāyavirodha*). This is because it contradicts the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the absence of contradiction regarding the distinction [between the Lord and the individual soul].
Furthermore, the phrase "the world is false" illustrates contradiction with one's own system. *9,439*
If the world were false, then by that same logic, falsity itself would also result in being false, which would entail its being real.
As for the phrase "for there is no difference," it refers to the contradiction with one's own action;
for by this very act of making a proposition, a distinction between the property to be proven (sādhya-dharma) and the locus (dharmin) is necessarily established.
It is more excessive than all other faults; it is the most excessively excessive.
He states the point to be proven regarding the example of mindfulness: "it is utterly to be abandoned."
Therefore,
this doctrine of the non-difference between the individual soul and the Lord, held by those who desire spiritual prosperity, must be accepted in its entirety.
This is the Lord's lack of lordship.
Regarding the point stated in the passage beginning with "by way of being a lord through a distinction of lordship," he also cites a Smṛti text, saying: "It is not improper."
Nothing whatsoever is improper for the Lord that is not inconsistent with His lordship;
indeed, only that which contradicts His lordship is truly improper.
Having reconciled all means of valid cognition with the Lord's sovereignty,
one should not, even if it were logically inconsistent, attribute anything improper to the Lord once His sovereignty is established.
"One should never apply even a name obtained through pride [to another]";
such indeed is the statement in the *Brahmatarka*... (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 3.2.150a–c).

Because there is nothing that is not possible for the Lord (īśa), and so forth, therefore [the phrase] "without contradicting the state of being the Lord" and so on is used. He who has established lordship is described as such; one should unite with that Lord.
One should know that [the Lord] exists;
this is because of the word "also" (api),
meaning "even by another," or "by the established reason of being the Lord."
He states the purpose of citing the Smṛti with the words "ataḥ" (therefore).
Therefore, what has been stated here is appropriate.
Therefore, it is established that the individual soul (*jīva*) is indeed absolutely distinct from Brahman.
Thus ends the section on "Comparison" (*upamādhikaraṇa*) in the illustrious *Nyāyasudhā*.
[======= Section 3.2.VII: The Section on Formlessness (*arūpādhikaraṇa*) =======]
Now, in the illustrious Nyāyasudhā, the section concerning the formless (Arūpādhikaraṇa).
// Oṃ. For that [the Tathāgata] is indeed formless, because it has that [consciousness] as its primary constituent. Oṃ.//

In this section, having established the formlessness of Brahman by means of the first sūtra, the second sūtra—“And like light, it is not purposeless”—addresses the objection that scriptural passages concerning its possession of form would otherwise be rendered meaningless; this is resolved by accepting that Brahman possesses a unique kind of form.
And as for this possession of a unique form:
It is understood from the commentary that this is supported by the two sūtras: "And it says 'that alone'" and "Furthermore, it shows [it] and is also remembered.
That, however, is untenable.
Because, if one were ultimately to admit that it possesses form, the statement "it is indeed formless" would result in being inexpressible;
and because there is no purpose for this investigation, he states the purport of the four sūtras with the words "And that... (sa ca).
For that [Self] is indeed formless, because it has that [consciousness] as its primary essence.
And because it does not possess a natural form, it is formless; yet its own nature, consisting of its qualities, is held to be its "form," which consists of a head, hands, feet, and so forth.
He is the Supreme Self.
The word "prakṛti" (primordial nature) is also indicative of other principles,
because He possesses a form that is non-material (*aprākṛta*).
Because it is devoid of a material form (*prākṛta-rūpa*).
If one were to say "consisting of qualities" (*guṇātmaka*), there would be the understanding that it consists of *sattva* and the other [qualities];
to exclude that, the word "own" (*sva*) is used.
The phrase "consisting of that" refers to those qualities such as bliss and so forth which constitute the very nature of the Supreme Self;
for by the word "form" (rūpa), there might otherwise be understood qualities such as whiteness and the like.
Therefore, the explanation "head, hands," and so on, has been provided.
Therefore, the remainder is "and he is possessed of form.
He shows the purpose of this investigation with the words "therefore":
"Therefore, there is no impermanence, nor indeed any contradiction with the two scriptural statements. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.2.152ab)
Impermanence consists in the state of being subject to birth and death;
it should also be understood that this does not mean the absence of beauty and such qualities.
And thus, devotion toward Him is appropriate—this is the implied conclusion.

Although the form of the Supreme Self exists, how then can it be designated as "formless" merely by its difference from what is commonly known? To resolve this doubt, the portion of the Sūtra beginning with "prakāśavat" has been explained in the Bhāṣya as having this purpose.

Now, if the form of the Lord is distinct from worldly forms, then regarding that [form], the word "rūpa"— (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the logical flow of the argument up to that point.)
The functioning [of the senses] would be impossible, because the apprehension of a relationship [between them and their objects] would be untenable.

Furthermore, the futility of the scriptural texts concerning the possession of form (rūpavattva) would be difficult to avoid. With this objection in mind, he explains [the passage] as a refutation, beginning with "Just as indeed... (yathā hi).
For just as the Veda declares that even when the light of fire has been set aside, the Self alone is the light, so too does it declare the Lord to be the light of the individual soul.

Regarding the phrase "of luminosity alone," it should be explained as follows: for it is well known that only solar and other such lights, which are themselves *taijasa* (luminous), are denoted by the word "luminosity" (*prakāśa*).
Even though [the Lord] has been set aside, this means even in the absence of His true nature (*tattva*).
The meaning is that the scriptural text, "His very self becomes his light," declares the Lord to be the light of the individual soul (*jīva*).
Likewise, the application of the term "form" (*rūpa*) to the form of the Blessed One, though it differs from worldly forms, is appropriate; this is the implied meaning.
The justification for this will be explained later under the section beginning with “*paramate*.”
Regarding the term *anusandheya* (to be connected): indeed, this section [of commentary] precedes the sūtra “And for this very reason, the simile” (*ata eva ca copamā*).
How, then, can there be an explanation later?
It is said:
for this very reason, the Sūtra states, "Not even from the standpoint of location."
The change in the order [of the topics] is for the purpose of indicating that this is connected by way of the subject matter (*adhikaraṇa*),
since the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) arises depending upon the established meaning of that [preceding topic].
And thus the Bhāṣya says: “Because it is so,” and so forth;
and here too: “In the forms of the Lord,” and so forth.

Now, why was this not done immediately after that? Because the meaning of the section concerning the possession of form (*arūpavattvādhikaraṇa*)—which was described as being connected by way of an introductory transition (*upodghāta*) as a reason for the meaning of the sūtra “ata eva ca”—does not constitute an interruption.

In order to elaborate further upon the nature of being the cause, the Teacher has employed the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase, "And because it is not of the nature of the original [state]," for it is indeed logical that there is absolute non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), who is bodiless even throughout the three periods of time.
Thus ends the section on the Formless (*arūpādhikaraṇa*). (9.4.44)
[======= JNys_3,2.VIII: The Section on Increase and Decrease =======] // Now begins the section on increase and decrease.
Oṃ. It possesses both increase and decrease because of its internal inclusion [of all things] and because of the consistency of both; thus it is so. Oṃ.
It is now established here that devotion, for the sake of which the greatness of the Blessed One is described, exists among persons in varying degrees;
for indeed,
devotion possesses the quality of increase and decrease.
Why?
Because Brahmā and others, as well as those such as ourselves, are included within the category of devotees.
Thus, only when this gradation of devotion is accepted does consistency arise for the Lord with respect to both groups.
This is incoherent;
for no connection is perceived between the reasoning and the matter asserted in the proposition.
To this, he replies: "tadbhakti" (*9,445*).
Thus, because both [increase and decrease] are included within it, there is a participation in increase and decrease;

through the gradation of that devotion, there is a gradation leading to liberation for all beings, from Brahmā downwards, according to their respective degrees of bliss and so forth. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 3.2.153) / (Brahmasūtra-bhāṣya 3.2.20)

The meaning is this: by the word "and" (*ca*), those such as ourselves are included; thus, for all beings, the gradation (*tāratamya*) of bliss and so forth leading to liberation—which follows the sequential order of the Vedic revelation without deviation—occurs precisely through the gradation of devotion to the Blessed Lord.
This is what is being stated.

It has already been established by the sūtra, "But because it is not apprehended like water, it is not so," that the fruit consisting of bliss and the like for one who is liberated is to be accomplished through devotion.
Furthermore, that [fruit] is understood from such scriptural passages as "Now, therefore, let there be an inquiry into bliss" to possess gradations;
and when there is a gradation in what is to be accomplished, a gradation in the means is necessarily required.
Otherwise, it would follow that it is causeless,
and it would also entail the inconsistency of God as the bestower of results;
yet this is not the case.
Therefore, devotion possesses the quality of increase and decrease.
Thus concludes the section on increase and decrease (*vṛddhihrāsādhikaraṇa*).
[======= JNys_3,2.IX: Section on Specific Locations (*sthānaviśeṣādhikaraṇa*) =======]
Now begins the section concerning specific locations.
Oṃ. [The self is all-pervading] because of its presence everywhere, like light and so forth. Oṃ.
(Oṃ, and because of the possibility [of rebirth], oṃ.)
Although this section follows immediately after [the section on] the opinion of others (*paramata*),
nevertheless, there is a connection between that [section] and this one as well;
for while this [section] introduces the subject matter, that [section] demonstrates the establishment of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Or rather, because the opponent's argument has been raised by this [text] and the subject matter introduced by it;
for instance: "The gradation of bliss among Brahmā and the others is not logically tenable."
This is because it is accepted that [the individual soul] is a reflection of the bliss of the Blessed One;
and because it has been stated in the sūtra "not even from the standpoint of location" (*na sthānataḥ*) that there is no gradation in the original object (the *bimba*);
otherwise, the consequence would follow that [the bliss] is accidental (*akasmikatva*).
Alternatively, the bliss of Brahmā and the others is not a reflection of the bliss of the Blessed One,
because they are mutually distinct and diverse.
And because there is an absence of variety in that which is intended to be the original object (*bimba*),
he clarifies this point here by saying "like a reflection" (*pratibimbavat*).
Due to the distinction of location, as in the case of light and so forth;
and like a reflection, their bliss and other qualities [are perceived] accordingly. (Manu 3.2.154ab)
Even if the bliss of these beings, beginning with Brahmā, exists like a reflection— that is,
it exists as something similar to well-known reflections—
it amounts to being a reflection of the bliss of the Blessed One.
Nevertheless, the remainder of the sentence is that they become mutually diverse.
How so?
By not transcending the diversity of the other contributing qualities (upādhiguṇa), such as devotion and the like, which serve as the means of accomplishment.
In this regard, the illustration is "like a reflection.

The meaning is as follows: just as reflections of the sun and so forth—though there is no diversity in the sun and so forth themselves—exhibit diversity due to the diversity of the qualities of their respective locations such as sun-crystals or water; it is the same here.
He states another reason for this diversity: "Nārāyaṇa," etc.
And because of the logical possibility;
and [he] is dependent upon the qualities of Nārāyaṇa... (Manu 3.2.154c).
And by the power of the original object (*bimba*), it is manifold; this is the meaning.

The fact that the quality of the locus and the capacity of the original object are the causal factors has been demonstrated in the *Nyāyavivaraṇa*. By this, the sūtra "and because of the logical consistency" (*upapatteśca*) is explained.
Some maintain the identity of the original object and its reflection.
Therefore, the state of being a reflection is explained as "Nārāyaṇa"; here,
*guṇa* refers to bliss (*ānanda*).
By the word "ca" (and), "that which is similar to it" is to be understood. To the question, "Why does it not become non-different from the original object (bimba)? he says: "Because it is too small."
... is extremely small in comparison to that. (Manu 3.2.154d)
Therefore, knowledge is always distinct from that of another.
"What is the reason? Because, in comparison with that [the Self], it is exceedingly small; therefore, it is always distinct.
Anticipating the inquiry as to why it is exceedingly small in comparison with that, he cites the scripture here: "Other... (anyat).
But the knowledge of living beings is one thing, while their bliss and lordship are another.
"Since that lordship belongs primarily to the Supreme Lord and only secondarily to the individual soul, according to the Śruti... (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.2.156a-c).
The connection is that Ānanda is [the bliss] of another and of the individual souls (jīvas). The same should be applied to the term "lordship" (īśatā) as well.
He states the reason by way of an illustration, namely, "supreme lordship."
The phrase "from this scripture" is to be connected with what precedes it.
Thus ends the section concerning specific locations (*sthānaviśeṣādhikaraṇa*).
Section on the Nature of the Protector =======] Now begins the section on the nature of the protector (*pālakatva*) in the illustrious Nyāyasudhā.
Oṃ. For [the scripture] negates the extent of the world as it has been described in its natural state; thereafter, it speaks further. Oṃ.

In this regard, the Bhāṣya, which aims to present the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), states: "He possesses only the status of being the agent of creation and dissolution, not that of a protector; for [protection] is established by itself.
That is incorrect.

Because the acceptance of [God] as the agent of creation and destruction would be purposeless; because the word "of this" (*asya*) is not perceived in the phrase "due to self-established existence" (*svataḥ siddheḥ*); and even if one were to supply the word "of persistence" (*sthiteḥ*), since that would entail resorting to the doctrine of inherent nature (*svabhāvavāda*), it would follow that creation and destruction are likewise equal [to persistence], making the acceptance of [God's] agency in them untenable. Therefore, he clarifies the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) with the words "creation... (*sṛṣṭīti*).
When it is stated that creation and destruction are dependent upon Him, [the response is:
"Because persistence is His very nature, there is no need for dependence on anything else."
When this has been stated and accepted by the proponent of the final view (siddhāntin), the following is the meaning:
the Lord’s role as a protector is not tenable, because [the purpose of] his existence is [already fulfilled].
And since that [maintenance] is established by its own nature (*svabhāva*), it does not depend upon Īśvara;
for it is accepted that Īśvara alone is the creator of the universe’s creation and destruction, and no other.
Thus, as long as he has not withdrawn [the world] after having created it, its maintenance is established by its own nature and does not depend on the activity of another.

If, indeed, there were another agent of creation and dissolution, then that indifferent being would require dependence upon Īśvara for the purpose of impelling him toward creation and for restraining him when he is engaged in dissolution;
yet such a thing does not exist.
Therefore, since there is no protectorship possible apart from indifference toward withdrawal, such is the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) here.

If that is so, then the established conclusion (siddhānta) is not tenable, because the reasoning based on the nature of things has not been refuted; therefore, he states the intention of the Sūtra: "Thus, not so."
... thus it is not logical. MĀnuv 3.2.156.
For the entire nature of everything is dependent upon the Lord.
That essential nature or property which is perceived as independent of anything else is called *svabhāva* (intrinsic nature).
This belongs to all things;
indeed, every such [nature] is dependent upon the Lord (*īśvara*).
Otherwise, because they would [then] possess independence, his lordship would be untenable;
furthermore, it would result in a contradiction with such scriptural passages as "All this indeed...
And his activity in the giving of food and so forth is quite manifest.
Thus concludes the section on the Protector (*pālakatva*).
Now begins the section on the Unmanifest (*avyakta*).
Oṃ, for it says that it is unmanifest; Oṃ.
In this context, the unmanifest nature of the Supreme Self was first established in detail.

Then, raising the objection that the means such as devotion would consequently be rendered useless, its perceptibility was also stated in the words: “And it is manifest, because it appears in action.”
Anticipating the objection that these two [statements] are contradictory, the Sūtra states: "Therefore, by the Infinite; for thus is the mark.
Since the resolution of this contradiction is not clearly perceived here, he explains its intended meaning: "Even though unmanifest," and so forth.
For it says that He is unmanifest:
"Though unmanifest, Hari is seen by His devotees through His own power. (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.2.23; Mahābhārata Anuśāsana Parvan 3.2.157cd)
Thus ends the section on the Unmanifest (*avyaktādhikaraṇa*). Now begins the section on the Designation of Both (*ubhayavyapadeśādhikaraṇa*).
Oṃ. But [the relationship between Brahman and the individual soul] is like that of a serpent and its coils, because both designations are used. Oṃ.
If the attributes, actions, and so forth of Īśvara are different from him, then—since *samavāya* (inherence) has been refuted—it is untenable for him to possess them.

If, on the other hand, they are non-different from him, then it is incorrect to say that he possesses knowledge and the like, or that he is an enjoyer of bliss and so forth; thus, in either case, devotion toward him is untenable. This being the position of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), the following is commenced. In this regard, the reason and the illustrative example are indicated [in the Sūtra].
But a thesis (*pratijñā*) does not consist in the formal adoption of a position (*pakṣa*).
It appears that even the implicit addition (*adhyāhāra*) is merely the adoption of a position regarding difference or non-difference by the force of the reason (*hetu*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
Therefore, he shows the thesis: "They are non-different from that."
But because both are designated, it is like a serpent and its coils.
All those qualities, though eternally non-different from it, exist specifically as qualities and as the possessor of qualities, and as the enjoyer and the enjoyed. (Māṇḍūkya-kārikā 3.2.158)
The word "eternal" (nitya) has the sense of restriction.

All the qualities and attributes belonging to the Supreme Lord are eternally non-different from Him; thus they are absolutely non-distinct. Nevertheless, by virtue of a specific power (*viśeṣa-śakti*), they exist in the relationship of quality and qualified, and so forth.
This might be the case.

Granted that there may be absolute non-difference between the Blessed One and qualities such as dimension (*parimāṇa*) and so forth—which persist as long as the substance exists—it is not tenable [to claim the same] for actions (*kriyā*) and qualities (*guṇa*) such as knowledge (*jñāna*), since these are understood to be impermanent through scriptural usage such as "he created," "he creates," "he will create," "he knew," "he knows," and "he will know. Therefore, he says: "by virtue of having a specific nature" (*viśeṣātmatayā*).
Because they exist eternally both as specific individualities and as an eternal power,
there is no impermanence in the dharmas such as action and the like.

The construction of the sentence is as follows: since those properties, such as action and the rest, which belong to the Supreme Lord, exist eternally by way of their eternal power (*nitya-śakti*), and because they can appropriately become objects of worldly transaction through manifestation in the form of specific individualities (*viśeṣātmatā*), they are not non-eternal. The detailed elaboration (*prapañca*) has already been provided previously.

But surely, the manifestation of actions and so forth is indeed impermanent; otherwise, the aforementioned conventional usages would result in being without a basis. Consequently, even though that manifestation is a property of the Blessed One, its absolute non-difference [from Him] is not tenable. To this, he says: "Not through a distinction... and so on.
And this nature of specific distinction is not impermanent... [MĀn 3.2.160ab]
This has been described as the objective basis for conventional usage.
Why? To this he says: "Because of capacity," etc.
...the state of being power;
that very [power] which... // MAnu 3.2.160bc //
The meaning is: because that specific nature is nothing other than the very form of power (*śakti*), and it has been stated that power is eternal; therefore [the object is eternal].
[Objection: If that is so, then there would be no distinction in conventional usage between "power" and "manifestation" (*vyakti*).
Furthermore, the lack of an objective basis for the aforementioned conventional expressions would not have been refuted; therefore, he says: "saviśeṣa" (with qualifications).
... it would be with distinction ... // MAnu 3.2.160 //
This individual is not non-different from power in an undifferentiated manner,
such that the aforementioned fault would arise; rather, [it is different].
It is indeed non-different from that which possesses distinctions.

If this "distinction," which is the cause for the accomplishment of everything, were different from the Blessed One, then the thesis that all his attributes are absolutely non-different from him would be undermined.
If, on the other hand, it were non-different, then it could not possess the status of being a "distinction."
Since that [cognition] too would not exist by terminating in its own nature alone, he says: "the particular" (viśeṣa).
... nor is this another distinction. MĀn 3.2.160d.
Nevertheless, it may be done especially for the sake of one's own maintenance.
The word "only" (*eva*) is used for emphasis.
Even this distinction was not made by the Blessed One as something separate; therefore, there is no loss of the original thesis.
Nevertheless, it may still possess the status of a specific qualification.
How so?
For this [entity], while being non-different, is not without distinction.
If that were the case, there would be an infinite regress through a succession of distinctions.
It would not [be possible].
Why? Because of the principle that a specific property (*viśeṣa*) cannot be its own establisher.
Thus has the proposition (*pratijñā*) been shown.
In that regard, the objections have been refuted;
and having stated this here as well,
it might be so.

If there were authoritative evidence for these points, we would perceive it; since we do not, he explains the reason given in the Sūtra—"on account of the designation of both"—as follows: "by way of being a specific [attribute]," and so forth.
Because it is specifically known through all means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).

The meaning is: "from the knowledge" (*vijñāteḥ*)—that is, from the fact that all two kinds of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), including Vedic statements, have established that qualities such as knowledge and so forth are attributes of the Lord, and by the force of the word "also" (*api*), are non-different from Him.
But how can it be "from the knowledge" (*vijñāteḥ*)? [Is it not rather *vijñātāt*? [This is because of the rule] "ātaścopasarge" (Pāṇini 3.3.106).
Because the suffix *ktin* subordinates the suffix *aṅ*,
it will occur by virtue of the rule: "The suffix *ktin* [is applied] after roots beginning with *nā*."
He explains this very point with the words: "He created."
For the distinction that "he created" and "he withdrew" is indeed understood;
yet by the very Vedic text itself, the identity of those [acts] as being one and the same is also perceived.
By the phrase "he created," he cites such scriptural passages as, "He created all this";
and [the phrase] "he resolved to eat that" [is cited].

By the phrase "he withdrew such [words]," and by the phrase "that [which consists of] bliss and so forth is that very Supreme Self," he [refers to] the scriptural passage beginning with "Bliss is Brahman."
This is the meaning:
"He created all this;
he, the bull, supports heaven and earth."
"It resolved to eat that;
it thought; it desired;
he who knows the bliss of Brahman."
From such scriptural passages as these, it is understood that creation and so forth are attributes (*viśeṣa*) or excellences (*atiśaya*) of Brahman, and not Brahman alone;
for if it were [Brahman] alone, the relationship between action and agent and so forth would be untenable.
"He understood: ‘Bliss is Brahman’."
The non-difference of that [Brahman] from Him is understood by the very scripture beginning with, "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, Infinite; It is to be perceived as one alone.
Thus, all this is postulated on the grounds that the two designations [of difference and non-difference] cannot otherwise be accounted for.
In all the attributes of Brahman, there is a non-difference from Brahman that is qualified by distinction (*saviśeṣa-atyantābheda*).

This includes: the eternality of activity (*kriyā*) and so forth; the nature of these as both potentiality (*śakti*) and manifestation (*vyakti*); the eternality of even that which is manifested; the non-difference of the manifested from its potential state; the qualified nature of the distinction itself; and the self-sustaining character of that distinction.
For if even one of these points were not postulated, the contradiction regarding the two types of designations cited above could not be resolved.
The preceding section of the text, up until the words "by way of illustration," is intended to elaborate upon this very point.
Now, [if] it is thought:

Let there be only difference between the attributes of Brahman and Brahman itself; the relationship of qualifier and qualified will exist through inherence (*samavāya*). Furthermore, the refutations of inherence will be reduced to fallacies due to their contradiction with scripture (*śruti*).
Or, even in the absence of inherence (*samavāya*), some such unique power (*mahimā*) is postulated as belonging to the property and the substratum themselves;

nor is there a contradiction with the scriptural texts on non-difference, because such usage is justified as a metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) based on the fact that [the qualities] are not adventitious (*anāgantuka*).
Therefore, what is the point of accepting distinctions and so forth by resorting to non-difference?
Another says: Brahman is indeed indivisible, and there is no distinction whatsoever within it;
nor is there any contradiction with other scriptural passages.

This is because objects such as ritual action have qualities as their domain, and since those qualities consist of illusion (*māyā*), they are charming only so long as they are not investigated; furthermore, expressions such as "bliss" (*ānanda*) can be understood as figurative (*upacarita*), just like the expression "the head of Rāhu."
But another says: "Since the consistency of both designations is established through difference and non-difference alone, what is the use of this conceptualization of non-difference with attributes?
This is not so;
for even by these three [modes], in the end, a distinction must necessarily be admitted within that which is non-different.

Then, with the intention that it would be better to accept that [distinction] from the very beginning, he says "Distinction" (bheda) in order to first cause the proponent of difference to accept a specific qualification.
If difference belongs to the qualified entity, how can that difference [itself] be distinct from the differentiator?
If a difference between Brahman and its specific attributes, such as knowledge and so forth, is admitted, then we ask:
does that difference exist together with the distinct entity, namely Brahman, and with the distinct attribute, namely knowledge and so forth?
How and of what kind is it to be understood?
Is it different or is it non-different?
He states the fault regarding the first [alternative] with the words: "If it were distinct... (bhinnaśced iti).
If it were distinct, there would be an infinite regress... // MAnu 3.2.163c //
If difference were distinct from the two things that differ, then that difference would likewise [require another difference], resulting in an infinite regress.

Indeed, the difference between a property and its substratum is accepted only for the sake of establishing their relationship as qualifier and qualified; and that difference is a cause for such [distinction] only when it is itself perceived.

And since that cognition occurs only through the status of qualifiers and so forth, the cognition of each subsequent distinction is necessarily required; thus, an infinite regress is firmly established.
Even if [the entity] were non-different, it must be stated whether it is non-different from that which possesses distinctions or non-different from that which lacks distinctions.
Regarding the first case, he states the fault: "If it were non-different... (*abhinnaśced iti*).
If it is indivisible, why was it not so before?
"Why not previously? means: why is the non-difference of properties from the substratum (dharmin) not accepted as being qualified? The sense is that it must indeed be accepted.

Even though [the relation] could be established through a qualification alone—just as difference is—without a further difference, there would be the fault of complexity (gaurava) in postulating a redundant chain; therefore, the conclusion is that it is better to accept the non-difference of properties from the substratum as being qualified.
To the objection that "let it be so," he says: "The distinction."
He does not accept that the distinction is non-different.
To begin with, a particular property (*viśeṣadharma*) is simply something distinct;

that is not accepted by the proponent of difference (*bhedavādin*). Since even the existence of a particular property is far from being admitted, this would constitute a departure from one's own established tenet (*apasiddhānta*).
And our desired [goal] would not be accomplished—this is the intention.
He refutes the second [position] with the words: "If it were non-different."
If it were non-different and without distinction, from where would that differentiation arise?

If difference were non-different from the two things that differ, and were moreover devoid of distinction, then how could there be its status as their difference—the state of "this is the difference between these two"—for it would not arise from anything at all?
This is because its belonging to those two or its being qualified by them is impossible without a distinction.
Furthermore, if it were merely that [non-distinct entity], then only the property and the substratum would exist, and difference would not exist.
And likewise, even the [distinction between] property and property-bearer would not exist;
or it would follow that only difference exists, and not property and property-bearer.
Consequently, even difference itself would not exist. *9,465*

Having accepted that difference is of the very nature of the thing that differs, he states another refutation against one who does not accept *viśeṣa* (ultimate particularity), beginning with the words "by this."
"That this one is distinct from that one"—this is precisely what constitutes differentiation;
since this very distinction is perceived in many ways, what further answer can there be? (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.2.165)

In the cognition "this jar is distinct," it is precisely that distinction which is perceived specifically as the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), and not the jar itself; rather, the jar is perceived as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*).
Likewise [in the case of] "by this" and "by that."
The use of the instrumental case in place of the ablative is due to the rule *vyatyayo bahulam* (various substitutions occur frequently),
or it is used in connection with the word *saha*.

In the statement "the jar is different from the pillar which is different from the cloth," this very difference is perceived as qualified by its association with a specific counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*).

Likewise, this object is distinct from the person by virtue of its curvature and its hollow interior; thus, this very difference is perceived specifically through a distinguishing attribute (*vyāvartaka-dharma*).
The object itself, however, is perceived merely through the contact of the senses.

Similarly, "this jar is distinct from this cloth, from this pillar, and from this wall"—this very difference is perceived in many ways through the cause of association with specific counter-correlatives (*pratiyogi*) as particularizing factors.
The jar, however, exists as a single entity;
therefore, difference is not the intrinsic nature (svarūpa) of the jar. What answer will you provide to that refutation of the difference in intrinsic nature which is asserted by others?
The meaning is: if a distinction is not admitted;

that is, if a distinction is not admitted, then it is also impossible to maintain that "the difference is non-different from the differentiator," because there exist many factors that establish a difference between the difference and the differentiator.
