The point is this: having established through their very qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) that those [differences] are otherwise established, one must state—on the strength of cognition—that the difference is non-different from the differentiator, and not otherwise. If it is argued: "No; for we shall provide the answer to the claim that a difference, such as mutual absence (*anyonyābhāva*), which is perceived as belonging to something (*tadīyatva*), as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*), as having a counter-correlative (*sapratiyogitva*), as possessing a mark (*liṅgitva*), and as being manifold (*bahutva*), is not accepted as being the very nature (*svarūpa*) of the differentiator. For that which is accepted as the nature of the thing is not perceived as having those properties of 'belonging to it' and so forth. [The author replies: No.
This is because this very [nature] is well-established, whereas for anything else it is absent;
otherwise, it would be merely stating another technical name for "difference" while it is actually the nature itself.
Furthermore, proponents of non-duality (advaitavādins) do not fail to accept the intrinsic nature (svarūpa).
So what is the use of this distinction?
This has been stated by means of the two words "sa" (he) and "eṣa" (this), which indicate well-known recognition.
If it is argued that [the application of these terms] is merely a metaphorical usage because of belonging to him (*tadīyatva*), etc., we say no.
Because the cognition is vivid, and because it is non-erroneous due to the absence of any subverting evidence;
this too has been stated by the words "it is seen. (9.468)
He states another refutation: "abhedeti" (regarding non-difference).
For indeed, non-difference and difference themselves constitute the essential nature of the possessor of distinctions.
The construction is as follows: it is not only the case for difference, but also for non-difference, that [the universal] is simply the essential nature (svarūpa) of the distinct particular;
this applies to one who accepts the non-difference of difference from the distinct particular, such as a jar.
Therefore, he must also admit that non-difference has the very nature of the jar, because it follows the same logical principle as difference; this is the meaning of the word "hi" (for).
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "Of those two also..."
And for those two as well... // Mānava-dharmaśāstra 3.2.166c //

The ellipsis is that non-difference must be accepted. [An objection is raised: "Let there be non-difference between difference and non-difference, both of which are absolutely non-different from the single jar; what follows from that? To this, he says: "Because of the lack of distinction."
For if there were no distinction between them, the two words would indeed be synonyms.

If there were absolute non-difference between difference and non-difference, and no specific distinction (viśeṣa) existed, then the words "non-difference" and "difference" would become synonyms, because they would denote the same object—just as the words "jar" (ghaṭa) and "pitcher" (kalaśa). This is the meaning of the word "hi" (for/indeed). To the objection that "let it be so," he replies: "abhedeti" (*9,469*).
And who could say that the words "non-difference" and "difference" are synonyms? 3.2.167ab.
Who would say "none"? No one at all; rather, everyone says that they are indeed synonyms. Therefore, this [claim] is unauthoritative and contradicts valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
This is what is meant:

Difference is non-different from that which possesses difference; by that same logic, non-difference is also [non-different] from it. Thus, those two are mutually non-different, and such is their identity.
Consequently, since the words "difference" and "non-difference" would result in being synonyms, this must be avoided solely by the force of a specific distinction (*viśeṣa*).
If that [distinction] is not admitted, the consequence would be unavoidable.
"Is it not proper, then, to establish that even the words 'the differentiated' (bheda) and 'that which differentiates' (bhedī) are synonyms?
True;
however, it was not stated [explicitly] so that students might investigate this for themselves. *9,470*
He raises an objection: "Difference."
If difference and non-difference from the distinct entity were mutually [established]... MĀnuv 3.2.167cd.

Even though difference and non-difference are non-different from the distinct object, the pot, they nevertheless possess mutual difference between themselves; thus, it does not follow that their respective words are synonyms. To the question, "In what way, then, are they qualified? he replies: "They are qualified."
... this is the distinction. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.2.167d)
The meaning is that even by one who accepts it in this way, a distinction must necessarily be accepted within the undifferentiated entity.
To the question "How so?", he says: "In the absence of distinction."

How can there be difference in that which is without distinction? Likewise, how can there be identity for one who possesses difference? Furthermore, the distinction between those two would arise merely from the fact of being the possessor of difference.

In the absence of any distinction, the difference [of one thing] would be non-different from the differentiator; likewise, the identity [of another thing] would be non-different from its differentiator, such as a jar.
Furthermore, how could that mutual difference and identity between those two be logically established?
Why would it not be so?
Because difference and non-difference are merely the possessor of difference;
otherwise, even a jar would have difference by itself.
[If that were not so,] there would be a mutual difference between difference and non-difference, which are non-different from the jar.

The point is that for the sake of logical consistency (*nirvāha*), non-difference must be accepted as being qualified (*saviśeṣa*) by means of the pot. He raises an objection with the words "of the distinct" (*bhedinaśca*).
If a distinction is perceived between the divider and the division, and likewise between the undivided and that which is divided... // MAnu 3.2.169a-c //
The word *ca* (and) has the sense of mutual conjunction;
the two words *eva* (only/precisely) serve to exclude any distinction or difference between them.
*Gamyate* means it is understood or accepted.
I accept that there is both non-difference and distinction between the difference and the differencer, namely the jar;
likewise, I accept that there is a qualified non-difference between that non-difference and its non-differencer.
Thus, since difference and non-difference do not consist solely in the jar, their mutual distinction is established, and therefore the two words are not synonyms.
Therefore, the point is that difference and non-difference must be accepted as being mutually non-different and yet distinct; thus, [the opponent's position] is untenable.

Even so, although it is already established that one who accepts a distinction between the property (dharma) and the substratum (dharmin) must ultimately admit a particularity (viśeṣa) in the non-different entity, the author—intending to show that the stated reality should not be abandoned—responds with the word "What? (kimiti).
... what difference is there between difference and non-difference? // MĀnuv_3.2.169d //
If there is thus a distinction between non-difference and difference, why is it postulated?
Even in those two cases, a non-difference characterized by distinction must be admitted. He states the reasoning for this: "by means of the qualifiers themselves."
If all transactions everywhere were conducted by means of distinctions alone,
then why would one postulate a separate category [of "difference"] at all, since that would only result in conceptual complexity?

If it is accepted that—in all cases where there is non-difference between the differentiated and the differentiator, or between the identical and the identical—the conventional usage is based specifically on the cultivation of their being "that alone" (tanmātratā), then the question arises: why is the difference between difference and non-difference postulated at all, given that it would only lead to conceptual complexity? This is a sarcastic remark.

Since everything—both difference and non-difference—is accounted for as being qualified by distinction (saviśeṣatva) just as in the case of a jar, the postulation of difference would involve conceptual over-elaboration (kalpanā-gaurava).

This is because it would entail the postulation of multiple categories as well as a twofold conceptualization; such is the sense. [The opponent asks: "Let this be so; what does that have to do with the present topic? To this, he replies: "Precisely by way of distinction."

If, even when the distinction is non-different from the distinct entity, there is the conventional usage of "belonging to it" and so forth—and if, even when [the universal] is non-different from the jar, there is the conventional usage of non-synonymous terms—this occurs solely by virtue of the *viśeṣa* (particularity), then why should the difference between the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*) be postulated merely for the sake of conceptual complexity? Even if one accepts a difference between the property and the substratum, a *viśeṣa* must ultimately be accepted; therefore, it is better to accept that [the *viśeṣa*] right from the beginning.
"Otherwise, there would be the consequence of the fault of conceptual complexity (*kalpanāgaurava*). By this, it is explained why [the distinction] was not previously stated.

If, out of fear of conceptual complexity, one accepts the non-difference of the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*), yet accepts a distinction for the sake of specific conventional usage; [then...]
In that case, let it be postulated in the same way for cows and horses as well, since there is no distinction [between them].
And if that were so, there would be no differentiation at all in the world; therefore, he says: "oneness" (aikya).
Due to the absence of the cognition of identity, there is indeed a difference between a cow and a horse.
Only difference (bheda) is admitted, not the particularity (viśeṣa).
The reading "of cow and horse" (gavaśvayoḥ) is a scribal error,
as it is not found in the root manuscripts.
To the question, "Even in the absence of the cognition of identity, why is a distinction not admitted? he says: "That very [thing]... and so forth.
For when there is the cognition "it is that very same [thing]," it is called a particularity (viśeṣa).
For, by means of the counter-argument regarding the property and the substratum (*dharmadharmipratibandha*), the opponent must establish a distinction between the cow and the horse;
yet no such lack of distinction exists there, because non-difference is accepted in that case due to the cognition of their identity.
And because that [distinction] does not exist here;
and because difference is established by perception, there is no burden of conceptual construction (kalpanā-gaurava).
Now, even the proponent of non-difference is made to accept a distinction—[as indicated by the phrase] "of Being-Consciousness, etc. (*saccidādeḥ*).
For even by a proponent of illusion (māyin), this distinction must be admitted in order to establish that existence, consciousness, and so forth are not synonymous. ... MAnu 3.2.172a-c.
"Even by the Māyin" means even by one who accepts that sentences whose objects are action and so forth have an illusory (māyika) object.
The reason for this is stated as: "for the purpose of establishing the non-synonymity of the collection of words beginning with 'Being' (sat) and 'Consciousness' (cit)."
"This" (*ayam*) refers to the cause for the application of non-synonymous terms.
The word "for" (*hi*) indicates that the existence of the particular (*viśeṣa*) in such a manner has been established by valid cognition (*pramita*).
This is what is being said:
Let it be granted for now that sentences concerning actions and the like have unreal objects;
nevertheless, sentences such as "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite" are indeed accepted by the opponent as having real objects.

Furthermore, if those words were restricted to an indivisible (akhaṇḍa) referent, then terms such as "truth" (satya), "knowledge" (jñāna), and so forth, having a single meaning, would become synonyms;
yet that is not tenable, because they are observed to be used together. Nor is it possible to admit a difference [between them].
Because it would contradict such scriptural passages as "one only, without a second," a distinction must be admitted even within reality. Furthermore,
its status as the ground for the application of non-synonymous terms is established by this very same presumption (arthāpatti).
"Because that [conceptualization] is constructed precisely as suchness. With this, he raises an objection based on the theory of exclusion (*apoha*), beginning with "If... (*yadīti*).
...if it is held that another word is intended to exclude [the preceding term] individually, even though there is no distinction in its meaning. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 3.2.172d–f)

If words such as "truth" and so forth were denotative of injunctions (*vidhi*), then because the qualifying attributes being enjoined—such as truthfulness and the like—would not exist in Brahman, and because its own essential nature is a single unity, they would become synonyms.
However, this is not the case, because these words denote the exclusion (*apoha*) of untruth and so forth. Furthermore, even if this is the case, they are not rendered purposeless.
This is because the qualifiers such as "Brahman is unreal" and so forth are imagined through delusion, and [the scripture] aims to negate them;
for there are indeed those who hold that Brahman does not exist, or that even if it exists, it is not knowledge, or that it is limited.
Such cognitions as "I know" and so forth belong to living beings.
Furthermore, the word *satya* (truth) does not express the exclusion (*apoha*) of even ignorance (*ajñāna*), such that one [word] alone would suffice;
therefore, there is neither synonymy nor redundancy.
Alternatively, words such as "satya" (truth) and so forth denote distinct meanings such as "truth-ness" and so on, and thus do not become synonyms.

However, since they function toward Brahman through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā), they do not impart their specific qualifiers to it. For the word "Gaṅgā," when applied to the riverbank, does not impart "Gaṅgā-ness" to that bank.

Nor should it be argued that because [the nature of Brahman] is thus characterized by a single [attribute], the others are redundant; for they are meaningful insofar as they individually exclude superimposed qualities such as unreality and the like. Furthermore, it is not the case that the definition is untenable due to the absence of an object for the acquisition of linguistic convention (*saṅgatigrahaṇa*).

The meaning of the objection is that since the words "satya" (truth) and "brahman" can be established as denoting the same object when they are understood to have a connection with the variegated [reality], they are neither synonyms nor redundant; thus,
the qualification "asatya" (unreal) [or "unreality"] is applied.
Or, "the qualification is superimposed"—
this is the connection [of the words] with "if this is accepted.
He refutes [this objection] with the word "illusion" (māyā).
Distinguished by the specific absence of any particularity of illusion, it may belong even to that which is real... [Mānava-dharmaśāstra 3.2.173a-c]
By the word "māyā," he expresses the state of being superimposed.
Thus, even when a false construction is imagined, the integrity of the Real is not established;
for it is unavoidable that it must be qualified by specific characteristics such as the absence of imagined unreality and the like—this is the meaning. (9.482)
He raises an objection: "And that... //
And if she is likewise... // MAnu 3.2.173cd //
The refutation of its indivisibility would occur if it were qualified by the attribute of being devoid of superimposed particulars;
but this is not the case.
Rather, that [indivisibility] too is merely superimposed, just like unreality and so forth.
The meaning is that the formlessness of space is not impaired by a superimposed form.
He refutes this, saying: "It would lead to an infinite regress."
... there is no finality. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.2.173d)
The word "of the sentence-meaning" is to be supplied [as the object].
If that were so, then no sentence-meaning would be established,
because it would not have been presented as possessing specific attributes such as truthfulness, nor as being excluded from [the opposite] such as untruthfulness.
For there is no sentence-meaning apart from relation and distinction.
If it is argued that Brahman alone is the sentence-meaning, we say no; because Brahman is self-luminous.

"And because exclusion (vyāvṛtti) is unreal"—this is the meaning of the objection: "Or rather, that [cognition] is indeed perceived, and it is established solely as the exclusion of its own absence, not as having Brahman as its object; therefore, how could its indivisibility (akhaṇḍatā) be contradicted?"
Even so, since the qualification consisting in the exclusion of its non-existence has not been avoided, the very integrity [of Brahman] is lost.
If that [qualification] is likewise [an exclusion], there is an infinite regress; thus the meaning of the refutation is that the knowledge of Brahman would be unstable.
Not only does the absence of difference in Brahman entail the redundancy of words and so forth, [but this further consequence follows].
He says "If" [in the verse] to address the question: "How could even a single word not apply there?"
If there were no distinction regarding truth, then there would be no such statement.
The meaning is that no word can function without depending on some cause such as a quality (*guṇa*), an action (*karman*), or the like.
He raises an objection: "But it is perceived by this [word]."
If it is observed by him, then... // MAnu 3.174c //
This fault would arise if Brahman were denotable by words;
but it is not so. Rather, it is only indicated by that word.
Indication (lakṣaṇā) does not depend on qualities, actions, and so forth;
for if it were so, it would indeed be nothing other than primary denotation (abhidhā). He refutes this [objection] with the words: "the indicated object" (lakṣyam).
"...it would also be characterized as the 'object to be defined' (lakṣya). Even if Brahman is accepted in this way, it would be characterized as the "object to be defined.
The meaning is that its status as an object to be defined cannot be avoided.
And this is merely an illustration; [the term] may indeed be qualified by its connection with the primary meaning and so forth as well.

If it is argued that "Brahman does not even possess the state of being indicated (lakṣyatva)," for even the word "indicated" is itself used through indication (lakṣaṇā) and not through the function of direct denotation (abhidhāna)—we say no.
In this sentence as well, because the word "lakṣya" (the object to be defined) is employed by the opponent, it acquires the specific quality of being that which is to be defined.
If it is argued that for that reason it too is indeed *lakṣya*, he replies with the word "punar" (again).
Furthermore, even if one were to examine the characteristics again and again, there would be an infinite regress.
The phrase "when secondary indication (lakṣaṇā) has been resorted to" is the ellipsis to be supplied. He raises an objection with the words "if."
If it were characterized by non-existence, then that would indeed be accepted by you.
The word "mate" (in their opinion) is the ellipsis [to be supplied].
Or, it is an indeclinable used in the sense of the instrumental case.
This refers to what was stated: that even for the Real (satya), there might be [the status of being an effect] as qualified by the qualification of being devoid of any specific illusory power (māyā).
Therefore, this is not undesirable,
because I accept that [Brahman] possesses a specific nature consisting of non-existence [of duality], as in the statement:
"There is no diversity here."
Thus, the Śruti indeed accepts non-existence in Brahman, just as in the statement, "There is no jar on this ground. As for what was said—
that such a statement would not be possible— it is not so.
That too is incorrect; for even in the absence of a cause consisting of a positive entity (*bhāva*), the application of a word is possible through a cause consisting of a non-entity (*abhāva*),
since it is accepted that [an object] possesses the property of being a non-entity.
By this, the claim that "it is the indicated object" (lakṣya) is also refuted;
the point is that it is logically possible for the word "indicated object" (lakṣyapada) itself to have apoha as its denotation.
To this, it must be said: why do you abandon the supreme final doctrine of indivisibility (akhaṇḍatva) and instead accept the possession of the property of non-existence?
Now, one might say:
"Indeed, words such as 'truth,' 'knowledge,' 'infinite,' 'consciousness,' and 'bliss' are heard in the scriptures with reference to Brahman;
yet it is not possible to accept their meaning as being of the nature of an injunction."

Because this contradicts such scriptural passages as "There is no diversity here," and because it has already been stated that there is no contradiction if one accepts the attributes of non-existence,
he says in response: "On account of non-omniscience, etc."
In this same way, you will also be free from such things as non-omniscience.
The ellipsis is "they must be accepted.
For just as the words "truth," "knowledge," and so forth are heard in scripture regarding Brahman,
so too is this [Brahman] "all-knowing."
"This one is the Lord of All"—

thus [you claim] that even such terms as "omniscient" and so forth likewise denote only the absence of non-omniscience and the like, just as those [other terms] denote only the absence of falsehood and the like. (By you.)
[These qualities] must indeed be accepted.

Consequently, the distinction that the statement "truth, knowledge," and so forth reveals reality (*tattvāvedaka*), whereas the statement regarding omniscience and so forth refers to Brahman as qualified by *māyā* (*māyāśabala*), is not tenable; this is the intended meaning. [An opponent might argue: "Let this distinction not exist; even the absence of non-omniscience and other such qualities is certainly accepted in Brahman. To this, he says: "At that time" (*tadā*).
In that case, there would indeed be omniscience, because both negative particles (nañ) have the sense of affirmation.
If the absence of omniscience and other such qualities in Brahmā is admitted, then the presence of qualities such as omniscience is indeed unavoidable.
Why?

The meaning is that, according to the maxim that "two negatives convey the original sense with an intensification," this will also apply to their [the Jains'] claim regarding the absence of non-omniscience and so forth; having stated this, he states the subverting argument (*bādhaka*) in the event of its non-acceptance, beginning with "If... (*yadi*).
If such [food] is not to be accepted...

If such a probandum— that the terms "omniscient" and so forth, when heard in reference to Brahman, convey the cessation of non-omniscience and the like— is not to be accepted, then the term "bliss" would likewise not exclude the absence of happiness, the term "truth" would not exclude unreality,
and the term "knowledge" would not exclude ignorance.

And the term "self" [would imply] non-selfhood; the ellipsis of the sentence is "because there would be no distinction. This is so that terms such as "bliss" (*ānanda*) do not fail to exclude [the opposite qualities] such as suffering (*asukha*).
To the question "What is the fault? he says: "Because of its lack of pleasure," and so forth.
... because of the non-cessation of non-happiness, and because of the cognition of non-existence, there would then be non-existence and so forth. (MAnu 3.2.177b–d)
The connection is: "because non-existence, ignorance, and so forth are not removed.
This is the meaning:
first of all, non-existence and the like are applicable to Brahman.
The scriptures, such as the statements "Being, Consciousness," and so forth, are set forth for the purpose of excluding that [misconception].
If even those do not exclude it, then it would follow that the non-existence and other such qualities of Brahman are indeed real.
Alternatively, by supplying the words "if it were not thus," one should apply this single sentence alone by mentally distinguishing its parts. *9,491*
He raises an objection: "Untruth, etc. (anṛtādi).
If it is accepted that each [vow] is opposed to falsehood and so forth, [then...]
Regarding this "truth-ness" and so forth:
the meaning is that,
at first glance, words such as "truth" and the like present themselves as qualifiers of truth-ness and so on.
Thereafter, they culminate in the removal of each respective opposing form,
as it has been said: "For, with respect to each object to be established, [the cognition] arises from the opposition of that which is opposed to it."
"One subsequently knows its absence, like [the absence of] the executioner from the place of execution.

Since it is well-established that the six qualifiers such as "truthfulness" (satyatva) and so forth are contradictory to their opposites such as "untruthfulness" (anṛtatva), how could there not be the exclusion of those [opposites]?
He says "even in the case of the inherent nature" (samavetaprakṛtau) with the words "anaiśvarye" (lack of sovereignty).
In the same way, why is the state of being opposed to lack of sovereignty not also prevented? (3.2.178cd)
The ellipsis [to be supplied] is: "of sovereignty and so forth, which are conferred by such titles as 'Lord of All' (*sarveśvara*) and the like.
He concludes with the verse beginning "akhaṇḍa" (unbroken).

Thus, even by one who maintains that the self is partless, a distinction must be accepted through a mind that is itself fragmented, because otherwise no understanding would be possible. (Manu 3.2.179)
Thus, the logical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows:
even by one who speaks without flaw, because of this very [fact] of being unimpaired by refutation;
for the reason is that there is no other way.
By "unbroken" (*akhaṇḍita*), it is meant being devoid of further conceptualization (*utprekṣā*).
Now, he causes the proponent of both difference and non-difference (*bhedābhedavādin*) to accept a specific qualification by stating "unbroken" (*akhaṇḍa*).

That [work] must indeed be borne upon the head with great reverence by both those who advocate its indivisibility and those who advocate its divisibility, and likewise by those who hold it to be both divisible and indivisible; for it is truly distinguished.

Since a distinction must therefore be admitted by both the proponents of the "unbroken" (*akhaṇḍa*) and the "broken" (*khaṇḍa*), for that very reason, a distinction must indeed be admitted between the "partially broken" (*khaṇḍākhaṇḍa*) and the proponent of the "partially broken" (*khaṇḍākhaṇḍavādin*).
[The term] *khaṇḍākhaṇḍena* is grammatically correct either as an indication (*upalakṣaṇā*)—as in the expression "the spears enter"—or by applying the rule *arśa-ādibhyo'c*.
To explain:

For one who asserts that there is both difference and non-difference between the property (dharma) and the substratum (dharmin), are those two admitted to be entirely different from them, or entirely non-different, or both different and non-different? Not the first, because it would lead to an infinite regress of differences.
Furthermore, if difference were its own nature (*svarūpa*) and one did not admit *viśeṣa*, it would be impossible for [the substrate] to belong to that [difference];
and because there is no relation between difference and non-difference—which are absolutely distinct—it would be impossible for [the substrate] to belong to that [difference].
Nor is the second [alternative] tenable.
Furthermore, because [the relationship of] belonging to that and so forth would be untenable,
and because the words "difference" and "non-difference" would result in being synonyms,
the third [option] is not [acceptable].
Because it would lead to an infinite regress;
for if difference and non-difference were identical in some cases, the aforementioned defects would follow.
Therefore, even by one who maintains both difference and non-difference, some distinction must be admitted in certain instances.

Thus, it is established that because the two designations [of difference and non-difference] cannot otherwise be accounted for, there is indeed an absolute non-difference characterized by specific distinctions among the attributes of the Blessed One.
Now, one might object: "This cannot be the intention of the author of the Sūtras, because he has employed such illustrations as the serpent and its coils."
For what is called a "snake-coil" is a particular kind of mutual conjunction of its constituent parts;
that [coil] is not absolutely non-different from the snake.

Furthermore, light is a distinct substance and is not non-different from the sun; therefore, even the illustrative example "like the substratum of light" is not applicable for demonstrating absolute non-difference.

Since the "prior-ness" of time consists in its connection with a past action, the phrase "not as before" is also consistent with the present context; therefore, he says: "nidarśana... (by way of illustration).
Therefore, by means of three illustrations, the Blessed One has declared with great emphasis the absolute non-difference of the qualities... [MĀnuv 3.2.181a-c]

The meaning is that, since this is so, through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), the non-difference of the Lord’s attributes from the Lord itself is established here as being qualified by distinction (*saviśeṣa*).

The intention is that one should understand that even the three illustrations [cited] are intended by the author of the Sūtras to be applicable to this non-difference qualified by distinction, in accordance with the evidence that leaves no other possibility (*niravakāśapramāṇa*).
In that context, although the serpent’s coil possesses both difference and non-difference, it is nevertheless employed to lead those of dull intellect to an understanding of non-difference,
just as in the expression, "medicinal herbs arise from the earth.
Furthermore, by the word *prakāśa*, radiant form (*bhāsvara-rūpa*) is intended.

And because it exists as long as the substance itself, that [light] is indeed absolutely non-different from the solar orb; furthermore, that "being in front" consists in a connection with a prior time, which is established for all the world. Now, one might ask: "Is one example sufficient? What is the purpose of three? To this it was said: "With care. (9.498)
Having thus explained the primary meaning of the section, he now demonstrates the meaning established by implication: "And that... (tacceti).
And that is not the theory of the connection of what has been expressed (nābhihitānvaya).

Therefore, precisely because the Blessed One has established that there is no distinction between the qualities of the Blessed One and the Blessed One himself, it follows that this view—that the cognition of syntactic relation (*anvaya*) arises from the meanings of words denoted by the words themselves—is not [the intended doctrine];
this is the remaining point.
The mention of "the relation of what is denoted" (*abhihitānvaya*) is merely illustrative.
Because all views other than the theory of the expression of the related (*anvitābhidhāna*), which will be discussed below, are untenable;
if, then, the theory of the relation of the expressed (*abhihitānvaya*) is untenable,
what path is intended by the author of the Sūtras?
For it is not possible that there can be a cognition of concomitance (anvaya-jñāna) without a means;
we maintain that it is the expression of what is concomitant (anvitābhidhāna).
With the intention of showing that even in that case there is a distinction, he says: "When... (yadā).
When there is a general release from all specific details,
the understanding of those specifics may arise even from a single word in the response.
The word *yadā* has the sense of *yadi* (if).
Although it says "of all particularities" (*aśeṣaviśeṣāṇām*), the meaning is "endowed with all particularities.
The word *eka* has its primary sense.
The meaning is that among the compounds, it is a single word [formed] with the first word, i.e., by the word *eka*.
For if it were a *karmadhāraya* compound, the word *ekapada*, being [the member] whose time [of occurrence] is prior, would have to be placed first according to the rule *pūrvakāla-eka-*.
Even so,
through the subsequent series of words, there is an understanding of a specific positive concomitance (*anvaya*).
This is what is meant:

All the words contained in the scriptural passages that establish Brahman—such as "Brahman is truth, knowledge, infinite," and "He who is all-knowing and all-perceiving"—denote meanings that are mutually connected.
Among them, the word *brahman* denotes Brahman as endowed with every particular attribute, such as truthfulness, omniscience, and so forth.
Nor, in this case, is there any redundancy among words such as "truth" and the rest.

Since the capacity of words lies in denoting what is related in a general sense (*sāmānyato 'nvitābhidhāna*), and not in denoting a specific relation, the word *brahman* brings about the cognition of Brahman as related to all compatible attributes in a general way. Consequently, the words "Real" (*satya*) and so forth serve to convey the cognition of specific relations, such as "related as reality" or "related as knowledge.

Indeed, it was already stated by the Author of the Sūtras in the first Sūtra that the theories of "denotation of the unrelated" (*abhihitānvaya*) and others are untenable, while the theory of "denotation of the related" (*anvitābhidhāna*) is tenable.
Why, then, describe this here as a *adhikaraṇasiddhānta* (a conclusion established by the context)?
It is said:
for by the word "ataḥ" (therefore), only this much is understood—that there exists a means for the comprehension of the logical connection (*anvaya*).
However, the distinction is not that it is neither the words themselves nor the meanings expressed by those words and so forth;
rather, in this regard, a challenge certainly arises as to what the intention of the author of the Sūtra was toward the commentator.
And for the purpose of resolving that, the description of the *adhikaraṇasiddhānta* (the established conclusion of a topic) is indeed appropriate.
Although it can be said that the intention of the author of the Sūtra is indeed established,
nevertheless, there is no fault in this effort, as it is an attempt to elaborate upon the arguments briefly explained therein under the guise of describing an *adhikaraṇasiddhānta*.
He shows the reason referred to by the word "that" (*tad*) with the words "since" (*yataḥ*).
Since there is no unity whatsoever among all distinct particulars, therefore... // MAnu 3.2.183a-c //
By the word "vastu," Brahman is meant;
and by the word "ca" (and), the particularity [of Brahman] is also included.

Therefore, the doctrines such as *abhihitānvaya* (the connection of what has been expressed) and so forth are not [valid]; rather, what indeed is this aforementioned method of *anvitābhidhāna* (the expression of what is already connected)? This is the implied conclusion (*śeṣa*).
For instance, it has already been established that attributes such as reality (*satyatva*) are absolutely non-different from Brahman; therefore,
it follows necessarily that the word *brahman*, which denotes Brahman, must also denote reality and the other such attributes.

However, if there is non-difference, there is no positive concomitance (anvaya) at all; how then could there be its expression? Furthermore, the undesirable consequence remains that there would be the expression of particulars. In this regard, the only solution is to accept that [the universal] possesses particularity (*saviśeṣatva*).
For even in the case of non-difference, it is possible for there to be a connection with the capacity for particularity and yet no expression of the particular. *9,508*
It might be argued as follows:
in this theory of the expression of the related (*anvitābhidhāna*), the comprehension of the relation with specific particulars would result in being entirely without a basis,
because all words possess the capacity to express the related only in a general sense.
Nor should it be said that the first word expresses the meaning in a general way (*sāmānyato 'nvitābhidhāyin*), while the subsequent one does so specifically (*viśeṣataḥ*);
for "being first" and so forth are not fixed [in their position].
For even in Vedic sentences, the word *brahman* is sometimes first and sometimes subsequent; therefore, he says: "in a general way."

... that which is known in a general sense may, through the power of another word, come to be known in a specific sense; by this means, there arises the expression of a related meaning (anvita-ukti). MAnu 3.2.183c–f.

An object known in a general way as being connected through each individual word may subsequently be known in a specific way as being connected by virtue of the power imparted by the proximity of other words.
For that reason, it follows—as the remainder of the argument—that the capacity of words to express what is already connected (*anvitābhidhāyitā*) is logically established. *9,510*

It is incorrect to claim that the theory of *anvitābhidhāna* (the denotation of words as already connected) has been established in the manner described by supporting the non-difference [of the word-meaning] with its qualifiers;
for this leads to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
For if there were non-difference between color and the jar, then when the jar is perceived by the sense of touch, color would also be perceived.
If it is argued that its apprehension is restricted without distinction, then a restriction would apply here as well.
If it is claimed that the statement regarding the distinction itself is what is restricted, [we reply: so be it.
Why is even the general statement not [considered] restricted?
If it is thought that this is merely stated as a possibility (*sambhāvanā*), then this is not an *adhikaraṇasiddhānta*.

For an *adhikaraṇasiddhānta* is that meaning which, when one thing is established, is established as a necessary consequence (*anuṣaṅgī*), and not the establishment of a mere possibility; therefore, he says: "only its own meaning" (*svārtha eva*).
Since it is only the object itself that is connected with some particularity by means of this [word],
it is indeed known through experience by that very expression "by this."
Since the meaning of words is necessarily connected with something by another—

whether that connection be with "truth" (*satyatva*) or "knowledge" (*jñānatva*)— it is established by experience that this specific connection with a particular attribute is understood precisely through the mention of those [attributes], namely, through the mention of the word "truth" and so forth.
Therefore, it is said that [the position] is logical; this is the remainder of the sense.

The meaning is that while individual words generally denote meanings as related (*anvitābhidhāyin*), the specific cognition of the related meaning (*viśeṣato 'nvitārthapratīti*) occurs through words whose capacities are established by their mutual proximity; this is established by experience.
This is what is meant:
first, it would follow that a designation of particulars occurs without distinction; however, that is not the case, because it contradicts experience.
Therefore, that [designation]...

A specific distinction must be postulated by way of its being a counter-obstructive factor (*pratibandhakatva*), and that [distinction] should be accepted exactly as it is experienced; thus, there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) whatsoever. Having thus established the theory of the expression of the related (*anvitābhidhāna*), he now demonstrates—by way of showing the subverting arguments (*bādhaka*) against not accepting the theory of the expression of the related—the untenability of the positions such as the expression of the already-expressed (*abhihitānvaya*), which was previously stated: *9,512* Thus, having established the theory of the expression of the related (*anvitābhidhāna*), he demonstrates the untenability of the positions such as the expression of the already-expressed (*abhihitānvaya*) and others, by means of presenting the subverting arguments (*bādhaka*) that arise if the theory of the expression of the related is not accepted: [The text continues: ... [he demonstrates]... by means of presenting the subverting arguments (*bādhaka*) that arise if the theory of the expression of the related is not accepted.
"If" means:
If this word were to express its own meaning here without any syntactical connection, then who would ever establish a connection for all the other words as well? (Manu Smṛti 3.2.185)
This [phrase] beginning with "Brahman" is the primordial state;
here, in the passage beginning with "True Knowledge," there are also other subsequent [states].
Likewise, if even individual words, being unconnected, were not to express their own meanings through connection, then who would effect the connection or the cognition of that connection?

The first word denotes that which is connected [with its meaning] in a general sense, without having obtained any assistance; however, the subsequent words, having obtained assistance from the very beginning, denote that which is connected in a specific sense.
To indicate this distinction, they are grasped separately by means of the phrase "these others."

Otherwise, if all the words situated in a sentence were not denoters of related meanings (*anvitābhidhāyin*), but rather denoted their own isolated meanings (*svārtha*) while remaining unrelated, then he would have stated that the cognition of syntactic relation (*anvaya*) would consequently become groundless. He elaborates on this very point in the verse beginning with "vyāpāra."
A word has no function other than the manifestation of its own meaning;
for even a person becomes one who has fulfilled his purpose by being addressed but once. (Manu Smṛti 3.2.186)
How can there be knowledge of the positive concomitance (anvaya) when it is not the meaning of the word? 3.2.187ab.
If the relation (*anvaya*) were not the meaning of the word—that is, if it were not denotable by the term—then how could there be any cognition of that relation?
It would be impossible, because no other means [of cognizing it] exists.

To explain: these [alternatives] are necessarily considered, either because they must precede the cognition of the relation or because they have been accepted as such by the proponents [of various theories].
Is it the words, or the speaker, or the word-meanings denoted by the words, or the sentence, or the final phoneme of the sentence, or the series of phonemes, or the *sphoṭa*, or the hearer?

Regarding this, [the author] states with the half-verse beginning "for this operation... that, insofar as the theory of the expression of related meanings (*anvitābhidhāna*) is not accepted, the status of the words as the means [of cognition] is not tenable.
It is well established that a word, as a linguistic unit, has no function other than the manifestation of its own meaning;
furthermore, syntactic relation (*anvaya*) is not denotable by a word.

How, then, can a word be a means for that knowledge? [The author] says "the speaker also" (*pumān api*) to show that even for the speaker, that [knowledge] does not exist; the ellipsis is "therefore he too is not a means. (9.513) This is because, for that reason, he also is not a means.
The mention of "once" (ekavāra) is for the purpose of indicating its extreme remoteness [from the final cognition],
because it has already been exhausted by the mere single utterance.
He states the defect in the view that word-meanings denoted by words bring about the understanding of their mutual connection (anvaya), beginning with the words "yadaiva" (at the very moment).
Whenever there is an utterance by them consisting of words whose meanings are not syntactically connected, [it is considered untruth].
The meaning of a word would be incoherent... MĀnUV 3.2.188a.
The connection is with the phrase "of that which has an unconnected meaning. The singular number is used for the genus. "By them" means by those [words] situated within the sentence.

If words, having conveyed their own respective meanings while remaining unconnected, then cease their operation, then it would follow that the word-meanings themselves— possessing expectancy and so forth— bring about the cognition of connection; in that case, the meaning of the word would remain unconnected [to others].

The meaning is that the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) would not be verbal in nature, and furthermore, another means of valid cognition called "the meaning of words" (*padārtha*) would have to be admitted.
This might be so.
If we were to say that it is the word-meanings themselves that convey the mutual connection (anvaya),
that is not the case; rather,
it is the meanings as expressed by the words that do so.
To the question, "In that case, how can positive concomitance (*anvaya*) be non-verbal?", he says: "No."
... for that logical connection does not serve that purpose. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.2.188b)
The meaning is that the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) established by the word-meanings is not the meaning of those words themselves;
for if that were the case, fire as presented by smoke perceived through direct perception would itself have to be an object of direct perception—this is the intended sense.
To the objection, "In that case, let the sentence itself be what conveys the syntactic connection," he says: "nirākāṅkṣa" (free from expectancy).
The wise declare that a sentence consists solely of words that are free from expectancy.
For one who does not accept the capacity of words to denote meaning through mutual connection (anvitābhidhāna), it is impossible to accept that a sentence conveys the cognition of that connection;
for the wise declare that words themselves constitute the sentence,
since there is no sentence apart from the words— this is the meaning.
Some maintain that a sentence is nothing other than a collection of words; in order to exclude this view, the wise have stated [the definition] as "that which is complete" (*nirākāṅkṣa*).
That [view] will be refuted later.
Furthermore, so that words such as "cow," "horse," "man," or "elephant" do not become sentences, the term "complete" is specified.

Since the absence of expectancy cannot be established in the absence of proximity (*sannidhāna*), proximity is already obtained through the very fact of being without expectancy; therefore, it was not mentioned separately.

Furthermore, in cases such as "one should sprinkle with fire" (*agninā siñcet*), because there is no cognition of syntactic connection even when there is an absence of semantic competency (*yogyatā*), and because it is irrelevant to the present context, competency has also not been mentioned.
[Objection: But by speaking in this way, you yourself have admitted that the sentence is something distinct from the words.

Just as a cloth is a specific modification of threads and is not merely the threads themselves, so too that specific modification of words characterized by their state of being free from expectancy (nirākāṅkṣatā) must be something distinct from the words; therefore, he says: "that [and] that."
And that state of being free from expectancy arises through the expression of those respective meanings.
The syntactic unity (*nirākāṅkṣatā*) of words is not a transformation (*vikriyā*), like a cloth [produced] from threads,
by which a sentence would exist as something distinct from the words;
rather, it is simply a quality of the person who hears them.
Inquiry (*jijñāsā*) is indeed expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*). And the state of being free from expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatā*) is the cessation of inquiry.
Since that state of being free from expectancy would arise through words, words are said to be "free from expectancy."
Furthermore, the state of having fulfilled its purpose (*nirākāṅkṣatākāritva*) is not a specific modification of words,
because that state is caused merely by the expression of the intended object,
and because that [expression] is their very nature.
Thus, it is stated that words which express the object sought to be known bring about the cessation of the desire to know (jijñāsā) and become free from expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣa*).

He establishes this—namely, that the listener’s state of being free from expectancy arises precisely through the expression of the object sought to be known—with the words "because [the purpose] is not fulfilled" (*apūrteḥ*).
First, a desire for the completion of those [unfulfilled] purposes is recognized.
When it is simply said, "Bring [it]," prior to the employment of words such as "cow" and so forth,
there exists a desire to know [what it is], such as "What [is it]? and so on.

This means that [the word] does not denote [its object], such as a cow and so forth, until there is a fulfillment of those objects—such as the action (*karman*) and others—that were intended to be inquired about.
What is meant is this:
verbal inquiry persists as long as the words [intended to express] those objects remain unfulfilled.

As long as those [meanings] have not been denoted, the expectancy does not cease; and once they have been denoted by those words, it ceases. Therefore, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is understood that the state of being free from expectancy arises precisely through the denotation of those respective meanings. As for the two positions—that the final letter of the sentence is [the cause] or that the entire series of letters is [the cause]—they are extremely weak and thus have not been refuted here.
As has been stated previously:

"In that case, let it be that the sentence itself—known as *sphoṭa*, from which the division into phonemes and words has been eliminated—is the conveyor of the syntactic relation (*anvaya*). Words, however, are employed merely as its manifestors. To this objection, he says: "Action" (*karma*) [verse 9.518].
But when the object, the agent, and the action have reached their completion, what other connection could there be?
In this context, the mention of "action" (*karman*) and so forth is illustrative;
the meaning is "of those categories of things that have been sought to be known.
The phrase "mutually connected" (*anyonyasaṃsṛṣṭānām*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].

When there is the expression "pūrta," the word "by means of words" (padaiḥ) is to be supplied as the ellipsis; "the connection would be what is to be established" (anvayo bhavet pratipādanīyaḥ) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
This is what is meant: [the meaning is that the connection between the words must be demonstrated].

One who asserts that the *sphoṭa* is the signifier of the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) must state the proof for its existence. If it is argued that this is because the cognition of the connection would otherwise be inexplicable, we say no; for it is possible for the words themselves to signify the connected meaning.
Furthermore, there is no such thing as a "positive concomitance" (anvaya) distinct from those [individual words] that needs to be established for the sake of which one would search for a *sphoṭa*.
He states the following as a refutation against not accepting this: "non-completion" (*apūrti*).
If there is no fulfillment by means of the words spoken, how can it be fulfilled by a human horn?
The non-fulfillment of the logical connection (*anvaya*) constitutes its non-expression.
By the phrase "by those that have been stated," he intends the established validity of the words; by the phrase "by a human horn" or "by a *sphoṭa*," he indicates its lack of authoritative basis.
"By that which is like a man's horn"—the ellipsis is "is fulfilled," meaning "is expressed.
This is what is meant:
for the proponent of words (*padavādin*), there is simplicity of conceptualization (*kalpanālāghava*) regarding the words already established as cognized in their related meanings.
This is because [the meaning] is conceptualized as being denoted by the name.

For the proponent of *sphoṭa*, however, there is complexity (*gaurava*), since two things must be postulated: the *sphoṭa* itself, which lacks any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and its capacity to convey the linguistic connection (*anvaya*). *9,520*
Let it then be the position of the new theory of abhihitānvaya (the relation of expressed meanings).

For if it were held that words cease their function after merely conveying word-meanings, and that the word-meanings themselves convey the syntactic relation (*anvaya*), then the aforementioned defect would indeed occur.
But this is not the case.
"But words themselves, having as their intermediate operation the presentation of word-meanings, bring about the cognition of syntactic relation (anvaya).
This is not so;
for if that were the case, it would follow that words possess a function that ceases after having been exercised.
To the question "What, then, is the fault?", he says: "If there is activity... and so forth.
If their activity [is inherent], then why does it not occur even when they are not mentioned? (Manu 3.2.191cd)

If, moreover, a "ceased operation" (viramyavyāpāra) is admitted even for insentient words, then we ask: why does a word that has not been uttered not also possess an operation in conveying the meaning of the word and so forth? He anticipates the answer: "Because it has been spoken" (ukta).
If it is argued that an operation is intended for the purpose of ensuring the presence [of the word] in the intellect when it has been uttered;

The suffix *kta* is used in the sense of the action itself (*bhāve*). "Being present in the intellect" means being an object of the intellect; for words are instruments of cognition, and not like the eyes and other senses, which [function] by their mere existence.
The intention is that since verbal expression (*ukti*) is a means to that knowledge, in the absence of such expression there is no operation because knowledge has not occurred;
this connects with the phrase "if this is accepted. *9,521*
Again, the proponent asks: "Because it resides in the intellect"?
Why would they not have made an effort long ago to remain established in the Buddha's teaching?
We ask you this: why do those words not make an effort even prior to the utterance, since their being known is necessary for the function of conveying the meaning of objects and so forth?
The sense of the question is: why do they not make an effort to become objects of cognition even without an utterance?

Alternatively, [the objection is]: "Why do they not impel that which remains silent for the sake of being uttered so as to become an object of cognition? He raises the answer with the words: "puruṣa... (by the person).
If their dependence upon the person [is established]...
This might be so if words were sentient;
but they are not.
Therefore, they are entirely dependent upon the person who speaks them.
When he manifests [the words] through pronunciation, they then come to reside within the intellect of the hearer and become capable of performing functions such as conveying the meaning of the word;

however, they do not perform anything themselves. If this is so, then even a function consisting of the subsequent communication of the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) is not possible for them; thus he says: "And afterwards... (*paścācca*).
And afterwards, she is equal [to him]. (Manu 3.219cd–220a)
The dependence on the person occurs subsequently, at the time of bringing about the comprehension of the syntactic connection (*anvaya*).
This is what is meant:

for if words were conscious, our purpose would not be fulfilled merely by their conveying the meanings of the word-objects when they are uttered together, but rather by their bringing about the comprehension of the syntactic connection.
Therefore, having reflected that positive concomitance (*anvaya*) must also be established by us, it would be appropriate to cease [the current argument];
yet this is not the case.
Otherwise, the aforementioned over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) remains exactly as stated.
It might be argued that [the auditory faculty] is the cause for the subsequent cognition (*anvayajñāna*) of the hearer;
however, it is merely the agent (*kartṛ*). Its cause, moreover, is now being investigated. *9,522*

If it is argued that the hearer, taking the words themselves—which express meanings that are not yet syntactically connected—as the instrument, strives for the cognition of the connection between those meanings recalled by them, the author replies to that with the words: "The person alone... (pumāneva).

If a male alone is subsequently sought for the purpose of establishing a connection among these [words], he alone [is the subject] even when there is the expression of other meanings by those words whose denotations were previously unconnected;
let him strive... [Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.2.193a-e].
By the word "anvaya" (syntactic connection), the cognition thereof is indicated. "Afterwards" means after the recollection of the word-meanings by means of the words;
the phrase "by the assistance of those [words] which express unconnected [meanings]" is the ellipsis to be supplied.
That [person] is indeed a man;
the word "utterance" (ukti) is an indicator for the knowledge that is its effect.
Even by means of words that do not explicitly express the syntactic connection (anvaya), if one understands that connection, [then that person is a man].
The meaning is that, in that case, one might also understand a horse and so forth by means of words such as "cow" and the like. He raises an objection: "By the word... and so on.
If it is argued that there is the power of the word [to denote it] there, that is certainly not the case.
The meaning is: since the word "cow" and others have no expressive power (*śakti*) at all with respect to a horse and so forth, how could that [horse] be understood by means of them?

If it is argued that "a sound is not perceived by the eye," then he says—in response—that this is the same in the present case as well: "How [could there be understanding] in the case of positive concomitance (*anvaya*)?"
... how [is it] in the case of a lineage? Mānava 3.2.193f.

The meaning is: how could one strive for the cognition of a relation by means of those [words] which lack the capacity for a relation? He summarizes the point stated in the verse beginning with "yadi ananvitam" (if it is unrelated) with the word "tat" (therefore).

Because it suffers from defects such as the excessive complexity of conceptual construction (*kalpanāgurutva*), and because it contradicts direct experience (*anubhūti*), the theory of *abhihitānvaya* must certainly be abandoned by the wise.
*Tat* means "therefore. *Tasyaiva vivaraṇam* (the explanation of that very point) begins with the words "conceptual construction" (*kalpanā*) and so forth.
The burden of conceptual construction (*kalpanā-gaurava*) was demonstrated by the first sūtra.
The term *abhihitānvaya* is an illustration of all the aforementioned positions.

To the question, "How is there a contradiction with experience? he says: "For when the word denoting the agent [is used]," because, when the word denoting the agent is expressed, there is a cognition of the general property (*dharma-sāmānya*).
For it is precisely because he seeks specific qualities that he asks in this manner.
The mention of the "agent" (kartṛ) is an indication for any related participant in general.
"Specific property" (viśeṣadharma) refers to the knowledge of that [property].
It is beyond dispute that when a word denoting an agent, such as "by Devadatta," is employed, the listener asks "Why? [seeking further specification].
And he asks precisely because he desires to know the specific properties, such as cooking,
etc.; and the desire to know the specific arises only from the knowledge of the general property.
And at that time, there is no other means for him to know the general property (dharma-sāmānya) of that [object] than the word;
therefore, it is understood that the word conveys the object as qualified by the general property.
To the question "Why [is this so]?"—meaning, from what does this [conclusion] arise due to the desire to know the particular (viśeṣa)—he says: "guṇa... (the quality...).
Because when the specific qualities, actions, and other attributes have been stated again, one becomes free from further expectancy... [Mānava-dharmaśāstra 3.2.196a-c]
"Free from desire" means one whose curiosity has ceased.
Therefore, the connection is that he asks precisely because he wishes to seek out a specific property.
This is what is being said:
The inquiry beginning with "What? which arises immediately after hearing words such as "agent" and so forth, is rooted in a desire to know (*jijñāsā*);
this is because it is an inquiry, like any accepted instance of such inquiry.
Furthermore, that desire to know has a specific property (*dharma*) as its object.
Because it ceases upon that statement,
as is commonly admitted;
and because the desire to know particulars is preceded by knowledge of the generality of the property, since it is a desire to know particulars, as is commonly admitted.
Furthermore, this knowledge of the universal [dharma] is produced by these words because it occurs immediately after them, just like that which is commonly accepted.

If it is argued that when the mere word-meaning has been denoted by the word, the knowledge of the universal property [dharma] arises through the force of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), we say no;
for it is illogical to abandon the perceived word and instead postulate an inference of something unperceived.

By this, the position that words denote [the meaning] as already endowed with particularities (*viśeṣānvitābhidhāna*) is also refuted. To the question, "Now that the positions such as *abhihitānvaya* have been shown to be abandoned, what relevance does this have to the present topic?", he says: "The words... (*śabdā iti*).
... words denote that which is possessed of [the universal]. (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 3.2.196d)
The meaning is that this very position— that all words, in their general application, denote their own respective objects as being possessed of [the universal]— is what must be accepted.
He concludes the subject matter directly to be established with the words "therefore" (*ataḥ*).
Therefore, the Blessed One alone possesses infinite qualities... // MAnu 3.2.197ab //
The meaning is that even though its nature consists of infinite qualities, its unity is not impaired,
nor is its infinity and quality-ness lost by being non-different from the One. And that [is the] incidental point [introduced by the words] "tacceti."
He concludes: "It is indeed one."
"But it is declared by all the Vedas that there is only one [debt]. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.2.197bc)
By the word "tu" (but), he indicates that [the Lord] is endowed with all attributes.
Thus ends the section on the "Description of Both" in the illustrious Nyāyasudhā.
[======= JNys_3,2.XIII: Parānandādhikaraṇam =======] // Now begins the section on Supreme Bliss (Parānanda) in the illustrious Nyāyasudhā.
Oṃ. [The Brahman is] different from the highest [individual soul], because of the designations of a bridge, measurement, connection, and difference. Oṃ.
Are the attributes of the Supreme Lord, such as bliss and so forth, similar in character to worldly bliss and the like, or are they distinct from them?
In the first case, no great esteem for Him is possible;
nor is the second case [tenable]. (9.526)
Because there is an absence of both a specific mode and a definite measure;
and because there exists a subverting argument— that those things under dispute possess worldly characteristics because they are denotable by words such as "bliss" (ānanda) and so forth—
otherwise, the application of words like "bliss" to them would not occur.
Because there is an absence of etymological derivation;
and because, since it is beyond the senses, in the absence of instruction or other means regarding it, one must resort solely to inference based on similarity.
And because that [reason] is unestablished, the consequence follows that there would be no knowability through the Vedas; it is for the purpose of resolving this that the following is commenced.
Since the removal of all suspected defects therein is not clearly perceived, he explains: "And those... (te ca).
[The Brahman is] higher than that [the individual soul], because of the designations of a bridge, measurement, connection, and distinction.
... And they (the worlds) are entirely distinct [from Him].
These qualities are not only non-different from the possessor of qualities; indeed, they are distinct from all worldly pleasures and the like.
To the question "In what way are they distinct?", he says: "All... [referring to the following verse].
All are the embodiments of all virtues and indeed the performers of all actions.
Bliss is also of the nature of knowledge, and knowledge is also of the nature of bliss, and so forth.
For pleasure and the like are not merely distinctions in the transformations of the internal organ;
rather, they are the agents of all things and the creators of the world and its origins.
The word "eva" (only/just) excludes figurative usage.
Since words would otherwise be synonyms—lacking plurality—if there were no mutual difference between them, he says "tathāpi" (nevertheless).
Nevertheless, they are also possessed of distinctions... // MĀnuv 3.2.198c //
The meaning is that even though there is no mutual difference [between them], the aforementioned fault does not apply; by this,
the manner of their distinction is shown.
And the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) will be explained;
thus, the first two sūtras have been interpreted.
To avoid the objection [of redundancy], there is the sūtra: "Oṃ, it is for the sake of the intellect (*buddhi*), like the feet, Oṃ."
He explains that as follows: "The wise one," etc.
It is for the sake of cognition, like a foot;
and also because it arises from the instruction of the learned.
And they are addressed by various such words... // Mānava-dharmaśāstra 3.2.199a //
Moreover, even so, they are expressed by various words. How is it that [this knowledge] is endowed with the linguistic proficiency of the wise?
For the wise, having directly realized the qualities of the Blessed One, can be made proficient by previous wise ones.
How can there be proficiency for those who are ignorant?
For such proficiency must exist; otherwise, the very state of being learned would be impossible. Therefore, he says: "And it is appropriate."
...and it is appropriate according to the instruction. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.2.199b)
It is appropriate that even those who are ignorant acquire proficiency through the instruction of the wise.
To the question, "How can there be instruction regarding that which transcends the senses? he says: "Anyā... (The other...).
The similarity to other [types of] bliss and so forth... // MAnu 3.2.199c //
The bliss of the Lord and so forth possesses a similarity to worldly bliss and the like;
therefore, the teaching that "whatever quality of the Lord is similar to our bliss is denoted by the word 'bliss' and so on" is logically consistent.
If that were so, there would be a contradiction between what precedes and what follows.

Since it was previously stated, "And they are distinct from all others," yet now there is an admission of similarity to other blisses and so forth, he says: "On account of favorability, etc. (ānukūlyādīti).
... [he should worship] the Supreme through conformity and so forth. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.2.199d)
Conformity is the unconditional state of being dear, which belongs to bliss;
the nature of being consciousness, which belongs to knowledge, and so forth.
The other [defects] consist of smallness, instability, and the like.

It is thus stated that since the grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*), such as conformity (*ānukūlya*) and so forth, exist, and since linguistic derivation (*vyutpatti*) is possible by relying upon them, the application of words such as "bliss" (*ānanda*) is logically justified; therefore, inference is not a determining factor.
[Objection: But why are distinct words not employed for the various distinct instances of bliss and so forth?
[Response: Because if that were the case, it would follow that there could be no entry of the intellect (*buddhi*) into those [instances].
To the question "Why is there no similarity in terms of smallness and so forth?", he says: "Because of fullness, etc."
"Their greatness, such as fullness and so forth, is heard in the Śruti as their distinctive quality.
He recites that Śruti passage: "Full," etc.
And when it is full, he is the controller of all without exception, the single-syllabled one, and the most excellent bliss.
This aggregate of qualities is Vāsudeva; he is indeed without parts.
This very Vedic scripture concerning Vāsudeva speaks of the supreme qualities of Hari.
Pūrṇa means one whose qualities are complete.
Uttama-sukha means the most excellent bliss, the supreme joy.
Ekala means solitary, alone, and independent of others.
"Soundless" (*sunisphala*) means entirely devoid of any differentiated parts.
[The scripture] speaks of the supreme, transcendent qualities of Hari.

A false interpretation of these topics has already been refuted in the very section beginning with "Not even from the standpoint of place" (*na sthānato 'pi*), and thus it is not pursued further here.
Thus ends the section on Supreme Bliss (*parānanda*).
*9,532* [======= JNys_3,2.XIV: Section on the Granting of the Fruit =======]
Now begins the section on the granting of the fruit.
// Oṃ. The fruit [arises] from this, because it is logical; oṃ.//
In this context, it has first been established through both scripture and reasoning that the fruits for living beings, such as heaven and hell, arise from the Lord alone.
To raise an objection to that, the Sūtra states: “Jaimini [holds that] dharma [is the cause], for that very reason.
This is its meaning.

If God is the cause of the fruit, does He depend upon merit and demerit or not? In the latter case, there arises the consequence of partiality and so forth, as well as the loss of the Veda’s authority.
In the former case, what is the use of a God, since the fruit is accomplished by the very action that He depends upon?
Otherwise, there would be the consequence of unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Nor is there a contradiction with the logical proof of its insentience (*acetanatva*);
for we do not say that it bestows the fruit of action like a king or similar authority, which would contradict its insentience.
But it is merely the cause;
nor is there any contradiction with the Śruti,
because merit and demerit, which are the causes of the fruits, are brought about by the Lord, and thus, for the sake of praising Him, He is figuratively designated as the cause of the fruits.
The Sūtra is for the purpose of providing a resolution: "Oṃ, but Bādarāyaṇa [holds] the former view, because of the mention of a reason. Oṃ.
Therefore, this was said:
"It is true that Īśvara depends upon dharma and adharma;
however, it is not logical to conclude that those two alone are the cause of the fruit."
For it is impossible to discard even Īśvara as a cause of results, since He is established by the Śruti as such;

and because there is no subverting evidence, it is untenable to assume that the Śruti has a figurative meaning; furthermore, the principle of complexity (gaurava) applies only to matters not supported by authoritative means of knowledge.
Nor should it be argued that if both the Supreme Brahman and karma were causes [of the result], there would be an equality of status;

for in the bestowing of the fruit, the Supreme Lord is designated as the agent (*kartṛ*), while karma is designated as the instrument (*karaṇa*), as seen in such expressions as "by merit, merit [is attained]. And it is well known that an instrument is that which is employed by an agent.
In this regard, the following objection is raised:
even so, if Īśvara depends upon karma in bestowing fruits, his sovereignty is not established in its non-figurative sense;
and consequently, there can be no excessive degree of veneration toward him.
He explains the preceding word as a rebuttal to this [objection]: "That very same... and so forth.
But Bādarāyaṇa [holds] that it is the former, because of the designation of a cause;
"The fruit [arises] from Him (the Lord), because that is logical.
He alone [is the cause] of all those residing in the state of individual souls, who are beginningless and beyond numbering.
Constantly perceiving both dharma and adharma, the Unborn One awakens them according to his own will.
To some of them, Acyuta himself bestows the fruit;
it is said that they never perform any distinction, such as instigation or the like. Therefore, he is independent in the primary sense of the term.
The state of being beginningless is stated with reference to the continuous flow [of time]. The connection is that [the Lord] awakens some [beings] and renders them active by Himself alone.
The sense is that He makes them instruments out of His own play (*līlā*), but it is not the case that He would be unable to grant [the fruits] without such instruments.
That which is mentioned here—the perception of merit and demerit, the impelling thereof, the granting of its results, and the Lord's state of not being impelled by those—is all [His work].

Thinking that when this very [topic] is investigated, it will generate great respect for it—let alone for the totality of all categories—the author first elaborates upon the nature of actions with the words "karmāṇi" (actions).
And all those actions are individually volitions;
though their bodies are insentient, they partake in the fruits of their own karma.
And in each of those [vows], there are likewise infinite duties of this kind;
and they are as follows... // MDh 3.205a-c //
The word "those" refers to the aforementioned qualifiers, beginning with "residing in all living beings.
The term "separate" means that they are the respective presiding agents over each individual merit (dharma) and demerit (adharma);
the phrase "non-conscious bodies" is stated in order to exclude those who are liberated (mukta).
And for that very reason, they partake of the fruits of their own karma; among those who possess the conceit of agency regarding their actions,
these [beings] are of such a kind— that is, they possess the qualities of sentience and so forth as previously described— and they remain engaged even in those very actions.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "Thus, of the Lord."
... such is the supreme, boundless power of the Lord. MAnu 3.205cd.
For one who possesses the vision and other qualities of such actions, [the result] is supreme because of being free from obstacles and the like.
To the question, "From where does such a nature of actions arise?", he says: "Only one... and so forth.
For indeed, the killing of a Brahmin is declared by Varāha and Hari to be one and the same.
It is by Hari alone, and not by a modern [author];
by the mention of "Varāha," it is indicated that this refers to the Vārāha Purāṇa;
the ellipsis is to be supplied as "manifested" in the form of sentience and so forth.
He demonstrates that very point: "By the hymn to Brahmapāra, she emerged from the king's body. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.2.206cd)
By the greatness of that hymn, she was again restored from her state of being a hunter;
having attained supreme knowledge, she likewise always obtained other [spiritual benefits] as well.
Thus indeed have the infinite various karmas ripening within saṃsāra been described by the Lord Kapila.
By this, they cause the entire history to be recalled in brief:
through the attainment of states such as that of a hunter, sentience and so forth are understood.
The word "tathā" (likewise) is used in the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*.
Other [sins] than the killing of a Brahmin have been declared separately,
such as by way of intentionality and so forth.
The word "hi" indicates that this is well-established in the supreme Sāṅkhya system.
To the question of how they are perceived as being conscious and so forth, it is said: "In saṃsāra...
He concludes the meaning of the verse with: "Therefore..."
Therefore, Janārdana, who possesses an infinite multitude of majestic qualities, is to be propitiated with supreme devotion; such is the meaning of the word "feet."
"Māhātmyam" means majesty; "śaktiḥ" means power; and "guṇāḥ" refers to qualities such as bliss and so forth.
By the meaning of the subsequent quarter-verse, [the author] indicates its connection with the word "ārādhya," meaning "to be propitiated" or "to be worshipped.
Thus ends [this commentary] on the *Anuvyākhyāna*, the well-composed work of the venerable Pūrṇaprajña Bhagavatpāda, by the ascetic named Praguṇajayatīrtha.

"By means of detachment."
Through detachment comes firmness of devotion; when worship by means of that occurs, there arises the direct perception of Viṣṇu—such is the sequence of the stages.

this meaning is as follows:
this chapter is, for the time being, an investigation of the means of proof (sādhana).

However, first detachment (vairāgya) must be accomplished;
by that, devotion (bhakti) arises.
For indeed, there can be no production of valid cognition regarding that which is to be adopted for one who possesses attachment to that which is to be rejected.
If it is argued that [devotion] is indeed seen [to exist],
that is not firm affection;
for this very reason, it is said to be "the firmness of devotion" (*bhaktidārḍhya*).
Through that dispassion and through the firmness of devotion, there arises meditative worship (*upāsanā*).

For it is not possible for one who possesses passion elsewhere, or who is devoid of devotion toward that [object], to engage in constant and uninterrupted contemplation. And when worship is practiced for an exceedingly long period of time, the Lord, being pleased, reveals Himself.
Since such is the sequence of detachment and the other [qualities], therefore this same sequence should also apply to these chapters (pādas) which have them as their subject matter.

Having thus stated the connection characterized by immediate succession among all four chapters contained in this book, and wishing— by way of that context— to explain the mutual connection of all the preceding sūtras starting from the first sūtra, he first restates the meaning of the first sūtra.
From the words "by means of reasoning" up to "the excellence of the teacher," [it is stated]:
"Having understood the meaning of the Vedas through reasoning, one should reject other traditions."
And one should remove any mutual contradictions found throughout the entire body of the texts.
Having become the internal *praṇava* because of its proximity [to the self],
