[the *praṇava* is established] due to the appearance of many contradictions [in the case of others] and because of the Vedic revelation associated with it.
Having resolved the contradictions among the Vedic texts from the skin up to the vital breaths,
and having set aside those points of conflict, he was gratified by their favor.
Having recognized the Lord as the creator of the body, and because of the recollection of Him as its father,
one should develop a special affection for Him that exceeds [affection for] His status as the creator of all things.

Having produced great respect for that [state] and, because of the extreme suffering elsewhere, having generated an even greater degree of dispassion by perceiving the superiority of its virtues; MĀnuv 3.3.6.
And because everything is under its control, having attained firmness in devotion,
one should strive for worship alone through the excellence of a distinguished teacher.
By the phrase "one should strive for worship alone" in that context, it is explained that the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*) must be undertaken.
All other explanations of the word *atha* are as follows:
although this [present discussion] was commenced with the intention of merely indicating the connection (*saṅgati*),
nevertheless, because the word *atha* had not been previously explained and because it is impossible to explain it in isolation, a restatement of the meaning of the sūtra has been made.

The summary is as follows: the meaning of the word *atha* (then/thereupon) is, in general, the possession of knowledge and other qualities regarding the entire subject matter investigated in the two preceding chapters.
The phrase "and the excellence of the teacher" is to be connected with every [qualification] mentioned.

In that context, by the expression "one who knows the meaning of the Vedas"—meaning that the Blessed Lord alone is the meaning of all the Vedas—the subject matter of the first chapter has been stated.
The ablative case in *yuktitaḥ* is used because of the elision of a verbal suffix ending in *-lyap*;
it means "having generally refuted arguments that contradict the meaning of the Vedas," referring to the first quarter of the second chapter.
The second quarter [of the verse] means "having generally refuted and rejected other systems than the Vaiṣṇava system, such as the Sāṅkhya and others.
The third and fourth quarters refer to "the mutual contradictions [within those systems]."

How then is there a distinction regarding the "division of the quarters"? To this, [the author] shows the specific feature of the fourth [quarter] by stating, "having become inclined toward the inner self," because many contradictions with reason appear;

thus, having refuted the contradiction between the words [of scripture] and the scriptures accompanied by reason, he says "of that" (*tasya*) in order to establish that the knowledge which resolves the contradiction with the scriptures concerning the inner self is the final one.
For internal phenomena, whether known falsely or correctly, attain the status of being the primary factor in bondage and liberation;
external phenomena do not do so in that way.

By the phrase "pertaining to the principle of Prāṇa" (prāṇatattvagāni), it is already understood that the subjects of the fourth quarter—which concern the primary vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa)—have their object of knowledge within the self (adhyātma).
Why, then, is this stated again? With the intention that this must be explained in detail because the desire to know depends upon its grace, he says: "by its grace" (tatprasāda).
"Anurañcitaḥ" means "made agreeable," that is to say, "made right.

By the words "the state of being the maker of the body" and so forth, the meaning is that one should understand the "omnipotence" (sarvakartṛtva) of the subject who "makes the threefold" (trivṛtkurvat), and having thereby become devoted to the Blessed Lord;
here too, the purpose of the repetition should be understood as before.

Having understood that [the world] is a means for extreme suffering, one should generate an even greater degree of dispassion (*vairāgya*) toward it than toward anything else; this refers to the third [type of person] and those following.
It is said to be "even greater" (*adhika*) because dispassion sometimes arises even in those who do not seek knowledge (*ajijñāsu*), and it is called "extreme" (*ati*) for that reason.

"By being superior in those qualities" refers to the second [type of guru]. Because it is under his control, "being under his control" is mentioned; and because devotion is established prior to that, "firmness" is stated.
Furthermore, since none of this occurs for one who has not served a guru, the word "distinguished" (*viśiṣya*) was employed. *10,9*
If it is asked, "What is the meaning of this word *atha*?
it is said:
although the word *atha* has many meanings, [it is used here in this specific sense].
Nevertheless, since other meanings are inappropriate here, there is no dispute that the meaning of "immediacy" (ānantarya) is accepted;
yet this immediacy must not be stated as referring to just anything,
for that would be redundant.

However, that without which the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*) does not occur, and in the presence of which it necessarily does occur, is precisely that which follows immediately [the qualification];
and such is the knowledge of the meaning of the Veda and so forth.
Furthermore, what is called "inquiry" (*jijñāsā*) is reflection (*manana*), which is synonymous with deliberation (*vicāra*).

And since that [enquiry] is not possible without hearing [the scriptures], therefore the knowledge produced by hearing all the objects of inquiry contained in this treatise is what precedes [the enquiry].
And when that exists, detachment and so forth necessarily arise for one born of a noble family, whose nature is *sāttvika*, and who has performed virtuous deeds in previous births.

As for the fourfold means—discrimination between eternal and non-eternal objects, the perfection of the means such as tranquility (*śama*) and self-restraint (*dama*), detachment from the enjoyment of fruits here and hereafter, and the desire for liberation—which others have stated to precede [the enquiry], that is [already] included within what we have stated.
Thus, it is not contradictory that [desire for liberation] is included therein.
The Teacher did not mention that those of the highest devotion lack the desire for liberation (*mumukṣutā*).

By this, the objection that there would be a circular dependency (*anyonyāśrayatva*)—namely, that dispassion and so forth, which are to be accomplished through the inquiry (*jijñāsā*), would themselves be the means for that [inquiry]—is also refuted.

For one of a sattvic nature who possesses a slight degree of detachment and so forth due to the influence of the company of the virtuous, there is an increase of that [detachment] through hearing (śravaṇa); and through reflection (manana) and other means, there is a further increase of it.
Having thus stated the meaning of the first sūtra, he explains its connection with the second sūtra by saying: "It is to be performed," etc.
When it is stated that "the inquiry into Brahman ought to be undertaken," a doubt arises as to why this should be so.
When this has been stated, the doubt arises: "Should it be performed, or should it not be performed because there is no purpose?
Here, by the word "doubt" (*saṃśaya*), error (*viparyaya*) is intended, due to their commonality as being false cognitions (*mithyājñāna*).
The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "When doubt exists, he said 'janmādyasya yataḥ' (from which the origin, etc., of this [world proceed]) in order to remove it.

Alternatively, it may be explained as: "When there is doubt as to whether [the inquiry] should be undertaken or not, and when the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) holds that it should not be undertaken because there is no purpose," he said so.
This is understood from what is about to be stated by the words "he said" (*ityāha*).

The connection [to the previous discussion] is as follows: Since the inquiry [into Brahman] has liberation as its purpose, how can there be any further doubt? To this he says: "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). This refers back to the word "therefore" in the first sūtra.
Even though "from him" has been stated, because no specific person is mentioned, [the question arises] again.

The connection with the preceding [passage] is as follows: although it has been stated by the word "ataḥ" (therefore) that the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) has liberation as its purpose, a doubt arises again because no specific reason for this purpose of liberation has been mentioned.
If that is so, then even by the Sūtra on "birth and so forth" (*janmādi-sūtra*), this suspicion is not removed;
for there too, liberation must indeed be explained as the meaning of the compound.
If it is argued that this was not stated specifically, we say no;
for [the text] explains it as "because no specific means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) was mentioned.
This is what is meant:

Even though it has been stated by the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) that the inquiry into Brahman (*brahmajijñāsā*) must be undertaken because its purpose is liberation (*mokṣa*), a doubt still certainly arises:
"Because no means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) has been mentioned therein.
If this is so, how would the second sūtra also remove this doubt?
For this point has not been established here by means of a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa); therefore, he explains it [with the words] "sṛṣṭi" etc.

"Because he is heard in scripture to be the agent of creation, bondage, liberation, and so forth, and because he is the giver of liberation and other such states, he alone is to be sought after by you.
Thus he spoke of that Supreme Brahman, known as Vyāsa, who possesses rays of knowledge. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.3.9)

The meaning is that because He is the giver of liberation and so forth on the basis of being heard from scripture, and because He is the giver of liberation and so forth, He must indeed be sought after by you who desire liberation; this is the point expressed by the *janmādi-sūtra*.
This is the underlying intention (*abhisandhi*).
In the aphorism "janmādy asya yataḥ," the phrase "is heard [in scripture]" is the ellipsis to be supplied.
Thus, it is stated that scripture is the authority for the Supreme Lord's status as the bestower of liberation.
Furthermore, in this context, the quality of being the bestower of liberation is primary.
However, the status of being the agent of creation and so forth is stated therein as the reason;
and this reason is a purely negative (kevalavyatirekin) one.
Furthermore, "being mentioned in scripture" is asserted in order to avoid the charge of that reason being unestablished (asiddhi).
In the rule "kṛtyānāṃ kartari vā," the word "vā" [indicates] that the genitive case is used.
But how can it be said, "of the agency in liberation and so forth," and so on?
For there is a prohibition against compounding a genitive with a word ending in the suffix -tṛ when the suffix occurs after the sense of an agent (kartari).
This suffix *tṛn* is prescribed in the sense of habit (*tacchīla*) and so forth.

Furthermore, because of the rule stating that there is an extension (*upasaṅkhyāna*) for words such as *gāmin* and *gamya* when combined with words such as *śrita*, a compound is formed with the second case ending [in *jñānaraśmayaḥ*].
Knowledge is like rays; thus, they are "knowledge-rays" (*jñānaraśmayaḥ*).
The meaning is "like one possessed of pervasive knowledge.

The specific mention [of Vyāsa] is made so that the disciples' devotion toward the author of the Sūtras might not diminish, based on the observation of the popular saying: "There was a certain sage named Apāṃtaratamas who became Vyāsa. *10,26*

Since it might be objected that the Lord's status as the means to liberation is irrelevant because there is no evidence for the inquiry (*jijñāsā*) being a means to liberation, he says: "By which very [means]..."
That very path by which bondage and liberation occur has been reached through inquiry;
the Lord, being well-pleased by this inquiry, shall grant him liberation.
"Release from bondage" (*bandhamokṣa*) means liberation from bondage;
it is a compound formed by the division of rules (*yogavibhāga*) according to the fifth case,
or it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*).
The word "yena" (by whom) implies "prasannena" (by one who is serene);
"gataḥ" means known,
because verbs meaning "to go" have the sense of "to understand."
The word "co" (ca) is used in the sense of "because.
The word "su" (well-) is used because mere clarity alone is not the means to liberation.
This [clarity] grants liberation to this living being (jīva), who is the seeker of knowledge regarding this Lord (Īśa).
This is what is meant:
the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) is not, for us, intended as a direct means to liberation;
rather, it is the Blessed Lord alone who is well-pleased.
And when he is known to be preeminent, one becomes well-pleased;
and the knowledge of his preeminence arises through the desire to know—thus it proceeds by way of a succession.
In this regard, the Blessed One’s status as the giver of liberation has been established by means of the aforementioned proofs.

It is established from common worldly experience itself that [a teacher] gives [instruction] only when pleased, that one becomes pleased through the knowledge of [the teacher's] excellence, and that [the teacher] is known as excellent;
what need is there for the presentation of formal means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) in this regard?
Therefore, the author of the Sūtras considers that the fact that the desire to know the Blessed One (*bhagavad-jijñāsā*) is the cause of liberation is already established.
"Is it not the case that in another place the connection of this sūtra was stated otherwise? True; even though that [other explanation] exists, this one has been stated as an alternative. *10,29*
Having stated the doubt to be dispelled by the third sūtra, he recites it as its refutation: "mokṣādīti" (beginning with liberation).

If it is asked, "How is it understood that the Lord is the giver of liberation and so forth? [the answer is: "Because He has the scripture as His source; for the giver of liberation is known through the scripture. (Manu Smṛti 3.3.11)
The connection is that the primary quality of being the giver of liberation, as well as the agency in creation and so forth, belong to the Lord alone.
How is this understood?
Not at all.
The sense is that others understand it in that way through various inferences and scriptures;
"if this is argued," the word "it has been stated there" is to be supplied as the remainder.
To explain how this Sūtra refutes such an objection, he comments: "For [the self] is to be known through the Śāstra."
The mention of "liberation" (mokṣa) is an elliptical indication for creation and the other cosmic functions as well.

Since the person who bestows liberation and so forth is the subject matter of scripture alone, therefore, he whom the Veda and other scriptures describe in such a manner is to be understood exactly as described; he is not to be imagined through inference or other means.
Why is it that the giver of liberation and the like is cognizable solely through scripture?
Intending to show that [the object] is established by exhaustion (*pariśeṣa*), he first refutes its being accessible through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) with the words "pratyakṣa... and so forth.
If liberation could somehow arise from things determined by direct perception,
why then would all these creatures be submerged in beginningless saṃsāra?
The meaning is: if [the Lord] who bestows liberation and so forth were perceptible— meaning,
by some means such as serving Him—
then everyone would be qualified [for that goal].
To the question, "If the giver of liberation were perceptible, why would all beings not be liberated?", he says: "Because...
"Since the certain cessation of suffering occurs through direct perception, all subjects—including kings and others—rush toward him alone. (Manu 3.3.13)

In order to dispel the doubt that [the self] does not run forth because it lacks the desire for liberation (amumukṣutva) due to its being a person (puruṣa), the nature of liberation has been explained as "the cessation of suffering.
For it is impossible that anyone who is suffering would not wish to abandon that suffering.
"From direct perception" means from that which is accessible through direct perception.
"A king and so forth" is stated by way of analogy. Alternatively, it means those wishing to abandon the suffering of poverty [should approach] a generous person as if he were a king and so forth.
He refutes the notion that [the self] is cognizable through inference with the words: "anumā" (inference).
If liberation were accessible through inference, then that very inference—
just as in the case of ordinary men— would preclude its being the bestower of liberation.
Only that which is accessible through the scriptures is certainly the sole bestower of liberation.
The meaning is: if someone were to be inferred as the giver of liberation;
[the response is that] inference itself—such as [an inference based on] being a person—is not applicable there because it possesses a counter-argument (sapratipakṣatva). This is the sense.
Intending to show that the scriptures are indeed incapable [of establishing the self] because their authority is not certain, he concludes the remaining point with the word "tad" (therefore).
Therefore, the construction is as follows: the person who bestows liberation must certainly be one accessible through the scriptures (*śāstra-gamya*) alone.
[Objection: "Let it be so; nevertheless, other things might also be accessible through the scriptures by virtue of being givers of liberation.

Anticipating this, and indicating the connection with the fourth aphorism—namely, that [liberation] occurs because of such an appearance—he explains the two words "tattasmāt" (therefore) as "śāstretyādi" (beginning with 'scriptures').
And according to the scriptures, there is no one other than Keśava who bestows liberation.
And since he alone is known through the scriptures as the giver of liberation, there is no one other than Keśava [who grants it].
But why is it he alone? To this, he explains the reason stated in the Sūtra: "For he is the giver of liberation."
For he who bestows liberation must be independent... // Mānava-dharmaśāstra 3.16a //
The logical connection (*anvaya*) is that He alone, being independent, must be the giver of liberation;
and this concordance with independence belongs to the Blessed Lord alone and not to others.
The intended meaning is that He in whom this is recognized in the Śruti and other scriptures is indeed the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu.

If it is asked, "Why should that which is dependent (*paratantra*) not grant liberation?"—does it grant liberation by itself, without depending on anything independent (*svatantra*), or does it grant it by depending on another independent entity?
Regarding the first case, he states the fault: "That which is dependent... [and so forth].
How can one who is dependent on others and exists under their own impulse be capable of attaining supreme liberation alone? (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 3.3.16b-d)
It is indeed dependent;
it is merely independent of others.

The intention is that if this [agent] were capable of liberating its own devotee without depending on anything else at all, then it would liberate itself as well, and thus it would not be subject to saṃsāra.
He refutes the second [alternative] with the words "anyā" (other).
If he were to grant liberation by means of another basis, then he alone would indeed grant it;
however, not being followed by him, he would not grant liberation through the words of another.

If it is argued that this intermediate lord (avāntareśvara) might grant liberation to his own devotee by relying upon another independent Viṣṇu, then it is indeed possible that he— being independent and not sought after or served by that seeker of liberation— would not grant liberation at all, merely because of the prayerful statement: "O other intermediate lord, grant liberation to my devotee."
The word "hi" (for) is used because it is so observed in the world.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "Therefore...
[Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.3.17ef]: "Therefore, for that purpose as well, Viṣṇu should be known by those seeking liberation."
For that purpose—that is, even for the sake of attaining liberation from intermediate lords—he is independent.
Thus, since the desire to know the Lord (Bhagavat-jijñāsā) is unavoidable, the conceptualization of intermediate lords as bestowers of liberation is useless; this is the intended meaning.
He explains the reason by another method: "Him alone," etc.

By the scriptural passages "whomsoever he [Brahman] chooses" and "him alone," those who proclaim the Veda understand that this [Brahman] alone is the source of the scriptures, and they do so with reverence. (Manu Smṛti 12.94)
By this [verse], he cites the Śruti passage: "He is attained by whomsoever He chooses," and the Śruti passage beginning with "And him alone.
Also: "Even knowing Him thus, one goes beyond death."
Thus, the Śruti is cited here;
by the supplementary statement, "There is no other path," its importance is understood.
Because He is the giver of liberation, the status of being the source of the scriptures belongs to Viṣṇu alone.
By this, it is stated that "samanvaya" (harmonious reconciliation) means the proper and respectful connection of the Śrutis [with Him].
Now, one might ask: on what basis is it said that in these two Śrutis, the Blessed Lord is referred to by the words "eṣaḥ" (this one) and "tam" (Him)?
Its ascertainment is achieved through a thorough consideration of the context and other such factors;
this is what has been stated by the proponents of the Veda.
Regarding this, he cites another scriptural passage: "He who... etc.
Those who know him thus become immortal... // Manu 3.19a //
"And those who know this become immortal"— this is the connection with what precedes, according to the Śruti.
This Śruti is cited separately for the purpose of critical inquiry (mīmāṃsā).
To the question, "Why is he called 'Hari' when addressed as 'a-trainam'?", he says: "Thus addressed."
... thus addressed, he went to the ocean. (Manu 3.19b)
That which is described in the Śruti as the knowledge that causes liberation— namely, "that which the sages weave within the ocean"— is said to be situated in the ocean;
and the meaning is that this is a characteristic mark (liṅga) of Hari.
He states another means of valid cognition: "That very [same thing]," etc.
"That alone is the supreme Brahman," as is determined by the Śruti.

The phrase "it is said" (ity uktaḥ) is understood to carry over [from the previous context]. By the Śruti text, "That indeed is the supreme Brahman of the seers," he has been determined to be Brahman.
This is what is meant:
when the word "this" (*enam*) is used, because the term "Brahman" (*brahma*) is heard and because that [term] is a name of the Blessed One, it is understood that this very person is the Blessed One.
Although the term "Brahman" has other applications as well, even so, those are merely secondary.
And it is not possible to understand it in this way here,
because that would contradict the restrictive determination "that very [thing].
Indeed, this [text] declares its primary Brahman-hood.
Otherwise, since the mere application of the word "Brahman" would be established by valid authority, its negation would be untenable.
He states another argument with the words "since": //
"From whom she was born," thus he speaks of creation... // Manu 3.20ab //
"From whom the source of the world was born"— this Śruti passage then describes the creation from that "Root Nature" (mūlaprakṛti) which was referred to by the words "He who [is] this.
And the status of being the cause of Root Nature cannot belong to anyone other than the Supreme Person.
For this reason also, he is the Blessed One (*bhagavān*).
By this, it should be understood that what was stated as "because his status as the agent of liberation and so forth is heard in scripture" has also been explained.
He concludes the second explanation of the reason with the word "therefore" (*tataḥ*).
... from that [Veda] comes Hari; it is understood that there is no other source for the scripture in the primary sense. (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 3.3.20b–d)

"Primarily" means, that is to say, by virtue of being the giver of liberation. He explains the reason stated in the Sūtra—"by scripture"—also as a refutation of what was previously asserted, namely, that the status of having scripture as its source (śāstrayonitva) is perceived for others as well as for Viṣṇu. Thus: "By scripture... [Śāstra...].
For its having the scripture as its source is known from the fact of its being in harmony [with it]. "Harmony" (anvaya) refers to the indicative marks such as logical consistency (*upapatti*).

Having raised the doubt that Brahman is inexpressible based on scriptural passages such as "from which words turn back," its expressibility is established in the section concerning the "contemplation" (*īkṣati-adhikaraṇa*).
That is inconsistent;

for it was not previously stated that [the Veda] is expressible [by other means], and because the status of being the source of the Śāstra could also be possible through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā) and so forth. Therefore, in order to connect the present section (adhikaraṇa), he explains the word "sam" as follows: "sam".
For by means of the prefix *upa*, the word *samiti* expresses its most primary meaning.
The primary and most eminent meaning is stated here,
because there is no reason for any restriction [of its scope].
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "In this way."

Thus, because the Śruti declares that Nārāyaṇa is the supreme and primary meaning, the Lord of the Vedas proclaimed "not what is not based on the Word" (nāśabdam) in order to establish this certainty. (Manu 3.3.22)

The connection is as follows: for the purpose of determining that Nārāyaṇa is the primary and most eminent meaning of the Śruti by virtue of being the giver of liberation and so forth; since the status of being the primary and most eminent meaning is expressed by the prefix *sam*, therefore, because such a logical consistency (*saṅgati*) exists, he declared [in the verse] "it is not without scriptural authority" (*nāśabdam*). Or [it may be read as]: "because of the existence of this consistency, he proclaimed [him to be the Supreme]. *10.37*
In this section, there is the sūtra "gatisāmānyāt.
Since that [sūtra] does not aim to establish that [the agent] is denotable by the verbal suffix (*vācyatā*), it was not explained previously.
Now, he states its connection [to the current topic] with the word "katham" (how?).
How is the connection [of the sacred texts] to be understood by men who know only a few branches?
The prefix *sam-* has two meanings: "primary" (*mukhyavṛtti*) and "all" (*sarva*).
Of these, the second meaning is implied here;
thus, these sūtras possess a single common subject matter (*ekādhikaraṇatva*).

Because the refutation of the objections regarding the meaning of the word "sam" (comprehensive) is one and the same, it is not possible to understand the concordance (*samanvaya*) of all the Vedas with the Supreme Lord as the cause of the origin and so forth of the world through such marks as the introductory passages (*upakrama*).
Why? Because...

Since for humans of short lifespan who possess limited wisdom and so forth, it is only possible to know a very small portion of the branches and Vedas, and thus knowledge of all the Vedas is impossible;
and since if the Vedas themselves were limited, their systematic reconciliation (*samanvaya*) could indeed be known even by people like us—therefore, he says: "The Vedas."
For the Veda is indeed infinite; thus the Śruti declares its infinity as well.
By this [verse], he cites the Vedic scripture: "The Vedas are indeed infinite.
The first word *hi* conveys the sense of the Vedic term *vai*;
the second *hi* indicates the well-known status of that scriptural statement.
The word *api* is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).
It means not only are there men who know but little of the Veda, but the Vedas themselves are also infinite.
The remainder [of the sentence] is "the infinity of the Vedas.

[Objection: Let it be that persons have little knowledge while the Vedas are infinite; even so, why is the knowledge of their systematic connection impossible? To this, he says: "ananta... (infinite).
The determination of infinite knowledge is like a means of crossing the great ocean of universal dissolution.

The phrase "of those who pierce even the smallest branch" continues [from the previous context]. The compound is formed through its expressive power (*gamakatvāt*), being comparable to the crossing over from the great ocean of dissolution;
it is like the expression "Devadatta’s teacher's house."
The sense is that it is impossible for one who does not know the nature of a particular sentence to determine its meaning by investigating its opening statement and so forth;
this is what is being said:
persons under dispute are not capable of knowing the synthesis of all the Vedas, because they do not know all the Vedas.

Whoever does not know a particular statement does not know its logical connection either, as is commonly agreed. Those who hold conflicting views are not capable of knowing all the Vedas, because they possess limited wisdom and so forth; for whoever possesses less wisdom than another does not know that [other's] knowledge, as is commonly agreed.
Or rather, the Vedas do not know this, because it transcends their wisdom and so forth.
He concludes the objection with the words: "Therefore, for this reason."
"...for this reason, no synthesis [of the teachings] is to be understood here.
Here, "here" refers to Viṣṇu.

Therefore, the intended meaning is that because there is a suspicion of different things being propounded in other Vedic branches (*śākhā*), it is not possible to ascertain the stated meaning [with certainty].
He introduces the sūtra as being for the purpose of refuting this [objection], stating: "Thus, having raised this doubt..."
To dispel such a doubt, that Compassionate One said: [Mānava-dharma-śāstra 3.25ab]
He says: "Because of the commonality of the goal" (*gatisāmānyāt*); the word "sūtra" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
Now, what is the meaning of this sūtra?

Since the realization of Brahman produced by all the branches (*śākhā*) is of a single form, all the branches indeed lead one to understand the Supreme Person alone as the cause of the world's birth and so forth; thus, it is not the case anywhere that...
If it is argued that a contrary interpretation might be suspected, [the author replies]:

"But has this not already been refuted by the objection that, because the Vedas are infinite, they cannot be fully known, and thus a definitive determination of their meaning through methods such as *upakrama* (opening statements) and so forth is far from possible?
To state the same thing again—what would be the point of this? Therefore, he states the intention (*abhisandhi*) of the author of the Sūtras: "It is impossible... and so on.
For even though this ocean of worldly existence has no further shore to cross,
I alone shall determine its end by the dissolution of every pore of my skin.
The phrase "by others than me" is the ellipsis [to be supplied].
By the word "hi," he accepts the proof adduced by the opponent.
"Uttāraṇa" means going to the further shore.
This means determining [the meaning] through methods such as context and so forth.
"Udī" means that which possesses water (*udaka*); the suffix *ini* is used here because the sense of "ground" (*bhūmi*) is intended.
The meaning is "the ocean. He is so described because he has dissolved [all things] into the pores of his skin.
The sense is that even the Veda, which is like the ocean of dissolution, is contained within my knowledge.
He explains this very point with the words "Even though" (*yadyapi*).
"Even though the meaning of the entire Veda is difficult to fathom for all human beings, it becomes as minute as an atom within the unmanifest space of my knowledge. (Manu 3.3.26)
Just as an atom is contained within unmanifest space, so too is it contained within my knowledge. The term "unmanifest" (avyākṛta) is employed because elemental space (bhūtākāśa) is limited;
for if there were no such distinction, what was stated in the preceding verse would appear partly contradictory and partly incoherent.
He summarizes his intention with the word "iti" (thus).
Thus revealing the state of being an object of knowledge for the entire Veda, the Lord of the Universe directly declared the uniformity of its interpretation.

By demonstrating, in the manner stated, that the entire Veda is directly knowable by Himself, He indicates the uniformity of its interpretation (*gatisāmānya*); however, this is not done without purpose, lest the aforementioned fault should arise.
The term "Lord of the Universe" (*viśvapati*) serves as the proof for His omniscience regarding all the Vedas;
for one who does not know what is to be protected cannot be a protector.
"And all the Vedas are contained within the Viśva"—this is what is meant by the author of the Sūtras. That is to say:
since it is impossible for anyone to know all the Vedas, is this knowledge of the concordance of all the Vedas being ascribed to Manu and others, or to me, the author of the Sūtras?
Even regarding the first [alternative], is it specifically or also generally?
We certainly accept the first;
as for the second, we shall explain it later.
The third [alternative] is not tenable, because it would result in the fallacies of non-establishment (*asiddhi*) and so forth for me, given my claim to omniscience.

If this were the case, and if someone else, like the author of the Sūtras, were to assert a commonality of understanding regarding other subjects, then there would again be no definitive conclusion; therefore, he says: "Who indeed... (*ko nāma*).
Who indeed, other than that single Bādarāyaṇa, could proclaim the commonality of destiny for those endowed with the infinite tradition, were it not for the sun of his knowledge?
"Jñānasūrya" means one who is like the sun through knowledge;
just as the sun is the illuminator of the universe by its own radiance, so too is this [person] through knowledge.
Because we see usage such as "vinā vātam" (without wind), the accusative case occurs even with "ṛte," just as it does with "vinā."
This is what is being said:
would an omniscient one speak of a commonality of destiny that is contrary [to reality], or would it be another?

Not the first [alternative], because it is impossible for there to be a contradiction between the statements of two omniscient beings; or, even if such a contradiction were possible, it would follow that both could not be omniscient.

Regarding the second [alternative], since it contradicts the words of the author of the Sūtra who is acknowledged by all to be omniscient, he would either be one of false views or a deceiver; thus, how can there be no certainty? Let it be granted that the Blessed One possesses knowledge of the commonality of destinies through his omniscience, but how does another person know for what purpose this treatise was composed? Therefore, he states another meaning of the Sūtra: "Another also... (*anyo 'pi*).
Even another person of small intelligence, knowing wealth consisting of four or five branches, might say it by way of inference through his favor. (Manu 3.29)

The construction is as follows: even another person of limited intelligence, by virtue of his faith in him, knowing four or five branches [of the Veda], might declare a commonality of understanding regarding the infinite wealth of the scriptures through inference.

The sense is this: taking as an example those branches by citing which the author of the Sūtras declared the concordance with the Supreme Lord, it is possible to infer that even those disputed branches—which share the status of being "branches"—are likewise devoted to Him; thus, it is logical for others also to possess knowledge of the commonality of their ultimate goal.
By this, the sūtra "from the inference based on the commonality of destiny" has been explained.

Now, one might object that it should be stated as "contained in four or five branches," because the numeral becomes a subordinate element (*upasarjana*) according to the rule *taddhitārthottarapadasamāhāre ca*.

In the case of "kaḍārāḥ karmadhāraye," the subordinate member will be placed at the end [of the compound]. Alternatively, the words "catuḥ" and "pañca" have the sense of a class (*varga*), as in the expression "if there were manifoldness (*prapañca*). (10.55)
Let this alone be the commentary on the Sūtra, because it serves as a means for the listener's comprehension;
not the former [explanation],
because it does not serve as a cause for dispelling doubt.

For the doubt of others is not dispelled merely by the fact that the author of the Sūtras, due to his omniscience, knows the commonality of the movements found in all the Vedas; therefore, he says: "in the primary sense."
Thus, because he is the Lord who primarily knows all states of existence in their universality,
his promise is firmly established and fulfilled even by the gods.
The connection is that he "made this vow.
"Primarily" means one who, without relying on inference and the like, possesses knowledge of the general nature of all the Vedas.
"Of the gods" refers to those of the highest qualification.
The particle *api* is used in the sense of a word-meaning (*padārtha*), meaning "possibility" (*śaṅkā*). For example: "There might even be honey."
It is fulfilled and resolved:

for those supreme practitioners who know the author of the Sūtra to be supremely authoritative, doubt is indeed dispelled by his mere likeness alone; thus, the previous explanation is intended for them.
But for others, there is the second [explanation].
The intention is that this is also the third [point] mentioned in the Commentary as "because of the scriptural statement regarding the commonality of destination" (*gatisāmānyaśruteḥ*).

Now, one might ask: "Since everything that was to be stated has already been said through these five sections (*pañcādhikaraṇī*), what is the purpose of the remainder of the chapter? To this, he says "Therefore... (*ataḥ*), demonstrating the connection in the form of an elaboration upon what has already been briefly stated.

Therefore, although the harmonious convergence (*samanvaya*) of all the Vedas is thus established, [the author], having clearly explained this meaning, has stated the convergence separately once again. (Manu 3.3.31)
The meaning is "by means of the preceding continuity.
The remainder [of the sentence] is "separately and in detail by means of the rest of the chapter.
In that regard, in the first quarter (pāda), the systematic application (*samanvaya*) of terms well-known in other [systems] is declared.
It has been stated that in the second [type], there are those well-known elsewhere that consist of logical marks (*liṅga*);
in the third, those of both forms that are well-known there and elsewhere;
and in the fourth, those well-known only elsewhere.
Establishing this sequence, he says: "In that regard..."

In this regard, first of all, there is the coordination (*samanvaya*) of words well-established elsewhere; here, they apply only to the literal meaning (*vācya*), like the breaking of a great wrestler. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.3.32)
Therein, in the first chapter, in the first quarter,
regarding words consisting of nouns,
In this context, regarding Viṣṇu, it is "thus" because it occurs similarly to the breaking of the great champions (mahāmalla).

The meaning is: just as when many wrestlers were standing as adversaries, the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa first brought about the defeat of the principal wrestlers, such as Cāṇūra and others, so too [is it here].
For regarding words well-established in both [contexts], the effort required is merely to exclude their established meaning elsewhere;
however, for those established elsewhere, it is necessary to establish their application to the Blessed One as well.
Therefore, these [words] hold primacy.

Words expressing gender (*liṅga*) denote properties (*dharma*) and produce the cognition of another [word] through mediation; however, words expressing substance (*sattva*), which consist of names (*nāman*), do so directly. Therefore, since there is a greater effort required for their coordination, names—which consist of words well-known in other contexts due to their predominance—are primary over those consisting of gender. Thus, in the first chapter, there is the coordination of these names.

It might be argued that, because the concordance (*samanvaya*) of words well-known in other [contexts]—which was mentioned in the fourth chapter—is more important than even this [present topic], it ought to come first;
for the state of being well-known in another [context] is stronger than being well-known elsewhere. To this he says: "From this" (*itaḥ*).
Even though this [result] is far more excessive, however, it pertains to that which is proclaimed in the fourth quarter [of the verse].

The connection [of the commentary] is as follows: although the samanvaya (harmonization) arising from the fourth quarter (the *turyapāda*) is even more extensive than this, it has not been presented here at the very beginning in this chapter;
nevertheless, because that samanvaya has also been stated here in brief by the words "But that [Brahman is known] from samanvaya" (*tattu samanvayāt*), the word "directly" (*añjasā*) was used.
The word "but" (tu) indicates that [the general rule] is not set aside because there exists a specific exception to it.
He demonstrates that very reason for the exception with the words: "because of the great conjunction" (mahāsamanvaya).
For in that great assembly, indeed, there is no entitlement for everyone.
In that [study of the Veda], the Brahmin alone is primarily authorized, while others are so in successive order;
and because it is difficult to master, it has not been directly declared as the first [duty] for others.

In that case, one might argue that [the scripture] should not be taught at all because there would be no qualified recipient; for one does not sing among the deaf while singing. To this it is replied: "Brahman alone.
Furthermore, since a scripture does not have only a single qualified recipient, it is stated: "other than that," and so forth.
The intention of the author of the Sūtras is as follows: having first stated the matter common to all qualified persons (*adhikārin*), he will subsequently explain that which is not common.
In that regard, this gradation (*tāratamya*) has been considered concerning the common [matter].
Furthermore, "and because it is difficult to understand" is another reason.
The meaning is: "because they have not first ascended to the Buddha [vehicle].
This is what is being said: although Brahmā and the others indeed possess primary eligibility for that [vehicle], [it is not so for others].
Nevertheless, there is indeed a slight degree of qualification for people such as ourselves.
This [specific] systematic connection does not first enter the intellect of those who are dull-witted;
rather, once the intellect is inclined toward Vedic proficiency through the knowledge of the common systematic connection, it gradually enters into that [specific connection] as well.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "Therefore" (ataḥ).
"But for the purpose of determining the meanings of words well-known elsewhere, the Lord first set forth [this work]... (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 3.3.35a–c).
The meaning is: because of its preeminence, its supreme importance, and because it has been established as something distinct from others.
The word "tu" (but) is used for emphasis.
Indicating the reason why the section concerning the "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) is placed at the beginning, he says: "In that regard" (*tatra*).
...In that regard, qualities such as bliss and so forth are determined, by relying on scripture and reasoning, to belong to the Lord alone. (Mānava-dharma-śāstra 3.3.35d–f)
In that context, regarding the elaboration of the concordance (*samanvaya*),
the word "first" (*prathamam*) is understood to carry over.
For in all virtuous states, bliss, consciousness, and so forth, are preeminent.

Therefore, the Teacher utters at the beginning an auspicious word connected with that [same] term. Since the *antaradhikaraṇa* and the *ākāśādhikaraṇa* are equally relevant to the sequence of the *ānandamayādhikaraṇa*, from what cause does this specific order arise? Indicating the reason for this, he states the purport of the *antaradhikaraṇa*: "The deity... and so forth.
All those who abide within other deities truly speak of Viṣṇu alone, by virtue of the underlying cause of the word's application.
Deities are indeed superior to insentient things;
therefore, those words denoting them possess a superiority over words denoting insentient things such as space.
All words [denote their objects] directly through their primary mode of expression (*vacana-vṛtti*), and not figuratively (*upacāra*).
How so?
Because the causes for both etymological (yoga) and conventional (rūḍhi) word-usage—such as frequent usage and so forth—are present in Hari.
Does it follow, then, that words have no usage whatsoever elsewhere?
Because it is determined that [the word "that"] refers specifically to Viṣṇu, he says: "due to association with Him."
... through association with that, by way of metaphorical designation.
In this world, those who speak of Viṣṇu as the supreme should speak of him alone as distinct from the other gods, on account of his possession of specific qualities.
The manner of metaphorical usage has already been explained.
To the question, "Why should there not be an equal application [of the term] in both cases, as with words such as 'akṣa' (die/axle)? he says: "In this case... (iha).

For words such as "Indra" denote qualities like supreme sovereignty; and since these qualities belong exclusively to the Blessed One, they must refer to Him alone as the primary and ultimate [referent],
rather than to another deity here.
Likewise, "not so" is the ellipsis [to be supplied].
Alternatively, the connection here with the preceding is "among these gods, because of association with them.
This also serves as an indicator for the excellence of the etymological basis (*rūḍhinimitta*).
Intending to show that in the subsequent sections as well, the sequence, the underlying cause, and so forth should be inferred by oneself, he says: "In this manner."
...and so it is for all others without exception.
The phrase "they shall declare Viṣṇu alone to be supreme" continues [from the previous verse].

Anticipating the objection—namely, that since words consisting of names well-known elsewhere are infinite, how can there be a conclusion to the quarters (of the Veda)—the author restates the meaning of the first quarter and states the connection with the second quarter while dispelling that doubt:
"Thus, 'elsewhere'... (*ityanyatra*).
Thus, when the entire collection of words "uru" (vast/great), which are well-known elsewhere,
is understood to have its application in Viṣṇu through these indicative marks, this constitutes the "samanvaya" (harmonious application).
"But if they were directed toward something else, there would be no correct convergence [of the Vedas];
thus, all marks without exception converge in Brahman alone. (Mānavadharmaśāstra 3.3.39)
He said: ... // Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.40a //

The intended meaning is that it is because they fall within the scope of the same underlying principle. The ellipsis to be supplied is: "When [the first point] is known by the first quarter [of the verse], a doubt arises."
How so?
For this grammatical connection consisting of names is generally stated by the force of gender;
and it is understood that genders belong to other things.
Consequently, because they are contradictory, the coherence perceived by them could not possibly be correct;
for the cognition of permanence does not arise correctly through [the reason of] being produced.
The word "iti" marks the end of the objection.
To avoid that [objection], [the author] states in the second quarter [of the sūtra]: "Of all the marks well-known elsewhere.

Now, one might object: "In that case, an investigation must be made here regarding those marks such as 'residing within the ocean' and so forth, which were stated as proofs in passages beginning with *antastaddharmopadeśāt* (Brahmasūtra 1.1.20)."
But it is not so;
for those things that have been stated are not being analyzed,
and those things that are being analyzed have not been stated.
It is said:

All words found in all the Vedas, even those well-known elsewhere, are indeed directed toward the Blessed Lord by virtue of all the indicative marks (liṅgas) heard here and there; such is the meaning of the first quarter [of the sūtra].
In that regard, what contradiction is there in setting aside those indicative marks which are beyond doubt and deliberating upon the others?
For this very reason, it was stated previously that [the cessation is] "without remainder" (*aśeṣataḥ*).
He explains the connection of this third term with the first and second [terms] by saying: "both" (*ubhaya*).

"...and because there would be a state of belonging to both [the individual and the universal], therefore, for the purpose of removing doubt regarding the gender and the word... (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.3.40a–c).

The state of having the Blessed One and others as their respective objects; therefore, the establishment of the fact that words well-known in other contexts refer to the Blessed One, as do words consisting of indicative marks (*liṅga*). *10.66*
But surely, the exclusion of its denoting anything else has already been established in that very same place by the words "not another" (*netara*) and so forth; so how can such a doubt arise?
Not so.
For the absence of intended meaning (*tātparya*) elsewhere has been demonstrated by the statement "it is not the other," and so forth;
however, the expressive power (*śakti*) certainly exists in both cases.
If that is so, then those very matters must be investigated once again.
O virtuous one! Among those very points, wherever there is an occasion for investigation, they are investigated.

When the movement of non-occurrence and so forth is easily understood in a certain place, it is proper to say that one should set that aside and suspect the presence of both [sides] elsewhere; thus it has been rightly stated.
And thus, there remains the doubt that the restrictive determination "that alone" (tattv-eva) would be untenable;
the sense is that he began the third quarter [of the verse] for the purpose of removing this doubt.
Alternatively, it may be connected with what is about to be said: "he said thus."
How is this doubt resolved in the third [chapter]? To address this, he states the intended meaning: "In both cases, because of the perception [of it]. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 3.3.40d) ...
in both cases, by virtue of being perceived.
The application of words currently in use, along with their gender, specifically pertains only to Hara.
[The word "Hari" applies] both there [in the primary sense] and elsewhere;

however, this is based on conventional usage (*pratīti*) and not on actual reality (*vastu*). Why is it that words with masculine gender (*saliṅga*), names, and genders are especially connected to Hari alone through the supreme primary function (*paramamukhya-vṛtti*) and through intentional focus (*tātparya*)?
To this he says: "That which... (*yad iti*).
... nor primarily anywhere else.
Words and indicative marks... [Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.3.42a]
The phrase "because it proceeds" is the ellipsis [to be supplied].
To the question "Why is this so?", he says: "Since... //
... because there is no independence anywhere else.
The word "there is independence" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
To the question, "Even in the absence of independence, why is there an absence of primary function (*mukhyavṛtti*) for words elsewhere?", he says: "In the case of those that are not independent."
In the case of dependent things, the basis for the application of a word is not primary.
Therefore... // Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.43a //

If it is argued that because other [deities] are not independent, and because qualities such as those that are the primary causes for the application of words are absent in them, words do not apply to them in a primary sense—let them not so apply; nevertheless, why is it that the specific concordance (*samanvaya*) belongs to Hara alone? To this, he says: "Therefore" (*ataḥ*).

The meaning is that for the other [term], there is an absence of primary denotation (*mukhyārthatva*). Indeed, a word must have a primary meaning; otherwise, a secondary meaning (*amukhya*) dependent upon it would be untenable.
And thus, when two possibilities arise and the primary sense of one is untenable, the primary sense of the other necessarily follows.
He states another argument with the words "yadadhīnāste" and so forth:
"Those [words], being dependent upon that, have attained the status of being the meaning of words."
But by means of even a very slight quality that serves as a cause for the application of a word, [one may be so designated].

Just as iron possesses the quality of burning [when heated], so too that very Lord, by virtue of His independence, must be accepted by the wise as the primary referent of the word "Self. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.3.44)
Thus he said: ... // MAnu 3.45a //

Those other entities, distinct from the Blessed One, depend upon that Blessed One through qualities and other factors which are extremely minor causes for the application of words; thus, while they have attained the status of being the referents of words, it is the Blessed One alone who is the primary locus (*īśa*), because he is the cause for the application of words without limit.
Furthermore, because of his independence, he must be accepted as the primary meaning of words.

In other [entities], the grounds for the application of words are indeed few, and even those are dependent on the Blessed One; however, in the Blessed One, they are infinite and not dependent on anything else— this being unproven, it has been stated by the wise (*manīṣibhiḥ*), that is,
by those possessing familiarity with the Vedas and other scriptures.

The meaning of a word that is dependent on something else is secondary (*amukhya*), whereas the other is primary (*mukhya*). Here is the illustration: just as iron, being dependent on another [fire], attains the state of being the referent of the word "burner" (*dāhaka*) when its capacity to burn is present; for this very reason, the word "it burns" (*dahati*) is used of it in a secondary sense, while it is used in a primary sense with respect to fire itself—such is the meaning. One might ask: "In this case, since the secondary nature of the other meaning is merely restated, is there not a tautology? To this he replies with the third quarter [of the verse]; the ellipsis is to be supplied as "he says. *10,69*
He establishes the connection with the fourth quarter [of the verse] by saying: "And thus."

And thus, even if it were established that all words without exception have Nārāyaṇa as their referent, it would not be appropriate in any way [to use them for other purposes]. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.3.45)
If it is argued that [the rule] would result in the attainment of even contradictory [acts], such as those that are inferior... // MĀnUV 3.3.46a-c //

The phrase "and thus" (*evañca*) is an elaboration of the preceding three quarters [of the verse]. Even though the application (*samanvaya*) of certain words to Nārāyaṇa has been established, the application of *all* words to Nārāyaṇa is not tenable; this is the remainder of the sense.

For it was asserted that the application of words such as "sufferer," "bound," and "inferior," as well as words whose objects are karma and so forth, is in no way possible—whether by etymological derivation (*yoga*) or by conventional usage (*rūḍhi*).
How so?
Because if the Blessed One were denotable by terms such as "inferior" (*avara*), it would follow that he possessed defects such as inferiority;
and this [consequence] contradicts all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
"And because of contradictions with the sequence of karma and so forth"—if this is argued, the remainder [of the sentence] is that "the author of the Sūtras has already provided a rebuttal to that.
To the question "How so?", he states the purport of the first section (adhikaraṇa): "Because of inferiority, etc."

"...for inferiority and so forth are indeed perceived in two ways. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.46cd). The grounds for the application of words such as "inferior" (*avara*) are perceived through the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
The word "indeed" (*hi*) indicates their well-known status.
To the question of how it is twofold, he says: "Of another," etc.
Even one who, being himself a stranger, becomes the cause of another's inferiority, is indeed the meaning of the word "inferior," just as a king might be victorious over another.
Another [is one] who experiences inferiority... // MĀnuv 3.48a //

The statement "being himself the Supreme" is not intended to state the etymological ground (*pravṛttinimitta*) for the term; rather, it is for the purpose of demonstrating that even though he is not inferior to himself, he is so in relation to others.
The meaning is that the single ground [for his being called "Supreme"] is his status as the controller of qualities such as non-inferiority in others.
The phrase "as follows" (*yathā*) indicates the demonstration of how this is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramita*).
The meaning is as follows: just as a king may be designated by the word "conqueror" because the victory achieved by his subjects depends upon him;
likewise, the sense of the word *avara* is a lineage (*anvaya*) that experiences inferiority (*avaratva*).
In other words, the possession of inferiority and so forth is another basis [for the application of the term].
And since this is well known, no formal proof has been stated.
To the question, "What follows from that regarding the subject at hand? he says: "Of those two... ... "The former exists in Keśava" (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.3.48b).
"Between those two causes of activity," the ellipsis being "therefore [the first] is denoted by words such as 'inferior' (avara) and so forth.
To the question, "Why is only the first accepted and not the second? he says: "The second..."
The second is the living being itself... // MAnu 3.48c //
The term "living being" (jīva) is also an elliptical designation for the insentient;
and if that were so, it would result in the loss of [the Lord's] status as the Supreme Lord—this is the meaning.
He states the conclusion of the section: "Because of independence."
... nor is there a refutation by virtue of independence. // MĀnuv 3.3.48d //
Of Hari... // Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.3.49a //
Since it is accepted that independence alone is the cause for [the Lord] being superior or inferior and so forth, the defect of Hari being inferior and such does not follow.
In this way, the purport of the subsequent section (*adhikaraṇa*) should also be stated.
By restating the subject matter of the first chapter, he states the connection with the second chapter: "In this way," etc. (*evam iti*). *10.71*
...Thus, when the concordance of all words has been stated in its entirety, since there can be no state of concordance for that which is devoid of contradiction,
therefore the Lord has effected the removal of all contradictions without exception. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.3.49)

"An explanation of all words and their meanings without exception"— this being stated, the connection is that the Lord has performed the removal of all contradictions in the second [chapter]. This refers specifically to the harmony (samanvaya) which is itself free from contradiction.
When the determination of the reality has been reached through both positive concomitance and non-contradiction, [the means of knowledge have fulfilled their purpose].
He states the connection of the third chapter with the words: "samanvaya" (beginning with *samanvaya*).
"What must be done by me?"—such indeed should be the thought of the qualified person.
This is an indication of the two chapters whose subject matter it is:
"What should be done by me for the sake of the determination of reality— that is, the determination of Brahman?"
This is the meaning:
although it has been stated that the inquiry into Brahman ought to be performed, and that it has indeed been performed;

Nevertheless, since the inquiry into Brahman, together with the inquiry into the means and the fruit, has been declared as something that must be undertaken, a question may arise in the mind of the qualified seeker who has already performed the inquiry into Brahman: "What is the means that I must perform, and of what nature is it?
If it is asked why such a question would not likewise arise regarding the fruit, the answer is that it certainly would.
However, since the means (*sādhana*) necessarily precedes the fruit (*phala*), the inquiry must first concern that [means];
this is precisely what is indicated by the word "only" (*eva*).
The remainder of the sentence is: "Therefore, the third chapter has commenced for that purpose. *10,73*
He clarifies the previously stated connection among these three quarters [of the verse] with the word "therein" (tatra).
In that regard, since devotion has been described as the means for warding off the succession of evils for those lacking it,

and since the entire collection of supreme qualities has been proclaimed, the practice of worship must indeed be performed with diligence as a constant duty in order to strengthen that devotion. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.3.51)
In that regard, in the third chapter,

for the purpose of prescribing devotion— that is, for the purpose of generating devotion and [consequently] for the purpose of detachment— for those who lack devotion, namely those who perform actions for the sake of desired fruits, the sinful, and the hateful.
That which was to be stated by the first quarter has been said;
that which expresses the infinite qualities of the Supreme Lord has been declared by the second.
Now, the meditation (upāsanā) is reached at the occasion for being explained in this [third] quarter.
Now, one might ask: what is the utility of devotion (*bhakti*) in meditation (*upāsanā*), such that it must immediately precede it? To this, he says: "Constantly" (*nityam*).
For meditation must always be performed with reverence,
since it is only through both reverence and continuity that an excellence of mental impression (*saṃskāra*) arises;
and reverence and continuity do not occur in one who lacks devotion toward meditation.
Thus, the connection is that meditation (*upāsanā*) must now be explained.
[Objection: If that is so, then meditation alone should be investigated.
Why is the thorough knowledge of all the scriptures investigated in the first section? To this he says: "That" (*sā*). (*10.75*)
And that worship is twofold: consisting of the study of the scriptures, and the higher [form] consisting of meditation... // Manu 3.52a-c //
That which has reached its proper occasion for being discussed is this very worship, and it is indeed of two kinds,
not of a single form.
How so?
One consists of the nature of the study of the treatises, and the other consists of the nature of meditation;
therefore, the inclusion of the first section within this [treatise] is appropriate.
Nevertheless, from where does this sequence arise?
Because meditative concentration (dhyāna) is to be accomplished through the practice of the treatises.
This very point has been stated by the phrase "by another" (parataḥ).
Since meditation (*dhyāna*) and concentration (*samādhi*) are not significantly different, concentration is also included by the term "meditation.

To address the question of how there can be only two types [of yoga] given that there exist other varieties of worship such as retention (*dhāraṇā*), withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), posture (*āsana*), restraint (*yama*), and observance (*niyama*), he says: "It is an ancillary (*tadaṅga*) to that."
...as well as its constituent parts, such as *dhāraṇā* (retention) and so forth. MAnu 3.52d.
That [study] is merely an auxiliary limb (*aṅga*) of that meditation (*dhyāna*), and not an independent form of worship (*upāsanā*).
This should be clearly understood from the Yogaśāstra.
Although the study of the scriptures is an auxiliary limb of meditation, it also possesses the status of an independent form of worship.

Because it is the cause for the direct realization of Brahman, and because it consists in the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind; or else, "it will come about through constant reflection upon the scriptures. (10.77)
What follows from this, if there are two kinds [of meditation] occurring at the occasion of worship?
To that he says: "In that way" (tathā).
Likewise, regarding this [third] quarter, Bādarāyaṇa has declared that meditation possesses both natures; he has explained it in detail, based on the sacred scriptures, with certainty.
Likewise, because it has reached its proper occasion,
the connection is "in this very [state]" and also "only through worship."
By this, he refutes the statement of the section's subject matter, which was that it will now be investigated whether the cognitions differ or not at each subsequent Vedānta text.
For instance: are there difference and non-difference?
Are they contradiction and non-contradiction, or rather, difference in characteristics and lack of difference in characteristics? Not the first.
Because the meaning has already been established;
as for the second [alternative], there is no attainment because Brahman is indivisible.
If it is argued that this inquiry concerns Brahman with attributes (saguṇa-brahman) and the vital breaths (prāṇa) and so forth, we say no.
Because it is not to be undertaken, as it is contrary to the subject matter and the purpose under discussion;
indeed, [it is contrary] along with the relevant object of knowledge (*prameya*).
Precisely for this reason, from the detailed explanation:
By this, the doubt that some topics might not be included is dispelled.
The mention of "scripture" (*śruti*) is illustrative.

Even though this is the occasion for explaining the connection (*saṅgati*), there is no fault in the fact that the explanation of the meaning of certain sūtras is intended precisely to support that connection.

Having thus stated the connection, he briefly sets forth the arguments for the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the arguments for the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) regarding the sections of this chapter, beginning with the words "separate perception" (*pṛthag-dṛṣṭi*).
Separate views, impossibility, lack of determination, combination, perception of distinction, failure of the effect, multiplicity of expression, and rapidity [are the causes of doubt]. (Manu 3.3.54)
Error, removal, a mark, lack of finality, lack of distinction, lack of purpose, over-extension, and reliance on what is not proximate. (3.55)
A superior cause, the desire for it, visible deformity, elevation, non-mention, lack of effort, firm bondage, and defeat [are the grounds for the loss of caste]. (Manu 3.56)

The attainment of equality with men, the renunciation of [worldly] attachments, the discernment of causes, freedom from delusion, the perception of distinctions, the absence of idle talk, equanimity toward virtues, and the vision of diversity [among beings].
The pursuit of forbidden paths is the obstacle; the desired fruit is non-conceptuality.
Purity, diversity, and being a limb [of the path] belong to the vision of non-distinction; this is the practice.
The arguments for the prima facie view, ease of understanding, the performance of injunctions, greatness, limited power, the fruit according to fitness, and rebirth. (Manu 3.59)
Equality of results, distinction, superiority of qualities, predominance,
action according to one's capacity, alliance, proof, strength, and submission.
The cause, the excellence of the effect, essential nature, the refutation of an entity,
counter-action, contradiction, connection, and non-deficiency.
Skill in the application of formative forces, self-determination according to one's will, mastery over material things, specific designation, lack of authority, preeminence, affection, and tradition.

Steadfastness, the attainment of what has been performed, the expansion of beginningless virtues, the excellence of the means of accomplishment, the various perspectives, instruction, and non-deficiency.
Absence of obstacles, absence of contradiction, excellence of qualities, and scriptural authority—
these are indeed the unimpeded arguments always employed in the determination of a tenet.
"The establishment of the validity of the established doctrine (siddhānta) through reasoning is 'always unimpeded'.
Thus end the sections of the Nyāyamālā. [======= JNys_3,3.I:
The Section on the Uniformity of Cognition across All Vedas (sarvavedāntapratyayādhikaraṇa) =======]
Now begins the section concerning the identity of all Vedāntic cognitions.
// Oṃ. The cognition [of Brahman] derived from all Vedānta texts is one and the same, because there is no difference in the injunctions and so forth. Oṃ.//

In this regard, when the doubt arises as to whether those seeking meditation and worship should understand [the teachings] through study, hearing, and reflection only within their own Vedic branch (*śākhā*), or rather through all the Vedas— given that the first position appears superior because the division of branches is well-known and otherwise inexplicable— the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is reached: "The cognition [arises] from all Vedāntas."

In this context, he explains the word "all" (*sarva*)—which has an unrestricted application—in order to dispel the misconception that it refers to [only] those perceived: "that which possesses power," and so forth.
The cognition [of Brahman] derived from all Vedānta texts is uniform because there is no difference in the injunctions and so forth;
thus, after having understood all the Vedas according to one's capacity, the meditation should take place. (Brahmasūtra 3.3.1; Manu-smṛti 3.3.65ab)

The grammatical identity of the agent is established by supplying the word "vijñāya" (having known) [from the preceding verse], as in "one who has known and remains [in that state]"; or alternatively, it means "one should practice meditation," or "one should perform meditation."
The word "bhavet" (should be) connects with the subsequent sentence.
In this context, it should have been stated simply that "one should know all the Vedas according to one's ability.
Nevertheless, it is stated in this way to demonstrate that the complete knowledge being described here is a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of meditation (*dhyāna*) and worship (*upāsana*).
And thus, by saying "and then" (*tataśca*), what was stated becomes explained.
To the objection, "Let the meaning remain exactly as it was heard; what is the use of this distinction?", he says: "In that regard" (*tatra*).
In that regard, the entire manifestation is indeed truly of Brahman alone.
For others besides those, it is held that there is complete knowledge according to their respective capacities.

In this regard, among the lay followers (*upāsakas*), since it is only appropriate that the complete comprehension of the entire Veda belongs to the Brāhmaṇa alone and not to others, it follows that for others, the comprehension of the whole [Veda] must be attained according to their respective fitness and capacity.
This is what is meant:
first of all, this Sūtra is common to all who are qualified.
Because that [knowledge] is understood through such arguments as the non-distinction of injunctions (*codanā*) and so forth,
and because it would otherwise follow that doubt and the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) are incoherent;
furthermore, it is not possible for everyone to possess knowledge of all the Vedas.
Because the Vedas are infinite and because men possess only limited wisdom and other such qualities, what was said is therefore appropriate.
Alternatively, this very point has already been stated by the phrase "it should be so in the first sentence itself," meaning that it would be logically established in exactly this way. Therefore,
when there arises the desire to know whose power of what kind [is involved], this sentence [is uttered].
The word "hi" indicates well-known fact.
Yoga is fitness.
Jñapti is the power of cognition. *10.85*
Indeed, it is in the context of being endowed with the fitness for worship that "the knowledge of all" is spoken of here;
and that [fitness] does not belong to one who knows only a small portion of the Vedas.
For it is said: "The Supreme Lord is to be sought through all the Vedas; He cannot be realized by those who know only a little of the Vedas."
Because of such scriptural passages as these,
the word "all" (sarva) must be explained in its primary sense alone.
Therefore, although for people like us it is impossible to possess knowledge of all the Vedas in this present life, [the term remains valid].
Nevertheless, one must postulate such a birth in which this [result] is possible; therefore, he says: "to that extent" (tāvatā).
By that much alone, every man indeed becomes fit for the service of the Lord.
"According to one's capacity, by means of mere knowledge"—this is the intended meaning. [The question is:
how is the knowledge of the Vedas useful for meditation and worship?
If it is argued that meditation is impossible in the absence of knowledge of the object to be meditated upon,
then, since it will be stated later that no one possesses meditation on the meaning of all the Vedas, knowledge of all the Vedas is not required.
This is true.

If it is argued that, even so, since meditation is impossible for one who has mastered only a single branch due to the suspicion that other branches state things differently, a thorough knowledge of all [Vedas] is necessary— this is not so; for it has already been stated that such a suspicion is dispelled by the inference based on the uniformity of the Vedic tradition (gatisāmānya).

Otherwise, due to mutual contradiction, the authority of the Vedas would be undermined. Therefore, the Śruti must be interpreted as "according to one's capacity. To show that knowledge of the Veda according to one's capacity is what is useful for the worship of the Lord, and that there is no necessity of knowing all the Vedas, he cites a Purāṇic statement beginning with "mahattvasya": [The text continues: "Because of its greatness... [and so forth].
"O Nārada, it is not at all the case that Janārdana attains satisfaction merely by one praising him after having known the supreme limit of his greatness. (Manu 3.3.67)
But for that devotee who always praises [Him] with unwavering devotion in accordance with self-knowledge, Hari is forever pleased.
From the context of such passages, there is omniscience appropriate to his capacity. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.69ab)
"Having known the further shore of greatness" refers to the state of knowing all the Vedas;
for without the Veda, O Blessed One, it is impossible to know greatness. "Let them praise" is also an elliptical expression that includes meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

Because the principle is the same, the phrase "it does not exist at all" is a negation of a restrictive rule; the remainder [of the thought] is that it is understood that "omniscience according to capacity" is useful for meditation.
How is it "according to capacity"?
Since an *avyayībhāva* compound is neuter, it should be understood that [the term] is used as appropriate.
True;
there is no fault here, for this is a compound meaning "knowledge of everything as it is appropriate."
Or rather, [the phrase] "just as" (yathā) means "in whatever way is appropriate," so that these two words are indeed distinct.
But surely, it is self-knowledge alone that is stated here as being useful for meditation (*upāsana*),
and not knowledge according to one's capacity (*yathāśakti-jñāna*).
Therefore, since this statement is not relevant to the present topic, he says: "The Self."
One attains conformity with self-knowledge through inquiry according to one's capacity.
The meaning is this: the conformity of this worship to the knowledge of the Self consists precisely in its being cultivated through inquiry into the Vedas according to one's capacity;
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the sentence being incoherent.

Since the restriction to all-encompassing knowledge has been rejected, when the question "But what [is to be done]? arises, it must be stated that knowledge is indeed to be pursued according to one's capacity.
But it is not knowledge of the self (*ātman*);
for knowledge of another has not been refuted previously.
Therefore, "knowledge of the self" must be explained simply as knowledge that is appropriate to the self.
From where does the knowledge of all the Vedas come? To this, it has been stated: "Because there is no difference in the injunctions (codanā) and so forth.

Since the division of the Vedic branches (śākhā-bheda) is well-established, it was explained that the injunctions and other elements are also situated within their specific [branches]. Therefore, the author of the Sūtras states another argument: "Om. Because of the study of one's own Veda (svādhyāya) being likewise [prescribed] in the Samācāra, and because of the qualification (adhikāra). Om.
There, he explains "hīyantaṃ" (the one who is declining) as "veda" (he knows).

For, because of the nature of Vedic recitation (*svādhyāya*) and because of the qualification for the *Samācāra* [section], as well as because of its similarity to the *Sava* sacrifice, the entire Veda must be mastered; otherwise, the futility of such statements as "the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayana*) shall take place" cannot be avoided. (Manu 3.3.70)
By the phrase "the entire Veda, along with its secret portions, must be mastered by the twice-born," he cites the Smṛti;
and by the phrase "one's own recitation (svādhyāya) should be performed," he cites the Śruti: "one's own recitation is to be studied."
Otherwise, if one were to accept knowledge of only one's own specific Vedic branch (*sva-śākhā-mātra*),

the following would be the case: because the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*)— that is, the injunction for Vedic study (*svādhyāya-vidhi*)— generally prescribes the study of all the Vedas, it follows as a logical reason that the knowledge of everything must be accepted.
This is because study does not terminate until the knowledge of the meaning is attained;
furthermore, if one were to accept that it refers only to the knowledge of one's own specific recension (*sva-śākhā*), this injunction would result in being purposeless.
