Nor should it be argued that, due to the well-known division of recensions, the word "one's own" (*sva*) is seen as equivalent to the word "entirety" (*kṛtsna*) in the term *svādhyāya*.
"Because it is logical that the division of the Vedic branches is caused by incapacity.
[Objection: But surely the author of the Sūtras has cited Smṛti as being based on Śruti by means of the word "hi"; how then can there be a reversal of this here?
It is replied:

The Sūtra follows the order of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), whereas the commentary follows the method of introduction (*upodghāta*); thus, there is no contradiction. By the very force of Śruti and Smṛti, it is inferred that, according to one's capacity, the thorough knowledge [of the Self] alone is the cause for freedom from doubt.
It is well known that repeated observation (*bhūyodarśana*) is a constituent factor of inference (*anumāna*).
[The opponent] says: study is not impelled by the injunction for study;
rather, it is impelled solely by the injunction for teaching.
Because the injunction for study lacks a person to be enjoined (*niyojya*).
For here, unlike [the injunction] "one desiring heaven should sacrifice," no person to be enjoined is heard;
nor can one be postulated as in the case of the Viśvajit sacrifice and others.

Since the accomplishment of study is achieved through the very injunction for teaching, there is no need for a separate [injunction] for it; nor should it be argued that the injunction for teaching is also devoid of a person to be enjoined (*niyojya*),
because one who desires to become a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇakāma*) is the one to be enjoined therein.

Because of the hearing of the ātmanepada ending in the rule, "One should initiate a Brahmin whose [proper] age has passed," and because the ātmanepada is prescribed for the root *nī* in the sense of "acting as a teacher" by the rule: "The restriction [of the ātmanepada applies] in the cases of honoring, lifting up, acting as a teacher, knowing, hiring, counting, and spending."

Because of the perception that the acts of initiation (*upanayana*) and teaching (*adhyāpana*) have a single agent in the injunction "he should teach him," and because teaching does not occur without study, the injunction for teaching itself— by means of the relationship of "taking up" (*upādāna*) characterized by the requirement of another for its own fulfillment— impels the act of study.
Furthermore, if study were to exist, there would be knowledge of the injunction, and from that, study; thus, there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*).
Therefore, this citation of a scriptural passage is not relevant here.
To this, it is replied:
This might be so if study were prompted by the injunction to teach;
but it is not so,
because teaching has livelihood as its purpose.

Because of the statement that "the three [higher] activities constitute one's livelihood," and because Vedic study is obligatory— as in the verse: "The twice-born who, without having studied the Vedas..."
This is because a transgression is heard to result from its non-performance;
furthermore, that which is eternal (nitya) is not joined with that which is non-eternal (anitya).
Moreover, if the purpose were fulfilled by teaching a single boy, it would follow that other boys would not study.

If it is argued that "he by whom one is brought [to a teacher] should be taught by him," then there would be an absence of study once the one who brought him has passed away. Furthermore, the objection regarding mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*) that was raised applies equally to such injunctions as "one should perform the morning twilight worship" (*prātaḥsandhyām upāsīta*).
If it is argued that this too is the rule for the teacher alone, based on such statements as "he should instruct him in the rules of purity and conduct," we say no; for [if that were so],
it would follow that those rules would cease to exist once the teacher has passed away.
Therefore, it must be accepted that the elders somehow bring about the boy's understanding of the injunctions for study and so forth; enough of this.
He explains the phrase "and because of [the evidence of] established practice" as follows: "even today," and so on.
...and because of his authority over right conduct:
"Even today, the gods and others always hear, reflect upon, and meditate according to their capacity upon that [Manu]. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.3.71a–c)
Since all knowledge is essential,
for that very reason even the gods and others continue to engage in hearing and reflection, and constantly practice meditation.
Otherwise, since those of great intelligence would be able to accomplish the hearing of each individual branch and so forth in a very short time, they would not be doing so even today.
"According to [their] fitness and according to [their] capacity" are qualifiers applied to each [of the categories].
Regarding the word "listening," the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) has been used.

When it was stated simply "and because of traditional practice" (*samācārāt*), one might ask how this can be so given that gods and others lack the qualification for the Vedas; therefore, the author of the Sūtras stated "and because of the qualification in traditional practice" (*adhikārācca*) to indicate that one should not forget the principle established in the *Devatādhikaraṇa*.

If even gods and others who possess the direct realization of Brahman still perform hearing [the scriptures] and other such practices, then it would follow that such realization is limitless; therefore, he says: "Nevertheless" (tathāpi).
Nevertheless, until the final determination of the truth is reached,
both hearing and reflection must indeed be practiced in every way.

Although the author of the Sūtras has accepted the conduct of the gods and others as authoritative, nevertheless, the reality— such as the Supreme Brahman and so forth— is determined by a correct, indirect, and certain conviction.
The first word "eva" (only) is connected with the phrase "precisely because of the determination of the reality.
The meaning of the word "hi" (for/because) is that hearing and so forth are the causes for the determination of the reality.
It is incorrect [to claim] that hearing and reflection must be performed until the determination of the reality is reached.

Since it is observed that even when a matter has been determined, doubt and the like may arise again due to the occurrence of other causes, making it impossible to definitively ascertain the determination of the object, he says: "matīti" (regarding cognition).
The supreme teacher knows the distinctions of intelligence, sacred learning, meditation, and time; for one who acts according to the path of his instruction, true insight shall indeed arise.
*Manī* means reflection; *śruti* means hearing.
*Uttamaḥ* refers to one who knows the fitness of the disciple.
This applies to one who is performing the hearing and other such practices.
"Vision" (darśana) is the direct realization of Brahman.
This is what is meant:
hearing and the other [means] are indeed for the purpose of the vision of Brahman.
Moreover, that means of accomplishment is not practiced in just any arbitrary way;
rather, as he will state, it must be preceded by a teacher who recognizes the disciple’s fitness and bestows [the instructions].
Therefore, such a teacher alone will instruct regarding the specific times for listening and so forth.
For beyond that point, even if hundreds of causes were to converge, there would be no arising of doubt or the like.
It is not logical to say that gods and others still perform hearing and so forth;
for it has been stated that hearing and the rest are the means for attaining the vision of reality (*tattvadarśana*). Thus, the vision [of reality] must already exist [in them].
Furthermore, because the vision of reality (*tattvadarśana*) is innate for gods and others—as it has been said:

"Those who have not attained the vision of Brahman do not reach the state of a god," and so forth—and because one who has already attained what is to be accomplished does not undertake further means of attainment, he says: "Hearing" (*śravaṇa*).
Hearing, reflection, and meditation on the realized truth lead to the attainment of extraordinary bliss... // MAnu 3.73a-c //

The construction [of the sentence] is as follows: even for a person who has seen the truth, hearing, reflection, and meditation are indeed appropriate for the attainment of a special bliss. If this is so, then how is it that the statement regarding hearing and the rest being the means to realization is not contradicted? To this he says: "of another."
... for the sight of another. // Manu 3.73d //
For one who has not yet perceived the reality, these practices such as hearing and so forth serve for the purpose of perception;
just as, according to the proponents of the doctrine of accumulation (*samuccayavādin*), actions prior to knowledge are for the sake of knowledge,
while those subsequent to it are for the sake of liberation.

Just as actions performed with desire are the cause of saṃsāra, while those performed without desire are the cause of knowledge, so too, for one who has not yet perceived the reality (*tattva*), hearing and the other [limbs of yoga] are for the sake of knowledge; thus there is no contradiction of what was previously stated.
However, for one who has perceived the reality, they are for the sake of special bliss; therefore, it is logical that even gods and others perform them.

Furthermore, the description of proper conduct was provided merely to reinforce the necessity of hearing and reflecting upon the meaning of the Vedas according to one's capacity; thus, it is not inconsistent.
As for the specific bliss, we shall explain it later.
It is incorrect to say that hearing and so forth must be performed solely in accordance with the instructions of a teacher who recognizes the disciple’s fitness.
Because such a guru is difficult to find, there would result the impossibility of hearing [the teachings] and so forth;

furthermore, even if such a guru were found, he is obtained only by a disciple who has performed the hearing and other practices and is endowed with internal spiritual power (*ādhyātmika-śakti*), and not by anyone else.
Thus, there would be a mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). To this, he says: "If... (verse 10.111).
If such a teacher is not available, one should perform the determined rites of hearing and so forth according to the established tenets of one who knows the final determination.
The scripture is determined to be twofold: that which has already been determined and that which is yet to be determined.
Of these, the first consists of the Brahmasūtras and so forth, while the second consists of the Vedas and so forth.
In that regard, one should practice hearing and so forth concerning what has been determined [by a teacher].
This means: from one who knows the determination according to the established tenets (*siddhānta*) of all the sciences.
This is what is being stated.
Even if the primary guru is not initially available, it does not follow that hearing [the scriptures] and other such practices become impossible;
for they can be accomplished even through a secondary guru.
In that regard, although a secondary guru may lack the capacity for an extremely profound exposition of the Vedas and other texts like the primary guru, an established exposition is indeed possible.
Nor should it be argued that even for one who has mastered the scriptures, the intended meaning remains difficult to grasp due to conflicting interpretations;
for even through a secondary teacher, such understanding is possible by following the treatises on the means composed by the Omniscient One.
And thus, when the secondary forms of hearing and so forth are performed, the primary teacher is also attained. (10.112)

If hearing and so forth from an omniscient Guru constitute the auxiliary means [to liberation], why is it not accepted that in the absence of such a Guru, there is simply an absence of hearing and so forth? What is the use of this secondary form of hearing and so forth? Furthermore, one might argue that the attainment of an omniscient Guru will occur through the accumulation of merit; to this, he says: "hearing and so forth... [referring to the necessity of the primary means].
Without hearing [the Veda] and so forth, it would not remain anywhere for even a single moment.

There are indeed Śruti and Smṛti texts—such as "Self-study and recitation alone," and "Nāka Maudgalya"—which signify that hearing [the teachings] and so forth must always be performed and not abandoned even for a moment.
In that context, a teacher who is omniscient is the ideal instrument;

however, in his absence, according to the maxim "when a quality is available, one should not resort to an improper alternative," hearing and so forth must certainly be carried out in whatever manner possible. This is the intended meaning.
But surely these very scriptural passages are of inconsistent meaning;
for when one encounters unavoidable disturbances such as sleep, it is impossible to perform hearing and so forth.
Indeed, it is not possible to enjoin the chewing of hair in the sky; therefore, he says: "Ati... [and so on].
But when it is impossible, such as during sleep and so forth, one should begin once again.
But when sleep and the like occur and cannot be avoided, one should perform hearing and the other practices immediately after they have passed away.
This is the intended meaning:

just as injunctions such as "one should offer the Agnihotra sacrifice in the evening and in the morning" are not rendered invalid even when obstacles such as the onset of illness arise, so it is in the present case as well.
If there is an absence of a teacher who knows the definitive conclusion, does it follow that hearing and so forth are also absent?
No; he says "in the absence" [to answer this].
In the absence of one who knows the definitive conclusions, he should always listen to the true scriptures... [Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.3.76]
Even in the absence of a teacher who knows the definitive conclusions, one should always listen to and reflect upon [the teachings] from whoever is available;
for it is not proper to abandon the primary [teacher] when the qualities [of the teaching] cannot be obtained— this is the intended meaning.

For the study of the Vedas and similar texts, an omniscient teacher is required; however, for the study of other [texts], one who knows how to determine their meaning and is nearly omniscient is required. Even in the absence of both types of teachers, if one were to undertake study and so forth, the understanding would be that it concerns false scriptures.
Therefore, it was said, "only true scriptures.
Since there is the possibility of over-extension by the phrase "one might hear from any kind whatsoever," he says, "If..."
...if an abundance of correct knowledge is observed.
If, in that person, an abundance of right knowledge and other virtues is perceived relative to oneself, then one should listen to him; however, not from one who is inferior,
because it would be useless.
The sense is that hearing and so forth are not for the sake of merely seeing [the truth].

When there is the expectation—given that it is impossible to provide a continuous exposition for a person who is superior by nature—asking whether there is simply an absence of hearing and so forth, he says: "Great fear. (*10.115*)
He should dispel the doubts of those devoted to Viṣṇu to the best of his ability, for [the failure to do so] is a great fear.

"He is naturally full of great fear," and his greatness is not through mere reputation alone, but rather through qualities such as devotion to Viṣṇu; this is stated in the passage beginning "to the devotees of Viṣṇu.
For it is he who, generating such respect, provides the commentary.
Furthermore, listening and the other practices performed with reverence alone are sufficient for the result.
It has been stated that the fruit of listening and so forth consists in the removal of doubt, ignorance, and error.

Even if it is impossible to listen to [the teachings] from a single source in their entirety, one should certainly engage in listening to even a single portion from many great teachers, according to one's capacity and as circumstances allow.
The sense is that even by him, there is the attainment of the fruit of hearing and so forth, which consists in the cutting away of doubt and the like.
To the question, "If there is no excellence [of knowledge] inherent in itself, how can there be hearing and so forth? he says: "Inherently" (svataḥ).
... if there is no one superior to himself, he should practice it himself and may also teach it to his disciples;
furthermore, this implies a mutual connection [between these acts].

Through the study of what has been heard and the practice of teaching, even those [teachings] give rise to the fruit of hearing and so forth by means of the emergence of fresh creative insight (*utprekṣā*).
However, one who explains while lacking proper hearing and so forth would incur sin through error.
To the question, "In that case, how can it be said that one should speak to disciples? he says: "The Real" (*sat*).
...the great path of the six established doctrines. *Mānava-dharmaśāstra* 3.3.77.
The connection is that one should say [this].
A tenet (siddhānta) is an object characterized by the conviction of its being authoritative;
however, there is no rule that it must be exclusively authoritative.
If that were the case, there would be no such thing as the doctrine of some that sound is eternal and the doctrine of others that it is non-eternal,
because it is impossible for both to be authoritative.
But this [cognition] is not like that;
rather, it is indeed authoritative (prāmāṇika), and for this reason it is called "existent" (sat).
The suffix *ṇic* has its own meaning (*svārthika*).
The meaning is "without abandoning.
Alternatively, it means "not causing the students to abandon [it].
We shall explain that the abandonment of the true doctrine (satsiddhānta) is itself the cause of great demerit (pratyavāya).

The meaning is that a minor error is indeed very small; however, one should not abandon the exposition of a work of great purpose on that account alone, for if that were the case, it would follow that one should refrain from sowing seeds out of fear of deer. *10,118*
What is this true doctrine (*satsiddhānta*) that is not to be abandoned? The true doctrine is twofold, distinguished as supreme (*para*) and inferior (*apara*).
Each of these is further twofold: the literal (*vācanika*) and the incidental (*ānuṣaṅgika*).
In this regard, he first states the supreme established doctrine (siddhānta) as it is taught in the scriptures: "Without remainder," and so forth.
The complete fulfillment of all virtues, the total eradication of all defects, and that everything else is dependent upon Viṣṇu—this is the correct determination. (Manu Smṛti 12.94)
"Another's system" (*anyattantra*) refers to that which is said to be the cause of the birth and so forth of the entire world.
"Determination" (*nirṇaya*) means that which is determined; it is a thorough determination based on scripture, namely the established tenet of another [school].
Indeed, this very point was stated in the *Janmādi-sūtra*, which is intent upon determining the nature of Brahman directly.
He states the opponent's established conclusion as a secondary consequence: "independence" (*svatantratva*).
It is always independent, and its differentiation occurs in every respect.
Independence (*svatantratva*) consists in having existence and other qualities that are under one's own control.
This refers to Viṣṇu.
The second occurrence of the word *tasya* ("of him") is connected with what follows later.
"And difference from everything" means absolute difference from primordial matter (*prakṛti*), the individual soul (*jīva*), and insentient objects (*jaḍa*).

But is this not also impossible? For it has already been stated [in the *Brahma-sūtras*] that "the existent [Brahman] is not the Self because it is not heard [in the Upanishads] as such," and "because of its being taught separately," and so forth.
How then is this a secondary tenet?
True;
nevertheless, because it was stated for the sake of its utility regarding the primary object of knowledge, there is no fault.
This is an elliptical expression for [the reasons] such as "being devoid of internal differentiation" (*svagatabhedavarjitatva*).
It connects with what will be stated later: "thus is the correct state" (*iti samyak sthitiḥ*).
To the question, "In what way is this [point] a secondary consequence (*anuṣaṅgika*)? he says: "of the absence of fault" (*adoṣatvasya*).
...for the purpose of establishing the absence of fault.
The ellipsis [to be supplied] is: "This point must be accepted for the purpose of establishing Viṣṇu’s faultlessness.
This is an illustration;
it should also be understood that [this applies to] his being complete with all auspicious qualities and his being the cause of the birth and so forth of the entire universe.
To the question, "How is that established by this? he says: "If..."
... that which exists when there is non-difference is its concomitant. (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 3.3.79d)
The connection with what precedes is as follows: "Because [otherwise] the consequence of Viṣṇu being connected with defects would follow if there were non-difference from the world.

Here too, the term "non-difference" (abheda) is an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa) of lack of independence (asvātantrya); and the phrase "consequent upon that" (tadanvaya) is likewise an indication of the absence of the perfection of qualities and so forth.
To prevent the understanding that the word "other" (anya) in the phrase "another's tantra" (anyattantra) refers to those who are not liberated, he says: "and being dependent on that."
And even for those who are liberated, there is dependence upon that [the Lord]. // MAnuBh 3.3.80ab //

The word "ca" (and) has the sense of a conjunction with the distinction that is about to be stated; "is to be accepted" is the ellipsis. For what purpose is this to be accepted? [One might ask: "Because it is also possible for the Sūtra beginning with 'janmādi' (origination, etc. to have as its subject matter those who are not yet liberated. To this, he says: "That... (*tad*).
... for the sake of fulfilling those qualities. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.80b)
For without being dependent upon them, His unimpeded sovereignty cannot be established;
and without that, the perfection of attributes does not occur.
This may be so.
If the liberated were distinct from the Supreme Self, it would not be so; why then [is it said they are] "dependent on that"? To this he says: "Even for the liberated... (muktānām api).
And there is also a distinction among those who are liberated... // Mānava 3.3.80c //
Furthermore, the absolute difference from the Supreme Self must be accepted;
by this, the statement “and His difference is from everything” is also explained.
To state the purpose [of the work], he prepares the introductory foundation with the words "nahi" (not indeed).
... for nowhere has it ever been observed that what is distinct becomes non-distinct. 3.80cd...

The non-difference of liberated souls from the Supreme Self cannot exist for those who were previously different, because the attainment of non-difference by one who was different is nowhere observed. To the question, "Is it not merely that it is not observed? What then? he says: "Of that... (tasya).
... its non-existence as well is accepted on the basis of experience.
The non-existence of the claim that "the divided becomes undivided" is established by experience;
therefore, one must simply state that even in saṃsāra, it is only those things that are already undivided whose lack of division is manifested in liberation.
To the objection, "Let it be so," he says: "pūrva... (as before).
If there were no distinction from the former state, the Lord would possess defects;
therefore, the established doctrine is that the liberated souls are entirely equal to Nārāyaṇa.
It has already been established that this saṃsāra, consisting of suffering and so forth, is real.
Therefore, if there were a difference between the individual souls (jīvas) and the Supreme Self (paramātman) even within saṃsāra, the latter would possess those defects.
The word "iti" is used here in the sense of a reason.

"Right standing" (samyak-sthiti) is the true doctrine; "subsidiary" (ānuṣaṅgika) means "the other," as is understood from the context. [Objection: But for what purpose is this extreme distinction, given that both difference and non-difference are established? To this he says: "Difference... (*bhedeti*).
Even if there is both difference and non-difference, faults would still arise by virtue of their non-difference.

Difference accompanied by non-difference is "difference-and-non-difference" (*bhedābheda*). Alternatively, it may be a singular collective compound (*dvandvaikavadbhāva*) according to the rule: "And [a compound] containing contradictory terms [is singular] when it does not denote a location."
Here too, according to the previous reasoning, both difference and non-difference must be accepted even within saṃsāra.
Consequently, by way of non-difference, the possibility of defects also arises.
If it is argued that their avoidance will occur through difference, then what is the use of this non-difference, which is as useless as the teat on the neck of a goat?
Now he states another established conclusion: "The state of being faultless," etc.
And the faultlessness of Ramā... Thus, like the Supreme Lord, Ramā is also faultless.

As it has been stated: “Desire and so forth [exist] there and there, from the abodes and so forth,” and “She is with the *samanā* up to the commencement of the path of transmigration, and immortality without having burned away [the body].”
By stating "the state of being without defects," he says "that" in order to dispel the misconception that there is also an absence of dependence [on others].
...and likewise its immediate succession. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.82d)
"Being immediately subsequent to the Supreme Lord" means being dependent upon Him;
or rather, by this [statement], he states another established conclusion—that subordination proceeds from the Blessed Lord alone.
This too has been stated: "And this very [conclusion] is the 'heat' (ūṣman) of the logical justification."
He states another established conclusion: "Brahman," etc.
Brahmā, Sarasvatī, Viṣṇu, Indra, Śeṣa, and Rudra, as well as their wives, Śakra, Kāma, and others, are likewise liberated in due order.
This should be known as the established doctrine of the virtuous.
The meaning is that they abide in liberation as well as in saṃsāra according to the sequence previously described.
Here, it should be understood that among those indicated by the copulative compound (dvandva), there is equality, whereas for others there is gradation (tāratamya).
This has been stated as "up to the final instruction" (*āmananāt*);
this is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*), and such things as the reality of the phenomenal world (*prapañca-satyatva*) are also to be included.
From where does this true established doctrine beginning with "endowed with all virtues" arise? To this he says: "It is determined."
...has been determined by Hari himself. (Manu 3.84b)
This was determined directly by the author of the Sūtras himself, Hari, and was not merely imagined as the meaning of the Sūtras through force;
this has indeed been demonstrated in various places, as it was stated:
"not abandoning the great established tenets."
To the question, "What is the fault in its abandonment? he says: "This... [etad iti].
Everything that is opposed to this leads solely to blinding darkness.
The meaning is that it is known as "existent. For it is indeed a contradictory cognition; its abandonment [is what is intended].
The ellipsis "it becomes for the blind" is to be supplied.
"Merely" means that it never leads to happiness.
To the question "Why is this so?", he says: "It is blind."
"The Veda declares most clearly that they enter into blinding darkness. (Manu 3.85ab)
He cites the Vedic scripture: "By this [path], those who worship ignorance enter into blinding darkness.
He will state that the meaning thus expressed is authoritative;
therefore, a cognition contrary to that [truth] is indeed ignorance.
By the phrase "it is extremely clear," he rejects the interpretation of others;
as we shall explain later.
But is it not the case that, in reality, the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is authoritative?
To the question of how that which has been introduced [as the subject] possesses authoritative status, he says: "Thus indeed... up to "...with reverence.
"Thus indeed all the Śrutis and the entire Pañcarātra [are authoritative]. (Manu 3.3.85cd)
The Mūlarāmāyaṇa, the Bhārata, all the Smṛtis, the Vaiṣṇava Purāṇas, and the two supreme systems of Sāṅkhya and Yoga. (Manu 3.3.86)
The Brahmatarka and the Mīmāṃsā constitute an infinite ocean of words;
following these are the logical arguments rooted in perception and scripture.
The direct perception of the Lord and of Rāmā and the others without exception—
whether they are liberated or not— is this very same supreme reality.
*ity eva* (thus indeed) is the restriction regarding the manner already stated; *etam evārtham* (this very meaning) is the restriction regarding the subject under discussion (*prakṛtadharmin*).
By this, it also excludes any transposition [of the terms].
The word "without remainder" (*aśeṣā*) is for the purpose of refuting the view that the portion of the Veda culminates in ritual action (*karman*) and so forth.
The word "then" (*atha*) signifies conjunction.
The word "entirety" (*akhilam*) is for the purpose of including even those passages concerning the birth of living beings and the like.
The phrase "the Mūlarāmāyaṇa alone" serves to exclude the various intermediate Rāmāyaṇas.
The word "akhilāḥ" (all) is used for the purpose of clarifying the scope of the plural number.
The term "Vaiṣṇava" is stated because other Purāṇas lack authority, as they are rooted in the Pāśupata and other such systems.
The word "parā" (the higher) is used to exclude the Sāṅkhya and Yoga systems that are directed toward this world,
because those two lack authoritative validity.
Mīmāṃsā is threefold.
The connection is that the Ocean of Words (*Śabdasāgara*) illuminates;
and the reasonings (*yukti*) that illuminate are those rooted in direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and scripture (*āgama*), not fallacious arguments (*ābhāsa*).
And it reveals [this] through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
By the word "only" (*eva*), it indicates the superiority of the direct perception of God (*īśvara-pratyakṣa*).
To the question of how the ritual sections (*karmakāṇḍa*) and so forth can reveal this meaning, it is said: "[it is] supreme" (*uttama*).
The intention is that although the meaning of the *karma* and other [sections] is superficially clear, this is the supreme meaning.

He precludes any alternative interpretation of the Vedas and so forth by stating: "He reveals it without leaving room for others," as in *Manu-smṛti* 3.3.89ab: "He respectfully illuminates [the Dharma], leaving no room for others."
This is an adverbial modifier.
By the word "respectfully," it indicates the presence of focused intent (*tātparya*) therein. For this purpose...
And the [scriptural] citations and so forth should be understood as already recited elsewhere (*10.132*).
It has been stated that one should always listen only to authentic scriptures (*sacchāstra*), while avoiding the great fallacy of false doctrines (*asatsiddhānta*).
Having thus defined the nature of those true doctrines, he explains this injunction—"one should always listen only to authentic scriptures"—with the words "And this very... (*etadeva ca*).
And this alone is the true scripture; anything other than that is a false scripture.
One should constantly study the true scripture and abandon false scripture.
This refers to the Vedas and so forth;
beyond that, there are those opposed to them and those indifferent to them.
The scriptural authority for this is explicit here, beginning with the words: "The Ṛgveda and the others, as well as the Mahābhārata."

While it should have been said that "one should not study bad treatises," the statement "one should abandon them" is intended to indicate that one must not merely remain indifferent toward them, but must also cultivate the knowledge [of their faults] as a means to that end. In this regard, the inclusion of "studying false scriptures" among the major sins (*pātaka*) serves as proof. Furthermore, the Teacher has elsewhere cited clear statements to this effect. *10,133*

It has been stated that one should study the true scripture, thereby establishing the necessity of hearing (śravaṇa) and reflection (manana); however, this is improper, because the vision of Brahman is possible through meditative concentration (nididhyāsana) alone, otherwise such [hearing and reflection] would be useless. To this, he says: "Without doubt... (asaṃśayena).
Without doubt, through the ascertainment of reality, there is the vision of Brahman.
By the word "doubt" (saṃśaya), error (viparyaya) is also indicated.
It should be understood that when certainty (nirṇaya) is attained, the vision of Brahman occurs through meditative contemplation (nididhyāsana).
This is what is meant:
It is true that profound meditation (*nididhyāsana*) is the means for the vision of Brahman;
however, for its accomplishment, both hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*) must also be performed.
For profound meditation is indeed the unerring contemplation of Brahman.
Since false reflection will be refuted in the fourth chapter,
and reflection upon that which is not known is impossible,
one must seek to hear [the teaching] for the sake of knowing it.

Furthermore, since even when an object has been heard, it may become false due to the arising of doubt or error through the appearance of fallacious marks (liṅgābhāsa), contemplation (manana) must also be accepted as the cause for its elimination.
Others, however,
maintain that hearing (śravaṇa) alone is the means for attaining direct knowledge of Brahman.
Reflection (*manana*) and meditative contemplation (*nididhyāsana*) are subsidiary factors (*aṅga*) that assist the fruit of hearing (*śravaṇa*).

For direct knowledge of Brahman (*brahmāparokṣajñāna*), which is intended for the uprooting of ignorance, is obstructed by mental distractions known as "doubt regarding possibility" (*asambhāvanā*) and "contrary conception" (*viparītabhāvanā*);
and reflection and the other practices remove these obstructions.
That is incorrect;
for nowhere is it observed that sound is a direct cause of perception,
and because it would follow that words concerning dharma and other such objects would likewise possess that same capacity, just like words concerning Brahman.

Furthermore, there is no specific reason by which we could understand that this status belongs only to that which has Brahman as its object, and not to that which has Dharma or other things as its object; consequently,
sound would have to be included therein by virtue of being subject to the definition of perception.
Now, it might be thought:
"The fact that a sentence such as 'You are the tenth' functions as the instrument for direct realization is indeed observed;
and it is not correct to claim that even in that case, the sense organ alone is the instrument and not the word."
Since the [causal efficacy] of sound is also established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), one might argue:
"Let the sense organ alone be the instrument (*karaṇa*), while sound is merely an auxiliary cause (*sahakārī*). If this is said, we reply: no, because the opposite could just as easily be maintained.
If it is asked, "Even so, what is the deciding factor?

we reply: because in some instances, even in the thickest darkness, and in other instances, even for one devoid of eyesight, the direct realization (*aparokṣa-pratīti*) "I am the tenth" is seen to arise from a verbal statement.
Furthermore, it is incorrect to claim that even a word whose object is dharma and the like must be a means for producing direct knowledge.
Because of the disparity:
for the word under discussion has as its object the immediate Brahman-Atman,
whereas another does not.
And there is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for its being the instrument for immediate knowledge,
but not for any other;
for instance:
The subject of dispute,
namely verbal cognition, is direct perception,
because its object is directly perceived, like the cognition of pleasure and so forth.

Immediacy (aparokṣatva) resides in the knowledge produced by Vedāntic sentences, because it is not the counter-positive of an absolute non-existence residing in immediate knowledge, just like "knowability" (jñānatva).
Nor is it the case that the word under dispute does not generate immediate knowledge.
It is not correct to argue that [the sentence] is like the sentences concerning the Jyotiṣṭoma and other sacrifices because it is a word;
for there is a deviation [from the rule] in cases such as "You are the tenth."
And it is heard [in scripture]: "He understood that from him; he shows the further shore of darkness.
Thus, the arising of immediate valid cognition occurs through instruction alone.
For this very reason, the definition of perception must be qualified by the condition of being distinct from sentences whose subject matter is Brahman and the Self.
To this it is replied:
as for the claim that the arising of immediate (aparokṣa) knowledge from such statements as "You are the tenth" is observed, that is inconsistent.

For the number ten is indeed produced by a relative cognition (apekṣābuddhi) or manifested by it; therefore, it is not perceived immediately through direct perception in the same way that color and other qualities are.
Then, just as the tenth person who completes the group of ten is likewise [ignorant],
so too, once indirect knowledge has first arisen through the word, immediate knowledge subsequently arises through perception aided by that [word].
Because of this [simultaneous] appearance, there is the misconception that there is only one immediate knowledge.
However, in cases such as darkness, the knowledge arising from a statement possesses no directness (aparokṣatva) whatsoever.
If it is argued that this dispute regarding experience is boundless,
the following must be said in response.
Is the capacity of a word to produce immediate perceptual knowledge its inherent nature (*svabhāva*), or is this capacity to produce immediate perceptual knowledge adventitious (*āgantuka*) to it?
In the first case, all words would possess such a capacity.
In the second case, the cause for this must be stated.
If it is argued that [the means of knowledge] has Brahman as its object,
then such [statements] as "You are the tenth" would not be a means for immediate knowledge, since they do not have that [Brahman] as their object.
Nor can it be said that [the means of knowledge] has an immediate object as its domain.

Because there is no such thing as "immediacy" (*aparokṣatva*) in an object that is distinct from being the object of immediate cognition, if one were to say that [the word] denotes [the object] by virtue of its being the object of this very cognition, there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*). However, if the intention is another cognition, then since even heaven and so forth are objects of immediate cognition for some people, a word whose object is that [heaven] would produce immediate cognition for us as well.
Even if [the object] is intended by a single person, since for some it is the object of non-perceptual knowledge, the word concerning that object would produce non-perceptual knowledge for us.

Furthermore, even if [the object] is intended by a single person, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that the perception of smoke would produce non-perceptual knowledge regarding fire already apprehended through direct perception.
If it is argued that such is the very nature of the word:

Even so, it would follow that the word "fire" could produce immediate perception (*aparokṣajñāna*). If you argue that this is not the case because [perception occurs] only when something is known as immediate, we say no; for if the word were the cause of immediate perception regarding a jar being apprehended by perception merely as a substratum (*dharmimātra*), it would follow that the word "this weighs one hundred palas" would likewise be the cause of immediate perception.

However, since the intended sense of "variety" (*prakāra*) is not applicable here, the identity of Brahman and the Self—which is the subject matter of statements such as "That thou art"—does not manifest as immediate perception (*aparokṣa*). For if it were so, the verbal testimony would be rendered useless. *10,142*
By this, the inference regarding its having an immediate object— namely, the argument beginning with "that which is immediacy," and so forth— is also refuted.
Since such an application could likewise be made in sentences concerning the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice and the like, it shares the same precarious status as a fallacious argument.

If it is argued that there is no contradiction whatsoever in the fact that sentences such as those concerning the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice lack the capacity to produce immediate (aparokṣa) knowledge, [we reply:
this is equally true for the Vedānta sentences as well.

If it is further argued that since transmigratory existence consists of ignorance (avidyā), and since ignorance cannot be eradicated without immediate knowledge, it follows that if the Vedānta sentences lacked the capacity to produce immediate knowledge, liberation (mokṣa) would be impossible—[we reply: No.
This is because the notion that [ignorance] is removable by knowledge has already been refuted,
and because it is logically established that nididhyāsana, which consists of one-pointedness of mind, is the means for attaining immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*).
If it is argued that the mind's status as a means for immediate knowledge is not observed anywhere else, [we reply:]...
If it is argued that this contradicts the scripture which says, "That which is not perceived by the word,
nor thought by the mind," we say no;
for that scripture is countered by the opposing scriptural statement, "This is to be attained by the mind alone."
If it is argued that this scriptural statement [regarding the cessation of speech] refers to the internal nature of one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgrya*),
then that too would pertain to a mind that is not yet matured.
Furthermore, how can the status of sound as a means for the knowledge of Brahman be accepted when it contradicts the scriptural text, "from which words turn back"?
However, scriptural passages such as "He desired to know that" (*tad dhāsya vijijñau*) are meaningful even in terms of indirect knowledge;
or rather, they declare that [such knowledge] is a means to direct realization through a traditional succession.
For the Smṛtis clearly state: "Having heard, reflected, and likewise meditated upon it, one abandons ignorance and its opposite."
"Having dispelled doubt, one attains the vision of Brahman"; and:

"As long as there is ignorance, so long shall there be the need for hearing; as long as there is lack of application, so long shall there be reflection; and as long as there is no direct perception, so long shall there be meditation; for where is that which has not been sublated?"
By this, it should be understood that the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding statements such as "Dharma exists" and the inference based on "being a word" (*śabdatva*) are likewise resolved.

For this very reason, [the objection] has also been refuted even when a qualification is added to the definition of perception (*pratyakṣa*), because [such an objection] lacks a basis (*nirnibandhanatvāt*). *10,147*

However, those who maintain that the word itself, having been engaged in producing immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*), produces it only after the obstacles such as incredulity (*asambhāvanā*) have been removed by means of reflection (*manana*) and meditative cultivation (*nididhyāsana*), should be asked:

prior to reflection and meditative cultivation, does this [word] produce immediate knowledge without having done anything at all, or does it do so by first producing mediate knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*)?
Not the first.

Because the absence of the arising of cognition from a word whose connection has been grasped would contradict valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Even in the second case, it would entail the fault of the word operating after having ceased its activity.
Therefore, it is better to assume that the word fulfills its purpose by that much alone; this is the general direction of the argument.
As for the statement that hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*) should be performed according to one's capacity, that is incorrect;
for since human capacities vary in degree, it would follow that hearing and the rest must also vary in degree.
Nor can it be said, "Let it be so."
This is because it would follow that the knowledge to be accomplished by them is of only one kind, rendering the various means redundant.
Nor should it be argued that since the Brahman to be known is immeasurable, the respective cognitions must also possess degrees of excellence;
for this does not avoid the redundancy, as the fruit thereof—liberation—is devoid of any gradation.
Indeed, a gradation in the destruction of bondage is not logically possible; therefore, he says: "Correctly" (*samyak*).
In accordance with the gradation of the correct or incorrect cognition [of dharma], there arises for men a result consisting of pleasure and pain, according to that gradation. (Manu 3.3.91)
"Viṣama" means contrary.
"Vijñāna" is simply knowledge (*jñāna*);
therefore, there is neither tautology nor contradiction.
The phrase "due to gradation" (tāratamyāt) means "endowed with gradation.
When it is said that there is a gradation between correct knowledge and erroneous knowledge, the understanding might arise that this refers to their mutual relationship.
To exclude that [misunderstanding], he explains by stating "and correct... (samyak ca).
And through correct and superior knowledge, there shall be an increase in happiness for human beings.
The indeclinable *samyak* means "correctly" or "properly. The word *ca* (and) has the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned.
From such middle knowledge (*madhyama-samyag-jñāna*), there arises a corresponding happiness.
From a small amount of right knowledge, [the result] is small;
likewise, from a greater amount of false knowledge, there is greater suffering, and so forth.
In this context, the statement regarding the gradation of suffering according to the gradation of false knowledge serves as an illustrative example.
Alternatively, it was stated that "one should abandon false treatises";
this [following] explanatory passage (arthavāda) serves to demonstrate the necessity of their absolute abandonment.
Liberation is not merely the destruction of bondage, but also [the attainment of] bliss.
The sense is that a gradation of that [intensity] is thus logically established.
He concludes the subject matter with the words "Therefore" (*ataḥ*).
Therefore, just as it is with one's own capacity, so too should be the hearing and the reflection.

But surely, since this is an *avyayībhāva* compound formed with the word "yathātmaśakti" according to the rule *yathātmaśakti*, and because it is an indeclinable by the rule *avyayībhāvaśca*, the third case ending should be elided after that indeclinable according to the rule *avyayād āpsupaḥ*—as in the example *yathātmaśaktyā*—so how is it [used here]?
It is replied: [The answer follows:]... [text continues] ...it is said.
The word *yathā* is a separate term connected with *samyagvāci*.
It refers to how the path of cessation was first taught by the Blessed One, and it is linked with the phrase beginning with "just as it was heard" (*yathāśravaṇam*).
Or, for the sake of similarity,
one should practice hearing and reflection by means of one's own capacity alone,
but not with respect to the subject matter of all the Vedic branches.
Nor is it restricted solely to the subject matter of one's own specific Vedic branch (*śākhā*).
Just as hearing (*śravaṇa*) and reflection (*manana*) are performed according to one's own capacity,
so too should one practice meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*) in that same manner.
And having performed that hearing and reflection, one should practice meditation (*kuvarnveti*).
Alternatively, the word *āś* following the avyayībhāva compound *yathā-ātma-śakti* signifies "properly" (*samyak*);
it is connected with the words beginning with "hearing."
Alternatively, there is an *avyayībhāva* compound of the word *yathā* with the word *ātman*;
thereafter, there is a *karmadhāraya* compound with the word *śakti*.
The meaning is: "by means of a capacity that conforms to [one's] fitness."

In this context, although the conclusion could have been made simply by stating that one should "hear" and "reflect" according to one's own capacity, more is said. This is for the purpose of concluding that what was stated regarding hearing and reflection also applies to their being limbs of *nididhyāsana* (meditative contemplation);

or else, it is for the sake of making known the specific distinction that one may act [even while practicing]. Furthermore, this alternative is determined in accordance with the instructions of the teacher.
Alternatively, the first half alone constitutes the conclusion of the subject matter (*adhikaraṇārtha*).
Therein, the phrase "one should practice" (*ācaret*), which is to be stated later, is connected by way of a "lion's glance" (*siṃhāvalokana*).
The word "thus established" (*siddham*) is to be understood as the ellipsis (*śeṣa*).
Thus concludes the section on the cognition of all Vedas (*sarvavedapratyayādhikaraṇa*). [======= JNys_3,3.II:
Section on the Summary (upasaṃhārādhikaraṇa) =======]
Now begins the section concerning the withdrawal [of the senses].
// Oṃ. There is a withdrawal [of the details] because there is no difference in the purpose, as in the case of the supplements to an injunction, and because it is the same; oṃ.//
In this context, it has been stated that the Supreme Self is to be meditated upon by synthesizing all the qualities and absences of defects mentioned in all the Vedas.
Intending to show that here too the word "all" functions without restriction according to the logic already established, he states the purport with the words: "Having performed... (kṛtvā).
Because there is no difference in meaning, the conclusion [of the meditation] is the same as in the case of the supplementary parts of an injunction;
having performed it, or even while performing it, one should practice *nididhyāsana*. (3-3-2)

The terms "hearing" (*śravaṇa*) and "reflection" (*manana*) likewise apply here, as does the phrase "according to one's own capacity. By this, [the Sūtra] states: "And because it is appropriate for what has been attained" (*prāpteśca samañjasam*).
The intended meaning (*tātparya*) of these and other such sūtras should also be understood as having been stated [previously].
Likewise, the meaning of [sūtras] such as “*tannirdhāraṇārthaniyamaḥ*” is [to be understood] through the explanation of the first section (*adhikaraṇa*).
Thus concludes the section on the Summary (*upasaṃhārādhikaraṇa*).
Now begins the section on the Subordinate Elements (*anubandhādhikaraṇa*).
Oṃ, [the suffix *aṇ* is applied] after words beginning with *anubandha*, etc. Oṃ.
In the Yogaśāstra, the restraints (yamas) and other practices are taught as limbs of spiritual discipline (upāsanā).
Regarding this, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) considers that the performance of the restraints is, first of all,
untenable.
The attainment of qualities such as devotion to Viṣṇu and the avoidance of defects such as attachment to sense objects constitute what is designated by the term *yama*.
This is because [these qualities] must be practiced according to the specific constraints of place, time, and state;
the enumeration of non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) and so forth is merely for the purpose of illustration, according to the teachings of Yoga.
In that regard, does the worship of the Yamas serve as a means for the arising [of the knowledge],
or for the arising of the knowledge of its fruit? It is not the first.
The second [alternative] is not tenable, because we observe that even those who harbor enmity constantly contemplate [the object], and because meditation consists of nothing more than that.

There is no evidence to suggest that worship accompanied by devotion and other such qualities alone produces the direct realization of Brahman, and not otherwise. Furthermore, [the scriptures state]: "The kings headed by Caidya [attained perfection] through hatred," and "Because of enmity, those kings... [and so forth].
In such passages as these, the fact that aversion is a means to liberation is first perceived;
furthermore, by the statement "having seen him alone, one is liberated, and not by any other," it is understood that liberation is to be accomplished solely through vision.
By reflecting upon both of these points, it is comprehended that aversion is a means to [attain] vision.
In this way, the status of postures (āsana), breath control (prāṇāyāma), and withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra) as auxiliary limbs (aṅga) must also be rejected.
Regarding that, the resolution is: "Because of the connection and so forth";
its meaning is: "Because of devotion and so forth."
In that regard, it is not known which position has been accepted and how the fault mentioned therein is avoided;
therefore, he explains by means of the passage beginning with "viṣayeṣu" and so forth.
And because of their consequences and other such factors; because of attachment to sense objects; because of doubt regarding the eternal;
and because of the mind’s longing for something else—the supreme state is not attained. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.3.93)
For this is indeed the statement of the *Bhārata*: "One who is free from these defects and endowed with constant practice beholds Vāsudeva. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.3.94)
Because of the pursuit of sense objects— that is,
toward the various objects of the senses other than liberation from the eternal Brahman—
the word *ākāṅkṣāt* (from the root *kāṅkṣ* with the suffix *ghañ*) means that one does not attain, nor does one perceive, the supreme Brahman.
The word *ca* (and) expresses a mutual conjunction;
the word *hi* means "because.
The ellipsis [to be supplied] is: "[it] states that defects such as contact with the object are obstacles to cognition."
Only one who is free from these defects becomes truly engaged in constant worship;
it should be understood that only such a person, through constant worship, perceives Vāsudeva.
This is what is meant:
First, we maintain that the restraints (*yama*) are auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the origination of worship (*upāsanā*);
for it is impossible for one who possesses attachment to sense objects and the like, and who is devoid of devotion, to perform worship constantly.
Indeed, [this is] not [possible] elsewhere.
It is logical that one whose mind is attached there and who is overwhelmed by affection would constantly contemplate that [object].
As for what was said here—that even those who are angry are seen to contemplate [the object] continuously like those who are affectionate—that is true.
Nevertheless, one must certainly accept the avoidance of contact with others and so forth.
Furthermore, there is no cause for hatred toward the Blessed One.
Even if hatred should arise in some due to the power of a defect in their disposition, such a form of reflection does not become a means for attaining knowledge;
rather, it must be accompanied by the aforementioned [virtues] and so forth. Thus, we also accept the second position.
Nor is there an absence of authoritative evidence in this regard,
because a statement from the *Mahābhārata* exists;
for in that passage, words such as "contact with objects" (*viṣayasaṃsarga*) serve as indicators (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the mere absence of self-restraint (*yama*).
It has been stated that "one who is free from these defects" because even the absence of devotion and so forth constitutes a defect.
He also provides the reasoning for why the restraints (*yamās*) must necessarily be practiced, stating: "The defects... (*doṣāḥ*).
The defects, bound to one from beginningless time, are the obstacles to liberation;
they generally exist within men, and for that reason, liberation does not arise.

Those defects, such as the absence of devotion to Viṣṇu and attachment to sense objects, which are obstacles to liberation, exist in abundance within men due to their beginningless connection [to them].
For that reason, their liberation does not arise.
This is what is meant:
Even for those who are fit for liberation and who desire liberation, liberation does not occur at this time.
One should consider why this is so.
If it is argued that it is because of the absence of the Lord’s grace, then one must ask: from where does that [grace] arise?
If it is argued that [this is] due to the absence of knowledge, from where does that [absence] itself arise?

If it is argued that it is due to the non-existence of the practice of meditation, no; for it will be explained later that even among those who harbor hatred, such practice may exist yet be non-existent [in its effect].
Furthermore, it must be stated why there is no practice of meditative absorption (dhyāna) either.
If you say it is because of the absence of hearing [the teachings] and so forth,
then why is that [hearing] also absent?
Therefore, it is understood that the defects themselves, by obstructing the arising of this or that [wholesome state], are the adversaries of liberation.
Nor is it correct to argue that it is impossible for adventitious defects to be the cause for the absence of beginningless liberation;
for they are beginningless by way of their continuous flow (*pravāha*).
And so it has been said:
"The qualities grasped by defects.
This might be the case.
There are some transmigrating souls, such as children, the simple-minded, and others, who are free from defects such as passion;
how then can it be said that defects are the cause of the absence of liberation? To this, he says: "All."
All these are seen among living beings according to their relative degrees.

Even among those living beings cited as being like children or the simple-minded, these very defects—such as the absence of devotion to the Blessed Lord—are indeed perceived through both direct observation and inference.
Furthermore, attachment, aversion, and so forth exist among men in varying degrees;
for they are of four kinds, distinguished as dormant (*prasupta*), attenuated (*tanu*), interrupted (*vicchinna*), and active (*udāra*).
Therefore, because those sublime [qualities] are absent in infants and others, there arises the misconception of their non-existence;
for even in them, desires such as for breast milk and so forth are observed, and thus there is scripture [to this effect], beginning with:
"Because of the lack of development in the womb and in infancy," and so on.
Thus, it is rightly said that all defects are indeed established by all means of valid cognition.
Nevertheless, it might be argued:
there exist transmigrating persons known as *ṛju* who are fit for attaining the state of Hiraṇyagarbha.
And it is not logical to say that they are faulty,
because that would contradict their uprightness (*ṛjutva*). "Upright," "correct," and "faultless" are synonymous.
To the question "How is that so?", he says: "Of the upright ones."
For those who are upright, there is only one [fault]: the absence of supreme enthusiasm.

Even for those who are upright, there exists a fault called "the avoidance of great exertion" for the sake of liberation; therefore, it is not incorrect that this was not mentioned, because otherwise liberation would be impossible to delay.
Nor does this contradict their uprightness.

Since he is indeed one [alone], the statement regarding his straightforwardness (*ṛjutva*) is intended to show the absence of a multitude of faults; the sense is that, as is observed in the case of those with little wealth, the term "destitute" (*niḥsva*) is applied even to one who possesses something. (10.165)
He resolves the contradiction in another way: "sa" (he).
Because it consists merely of a small degree of merit, it is not contradicted by its status as a non-external [act].
This is the fault called "the absence of supreme enthusiasm.
Although the lack of great effort is indeed a fault because it is to be abandoned,
nevertheless, it is not of a positive nature like attachment and so forth.
Nor is it of the nature of an absence of qualities;

rather, it is merely a state of deficiency in qualities characterized by enthusiasm, and thus it is called "non-fault" (*adoṣa*), which does not contradict its being [a form of] crookedness (*nārjutva*).
What follows from this, if faults are thus the causes of saṃsāra and obstacles to liberation? To this he says: "Therefore... (*ataḥ*).

Therefore, for one who desires the goals of human existence (*puruṣārtha*), supreme devotion should be practiced toward Viṣṇu and toward his devotees, such as Ramā and others, according to their relative gradation.
This [injunction] is also an illustration for all [deities] beginning with Yama.
The goal of human endeavor is liberation (*mokṣa*).
This is the summary here:
those defects such as the absence of devotion to Viṣṇu and attachment to sense objects must be abandoned by one who possesses the desire for liberation and so forth.
Because it is opposed to liberation and other such goals.
Whatever is opposed to something is seen to be abandoned by one who desires that thing;
just as unwholesome food, which is opposed to health, is abandoned by one who desires health.
And thus it is established that devotion to Viṣṇu and so forth must be practiced;
for without the performance of positive states of being, the abandonment of negative states is impossible.
He explains what was stated—that [devotion] toward Viṣṇu is supreme while toward others it is of varying degrees—with the words "one's own regard" (svādara).
For respect toward all living beings is indeed established by their very nature;
it is even greater toward those who are superior to oneself, in accordance with that degree of superiority.
One who desires welfare in every way must perform [the rites] ending with Vāsudeva.
"Veneration" (ādara) means affection (*sneha*).

"Established by its very nature" (*svabhāvataḥ saṃsiddha*) means that it is established from beginningless time, without depending on the performance of services and so forth; this is the meaning of the word *hi*.
For otherwise, there would be no such aspiration as, "I must always be happy and never suffer. This is the sense of the word *hi*.
Therefore, one should show greater reverence toward those who are directly superior to oneself than the reverence shown toward one's own objects;
in this manner, one should show increasing reverence according to their respective degrees of superiority, culminating in Vāsudeva,
for whom reverence is unsurpassed.
The "auspicious" refers to the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and so forth; this will be explained in the section on rebirth (*upapāda*).
The auxiliary factors (*aṅga*) are of many kinds, distinguished as those to be practiced once, those to be practiced repeatedly, and those to be practiced constantly.
But as to the question "How is this so?", he says: "No."
One should never abandon it, but rather increase it gradually.

One should not only not abandon that respect for Viṣṇu and the others, but should also increase it over time. In response to the expectation of how this should be done toward those who are one's equals or those inferior to oneself, he says: "toward equals," and so forth.
One should feel affection for equals as for oneself, and compassion for others who are virtuous;
by acting thus, the Lord is quickly perceived through direct realization.
The word "should be done" (kartavya) carries over from the previous context.
Therefore, compassion should be exercised toward those who are inferior, rather than toward those who are superior or equal.
If it were stated simply "toward those who are good" (satsu), then there would be the undesirable consequence of it applying even to those who are superior or equal.
If it were stated merely as "other than that," there would be the undesirable consequence [of the rule applying] even to non-existent things.

Therefore, it should also be applied as follows: toward those who are ignorant other than those three groups, one maintains equanimity; and toward those who are contrary [to the Dharma], one maintains contrariety.

When this is practiced, there is the worship of the Yamas, the arising of knowledge, and the excellence of liberation; to indicate that these constitute auxiliary elements (*aṅga*), there is the diverse expression: "The Lord is seen quickly by one who desires the human goal and seeks what is auspicious.
For this very reason, all three are mentioned together in the conclusion. (10.169)
Even regarding the abandonment of defects, there is a distinction.

For passion and the like expand the cycle of saṃsāra, whereas perverted knowledge and the like lead constantly to hell; therefore, with the intention that these must be abandoned more urgently than passion and the like, he cites the scripture on that point: "That... (tad).
He who perceives equality with Viṣṇu even in the liberation of Ramā, Brahmā, Śiva, and others, shall go to that blinding darkness.
How much more so for one who perceives superiority, or even for one who perceives the absence of his virtues;
likewise for one who perceives faults, for one who perceives non-difference, and for one who perceives both.
Thus says the sacred revelation... [Manu 3.103a]
That is well known.
It is not only in *saṃsāra* but even in liberation (*mukti*) that there is equality in some way or by some attribute.

Since it is observed that Lakṣmī, Brahmā, Śiva, and others perceive Viṣṇu as superior, it goes without saying that the person [who denies this] attains blinding darkness; thus the point should be applied.

He concludes the proof of his own position regarding both difference and non-difference with the words "by that" (*tena*): [it is for one who perceives] the absence of qualities in Viṣṇu, and the non-difference of Viṣṇu from souls and insentient matter.
... endowed with those aforementioned qualities, one should worship Hari; by that alone is liberation born.
[Endowed] with the previously mentioned qualities, such as the avoidance of contact with sense objects and so forth.
Alternatively, one who is endowed with the qualities and limbs such as *yama* and the rest as fully proclaimed in the Yogaśāstra—
by means of that very same kind of worship, having seen Hari, liberation arises for one who exhausts their karma.
Now, he refutes what was stated by the opponent— that even for those who hate the Lord, liberation is spoken of in the Purāṇas— with the words "from hatred."
That which is spoken out of hatred, and that which contradicts the words of the Vedas; MĀn 3.104ab.
Therefore, the intention is that it must be explained otherwise;
and he will state that manner [of explanation].
To the question, "What is that scriptural passage? [he says]: "May we not [fall] to those thieves who, in the place of the oppressors, are greedy for food—those enemies who are devoid of compassion."
He recites this for that purpose: "The enemies," and so forth.
But those enemies of Rāma who, out of hostility, are indifferent toward him,
remain forever situated in the blinding darkness of the state of malice.
Those who hate Hari go to darkness, as do those who identify with him [as being non-different from him],
as well as those who know his state of being devoid of qualities (nirguṇatva), and even those who perceive his faults.

*Rāma* is one who possesses delight (*ramaṇa*); thus, *rāmī* refers to the Blessed One’s name. Those who have departed from that [name] and are turned away from him are called *nirāmiṇaḥ*. For this very reason, they are his enemies.
The phrase "the locus of malice" (*abhidrohapada*) is itself explained by the term "blind darkness" (*andhatamasi*).
The ellipsis "they remain ever-present" is to be supplied.

By this [verse], those enemies who are devoid of compassion (nirāmiṇaḥ) and who are greedy for food and enjoyments— those who are malicious (abhidruh), fit to stand in the place of universal treachery (abhito drohasya pade)— from such thieves (stenebhyaḥ), do not speak of us.
For the construction "one who has heard from us does not deserve suffering" is thus indicated.
And this is the speech of the Knowledge-Goddess addressed to Vāyu.
[This applies] to him who is non-different from that [Vāyu], namely Hari, the proponent of the non-difference of the individual soul and so forth. (10.172)
To the question, "How is this not in contradiction with the sūtra? he says: "ityādi" (and so forth).
From such a collection of scriptural passages as these, it follows that darkness falls upon the hater.
Intending to show that the teaching of liberation for those who harbor hatred is contrary to tradition (smṛti), he recites them [the verses], beginning with "Hiraṇyakaśipu... and so forth.
And Hiraṇyakaśipu also, O Blessed One, having been pierced by the darkness [of ignorance] through the censure of the Lord,
passed away due to the power of his son Prahlāda.
Since my father censured me for my devotion to you, though he was himself possessed of sin,
may my father therefore be purified from that wretched and insurmountable evil.
He who, hearing reproach of the Blessed One or of others devoted to him,
does not depart from that [situation], he too goes to hell, fallen from his merit.
Fools disregard me when I have assumed a human form, being ignorant of my supreme nature as the Great Lord of all beings. (Manu Smṛti 3.109)
Futile are their hopes, futile their actions, and futile their knowledge;
devoid of discernment, they have taken refuge in a delusive nature that is both demonic and asuric.

Those malicious people who hate me in their own bodies and in the bodies of others— I cast those cruel haters, the lowest of men, perpetually into transmigrations within only the inauspicious wombs of the asuras.
Having entered the womb of an asura, deluded from birth to birth,
they fail to reach me, O son of Kuntī, and from there they go to the lowest state.
How could he who hates the Lord Nārāyaṇa, the best of the wise gods, not become an object of hatred for anyone as long as the world endures? (Manu 3.113)
"O best of the wise, the ancestors of one who hates the Lord Nārāyaṇa, the supreme deity, sink into hell for eternal years"—
from such a collection of scriptural passages, it follows that for the hater, there is only darkness. (Manu 3.114)
One who intends to enter is the object of the possibility [of being bitten];
for there is the rule that "in cases of apprehension, the addition applies even to insentient things," as in the expression, "the dog is about to die."
Through this failure to abandon [me], he has fallen into darkness. My father has censured me for my sake;
he has become sinful and guilty toward me and regarding my interests.
Therefore, from the sin born of the offense of censuring Viṣṇu and His devotees— which leads to eternal hell—
it is well known that such censure and the like are rooted in hatred.
This is a statement by Prahlāda addressed to Narahari.
If even one who hears reproach falls downward from that state, then what need be said of the reproacher? "Human-like" means similar to a human being.
Those who disregard me become possessed of vain hopes and desires;
not even a trace of happiness shall accrue to them.
[I am] situated as the impeller within the bodies of both self and others.
The *saṃsāra*s are bodies, so called because beings transmigrate within them;
its explanation is given in the passage beginning with "among the *āsura* [beings]," and so forth.
*Loka* means people; *tasyānta* refers to those ending with the *caṇḍāla*s and others.
To the question, "How is this in conflict with the Smṛti?", he says: "ityādi" (and so forth).
From such a collection of statements as these, it follows that for those who harbor hatred, there is only darkness.
The word "is known" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
The particle *tu* indicates that even darkness is without rising [from it].
Therefore, it is established that the limbs beginning with restraint (*yama*) must necessarily be practiced.
Thus ends the section on the "Ancillary Elements" (*anubandha*) in the illustrious *Nyāyasudhā*. [10.177] Now begins the section on "Knowledge" (*vidyā*) in the illustrious *Nyāyasudhā*.
// Oṃ. But it is knowledge alone [that is the means], because of the definitive determination; Oṃ.//

Although this section [the adhikaraṇa] should properly have come before the discussion beginning with "from the connection and so forth" (anubandhādibhyaḥ), nevertheless, since the opportunity to establish its efficacy arises only when the nature of meditation (upāsanā) has been understood— and not otherwise—
it has been explained out of its sequential order.
For instance:
The worship of the Blessed One should not be performed because it is useless;
nor for the sake of direct realization,
since that too is useless.
Nor should it be said that this [devotion] has liberation as its purpose, because according to the Cārvākas and others, liberation does not exist at all;

or, even if it does exist, it is—according to the systems of the Jainas and others—accomplished by other means. This [work] is commenced in order to establish both the existence of liberation and the fact that even that is accomplished through the vision of the Blessed Lord.
Although the doctrines of the Cārvākas and others have already been refuted in the *Samayapāda*,
this present effort is nevertheless undertaken for the purpose of specifically demonstrating the defects regarding liberation, its means, and the ether (*viyat*).
In that regard, he first restates the Cārvāka position with the words "Not at all" (*naiva*).
"But it is knowledge alone [that leads to liberation], because of the definitive determination [of scripture].
"There is no liberation at all," so say those who stand by the Lokāyata doctrine. (Manu 3.3.115ab)
The word "eva" (only/just) is intended to indicate the negation of its own essential nature (*svarūpa*).
Otherwise, a negation based on a connection with a specific person and so forth might also be understood.
Therefore, the remainder [of the sense] is that meditation (*upāsana*) would be purposeless.
If so, what then is the human goal? To this he says: "Experience" (bhoga).
...enjoyment. // Mānava-dharmaśāstra 3.115c //

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: they say that enjoyment (*bhoga*)—the experience of the pleasures of sense objects such as garlands and sandalwood—is the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*).
And he states that this enjoyment pertains only to this world, not to states such as heaven, by saying "the body," etc.
... up to the very body ... // MAnu 3.115c //
The meaning is "until the fall of the body.
Why is there an absence of heaven and liberation? To this he says: "reduction to ashes."
... from that, there would be reduction to ashes. (Manu 3.115d)
Thus... (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 3.116a) *10,179*:
After that fall, the body shall be reduced to ashes.
This is what is meant.
The attainment of heaven and liberation for the self must be discussed as occurring after the fall of the body;
yet the self does not exist apart from the body,
and the body certainly perishes immediately after its fall.
"Then, to whom would those two belong?"—
this is the connection with the words "thus they said.
Or, the word "iti" marks the end of the doubt.
Refuting this very point on the grounds of a lack of valid means of cognition (pramāṇa), he first asks: "That" (tad).
... by what authority has that been seen? ... // MAnu 3.116ab //
He refers back to that with the words "liberation does not exist at all," which constitutes the meaning of the sentence. By what means?
The meaning is: by perception or by something other than that.
It has been seen and understood.
With the intention that the second [point] cannot be accepted by the Cārvāka, he says: "By perception," and so forth.
... by one who speaks from direct perception. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.116b)
This is connected with what precedes: by one who accepts that perception alone is the valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and nothing else.
He refutes the first [position] with "No" (*na hi*).
For the non-existence of liberation is not determined by the means of perception alone.

To begin with, inference and the like do not constitute a means of valid cognition for another; that is to say, they are not [means of knowledge] by means of that perception which is accepted as a valid cognition. For what is called "liberation" (mokṣa) is specifically the attainment of supreme bliss and the absolute cessation of suffering.
And its absence should be understood as follows:

there is no person whatsoever who experiences supreme bliss; rather, everyone is suffering. Now, the happiness, suffering, or their absences residing in one person are not objects of perception for another person. Therefore, how could the non-existence of liberation be determined through direct perception? This is the meaning of the word "hi" (for/indeed). *10,181*
Let it not be that the certainty of the non-existence of liberation follows from the absence of a means of valid cognition;
for in this case, the certainty of its existence is indeed difficult to establish,
precisely because of the absence of a means of valid cognition.
In that case, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is the valid means of knowledge;

for there is no capacity in another’s perception to perceive the supreme bliss or the absence of suffering residing in another person. Rather, it is precisely that absence, as it pertains to oneself, that is perceived through direct perception.
Nor is it other than perception, because its validity is established by that [perception].

Consequently, due to the absence of any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) to either prove or disprove it, there would be either non-comprehension or constant doubt regarding liberation; thus, the performance of meditative worship (upāsanā) would not be possible.
Not so;
for the determination of liberation is indeed possible through perception.
As to the objection that perception lacks the capacity to function in that regard, he replies: "It is possible. (*ghaṭate*) [10.182]
But the vision of liberation is appropriate for a person of great excellence.
Although the perception of ordinary beings is not capable of apprehending liberation,
nevertheless, it is indeed appropriate to ascertain liberation through the perception of the Great Being (mahattamapuruṣa).
The sense is that the understanding of his perception will come about for others through his word.
