Now, an objection is raised: "In the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti*, a genitive case ought to occur; how then can there be a third case?
The genitive is prescribed when there is the intention to express the 'remainder' (*śeṣa*), and here there is no such intention to express the remainder. If this is argued, it is not so.
Since the mention of "the remainder" (*śeṣa*) has been excluded in this yoga,
it is said:
this third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used in the sense of a cause (*hetu*).
It is not by means of the agent or the instrument;
that is to say, it is not by means of the perception belonging to that Great Person (mahīyas) who is the cause or the instrument.
Thus, the vision of liberation—that is, the certainty regarding the actual existence of liberation—is possible for others.
Alternatively, the direct perception regarding liberation is established.
How so?
Because we maintain that liberation is perceived by the Great Person (*mahāpuruṣa*); such is the construction [of the sentence].
Alternatively, there is no fault in supplying the word "being performed" (*kriyamāṇā*). If that is the case, then it can certainly be argued by me as well:
although the absence of liberation for those like us, which resides in other persons, is not perceptible [to us].
Nevertheless, for a great man who is a teacher of Lokāyata, [the truth] is indeed perceptible;
and our understanding of that will come about through his word.
And since there would thus be a lack of certainty due to the presence of a counter-argument, he says: "No."
But there is no greatness whatsoever in the one who says "no. (Manu 3.117cd)
The connection is as follows: "I perceive through direct experience that liberation does not exist at all, whether present or future, in any person whatsoever.
The word *eva* (only) implies that even greatness itself does not exist, so how could there be anything greater? Alternatively, the word *tu* (but/however) carries this sense.
Here, "greatness" is required in its many various forms.
These are: the direct perception of objects not perceptible to other persons, the possession of extraordinary qualities conducive thereto, and the quality of speaking in accordance with reality.
Not even one of these modes exists in the teacher of the Lokāyata;
how, then, could there be any suspicion of counter-argument against him by those great beings who proclaim liberation?
To the question "Why?", he says: "Establishing..."
How can one who accomplishes what is common to all be considered a person of distinction?
By establishing the non-existence of dharma and so forth, the teacher of the Lokāyata school asserts the equality of all persons; how then does he become superior to others?
Not in any way.

This is what is meant: [the opponent] argues that since there is no distinction between people regarding the absence of dharma and the like, the Lokāyata teacher cannot claim any superiority over others.

The teacher of the Lokāyata school ought to possess a distinction over others in his direct realization of the absence of liberation residing in other persons, which is not perceptible to those other persons;
otherwise, that same consequence would apply to the others as well.
Yet, such a distinction does not exist.
A specific dharma produced by austerity or yoga is likewise established by him [the opponent] himself to be non-existent in his own case, just as it is in the case of others. Therefore,
due to the absence of such a cause, it is certain that he too lacks the direct realization of the absence of liberation for other persons, just like anyone else.
Therefore, his statement that "I directly perceive the absence of liberation" is indeed false.
If it is argued that the excellence [of the mind] is simply a specific transformation of the elements (*bhūta*),
is that [excellence] perceptible or imperceptible?
Not the first,
because it is not perceived;
for there is no evidence that something of such-and-such a nature can be the cause of the result under discussion.
Otherwise, there would be the fault of over-extension (*atiprasakti*).
Nor is the second [alternative] possible;
for by that very person who denies supersensible objects (*atīndriyārtha*), the absence of such [knowledge] in himself has been established, just as it is in others. *10,189*
Just as you assert that there is no Great Being who directly perceives the absence of liberation, so too do I say:
there is indeed no such exalted person who might behold liberation through direct perception,
because of the lack of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
And thus, there would again be a lack of certainty; therefore, he says: "They are seen."
Moreover, men are seen in this world who know both the higher and the lower.
Those who possess direct vision, who are established in yoga, and whose eyes are stainless,
having seen the deity directly, obtain prosperity through its grace.
...who have reached the further shore of knowledge and discernment. // MAnu 3.120a //
The sense is that it is not merely one;
they are Vasiṣṭha and others, in this very world on this terrestrial sphere.
He states their greatness as follows: "They have reached the further shore of knowledge and realization."
In this context, by means of the two subjects, the two objects are indicated:
those who fully know the forms of both the general and the particular;
not only those who know all that is present, but indeed those who know both the higher and the lower as well.
Therefore, what is the use of inference and the like? He says "no," adding: "and because it is immediate perception."
To the question, "What is their distinction from people like us?", it is said: "Established in yoga and possessing stainless vision.

They possess divine vision due to the extraordinary unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) produced by being established in yoga. To the objection, "What is the use of that alone?", he says: "Direct perception" (*pratyakṣam*).
Having directly perceived the Supreme Deity through the power of yoga, they possess sovereignty such as illumination attained by her grace.

Vasiṣṭha and others, directly perceiving liberation residing in the Supreme Person with their divine vision perfected by yogic power, are seen by direct perception itself; therefore, it is not the case that there is no certainty regarding liberation.
To the objection that "they do not exist because they are not perceived by people like us," he says: "They are denied."
...how can they be prohibited by men? (Manu 3.120b)
By the word "by men," he indicates those of meager fortune who are acquainted with secluded places;
for they do not frequent the merchant streets where they might be discovered by you.
The meaning is that because they are beyond reach due to such distance, they cannot be negated even if they are not perceived.
[Objection: Surely there is no disagreement regarding the mere nature of the Puruṣa;
but from what source does their greatness derive? To this he says: "And it is seen," etc. (10.191).
It is not merely that they are men; rather, their extreme majesty and greatness are observed.
How so?
Because they possess exceedingly great power.
This is what is meant:
indeed, we observe such things as the covering of the Vindhya mountains and the drinking of the ocean; these are their exceedingly great powers, and they are the effects of great sovereignty.
Furthermore, effects cannot exist without causes;
and since among those of great sovereignty there is a luminosity known by the name of omniscience, their status as supreme beings is established.
[Objection: But how is it established for others that he possesses direct perception regarding the subject of liberation?
If it is argued that [the world's practice] is due to their words, we say no; for it is possible that they are deceivers. To this, he says: "If..."
If even those [means] are prohibited, why is your own speech not also prohibited?
For deception is rooted in a motive,
and no investigation of motives is possible for them,
because they possess all sovereignty.
Furthermore, because no other purpose [for their teaching] is established,
even such yogis, if they were deceivers, would be refuted; that is to say,
their statement would be rejected on the grounds that it is rooted in deception.

In that case, why is the doctrine of the Lokāyata teacher accepted by you not likewise refuted? It too should be disregarded, having been conceived as being rooted in deception; such is the meaning, since there is no distinction between them.
By this, the following point is also refuted:

"Even though we do not perceive yogins because of the extreme distance [between us], from where are we to learn of their greatness and the statement concerning that which is the object of their own direct perception?
If you say, 'From the Itihāsas and Purāṇas,' then no."
"Because they lack authority. For their lack of validity is to be inferred through the observation of defects;
yet, no such valid means of cognition exists in that regard.

If validity were denied simply on the grounds of being a statement, then it would follow that even the words of the Cārvāka teachers must be denied as valid. If you argue that the words of the Cārvāka teachers are rejected because of a suspicion of deception, whereas their validity is ascertained through corroboration by perception, [the author] replies that this is the same in the present case as well—namely, "that which has been said. (*10,193*) Thus he says: "yad ukteti" (as for what was said).
The authority of the words he has spoken is perceived through direct perception.

The connection with the preceding [sentence] is as follows: "those yogis by whom the validity of the statements uttered [by them] is perceived through direct perception and in accordance with direct perception, they too [are included].
To the question "How so?", he says: "even Varāha and others."
For even boons and other gifts granted by him always indeed become true.
The boons and curses bestowed by those yogis always become true without fail;
for this reason— connecting with what precedes—
it is perceived directly that whatever they say while being pleased, such as "this good fortune shall be yours," or while being angry, such as "this misfortune shall be yours," happens exactly so.
Thus it may be argued:
let that person's statement be authoritative with respect to an object suitable for direct perception, by virtue of its correspondence with such perception.
"But how is it in the case of supersensuous matters such as liberation?
If that is so, then the words of the Lokāyata teacher should also be authoritative regarding objects suitable for perception, by virtue of their correspondence with direct experience;
but as for supersensuous matters such as the non-existence of liberation, the question "how? remains exactly the same.

Now, you might think: "Insofar as his words concern objects amenable to perception, they are indeed found to be consistent with direct perception; therefore, we place our trust in him even regarding supersensible objects, because such is observed in the world."
This is the same in the present case as well;
this is expressed by the word "api" (also/even), which serves to include what has not been explicitly stated.
Thus, the validity of the claim that yogis possess direct perception of liberation is established in order to refute the existence of a counter-argument (*satpratipakṣatā*).

The lack of authority of the teacher of the Lokāyata has already been established by his assertion that liberation does not exist, which is [contradicted by] perception. He establishes that lack of authority by another reason as well: "The lack of authority," etc.
And from what is spoken by such a person, non-authoritativeness is determined as being mere idle speech.
In the *Hetusamuccaya*, the word "ca" (and) functions as a conjunction.
The term "vṛthāvācā" is an expression where the abstract state (*bhāva*) is the primary referent;
for if it were stated simply as "because of futility" (*vṛthātvāt*), there would be a logical deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of seeing grass and such things.
The mention of "speech" (vāk) is for that purpose.
To the question, "In what way is the teaching of the Lokāyata teacher useless? he says: "For not... (na hi).
For there is no purpose whatsoever in preventing [others] from the next world.

It is well known that there is no purpose whatsoever to be gained by denying the next world, liberation, and so forth, through the demonstration of their non-existence. To illustrate this: the purpose for stating such things must be either unseen (adṛṣṭa) or seen (dṛṣṭa).
It cannot first be the unseen (adṛṣṭa), because that would preclude the existence of another world;
for the unseen must be either something to be experienced in heaven and so forth, or something to be experienced in this very life through another body.
Not the first, because the existence of heaven and other such realms in the afterlife has been refuted by the opponent.
Not the second.
Because the proponent of the doctrine that the body is the self negates the existence of another world— that is, a subsequent body—
and because no benefit is observed for either the teacher or the student in terms of wealth or the fulfillment of desires. *10,195*

The purpose of the Teacher is the benefit of others, consisting in the cessation of the obstruction to the enjoyment of desires for those living beings whose enjoyment of desire is restricted by Vedic injunctions that establish the rules of dharma and adharma; this is achieved by demonstrating the non-existence of dharma and so forth [for the Teacher himself].

This benefit of others, in the form of the cessation of the obstruction to the enjoyment of desires through the demonstration of the non-existence of dharma and so forth for living beings, is indeed the aim of the Teacher.
Although assistance is not a purpose in its own right,
nor is it a purpose by virtue of being an unseen cause,
nevertheless, they do indeed act for the benefit of the benefactor.
Furthermore, the sole purpose for those to be trained is precisely the cessation of the obstruction to the enjoyment of sensual pleasures;
so how can it be said that [the teaching] is in vain? To this, he says: "Speech in vain."
If he should kill [an animal] for useless speech, what would be the answer to that?
In this context, "vain speech" (*vṛthāvāc*) is the indication of the probandum (*sādhya*).
Even so, the state of being vain speech is not to be avoided;
or alternatively, it means speech devoid of any invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭaprayojana*).

If someone were to kill that teacher or his disciple in vain, what would be the consequence for him? Nothing at all. This is what is meant: The Blessed One has said: "O monks, there are five persons who, even if they shed a great deal of blood, do not thereby create a grave offense or incur a karmic result leading to rebirth in the lower realms, nor do they produce much demerit. Which five? They are: one who kills himself; one who kills another who is killing him; one who kills a person who has already committed a grave offense; one who kills a person who is insane; and one who kills a person who is delirious with pain. These, O monks, are the five persons who, even if they shed a great deal of blood, do not thereby create a grave offense or incur a karmic result leading to rebirth in the lower realms, nor do they produce much demerit. This is the meaning of the Blessed One’s statement. For it is said: "There is no offense for one who kills a person who is insane, nor for one who kills a person who is delirious with pain, nor for one who kills a person who is committing a grave offense, nor for one who kills a person who is killing him, nor for one who kills himself. Furthermore, it is said: "If one kills a person who is insane, or a person who is delirious with pain, or a person who is committing a grave offense, or a person who is killing him, or if one kills oneself—even if one sheds a great deal of blood—there is no grave offense, nor is there a karmic result leading to rebirth in the lower realms, nor is much demerit produced. Therefore, this is the reason why there is no offense in these cases. It is not that the Blessed One intended to permit the taking of life; rather, he spoke thus because there is no offense when one kills those who are insane and so forth. Thus, the Blessed One taught that there is no offense for one who kills a person who is insane and so forth, but he did not teach that there is no offense for one who kills a person who is not insane and so forth. If a teacher were to instruct a student, saying, "Dharma and Adharma do not exist at all; therefore, you must indulge in sensual pleasures without restraint," and the student, for the sake of seizing the teacher's beautiful wife and other possessions, were actually to kill him—
what remedy would there be for the teacher in that case?
Because of the Vedic teaching that doing harm to one who has been helpful is a cause for great demerit (*pratyavāya*), he has been made to abandon it by that very [teaching].
Furthermore, the notion that "one should return a favor to the benefactor" holds true only when there exists the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of merit and so forth;
however, that [impression] has been completely eradicated by him.

Therefore, there is no purpose whatsoever for the teacher; on the contrary, there is only misfortune characterized by the loss of his own life. Likewise, for those to be trained, there would be engagement only in mutual plundering of wealth and women, or in mutual slaughter and the like, rather than in the enjoyment of sensual pleasures. For even a slight enjoyment of sensual pleasure, when overwhelmed by great misfortune, is itself a misfortune.
Granted that the teaching of the Lokāyata masters is thus futile and a cause of harm; nevertheless, why is it invalid? To this he says: "sva... (his own...).
What man of intelligence would speak so as to bring about the ruin of his own life?
The word "own" (sva-) is indicative of others as well;
the ellipsis is "and futile.
From the fact that he speaks words that are both futile and causes of harm, the lack of discernment on the part of the Lokāyata teacher is inferred.
The ellipsis [to be supplied] is that, therefore, that statement lacks authority (*aprāmāṇya*).
And this point has already been stated in the section on the purpose (*prayojanādhikaraṇa*) [*10.197*].
To cause the aforementioned matter to enter the intellect, he states it in brief: "Authority" (*prāmāṇya*).
Could there even be doubt regarding the authority of those two men?
For one who is ignorant, there is the possibility of speech contrary to his own life, as well as that which contradicts what is perceived.
He who hears the words of gods beyond the reach of the senses, who has seen both the higher and the lower,
and who makes known all that is past and future through his experience of the worlds—
[in this context] by the word "authority" (*prāmāṇya*), reliability (*āptatva*) is meant.
The word *kim* is used in the sense of an objection;
the word *api* expresses censure;
and *sva* is an elliptical expression (standing for more).
"Of much that is seen"—that is, even of much that is fit to be perceived.
The word "ca" (and) serves to include further qualifications.
The phrase "by the speech of a deity" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) that also includes other supersensible means of knowledge.
Having brought all that he has said into conformity with direct perception, thereby attaining public experience and public confidence, one might ask:

would there still be doubt regarding the authority of even those two types of persons—the teacher of the Lokāyata school, characterized by such qualities as making statements contrary to his own life, and the yogi, characterized by such qualities as hearing the words of supersensuous deities—or would there not?
Indeed, there would be none at all.

However, the construction is as follows: the lack of authority of the first [statement] and the very authority of the second are determined. Thus, with respect to a materialist teacher (*lokāyatācārya*)—who, due to the absence of such causes, has not been suspected of possessing supersensible knowledge, yet who is suspected of being deceptive because of his lustfulness and so forth—in contrast to a yogi whose words accord with direct perception and who is utterly unsuspected of being a deceiver because he possesses all sovereignty attained through omniscience by means of the perfection of yogic power; *10,199* [The text continues: ...[the determination of authority]. (Note: The provided fragment ends mid-sentence regarding the contrast).
It has been stated that liberation is not established by the perception understood from the statement of that [Veda], because it is impossible for it to be an antidote.

Now, one who wishes to establish that [liberation] even by means of the Veda, [addresses] one who disputes its authority: "Is the Veda's lack of authority asserted because it is devoid of corroboration?"

Or [it is invalid] because it is a statement, like the statement of a madman; or else, because it lacks a determined particularity, like the statement of a madman; or else, because it is sublated. Having thus proposed these alternatives, regarding the first one as well, he refutes the first option—namely, whether there is no corroboration for the whole or for a part—by saying "therefore" (*ataḥ*).
Therefore, because it is clearly accessible through direct perception and because the Veda alone is the source of knowledge.
The meaning is that the attainment of the fruit [of action] is observed for those who perform Vedic rites;
this is because it is accessible through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and is established through corroboration by direct perception. And the word "ca" (and) is used in the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*.
Regarding the claim that "liberation is established through the Veda," it is stated that by this [argument],
the assertion that no part of the entire Veda accords with other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is unproven;
for it is observed that there is agreement with other means of knowledge in those portions of the Veda which teach yoga and the like as means for attaining sovereignty and other such powers.
Furthermore, the Vedic passages that establish liberation should be understood as having been cited in various places [in this very work].
If it is argued that a discrepancy with the results of the Vedas is observed, we say no;
for it has already been stated previously that such discrepancies are caused by defects in the agent, the ritual action, and so forth.
This has been stated clearly as "sphuṭam" (it is evident).
He refutes the second [alternative] regarding the first [case] with the words "yadi" (if).
If the scripture lacks authority, then the same would be true for that which is perceived by the senses.

If it is argued that because a specific portion lacks corroboration, the entire scripture (āgama) is not authoritative— that is, it is invalid— then sensory perception (akṣaja) alone would likewise be invalid;
for there is an absence of corroboration for perceptions whose objects are pleasure and the like.

If it is asserted that a portion of the Veda lacks authority precisely because it is devoid of corroboration, then perceptual cognition whose objects are our own pleasure and so forth would necessarily be invalid as well.
Although the corroboration of yogic perception has been mentioned previously, this statement should be understood as being made in comparison to other means of valid cognition.

It might be argued: "Perception is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by its very nature; what need is there for corroboration in that case? To this he says: "If the validity of that which arises from the senses... (10.200). "If the validity of that which arises from the senses were [intrinsic], how could it not also belong to scripture? (Manu 3.3.126cd).

If the validity of sensory perception were intrinsic (*svataḥ*) even without corroboration, then why would the validity of scripture (*āgama*) not also be intrinsic? Since there is no distinction [between the two], it certainly would be so. He refutes the second [position] with the words: "If [it is argued that] of scripture...
If it is claimed that scripture lacks authority merely because it is a verbal statement, like the speech of a madman;

In that case, because it is produced by the senses (*akṣaja*), the sensory cognition of pillars and so forth would also be invalid, just like the sensory cognition of objects such as silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, since there is no distinction between them.
To the objection that sensory cognition regarding pillars and the like is valid because it is free from defects, he says: "If [it were] sensory... (*yadyakṣajasya*).
If sense-perception directed toward objects such as pillars were to possess validity because of being free from defects, then why should scripture not likewise possess it for that very same reason?
For it is impossible for that which is not of human origin (apauruṣeya) to be subject to defects.

Although one could have stated it simply as "of the Veda" following the initial introduction, the author says "of scripture" (āgamasya) in order to indicate that, by this very same logic, the validity of even human-authored scripture must be established.
He refutes the third [position] with the words: "In the world... (loka).
And the distinction from worldly speech is established by its non-deviation [from truth].
The Veda is distinguished from the speech of madmen and others by its non-deviation, that is,
by its freedom from sublation.
For the Vedic meaning is not established by direct perception, such that it would find scope there as a sublater [of perception]. By this, the fourth [position] is also refuted.

Thus, the inference—namely, that "the activity of yogins who possess detachment from the enjoyment of fruits here and in the hereafter, which aims to establish liberation through both perception and scripture, is fruitful because it is the activity of a discerning person, like [any] accepted [activity]"—is also [established].
This has been indicated;
furthermore, the validity of inference (*anumāna*) has already been established previously. Others, however, do not infer in this manner.
"The continuum of suffering is absolutely severed because it is a continuum, like the continuum of a lamp’s flame"—
this is incorrect; for if one takes the entire continuum of suffering belonging to all living beings as the subject of the inference, the reason is contradicted in part.

This is because some eternal transmigrators (*nityasaṃsārin*) have been accepted by those [opponents] as well, and because [their existence] will be established [later]. Furthermore, if one were to take as the subject the continuum of suffering belonging to a living being distinct from them, there would be a fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in that very case;
moreover, there would be a fallacy of deviation in the continuum of color and other qualities of the atoms of earth (*pārthivaparamāṇu*).
If it is argued that even that [consciousness] would be utterly severed due to the absence of fruits and roots in the case of universal liberation, we say no;
for the position of universal liberation is itself about to be refuted,
and because there is a deviation [from the rule] in the continuum of the moments of time.
Furthermore, by the term "continuum of suffering," are the sufferings themselves meant, or some property thereof?
In the first case, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*),
because even one who does not accept liberation must admit that sufferings are perishable.
If it is argued that for this very reason it was said "absolutely," what is the meaning of this? Does it mean that all sufferings whatsoever are cut off?
Or [is it that] they are cut off without remainder?
Or else, [is it] because no other suffering arises there?
Not the first.
Because there is no escape from the fault of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*),
since the impermanence of all sufferings is accepted by the opponent;
for this very reason, the second [alternative] is not tenable.
For suffering is not a composite substance,
such that one might suspect it could be cut off with a remainder; thus,
the third [alternative] is not tenable.
Because the example lacks the property to be proven;
for the continuum of a lamp’s flame is not cut off in this manner,
since it is possible for another flame to arise right there again.
The second [alternative] is not tenable;
for birth is either the nature of suffering or something other than that.
In the first case, there is a departure from one's own established tenet (*apasiddhānta*).
Because the eternality of the genus (jāti) is accepted [by the opponent],
the second [alternative] is not tenable;
for there is the fallacy of the unestablished locus (āśrayāsiddhi).

This is because no property distinct from the universal (*jāti*) is admitted in the case of qualities (*guṇa*). Even if such a property were admitted, it would result in a different entity (*arthāntara*).
For liberation is not established merely by the destruction of some particular property of suffering. *10,206*

The argument that "the self, at some time, must have all its specific qualities destroyed because, while being omnipresent, it possesses specific qualities of an effect— just like space in the state of the great dissolution (mahāpralaya)" is untenable;
for if "all selves" are taken as the subject of the proposition, there is a contradiction regarding the self of the Supreme Lord (parameśvara),
and [furthermore], the reason is unestablished (asiddha).

Even if the individual soul (*jīvātman*) is taken as the subject of the proposition, there is a contradiction, because it has already been admitted that individual souls possess exclusively the nature of being subject to transmigratory existence (*saṃsārin*). If, on the other hand, a soul distinct from that [Brahman] is taken as the subject, the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to that very same case;
furthermore, the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*) because individual souls lack omnipresence (*vibhutva*).
If it is argued that the meaning of the proposition is that "the nature of self (ātmatva) resides in a substance whose specific qualities have all been destroyed at some time," this is not so;
for if that were the case, it would result in the fallacy of the reason (*hetu*) being unestablished (*asiddhi*).
Nor can it be argued that "being a genus" (*jātitva*) is the reason.
This is because the defects of the previous inference have not been avoided,
and because [the reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) and so forth.
If it is argued that the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*) is "residing in a substance devoid of all specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*)," we say no.
If it is argued that there is no fault because the production of only substances possessing qualities has been established,
and because the reason (hetu) is "being a genus residing in that which possesses particular qualities which are effects of an all-pervading [substance]," we say no;
for the phrase "possessing particular qualities which are effects" is redundant.
Because even upon the abandonment of that [suffering], it remains a distinct entity;

and because it will be stated later that liberation is not the destruction of all specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*). By this, the following qualified negative inference (*viśiṣṭavyatirekyanumāna*) is also refuted: "Devadatta is the locus of the destruction of suffering that is co-temporal with Devadatta’s own demerit (*adharma*) and does not reside in Devadatta himself, because he possesses suffering, like Yajñadatta."
This has been refuted;

since the objection regarding it being a different entity has been avoided, let this elaboration suffice. Now, he restates the Jain-proposed means for achieving liberation in order to refute it: "It exists," etc.
"There is liberation through dharma and also through knowledge of reality as it is.
This is the connection: the Jains say that this established existence of liberation is excellent;
and if the reality of liberation is accepted, then its means of accomplishment must also necessarily be accepted.
And thus, with the intention of asking what contradiction there could be, he asks: "api" (even).
The meaning is: "What then? He provides the answer: "By means of the Dharma."
They say that [liberation] is attainable.
Furthermore, the particle "api" (also) implies a mutual conjunction;
for although the Jainas accept both liberation and its means, they nevertheless disagree regarding their specific nature.
The intention is that they declare liberation to be achievable through the combination of right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*) and right conduct (*samyak-cāritrya*).

If "right vision" (*samyag-darśana*) is direct, immediate knowledge (*aparokṣa-jñāna*), then it is already included by the term "truth" (*yathārtha*); and if it is the observance of one's own religious vows (*svasamaya-paripālana*), then it is included by the term "dharma. Thus, the mention of both [knowledge and conduct] is intended to indicate that their separate mention [as distinct categories] would otherwise be redundant.
We also accept, in some sense, that liberation is to be accomplished through the accumulation of the knowledge of dharmas;
therefore, immediately after the discussion of disagreement, he shows [this] with the words: "validity."
And the authority of inference is [established] for the purpose of proving the Jina’s status as a reliable person (āpta).
And from his words, there arises the correct knowledge and discernment of dharma.
From the inference such as "the Jina is authoritative because his speech is unerring," and—
by virtue of the word "and"— from the speech of those who have seen the Jina;
that is, from his speech, which is the speech of the Jina.
Thus the Jains say;
they assert the attainment of the means to liberation from the words of the Jina, whose status as an authoritative person (āpta) is understood through inference and other means,
but not from the Veda as a self-evident authority— this is their intention.

If it is argued that, having begun by showing the disagreement regarding the means to liberation (*mokṣa-sādhana*), it is irrelevant to demonstrate the disagreement regarding the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-vipratipatti*), we say no; for even that which makes the means known is itself a means. He also demonstrates the disagreement regarding the very nature of the knowledge of Dharma, [beginning with] the word "Dharma."
For dharma is nothing other than non-violence; knowledge is the perception of the true person.
Thus say the Jainas... // MAnu 3.129a //
That in which non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) is supreme—that is, the primary element—is described as such.

Since this is also agreed upon by us, it is stated that other sacrifices and the like, accompanied by violence, are not *dharma*. The perception of the person (*pudgala*) as the body, in the form of being distinct from the self (*ātman*), [is what is meant].
Alternatively, it is the vision of the person (pudgala) or self as distinct from the body and so forth.
Here too, the phrase "nothing other than what is intended by the proponent" carries over. He refutes this, asking: "How?"
...how could that be authoritative by means of inference? MAnu 3.129ab.
How could that word of the Jina be understood to be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by means of inference?

The meaning is that what was stated— that one ascertains the validity of the Jina’s word which teaches the Dharma and knowledge that are the means to liberation through an inference based on its being the word of a reliable authority (*āptavākya*), after first determining the Jina’s reliability through inference and his word— does not hold up.
To explain the reason why [the opponent's position] is untenable, he first states the nature of perception, inference, and scripture in sequence as an introduction: "The objects... and so forth.
For a sense organ directed toward its object is called "perception" (pratyakṣa); following the etymology of the word *pratyakṣa*, it is proclaimed as "inference" (anumā). 3.3.129c–f.
Because it causes both dharma and adharma to reach the supreme state on all sides,
and because it possesses other qualities beyond the reach of the senses, it is therefore known as Āgama.
The sense organ (*akṣa*) is that which is faultless (*adoṣa*) when it is in proximity (*sannikṛṣṭa*) with its respective faultless objects (*viṣaya*).
The singular number is used to denote the class.

The meaning is that perception (*pratyakṣa*) is that [cognition] which arises from a sense organ that is faultless because it is in proximity with its own specific object, as determined through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
By this, it is indicated that this is a *prādi-samāsa* (compound with prefixes) and not an *avyayībhāva* (indeclinable compound);
for if that were the case, the genitive case ending in *pratyakṣasya* would not be heard.
Even though *pratyakṣa* [could be analyzed as] "the sense-organ (*akṣa*) directed toward (*prati*) [the object]."
Nevertheless, he indicates with the word "hi" that there is a connection between objects by way of their fitness (*yogyatā*),
because this follows from the term "perception" (*pratyakṣa*). Validity [of knowledge] exists precisely in accordance with perception and scripture (*āgama*).
And "conformity" consists in possessing the property (dharmin) and so forth as apprehended therein, and having an object that is uncontradicted and non-obstructed;
"is proclaimed as inference" is the ellipsis.
That inference which is well-known is proclaimed as "inference" on account of this cause.
Although inference (anumā) has been followed [as the primary means], nevertheless, by implication, there is a connection with perception (pratyakṣa) and the other [means of knowledge].
It was stated previously that even an inference rooted in another inference ultimately has its root in perception and so forth.
By the explanatory gloss on "ā" as "from all sides" (samantāt), the meaning is clarified.
The word "correctly" (samyak) should also be understood [as part of the compound].
It causes one to go, that is, it makes known;
this is a metaphorical attribution of agency to the instrument.

This is because the suffix *ap* is prescribed after the roots *grah*, *vṛdh*, *niści*, and *gam* when the agent (*kartṛ*) is not the factor [of the action], or when the action itself (*bhāva*) is expressed.

Furthermore, this explanation should be understood as referring to objects that are beyond the scope of inference; and whatever is other than dharma and so forth, even if it is supersensuous (*atīndriya*), is also included by the word "even" (*api*).
The word *tu* is used for emphasis;
it is connected with the phrase "by that very [means].
Although *āgama* is so called because everything (*ā*) is understood (*gamya*) correctly and completely (*samantāt*) by means of it.
Nevertheless, because it would be useless regarding an object already reached by perception or inference, it is said to concern even that which is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*).
The explanation of this begins with the word "dharma" and so forth;
such is the scripture (*āgama*) that is well-known.

One should not think that this is merely an etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) of words such as "perception" (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth, nor that there is a rule that a meaning obtainable through etymology must necessarily exist in a way that avoids over-extension (*ativyāpti*), because such meanings are absent in cases like *vyāghraparṇī*. With this intention, he says: "By this... (*eteneti*).
For this very reason, each of those is accepted as a valid means of knowledge.

The status of being "perception" and so forth for perception and the other means of knowledge is held by the authoritative teachers (prāmāṇika) to be their very nature as perception and so on—that is, their being denotable by the terms "perception" and so forth.
This is precisely the basis for the application of the terms "perception" and so forth to perception and the rest;
it is not merely a meaning obtainable through etymological derivation. This is the sense.
Why is this so? To this he says: "For its own nature... (svarūpaṃ hi).
For that is indeed their own true nature... // Mānava-dharmaśāstra 3.3.131c //

The meaning is that the nature and definition (*lakṣaṇa*) of these means of knowledge, such as perception and the rest, consists in their having sense organs that are free from defects and in close proximity to the object to be defined.
For a definition is indeed the ground for the application of a word.
To the question "Why is this so?", he says: "Otherwise... [and so forth].
... because it possesses the status of being established otherwise.
And its establishment is by means other than that;
the meaning is that it is impossible to define the characteristics of perception and the other [means of knowledge] in any other way.
Thus it has been said: [10.227]
If that is so, what follows regarding the nature of perception and the other means of knowledge? To this, he says: "Therefore" (ataḥ).
Therefore, how could inference show either the Dharma or even the person?
The word *anumeyam* refers to the word of the Jina whose validity is understood through inference (*anumāna*).
The two particles *ca* and *api* serve to indicate mutual conjunction.
*Darśayet* means "should demonstrate" or "should establish."
This is what is meant:
when it is said that the establishment of phenomena and so forth proceeds from the words of the Victor, what is stated to be the means of valid cognition?
If you say "scriptural authority" (āgama), then no.
Because scripture is defined as that which establishes an object not already apprehended through valid means such as direct perception,
and because that [status] is not established for the words of the Jina.

For the Jina has composed his speech either after perceiving an object through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or otherwise. In the second case, since it would be a human composition lacking a foundation, its correctness would be as difficult to find as that of the words of a madman.
In the first case, if [the object] is understood through perception or inference, it is impossible for there to be a lack of correspondence with the reality of an object not previously apprehended.
If [the validity] is established by another statement, then it results in a blind tradition (*andhaparamparā*) and is therefore once again invalid.

By this, the inference of those who follow the Jina— namely, "The subject under dispute is authoritative because it is the word of a reliable person (*āpta*), and the Jina is reliable because his speech is unerring"— as well as the words of the Jina himself, are refuted.
For instance:
a statement whose object is the reliability [of a speaker] is indeed incorrect if it is baseless;
the same applies even if it is rooted in another statement.
Nor is perception the basis [for this knowledge],
because perception belongs to a sense organ that is directed toward its objects;
and a mental state of another person, whose nature is not directly accessible, does not attain the status of being an object of immediate perception.
Therefore, it must be stated that this is rooted in inference based on such qualities as having unerring speech; yet this [speech] itself is not an inference,
because only that which makes an object known by following upon perception and other means of valid cognition is considered an inference.
And this [reason] does not apply to the present case.

For if the phrase "because it is the word of a reliable person" (āptavākyatvāt) is taken in its literal sense, there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) in the case of a statement by someone who is reliable but deceitful or ignorant. If the intended meaning is "because it is a statement rooted in reliability," then the qualification is unestablished (viśeṣaṇāsiddhi).
Indeed, attainment (*āpti*) is characterized by the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) and so forth.
In that regard, first of all, the knowledge of reality concerning objects such as *dharma* is not produced by the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the Victor,
because direct perception belongs to a sense-faculty (*akṣa*) that is situated in relation to its respective objects.
Furthermore, because dharma and so forth are not objects of the senses;
or, if they were such, it would follow that others could also attain their realization.
For this very reason, [the knowledge of dharma] is not produced by inference.
If, however, one accepts other [independent] statements, it would be nothing more than a blind tradition (*andhaparamparā*).
Likewise, even the absence of a desire to deceive (*avipralipsā*) is difficult to ascertain.
For this very reason, the inference that establishes the status of a reliable authority (*āptatva*) is subject to the fallacy of being "overturned by the lapse of time" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*).
This is because [the inference] is sublated by the aforementioned method of pervasion (*vyāpti*).
If it is argued that there is no contradiction because this person's perception operates upon objects not perceived by others, we say no;
for it is countered by a valid opposing argument (*satpratipakṣa*) based on [his] being a human being (*puruṣatva*), and so forth.
And [the definition] "one whose speech is unerring" applies either in some cases, in the specific context at hand, or everywhere.
It cannot be the first [option],
because there is no pervasion (vyāpti) such that whoever is unerring in speech in some instance is necessarily an authoritative person (āpta) regarding that particular subject matter.
Not the second,
because there is no means of discerning it;
for this [distinction] is indeed to be inferred from the attainment of the fruit.
For this very reason, the third [alternative] is also not tenable.
As for the mark (liṅga) that is asserted—namely, being free from perspiration and so forth—that is, first of all, unestablished due to doubt;
furthermore, it is otherwise established as possible through the use of medicinal herbs and the like.

Nor does this [objection] apply even to the statements of Manu and others, because, being of non-human origin (*apauruṣeya*), they are rooted in the Veda without depending on any other source. As it is said: "Whatever Manu has spoken is indeed a remedy."
This is because the status of being an authoritative person (*āpta*) and so forth is ascertained by the Veda itself through such statements.

Therefore, since perception and the other means of knowledge possess the characteristics already described, while these [characteristics] are absent in the case of the perception of the Jina and those shown by him, in the inferences proposed by others, and in the words of the Jina and others, it is incorrect to claim that the establishment of *dharma* and so forth proceeds from the words of the Jina—words whose authoritativeness is supposedly established through inference and the like.
Thus, it is established by the absence of any determining factor that the Jina’s speech is not merely free from error.
However, with the intention that [this applies] even from the state of a lapse, he says: "In its own nature" (*svarūpe*).
Regarding the faults of a person, it has been said: ... (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 3.3.132cd).
This is a locative of object (*viṣayasaptamī*).

By the logic of *ta-ni-ru-yukta*, the word "non-person" (*apudgala*) refers to a self that is either different from the person—that is, the body—or similar to it; or else, it is expressed by the word "person" (*pudgala*) itself.
This has been stated [in the verse]: "And thus the self [is not perceived] in its entirety," and so forth.
The meaning is this:
the Jina has stated that the nature of the self is the size of the body and possesses form;
since that [view] was previously refuted, he is one whose speech is faltering.

Although the sevenfold predication (*saptabhaṅginaya*) taught by him has also been refuted, this statement is nevertheless made specifically to demonstrate the fallacy regarding that very "vision of the person" (*pudgaladarśana*) which was described as the means for attaining liberation.
[Objection: But is not this also already established by the preceding sentence?
[Reply: True.
There is no fault in saying that the subsequent binding is for the purpose of elaboration (*prapañca*).
By means of another method, he demonstrates the deviation from the words of the Jina regarding the nature of the self: "It is bliss alone," and so forth.
... and even bliss itself;
he does not conceive of a person (pudgala)... // MĀnuv 3.132cd //
Here too, by the terms "non-person" (apudgala) and "person" (pudgala), the self (ātman) is meant.
Those who know reality consider the self to be identical with bliss, as being absolutely non-different from bliss;
the Victor (Jina), however, does not consider it to be that very bliss.
He speaks of seven modes, such as being distinct and so forth;

however, this is refuted by the rejection of that method of the sevenfold predication (*saptabhaṅgī*) and by proving the absolute non-difference of the Self from pleasure and the like, just as [the Self] is not different from its masculinity and other attributes.
Therefore, the implication is that this person’s speech is faltering. *10,234*
For this reason as well, he says "so it is" with the words beginning with "suffering."
...the absence of suffering is indeed happiness. (Manu 3.132f)
The word *tu* serves to exclude the self (*ātman*).
The word *iti* indicates a reason.
It is to be connected with what precedes.
Because the self is a positive entity (bhāva),
whereas happiness is the absence of suffering (duḥkhābhāva);
and it is never observed that two things of contradictory natures are absolutely identical.
Therefore, the Jina declares that the self is not absolutely non-different from pleasure;
and since that [declaration] is incorrect, he is one whose speech has faltered.
To the question "Why is it incorrect?", he says: "only... (mātra).
Because it is observed that there is an increase in pleasure beyond the mere enjoyment of the objects of the senses.
The *mātrās* are the objects of sense, such as sound and so forth, because they are measured (*mīyante*).
"Experience" (*bhoga*) means direct perception;
this is also an elliptical expression [for other related factors].
It should also be understood that this is because one observes a diminution of pleasure when there is a diminution of the enjoyment of sense objects.

The meaning is that the claim that pleasure is merely the absence of suffering is untenable, as it contradicts valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); for pleasure, like suffering and so forth, is a positive entity (*bhāva*) characterized by degrees of intensity.
To establish that pleasure possesses such gradations, the word "because of observation" (*darśanāt*) indicates direct perception (*sākṣin*) as the proof in this matter.

However, for one who is still in disagreement even with that, the phrase "beyond the enjoyment of objects" (*mātrābhogātirekeṇa*) was stated to indicate the undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭaprasaṅga*).
For if pleasure were unsurpassed (*niratiśaya*), then the acquisition of objects beyond the mere enjoyment of them would be useless for those possessed of discernment;
yet such [acquisition] is observed. *10,235*

Now, it may be argued that pleasure is not possessed of degrees of intensity; rather, it is suffering that exists as a positive entity and is possessed of degrees of intensity, and the absence of that [suffering] is pleasure.
Thus, it is understood that to the extent that [suffering] ceases, to that same extent there is pleasure.

Furthermore, we do not intend to establish that the perception of degrees of intensity is real, when it is actually caused by limiting conditions (upādhi) in the form of its counter-correlate (pratiyogin).

And the excessive grasping for the enjoyment of sense objects is for the purpose of averting an excess of suffering, because the absence of suffering is to be accomplished through the enjoyment of sense objects; therefore, he says: "of pleasure."
By what means is there an absence of happiness? ... MĀnuv 3.133c.

This description of [the self] as being conditioned by adjuncts (aupādhika) might hold true if the non-existence of pleasure were established by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). The meaning is that the non-existence of pleasure is not established by any means of valid cognition whatsoever.
In the same way, he states the refutation against the description of dependence (*pratītya*) and so forth as being merely conditional (*aupādhika*), beginning with "And not" (*na ca*).
...and there would be nothing; what, then, would be the reversal? (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 3.133d)
If it is assumed, without any basis whatsoever, that the observation of degrees in pleasure and so forth is merely conditional (*aupādhika*),
then pleasure would be a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*) and suffering its absence (*tadabhāva*).
In that case, the observation of degrees [in suffering] would be caused by the conditioning factor (*upādhi*) of its counter-correlative, namely pleasure.
And why could there not also be the opposite of what others have stated—that things such as snakes and thorns exist for the sake of producing pleasure?
Indeed, it could be so.
Therefore, since no distinction can be perceived between the two, one must admit that both possess an intrinsic gradation of existence.

If it is argued: "Since there is a valid means of cognition (pramāṇa)—namely, that 'the non-existence of pleasure is a real entity because it possesses the nature of an entity, like the commonly accepted absence [of something]'—how can it be said by anyone that pleasure is non-existent?
[We reply: In the view of one who speaks thus, does some entity exist, or are all things indeed non-entities?
He states the fault in the first case with the words: "If... (yadīti).
If even some entity were to exist, how could it possess the nature of non-existence?
In the view of one who infers the non-existence of pleasure by treating it as a real entity (*vastu*), if some object were indeed an existent (*bhāva*),
then how could that very pleasure be non-existent?
On the contrary, even an object accepted as an existent would have to be non-existent.
Otherwise, there would be the consequence of a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the property of being a real entity (*vastutva*) in that case.
[Objection: But surely all categories (*padārtha*) are indeed non-existents (*abhāva*); thus, the aforementioned fault does not apply.

Even so, because it would follow that jars and the like are beginningless, it is untenable for them to possess prior non-existence (*prāg-abhāva*), destructional non-existence (*pradhvaṃsa-abhāva*), or absolute non-existence (*atyanta-abhāva*).
Nevertheless, mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) is indeed logical;
for the mutual non-existence of a cloth and so forth in a jar is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
and mutual non-existence does not exist as something other than its locus (*dharmin*).
Therefore, the pot itself is the mutual absence (anyonyābhāva) of the cloth and so forth; likewise for the cloth and the rest. Thus, he raises the second objection: "If all [are mutual absences]..."
If all non-existents were mutually [non-existent] in this way...
The meaning is: "If you think that all things whatsoever would be mutual non-existences (anyonyābhāva), [the author] states the reply: 'Because of being an entity' (bhāvatvāt)."
... by means of cultivation. MĀnuv 3.3.134d.
If there were the state of being the absence of an absence, what would be lost for us then?
By thus establishing that all things consist of mutual non-existence, what of ours would be undermined?
Nothing at all.
How so?
Because the state of being the absence of non-existence would itself be existence.
This is what is meant:
Is the non-existence being established as the nature of pleasure (sukha) one of the three types beginning with prior non-existence (prāgabhāva),
or is it mutual non-existence (anyonyābhāva),
or rather a general absence (sāmānya)?
In the first case, there is an avoidance of the previously mentioned fault;
however, in the second and third cases, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanam*),
because we too accept that all things, including pleasure and so forth, possess the nature of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāvatā*).
Nor is there a contradiction with the acceptance of its being an entity (bhāvatva),
for pleasure is indeed the mutual absence of other things, such as the mutual absence of pain and so forth.
And the absence of non-existence is indeed existence.
Such a nature of non-existence does not contradict the essential nature of pleasure, because the self (ātman) is likewise of that same nature. *10,239*

It has been stated that the non-existence of non-existence would be existence itself; in order to demonstrate this, he first states the essential nature of existence and non-existence: "The state of being existent... and so forth.
Existence is the nature of affirmation; non-existence is the state of negation.
The construction is as follows: "being a positive entity" (bhāvatva) means having the nature of an affirmation, while "being a negative entity" (abhāvatva) means having the nature of a negation.
The abstract suffix (*bhāva-pratyaya*) is used for the purpose of extracting the ground for the application of the term;
otherwise, it would be like the case of "Indra" and "Purandara."
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "Of the negation... and so forth.
Even the negation of a negation would necessarily result in a positive state of being.
Since "non-existence" (abhāva) is by definition a negation, the phrase "the non-existence of non-existence" would mean a negation of a negation; and that,
by the force of observation, would be nothing other than an affirmation (vidhi).
For it has been observed that the prohibition [of *na*] in the rule “*neyaṅuvaṅsthānau*” is a positive injunction (*vidhi*) that prohibits [the application of] “*astrī*”.
And this will be explained later.
And it has been stated that "existence" (*bhāva*) is indeed a positive entity (*vidhi*).
Therefore, it is logical that the non-existence of non-existence (*abhāvābhāvatā*) is simply existence itself.

If this were so, however, the rule established elsewhere—that substances (*dravya*) and so forth are existents (*bhāva*), while prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and so forth are non-existents (*abhāva*)—would not hold.

Since even in the case of a jar, the negation "not a cloth" exhibits a negative form, while "it is a knowable object" exhibits a positive form, [the author] recalls what was stated previously with the words "firstly."
But the first practice is that which determines existence and non-existence.
This has already been explained [in verse 10.241].
Thus, by demonstrating that the Conqueror (Jina) possesses faltering speech, it has been stated that the means for liberation taught by him lacks authoritative validity (*aprāmāṇikatva*).

Furthermore, showing its contradiction with reason, he refutes the first alternative—namely, whether the self-knowledge said to be the means for liberation functions directly or through the mediation of the self’s purification—with the words "And not" (*na ca*).
And consciousness of a person never anywhere bestows liberation.
The knowledge of the self does not bestow liberation because it is insentient, like a cloth; this is the remainder [of the argument].
He establishes the pervasion (vyāpti) of this [reason] with the words "in some cases" (kvacit).
The word "not" (neti) carries over;
and [the phrase] "granting liberation" (mokṣada) is also [to be supplied]. Furthermore, that [term "liberation"] has the abstract state (bhāva) as its primary meaning.
For nowhere has the capacity to grant liberation been observed in that which is insentient,
such that there would be no pervasion [of the rule];
the fact that karma possesses such a nature will be refuted later.
It is well known that knowledge is indeed consciousness itself, and not something insentient.
He refutes the second [position]—that the Self, when known and propitiated, bestows liberation—with the words "because of lack of independence" (*asvātantryāt*).
Because the person lacks independence, it does not grant happiness even when known.
Even the self, when known, does not bestow happiness nor grant liberation;
why? Because the person (pudgala) lacks independence regarding the self.
By the word "hi" (for/since), he indicates that the pervasion [of the reason] is clear in the case of cloth and so forth.

And lack of independence will be understood immediately thereafter. It is stated that he "bestows happiness" in order to indicate that even the bestowal of mere happiness upon the self is not possible, let alone the bestowal of liberation consisting of infinite happiness.
He refutes both positions by means of another reason: "For indeed, it is not so"—*na hīti*.
For the state of being an afflicted person does not cease merely through the thorough knowledge of that affliction. (Manu 3.138ab)
The knowledge of the self (*ātman*) is not the cause for the absolute cessation of suffering, because it is a cognition of that which possesses suffering, like the cognition of Devadatta.
Even by the Jaina, it is stated that the knowledge of one's own self alone is the means to liberation, not merely the knowledge of a self in general.
The term "suffering" was used to exclude the possibility of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the knowledge of God (*īśvara*).

If one intends to express that even this [meditation] lacks the status of being a direct means to liberation, one should simply state "because it is knowledge" (*jñānatvāt*). Alternatively, the intended meaning is as follows: the self is incapable of removing suffering;
because it possesses suffering, it does not remove that which is harmful to it, just as a poor person is incapable of removing his own poverty. This is the essential point.
By the statement that [the self] is subject to suffering, its lack of independence is established; for if it were independent, it would never become miserable. This might be argued:
"The knowledge of the self does not bestow liberation, as Devadatta gives a cow."
However, just as light dispels darkness, [the knowledge of the Self] removes suffering due to their mutual opposition;
in that case, what can insentience do?

Furthermore, it is not merely the knowledge of the Self that is opposed to one's own suffering, but rather the knowledge of the Self as its own object; thus, suspecting that the second reason is also inconclusive, he says: "If... (yadi).

If one could somehow become free from suffering through the knowledge of the person (pudgala), then even one possessed of a body would not suffer; for what could ever be superior to knowledge? (Manusmṛti 3.138c–f)
In no way [can this be so], because suffering and self-knowledge are contradictory.
If that is the case, why would one who possesses a body not always and continuously be free from suffering after the time of knowledge? Indeed, he would be so.
This is what is meant:

Indeed, light, by virtue of its opposition to darkness, dispels it immediately upon its own arising and not with delay; for if there were a delay, the very nature of their opposition could not be maintained. Likewise, if the knowledge of the reality of the Self, being opposed to suffering and other evils, were to make the Self liberated by dispelling them, [it would do so immediately].
In that case, the Jinas and others, being endowed with the knowledge of reality, would have been liberated immediately upon the arising of that knowledge;
yet this is not so,
because they are perceived as possessing bodies and other such attributes.
And because such things as suffering cannot be avoided;
the words "always" and so forth are stated in order to refute the charge of over-extension (*iṣṭāpatti*).
Here, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows:
Suffering and so forth do not stand in opposition to the knowledge of the true nature of the self (*ātmatattvajñāna*), because they coexist with it for a long time, just as is commonly accepted.
Furthermore, the knowledge of the true nature of the self is not singular until liberation,
since cognitions are observed to be momentary.

And thus, that final cognition of the Jina, immediately after which liberation is desired, is not the means for achieving liberation because it is a cognition of the self, just like the first and subsequent cognitions;
otherwise, it would bring about liberation at the very outset, as there would be no distinction [between them].
[Objection: But surely you yourselves accept that the cognition of God (Īśvara) is the means for achieving liberation?
Since this same refutation applies there as well, he says: "The Lord," etc.
For one who maintains that God is the Lord,
liberation would occur after some time has passed, in accordance with the will of the Lord, following the Lord's creative decree.
This is the intended meaning.
We do not say that knowledge of God is the means to liberation;
rather, it is the Supreme Lord himself who is gracious.
Knowledge, however, is proclaimed as the means to liberation because it is the means for attaining His grace.
And that conscious being forms some conception of time, thinking, "At this moment, I shall release him.
In accordance with that conception, he indeed becomes released; thus, there is no fault whatsoever.
Just as a lord, though pleased by a brahmin’s learning, conduct, and so forth, mentally resolves:
"At the next solar eclipse, I shall give a cow to him";
even though the lord is pleased by that brahmin’s learning, conduct, and so forth, he mentally resolves thus.
"I shall give this man a cow during the next solar eclipse.
Following that [promise], he receives a cow from him in exactly that manner.
Having thus refuted the status of knowledge of the Self as a means to liberation, he likewise refutes that of Dharma—stating "karma" [is not the cause]. (10.248)
Moreover, the state of being the cause of karma does not exist anywhere because [inanimate matter] lacks consciousness.
The state of being a cause by means of action is "karmahetutva" with respect to liberation;
alternatively, "karmahetutva" is a *bahuvrīhi* compound,
for which the word "mokṣasya" (of liberation) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
The word "tu" (but) is used for emphasis;
it connects with the phrase "not at all.
This is because action is devoid of consciousness.
The meaning is that the disputed action cannot be a means to liberation because it is insentient, like a cloth.
He establishes the pervasion [of the reason] with the words "for not... (na hi).
The word "no" (na) is connected to both [clauses].
For we do not agree anywhere that insentient things possess the quality of being a means to liberation;
thus, the meaning is that there is no lack of pervasion (vyāpti) in this case.
If it is argued: "Even though it is insentient, why should this specific action not be a means for attaining liberation?
[We reply: Is the action being performed until the attainment of liberation one and the same, or is it manifold?
It cannot be the first case.
Because multiple actions are observed, and because a new karma arises with each individual action;
furthermore, if there were only oneness, it would result in either the birth of what is already born, the futility of actions, or the occurrence of activity after having ceased.
Having granted [for the sake of argument] that there is unity [of the self], he states the subverting argument:
"Just as there would now be no cause for the dissolution of all suffering, so too there would be none hereafter... (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 3.3.140a–c).
Just as an action that has arisen after the initial performance does not become the cause of liberation at the time of the dissolution of all suffering,
so too it would not be the cause of liberation at the intended later time either;
the reason being "because it is an action," this is the implied sense.
Because even a single action differs according to the distinction of time, its status as either a thesis (pakṣa) or a similar instance (sapakṣa) is appropriate;
however, in the case of the opposing view (vipakṣa), it would establish liberation immediately after arising, since there would be no distinction.
Regarding the second [position] as well, he states the subverting proof (bādhaka-pramāṇa): "Without remainder... and so forth.
In this context, "now" (atra idānīm) refers to the present manifestation of karma;
"the subsequent" (uttaram) refers to the final one;
the rest is the same.
Furthermore, actions other than the final action do not possess the quality of being a means to liberation;
for if that were the case, it would follow that liberation must occur immediately after them.
Nor can it be said that the final action, when assisted by preceding ones, is the means to liberation.
This is because, in the absence of a fixed limit (*iyattā*), it would follow that there is no determinate cause;

for there is no authoritative rule (*pramāṇa*) establishing the necessity that immediately after the arising of knowledge, one must attain liberation only after performing exactly so many actions within exactly so much time.
Nor is such a view accepted by the Jainas.
Because it is accepted that the Victors appear at different times, he provides a clarification of this appearance with the words: "The view... (*dṛṣṭi*).
... because it is an inference based on what has been previously seen.

The meaning is that because this [inference] is preceded by a view and possesses a pervasion (*vyāpti*) established by valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is therefore a true inference and not a fallacy (*ābhāsa*). As for what was stated— that [it proceeds] "in accordance with the creation of a Lord" (Īśvara)— that is incorrect.
If it is argued that there is no evidence for the claim that liberation follows from the grace of the Lord through knowledge and so forth, we say no; for such scriptural testimony exists,
and its authority has already been established.
Without even extracting [the point] from what has appeared, he also states an inference: "The view," and so forth.
If the knowledge of another who is capable [of teaching] produces that same joy, then the destruction of bondage would occur by that very means; what fault could there possibly be in this?
The cognition of another who is capable [of liberation] is "distinguished cognition," which means the cognition of the excellence of qualities and so forth;
if it is inferred that this produces joy,
and if it is further inferred that the destruction of bondage occurs through that very joy.
In that case, what indeed is the refutation?
None at all.
Why?
The meaning is that inference is preceded by perception and possesses a pervasion (vyāpti) and so forth established by the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
This has been stated merely for the sake of the subject matter;
however, this is the actual procedure of its formal application (prayoga).

The destruction of the bonds of *saṃsāra* is caused by affection for another capable person, because it is a destruction of bonds, like the destruction of the shackles binding a servant who depends on the favor of a king.

And that person is none other than Īśvara. The disputed affection arises from the knowledge of excellence in qualities and so forth, because it is affection [for a superior], like affection for a king.
Even the grace of Īśvara, which arises through karma and other factors, occurs only when there is knowledge of the excellence of his qualities; thus, there is no fault.

Alternatively, that [knowledge] which has Īśvara as its object exists because it is a cognition of the excellence of qualities, just like the [cognition] under discussion. Nor is there a fault resulting from the proof of Īśvara.
Because that [existence] has already been established by the first inference; this is what was meant by the statement, "of another [cause] which is capable. [Objection:
But I can also infer the opposite of this.
If it is argued that there is therefore a counter-balanced reason (*satpratipakṣatā*), [we ask]:
is it inferred that the destruction of bondage under dispute is based on one's own knowledge, or that it is not based on the favoring of others?
Regarding the first case, he states the fault: "From one's own knowledge," etc.
By whom and where has the destruction of bondage ever been seen through one's own knowledge? MĀnuv 3.3.142ab
The phrase "is seen" should be interpreted with a change in intonation (*kāku*) as "is not seen";
thus, the intended meaning is that there is an absence of pervasion (*vyāpti*).

In the second case, however, because [the reason] consists of the "removal of bondage," there is an inconclusiveness (*vyabhicāra*) due to instances such as the removal of shackles which depends upon the favor of a king.
If it is argued that some abandonment of bondage is observed to occur independently of another's favor,
and therefore there is a deviation from the rule even for you [the opponent], we say no; for such cases are equivalent to the subject of the thesis (*pakṣatulyatva*).
For the path of those who know the truth is this: the cessation of all undesirable states depends upon the grace of the Lord.
As for the objection that if dharma and knowledge were the means to liberation, liberation would occur at that very moment—that is incorrect, because of the presence of karma as an obstacle.
For a cause does not cease to be a cause simply because it fails to produce its effect due to the presence of an obstructing factor; otherwise, there would be an over-extension of the principle.
Indeed, action is of many kinds.

If it is argued that although karma such as the obscuration of knowledge (*jñānāvaraṇīya*) has indeed ceased through knowledge alone, nevertheless causes such as [the remaining] lifespan (*āyus*) still exist;
This assumption of the existence of an obstacle might be valid if [it were the case that] "dharma consists of non-violence and so forth,
the knowledge of the self— characterized by its being the size of the body and so on— is the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna), and both this dharma and this knowledge are the means to liberation."
Thus, this matter would be established by valid cognition;
however, it is not so.

Intending to show that an analogous [argument] regarding auspiciousness (*kalyāṇa*) would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), he states—beginning with "And of non-violence" (*ahiṃsāyāśca*)—that there is first of all no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the essential nature of dharma and so forth.
And by what means of valid cognition is the fact that non-violence is dharma understood?
The word "ca" (and) is for the purpose of including knowledge;
alternatively, it is for the purpose of compounding [the practice] with eating at the seventh watch and so forth,
and it serves as an indicator for specific types of knowledge.
If it is argued that [the truth] is understood through the word of the Jina, we say no;
for it has already been stated that there is no means of establishing its authority.
Furthermore, he states that the word of the Jina is countered by an opposing argument: "of violence alone," and so forth.
If it were asserted that violence itself is dharma, what would be the reply?
In this case as well, the illustration should be understood as before.
If one who has understood from the words of the Jina that non-violence is the Dharma is told by a different teacher that violence itself is the Dharma, what answer could there be? None at all.
And thus, there would be no certainty regarding the Dharma.
If it is argued that a teacher who has broken his vows is not authoritative, then how is the Jina authoritative?
[Because he possesses] omniscience...
If it is argued that this is because [the Buddha] is endowed with all virtues,
then this applies equally even to a teacher of a different tradition.
If it is argued that those virtues do not exist in him according to authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), [then the same objection applies].
Even regarding the Jina, by what means are they established?
If it is argued that their establishment therein occurs through the word of those who have seen the Jina,
then the same applies elsewhere as well.
If it is argued that those who perceive a different teacher are deluded or deceivers,

then why is this not also the case for those who perceive the Jina? Now, he states [the verse] beginning with "of dharma" (*dharmasya*) to show that even the status of dharma and so forth as a means to liberation lacks authoritative proof.
By whom, moreover, is it understood that dharma is the cause of happiness?
Liberation is happiness; it is determined by the word of the Victor. To one who asserts this, he says—as before—that there is a counter-position: "of killing," and so forth.
By what means of knowledge is the fact that killing can be a cause of liberation prevented?
The ellipsis [to be supplied] is that "the state of being the cause of liberation was stated by a certain teacher.
In the rule *hanasta ca*, the term *supi* does not carry over. However, *brahmahatyā* and other such terms are genitive compounds (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*).

Therefore, the term *hata* (killed) is correct. For it is entirely improper [to claim] that the Jains' means of attaining liberation is valid, since they assert that a sacrifice characterized by violence is a cause of liberation, following such scriptural passages as: "Indeed, for those who perform the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, their merit becomes inexhaustible. *10,264*
Now, refuting the means for attaining liberation as accepted by the Buddhists, he first sets aside what has been stated by the proponents of emptiness (śūnyavādins): "And not... and so forth.
And liberation cannot be attained in any way whatsoever merely through the thorough knowledge of emptiness, nor even by the cultivation of emptiness.
The thorough knowledge that the entire reality is indeed emptiness, upon which [all things] are superimposed;
likewise, by means of the meditation on emptiness and the contemplation of emptiness;
and furthermore, "api ca" (moreover) indicates a mutual conjunction.
The connection is that liberation would not occur.
And as to how it would not, he explains this by stating:

because there is a lack of valid evidence (*pramāṇa*) for the claim that the thorough knowledge of emptiness and so forth is the means to liberation, and because that [claim] contradicts the aforementioned valid evidence regarding the abandonment of bondage.
Alternatively, does the thorough knowledge of emptiness and so forth accomplish liberation by itself, or by generating faith in emptiness?
It is not the first case,
because it is insentient, like a cloth.
Not the second [alternative], because one does not admit that emptiness possesses the quality of clarity; otherwise, there would be a contradiction of its very nature as emptiness. *10,265*
It might be argued as follows:
bondage is indeed superimposition (adhyāsa) caused by ignorance (ajñāna), which is designated as conventional reality (saṃvṛti);
