and this conventional reality is sublated by the knowledge of emptiness (śūnyajñāna), its opposite.
Therefore, since even the superimposition of bondage has its root in that [ignorance], what will [attributes] such as insentience accomplish? Nor is such a cultivation (bhāvanā) useless,
for it serves the purpose of removing non-apprehension and contrary apprehension.
Not so;
for the superimposition of bondage has already been refuted.
Granting the objection for the sake of argument, he says: "If..."
...if that is so, why is he not [considered one] now? (Manu 3.144d)
The entire passage beginning with "from the thorough knowledge of emptiness" follows here.

If it is argued that liberation occurs in some way through the knowledge of emptiness according to the manner of the doubt raised, then why would that liberation not occur at this very moment, in the instant immediately following the arising of that knowledge?
The intention is that it ought to occur precisely then.
For there is no delay in a lamp’s dispelling of darkness, which is its opposite;
yet the opponent accepts that persons continue to transmigrate even immediately after the knowledge of emptiness.
If it is argued that the delay is due to the presence of non-conception and contrary mental cultivation, [we reply:]...
Do they cease within the activity of conventional reality or not?
In the second case, there would be no cessation at all, just as with emptiness. In the first case, once conventional reality has ceased, how could that [activity] not cease?
Otherwise, there would either be no cessation of conventional reality, or these two would not be its effects.
And if conventional reality does not cease, how could it be opposed by knowledge?
Furthermore, how could it cease even later? *10,266*

Now, one might object: "Just as in your view the state of saṃsāra persists even after the arising of knowledge, why should it not be so in our view as well? To this, he states the difference with the word *para*.
For one who desires to please others, delay may indeed be appropriate;
but if [the action] were not dependent on human desire, by what could delay be caused?
Even for one who has performed his own duty, if he desires to please another, it is indeed appropriate that there be a delay in obtaining the fruit;

for such is seen in the world. However, if one does not maintain that liberation depends upon the grace of another person, then mere knowledge of emptiness, because it is opposed to bondage, [destroys] bondage.
If it is accepted that [ignorance] causes [the body] to cease, then what could be the basis for any delay in liberation immediately following the arising of knowledge?
For that which is postulated as an obstacle would, by virtue of being a conventional body, be contradictory to knowledge;
indeed, there is no delay in the cessation of a dream-bondage after one has awakened.
Even in matters that do not depend on the favor of others, there is delay;

for instance, even when the consumption of *trivṛt* root and so forth has been performed, a delay in purging is observed. Therefore, how can it be said that in the absence of dependence on human desire, no delay would occur?
To this he replies: "Also elsewhere."
In other cases as well, there may be delays caused by the will of the Lord.
Except for liberation;
the cause [of the world's duration] is simply the will of the Lord (Īśvara) that "let this be so for such a length of time.
To the question, "Why is the will of the Lord postulated here as the cause? he says: "Otherwise... (anyathā).
Otherwise, if there were a cause, why would the effect not be produced? (3.146cd)

If the non-conception of God’s will were the cause [of the absence of the effect], then, just as the three-fold root-herb (*trivṛt*) is the cause of purgation and so forth, if that [herb] were present, why would the effect—purgation and the like—not arise?
It certainly would arise.
It is precisely because the effect does not arise that a deficiency in the causal complex (*sāmagrīvaikalya*) is postulated.

Nor can it be said that there is a deficiency in the visible cause here; rather, the will of the Supreme Lord alone must be postulated. Furthermore, it is not reasonable to postulate a deficiency in the *dharma*.
Furthermore, it would follow that the effect could not arise even at a later time;
for no dharma whatsoever is performed in the interval between them.
If it is argued that the dharma exists [at that later time] but had previously not attained its operation, [we reply:]...
What is this so-called "function" (vṛtti)?
Is it a causal relationship, or is it the association with auxiliary factors?
It cannot be the former.
This is because it is being investigated why there is no instrument at all.
As for the second [alternative], that very thing is called the will of God acting as a cooperative cause.
If it is argued that the effect does not arise because the medicine does not pervade the internal state of the body, we say no.

"Because that too would be impossible without the will of God. Furthermore, even for those who consider themselves to have attained the means [to liberation], other disputants might somehow claim that there is a deficiency in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) or the presence of an obstacle (*pratibandhaka*) causing the delay in liberation; however, this cannot be said by a Buddhist. Bearing this intention in mind, he says: "When the cause exists... (*kāraṇe sati*).
For when the cause exists, the existence of the effect is indeed strictly determined.

In the view of this Buddhist, the production of an effect when a cause exists is strictly determined; it is not, as in other systems, merely contingent upon the presence of an unobstructed causal complex (*kāraṇasāmagrī*).
This is because that which is capable cannot be delayed—this is the meaning of the word "for" (*hi*) in his statement.
Therefore, it is established that emptiness, consciousness, and so forth, are not the means to liberation.
He refutes the means to liberation propounded by the Vijñānavādin with the verse beginning "vijñāna" (consciousness).
For the Vijñānavādins as well,
liberation is nowhere possible through the realization of the non-duality of consciousness, nor through the cultivation of consciousness.
"Dvita" itself is "dvaita"; the suffix *aṇ* is used in its own sense. That which is not duality (*dvaita*) is non-duality (*advaita*).
The non-duality of consciousness is "consciousness-non-duality" (*vijñānādvaita*);
it is so called because of the realization that consciousness alone is the single reality and that nothing else exists apart from it.
It is through the cultivation of consciousness—that is, through the meditation on the non-duality of consciousness.
The first word "ca" (and) serves to collect [the arguments] of the proponent;
the second "ca" collects the means of proof (*sādhana*); and the word "eva" (only/just) is connected with the first [clause], "does not at all occur."
The second [clause], however, is for the purpose of restricting the proof;
it establishes that [the position] belongs to the Vijñānavādins by means of those two proofs.

The meaning is that the means to liberation taught by the Vijñānavādin—such as the realization of the non-duality of consciousness (*vijñānādvaitavedana*) and so forth—is simply not tenable due to the force of the logical arguments.

Alternatively, the construction is as follows: "For the Vijñānavādin," meaning that for him, liberation is not at all possible or achieved through the realization of the non-duality of consciousness and so forth as propounded by him. Why? To remind [the reader] of everything previously stated, [the author says]: "For at some time, he... and so on.
It has been stated that [liberation] does not occur only at the time following the arising of knowledge.
Now, he refutes the means for achieving liberation as favored by the Vaibhāṣikas and Sautrāntikas with the word "antar" (within).
Because he perceives the momentariness of both internal cognition and external objects,
and because he practices according to the taught path, he is not liberated due to the absence of valid means of knowledge.
This is an elliptical expression for the knowledge residing within the body.
It refers to the experience of the momentariness of consciousness, sensation, perception, mental formations, and external form.
The person is not liberated by means of momentariness according to the stated path;
for what reason? Because there is a lack of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding this matter.
Since faults such as the acquisition of what was not done (*akṛtābhyāgama*) and the loss of what was done (*kṛtavipraṇāśa*) are indeed manifest, they have not been explicitly stated.

Having thus refuted the non-Vedic doctrines, while now refuting those that are Vedic, [the author] first restates the means to liberation according to the Sāṅkhya teaching, beginning with the words "From primordial nature" (*prakṛteḥ*).
"The discrimination between primordial nature (prakṛti) and the person (puruṣa) is the means to liberation"—with such a doubt... [Mānava-dharmaśāstra 3.3.149a-c]

The Sāṅkhyas declare that "discrimination" (viveka) is the perception of the difference between primordial nature (*prakṛti*), which consists of the internal organ and so forth, and the person (*puruṣa*), one's own self, both in terms of their essential nature and their attributes.
He refutes this with the words: "And not... (*na ca*).
There is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for this point.
How is it that he does not exist?
"He who knows this Person and Nature along with its qualities— no matter how he may conduct himself— he is not born again."

Because there exist scriptural authorities such as, "Those who thus perceive the distinction between the field and the knower of the field, and the liberation from the material nature (bhūtaprakṛti), by means of the eye of knowledge, they go to the Supreme," it is said [in the commentary]: "by the grace of the Lord."
And there is no pride in this [knowledge], because it arises from the grace of the Lord.
The meaning is that there is no authoritative proof for the claim that the discrimination between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* alone, without the grace of the Lord (*īśa*), is the means to liberation.
This is the intended point: it is indeed true that the discrimination between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* is a means to liberation.
However, it serves as a means for attaining the grace of the Blessed One;
for when there is discrimination between primordial nature (prakṛti) and the person (puruṣa), detachment arises in the person.
For one who has become detached, the grace of the Blessed One is attained through devotion and other such means.
And these statements have that [liberation] as their purpose.
However, by the atheistic Sāṅkhya, the state of being the direct means to liberation is asserted for the discrimination between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*;
yet there is no authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*) for that specific distinction.

Now, it may be argued that these statements establish that the discrimination between primordial matter (prakṛti) and the person (puruṣa) is indeed a means to liberation, and there is no reason to assume an indirect succession;
therefore, these [discriminations] themselves possess authority as direct means. To this, he says: "The Śrutis... [etc.].
Since the Śrutis and Smṛtis declare that liberation is attained through the grace of the Lord according to fixed rules, how could it possibly exist without Him?

The meaning is that [the Lord is known] through such Vedic texts as "By whose grace... and so forth, and through such Smṛti texts as "Viṣṇu is the giver of knowledge to the ignorant," and so forth; it does not mean that he is known through the words of ordinary men, because of the word "eva" (only).
When, because of which;
by means of restriction, self-establishment, and exclusion of others;
not by anything else.
Because of the statement "that alone is the one," liberation would arise from that very serenity.

The sense is that, because there exists a powerful subverting factor (*bādhaka*), it is more reasonable to regard those statements as merely traditional (*pāramparya*), like the saying, "We live by the plow.
He refutes the means to liberation (*mokṣasādhana*) propounded by the Vaiśeṣikas and others with the verse beginning "Kaṇāda... (*kaṇāda...*).
Kaṇāda, Yoga, and Akṣapāda as well... // MAnu 3.151ab //
By the word "yoga," Patañjali, the author of the *Yogānuśāsana*, is indicated;
the phrase "speakers of what is untenable" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
The meaning of the particle *api* is that it is not only the Sāṅkhyas and others [who are so].
Now, do these three systems not all maintain that liberation is to be accomplished through the grace of the Lord?

For instance, although the Vaiśeṣika has stated that the knowledge of the truth regarding the similarities and differences among the categories such as substance and so forth is the cause of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*),
even so, it is not [the cause] directly.
But it is only through the gateway of Dharma;
otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the Sūtra which states: "Dharma is that from which the attainment of worldly prosperity and the supreme good results.
Furthermore, even Dharma is not the direct cause of liberation.
Rather, it is indeed assisted by the grace of Īśvara,
as it has been said:
"And that [knowledge] arises solely from dharma manifested through the impulsion of Īśvara."
And it is clearly stated: "I bow to that Lord, by whose releasing of the bound one is satisfied, and by whose binding again one is dissatisfied; this entire universe is his prison.

Although Akṣapāda (Gautama) says that the attainment of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) results from the knowledge of the reality of the sixteen categories beginning with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), nevertheless, the knowledge of the reality of the fifteen categories beginning with the means of valid cognition has as its cause only the knowledge of the reality of the twelve kinds of objects of knowledge (*prameya*), such as the self (*ātman*).

The objects of valid cognition (*prameya*), however, are the self, body, sense organs, objects, intellect, mind, activity, defects, rebirth, fruit, suffering, and liberation; this is because of the use of the word "however" (*tu*).
Even the knowledge of the self and so forth is not a direct means to liberation;
rather, it is [a means] only when accompanied by the grace of the Supreme Lord.
"The wise declare that He is the path to heaven and liberation; therefore,
here this Supreme Self is described as the object of worship"—
so says the statement of those who know the tradition.
Now, as to how he speaks what is untenable, he says: "Of the Lord," etc.
... by the grace of the Lord;
even those who speak of liberation say thus... // MAnu 3.151bc //
Even those who claim that liberation comes from the grace of Īśvara speak something improper; the meaning is that they are speakers of what is logically untenable.
For instance, although the Vaiśeṣikas accept the grace of Īśvara, they do so only as a cooperative cause for dharma.
Because of the statement, "manifested by the injunction of the Lord" (*īśvaracodanābhivyaktāt*),
Patañjali likewise declares that devotion to the Lord (*īśvarapraṇidhāna*) is of equal status with austerity, self-study, and so forth.
The Naiyāyikas also maintain that the knowledge of the reality of the Self alone is the means to liberation, while grace from the Lord is merely an auxiliary factor.
This is because it has been explained in exactly that way in the second aphorism.
Furthermore, the Śruti and Smṛti texts declare that all things, such as dharma and so forth, are means for attaining the grace of the Blessed Lord, either directly or indirectly;
yet they state that the grace of the Blessed Lord itself, being independent of anything else, is the direct means to liberation.
“Having set aside all that, there may be a means for liberation;
but for one who has not set aside anything at all, there is no direct vision for the sake of release”—and so forth.
Therefore, how could they not be proponents of an untenable doctrine? *10,286*
For this reason as well, he says that [the opponent] speaks what is untenable: "And from enjoyment alone... and so forth.
...and they say that the exhaustion of karmas occurs through enjoyment alone. ... // Mānava-dharmaśāstra 3.3.151cd //
The Vaiśeṣikas and others, though appearing like knowers of reality, do not believe that prior karmas are destroyed by knowledge alone;

rather, they assert that through the power of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), by manifesting an immeasurable array of bodies, the knower of reality (*jñānin*) consolidates even infinite karmas—even those with adverse ripening times—and destroys them solely by experiencing their fruits as pleasure and pain. Therefore:
This means "speaking what is untenable. But [one might object]: "This is irrelevant, because the investigation into the means of liberation is the subject at hand."
Not so;
for bondage consists of ignorance, desire, action, and so forth.
Therefore, since liberation is the cessation of that [bondage], how could the destruction of karma and afflictions not be liberation?
And it will be stated later:
"the destruction of karma, as well as the departure [of the soul]," and so forth.
Therefore, this inquiry has as its object only the means for attaining liberation.

Even though they speak thus, how can they be said to be speakers of what is untenable? To this he says, "Because this matter lacks authoritative proof," and continues with: "And why [is this so], when the Lord of the World is propitiated? (Manu 3.151ef).
From what authority, indeed, is this to be understood—that even for the wise, the exhaustion of karmas occurs only through the experience of their fruits?
From none whatsoever.

Since liberation is impossible for those whose karmas are not exhausted, and since there is no other cause for that exhaustion, it is postulated that the very perception of supreme happiness and suffering is the cause of that exhaustion; therefore, he says: "serene" (prasanna).
The phrase "whence is this? continues [from the previous context].

The intention is: since it is established in another way that the Blessed One, being pleased by knowledge, destroys even those karmas whose fruits have not yet been experienced, whence is this [claim] to be inferred?
Furthermore, one should not raise the doubt: "How can the Blessed One desire the destruction of karma that has not yet yielded its fruit?"
With the intention that his sovereignty is unimpeded in every respect, it is said that he is the "Lord of the World" (jagadīśvara).
This is merely a plausible supposition and not something established by valid cognition (pramita).
To the question, "How else could this be explained? he says: "It is divided."
The knot of the heart is broken, all doubts are cut asunder,
and his karmas are exhausted when that which is both high and low is seen.
"The knot of the heart is rent asunder, all doubts are cut away,
and one's karmas are exhausted upon seeing the Lord, the Self, even here and now"—
since this is established by such statements from the Śruti, Purāṇas, and other sources, it cannot be otherwise. (Manu Smṛti 3.3.153)
Ignorance is the knot of the heart;
because he is both supreme and inferior, he is Parāvara.
[This applies] to the Lord of the World, who has spread his qualities throughout the self.
The first is a statement from the Kaṭha Śruti; the second is a statement from the Bhāgavata;
by the word "etcetera," the statements from the Itihāsas to be mentioned later are included.

Otherwise, since the exhaustion and destruction of actions would be certain through the mere experience of their fruits even without the grace of the Lord, the [proposed] justification would be entirely different. If it is argued: "In this context, it is said that 'actions perish when the Supreme Lord is seen,' but not that they perish by the act of seeing; therefore, there is no contradiction even if one explains it as being through experience," we say: no.
If that were the case, it would follow that one must admit that even the severing of the knot of the heart and the cutting away of doubt are achievable by other means;

furthermore, it would contradict the use of the word "only" (*eva*) in the phrase "in this very life" (*dṛṣṭa eva*). Moreover, since the exhaustion [of karma] through experience is common to all, the qualification "through vision" (*darśana*) would be redundant.
If it is argued that the distinction [between the ignorant and the wise] is logical because the ignorant person is not able to exhaust all karmas through experience—
due to their great number and the fact that their ripening occurs at uneven times—

whereas the wise person, by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), creates a manifold array of bodies (*kāyavyūha*), gathers them all together, and destroys them without experiencing the results, then from where does this conception arise?

If it is argued that [the meaning] is established by presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) alone, we say no; for the establishment of presumptive testimony depends upon the alternative interpretation of the statements we have cited,

while the establishment of those statements' alternative interpretation depends upon the establishment of the presumptive testimony— thus there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).

If it is argued that there is a mutual dependence (*parasparāśraya*) for you as well— namely, that the refutation of *arthāpatti* occurs when the misinterpretation of statements has been refuted, and the refutation of the misinterpretation of statements occurs when *arthāpatti* has been refuted—
we say no; for [the misinterpretation] has already been shown to have no scope by means of restrictive particles (*avadhāraṇa*) and the like.
"Lord Hari, when pleased, shatters the accumulation of karma"—since such statements, which leave no room for other interpretations, have been cited elsewhere;
and for this very reason, it is said: "Karma is not exhausted even in hundreds of millions of kalpas without being experienced."

Such general statements as these refer to those who lack knowledge; even for the wise, they refer to the subject of *prārabdha-karma* (commenced karma). "O lord of men, the Self indeed has many bodies... [and so forth].
Having attained the power of yoga, he should act through those [faculties] and traverse the entire earth;
with some he may enjoy sense-objects, while with others he should perform severe austerity;
and he may withdraw them again, just as the sun withdraws its masses of radiance.
Statements such as these refer to the *prārabdha-karma* (commenced karma) of the wise, because the destruction of *prārabdha-karma* will be explained by the force of specific scriptural declarations.
For this very reason: "From knowledge alone, upon the exhaustion of all karma, liberation occurs at that very moment."
But this is not so;
since those liberated while living (jīvanmukta) are observed [to exist], this objection has no basis. *10,291*

As for the inference: "The subject under dispute (the karma) is destructible by the enjoyment of its fruit, because it is karma, like karma that is commonly accepted [as such]," this is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to karma for which an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) has been performed.
We shall refute later the claim that expiation is not a cause for the destruction of karma.
If you argue that the reason is "being karma for which no expiation has been performed," then what is this so-called "expiation"?
If it is argued that [penance] is a specific vow prescribed for the purpose of removing sin,
then there would be a deviation [from the rule] in cases where karma is destroyed through the grace of great beings and the like.
If it is further argued that what is intended by "prāyaścitta" is merely the cause for the removal of sin, we say no.
Nevertheless, there is a deviation [from the rule] when merit is destroyed by great contempt and the like.
If it is argued that the reason is "the state of being an action devoid of any other cause for its destruction," then does the injunction itself imply the status of being the cause?
If that were the case, then even meditative concentration (*samādhi*) would not be the cause for such things as the emanation of a multitude of bodies;
if you argue that it is acceptable to accept a result mentioned in an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*),
then the same applies to the present case as well.
For it has been stated that there is no contradiction here;
moreover, the quality of being non-worldly (*alaukikatva*) is common to both cases.
Furthermore, according to this view, there is never any exhaustion of karma.
Furthermore, because it acts again even at the time of experiencing [the fruit],
it is impossible that it does not act;
for "no one [remains inactive] even for a single moment."
Because it has been stated thus:
if it is argued that even activity being performed does not produce the unseen (adṛṣṭa), we say no,
because that would contradict the Śruti and Smṛti.
For the wise, by the power of their knowledge, it is so; thus, other scriptural passages and the like refer to other subjects, such as:
"Just as [water does not cling] to a lotus leaf," and "Having deposited all actions in Brahman."

If it is argued that this is postulated on the strength of such scriptural and traditional texts (*śruti-smṛti*), then why is this same principle not accepted with regard to past actions as well? [The opponent replies:
"Because of the absence of passion (*rāga*) and hatred (*dveṣa*), there is no activity that serves as the cause for unseen merit or demerit (*adṛṣṭa*)."
As it has been said:
"For one whose afflictions have been eliminated, [worldly] activity does not constitute an obstacle.
This is not so.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that the killing of a Brahmin committed through negligence and the like would not be a cause of unrighteousness; enough of this.
He refutes the means to liberation taught by the Pāśupatas and others with the words "And not... (*na ca*).
Nor [is it attained] through the grace of Śiva and others as taught by the Pāśupatas and other [sects].
By the word "Pāśupata," all four types [of Pāśupatas] are included;
by the word "and others" (*ādi*), the Skānda, Saura, and so forth are meant.
By the second word, "ādi" (and so forth), [the systems of] Skanda and others are included.
The ellipsis is that liberation arises from grace (*anugraha*).
Now, one might object: the phrase "as stated in the Pāśupata and other [systems]" cannot be a qualifier of grace.
Because a compound cannot be formed due to a lack of semantic capacity;
if that were the case, it would have to be "pāśupatādy-uktāt" (from what is taught by the Pāśupatas and others).
For this very reason, it is not a qualifier of liberation (*mokṣa*).
If that were the case, it would follow that [the term] is stated by the Pāśupatas and others; however, if it were a qualifier of Śiva and so forth, it would be redundant. To this, it is replied:
Let it be that *anugraha* (favor) is the qualifier;
in that case, the compound *śivādyanugrahaḥ* is simply a genitive-tatpuruṣa compound. The non-elision (*aluk*) of the genitive case-ending is according to the rule *ṣaṣṭhyā ākrośe*.
The purpose [of this work] is also to resolve contradictions with such scriptural passages as, "Having known Śiva, one attains ultimate peace.
For liberation is indeed sought through the grace of that Supreme Śiva, who is not touched even slightly by the attributes of saṃsāra.
"But for one who is possessed of ignorance and the like, and is thus known [to be such], it is said that there is no liberation through their grace.
"Liberation and knowledge, as well as the distinction of those going to the state of liberation, occur gradually;
for the lower ones, this happens through the favor of those higher, and not otherwise."
In order to avoid contradiction with such statements as these, the term "grace" (*anugraha*) has been specified as being that which is taught by the Pāśupatas and others.
It is indeed accepted that the grace of Śiva and others—which serves as a means for the Lord’s favor—is a cause of liberation;
however, it is not the [grace] taught by the Pāśupatas and others that is an independent means.
Alternatively, *pāśupatādyuktā* may also be read as a separate word; in this case,
the ablative case ending is elided by the rule *supāṃ suluk*,
or the nominative case ending is elided.
And this is a qualification of liberation;
the purpose of specifying the proponent therein must indeed be stated. Or rather, let it remain as it was heard [in the original], referring specifically to Śiva and the others.

The meaning is that for those such as Śiva who are said by the Pāśupatas and others to be objects of independent worship, there is no grace whatsoever toward those who worship them in that manner; on the contrary, there is only wrath. Therefore, liberation through grace is utterly cast aside. *10,298*
To the question, "Why is there no liberation through the grace of Śiva and others? he says: "Not by another."
For it is stated in the Śruti that there is no other path than through the knowledge of the Puruṣa.

In the Śruti, in the passage beginning "The Puruṣa with a thousand heads," immortality is indeed declared through the negation of anything other than the knowledge of the Puruṣa who is the subject under discussion; therefore, it is the grace of Puruṣottama alone, impelled by knowledge, that is the cause of liberation, and not the grace of Śiva or others. Now, one might object: "In the Puruṣasūkta, it is only the *paśu-puruṣa* (the bound soul) that is expounded, not Viṣṇu; so how can this mantra be cited as proof for the fact that knowledge of Viṣṇu is the means to liberation?"

If it is argued that even the knowledge of the individual soul (paśu) and the person (puruṣa) is extremely useful for the grace of the Lord of Beasts (Paśupati), and is therefore called a means to liberation,
and that nothing else [is so], and that this is not contradictory because the fruit does not arise from abandoning the means to the means just as one would abandon the means itself— [we reply: no.
Is this [objection] based on the absence of the primary denotative power (*śakti*) of the word "Puruṣa" in Viṣṇu, or on the absence of any indicator of its intended meaning (*tātparya*),
or on the existence of a subverting argument (*bādhaka*)?
Not the first [alternative], because the word *puruṣa* is used for Hari in the *Nārāyaṇānuvāka*; thus he says: "All."
All moments were born from that Puruṣa who is lightning;
thus the word "Puruṣa" is applied to Hari, who reclines upon the ocean.
Immortality is not stated to result merely from the knowledge of the Person (puruṣa);
rather, the word "Person" (puruṣa) is also applied to Hari.

To the objection that even though He is called "the Person of lightning," why might this not refer to the Person among animals (paśupuruṣa), it is said: "He who lies upon the ocean" (abdhiśaya), meaning "on the further shore of the waters" (ambhasya pāre).

Because the quality of reclining upon the ocean is heard in this person in the passage beginning with "yam antaḥ samudre," and because his status as a mark of Viṣṇu is understood from such statements as "the end-maker reclining on the great ocean," [the author] says "na tasya" (not of him) to show that this is Nārāyaṇa and not Paśupati.
"No one has mastery over him; his name is 'Great Renown'";
thus the lordship over him is itself prohibited by the Veda.
"Viṣṇu Nārāyaṇa, Hari, is eternally supreme over all and is everything"—by this statement of His being superior to all, even equality is excluded. (Manusmṛti 3.3.157)
Of that person:
[the word "īśe" (he rules) is used] because of the rule "vyatyayo bahulam" (there is much substitution);
the genitive case is used according to the rule "adhīgarthadayeṣāṃ karmaṇi" (the genitive is used for the object of verbs meaning 'to remember,' 'to rule,' and 'to pity').

"Mahat" and "Yaśas" are the names of that Puruṣa. In the *Śruti*, within the *Nārāyaṇa-anuvāka*, by the statement "na tasya" ("not his"), the lordship over that Puruṣa is explicitly denied by [the Lord] himself. And because he is both supreme (*parama*) and food (*aśa*), he is the Supreme Food (*paramāśa*).
Alternatively, by changing the gender, it may be read as "paramam" (the supreme).
"Viśvam" means full.
In the *Nārāyaṇānuvāka*, the scriptural passage beginning with "viśvataḥ" declares that this Puruṣa is superior to all; by this statement, even that [notion of fullness] is set aside.
For it is not logical that one who is supreme should have an equal.
To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "Equal."
Because he lacks concentration, he is not even a figurative man.
The term *samādhika* is a compound formed by treating the two members as a single unit (*dvandvaikyavadbhāva*).
This refers to what is described in the *Nārāyaṇānuvāka*.

One whose movement (*cāra*) is "near" (*upa*)—that is, one who has become subordinate (*upasarjanabhūta*) to the Pradhāna—is a "man of metaphorical usage" (*upacārapumān*), meaning he is not the *paśu-puruṣa* (the bound individual soul).
It has not been stated that this person is Hari himself—known by names such as Nārāyaṇa—because he can be known as such only by his disciples.

Since the absence of a superior lord and the state of being supreme over all, which are understood from that [text], as well as the absence of an equal, are impossible in the case of a sacrificial animal (paśu), this word "Puruṣa" does not refer to that.
Rather, let it be that it refers exclusively to Viṣṇu, by virtue of names such as Nārāyaṇa and by marks such as reclining upon the ocean.

The expressive power (*vācakatva-śakti*) of the word "puruṣa" for Viṣṇu is not established by that alone, because its usage can be accounted for even through a non-primary mode of application (*amukhyā vṛtti*); therefore, he says: "sameti" (it is equal).

This Viṣṇu is not the object of the word "Puruṣa" by way of metaphorical usage (upacāra), but rather by its primary sense (mukhyavṛtti) alone. Why? Because metaphorical usage is postulated only when the primary sense is impossible.

The primary meaning of the word *puruṣa* is "fullness," and that is appropriate for Viṣṇu alone because He is devoid of anything equal or superior. [Objection: "Granted that the word *puruṣa* has this denotative power (*vācakatva-śakti*) with respect to Viṣṇu, nevertheless, since there is no indicative evidence (*jñāpaka*) in the *Puruṣasūkta* to show it refers to Him, it cannot be taken as being about Him. To refute this second point, he says: "It is *puruṣa* itself."
The Person alone is all this—whatever has been and whatever is to be;
moreover, he is the lord of immortality, as well as of that which grows by means of food.

The Veda declares that he possesses the state of being both the liberated and the supreme lord: "Whatever has been, whatever is to be, and whatever exists—this entire universe, though unliberated, is indeed the Puruṣa;
it is entirely dependent upon the Puruṣa."
Since, in this way, food surpasses— that is, transcends— food that has not been released (i.e.,

food belonging to those who are not liberated), meaning it has the unreleased as its sovereign; therefore, because of the non-difference between the state and the possessor of the state (*bhāva-bhāvitr-abheda*), he is also the lord (*īśāna*) of the class of the liberated with respect to immortality.

If the world were independent in *saṃsāra*, or if it were independent in liberation (*mukti*), then a wise person would not seek liberation; therefore, even in liberation, the world remains dependent on Him. Thus, that *śruti*—the mantra from the *Puruṣasūkta*—declares His status as the Supreme Lord over both the liberated and the unliberated.

Furthermore, through such passages as "That is the supreme goal of the liberated," it is understood that this belongs to Viṣṇu alone, and is entirely impossible for any other being (*paśu*). Therefore, it is known that the *Puruṣasūkta* refers exclusively to Viṣṇu.

But surely, since it is said here that "the Puruṣa alone is all this," the Puruṣa's very nature as the self of everything has been declared; so how can the Śruti speak of him as being the liberated, the unliberated, and the Supreme Lord? To this, he replies: "Amṛta... (immortal).
From the word of Amṛteśāna, the lordship over all is declared.

The term "Īśāna" is an indication where the abstract state (bhāva) is the primary meaning. Since the state of being the Lord of liberation is mentioned in the second half [of the verse], it should be understood that in the first half, the lordship over all that is *not* liberated is what is proclaimed,
and not [the lordship over] everything.
No proponent whatsoever accepts a distinction in liberation and non-distinction in non-liberation;
nor is such a position tenable, because no distinction is observed in what was previously undivided. (10.305)
He states another reason with the words "yadi" (if).
If it is said that "the Lord is all," then that [distinction] is in vain.

If the state of being the All (sarvatva) had been declared for the Person in the first half [of the verse], then the word "uta" in the second half—namely, in the phrase "the Lord of immortality" (amṛtatvasya u īśānaḥ)—would be redundant.
To the question "How so?", he says: "The word 'uta'..."
The word "uta" (or) expresses the conjunction of this with lordship.
The word "uta" situated in the second half [of the verse] would express a conjunction of two lordships,
because no other meaning is possible;
and there is no occasion for a statement of their conjunction unless both lordships have been mentioned.
Therefore, the word "uta" is indeed useless.
He states another argument: "by the Puruṣa alone."
And regarding him, the Brāhmaṇa declares: "This [universe] is pervaded by the Puruṣa. (MDh 3.161ab)

"The Puruṣa alone is all this"—by which it is meant that all this, from the grass up to the dung-heap, is pervaded by the Puruṣa; [the claim] that "everything is the Blessed Lord" is indeed a false view (mithyādṛṣṭi). Furthermore, a Brāhmaṇa passage from another Vedic branch, which engages with that mantra, states that it is merely an explanatory commentary (vyākhyāna) upon that mantra; therefore, "being everything" is not its intended meaning.
It is pervaded and brought under control;
by this, the view that the word "uta" has the sense of a conjunction (*samuccaya*) regarding the property-bearer (*dharmin*) is also refuted. *10,306*
Furthermore, he states that the meaning of the first half-verse is precisely "lordship over all" (sarveśatva) and not merely "universality" (sarvatva): "etāvān iti."
"Such is his greatness"—for that is indeed a statement concerning his majesty.
The phrase "because of this statement" is the ellipsis [to be supplied].

From the force of the subsequent sentence—"Of this person, such is the greatness as was stated in the preceding sentence"—it is first understood that the statement "this is indeed that Person" is a word expressive of the greatness of that Person. Consequently, it must be explained in such a way that it serves as a presentation of that greatness.
And its greatness does not consist in being the self of all, because that would be a cause for diminution;
rather, it consists solely in sovereignty over all.
Nor is there any statement regarding greatness (*mahiman*) other than that [of the Self], because there is no reason for such a restriction. *10,307*
For this reason as well, he says "so 'mṛtasya" (of that which is immortal) to show that this is indeed so.
"He is the lord of immortality and fearlessness, having transcended mortal food"—
thus, after restating the sovereignty over the unliberated mentioned in the first half of the verse, [the text continues].
And "He is the Lord of immortality" establishes his lordship over the state of liberation.
The word "iti" implies "because of the statement of the Bhāgavata.
Having restated [the fact] by means of the statement "that which grows by food," the word "iti" implies "as the reason";
thus the Śruti enjoins it.
This is the meaning:
it is understood that in the second half-verse, the Śruti recognizes the state of being liberated as the sovereign power (adhipatya), taking the state of not yet being liberated as the cause;
for, in the context of the commentary on the Puruṣasūkta, the second half-verse is explained in exactly that way by the statement of the Bhāgavata: "He [is] of the immortal."

For this very reason, the interpretation— "He is the lord (*īśāna*) of that immortality (*amṛtatva*) and godhood (*devatva*) which grows, ascends, and increases through divine enjoyment consisting of food"—
is incorrect. For,

with the intention of expressing the identity between the state (*bhāva*) and the possessor of the state (*bhavitṛ*), the phrase "of immortality" (*amṛtatvasya*) has been explained as "of the immortal" (*amṛtasya*).

And it was stated "of the fearless" (*abhayasya*) precisely for the purpose of excluding the gods; furthermore, it has been explained that the instrumental case in "by food" (*annena*) functions as the accusative; and since "food" is not self-evident [in this context], it was specified as "mortal" (*martyam*).
Thus, this meaning of the latter half [of the verse] is consistent only with our own interpretation of the former half.
In the former half, non-liberated sovereignty (*amuktādhipatya*) is enjoined;
in the latter half, the Śruti reiterates that aforementioned non-liberated sovereignty as the cause and enjoins the Puruṣa’s status as the Lord of liberation.
However, in the interpretation of others, [the argument] is indeed untenable due to mutual contradiction.
By this [it is shown that], if the word "Puruṣa" were to have Viṣṇu as its referent, the fact of being the self of all (*sarvātmakatva*) would be a subverting factor;
for even you do not admit that Viṣṇu is the self of all.
"The state of being an element (bhūtatva) and so forth is appropriate for the sacrificial animal because of its connection with a body"—thus the third position is also refuted.
He concludes: "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). *10.309*
Therefore, liberation comes only from the thorough knowledge of Viṣṇu, and not from anything else.
Through thorough knowledge arising from thorough knowledge, and through the clarity born thereof,
as well as through the grace of others such as Śiva and so forth,
even the Pāśupatas who possess knowledge declare that the exhaustion of karma occurs only through experience.
He states that even this is untenable, beginning with "tadyathā" (for example).
"‘Just as the tuft of a reed-stalk thrown into a fire is consumed, even so are all his evils consumed,’ according to the Śruti.
[Regarding the form *iṣīkā*], the shortening of the vowel does not occur because of the rule: ‘In the case of *iṣīkā*, *eṣīkā*, and *mālā*, when they mean a mat, cotton, and a wreath respectively.’"
"Protaṃ praviṣyam" means it would be consumed; "pradūyeta" means it would be scorched, or it would be reduced to ashes—
such is the illustration.
For this knower,
they are "consumed," meaning they perish;
the word "ca" (and) serves to include the previously cited scriptural passages.
"From that very [source]" means from the very knowledge of Viṣṇu. Now, one might object:

"In this scriptural passage, the burning away (*paritāpa*) of actions by the knower is heard, but not their destruction by knowledge; therefore, this is not the intended meaning. To address this, he cites the designation of the Lord's own words, beginning with "Just as... (*yathā*).
Just as a kindled fire reduces fuel to ashes, O Arjuna,
so does the fire of knowledge reduce all actions to ashes.

Although the causality of knowledge is clearly perceived here, it is not understood what is to be imagined regarding the "reduction of karmas to ashes," since that is impossible in its primary sense; therefore, he recites another passage: "All... etc.

The meaning stated [in this verse] is also understood from such words of the Blessed One as: "Abandoning all duties, take refuge in me alone; I shall liberate you from all sins; do not grieve. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.3.165)

The non-Vaiṣṇava doctrines and those concerning objects of desire have been explained elsewhere by the venerable Bhagavatpāda himself in such passages as: "And the taking of refuge [is preceded] by the realization of [the Lord's] supreme excellence," and so forth.
Therefore, I am pleased;
do not grieve.
You shall not grieve; you will be liberated.
The phrase "by the word 'etcetera'" includes [quotations] such as "of one who has gone beyond attachment, who is liberated"; this is the connection with the words of the Blessed One.
Alternatively, the meaning stated by the Śruti, namely "tadyathā" (just as), is determined by the words of the Blessed One. *10,311*
He restates the means to liberation according to the Bhāṭṭas: "The eternal," etc.
Performing the obligatory and occasional rites while abandoning others,
he is liberated from the cycle of transmigration...
That which is called "obligatory" (nitya) is that in the non-performance of which there is sin.
That which is prescribed by taking as its basis a specific occasion such as being a Brahmin and so forth is called *naimittika*;
for example, the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā-vandana*) and the like.

That which is prescribed by taking as its basis an incidental occasion, such that there is a transgression (*pratyavāya*) if it is not performed, is called *naimittika* when it is enjoined upon the occurrence of an adventitious cause such as the death of a parent.
For example, the ancestral śrāddha rites and so forth;
as well as other optional (kāmya) and prohibited (niṣiddha) acts.
In these cases, there is a fruit when the action is performed, but no transgression (pratyavāya) when it is not performed.
The signless state regarding sensual desires arises from the desire for them,
as in the case of the Jyotiṣṭoma and other such sacrifices;
that which is prohibited is forbidden.
Just as in the case of killing a Brahmin and so forth;
and the meaning of the word "ca" (and) is that one exhausts the accumulated karma through experience.
This is the intended sense.
For saṃsāra consists of pleasure, pain, and their causes;
and it has karma alone as its motive.
However, through the non-performance of obligatory and occasional rites, due to the accumulation of demerit (*adharma*), he comes to obtain suffering and its means.
The same applies to the performance of prohibited acts.
However, by performing acts for the sake of desired results (*kāmyakarman*), the attainment of happiness and its means arises through the production of merit (*dharma*).
One who seeks liberation (*mumukṣu*), on the other hand, performs only the obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites at all times.
He abandons what is prohibited, and thus there is no accumulation of demerit (*adharma*);
he also abandons what is desired for its fruits, and thus there is no accumulation of merit (*dharma*).
In this way, by preventing the future arising of merit and demerit and by exhausting those previously acquired through experience, one is liberated from a cycle of existence that is devoid of seeds.
As it has been said:

"One who seeks liberation should not engage in actions that are either desired or prohibited; however, one should perform obligatory and occasional rites with the desire to avoid the arising of transgression."
Furthermore, there is no fifth category of action such that the arising of merit or demerit would occur whether it is performed or not performed.
He refutes this with the words: "This also... (*etad api*).
... this too has been refuted by this [statement];
for the King of the Vedas himself declares this very same meaning: "It is knowledge alone. (Manu 3.3.166d–f)
By this Vedic statement, "There is no other path," which negates any means for liberation other than knowledge of the Lord;
furthermore, the obligatory and occasional performance of rituals with complete regularity and correctness is simply impossible.
As it is said: "The gods perform the entire prescribed [duty], the sages half of it, and humans one-tenth."
This is because of such scriptural passages as these.
Nor is the non-performance of prohibited acts possible,
since mental, vocal, and physical lapses committed through negligence are unavoidable.
If it is argued that their destruction occurs through expiation (*prāyaścitta*), we say no;
for even expiation is impossible to perform correctly.
Furthermore, the destruction of previously accumulated karma through its mere experience is utterly inconceivable.
"Because it is infinite"—this is sufficient.
Now, one might ask: "Why is all this being described when it is not mentioned in the Sūtra? To this, he says: "Knowledge alone," and so forth.
The King of the Vedas himself declares this very same point: "Knowledge alone [is the cause]. (Manu 3.166ef)

However, by the sūtra "But [it is] knowledge alone, because of the determination," it is stated that [the soul] is itself [knowledge], and not [knowledge] in a figurative sense. The Vājasaneyins study [as follows]:
"He saw thirty-six thousand fires of his own self, consisting of the suns, made of mind, built of mind," and so forth.
Regarding this, there is a doubt:
Are these fires subordinate to ritual action and part of its remnants, or are they independent, consisting solely of knowledge (*vidyā*)?

Since the context concerns the fire consisting of ritual action (*kriyāmaya*), it might be argued that this instruction refers specifically to that; however, it is replied: these fires consist of knowledge (*vidyātmaka*) alone and are not subordinate to ritual action, because of the definitive statement, "These indeed are piled by knowledge alone" (*vidyācita*).

Thus, with the intention that the explanation of others is indeed false, he stated "this very meaning," because such reflection would be fruitless; for in both cases, its purpose is simply spiritual progress (*abhyudaya*).

"But how can one who possesses discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities, who is endowed with tranquility, self-control, and other virtues, who is possessed of dispassion toward all enjoyments, and who desires liberation— such a person indicated as the qualified seeker by the word 'atha' (*atha*) in the *Uttaramīmāṃsā*— engage in these trivial deliberations?

Having thus refuted the views raised as prima facie arguments (*pūrvapakṣa*) by the author of the Sūtras, [the author] now refutes the views of those commentators on the Sūtras who speak otherwise, specifically those who maintain the doctrine of the necessity of combining [all means].
He first refutes that opinion with the words "vineti" (it leads away).
"That there can be no liberation without action, even through knowledge"—this is the Vedic revelation;
for it respectfully prohibits any other path with the words, "There is indeed no other way. (Manu Smṛti 3.3.167)
The Blessed One’s path is this: the mere cessation of saṃsāra occurs through knowledge alone, whereas the increase of bliss occurs only through knowledge that is dependent upon karma;
as he will state later: "And by way of being a cooperative cause."

Therefore, rather than stating that liberation results from both knowledge and action, it is said that there is no liberation through knowledge alone without action, but rather [liberation] is attained through knowledge accompanied by action.
This very view is clearly refuted by the Vedic scripture which states, "That alone is the bridge; there is no other path.

Having stated that knowledge alone is the means to liberation in the words "Having known Him thus," the subsequent statement "there is no other path" makes it clear that this [requirement of action] is intended with great emphasis.
Furthermore, there is no evidence whatsoever for a rule of conjunction [between the two paths],
because such passages as "They enter into blinding darkness" have other meanings;
just as food joined with honey, and honey joined with food.
Thus, because [statements] such as "Austerity and knowledge, when combined, are a great medicine" have as their object indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*),
and even if they were to have as their object direct knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*), they serve the purpose of increasing bliss. (10.319)
The proponents of Māyāvāda say:
liberation is twofold, distinguished as higher and lower. Among these, the lower is characterized by the attainment of Vaikuṇṭha, Satyaloka, and other such realms.
The latter, however, consists in abiding in non-dual Brahman when ignorance has ceased.
For the former [type of aspirant], the means is meditation on symbols and the like performed in a different manner;
for the latter, however, it is the knowledge of unity.
In this regard, he first refutes the notion that meditating upon Him in another way can be a means for attaining Vaikuṇṭha and other realms, by stating: "anyathā" (in another way).
Furthermore, she respectfully forbids him from worshipping in any other way, saying, "He is thus. MAnu 3.168a-c.
By stating "in this very manner as it exists, and not otherwise," the Śruti precludes even meditating upon [Brahman] in any other way as a means to achieve the human goal (puruṣārtha);
it does so not only regarding positions distinct from the knowledge of the Supreme Person.
By the word "Him" (tam), the attainment of knowledge in accordance with reality is already established.
Since it is logical to refer back to the subject under discussion in its entirety—including its specific modes—it is illogical to assume that it refers only to a single part.
Nevertheless, when he says "that which is thus," it is for the purpose of indicating special regard [for that part].
Let this scripture have as its subject matter supreme liberation (*paramamokṣa*).
But another might argue that the human goal will be achieved through a different mode of meditation; therefore, he says: "No."
... "not as a mere representative," says the Lord. (Manu 3.168d)
“The author of the Sūtras will state [in the sūtra], ‘Not in a symbol, for he is not that,’ that meditating on [Brahman] otherwise is in every way improper;
therefore, that [meditation on a symbol] is not a cause for even a fraction of the human goal. *10,320*
To one who says, "I shall state another meaning of the Sūtra," he points out the contradiction with the Śruti, saying: "The blind... and so forth.
"And those who worship ignorance enter into blind darkness"—
because of this contradiction with the Śruti, there can be no other form of worship.
The phrase "the means for achieving the goals of human life" is the ellipsis [to be supplied].
As for the scriptural citation (*śruti*), it has been explained elsewhere by way of demonstrating its agreement with the *smṛti*.
Now, he refutes the claim that the knowledge of oneness is the means for supreme liberation, stating: "And not... (*na ca*).
Nor is one liberated by the cognition of oneness, according to the principle already stated.
The word "ca" (and) is used for emphasis:
even from the cognition of oneness, a person is not liberated from saṃsāra.
Why?

According to the logic already stated, having declared that knowledge of the Blessed One— who is endowed with such great majesty as having a thousand heads— is the means for attaining immortality in the passage "Knowing Him thus," [the text] states "There is no other path" to indicate the absence of any other means.
If it is argued that the oneness stated in the passage "The Person alone is all this" is what is referred to by the word "thus" (evam), we say no;
for, according to the reasoning already set forth, that sentence does not have oneness as its subject matter.

“Furthermore, scriptural passages such as ‘Whosoever among the gods awakens to this’ do not state that the knowledge of oneness is the means to liberation, according to the principle already stated— that [the soul] has the qualities of Brahman as its essence.
Moreover, it is established by the principle already stated— that there is a separate teaching [of the two]— that the knowledge of oneness is a form of erroneous knowledge.”
It has been stated that false knowledge is a means to what is harmful.
Furthermore, the knowledge of non-duality (advaitajñāna) does not function as a means to liberation in the manner of sacrifices or service to a king;
rather, it functions by way of being the opposite of ignorance (avidyā).
When ignorance has ceased through the realization of non-duality—which is its opposite—the bondage that has that [ignorance] as its material cause ceases of its own accord.
Consequently, it would follow that for those who have realized non-duality, the perception of duality such as the body and so forth would cease in the very next moment;
yet, liberation while living (jīvanmukti) is indeed accepted.

If it is argued that even when ignorance (*avidyā*) has ceased through knowledge, the perception of duality continues due to its residual impression (*saṃskāra*), we say no; for since the residual impression is an effect of ignorance, its continued existence is untenable once its material cause has ceased. Indeed, it is never observed that an effect persists once its material cause has been removed.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of its being real;

for since that [duality] has not ceased even when knowledge arises, and because there is no other means to remove it, it would persist forever, and thus the cessation of the perception of duality would never occur.
Furthermore, it is logically untenable for the unattached Self to be the substratum of the formative impressions (*saṃskāra*) without any connection to ignorance (*avidyā*).
By this, the claim that the persistence of dualistic perception occurs due to the force of *prārabdha* karma is also refuted.
If it is argued that although ignorance has been removed by knowledge, it persists for some time according to the analogy of a burnt cloth,
thereby accounting for the continued appearance of duality— this is not so;
for if there were no cause for its absolute cessation, it would follow that the perception of duality could never cease.

By this, the position that ignorance persists as a residue (*avidyā-leśa*) is also refuted. For a "residue" would have to be either a constituent part (*avayava*), like a thread in a cloth; or a spatial portion (*pradeśa*); or a property (*dharma*).
It cannot be the first.
Because ignorance is not something produced,
the second [alternative] is not tenable;
for we do not admit that it has spatial locations.
Nor is it the third [alternative], because when the locus (*pradeśin*) has ceased, it is impossible for the spatial parts (*pradeśa*) to remain; furthermore,
it is illogical that the attributes (*dharma*) should not cease when the substratum (*dharmin*) has departed.
Now, it might be thought: although ignorance, which is the fundamental cause of saṃsāra, is indeed one,
it nevertheless possesses many modes.
Among these, the first is the cause of the delusion that bondage is ultimately real;
the second is the conceptualizer of things as having causal efficacy;
and the third is the conceptualizer of the form of the object appearing in immediate perception.
In that state, through the firm conviction in the reality of non-duality (*advaita*), the mental mode that imagines the reality of the entire world of duality (*dvaita*) ceases.

The form of *māyā*, which is the material cause of the phenomenal world capable of purposeful action (*arthakriyā-samartha*), dissolves upon the direct realization of truth (*tattva-sākṣātkāra*). However, the residual trace of *māyā* (*māyā-leśa*), which produces objects capable of appearing as immediate perception, has ceased for one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*); it remains hidden during the state of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), but persists at other times as the cause of the appearance of the semblance of a body.
But [the claim] that it ceases at the conclusion of the experience of the fruits of *prārabdha* karma is incorrect,
because this conceptualization lacks any basis in valid authority (*pramāṇa*).
If it is argued that the scriptural text, "Indra moves in manifold forms through his powers (māyā)," is the authority here, we say no;
for this passage establishes the power of the Supreme Lord,
and there is no appearance of establishing a māyā in the form of something indefinable that is sublatable by knowledge.
In the Śvetāśvatara mantra as well, it is stated: "From meditating upon Him, from union with Him, and from becoming His true nature, there is ultimately the cessation of universal illusion.
This means that through repeated application of the mind to Him, there arises a state of being His true nature—that is, the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna).

From that which has arisen, through meditation upon and the grace of that Supreme Lord, at the conclusion of the exhaustion of karma, the cessation of the illusion that binds the universe occurs. Thus it is said.
However, there is no gradual cessation—characterized by sublation—of the forms of indeterminable ignorance.
Furthermore, as for that which is said to persist even after the magician has departed, does the knowledge of reality oppose it or not?
In the first case, how is it that it does not cease?
In the second case, it would not be ceased by knowledge;
and if that were so, it would be real.
By asserting that it ceases when karma is exhausted, one would be stating that karma is its cause.
Otherwise, its cessation would be impossible upon the cessation of that [avidyā].
Now, you might think: "Knowledge alone is the remover of even a trace of avidyā."
However, [the opponent argues] that it does not cause [the body] to cease because it is obstructed by powerful *prārabdha-karma*;
rather, it causes it to cease once the obstruction is exhausted through the experience of its fruits.
That too is incorrect.
Because it is impossible for karma to persist without a basis (*anupādāna*).

If it is argued that this very trace of ignorance (*avidyā-leśa*) is the basis for karma, we say no; for this would result in the fallacy of mutual dependence (*parasparāśraya*), wherein the persistence of karma depends on the persistence of the trace of ignorance, and the persistence of the trace of ignorance depends on the persistence of karma.
Because it remains a defect even during its persistence, just as it was at the time of its origination;
furthermore, there is no other clear evidence for this point.
Therefore, let there be no mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*) regarding its persistence.
But this [distinction] certainly exists in the case of informative cognition (*jñapti*).
If it is argued that this matter must be postulated because liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) would otherwise be impossible, we say no;

for since everything is accounted for by accepting the fact—established by all the Śrutis, Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and so forth—that liberation occurs solely through the grace of the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*), there is no room for such a postulation.
He concludes the subject matter of the section with the words: "Thus, all this."
Having thus fully understood everything through all means of reasoning and traditional scriptures,
one should constantly worship Hari by means of His very qualities through one's own yoga.
It is untenable to claim that liberation does not exist at all, or that it is achievable through some other means apart from the Self. On the contrary,

when the internal organ of a supreme devotee (*paramabhāgavata*) has been purified by the performance of actions prescribed in the Vedas and other scriptures for the sake of the Lord without desire, and when— upon the destruction of defects such as passion— devotion to the Lord has arisen, he engages in the practice of hearing, reflection, and meditative concentration (*nididhyāsana*), culminating in the direct realization of the Lord.

Upon his birth, the Lord became pleased; having destroyed all *karmas* except for those that have already begun (*prārabdha*), He established a certain period of time for the sake of engaging in the *bhāgavata-dharma*.

Having reserved the *prārabdha-karmas* for that purpose, once their fruits have been experienced, He destroys even those and liberates him from the bondage of *prakṛti*. Having made this entire promise, [He acts] through the *guṇas* alone, and not otherwise.
With the words "He would weep," etc., he restates the meaning of the portion of the Sūtra beginning with "Even though [the qualities] are perceived as non-existent" and "And because it is the same.

The word "is appropriate" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. [This applies] only according to one's own capacity, and not by transgressing that capacity; this is established by the Sūtra beginning with "And because of the attainment," etc.
Thus is the restatement of the meaning of the Sūtra;
and the purpose is to indicate the connection with what follows.
It has been said: "by virtue of one's own fitness."
He explains that very fitness [of the word "Brahman"] with the words: "Brahman..."
Brahmā [is superior] by virtue of all qualities and by the generality of his actions;
Rudra by the generality of his qualities; and the others by the generality of their substance—this is the connection with the word "Brahmā" alone.
"By all [means] declared in the Vedas";
the word "ca" (and) serves to include both actions and substances;
the phrase "one should worship Hari" is understood to carry over.

The meaning is that Brahman alone is fit to worship Hari, who possesses infinite forms due to being endowed with all the qualities and activities mentioned in the Vedas; the word "ca" (but) has the sense of "tu" (however). Sarasvatī, however, worships him through the generalization of activity by means of the contraction of activity.
The meaning is that he worships Hari, who possesses infinite forms by virtue of being endowed with all the qualities mentioned in the Vedas;
he includes such actions as the "three-stride" (trivikrama) within His eternal strides and so forth.
By means of the commonality of qualities, he worships all His forms.
The meaning is that it contracts qualities and actions.
"Others" refers to Śakra and the rest.
As for substances and forms, the contraction of their qualities and actions is already established.
By this, the purport of the section beginning with “And likewise, because there is no difference, [the meditation] is the same” has been stated.
This section, however, precedes the one beginning with “But it is indeed the knowledge, because of the determination.”
Why, then, is there an explanation by way of transposition?
It is said:
because the object of cognition (*prameya*) is easily grasped when the context (*prakaraṇa*) is purified, the sequence has been broken.
For instance: since no inquiry whatsoever can find scope unless the essential nature of meditation (*upāsana*) is determined, its nature was first demonstrated;
thereafter, its necessity as a duty was established.
Immediately thereafter, when there arises a desire to know the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) for that [meditation], an inquiry into its suitability (*yogyatā*) and so forth follows.
Thus concludes the section on Knowledge (*vidyādhikaraṇa*).
[======= Section on the Duration of Authority (yāvadadhikārādhikaraṇa) =======]
Now begins the section on the extent of the functional capacity.
Oṃ. Those who hold office remain in their positions for as long as their term of authority lasts. Oṃ.
This has been explained in the commentary by the words "etad yathā-yathā" and so forth; however, that is not clear,
because the specific qualification of the governing context (*adhikāra*) is not stated as the cause.
Because by stating "in liberation," it is understood that this is not so in saṃsāra;
because by the mention of mere bliss, the exclusion of other qualities follows;
and because there is no specification of the substrata.
Therefore, he explains it clearly: "The qualification," etc.
The continued existence of those entrusted with office lasts as long as their term of office.
Through their specific offices, there is a distinction among deities and others by means of devotion, knowledge, bliss, and so forth.
"Adhikāra" means fitness.
Here, by the general statement, it is understood to apply both to liberation and to saṃsāra.
To the question, "If that is so, why was it said 'in liberation'?", he replies: "And in mokṣa."
... and especially with regard to liberation.
The general meaning is this; specifically, however, the connection is that it is liberation alone [that is attained].
In saṃsāra, due to the power of distraction, one's capacity to follow [one's] fitness is somewhat impaired.
Since devotion and so forth occur as a rule only according to one’s capacity due to the absence of such [capacities] in liberation, it was stated "in liberation.

If that were so, one might raise the objection that for those who are liberated, there would be the undesirable consequence of mutual hatred, envy, and so on, which would contradict their state of liberation; to resolve this doubt, the Sūtra states: “But there is no contradiction regarding the cognitions of the Imperishable, because of the commonality and its presence, as in the case of the Aupasadā [mantras]; that has been explained.”
This too is unclear;

for in the phrase "due to the equality of the absence of defects," no purpose for the word "equality" (sāmya) is seen. Furthermore, the expression "because there is [something] other than those who are superior" is understood to mean "because of their arising."
Furthermore, it is incorrect to say "like a disciple," because even in some cases, a disciple is seen to harbor hatred and other such feelings toward his teacher.
Therefore, he explains [the meaning] as "not."
"But there is an inclusion of those who hold views based on letters [of the Veda], due to the commonality and the presence of that [nature]; it is like the Aupasadā [rite]. This has been stated:

'There is no contradiction by that much, because [the teaching] is entirely faultless; for the views of others and those inferior to them are in every respect mere fallacies. (Brahmasūtra 3.3.33) (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 3.3.173)
To that extent, because of mutual inequality, there would be the consequence of hatred and so forth, which constitutes a contradiction to liberation.
The meaning of the word "equality" (sāmya) is "in its entirety.
The phrase "from those who are superior" is explained as being due to [the opponent's] fallacious appearance (ābhāsatva).
The construction is: "and because all those inferior to that are mere appearances.
Explaining this very point, he analyzes the example with the words: "since..."

Since all qualities and all actions of those who come later are invariably based upon the great favor of their predecessors, they should never harbor envy or similar feelings toward them, just as a good disciple does not feel such toward his teacher. (Manu 3.174)
The meaning is "like that of a good disciple toward his guru.
The Teacher will clarify this further below (*10.324*).
However, the ancient commentators on the Vṛtti explain these two sūtras differently.
Regarding the doubt as to whether liberation occurs for the wise immediately upon the arising of knowledge or not—if the former position were held, this is said in response:
