however, its efficacy regarding other objects is established. Even though this was accomplished by the practitioner solely for the sake of liberation, nevertheless, its capacity regarding those other objects arises from the power of its own nature.
Just as fire, although produced for the purpose of burning, also illuminates by virtue of its own nature;
thus [says] Bādarāyaṇa: "Oṃ, the human goal [is attained] from this [Veda], because of the word [itself]; Oṃ."

Regarding the doubt as to whether knowledge is a means to liberation through its entry into ritual action (*karma*), or whether it is an independent means, some explain that this [passage] establishes that independent knowledge alone is the means to liberation; however, that is incorrect,
because this very point has already been established by the statement "knowledge alone" (*vidyaiva*).

However, when the doubt arises as to whether knowledge accomplishes liberation alone or other human goals as well— and when the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) has been reached that knowledge accomplishes liberation alone because the wise have no attachment toward other persons— the author, intending to state the solution, explains this much: "Therefore, the human goal [arises] from this," beginning with the word "evam" (thus).
"Therefore, the human goal [is attained] from the Word," so says Bādarāyaṇa.
Thus, from the constant vision of the Lord, which has arisen free from defect, there is the attainment of the desired fruit... *11,2*

Therefore, the reference to "knowledge" (*jñāna*) as the subject of the pronoun *ataḥ* is not tenable, because in the preceding context, it was meditation (*upāsana*) alone that was the primary topic; for this reason, it was stated: "thus having arisen.
Indeed, meditation was not introduced as an independent subject, but rather for the purpose of beholding the Blessed Lord.
Therefore, the sense is that this too is indeed the subject at hand by virtue of being the goal to be accomplished.
Thus,
the mention of the Lord's faultlessness arising from the aforementioned form of worship should be understood as the introductory premise (*pātanikārtha*) for establishing that point.

Alternatively, if it were stated simply as "from the vision of the Blessed One," then even the vision of the Lord's incarnations by the Daityas and others would have to be considered a cause for the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*).
If it is argued that this is already precluded by the phrase "having arisen [in this way]," we say no;
for that phrase has fulfilled its purpose merely in demonstrating the relevant context (*prakṛtatā*).
If it is argued that, therefore, there is no vision of the image for them, let it not be so;
for that [vision] has liberation as its purpose.
But here, since another human goal (puruṣārtha) is under discussion,
it is therefore stated that [liberation comes] "from the faultless vision of the Blessed One.
By using the term "Blessed One" (bhagavat), he refutes the notion that non-dual knowledge (advaitajñāna) is what is intended here.

Because of the statement that "knowledge is fruit-bearing starting from the moment of its arising until its own [final] emergence," the attainment of the desired fruit occurs; thus, it excludes liberation alone. But is this not incorrect?
Since it is observed that even the intentions of the wise are sometimes rendered fruitless, he says: "Of that which has been commenced."
... because of not overstepping what has been undertaken. (Manu 3.4d)

The connection with the preceding [text] is as follows: "without overstepping the karma that has already begun" (*prārabdhakarma*). For knowledge obstructed by *prārabdha* does not even bring about liberation; therefore, it is an obstacle to that [liberation].
Even the intentions of the wise might become futile due to [the power of] destiny.
To show that there is a distinction even though knowledge is a cause for the goals of human life, he says: "O God."
For gods, sages, humans, and others, according to their respective species.
Here, by the word "jāti" (caste), the capable person is meant;
the connection is that the attainment of the desired fruit occurs.
By this, the intended meaning of the [sūtra] "not because of non-distinction" (*nāviśeṣāt*) is also stated. *11,5*
In this regard, knowledge (*jñāna*) is not itself an independent means for attaining heaven and other such goals; rather, it is action (*karman*) alone that is so.

Knowledge, however, is described as a means [to those goals] because it is a subordinate element (*śeṣa*) of action. This subordination is established by action alone, insofar as it bestows an excellence upon the human goal (*puruṣārtha*); thus, because it is subordinate, it is merely a commendatory statement regarding the human goal.

Having raised the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) through such sūtras as "As in other cases, so [says] Jaimini," the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) was established by Bādarāyaṇa himself in statements such as "But because of the additional instruction" and "Because it is seen to be so," demonstrating that knowledge independent of ritual action is itself the means for attaining heaven and other goals.
In this regard, the refutation of the proofs adduced by the proponent of the prima facie view is clearly set forth in the Bhāṣya.
To address how the contradiction with Jaimini’s view is to be resolved, he says: "That which was stated by Jaimini."
That which was declared by Jaimini pertains to human beings, as well as certain specific distinctions among them.
The fact that only action accompanied by knowledge is the means for attaining heaven and so forth is the domain of human knowers.
This is not merely what was stated by Jaimini; rather, others know that heaven and the like are attained through action alone and not by any other means:
"The invisible result (adṛṣṭa) itself is not perceived as being seen through knowledge."
Thus, those specific [doctrines] mentioned in the passage beginning with "some learned ones have said" and so forth, which are partial aspects of Jaimini’s system, belong to humans as well.
If one asks, "In what way are these partial aspects of Jaimini’s system? [the answer follows].
We say that they are similar insofar as both independent cognition and [Vedic injunction] serve as the means for attaining heaven and other such goals.
Just as humans are also divided into superior, middling, and inferior types, they indeed become subjects of diverse opinions according to their respective capacities.
Having thus explained the scope of Jaimini’s doctrine, he shows the scope of the author of the Sūtras’ doctrine with the words: "The universal."
The general rule has been proclaimed by the Blessed One...
The Blessed One has taught only in general that knowledge is the means for accomplishing all human goals;
he did not specify that knowledge must reside in a particular type of person.
Therefore, because these two views are determined by their respective general and specific scopes, there is no contradiction between them.
But surely, even a generality must reside in some particular instance; where then does this [generality] itself reside? To this he says: "Of the gods and so forth."
The doctrine of the Blessed One, having been specifically set aside by exceptions, remains established as pertaining to the domain of gods and so forth;
for although this matter is established from worldly experience itself—
that what remains as a generality is that which has excluded the scope of exceptions.
Nevertheless, for the sake of those with dull understanding, it has been stated by the Teachers.
He demonstrates the difference in the objects of the two views by means of another method, [saying]: "It is powerful."
When there is the presence of a powerful contradiction, the teaching of Jaimini and others is accepted.
In this context as well, the term "general statement" (*sāmānya*) refers to what was spoken by the Blessed One.
The Blessed One stated in general that knowledge is the means for accomplishing all human goals (*puruṣārtha*).

However, Jaimini and others, intending that knowledge does not function as a means to human goals when powerful obstructing karma exists, have stated that the attainment of heaven and other such results does not occur through independent knowledge alone.
Consequently, there is no contradiction because [the two] have general and particular objects as their respective domains.
Thus, the Blessed One’s doctrine stands as the object of unimpeded knowledge,
as it has been said:
"Because of the non-transgression of what has been undertaken.

Now, it cannot be said that this is not the subject matter of the views of Jaimini and others; for when there is a powerful contradiction, it is impossible for even ritual action (*karman*) to be a means for attaining heaven and so forth.
Not so;
for there is no rule that whatever action is an obstacle to a cognition is likewise an obstacle to that [cognition's] object,
since we observe otherwise in the world.
If it is asked, "How can this be so when there exists karma that obstructs the fruit? [the answer is:
in that case, the very karma that is the means to heaven and so forth does not arise;
or, even if it has arisen, it remains obstructed—what contradiction is there?
For it has been stated that the reasoning of Jaimini and others is not accepted in every case where a powerful contradiction exists;
and this established rule must be supplemented by the preceding established rule.
"Otherwise, a contradiction would arise.
Thus concludes the section on the purpose of the person (*puruṣārthādhikaraṇa*). [======= Section on Acting According to One's Will (Kāmacārādhikaraṇa) =======]
Now begins the section concerning acting according to one's own will.
Oṃ. Or rather, there is approval for the praise. Oṃ.
In this section, the existence of a distinction based on the right and wrong activities of the knower is established.

Thus, since this [section] aims to establish the general case of the ignorant, its inclusion within this quarter (pāda), which intends to demonstrate the power of knowledge, is not possible; therefore, he states the purport of the section:
"vikarma... (regarding forbidden action).
Or rather, it is for the sake of praise;
there is no taint from improper action anywhere for those who possess right view.

Although here the existence of a distinction between the wise and the ignorant is established explicitly through their respective engagement in right and wrong actions, nevertheless, the inclusion [of this verse] here is justified because it results in the attainment of the following meaning: that for those possessing right vision (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), there is never, in any case, the taint of performing prohibited acts (*vikarma*) in the manner to be described.
For the point is that the absence of the taint of prohibited acts does not exist for the ignorant.
As it has been said: "And some [hold that there is] freedom of action.

If it is asked, "In the absence of any taint from improper actions (*vikarma*), how can a distinction be admitted on account of engagement in what is not right?"—the answer is that a distinction is accepted for one who performs improper actions due to the loss of qualities such as bliss and the like.
It will be stated later that "the ointment is different from that.
In response to the inquiry as to whether for all wise ones there is the occurrence of improper action and the loss of qualities, he says: "and the loss of qualities."
And there is no loss of qualities for Brahman, because it is immutable.

For Brahman, however, there is no improper action whatsoever,
according to such statements as: "O dear one, my speech is never observed to be false."
There is no loss of qualities due to improper action (*vikarma*).
Even for the gods other than Hiraṇyagarbha, there is generally neither improper action nor loss of qualities;
however, the meaning is that there is a slight loss of qualities caused by minor improper action. (11.14)

If a transformation of the gods were possible, and by that [transformation] there were a loss of qualities such as bliss, then the scriptural rule—"this one is inferior to that by this much," "this one is superior to that by this much," or "this one is equal to that"—would be violated;
and thus the scripture would lose its authority.

Furthermore, a series of transformations of the counter-correlates (pratiyogi-paramparā-vikṛti) is not supported by any means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa). Therefore, he says: "of that which is already established" (kḷptasya).
... but in no way for that which has been prepared [for another]. *Mānava-dharmaśāstra* 3.4.5b.
The word "no loss" (*hāniḥ na*) carries over from the previous context.
The meaning is that for whichever deity whatever degree of excellence has been established, there is no loss whatsoever of that through any kind of improper action (*vikarma*).
If one asks, "In that case, what is the meaning of the statement that for deities there is a slight loss of excellence due to improper action? he says: "attained" (*prāpta*).
A loss of what has been acquired may occur at some point due to a great transgression.
By the word *prāpta*, that which is already present is meant.
Among the gods, nothing is lost by even a slight transgression (*vikarman*);
however, by a great transgression, there is only a diminution of the very quality already possessed.
It would be so.

For the sake of fulfilling one's own capacity, one should practice the means [of attainment] only to that extent; if one were to perform practices beyond that, there would be the consequence of [excessive] bliss and so forth, which ought not to exist.
If the gods were to perform practices exceeding what is required for the fulfillment of their own capacity, then the rule of gradation (tāratamya) would be violated.
For a deity who, having performed the means of worship without deficiency, does not commit a great transgression, must certainly be endowed with that quality;
for it is impossible that the propitiation of the Lord should be fruitless.
Nor is there any proof for the occurrence of a transformation in others at that very moment.
And because of that, the scripture would lack authority; therefore, he says: "Nevertheless."
Nevertheless, that is indeed established... // MAnu 3.4.5e //
Although the gods perform practices even beyond what is required for their own fulfillment,
nevertheless, a great and fixed transgression (vikarma) is ordained for them that obstructs those very practices:
"An effort exceeding one's own authority is in no way possible."
Because of the statement, "If one exerts some excessive effort, some fault might arise," it was said: "But for that which is already established, however it may be, it remains established as such."
He states the proof for both [positions] with the words: "Therefore..."
Therefore, there is no fixed rule regarding the time [of study].

The meaning is that because there is no deficiency in what has been prescribed, and because there is a rule regarding the attainment of results through further performance, there is no violation of the scriptural rules concerning gradations [of practice].
He cites an example of the stated point: "Like the moon," etc.
And for both Candra and Sugrīva, because they took wives who were their own superiors,
there was no loss of what had been acquired, nor indeed any loss of what had been ordained.
The word *ca* has the sense of "just as" (*yathā*).

Furthermore, there is even a decrease in the bliss of humans and others due to their improper actions (*vikarman*).
There would be a particular loss of merit in liberation through the offense of those who are in their exaltation.
It has been stated that for the gods, there is only the loss of what is acquired (*prasaktahāni*) through their improper action, but not the loss of what is already established (*kḷptahāni*).
In response to the inquiry as to how it is for those other than them, he says: "There is also diminution" (*hrāso 'pi*).
The word "even" (api) in the phrase "even of that which has been fashioned" (kḷptasyāpi) serves to include other cases as well.
The term "of bliss" (ānandasya) is an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa). "Diminution" (hrāsa) means non-manifestation.
And if that [attainment] were dependent on the will of Īśvara,
then since the veils of *prakṛti* and so forth have already been dispelled,
he says "specifically" (*viśeṣeṇa*) while determining it even in the case of improper actions (*vikarma*).
Due to an offense against one's own superior object, there occurs a specific diminution of bliss. "And some say [this applies] even by acting according to one's desire. Oṃ.
It might be argued as follows:

in this section, by the sūtra "and [the absence of stain] from an act done after knowledge, according to one's own will" (kāmacāreṇa caika iti), the absence of any taint for the knower due to an improper action (*vikarman*) performed after the arising of knowledge is stated;
likewise, by the sūtra "and [the destruction] of those prior to it by sublation" (tathopamardaṃ ca), the destruction of actions prior to knowledge by means of that knowledge is stated.
Both of these points are stated in the fourth chapter by the sūtra: "Upon attaining that [knowledge], there is the non-clinging and destruction of future and past sins.

If one asks how, then, this constitutes the fault of redundancy, he removes the charge of redundancy regarding the phrase "and one [is liberated] at will" by stating: "of that which follows knowledge."
And some say that by acting out of desire;
in the fourth [case], it is stated that there is no taint for one whose sin is overcome by knowledge.
In the fourth chapter, by the phrase "the non-adhesion of subsequent sin," the non-adhesion of sin following knowledge—that is, the absence of its fruit such as rebirth in hell—is stated.
He states another subject: "and impurity, etc."
The result of that [practice] is that impurity and other such conditions shall not affect him.

By the phrase "the non-clinging of future sin," it is stated that for this man of knowledge, the fruit of that [sin]—namely, impurity, unfitness for conversation, and so forth, which are the fruits of subsequent sins—shall not occur.
To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "In this regard... (atra).
In this context, the certainty of liberation as the very fruit of knowledge is stated.
In this third chapter, by the statement "and one [acts] according to his own will," the certainty of liberation as the fruit of knowledge is established;
the meaning expressed here is that the sins committed by a knower are unable to obstruct liberation, which is the fruit of knowledge.
Therefore, there is no fault of redundancy.
Oṃ, and the crushing [of obstacles], Oṃ!
To avoid the second redundancy and to explain the intended meaning of the term "upamarda," he says: "prārabdha... (beginning with the word *prārabdha*).
And there is the wearing away [of karma] (upamarda),

which occurs through knowledge regarding that portion already experienced— though it is unalterable once obtained, like death resulting from consuming poison— which arises solely from karma already set in motion.
...is declared here as "upamarda" (suppression)... // Manu 3.4.9a-e //
In the first half of the fourth chapter, the destruction of the essential nature [of karma] is described,
because of the statement "only that whose effects have not yet begun.
However, here in this third chapter, by the sūtra beginning with "and the crushing," the crushing of the fruit born of commenced karma by means of perfect knowledge is proclaimed.
However, this does not mean the destruction of either *prārabdha* (commenced) or *aprārabdha* (uncommenced) karma; thus, there is no fault of tautology.
Now, one might object: "Why was it not simply stated here that [the destruction is] of *prārabdha* karma? What is the purpose of mentioning the 'grasping of the fruit produced by it'?
This doubt should certainly not be raised.
For it has been stated, "But the others [are destroyed] by experience," which declares that *prārabdha* karma is destroyed only through experience;
thus, there would be a contradiction if one were to accept that it is destroyed by consciousness (*saṃvit*).
However, the slight destruction [of karma] occurs precisely through the medium of the fruit,
because actions are partless (*nirbhāga*).
But would it not follow that, by implication, the destruction of the fruit is itself stated to be the destruction of the action?
And thus, since the contradiction with the Sūtra "by means of experience" (bhogena) remains as it was, it is said: "of that which has been partially experienced.

It is not stated that there is a complete destruction of all the fruits of *prārabdha* karma by means of realization; rather, it is of that which has been partially experienced. Therefore, there is no contradiction with the Sūtra.
The sense is that karmas do not cause the knower to experience their own fruit as long as there remains one who is ignorant.
As it has been said:
"O dear one, no person whatsoever shall ever, in any way, wander through the cycle of worldly existence like others, provided they serve Mukunda."

Now, one might object: "Since it is traditionally taught that 'the performed action, whether auspicious or inauspicious, must necessarily be experienced,' and because the experience of the fruits of *prārabdha* (commenced) karma is remembered as being unavoidable, how can this [liberation] be possible? To this, it is said: "even of that which has been reached and is irreversible.
The meaning is: even of that which has presented itself and is impossible to avoid.
The meaning is: "even though it has occurred [in the mind] as something that cannot be turned back.
While it would have been sufficient to say merely "even of that which is irreversible," by using the term "that which has occurred" (*prāptasya*), he indicates the removal of a contradiction.
He provides an illustration for this: "poison," etc. (*viṣeti*).
Just as death resulting from the consumption of poison is indeed certain due to its irreversibility, yet it is not absolutely irreversible—
since recovery is seen through mantras, medicines, and the like that counteract poison—
so too the experience of the fruits of *prārabdha* karma is indeed certain due to its irreversibility, yet it is not absolutely irreversible.
Since it will be demonstrated later that cessation [of bondage] occurs through knowledge and other means,
the meaning of the statement "it must necessarily be experienced" should be understood as being like the statement "death is inevitable from consuming poison.
Generally speaking, the fruits of *prārabdha* karma must indeed be experienced.

Regarding the statement, "But they are crushed by means of exception," in response to the inquiry as to whether the crushing of the fruits of the *prārabdha* karma for all knowers (*jñānin*) is of one kind only or of various kinds, he says: "Of the gods and so forth.
In response to the inquiry as to whether the crushing of the fruits of the *prārabdha* karma for all knowers is of one kind only or of various kinds, he says: "Of the gods and so forth."
... for the gods and the others, respectively. (Manu 3.4.9)
"For those whose knowledge is greater, [their capacity] is greater," and so forth.
By this, the application of the sūtra "Not so, because there is no distinction," which is recited in the middle, is shown both in relation to what precedes and what follows.
This is what has been stated:
there is no destruction of *prārabdha* karma except through its experience;
however, it has been said that by the knowledge of Brahman, there occurs a diminution of its fruit.
In this regard, some hold the view:
"The majesty of the knowledge of Brahman is indeed inconceivable;
therefore, by its power, even those karmas that have already begun to bear fruit—as if they had not yet begun—are exhausted without their results being experienced."
Statements such as "Action that has not been experienced does not perish" refer to those who lack knowledge;
consequently, the word "all" in the passage "The fire of knowledge consumes all actions" remains uncontradicted.
Others, however, maintain that even those *prārabdha* (commenced) actions, empowered by the will of the Supreme Lord, necessarily yield their own respective fruits.
"There is no diminution of the fruit whatsoever.
Regarding this, he first refutes the initial position with the words "in its entirety" (*sarvātmanā*).
For indeed, the complete enjoyment [of results] belongs only to *prārabdha* (commenced) karma;

it would not occur even for one who has realized Brahman... // Mānava-dharmaśāstra 3.4.10a-c // Even for one who has realized Brahman, there would certainly be no complete enjoyment of *prārabdha* karma.
The meaning is that the view— that even those karmas already set in motion (prārabdha) are exhausted through the knowledge of Brahman alone, without the experience of their fruits—
is untenable; for if that were the case, there would be no remaining in the state of saṃsāra for those who know Brahman, because [their karma] would be seedless.
If it is argued that they assume bodies solely for the sake of favoring the world, we say no;
for in the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, there are abundant instances of their undergoing suffering due to causes such as curses.
Furthermore, the meaning of the word "hi" (for) is that the persistence of karma is understood from scriptural texts such as, "For him, there is delay only so long," and so forth.
To refute the second opinion, he says: "phalet" (it would bear fruit).
...but there is indeed a diminution of the fruit. (Manu 3.4.10d)
The phrase "of the karma already begun" (prārabdhasya karmaṇaḥ) continues [from the previous context].

The meaning is that this is based on scripture (āgama), which states: "Having uttered 'Om' and perceived this inner Self, and having destroyed both merit and sin, they act according to their desire and follow after Brahman."

To one who, having explained that the scope of *prārabdha* karma is determined by scripture, might say that there is not even the slightest diminution of the fruit of *prārabdha* karma, he replies with the words "sarvātmanā" (in every respect).
If there were a total loss of the fruit for karma that has not yet begun [to bear fruit], then the injunctions regarding optional rites would be rendered useless. ... (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 3.4.11a–c)
The meaning is "even slightly.

Here, the rules for expiation (*prāyaścitta*) intended for the purpose of removing diseases resulting from the ripening of karma such as the killing of a Brahmin are what are meant by "optional rules" (*kāmyavidhi*).
This is the sequence of subsequent steps here.

"An assassin of a Brahmin shall suffer from consumption," according to this traditional legal text (smṛti), consumption and similar ailments are indeed the fruit of killing a Brahmin and other such acts.
Therefore, the consumption and so forth produced therein are precisely the "commenced karma" (prārabdha) resulting from the killing of a Brahmin and the like.
Moreover, since cessation is observed through the performance of expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for that which consists of the exhaustion of the fruits of commenced karma (*prārabdhakarman*),
how can it be said that the fruit of commenced karma is not subject to annihilation in any way whatsoever?
Now, one might think:

Expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is not the cause for the cessation of [the fruit of] decay; rather, it is simply the exhaustion of karma that has begun to yield its experience (*bhoga*). If that were the case, the scope of expiation would become useless.
If it is argued that expiations will be merely occasional rites (*naimittika*), like [the offering of] a cow upon the burning of a house, we say no.

Since these [rites] are enjoined in conjunction with [results such as] the destruction [of sins] and so forth, it is illogical to postulate another result when the possibility of that very [destruction] as their fruit exists. Furthermore, the necessary posteriority [of the result to the action] remains unestablished here; this is what is meant by the term "kāmya" (optional/for the sake of a desired result).
If it is argued that, nevertheless, the knowledge of Brahman is not enjoined for that purpose, we say no;
for an injunction is postulated precisely by resorting to the result [itself].
By this very logic, the absence of the capacity of expiatory rites (prāyaścitta) to destroy karma is also refuted.
If that were the case, it would follow that the injunctions for expiation (prāyaścitta) are rendered useless;
furthermore, the view that [the fruit] is occasional (naimittika) has already been refuted because it entails the abandonment of what is perceived and the acquisition of what is unperceived.
Now, action possesses a twofold power.
One [type of demerit] indeed produces its fruit, while the other is the cause for being excluded from social intercourse.

If it is argued that the second is removed by means of penances (*prāyaścitta*), then this same logic applies to the penances for the ripening of karma as well; how then can there not be a sublation [of those karmas]?
Furthermore, not every disease nor every sin is a cause for being excluded from social intercourse; if that were so, penance would be rendered entirely useless.

Moreover, even one afflicted by consumption, leprosy, or similar ailments does not become fit for social intercourse merely by performing penance, but only upon the actual disappearance of the consumption and other such conditions;
therefore, it must be admitted that the purpose of penances is precisely to bring about the removal of those [defects].
Furthermore, there would be the consequence that expiatory rites for those facing death would become meaningless.
If it is argued that such [rites] exist for the sake of establishing social practices such as ancestral offerings (*śrāddha*), we say no;
for this would lead to the undesirable conclusion that they are absent for wandering mendicants (*parivrājaka*). Enough of this.
He summarizes: "Thus it has been said."

The word *iti* has the sense of "therefore. Although the exhaustion of commenced actions occurs only through their fruition, there nevertheless exists a reduction of the fruit; thus, the stated rule becomes justified—this is the remainder of the sense.
Regarding the meaning stated in the passage beginning with "Thus, the description of what has arisen," he cites the consensus of tradition (smṛtisammati) by saying "evamādi" and so forth.
Thus it has been clearly declared even today in the Tantrabhāgavata.
By the word "etc. (ādi), other [passages] relevant to this are included;
the meaning of the particle "api" is that they are also cited in the Bhāṣya and other works.

or else, it is a conjunction with the subject matter of the [current] section;
or else, by the phrase "and so forth" (*evamādi*), the subject matter of both sections is included.

In the section on the human goal (*puruṣārtha-adhikaraṇa*) and the section on praise (*stuti-adhikaraṇa*), the gradation of the fruit of knowledge was stated;
since that [gradation] regarding worldly fruits is not disputed, the subsequent text is intended to establish it with respect to the state of liberation (*mukti*).

For those who do not admit any distinction whatsoever in liberation, and for those who, even while admitting distinction, do not accept [qualities] such as bliss, there is no occasion for proving gradation; rather,
it is precisely the proof of distinction and so forth that must be undertaken,
and this will be done in the fourth chapter.

Furthermore, for those who, while accepting distinctions such as bliss (*ānanda*) and so forth, nevertheless do not admit a gradation (*tāratamya*) among them, this effort is made. There is no fault, as this is merely an elaboration of the meaning of the scriptural passage "as long as the office lasts" (*yāvad-adhikāram*). In that regard, he first establishes the gradation of bliss in liberation through reasoning, beginning with the words "the gradation."

If there were no gradation in the fruit [of their actions], how could the Śruti speak of Brahmā and the others as being "free from sin" and "unassailed by desire," and having declared their liberation,
further describe their respective gradations of bliss individually? (Manu Smṛti 3.4.12)

If there were no gradation (*tāratamya*) in the bliss of liberation— the fruit of knowledge— attained by Brahmā and the others, then how could the Vājasaneyins’ scripture, beginning with "He who is indeed the most successful among men," and the Taittirīyas’ scripture, beginning with "This is the inquiry into bliss," declare a gradation of bliss for those beings starting with Brahmā?
Without stating that "all [levels of bliss] increase a hundredfold each subsequent stage," the text speaks of them individually;
by this, one understands that there is a specific intended meaning (*tātparya*) therein.

To the objection—"What is the connection between the bliss of Brahmā and the others which the Śruti declares, and that which is established for the liberated souls?"—it is said: "free from blemish" (*avṛjina*).
And there are such passages as, "He who is a *śrotriya*, free from evil, and unhurt by desire," and so forth;
and the second [type of evidence] is the phrase, "of the *śrotriya* who is unhurt by desire.
Although it has been stated elsewhere that even the status of being a *śrotriya* is an indicator of liberation.

Nevertheless, because that [liberation] is to be accomplished through many preparations, it was not mentioned; yet, having declared liberation, he speaks of the gradations of bliss for those liberated ones.
The two words "ca" (and) indicate a mutual conjunction.
It will be understood later that the Taittirīya Śruti is also implied here. *11,33*

Anticipating the objection that the gradation of bliss mentioned in the two scriptural passages pertains only to the realm of transmigratory existence and not to liberation, he offers a rebuttal with the words: "In transmigratory existence..."
If this gradation exists only within saṃsāra and not in its primary sense,
then the meaning of the term "unassailed by desire" and our state of being free from sin would not exist.

This gradation has been stated [in the verse]; however, when "saṃsāra" alone is mentioned, it is not undesirable to the proponent (siddhāntin), because the subject matter of both the liberated and the unliberated will be explained later.
Therefore, what was said by the phrase "for this very reason" is an elaboration of that [point] itself, namely, that [the gradation] is not primary.
The suffix *tasi* is used in the sense of the locative case (*saptamī*).

The meaning is: "If it is argued that this gradation exists only within *saṃsāra* and not in liberation (*mokṣa*), which is the primary goal of human life (*puruṣārtha*)," then the meaning of the term *akāmahata*—namely, the state of being unassailed by desire (*akāmahatatva*) and the state of being free from evil (*avṛjinatva*)—would not apply [to liberation].
The word "proper" (*yuktam*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
For instance:

when it is said, "one who is learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), free from evil (*avṛjin*), and not overcome by desire (*akāmahata*)"—that is, regarding both "the one learned in the Vedas" and "the one not overcome by desire"—are such qualities as being "not overcome by desire" qualifiers of those transmigrating beings under discussion, or are they intended for the purpose of including other [kinds of] transmigrating beings?
Not the first,
because a qualification is meaningful only when [the qualified] is possible or when there is ambiguity;
and there are no such beings as Brahmā and others who possess qualities such as being unlearned in the Vedas (*aśrotriya*).
By this, [the objection] that this [definition] would serve to exclude deviation is addressed;
nor is it possible for those in saṃsāra to be "unassailed by desire" and so forth.
For this very reason, the second [alternative] is also refuted. (11.34)
But is it not the case that even among those in saṃsāra, qualities such as being unhurt by desire can somehow exist?
True;
we say that they do not exist in the primary sense.
Furthermore, it is not reasonable to accept a secondary meaning in the absence of a subverting reason (*bādhaka*).
By this, the statement "having declared liberation for one who is free from crookedness and untouched by desire" is explained.

To show how being untouched by desire and so forth is impossible for those in transmigratory existence (*saṃsārin*), he first establishes the impossibility of being untouched by desire with the words "of desire" (*kāmasya*).
"Wherever the desires of desire are attained, there make me immortal"—thus the Veda declares the defining characteristic of liberation, and it is an authoritative testimony. (Manu 3.4.14)
Whence else could there be an assault of desire? ... // MAnu 3.4.15a //
"In that world where the desires—that is, the objects of longing—of one's wish are obtained and fulfilled, make me there immortal and liberated"; this is a prayer addressed to Vāyu.

Because of this [statement], the Śruti declares the state of having all desires fulfilled (*āptakāmatva*) as the defining characteristic of liberation (*mukti*), since a qualifying attribute serves the purpose of excluding its opposite.

Because it is impossible to subvert the Śruti, which is more powerful due to its lack of room for alternative interpretation (*niravakāśatva*) and other reasons, how could the state of being unassailed by desire (*akāmahatatva*)— which is the removal of desires— possibly exist anywhere other than in the liberated one?

Since the Śruti declares that the fulfillment of all desires (*āptakāmatva*) is the defining characteristic of the liberated, such a state would be impossible among those in the cycle of transmigration (*saṃsārin*).
But how is it that being unaffected by desire is impossible? To this he says: "Having obtained... and so forth.
... that [state] belongs to one whose desires have been fulfilled. (Manu 3.4.15b)
That is the destruction by desire.
The cause of being undestroyed by desire is the state of having attained all desires. And in the absence of the cause, there can be no occurrence of that which is produced by it.
In this regard, it has been stated that the cause (nimitta)—namely, the state of having one's desires fulfilled (āptakāmatva)—is not possible among those subject to saṃsāra;
therefore, the effect (naimittika), which is the state of being unhurt by desire (akāmahatatva), is also impossible there.
He explains that the state of having one's desires fulfilled is the cause for the state of being unhurt by desire with the words: "without effort" (aprayatnena).
When the attainment of desires occurs without effort, that alone is the state of being unhurt by desire; how could it be otherwise?

The connection is with the term *sākāmahatā*. The meaning is that it is that which is understood from the word *akāmahata*. Otherwise, if there were no attainment of desires despite effort, for what reason indeed would there not be [the state of] being "great through the absence of desire"? For there would be no reason at all; thus, positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) have been stated.
This is what is meant:
being struck by desire (*kāmahatatā*) is indeed affliction caused by desire, and the absence of that is "not being struck by desire" (*akāmahatatā*).

Furthermore, it is established by experience that the absence of affliction caused by the objects of desire occurs only through the effortless attainment of those respective objects, and not otherwise.
Therefore, the relationship of cause and effect between the state of having one's desires fulfilled and the state of being unhurt by desire is indeed logical.
However, there is no such restrictive rule that this [state of being unhurt by desire] belongs only to one whose desires have been fulfilled.
If it is argued that the absence of affliction caused by the signs of desire does not occur otherwise [than through the absence of desire itself],
because even when desire exists, the absence of affliction caused by its signs is possible— [we ask:

Is this merely pointing out a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in what was stated, or is it being hoped that even among those transmigrating beings under discussion, the state of being "unassailed by desire" (*akāmahata*) is possible simply by virtue of being "desireless" (*akāmatva*), despite the absence of having all desires fulfilled (*āptakāmatva*)?
Not the first,
because of the addition of qualifiers according to the reasoning to be stated later;
nor the second.

Intending to show that this contradicts the inference—"Brahmā and others are not devoid of desire, because they possess unslumbering and non-deluded consciousness, like Devadatta"—he establishes the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of that inference with the words "of the conscious being" (*cetanasya*).
But where has it ever been seen that one who is conscious and not asleep is devoid of desire? (Manu 3.4.16ab)

The term "of the conscious being" (*cetana*) is stated in order to avoid the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of jars and the like. The term "of one who is not asleep" (*asupta*) is used to avoid that [fallacy] in the case of those who are asleep or unconscious;
it should also be understood as "of one who is not deluded" (*amugdha*).
Objection: But in deep sleep and in a state of fainting, one indeed does not cognize;
therefore, since the exclusion of those states is already established by the term "of the conscious one" (*cetana*) alone, the qualification is redundant.
Reply: Not so.
This is because by the word "conscious" (cetana), only the state of being a self (ātmatva) is intended.

For if the connection with consciousness (caitanya) were intended, then the opponent—fearing the audacity of having to accept the absence of desire—might also have to accept the absence of consciousness in Brahmā and others; thus, [the reason] would be unestablished (asiddhi).
This very point is indicated by the word "but" (tu).
The word "where" (*kutra*) is used in the sense of an objection.
The word "for" (*hi*) implies the reason that pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established;
or rather, the qualification "being awake" (*asuptatva*) and so forth need not be included as a property of the logical reason (*hetu*).
And this being the case, there is no risk of the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*),
because even during deep sleep and similar states, desire exists within the Self.
Nor does this lead to a contradiction with such scriptural passages as, "Where one is asleep and desires no desire whatsoever," or with the fact of non-perception [of desire in that state].

Since even for those desires that exist at that time, their non-perception and the conventional designation of their absence according to scripture are both possible due to their unmanifest state, the author—intending to show that the preceding qualification was employed with reference to manifest desires—states: "It is simply non-manifestation. (*11.38*)
The non-manifestation of desires is not their destruction, nor is it the case for delusion and sleep.
Destruction (*nāśa*) is non-existence (*abhāva*).
"Sleep" (*suptam*) means the state of sleeping (*suptiḥ*); the suffix *kta* is used here in the neuter gender to denote an abstract state (*bhāve*). (Pāṇini 3.3.114)
This might be the case: once the existence of desire during sleep and so forth is established, the postulation of the unmanifest (avyakti) is logical.
But how is that very [existence] established? To this he says: "yatkāmaḥ" (one who has a desire for what).
Why does one wake up with the very same desire with which one fell asleep? Why does one speak even against one's will? How can there be a lack of desire while one is asleep? (Manu 3.4.17)
Delusion (*moha*) is also to be understood here.
After the word "speaks" (*vyāharati*), the phrase "because of which" (*yataḥ tasmāt*) is to be supplied.
It is established by experience that Devadatta, desiring food and so forth, falls asleep and the like, yet when awakened, he sometimes speaks of that very same thing.
Therefore, from that specific utterance, it is inferred that he had a desire for that at that time and in that place;
yet that desire did not arise immediately after his rising, because Devadatta was still unconscious at that moment.
Indeed, the arising of desire occurs only when there is a broad perception [of an object] and a cognition that it is a means to achieve what is desired;

nor can this causal complex for desire be postulated as occurring spontaneously. Therefore, one must accept that the very same prior desire, which existed more intensely (or was unmanifest) during states such as deep sleep, persists and is subsequently manifested through the gradual acquisition of auxiliary conditions.
And so Patañjali has said:
"Ignorance is the field for the others—namely, those that are dormant, attenuated, interrupted, and active.
Since this is so, how could the Self be devoid of desire during states such as dormancy? (11.41)
But surely this reason, "being conscious," whether taken alone or as qualified, is inconclusive with respect to liberated beings (*mukta*), because they lack desire; to this he says: "all," etc.
He obtains all desires and, attaining liberation, goes together with Brahmā;
there he wanders about, laughing, playing, and experiencing delight.
"Taking whatever he desires as food, assuming whatever form he desires, and wandering through these worlds,
he remains singing the Sāman as one who is liberated"— this is established by the great authority of such scriptural passages.
How could one who is free from desire be liberated? ... // MAnu 3.4.20a //
By this [phrase], he cites the Śruti passage: “He enjoys all desires together with the wise Brahman”;
and by the word *paryeti* (he goes around), he cites: “There he moves about, laughing, playing, and rejoicing.”
The form *jakṣan* is correct because it belongs to the Vedic language.
By the term *kāmānnī*, [the text refers to] the passage: "Moving through these worlds at will, assuming forms at will, he sits singing this Sāman."
By the word "etcetera" (ādipadena), there is an inclusion of passages such as "he becomes one-fold.
The ellipsis to be supplied is: "because of the understanding that desire exists by force [of these texts].
Even though these scriptural passages do not explicitly state the existence of desire for one who is liberated;
Nevertheless, by virtue of its capacity, it indeed makes that [meaning] understood.

This is what is meant by the phrase "by the force of direct statement" (*śrutibalāt*). And since that capacity is indeed non-deviant and not merely a matter of possibility, he expresses this with the word *sat* ("existent").
For instance:
objects are called "desires" (kāma) because they are the objects of desire,
since the suffix *ghañ* is prescribed after a verbal root in the sense of the object (*karman*).
And regarding the statement, "By that, he enjoys all desires," because of its proximity, it would mean that he enjoys those objects which have become the objects of his desire through his actions;
for what kind of attainment of desires could there be for one who is free from desire and is like a stone?
Furthermore, activities such as wandering about, which are the effects of desire, are not possible without desire.
The recollection of women by one who is free from desire is utterly impossible;
furthermore, food and other such things possess the nature of objects of desire precisely because they are desirable—thus, as before, there is an understanding of "desire" (kāma).

Although there are clear scriptural statements here such as, "If he becomes desirous of the world of the fathers," and so forth, these examples are nevertheless provided so that the disciples may reflect upon the underlying reasoning.
"Because the liberated one lacks desire, there is no inconclusiveness of the reason.
[Objection: But even in the absence of desire for the liberated, it is said: "When all desires that dwell in his heart are released, then the mortal becomes immortal; here he attains Brahman."*11,43*
There is a scriptural passage beginning with these words.
To the question, "How then is the possession of desires ascertained?", he says: "The desires which belong to him."
"...the desires that reside in his heart"—
thus the Śruti speaks precisely of the liberation of those desires situated within the internal organ.
The grammatical connection is "thus says the Śruti";
and the phrase "only for those situated within the internal organ" means that it is not so in every respect.
The word *hi* has the sense of "because";
therefore, the connection is: "How could one who is free from desire be liberated?
To the question, "Why is the meaning of the scripture restricted [in this way]?", he says: "In the heart alone," and so forth.
... "in the heart"—if this were not so, the qualification would be meaningless. Mānava 3.4.20ef.
If this scriptural passage were not explained according to the manner stated above—
that is to say, if it were explained in every respect as being intended to convey the absence of desire—
then the qualification of desires as "residing in the heart" would be entirely redundant.
Because there is nothing else to be excluded,

the Śruti, by employing this qualification, conveys this meaning: that in liberation there is an absence of only those desires which are transformations of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), due to the very non-existence of the internal organ itself, but not because of the persistence of all desires that constitute its essential nature.
This might be so,
if this were a qualification;
but it is not so.
Because there is nothing to be excluded [from the mind].
According to the Śruti statement, "All this is indeed the mind," it is understood that all desires are merely transformations of the mind and that desire is not an attribute of the Self.
Therefore, suspecting that the phrase "residing in the heart" is merely a description of their essential nature, he refutes this with the words: "only in the heart."
The view that "this [Veda] is their refuge in the heart" does not appear as a tenable position.
It shines— that is, it appears splendid— within the internal organ alone, in relation to those desires.
To the question "Why does he not speak?", he says: "Of those who are liberated."
The scripture states in various branches that even for those who are liberated, there is the fulfillment of their desires.
The meaning is "even for those devoid of the internal organ" (antaḥkaraṇa).
The connection is: "therefore it does not shine," because of which [reason].
The scripture has been cited previously.
But surely this is incorrect;
for it is argued that this scripture, which was presented as an opponent to the previously cited scripture, is likewise subject to sublation.
Not so.
Because the previously cited scripture possesses greater force and is thus capable of sublation;
for instance,
the scriptural injunction regarding desire (*kāma-śruti*) is indeed without any other scope [for application].
However, the scriptural statement regarding the non-existence of that [mind] has scope according to the manner already explained;
even when there is doubt as to whether it is intended as a description of the nature of the qualifier, it does not lack scope.
All of this—that the scriptural statement "all this is mind alone" also has scope—was stated in the *Sāṅkhyādhikaraṇa*.
Furthermore, the scriptural injunction regarding desire exists in all branches (śākhās), as it has been cited in that very manner;
whereas the scriptural statement regarding its absence occurs only in certain places. Therefore, how can there not be a relationship of sublation and that which is sublated?
This is what was stated as "in the separate branches.
He concludes the meaning expressed by the verse beginning with "where [the desire] of one," with the words "therefore" (*ataḥ*).
Therefore, freedom from being overcome by desire belongs primarily only to those who are liberated.

The meaning is as follows: the absence of affliction caused by the signs of desire (*kāmanimittopadrava*), which is the state of being unhurt by desire (*akāmahatatva*), is established precisely through the states of being without desire (*akāmatva*) and having attained all desires (*āptakāmatva*).

Since the state of being without desire is impossible in anything other than a conscious being (*cetana*), and since the state of having attained all desires—being the very definition of liberation—is possible only there and impossible in those who are not liberated, it is established that this quality belongs exclusively to the liberated. This is the remainder of the argument. *11,46*
True. While, according to the primary sense, the state of being unassailed by desire is possible only for those who are liberated,
nevertheless, because of the absence of the many afflictions caused by desire, it is indeed applicable— even if only in a secondary sense— to Brahmā and others as well.
If it is asked, "In that case, why should transmigrating beings themselves not be what is propounded by the Śruti?"—
is the abandonment of the primary meaning made because of the existence of a subverting factor (bādhaka), or is it done in vain?
It is not the first [alternative].
Because that [primary object] is absent,
and because fallacious sublaters (bādhakābhāsa) will be refuted later,
he refutes the second [position] with the words: "of the primary meaning" (mukhyārthasya).
The pointlessness of abandoning the primary meaning is an ornament only for those who employ deceptive means.
Only those who lack discernment, such as the proponents of Māyā and others, abandon the primary meaning without any subverting evidence;
for they reject the Supreme Lord as the literal referent and instead accept the definition of the Nirguṇa (the qualityless).
But this is not the case for the knowers of Nyāya.
Freedom from sin, freedom from suffering, and freedom from crookedness are declared here [to be the results].

Having thus stated the impossibility of being untouched by desire (*akāmahatatva*) in those who are not liberated, and now intending to state [the impossibility] of being free from crookedness (*avṛjinatva*) as well, he first explains that freedom from crookedness: "being sinless" (*apāpatva*).
The construction here is as follows: "being free from crookedness" (avṛjinatva) means, first of all, being free from evil (apāpatva) and being free from suffering (aduḥkhatva).
To the question "Why is this so?", he says: "Because it is unpleasant" (apriyam).
The unpleasant, the crooked, suffering, and the sting—these are what is meant by "it is said. (Manu 3.23cd)
"Because it is the cause of that, it is called 'pāpa' or 'vṛjina'";
thus was the meaning of the name explained by the Lord himself in the *Śabdanirṇaya*.
The connection is that [it] is expressed by words such as "suffering" and "unpleasant.
Because it is the cause of that— that is, because it is the cause of suffering—
it is like saying, "curd and cucumber are fever," where they are perceived as being directly the fever itself.
By this it is stated that the word *vṛjina* is primary in the sense of suffering (*duḥkha*),
while its application to sin (*pāpa*) is based on the principle of denoting that which is for the sake of that [suffering].
For this very reason, the word "or" (*vā*) is used.
The meaning of the word *nāman* is the meaning of the word *vṛjina*.

The point is that if the word *vṛjina* has meanings such as "suffering," then it is already established that the word *avṛjina* has meanings such as "absence of suffering. To the question, "What follows if being free from sin (*apāpatva*) and so forth is the meaning of the word *avṛjina*? he says: "And being free from sin... (*apāpatvaṃ ca*).
Indeed, as long as saṃsāra exists, there is no absence of sin for this person;
for even for the man of knowledge, there remains the suffering resulting from previously commenced sin.
The word "ca" (and) has the sense of a conjunction of what is about to be stated. "Of this jīva":
the word "hi" (for/indeed) is for the purpose of indicating the reason, namely "because of being subject to transmigratory existence."

Regarding the scriptural passage beginning with "like the tuft of a reed," since there is an absence of sin for the knower, one might ask how this [scripture] can be so; therefore, it is said that [the scripture concerns] "that which has begun.
The sense is that the scripture refers to what has not yet begun (*anārabdha*).
The connection is that even for the knower, there certainly exists sin that has already begun (*ārabdha*).
The meaning of the word "hi" (for/indeed) is that suffering certainly exists because of the presence of evil.
Therefore, it is established that freedom from blemish (*avṛjinatva*) is also impossible except for those who are liberated.
Some explain this scriptural passage otherwise.

Furthermore, the scriptural statement, "He who is learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), free from evil (*avṛjin*), and untouched by desire (*akāmahata*)," as well as the phrase "of one learned in the Vedas and untouched by desire," is not intended for the inclusion of liberated beings (*mukta*).
Rather, it refers specifically to human *gandharvas* and others under discussion;
nor is such a state impossible in their case.
Because of the traditional teaching (smaraṇa) that "a Śrotriya is one who has studied the Veda," the word *śrotriya* has as its cause the mastery of the Vedas (*chandas*).

Furthermore, since humans, Gandharvas, and others are almost like omniscient beings, even though the presence of commenced karma (*prārabdha-pāpa*) may exist, they do not commit sin at that time; thus they are described as being "free from blemish" (*avṛjina*).
And because they are endowed with dispassion toward sense objects, they are "unassailed by desire" (*akāmahata*).
Nor is it correct to say that [the qualification] is redundant because there is nothing to be excluded;
for we do not state "being a Vedic scholar" (*śrotriya*) and so forth as a qualifying attribute.

Rather, when it has been stated that human *gandharvas* possess a hundredfold more bliss than humans, this [qualification] is mentioned in response to the expectation for a reason regarding that matter.

Thus, when there arises the inquiry as to why the gods' gandharvas are said to possess a hundredfold greater bliss than the human gandharvas, the reasons such as being learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) are stated.
This applies likewise to the subsequent cases as well.
Nor should it be argued: "How can qualities such as being learned in the Vedas, which exist in all [the preceding stages], be the cause for the excellence of bliss?"
"A human gandharva is even more distinguished than a human because he is a *śrotriya*, free from vice, and not overcome by desire.
Since each subsequent one possesses qualities such as being a *śrotriya* to a greater degree than each preceding one described, this is the explanation.
He refutes that [interpretation] with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*).
Therefore, the notion that "from each [of these] there is a lack of desire" is an assumption not found in the scripture.
This is the meaning:
therefore, compared to each preceding item previously specified, each subsequent one possesses a greater degree of lack of desire (*akāmatva*).
This is an illustrative indication (*upalakṣaṇa*).
If one were to explain it as "and [the status of] a *śrotriya* and so forth," there would be the postulation of what was not heard in the text;
for in that case, one would have to postulate both "therefore" (*tasmāt*) and "with excellence" (*atiśayena*), which are not explicitly stated.
Otherwise, the intended meaning could not be obtained.
He states another fault: "akāma... etc.
By the statement "struck by lack of desire," the abandonment of what has been heard is also clearly implied.

Since it is stated that [the person] is "struck down by desire for what has been heard," and since the opponent has explained [the compound] as "desireless" (*akāma*), the abandonment of the word "heard" (*śruta*) and its replacement by the word "struck down" (*hata*) also becomes evident.
For there is no purpose whatsoever for the word "struck down" [in this context].
Therefore, because it entails the abandonment of what is heard in the text and the adoption of what is not, this interpretation is incorrect. *11,52*
Others, however, explain it thus:
the phrases "he who is a *śrotriya*" and "of a *śrotriya*" refer neither to those already mentioned nor to the human *gandharvas* and so forth under discussion, but rather to other persons.
For it is as follows:

The bliss of human *gandharvas* is a hundred times that of humans, Ānanda. Furthermore, for another who is learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), free from blemish (*avṛjin*), and devoid of desire for the state of a human *gandharva*, his bliss is likewise a hundred times that of humans and equal to that of a human *gandharva*. Thus, it is stated here that for one who is free from desire regarding various states, there is a corresponding equality of bliss with those respective states.
Nor should it be argued: "Since those who are dispassionate have no desire for anything at all, how can this statement regarding gradation be made?
For what is intended here is the existence of desire in states other than that [of total dispassion].
Indeed, the meaning sought to be established here is: "Whoever is liberated from a certain amount of exertion, he possesses a corresponding degree of bliss."
This too is refuted by the very consequence of abandoning what is heard and imagining what is not heard;
for here too, the word *hata* would have to be supplied because it lacks a purpose,
and the phrases *tasmin pade* and *sakāme* would have to be imagined elsewhere.
He states an additional fault with the words "in some cases" (kutracit).

"In some cases, due to the absence of desire in a man who possesses desire, there is the experience of the enjoyment of happiness like that of Indra and others; this [claim] contradicts experience. In the interpretation that "in certain instances—namely, in positions other than those of Indra and others—a man possessed of desire experiences the enjoyment of a happiness equal to that of Indra and others because his desire for those specific positions is absent," there is a contradiction with experience (*anubhavavirodha*).

For one who does not desire sovereignty, the fact that the experience of pleasure equal to that of a king is sublated by actual experience is evident. If it is argued that the reality should not be sought because of the praise of dispassion (*vairāgya*), we say no; this Self is of the nature of infinite bliss, but it does not manifest as such due to the obscuration caused by afflictions such as desire.

Therefore, since this section has been introduced for the purpose of demonstrating the principle that to the extent that desire is exhausted, to that same extent an increase in bliss is observed, [one might object]: "The intent here is directed toward the increase of bliss, and one should not place excessive emphasis on the hundredfold multiplication. If you say this, we reply: no.
Because one who desires the position of Indra does not perceive any particular excellence of bliss compared to one who desires the position of a god;
therefore, what is the meaning of the Vedic text? To this he says: "Therefore... (*tasmāt*).

Therefore, having separately stated the gradations of happiness for those who are not yet liberated, the Śruti declares, "And he [is the one] among the liberated," thus expressing the gradation of happiness even for those who are liberated; this is indeed elegant... // MAnu 3.4.28a-e //
Since the perception of a different meaning has been refuted,
the gradations of happiness associated with non-liberated beings such as humans and others are stated individually by the phrases "those who [have a hundred]," and so forth; then,
by the phrases "he who" and "of the learned one," the gradations of happiness among liberated humans, gandharvas, and others are expressed.
The explanation that "the Śruti says so by means of extended application (atideśa)" is indeed elegant.
[Objection: But if this were the case, the fault of syntactical split (vākyabheda) would arise.
[Response: Not so.
He says "and that" (tacceti), because of the existence of an indicator (jñāpaka).
And that [is] understood from the word "and" (ca) itself.
The fact that the subject matter of the sentence beginning with "yaśca" is something other than what has been under discussion is understood by the word "ca" (and) itself;
the meaning is: how much more so when there is the aforementioned logical inconsistency within a single sentence?
For this word "ca" is perceived as an indicator of conjunction (*samuccaya*).
Likewise, one says "Devadatta the wealthy" and "Yajñadatta [the wealthy]";
however, such a construction is not appropriate when there is identity of referent.
For one does not employ the expression, "Vasiṣṭha is the most proficient in the Vedas and the husband of Arundhatī."
If it is asked, "Why should the word *ca* not signify a conjunction of qualifiers?"—we say no;
because there is no subverting reason (*bādhaka*) for its primary meaning, it is improper to abandon it.
Furthermore, a shift in the syntactical construction (*vacanavyatyaya*) is quite evident when [the sentence] is taken as a single unified statement.

Indeed, that which is the hundredfold bliss of the gods by birth through karma is but a single unit of the bliss of the gods by birth (ājānadeva), provided they are learned in the Vedas, free from evil, and untouched by desire.
Likewise, that which is a hundred human joys is one joy of the human *gandharvas*, for those who are learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) and are unaffected by desire (*akāmahata*). [Objection:
If this is so, then how is it that the passage from the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* was explained in the Commentary as referring only to those who have just been liberated?
[Response: The phrase "and whoever" (*yaśca*) is stated with the intent of including a specific qualification.
This is the intention of the author of the Bhāṣya:
in every respect, these two statements have distinct objects;
even if one were to assume they form a single syntactical unit, let it be taken as referring only to those who have been liberated.
In that regard, because the logical impossibilities (*anupapatti*) are few,
it is not the case that [the teaching] has as its object only those who are not yet liberated, due to the abundance of logical impossibilities.

It is incorrect to say that two scriptural passages declare that for those from humans up to Hiraṇyagarbha— both those who are not liberated and those who are liberated— the bliss increases hundredfold at each successive stage.
The teaching regarding the "delight of men" [is given] because there is no mention of liberation.

Anticipating the objection that "nothing else, such as freedom from being overcome by desire and so forth, is heard of there," he explains the meaning of the scripture with the passage beginning with "attained" and ending with "beholds."
In that regard, first, the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka* shows the indicator for one who has been liberated as a human being: "He is successful" (*rāddha*).
"One who is *rāddha* (successful) is one who has attained perfection (*saṃsiddha*); thus he is understood to be liberated (*mukta*) alone.

One joined with the virtuous Viṣṇu is considered a liberated youth. In the opening sentence, "He who among men is *rāddha*, that is, prosperous," the word *rāddha* refers exclusively to the liberated one, not to one who is unliberated.

By what function [is it denoted]? By primary denotation (abhidhā) alone, and not by metaphorical indication (upacāra), such that the impossibility of the primary meaning and so forth would need to be explained.
How so? Because it is "well-established" (saṃsiddha).
This is what is meant:
the root *rādh* is recited in the sense of "accomplishment" (*saṃsiddhi*).

And regarding the root *rādh*, [it is stated in Pāṇini 3.4.72]: "The suffix *ktvā* (or *lyap*) is optionally used after roots meaning 'motion' (*gatyartha*), those that are 'intransitive' (*akarmaka*), as well as *śliṣ*, *śīṅ*, *sthā*, *āsa*, *vas*, *jan*, *ruh*, and *jṛ*."
Thus, because the root is intransitive, the suffix *kta* denotes the agent;
consequently, it is said that he is "accomplished" (*rāddha*) or "perfected" (*saṃsiddha*).
And this perfection is indeed liberation, because it is a "correct accomplishment" (*samīcīna-siddhi*) by virtue of its permanence and its being unmixed with suffering.
The other [state] is not [the meaning], because it is improper due to its impermanence and its being permeated by suffering;
and when the primary meaning is possible, one cannot accept a secondary meaning.
Thus, the word "prosperous" (*samṛddha*) also denotes only the liberated one.
Because perfect greed (*samyag-ṛddhi*) is impossible without liberation (*mukti*).
However, [the status of] being the sovereign (*adhipati*) and so forth for others is common to both those who are liberated and those who are not.
And how it is possible in the case of one who is liberated has been explained in the Bhāṣya. *11,60*

Now, demonstrating the evidence from the Taittirīya Śruti that indicates the liberated human being, he explains the words beginning with "yuvā syāt" (he should be young) as follows: "sādhunā" (by means of what is good).
One who is joined with a virtuous Viṣṇu is considered a virtuous youth who is liberated.
Since youth is eternal for this liberated one, he is "the Youthful" (Yuvan); and because he has attained the fruit of study, he is called an "Adhyāyaka" (one who studies).
He is praised as "learned" (āśiṣṭa) because he has attained the bliss of the cessation [of mental fluctuations],
and he is designated as "most steadfast" (dṛḍhiṣṭha) because he remains established without deviation.
And by his very nature, he becomes strong and liberated alone.
For one who is faultless is called "good" (*sādhu*); and there is no one other than Viṣṇu who is faultless. Therefore, it is said, "by the good Viṣṇu."

When the word *sādhu* is used as an upapada at the end of the third case, from the root *yu* (meaning "to mix") with the suffix *kvanip*— according to the rule "it is seen after others as well"— the form *sādhuyuv* arises;
or alternatively, from the root *yuj*.
This is the form of the word *yoga*.
By the force of the inclusion of the root *dṛś* (to see), there is an elision of the final part of the verbal root.
Thus, it is stated that one possesses liberation characterized by proximity to the Blessed One.
The term *yuva* (the youthful) is explained first, even though it occurs later in the sequence, because the word *yuva*—which denotes excellence—is an indicator of the liberated one (*mukta*).
Although the word *yuva* is based on the occasion of youth, nevertheless, between the primary and the secondary meanings, understanding applies to the primary; thus, eternal youth must be accepted.

And that [eternal youth] is appropriate only for this liberated human being, not for one in the cycle of transmigration (*saṃsārin*); for this reason, he who is "youthful" is indeed the liberated one.

Although the word *adhyāyaka*— derived from the root *iṅ* meaning "to study," preceded by the prefixes *āṅ* and *adhi*, and formed with the suffix *ṇvul*— denotes one who performs correct study, nevertheless,
because the context here concerns human goals (*puruṣārtha*) and study itself is not a human goal, this term must be interpreted as indicating the attainment of the fruit of study.
And that fruit of study has been obtained by him alone [the teacher] through his liberation.
Because liberation alone is its fruit,
for that reason the teacher is said to be truly liberated.
He is an "āśa" because he possesses tranquility (*śama*) completely and in every respect.
One who is most swift (*āśiṣṭha*) is so because of extreme speed;
and "rightness" (*samyaktva*) and so forth consist precisely in the absence of decline and the like.
Therefore, by virtue of attaining full bliss according to one's fitness for non-decline, the liberated one alone is proclaimed as "most swift."
For "firm" (*dṛḍha*) is [the form] without modification;
"most firm" (*dṛḍhiṣṭha*) means exceedingly firm.
Because it is Vedic, the substitution of *ṛ* for *ṛt* applies according to the rule: "The *ṛ* of a light syllable followed by a consonant [is replaced by *ra*]."
This is not so;
for one who remains liberated, there is no attainment of anything other [than that state], and because he is supremely changeless, he is called "most firm" (*dṛḍhiṣṭha*).
One who possesses strength is "strong" (*balī*).
"Balistha" means exceedingly powerful;
and "exceedingly" refers to being natural.
One who is powerful by nature becomes liberated solely through that [nature].
"Not one who is not liberated;
therefore, he alone is called the most powerful.
[Objection: But for one who is liberated, it is said: "This entire earth might be full of wealth for him."
To the question, "How is it appropriate to speak of his being a lord of the earth filled with wealth? he says: "Of him..."
"This earth belongs to him," and so forth, is said with reference to his prior state of existence.
The state of being "prior" is non-liberation; for it is with the intention of referring to both liberated and unliberated humans that the passage beginning with "he may be young" was commenced.

In this context, the meaning is that while the passage beginning with "he may be young" establishes the liberated one, the subsequent statement beginning with "of him" (*tasya*) proceeds with the intention of referring to the unliberated.
By this very principle, other passages such as "the lord of others" and so forth should be understood as pertaining to the unliberated.

Now, one might raise the objection that if it is admitted that passages such as "one should be young" refer both to the liberated and the unliberated, there would be a contradiction with the perception that they have a single subject matter. To dispel this doubt, instead of simply saying "the liberated," the term "prior state" (*pūrvabhāva*) is used.
It is the very same conscious being who is denoted by words such as "young"; it is merely through the distinction of its various states that these specific attributes are established.
The single conscious entity alone is denoted by words such as "youth" and so forth;
its specific qualifiers are established according to the differences in its states.
Therefore, the appearance of a single object is not untenable. *11.66*

Thus, by describing [the passage] from the Vājasaneyi Śruti beginning with "He who, indeed, among men... and ending with "...is the most perfect," as well as the Taittirīya Śruti beginning with "He should be young... and ending with "...should be full," as referring to both the liberated and the non-liberated, [it is shown that] "that is the supreme bliss of men. Then...

Since it is established that the statement, "Whatever is a hundredfold joy of men, that is one human joy," refers to both the liberated and the unliberated, [the author] explains the passage from the Taittirīya Śruti—"That is one joy of the human Gandharvas, and of the learned man who is untouched by desire"—as follows: "That is one... and so forth.
Having stated that "he alone" experiences happiness within the course of worldly existence,
he further declares that for the Vedic scholar there is a hundredfold nature of liberation.
"Having spoken of the happiness pertaining to saṃsāra" means having spoken of the happiness of a worldly human being, which is a hundred times greater than [the happiness of] other worldly humans.

"The state of being a hundred times greater than the liberated" means that the scripture— this being the understood remainder of the sentence— declares that the liberated gandharva possesses a nature of happiness that is a hundred times greater than the happiness of a liberated human being.

Intending to show that by this very same logic, the passage beginning with "those who are the hundred joys of the human Gandharvas" should be explained, he says—referring to the statements "he is one" and "of the Śrotriya"—"saṃsāragāditi. (*11,67*)
And from one who has entered the cycle of existence, for one who has likewise entered the cycle of existence, [the merit] is more than a hundredfold;
for one who is liberated, for one who is liberated... // MDh 3.134a-c //
The meaning is: compared to the happiness of worldly humans, gandharvas, and so forth.
Having stated that the happiness of those belonging to the realms of cyclic existence—such as gods and gandharvas—is more than a hundredfold, exceeding it by a factor of one hundred;

the phrase "of the liberated from the liberated" means that he declares the happiness of liberated gods, gandharvas, and so forth, to be a hundred times greater than the happiness of liberated humans, gandharvas, and so forth.

By this, it is stated that having referred to both "those hundred" and "this one" together as a single expression, their respective states of possessing a hundredfold bliss are then described separately through the phrases "he is one" and "of the learned Śrotriya.
In this very manner, the Vājasaneyi-śruti passage beginning with "that one [bliss] of the ancestors," and so forth, is also to be explained.
Since the word "liberated" (mukta) is heard at the outset, [it refers to one] born [in that state]...

Because of the hearing of the phrase "and he who is a Śrotriya" [in the verse] beginning with "to a god, etc.," the phrase "and he who is a Śrotriya" must also be understood as recurring in the middle [of the passage].
As for the contradiction between the two scriptural passages, it has been resolved elsewhere by the venerable Bhagavatpāda.
He concludes the explanation of the two scriptural passages with the words: "it would be appropriate."
...it would be appropriate for one who has observed what is declared in the Śruti.
For one who looks upon what is stated in the Śruti, observing it and investigating it thoroughly, this very explanation would be appropriate by means of the intellect (*mati*).
Alternatively, "looking upon" (*abhivīkṣa*) means observation, which is thorough investigation; therefore, this alone, as stated in the Śruti, would be appropriate.
Having thus established the gradation in liberation through the Śruti, he establishes it further through reasoning with the words, "And it is reasonable."
And it is logical that, due to the superiority of their means of accomplishment, there is a superiority of what is to be accomplished among the gods and others.

The meaning is that in the case of the gods and others, the superiority of the goal (sādhya) over humans and others—the superiority of the fruit attained upon liberation—is both logical and inferred because of the superiority of the means (sādhana).
What is being stated is this: the gods and others possess a superior fruit of liberation compared to humans and others, because they possess superior means relative to them.
To the objection that this reason is "inconclusive" (aprayojaka) due to the absence of a subverting argument (bādhaka) in the contrary case, he says: "Not [a matter of] superiority."
