If there were no excellence in the goal to be accomplished, why would there be effort in the means?
The words "in the case of liquor and so forth" (surādiṣu) and "from humans and so forth" (mānuṣādibhyaḥ) carry over [from the previous rule].
This applies when there is an instrument (sādhana), or an excess of instruments (sādhanādhikye).
If gods and others did not possess superior pearls compared to humans and others, then they would not exert effort for the sake of attaining those superior results.

Furthermore, those who undertake excessive effort for the sake of a result that is not superior would not be considered discerning. Thus, because there is a subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against the contrary position, the reason is not "unestablished" (*aprayojaka*).
To the objection that it might be "unestablished in its own nature" (*svarūpāsiddha*) due to a lack of evidence, he says: "And effort... (*yatnaśca*).
And a truly great effort is observed on the part of those high-souled ones.

The great effort and the superior performance of the means for liberation by those gods and others—who are to be inferred from their possession of great fruits—compared to humans and the like, is indeed seen through the instruments of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
The intention is that we shall also state those [means].
He establishes the pervasion (*vyāpti*) with the words "where... (*yatra*).
Where there is an abundance of means, there an abundance of results is invariably seen. // MAnu 3.4.36c-e //
In whatever person there is an abundance of means relative to something else, an abundance of the result relative to that same thing is invariably observed;
this is seen in the world among farmers, merchants, royal servants, and others, as well as in the Veda among those who have established the sacred fires and so forth.

The meaning is that, by the rule that "whoever possesses a superior means of accomplishment (sādhana) possesses a superior result of accomplishment (sādhya)," this is indeed perceived through those respective means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).

However, one who is ignorant of the gradations in the fruits of establishing sacred fires and so forth, and who— observing in cases such as plowing— that the gradation in grain and the like depends on other causes and is not governed by the gradation in means such as plowing, might disagree even regarding the illustrative examples (dṛṣṭānta).
He replies to that with the words: "If not."
...if not, they would not easily exert effort. MĀnuv 3.4.36ef.

If, in both the world and the Veda, an increase in the means did not result in an increase in the result, then no one would directly undertake the effort of practicing superior means; rather, they would perform them all equally.
Otherwise, they would not be considered discerning persons (*prekṣāvant*).
For if the same amount of heaven obtained by the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādhāna*) were also obtained by the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*), no one would engage in the horse sacrifice;
or, if they did engage in it, they would be lacking in intelligence.
If the gain of grain from plowing a mere *droṇa* or *āḍhaka* of land were equal to that [gain of heaven], [then no one would engage in agriculture].
If the unseen [cause] were excluded from the category of "existence," no one would engage in it;
and if that were the case, it would be ineffective.
Since visible factors such as rain and invisible factors such as merit (*dharma*) are indeed included within the means of accomplishment, one should not suspect any logical deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

In this way, humans and others receive a lesser fruit of liberation than gods and others, because they possess fewer means in comparison to them; for it is observed that whoever possesses fewer means relative to another obtains a lesser fruit from that person, as is commonly acknowledged.

Gods and others down to humans possess gradations in their fruits regarding liberation, because they are endowed with gradations in their means; for those who possess gradations in their means produce those who possess gradations in their results, as is commonly acknowledged.

In this regard, one should also consider the following inference: "The fruits of liberation for those ranging from Brahmā down to humans possess gradations, because they are accomplished by means that possess gradations, just like [worldly] consensus.
Furthermore, favorable reasoning (*anukūlatarka*) and so forth should be inferred as before.
This might be argued:
It has been established in the *Guṇopasaṃhāra-pāda* that even those who are liberated continue to perform meditation (*upāsana*) and ritual action (*karman*).
Furthermore, there is no restrictive rule that their performance must be of only one kind.

Thus, although there may be a gradation in their meditations and so forth, since there is an absence of any corresponding gradation in the fruits produced by them, the inferential arguments (anumāna) accompanied by reasoning (*satarka*) are indeed untenable.
If it is argued that a practice performed by those who are already liberated cannot truly be a "means" because there is no longer anything to be accomplished, we reply:
this is not so, for it is logically consistent that even a superior practice performed by those who are not yet liberated (or by those seeking liberation) functions as such a means.
And since the performance [of the rite] will not be of the nature of mere play like that of a liberated being, he says: "With difficulty" (kṛcchreṇa).
It is because it is accomplished with difficulty that it is not described as being like that of a liberated being. (Manu 3.4.37ab)

Because those seeking liberation (mumukṣus) perform the practice of the means with great difficulty, their performance is not like that of the liberated ones, who act with ease. By the addition of this qualification, fallacies such as inconclusiveness (anaikāntya) are avoided. Furthermore, since there is an absence of difficulty for the liberated and their activity is seen to differ from mere play (līlā), any argument for an alternative explanation (anyathāsiddhi) is also refuted.
It is thus stated that play (*līlā*) is not something involving hardship.
To the question, "What is the authority for the performance of spiritual means by those seeking liberation through hardship?", he says: "It is proclaimed."
The meaning is that this is proclaimed by means of scripture (*āgama*).
He recites that scripture: "For ten kalpas, austerity was practiced by Rudra in the salt ocean. (11.78) For ten kalpas, austerity was practiced by Rudra in the salt ocean.
Having abandoned all pleasures with a mind afflicted by the salt-water [of worldly existence].
For ten million years, Śakra drank smoke with extreme suffering;
and for ten thousand years, Sūrya performed austerities with his head hanging downwards.
Having renounced pleasure through great hardship by means of dharma, he who slept in the open air drank my nectar with the utmost reverence for a thousand years.
"For even those who know the Veda exert effort with extreme difficulty...
(Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.4.40a–c).
A *kalpa* is a day of Brahmā;

it is neuter because it belongs to the class beginning with *pātra*. The accusative case is used according to the rule "the accusative is employed [to denote] uninterrupted connection (*atyantasaṃyoga*) with time or distance."
Alternatively, "ten kalpas" is a bahuvrīhi compound serving as an adjective qualifying austerity (*tapas*). A "thousandfold assembly" (*sāhasraḥ saṅghaḥ*) is one whose measure is a thousand.
Because the suffix *aṇ* is prescribed [by Pāṇini 5.1.27] in the sense of "that is its measure" (*tad-asya parimāṇam*) for words such as *śatamāna*, *viṃśatika*, *sahasra*, and *vasana*;

others also exert effort with great difficulty, but is it for the sake of results in this world? No, it is said: "even for those who know Brahman. By this, detachment from sense objects (*viṣaya-vairāgya*) is indicated.
Since the gradations of liberation resulting from the practice of spiritual means following the knowledge of Brahman will be established later on, only the general principle is intended here.
The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the sentence. *11.86*
He concludes the inference with the words "etad" (this).
...how can all this [be so] when there is no distinction in liberation? (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.4.40cd)
All of this is the performance of the means with difficulty;
"viśeṣa" means variety;
the suffix *tasi* is used in the sense of the locative case.
How is this logical?
The remainder [of the sentence] is: "Therefore, by this, a distinction in liberation is established.
This might be so.
"The inference of gradation in liberation is *kālātyayāpadiṣṭa* (annulled by the lapse of time),
because it contradicts such scriptural passages as 'He attains supreme equality'.
Not so.

Intending to show that scripture cannot be a sublater [of other means] because it is itself sublated by both Śruti and Smṛti, he first cites the Śruti and Smṛti passages that speak of gradations in liberation: "The divine... and so forth.
"The divine nature leads to liberation, while the demoniacal is considered bondage"—
thus has the distinction regarding liberation been declared by the Blessed One himself. Therefore,
you should devote yourselves to Him alone through the functions of the self, by means of the qualities of mind, speech, and body, and through your own duties.
Those free from deceit [should worship] the lotus feet of the wish-fulfilling tree for the sake of accomplishing their goals according to their respective capacities.
Friends with eyes and ears have become unequal in their mental speed;
some appear reaching only to the mouth, others to the armpits, while still others look like deep lakes after bathing.
And such statements as these clearly declare the gradations leading to liberation. 3.4.44.
Sampad is fitness;
vimokṣa is distinguished liberation;
nibandha is bondage in a low place within blinding darkness.
The dative case is used in the sense of "for the sake of that" (tādarthye).
The word *ca* has the meaning of *eva* (only/indeed).
Thus, it results in the sense: "it was spoken by the Blessed One himself."
Otherwise, the prefix *vi-* would be rendered meaningless.
"Tameva" (him alone) refers to Pṛthu’s words addressed to the sages;
"taṃ" means Viṣṇu alone.

"By their own activities" is an elaboration of that very [term], meaning "by their own actions consisting of the works of mind, speech, and body. "Devoid of guile" means free from deceit; "desireless" means free from longing.

"For the accomplishment of liberation"—that is, for the attainment of the determined goal of liberation according to one's qualification and capacity—is a statement regarding the gradations of liberation.
Because it has been stated that they are "free from guile" (amāyinaḥ), the word *artha* refers specifically to liberation (*mokṣa*).
[The term] *akṣaṇvantaḥ* means "possessing eyes";
the augment *nuṭ* is applied according to the rule *ano nuṭ*.

Possessing ears and having attained the fruits of all their senses, they were friends to one another and liberated. In terms of mental speed— where "mental speed" refers to the excellence of wisdom— the plural number is used in the sense of "and so forth"— they became unequal in their qualities such as knowledge, being endowed with varying degrees of superiority.
Furthermore, a gradation in proximity to the Blessed One is stated:
among them, some possess *ādadhras*, which is the absence of the sound "āsya" (mouth).
[The term] *ādadhras* means that for them there exists the immortal (*amṛta*) whose measure is the mouth; thus, by the rule *arśa-ādibhyo 'c*, the suffix *ac* is applied.
They are said to be "far away" because they dwell within the nectar-treasury that is the measure of their mouths;
or else, just as there is the word *taratama* (comparative/superlative), there is also the word *dadhnā* (instrumental singular) even when not functioning as a suffix.
Thus, the meaning is that they are perfectly immersed in curd (*dadhi*).
Some have entered the *kakṣa* forest, which is near the *kakṣā* (the armpit);
here, the word *u* has the sense of *eva* (only).
This means that they are solely devoted to sporting in the forests of Śvetadvīpa; thus, their intermediate state is described.
By the rule *āñjaseḥ asuk*, the suffix *asuk* is applied [to form *āñjasas*]. According to some, the forms *snātvaḥ* and *snātavyāḥ* are derived [from the root *snā*].
By the rule *kṛtyārthe tavai-ken-kenya-tvanaḥ*, the suffix *tvan* is applied.
Deep as if with their own hearts, they beheld the Supreme Lord;
by this, extreme proximity is expressed.
"Having heard [this], Viṣṇu is the fruit of the ears"—
since this mantra has been explained by such Smṛti passages, no other meaning should be imagined.
By the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and so forth," he includes the previously cited Śruti texts of the Kaṇva and Taittirīya schools.
This is clearly untenable.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says:
"By what [means] is that similarity perceived among those who are liberated? (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 3.4.44cd).

Therefore, because it is sublated by Śruti and Smṛti which leave no room for other interpretations, the meaning is that the passage cited cannot have that [literal] sense as its purport; by whom? By no one at all. If so, what then is its meaning? To this he says: "duḥkhādi... (beginning with suffering).
And the equality consisting in the absence of suffering and so forth is understood as the meaning of the statement regarding equality.
The word *ca* (and) is used for emphasis, or to include the equality with supreme bliss;
as it has been said:
"The absence of suffering is supreme bliss; the distinction of the marks is considered equal."
This inference is not merely conjectured;
rather, it is established by scripture (āgama).
With the intention of showing how, therefore, there can be no suspicion of the fallacy of "transcending the time" (kālātīta), he says: "By devotion and so forth."
For it is stated in the *Bhārata* that when qualities such as devotion are present, there is indeed incomparability... [Mānava Dharmaśāstra 3.4.45c–e].

When there is the presence of qualities such as devotion (bhakti) in varying degrees, the inequality of the fruit of liberation arises by reason of that very gradation of the qualities of the means, such as devotion; that is to say, it is caused by the differences in those qualities. This has been stated not only by us, but also in the *Bhārata*.
The word "hi" indicates that which is well-known in that statement.
For example, in the phrase "for when there is a quality, they proclaim inequality," the meaning is:
"when a virtuous quality such as devotion and so forth is present in an unequal degree, they indeed declare that the result is also unequal."
It has been stated that the gradation of means is observed through authoritative sources (*pramāṇa*).
To the question "Which are those?", one sentence is first cited to demonstrate performance with difficulty (*kṛcchra*);
then he says "sādhan... [and so on], indicating that there are others as well.
...the excellence of the means is also stated in every case. // MAnu 3.4.45ef //
The diversity of the practices for practitioners is found everywhere in the scriptures.
He recites those statements, beginning with: "It is difficult to understand."
The nature of the Lord, who is of terrible form and the destroyer of the three worlds, is difficult to comprehend even for the gods, the sages, the perfected ones (siddhas), and the great yogis.
The wheel of meditation of the Lord Nṛsiṃha is difficult for gods and others to comprehend;
thus he is so described because his form is "ghora," meaning terrifying. He is one whose nature it is to destroy the three worlds.

By the word "eva" (indeed), he states that the Great Yogins are not so merely by name, but in fact according to their actual state; this is what is expressed by the passage beginning with "nityamuktaiḥ" (by those who are eternally liberated).
By those who are ever-diligent, highly fortunate, liberated from the fear of afflictions, possessed of great energy and great fortitude, established in goodness, and resolute; (4.47)

By those who know the origin and dissolution of the knowledge of the past and the future, and who are endowed with purity, self-study, contentment, austerity, truthfulness, and compassion; Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.4.48.
How much less so by mortals who are beset by fear, delusion, distraction, and the affliction of disease,
and whose lifespan, vigor, intellect, fortitude, resolve, learning, and vows are all meager?
"Always" means by those who are diligent in meditation and so forth.
"Fortune" (*bhāga*) refers to good luck, such as mastery over the senses.
"Delusion" (*moha*) is false knowledge.

The afflictions are those of ignorance; "trepidation" is the fear of obstacles and the like. They are not only constantly engaged, but that engagement is said to be "great" because of their great enthusiasm.
"By those who are always abundant in the qualities of a being" means by those whose resolve is determination.
By the word "knowledge," the object of knowledge is indicated.
They are so described because it is their nature to know past and future cognitions, as well as manifestation and dissolution—that is, creation and withdrawal.
Because the knowledge of manifestation and dissolution yields such great fruit, it is mentioned separately.
It goes without saying that this is difficult for mortals to understand.
Dhvaṃsa is the dissolution of the mind;
moha is ignorance;
śruti is hearing.
In this passage from the Vaihāyasasaṃhitā, it is clearly understood that for human beings, the means [of attainment] are slight compared to those of the gods and others.
If it is argued that these will become greater immediately after the departure from the state of humanity, we say no;
for it will be stated immediately thereafter that the state of being human and so forth does not depart. *11,101*
O God, it is difficult for anyone other than me to know You, who are both intoxicated and free from intoxication;
only Brahman knows something of You, for indeed no one else does.
"Alas! is the Vedic utterance; "intoxication and non-intoxication" refers to being the cause of pleasure and pain for both gods and demons.
By this, it is stated that Yama possesses greater knowledge than others.
By the phrase "Brahman alone," [it refers to] Brahman;
for this very reason, the expression "other than me" (madanya) should be explained as meaning "excluding those beginning with Brahmā.
Even among the liberated ones and the perfected beings (siddhas), he who has Nārāyaṇa as his supreme goal [is the foremost].
O Mahāmati, one whose self is perfectly tranquil is extremely difficult to find, even among ten million.

In the statement of the *Bhāgavata*, "Among millions of liberated ones"—meaning those perfected knowers who are free from the egoistic conceit of the body and so forth—"one who is solely devoted to Nārāyaṇa, whose self is perfectly tranquil, is extremely rare; indeed, only such a person exists.
[This is contrasted with] "But all those whose goal is Nārāyaṇa are tranquil-souled"; through this, the gradation of the means (*sādhana*) is clearly perceived.
In this verse, detachment (*vairāgya*) and devotion (*bhakti*) are expressed by the two qualifiers.
"From whom this creation has come into being—whether he fashioned it or whether he did not;
he who is its overseer in the highest heaven—he indeed knows it, or perhaps he does not know. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.4.52)
This is the meaning of the mantra "iyam visṛṣṭiḥ":
this manifold creation, established through perception and other means of knowledge, has come forth from Hiraṇyagarbha on all sides;

and as for him who is the supervisor and lord of this phenomenal world, even he—whether he knows the Supreme Self in the supreme sky, that is, in the space of the heart, or whether he does not, or whether he holds it so or not.
"Aṅga" is an address to someone.
Compared to others, he meditates and knows [the truth] more fully, yet he does not meditate or know it in its entirety.

In the word "vyomni," there is elision (*luk*) of the locative case ending; by the rule "yo 'sya so 'ṅga" and "prakṛtyāntaḥpādam avyaparaḥ," there is the preservation of the original form (*prakṛtibhāva*).
He who has himself realized the manifestation of his own self-illusion—how could others, such as the wind-god, know him?
Even Brahmā does not truly know him here; how then could other gods, lords of sages, or mortals?
In these statements of the Bhāgavata, beginning with "He who [knows] his own self-illusion," the gradation of knowledge is understood through the expression of *kaimutya* (a fortiori).
The Blessed One, being himself possessed of knowledge, has personally attained the expansion—the full extent—of the power of his own self-illusion, which is the majesty of his essential nature.
This is a statement of Brahmā.

I bow to that Hari among living beings here, to you whose essence is immeasurable, the source of Dharma and the other goals of life; you who are beyond the guṇas and the supreme limit— I do not know you, so how could others?
Reality is its own nature;
origination is its cause;
whose true limit is merely the correct direction.
This is the word of Brahmā:
"Neither I, O sages, nor Marīci and the other chief seers—who are indeed attached to material existence—know that which has been created by Him;
for even the lords of Daityas and mortals have their minds stolen by His Māyā, how much more so those whose conduct is eternally unwholesome? (Manu 3.4.55)
"I am not another's life"—this is the word of Śiva. "That which was composed" refers to whose life story [was told].
"O Lord" (īśa) is an address to the Blessed One.
I am Mahendra, Nirṛti, Pracetas, Soma, Agni, Īśa, Pavana, Arka, and Viriñca;
likewise the Ādityas, Viśvedevas, Vasus, Sādhyas, the hosts of Maruts, and the hosts of Rudras along with the Siddhas. (Manu Smṛti 3.4.56)

And others who are creators of the universe, lords of the immortals, such as Bhṛgu and the rest— who, though their nature is dominated by goodness (sattva), are touched by illusion and do not know His purpose, even though they are untouched by passion (rajas) and darkness (tamas)— how much less so those other than them?
O King, Brahmā is traditionally held to have been born from the primordial waters; immediately after that deity, he knows the foremost of gods, and even more than that, he is superior to him.
"I am [he]"—this is the statement of Yama.
The "sought" (īhita) is that which is desired;
it is traditionally held to be at the beginning of all conceptual proliferation (prapañca),
being measured as the primordial [state].
Therefore, they will not surpass this class of the knowers (jñānin) by much, nor even more, nor with any excellence; indeed, they will not surpass them in any way, even in liberation.
Through the yoga of devotion to me and through knowledge, you shall surpass all others.
Just as a distinction in devotion is seen here toward Puruṣottama,
so too is there a distinction in liberation for the knowers when the subtle body is cast off.
Even though all the gods and others have attained union [with the Supreme],
they nevertheless remain in a state of gradation, for there is indeed a gradation in their means of attainment.
Among thousands of men, scarcely one strives for perfection;
and even among those who strive and attain perfection, scarcely one knows Me in truth.
"Na tvām" (not you) is the Lord's speech addressed to Brahmā;
"atra" means in this saṃsāra; "liṅgabhedane" means when the dissolution of the subtle body (liṅga-śarīra) has occurred.
For the sake of the attainment of knowledge;
among those who strive, some become accomplished (*siddha*);
this should be construed as "among those who are accomplished."
"In reality" means predominantly.
And "to know even one [verse] in reality" is as follows:
"He who shall declare this supreme secret among My devotees..."
Having established supreme devotion toward me, he will come to me alone, without a doubt.
And among humans, there shall be no one who does more for me than he;
nor shall there be anyone else on earth dearer to me than he.
And whoever shall study this dialogue of ours concerning dharma, by that sacrifice of knowledge I shall be worshipped; such is my conviction.

Even that man who, being faithful and free from malice, should merely listen to this [work], he too, being liberated, shall attain the auspicious worlds of those who perform meritorious deeds. *Note:* By the words "he who" (*ya imam*), the relative degrees of merit for the expounder, the student, and the listener are stated.
And it has been stated elsewhere that an abundance of exposition and so forth is a means to liberation for each individual:
"Some perceive the Self within the self by means of meditation; others by means of Sāṅkhya-yoga, and still others by means of karma-yoga. (Manu 3.4.67)
But others, not knowing this, worship having heard it from others;
they too, being devoted to what they have heard, certainly cross over death.
Regarding the phrase "by means of meditation" (*dhyānena*), one should consult the commentary on the *Gītātātparya* composed by the venerable Śaṅkarabhagavatpāda:
"The Lord Viṣṇu, though possessing all forms, always perceives his own self along with all its subtlest and complete particulars. (Manusmṛti 3.4.69)
And nowhere else has anything else been seen by him in such a manner;
however, even Ramā beholds the Lord everywhere and at all times.
However, they do not perceive him as superior to others through all his specific qualities;
for he indeed perceives himself and everything else in their entirety at all times.
Brahmā indeed perceives the all-pervading [Self] as superior even to the qualities (guṇas);
however, one who has not attained liberation does not perceive it in that way at all times.
But one who is liberated should always perceive [the world] as being all-pervasive;
he would never be able to perceive particularities as one perceives wealth.

One should always perceive one's own self and others through all their specific qualities; likewise, speech perceives as many particulars, yet it does not see Hari— who is beyond the three gunas— as pervading [all] with a hundredfold [qualities].
By the words "with the most subtle," etc., the gradation of knowledge among all [beings] is stated. He sees even the entire universe as other than himself; however, what is it that he sees?
In that case, the meaning of the question is: "Why is she not equal to the Blessed One?

Even though she perceives [Viṣṇu] as superior to other groups of knowledge, she does not perceive Him as endowed with all His specific attributes, nor does she perceive anything else besides Viṣṇu and herself.
She might, however, perceive [him] as superior to others such as Sarasvatī.
A distinction is stated even for Brahmā based on the difference in his states, but not with respect to all [of them].
Likewise, it is due to his omnipresence, his possession of superior qualities as perceived through Sarasvatī and others, and his being present everywhere.
By the word "ca" (and), he conjoins the possession of the aforementioned qualities.
Then, the question "Why is there equality with Ramā for the liberated Brahman? is posed by the words "But rather... (api tu).
To perform a vision [of the truth],
it is different from that of the Blessed One;
just as Brahmā does not see what has not been seen by Rāmā.
As many as are seen by Brahmā, so many [he sees];
Giriśa and Garuḍa likewise see Hari as having entered into pure darkness;
yet even they do not see the specific distinctions perceived by Vāṇī.
Umā and Suparṇī perceive everything up to the Great Principle (mahattattva),
but they never perceive the specific objects (viśeṣa) perceived by Rudra.
Except for the liberated ones, all the gods— including Indra, Kāma, and Brahmā, down to the level of the ego— know both their own true nature and other natures.

Manu, Dakṣa, and the others, perceiving Hari abiding in the principle of the intellect (buddhi), behold the Supreme Lord as situated in the mind (manas), while Soma and Sūrya behold Him likewise. || 3.78 ||
Other gods always perceive Viṣṇu as abiding within the elements; after many thousands of years, they perceive him here and there within the principle of Mahat.
Others, according to their capacity, perceive Hari residing within the cosmic egg;
some perceive him as the Lord of Śvetadvīpa within their hearts; and even there, some at certain times behold Keśava.
The connection is that [he] perceives only the quality of darkness (tamas).
This applies individually to each verb beginning with "paśyet" (he may see).
"Another form" refers to a form inferior to one's own.
"By means of many thousands of years" means by means of the practice performed for many thousands of years.
"In various places" refers to the divisions of the *mahat-tattva*.
Some, however, [worship] the Lord of Śvetadvīpa alone, according to their respective fitness;
in that regard, [the worship] is also performed in the heart. *11.116*
Since the gradation in the perception of specific qualities was not clearly stated as it is in the case of perceiving magnitude, he says: "Umā."
O Umā, as many infinite portions of Vāsudeva’s specific qualities as were previously perceived, those very same ones are subsequently discerned when they are described.
And those who desire Indra and the other gods perceive the specific qualities residing in Brahman as being only a hundredth part of what is found in those awakened by Umā and the others.
However, those mentioned later and later, up to Umā, perceive only infinite portions of Vāsudeva’s specific qualities that were not perceived by those mentioned earlier;
this includes Śakra, Kāma, and so forth—the word "ca" (and) having the sense of "but.
The word "eva" (only/just) is to be construed with "by Umā and the others alone."
"In the awakened ones" (*prabuddhebhyaḥ*) is used in the sense of the genitive case, as before;
"they declare" (*cakṣate*) means they see.
He states the purpose of the statements cited [above] with the words "beginning with 'thus'" (*ityādi*).
Thus, from such statements in the Vedas and Smṛtis,
a gradation of both the liberated souls and their means of attainment is seen according to their true nature.
"According to reality."
The meaning is that it is not in the form of a restatement of another's view.
The construction is "of both the liberated ones and the means.
Indeed, within certain very specific passages cited for the purpose of demonstrating the gradation of the means, a gradation among the liberated ones is perceived.
The meaning is that even that [distinction] must be accepted because it is the subject under discussion (*prakṛtatvāt*).

To the objection that while there may be a gradation among the means for those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), there should not be a gradation in liberation itself, a refutation was previously stated.
Now he says—[beginning with] "sādhye"—that this very objection is untenable, let alone the statement of its refutation.
There is a dissimilarity between the probandum and the probans... // MAnu 3.4.84a //
By what seed is this dissimilarity between the probandum and the probans—the probandum being non-variegated and the probans being variegated—conceived or even suspected? By none at all.
This is the intended meaning:
indeed, a suspicion that the subject (pakṣa) might be a counter-example (vipakṣa) could only arise from some specific ground.
One who suspects [the inference] to be "seedless" (nirbīja)—being neither a worldly person nor an investigator—is to be disregarded like a madman.
And the "seed" consists either in the observation of deviation (vyabhicāra) or the observation of a limiting condition (upādhi), or the suspicion of one of these two.
Of these, the first does not exist here.
This is what he says: "the unseen" (adṛṣṭa).
... by whom can that which is unseen be imagined?

Nor is the second [alternative] possible; for since the presence of the probandum (*sādhya*) in the subject (*pakṣa*) is established by scripture and other means, any suspected factor would necessarily lack pervasion of the probandum (*sādhyavyāpakatva*), and thus cannot function as a limiting condition (*upādhi*).
Furthermore, even if it were present in the subject, it would be a pervader of the probans (*sādhanavyāpaka*).
For this very reason, even the suspicion of a limiting adjunct (upādhi) is dispelled,
and consequently, the suspicion of inconstancy (vyabhicāra) is also removed,
because pervasion (vyāpti) has been established by the cited statements.

Therefore, due to the absence of a seed [for such a distinction], this very suspicion is untenable. Keeping in mind another inference—namely, that "the Lord bestows diverse fruits upon those seeking liberation because He is propitiated by diverse means, since He is the giver of fruits in dependence upon diverse means"—he states the subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against the contrary position (*vipakṣa*) in order to refute the establishment of an alternative [cause]: "Inequality" (*vaiṣamyam*).
By that [act], both partiality and cruelty would also accrue to another.
By that disparity between the goal and the means;
and the second word "ca" (and) is for the purpose of indicating another proof:
if God were to grant a fruit equal to one who has performed great exertions to one who has performed only slight exertions.
In that case, it would follow that He is partial;
or, if He were to grant a result equal to one who has performed only a small means to one who has performed the great means,
then He would be merciless— this is the meaning.

It is not the case that the charge of partiality and other faults against the Lord is unavoidable, because He is not the cause of suffering and so forth; therefore, he says: "Because [the Lord] is dependent.
And these two [objections] were refuted by the Lord of Knowledge (Vidyādhīśa) with the words, "Because [He] is dependent" (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 3.4.84ef).
By this, he cites the sūtra: "Or [the objection regarding] partiality and cruelty [is refuted] because [God] has regard for [other factors]";
the connection is with the words "those two."
Those two defects are characterized by partiality and cruelty;
for whatever is contradicted by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) or lacks scriptural authority is called "undesirable" (*aniṣṭa*),
such as partiality and the like.
Since this has been refuted by the author of the *Īśvara-sūtra*, how could it not be undesirable as being contrary to valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?
There is no inconsistency in making this effort for the sake of those who accept the authority of that very sūtra.
However, for those who do not accept the authority of the Sūtras and instead maintain that the Lord's possession of partiality and so forth is acceptable,
the masculine gender is used to indicate that partiality and the like are defects, serving as the reason for the Veda’s lack of authority.
Otherwise, by virtue of the context, he would have said, "they are excluded."

If it is argued that one can understand [the meaning] as "even in the case of the neuter usage, [it refers to] a fault," we say no; for the statement "those two, namely partiality and cruelty" is complete in itself and requires nothing further. He establishes the conclusion of the reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga) by reversing [the premise] with the words "because of the gradation" (*tāratamyāt*).
Due to the gradations of the means of accomplishment, there is a corresponding gradation in what is to be accomplished;
yet, because the Lord is sovereign, He remains forever the cause of non-differentiation and so forth in the Supreme Lord.

Because the means [of accomplishment] possess degrees of intensity, the goal accomplished—which arises from the Lord at all times according to fixed rule—would necessarily possess degrees of intensity; this would constitute a reason for partiality and other defects in the Supreme Lord.
Indeed, a reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga) reaches its conclusion through the reversal of the premise when the reversal of the consequence serves as its logical warrant.
For the reversal of "being without fire" establishes the reversal of "being without smoke."
And this is relevant to the present topic.

Alternatively, since it may be asked how inequality and so forth were refuted by the author of the Sūtras, he explains the relationship of cause and effect between dependence and the absence of inequality and so forth with the words: "Because of gradation" (tāratamyāt).
The previous interpretation remains the same.

This effort by the author of the Sūtra to avoid [the charge of] partiality (*vaiṣamya*) and so forth by accepting that [the cognition] depends on the prior action of preparing the means of proof (*sādhana-saṃskāra-pūrvakarman*) is useless;
for even if that [partiality] is avoided regarding the result, it cannot be avoided regarding the means of proof and so forth.
For instance:
does the Supreme Lord possess the status of an instigator (prayojaka) regarding the creation and so forth? If the position is that He does not, then His status as the Supreme Lord is lost.
One might ask: "Since one who employs various means without a motive would inevitably fall into partiality and so forth, how can this untenable [objection] serve as a refutation of the Sūtra?
Do not say so; for the author of the Sūtra himself has already rejected this objection, as he states: "In [the case of] independence... (svātantrye).
"Even though the Supreme Lord possesses absolute sovereignty regarding the means of accomplishment and so forth,
there is no fault in His dependence upon beginningless diversity"— such is His teaching.
Sovereignty [is established] because of being the instigating agent;
variety [is established] because of the means and so forth—
this is the ellipsis for "because of impelling with reference to."

A "defect" (*doṣa*) is such things as inequality and so forth. The "word of him" refers to the word of the author of the Sūtras. [Objection: But in this way, would there not be the defect of Hari losing his independence (*svātantrya*) because he is everywhere dependent? To this, he says: "Independence... (*svatantrye*).
This fault also does not exist. How so?

Because there is that statement which establishes this meaning: even though the Supreme Lord possesses independence regarding the means of accomplishment and so forth, he acts as an impeller by depending on the beginningless diversity of his own will. Thus it is said.
To the question "What is that statement? he recites two successive sūtras, beginning with: "Because of beginninglessness."
For it has been stated that this is logical because there is no beginning.
Therein, in order to avoid the first objection, he cites the sūtra: “If it be argued that there is no [creation] because of the non-differentiation of karma, we say no, because of beginninglessness”;
and to avoid the second objection, he cites: “And it is logical.”
Having thus refuted the possibility of inference being established otherwise, he refutes sublation (bādha) and counter-inference (pratirodha) with the words "apekṣya" and so forth.
The existence of the goal (upeya) in such a manner depends upon the diversity of the means (upāya);
with what [principle] of mine would this be in conflict? ... MAnu 3.4.87a-c.

The phrase "is being established" is the ellipsis for "the persistence [of things] as they are is being brought about by the Lord of the Uneven. By what? By no means whatsoever. By me? By the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
By what? By none at all.
The intention is that [the verse] beginning with "supreme equality" (*paramaṃ sāmyam*) has been explained otherwise.
To establish the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) for inference and other means of knowledge, he states an illustrative example: "Even in the case of a king and so forth.
(Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.4.87d) ... [it is] seen even in the case of a king and so forth.

The meaning is that in a discerning king and others, the granting of results corresponding to service is observed, whereas in one who lacks discernment and acts perversely, partiality and so forth are seen. He states another refutation against the assumption of a disparity between the means and the end: "Renunciation," etc.
The renunciation of what is seen and the postulation of what is unseen are extremely difficult for anyone other than a magician to accomplish. (Manu Smṛti 3.4.88a–c)

Since it is observed everywhere that the probandum and the probans possess a uniform nature, and since their dissimilarity is never observed anywhere, one who suspects such a dissimilarity in the present case would incur the two faults of abandoning what is observed and imagining what is unobserved; yet it cannot be said that these two [faults] do not exist, because they are not accepted by any discerning person—thus he says: "It is very difficult."
The proponents of Māyā abandon what is perceived, such as the reality of the phenomenal world (prapañca),
and they postulate what is unperceived, such as its being indescribable (anirvācya) and so forth;
therefore, it is said [in the verse] "by one other than the Māyā-vādins."
And its application occurs later on.
To the question, "What fault is there for those who perform acts such as the renunciation of what has been seen, even if not performed by others? he says: "Why is that? (tatkimiti).
... so what need is there for other disputants? (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.4.88d)
Deceitful people are followed here... // MAnu 3.4.89a //
Then what? This is a question with a hidden intention (*gūḍhābhiprāya*),
concerning the matter of performing practices such as the renunciation of [worldly] views.
"They are followed" means they are pursued.
This is what is being said:

for those who criticize the proponents of illusion (māyāvādins) by charging them with the abandonment of views and so forth, there would be a self-contradiction if they themselves were to commit such abandonment of views and so forth in this context. *11,132*
Anticipating the objection that there is a dissimilarity between the probandum and the probans, he states another undesirable consequence: "śruta... and so forth.

Since the similarity between the probandum and the probans has been stated according to the manner explained above, whereas otherwise it would not have been stated, if one were to accept dissimilarity (*vairūpya*) here, there would be both the abandonment of what is stated (*śrutahāni*) and the acceptance of what is not stated (*aśrutagraha*).
For the proponent who employs "in the mark" (*liṅge*) as a qualifier for those two [the probandum and the probans], this very intention has already been stated.

Indeed, the proponents of Māyā (*māyāvādinaḥ*), abandoning the Brahman endowed with omniscience and other qualities as it is stated in scripture, resort instead to the unqualified (*nirguṇa*) Brahman which is not so stated.
He states another objection for those who perform the fourfold [acts] beginning with the renunciation of what has been seen: "That... (tad).
...the loss of what has been heard and the grasping of what has not been heard; even these are signs of those who employ deceit—what faults could be greater than those? (Manu 3.4.89b–d)
That [occurs] there among the natural faults;
from that, this [arises] through the abandonment of what has been seen;
[those who are] excessive are excluded.
The meaning is that if one were to perform the abandonment of what is seen (*dṛṣṭa*) and so forth, other things established by valid cognition would also have to be abandoned;

and if one were to perform the postulation of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) and so forth, other things not based on valid authority (*aprāmāṇika*) would also have to be postulated. This is the intended sense.
It might be argued as follows:

If the liberated were possessed of degrees of excellence, they would consequently be subject to mutual hatred; thus, the inference of gradations among the liberated is refuted by a counter-reasoning (pratikūlatarka). To this, he says: "niśśeṣa... (without remainder).
For those whose faults have been entirely eliminated through many births, direct perception of Hari indeed arises; how then could hatred, envy, or the like exist for them?
Those from whom faults have departed entirely are described as such;
the phrase "for those possessing hearing and so forth" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
For them, there is the direct perception (*āparokṣya*) of Hari—that is, Hari's manifestation before their eyes.
This is the meaning.
The word *hi* indicates that this point has already been established in the section beginning with "from the [mention of] the continuations and so forth" (*anubandhādibhyaḥ*).
Alternatively, it is used in the sense of "because."
The meaning is that faults such as hatred and envy arise from that [cause]; therefore, how could they be attributed to those who are liberated?
This is what is being said:
those who possess degrees of variation are observed to possess hatred and so forth, just like worldly persons; indeed, this is the pervasion (*vyāpti*) that must be stated here.
But it is not so;
for in the case of worldly beings possessing hatred and the like, being possessed of defects (*doṣitva*) alone is the determining factor.
This is because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is observed that wherever there is the possession of hatred and the like, there is the possession of defects.
Furthermore, the state of being possessed of defects is not possible in those who are liberated;
for it must be said that their defects are adventitious (aupādhika), since it is impossible to even suspect that they possess innate (svābhāvika) defects.
And those [obstacles] have for the most part already departed even before the arising of the direct realization of the Blessed One;
moreover, they are destroyed by that realization along with their very roots.
Furthermore, in liberation, because the limiting adjunct itself has vanished, it is not possible for them to remain even in the slightest degree.

Therefore, due to the absence of the pervader (vyāpaka), there is also the absence of the pervaded (vyāpya). Now, one might object: "The opponent does not seek to prove that those who are liberated possess hatred and so forth; rather, he merely seeks to show this as a logical consequence (āpādya). Consequently, it is irrelevant to attempt to prove their exclusion from those [qualities]."
Not so;
for it is precisely the *upādhi* that has been discussed here in relation to the pervasion (*vyāpti*) which serves as the foundation of reasoning (*tarka*).

And since its exclusion from the subject (*pakṣa*) and its capacity to exclude the intended property by means of its own exclusion must necessarily be established, it is for this purpose that its demonstration is being undertaken.

In this context, hatred, envy, distress, malice toward others, aversion, effort, and desire are the pervaded (vyāpya), while ignorance, egoism, and so forth are the pervaders (vyāpaka); such is the distinction.

To make even the opponent accept the point that it is precisely the defects (doṣas) that act as the motivators for hatred and the rest, he employs a counter-example (pratibandī), saying: "they would be... [verse 11.136].
If envy and the like were to arise even toward equals, why would they not arise toward you?
If it is admitted that there is a gradation [among the liberated], and if envy and the like are asserted to exist [in them],
then why would they not also exist when the liberated are admitted to be equal?
If you say, "If the liberated were possessed of gradation, they would possess hatred and the like," then you must state that they do not possess hatred and the like, and therefore they are equal.
Nor can equality even be admitted;
for if the liberated were equal [to the bound], they would possess hatred and so forth, because there too the undesirable consequence would follow—this is the meaning.

To the question, "How does the consequence of hatred and so forth follow from equality?", he says, "Those who are being tormented," etc., indicating that, just as in the case of the opponent's own position, equality is observed to be accompanied by hatred and the like.
Even those who are possessed of hatred, envy, and other such passions are seen performing austerities when they observe others of equal status;
in this world, it is these very defects that are the cause.
It is not mere equality in existence that is intended as the cause [of non-discrimination], for that would lead to an over-extension;
rather, it is the very vision of equality that is meant. With this intention, it is said: "having seen them as equal."
He states the purpose of employing a counter-objection (pratibandī) with the words: "The faults... (doṣā iti).
The singular number [in the word "cause"] indicates that the causes are the faults (doṣas) alone when they are combined.
Thus, when we have pointed out this over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) to the proponent of equality, he must say this:
"In this world, the faults alone are the cause of hatred and so forth."
This is because that [distinction] is determined through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*),
and not because of similarity;
for even when similarity exists, [the distinction] is absent among friends.
Because [the effect] occurs even when [the cause] is absent in some cases,
and because there are no defects in liberated beings,
therefore, even though there is equality, [it is not dual].
Regarding the phrase "the consequence of faults and so forth" (*doṣādiprasaṅga*), [the author] asks "What follows from this? and says: "If... (*yadīti*).
If it is free from fault, why is it excessively criticized?
If, in this way, faults alone are the cause of hatred and so forth, then in that case, freedom from fault has been accepted regarding those who are liberated.

Then, by what is it being refuted through the acceptance of an excess or a deficiency? Nothing at all. Even by one who accepts equality, the occurrence of hatred and so forth must be prevented precisely by means of faultlessness itself.
Even by us who accept gradation (*tāratamya*), it will be refuted in exactly the same manner.
However, this much is the distinction: that while gradation is established by valid cognition (*pramita*), equality is not; such is the meaning of the whole passage.
He raises a doubt with the words "yadi" (if).
If envy and the like are prevented because of the absence of seeing another [possessing what one desires],
this might be so if we were to prevent hatred and so forth on the grounds that they are equally prone to arise;
but it is not thus.
Is it merely the state of equality that is not a cause for hatred and so forth? No, because that would lead to an over-extension [of the argument]. Rather, it is the vision of equality.
And one who is liberated does not perceive another liberated being as unequal; therefore, there is no hatred or the like.
In that case, it can be argued as a rebuttal: "The mere existence of gradation is not the cause of hatred and the like; rather, it is the perception of another as being superior to oneself.
And a liberated soul does not perceive another liberated soul as superior to itself.
Therefore, even though gradation exists, there is no possibility of hatred and so forth; why, then, should you not be satisfied with this? This is the response that can be stated here.
Nevertheless, because that [perception] is not real, he refutes the absence of other perceptions by stating "due to non-perception."
How can lack of interest and other such states be prevented by him through non-seeing?

In this way, while one prevents hatred and the like by means of the absence of seeing other [objects], how is dissatisfaction (*arati*) and so forth—which arise from not seeing [the desired object]—prevented by him?
Dissatisfaction is the absence of pleasure;
by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), languor (*tandrī*) and fear (*bhaya*) are included.
This is what is meant:
this rebuttal would be valid if it were possible for one who is liberated to lack the vision of anything else;
but it is not so.
For one who is liberated is certainly not insentient,
as that would entail the consequence of contradicting your own tenets.
Consequently, if there were an absence of seeing other things while being sentient, it would follow that there would be dissatisfaction and so forth.

[Objection: Surely it is only those whose minds are directed outward who experience dissatisfaction and so forth when there is no other object of perception, and not those who are liberated; therefore, the consequence of dissatisfaction and so forth does not apply [to the liberated]. To this, he says: "Even for Brahman... (brahmaṇo 'pi).
Even Brahmā was seen to feel dissatisfaction when he was previously alone, according to the Śruti.
"Whose knowledge is unimpeded, as are his dispassion, sovereignty, and virtue— this fourfold set is innate to the Lord of the World";
the meaning is that this applies even to one who is thus measured [by such attributes].

"In the beginning" means in the primordial time. "In the Śrutis"—the singular number is used here to denote the class. He recites those Śrutis according to their meaning, beginning with "Not indeed... (*naiva*). (11.139)
He did not find delight being alone; since he did not find delight anywhere, he desired a second. For this reason, the Vedas have declared thus.
By this, he indeed took up the statement: "He did not rejoice; therefore, one who is alone does not rejoice; he desired a second.
This might be so, provided that the mere absence of the perception of another were the cause of his lack of joy and so forth.
But this is not the case;

rather, there is an absence [of seeing] when there is a desire to see something else. However, for one who is liberated, there is no such desire at all; therefore, even though there is an absence of seeing other things, it does not follow that there is non-existence and so forth. Anticipating this objection, he says: "If... (yadi).
If it is imagined that there is no desire for that [result] at all, such an assumption is false;
why not simply accept the very faultlessness declared by the Śruti? 3.4.94.
The construction is as follows: "In that case," meaning regarding liberation;
"in that other sphere of perception," meaning there is no desire at all; therefore, it is falsely imagined that "if [it were so]," and so forth.
The phrase "the knot of the heart is severed," and so forth, is what is stated by the Śruti; the connection is that [this occurs] directly by the Śruti itself.
The word "then" (tahiṃ) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
Alternatively, the word "tat" (that) has the sense of "tarhi" (then).
This is what is meant:

having admitted the equality of those who are liberated, and because they lack the perception of anything else, they abandon hatred and the like; and because they lack the desire to perceive anything else, they avoid non-delight and so forth. Thus, there would be the postulation of many things not supported by authoritative means of knowledge (*apramāṇika*), as well as the abandonment of that which is supported by authoritative means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*).
They would both exist; for, due to the absence of any observation of a commonality, non-existences, as well as the absences of desire and so forth, lack any basis in valid cognition (*prāmāṇika*),
whereas gradations and the like do possess such a basis.
Therefore, having accepted the gradation [of qualities], one should accept the scriptural teaching of faultlessness in order to eliminate hatred and the like.
By this, the doubt that "one must either accept gradation or equality and then effect the removal of hatred and so forth by means of faultlessness" is also to be understood as refuted.
He states clearly what has already been said: "And gradation... and so on.
Having completely set aside gradations of status, desire, and even what has been heard,
by what logic could one who considers himself wise imagine an equality regarding what has not been heard?
One should also understand that "another view" is to be included here as well.
“He who among men has attained success,
where desires are fulfilled—
those friends who possess eyes and possess ears.”
Thus it has been heard in such passages.
For friendship is not possible in the absence of seeing another.
The term "equality" (samatā) is also an indicator for the absence of the desire to see another.

"One who considers [only] reasoning" (*yuktamānin*) means one who possesses great esteem for reasoning; the sense is that no one would conceive [a doctrine] in such a way [if they truly valued reasoning].
For reasoning—whose other name is *tarka* (hypothetical reductio)—is characterized by the consequence of abandoning what is authoritative and accepting what is non-authoritative.

Now, one might object: "Even if equality (*samatā*) is not explicitly mentioned [in scripture], it is not unauthoritative; for scripture alone is not the sole authority. To this, he says: "What is that? (kiṃ tad iti).
What measure of equality is perceived by you in those who are liberated?
There is nothing other than the cutting of that [wood];
therefore, in the absence of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), its lack of authority is established precisely because it has not been heard [in scripture].
He concludes what was stated in the passage beginning with "because of the absence of seeing anything else" by saying "in vain."
Why is this insistence so futile, resulting in the loss of what has been heard and the grasping of what has not been heard?
"By what? means by no cause whatsoever.
"Loss of what was heard and grasping of what was not heard" is a dvandva compound treated as a singular;
or it may mean "grasping of what was not heard accompanied by the loss of what was heard."
This is a locative of reference (*viṣayasaptamī*).
Therefore, the sense is that there is no [logical] necessity.
He states another inference regarding the gradations among those who are liberated: "Even in liberation... (*mokṣe 'pi*) // 11.142 //
Even in liberation there is gradation, because of its conscious nature, just as it was before.
"Attained here with gradation" means that it possesses gradation.

"In the past" refers to within saṃsāra. Now, one might object: if this is being proven—that whatever exists in this saṃsāra is attained with gradation—then the qualification [in the thesis] is employed to avoid the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) regarding liberation (*mokṣa*) as well.

Or alternatively: by the phrase "even in liberation," having made the liberated one the subject (*pakṣa*), it is established that there is gradation (*tāratamya*). That is to say, having made the liberated one the subject, it is proven that there exists a hierarchy.

In this regard, it may be argued that the qualification "even in liberation" is employed to avoid the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) according to the aforementioned gradations.
This is not the first [position], because since even the state of being eternally transmigratory (*nityasaṃsāritva*) is possible, there would be the consequence of sublation (*bādhā*).
Even if one were to include as the subject (pakṣa) a specific person for whom liberation is certain, the example would still lack the property to be proven (sādhyavikala);
for a transmigrating being does not possess a gradation of having reached liberation.
Furthermore, in the second case, the word "api" (also/even) is redundant.
Furthermore, because it possesses a prior gradation, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*).
Even in the third case, the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is likewise devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*).
Moreover, "possessing a gradation" means either the existence of both inferior and superior states, or the existence of one or the other. *11,143*

In the first case, there is the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) with respect to the Supreme Lord; in the second case, there is the proving of what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*),
because the opponent himself accepts that even liberated beings possess superiority over those who are not yet liberated.
If it is argued that there is a fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in proving the superiority of the liberated ones regarding Devadatta, how is this to be understood?
It is said:
the intended meaning here is that the liberated ones at that time possess mutual gradations because they are conscious, just like those in saṃsāra.
Furthermore, "gradation" (tāratamya) consists of either inferiority relative to something or superiority relative to something; thus, neither of the aforementioned faults applies.
Moreover, if one were to reject the universal by means of excluding its particulars, it would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).

Alternatively, the meaning of the proposition should be stated as follows: the liberated one, who exists in the moment immediately following [the attainment of] devotion, was previously endowed with a nature characterized by both superiority and inferiority, and even now he remains endowed with those two.
"The pervasion must be stated in a general sense alone. [The author] raises this objection and then refutes it with the words, "it has been said."
When this was said, what was your reply? ... // Mānava-dharmaśāstra 3.4.97c //

The meaning is that once it has been stated and answered—since both pervasion (*vyāpti*) and the property of being a predicate of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) have been established through valid cognition—there is no further rejoinder possible.
To the objection that "the inference has a sublated object" (*bādhitaviṣaya*), he says: "It is a conceptual construction" (*kalpanā*).
... for those who maintain that [the world] is mere conceptual construction.
"He speaks by mere imagination" means he is described as such because his statement is connected with what preceded it.

Since the Vedic scriptures have other meanings and there is an absence of any other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), what is your answer to one who asserts, based solely on his own conjecture, that there is no gradation among those who are liberated?

If it were to be inferred in this manner, then one might also infer that liberated beings are possessed of suffering and so forth because they are conscious, like those in saṃsāra; thus, such an inference is refuted by the fault of over-extension (atiprasaṅga). Therefore, he says: "And not... (na ca).
And one should not imagine suffering and so forth... // MAnu 3.4.98a //
That which is to be conceptualized is the object of inference for one who is liberated.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of such qualities as the non-perfection of bliss is intended.
To the question "Why?", he says: "Because of the absence of suffering," and so forth.
...by the force of the scriptural statement that [the self] is devoid of suffering. (Manu 3.4.98b)
In this case as well, the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) is to be understood.
This is the intended meaning:

indeed, this undesirable consequence (*atiprasaṅga*) is to be stated with the intention that [the cases] share the same status regarding their logical connection and security (*yogakṣema*), and not otherwise, because there would be a lack of pervasion (*vyāpti*).
And that [reason] does not exist in the present case,
because it is sublated by the scripture which establishes that the one who brings about suffering and so forth is free from suffering and so forth;
for scripture, being authorless and being the apprehender of the subject (*dharmin*), is more powerful than inference.
"And because the inference based on gradation is uncontradicted.

(*11,148*) Explaining this very point, he first cites the scriptural passages establishing that the liberated one is free from suffering and so forth, and then states their intended meaning with the verse beginning "śokam":
"The knower of the Self transcends sorrow; having crossed over, he partakes in no suffering whatsoever. (*Manu 3.4.98cd*)
By this, one becomes truly joyful and never grieves;
he is the partaker of sin-destroying food, the father-nourisher, the well-wisher, and the lord here on earth.

"Whatever end one desires to reach, that one shall attain here through resolve"—such scriptural passages are the authority for the attainment of freedom from suffering and other such perfections. (Manu 3.4.100)
He cites the Vedic scripture: "The knower of the Self crosses over sorrow.
Here, *vettā* means "the knower" (*veditā*), or it is a form of the root *vid* in the sense of "to investigate" (*vicāraṇā*).

By the phrase "having crossed over all," it is meant that he has indeed then crossed over all sorrows. By the phrase "not partaking of suffering," it is meant that he does not touch upon any lack of bliss.
By the word "by which," it is meant: "That indeed is the mind of the individual soul (*jīva*), by which one becomes truly blissful and, moreover, does not grieve."

Although the absence of sorrow is already established by the word *eva*, the reason why it is stated again as "he does not grieve" (*na śocati*) is to indicate that this occurs "at any time" (*kadācana*).
By the phrase "free from the touch of sin" (*akilbiṣaspṛt*), it is meant that "all his friends rejoice in the fame that has come to him, through a friend who is a conqueror in the assembly."
"O sinless one, the father is indeed the protector of these; he becomes a helpful friend for the sake of the swift ones"—thus [is] the mantra (Ṛgveda 10.71.10).
All are friends to one another, liberated by the welcome that has arrived, which is glorious (or possessed of fame).
One who endures the assembly is called *sabhāsahaḥ*; the suffix *-aṇ* is applied here in the sense of "skillful" (*karmaṇya*).
By means of that friendship with the Supreme Lord as the cause, they rejoice.
How so?
For indeed, because the Lord (Īśvara) is one who "strives against" (spṛt)— that is, one who cannot endure— the suffering of these liberated ones;
the word *spṛt* is derived from another verbal root meaning "to strive," followed by the suffix *kvip*.
"Pitṛṣaṇiḥ" means the giver of food;
for according to scripture, "food is indeed the father," and the root *ṣaṇ* means "to give."
The suffix -ika is applied here.
*Ara* means "free from impurity" (*mala*).
It is beneficial for the *vājin*, that is, for the sense faculty (*indriya*).

According to the Vedic scripture, "The sense-organ is indeed the steed," in this context of liberation, by the phrase "whichever [he desires]," it is meant that whatever end he becomes desirous of, that comes to him through his mere volition.
The final state is here in liberation; it is the perfection consisting of the absence of suffering and so forth for those who are liberated.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "Therefore" (ataḥ).
Therefore, there is no room here for inference based on suffering and the like.

The meaning is that it is contradicted by scripture (*śruti*). Furthermore, it should be understood here that the proposition— that those who are liberated (*mukta*) are possessed of suffering and so forth— is also self-contradictory.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "By way of gradation... (tāratamya).
Therefore, an inference based on gradation would not lead to an over-extension of the principle.
Therefore, because there is no sublation [of the opponent's view] and because there is an absence of equal status in terms of logical security (*yogakṣema*),
he concludes the proof for the gradation of liberation with the verse beginning "śruti" (verse 11.155).
Thus, this gradation is discerned solely through the power of scripture and reasoning;
therefore, who here is able to create a contradiction even regarding liberation?
It is clearly discerned and correctly experienced;
there are no disputants at all regarding this matter of the gradations of liberation.
Thus concludes the section on acting according to one's own will.
[======= JNys_3,4.III: The Section Concerning the Topic of Both Marks =======] // Now, the section concerning the topic of both marks //
Oṃ. But in every way, it is those very [entities] [that are the cause], because of both marks. Oṃ.
Oṃ. Nor is there [a loss of status] even for one holding an office, because of the inference of falling [from grace], since that [office] is incompatible [with such a state]. Oṃ.
In this regard, it was stated in the first section that the attainment of knowledge occurs only for those who possess beginningless fitness for knowledge, and not for others;
and in the second, it was declared that the attainment of the status of deities and so forth belongs only to those endowed with beginningless fitness for such states, and not to others.

This manifold beginningless fitness of living beings—which results in the attainment of higher or lower degrees through various well-known causes—is not accepted by those disputants who [deny its existence]; therefore, in order to establish it, he says:
"Beginningless."
In every respect, those [two] alone [are the authorities], because of the evidence of both [scriptural] marks (liṅga).
Nor is there an authority for one who has fallen [from his status], because such a fall is inferred and because [the office] is incompatible with that state.
And [this applies to] beginningless fitness, which extends as far as the end of the Kali age and the Lord of Speech (Brahmā).
"Who is able to restrain [the power of knowledge] when it is aroused by the force of reasoning and scripture?
This means that there is not only a gradation among those who are liberated;
by this, it is stated that this [difference in power] is also a proof for the gradation of liberation itself.
Because it is beginningless and eternal;
the word "eva" (only/just) is connected with "ka" (who);
that which has Kali, Vāṇī, and Īśvara as its limits is described as such.
The Kali age is the limit of the succession of the decline of human capacity, while the Lord of Speech (Brahmā) is the limit of its succession of increase.
[The opponent asks:

"How is it established by reason and scripture? To this, [the author] first states that [capacity] with respect to one who has great regard for reason alone—due to the conceit that the scriptures are open to interpretation—saying: "Of Brahmā... [and so forth].

Time other than that of Brahmā is characterized by excess and is subject to dispute; let one who considers himself a knower of the Mānavadharma not think that "this time is indeed as [described] here," and so forth. (Manu 3.104)
It is universally accepted that in the present time, Brahmā is supreme;
therefore, it is said that time—which is the subject of dispute—is the one who disputes.
Time other than the present great aeon (*mahākalpa*), namely the past and the future, is endowed with whatever superiority belongs to this Brahmā beyond [the present].
The phrase "kālo hi" means "because it is time. This refers to the present time, for example.

By the word "ādi" (and so forth), there is an inclusion of such arguments as: "This [Brahman] is superior to others even in past times and so on, because He is Brahman, just like the Brahman existing in those times."
One who esteems inference and possesses great regard for it should apply themselves toward awakening, or toward the realization of one who esteems inference.
If it is argued: "How can there be inference [regarding Brahman], given that there is no connection with time due to its transcendence?"—it is not so.

This is because those who maintain the validity of inference through a traditional connection (*paramparāsambandha*) accept that inferences such as "this time is possessed of human-authored speech that lacks contemporaneity with anything other than the Veda" do not apply; this is what is meant by the phrase "by those who hold [inference] to be authoritative. Even at a time when words and so forth did not exist for Brahmā, the fact that his capacity alone was established as supreme over all proves that an eternal, beginningless, and supremely excellent capacity is established.
This might be so:
this proposition is contradicted by valid cognition,
and the example is devoid of the property to be proven.
For this word "other" (anya), by virtue of the context, refers to everything distinct from Brahman.

In that regard, there is no superiority of Hari over Mahālakṣmī or of [Brahmā] over the upright ones (ṛju) throughout the three periods of time; because it is established that Hari and Śrī possess superiority while the upright ones possess equality, he says: "the word 'other'."
The word "other" (anya), when employed with the intention of expressing something other than Hari, Śrī, or one's own self,
does not constitute a fault at all.
By the word "own" (sva), Brahman is denoted; and it is that which is to be repeated [in the compound], as in the expression "the own and those equal to the own."

When the speaker himself explains his own intended meaning, what need is there for context and the like? For they would be useful only in its absence. However, in formal debate, it must be stated quite explicitly.

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that even [fallacies such as] shifting the thesis (*pratijñāntara*) and so forth could be avoided in this same manner. [The objection that] "the reason for sublation (*bādhā*) and so forth does not at all constitute a fault" is not correct.
He extends the stated principle to other cases as well with the words: "and in the case of Rudra and others."
...and [the same applies] to Rudra and others, according to reason.
The meaning is that, by this very method, the fitness of Rudra and others for the *sāman* chants and so forth must also be established through reasoning.
[The argument is: "The subject under dispute, this time of Rudra, is endowed with a superiority distinct from that of Īśvara and others, because it is time, like this [present] time," and so on.
[Objection: Well then, all liberated beings (*mukta*) are indeed superior to Brahmā, because they are liberated while he is still subject to transmigratory existence (*saṃsārin*).
Therefore, since one might ask why those other words are not also included in the explanation of "other words," he says: "But as for their being the best..."
But even for the liberated, there can be no superiority over Brahman.
Therefore, the implication is that there is no fault in not apprehending that [universal].
To the question "How so?", he says: "The manifestation... (vyaktiḥ).
There may indeed be the manifestation of happiness, but there is no increase in that happiness.
The first word "tu" (but) has the sense of restriction;
it is connected with the phrase "only the individual.
The word "ca" (and) has the sense of a conjunction of other qualities and applies to both instances.

In liberation, there is merely the manifestation—characterized by experience—of the very nature of bliss and so forth that already existed previously, through the removal of the veil of ignorance and the like; nothing additional is produced.
For if that were the case, it would follow that [liberation] is impermanent.
Furthermore, the nature of others is not something additional to the nature of Brahman.
Furthermore, polished bell-metal does not become superior to unpolished gold.
By this, the reason based on being "liberated" (muktatva) is also refuted.
To show that it is not only the case that liberated souls have no superiority over Brahman, but rather [the opposite], he says: "baleti" (by force).
And Brahman is always superior to them in strength and knowledge. (Manu 3.107ab)
This is an indication of other qualities as well:
[they exist] always, both in saṃsāra and in liberation.
By this, the inclusion of that [quality] by means of the word "equal" (*sama*) is also refuted. (11.163)

[Objection: But surely, by this same logic, there would also follow the undesirable consequence of an inference such as: "The time under dispute is endowed with an abundance [of dharma] relative to this king, because it is time, like a time that is commonly accepted. To this he says: "But regarding abundance... — "But no proof whatsoever is perceived for the non-eternality of abundance. (Manu 3.4.107cd)

The word "of Brahmā" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. In the phrase "in [the case of] non-eternality," the term also implies "having a beginning. The particle *tu* (but) serves to exclude the superiority [of the status] of kings and others.
The intention is that there is no over-extension [of the argument] because of the distinction between the presence and absence of sublation (*bādhaka*).

Having thus established that the various kinds of capacities (*yogyatā*) among living beings, beginning with Brahmā, are beginningless and eternal, he now seeks to establish this also through scripture (*āgama*), first reciting the Vedic verses, starting with "I hear the Hero" (*śṛṇve vīraḥ*).
The hero is heard of as subduing every fierce one, leading each one beyond [his power];
the king of both worlds, increasing his own might, Indra drives away the tribes of men.
The Hero is one who has reached the ultimate limit;
Indra is the Supreme Lord.

Subduing every fierce being—that is, bringing all those of wicked nature to hell, while leading others, those of virtuous nature, across to the other side—he causes them to transcend saṃsāra most thoroughly, as they blaze forth with an excellence beyond their own individual fitness.
"Dveṣī" means one whose hatred increases. "Śṛṇve" means he is heard of.
From where? Because he is the king of both groups, namely the gods and the asuras.
Moreover, Indra constantly shakes and overturns men, clans, and subjects;
he casts aside the friendships of former times and, moving forward, goes toward others. Shaking off his unfulfilled deeds, Indra traverses many autumns.

He turns away from the friendships of the former; in the past mantra, he abandons the friendships with the fierce ones previously mentioned. Hastening exceedingly with others, the virtuous ones, he comes to the experiences of the present.

Shaking off those [beings] who are devoid of right experience, Indra, while abiding in this contemptible cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), has crossed many autumns— past years— and crosses over those of the present;
he will also cross over those yet to come.
In these two mantras, it is heard that from time immemorial the asuras lack devotion to the Blessed One and attain eternal hell;
the gods always devote themselves to the Blessed One and attain liberation;
and for humans, there is perpetual saṃsāra.
Day after day, he drove away the similar black ones from their dwelling places to another side;
the bull, desiring wealth, slew the two Dāsas, Varcin and Śambara, within the enclosure of the waters.

Day after day, as the showerer of benefits, the Supreme Lord, Vṛṣabha, constantly drives away—by the mere fact of His consciousness—the dark, tamasic creatures; whom does He ward off from the other half of His own abode?
Furthermore, He struck down the two Dāsas, the two Dasyus who sought to seize the world, Varcin and Śambara, within the vast expanse of the waters upon the shore of the ocean.
In this regard, it is understood that for the Daityas there is never liberation.
