The gods worshipped him as *bhūti* (prosperity); therefore they prospered. Even today, when one sleeps, one breathes out saying "bhū-bhūḥ" (prosperity, prosperity). The Asuras worshipped him as *abhūti* (non-prosperity); consequently, they were utterly defeated. Just as a weaver takes a measure of thread and weaves another, newer, and more beautiful form, even so does this Self [transform] this...
Having destroyed the body and caused ignorance to depart, he assumes another form that is newer and more auspicious— whether that of the ancestors,
or of the Gandharvas, or of the gods, or of Prajāpati, or of Brahmā, or of other beings.
This is called "prosperity" (bhūti).
To that Supreme Lord;
*bhūti* means the form of sovereignty;
the ellipsis is "they became liberated."
Now, at this very moment, the wind has fallen asleep;
they have become utterly defeated and have reached the eternal hell.
Herein it is heard that through the correct and the contrary modes of worship of the gods and the asuras, there is the attainment of liberation and darkness respectively.
By this, it is understood that the states of being a deity and an asura are innate (*sahaja*).
This is illustrated by the following example which is about to be explained:
just as a goldsmith (*peśaskāra*) [takes] a measure, a portion, of *peśas*, that is, of gold.
Form, such as a necklace and so forth, appears as if it were something else, newer, prior to its experience; it appears more beautiful due to the removal of impurities.

The Self is the Supreme Self of other beings, the best among men. In this regard, just as the state of being a *rucaka* (necklace) or other ornaments is produced from gold alone by a goldsmith and not from any other substance whatsoever, so too liberation is brought about by the Lord only for those who are fit for liberation, and not for others.
It is understood.
Now, he recites the traditional authorities (*smṛtis*) on this very point: "They go," and so forth.
They swiftly attain the supreme perfection pertaining to this world and the next—
a state that is unattainable by all the asuras, imperishable, and free from affliction;
no men reach that goal except for the devotees of the Lord.

Having previously stated— in the context of the "Satya Yuga"— that those whose nature is that of the [divine] deities attain the fruit of liberation and so forth by means of the word "they go," and having stated that for the *asuras* there is no attainment of that state, and for humans "that goal is not attained," it is now said that there is never such attainment for them:
"The deluded disregard me when I have assumed a human form."
Not knowing my supreme nature as the Great Lord of all beings.
"Those whose hopes are vain, whose actions are vain, whose knowledge is vain, and who are devoid of discernment,
have resorted to a delusive nature, that of Rākṣasas and Asuras.

By the phrase "despising [the Lord]," it is stated that for those possessing the nature of Rākṣasas and others— characterized by such things as contempt for the Blessed One— there is never the attainment of the goals of human life (puruṣārtha).
"Nature" means inherent disposition.
But those great-souled ones, O Pārtha, who have taken refuge in my divine nature, worship me with undistracted minds, knowing me as the imperishable source of all beings. (Manu 3.4.116)
In the phrase "of the high-souled one" (*mahātmanaḥ*), it is understood that divinity—characterized by the worship of the Blessed One and so forth—is his very nature.
Fearlessness, purity of being, steadfastness in the yoga of knowledge, charity, self-restraint, sacrifice, study of the scriptures, austerity, and uprightness; (Manu 3.4.117)
Non-violence, truthfulness, freedom from anger, renunciation, tranquility, absence of malice, compassion for all beings, lack of greed, gentleness, modesty, and steadiness. (Manu 3.118)
Splendor, forgiveness, fortitude, purity, non-malice, and absence of excessive pride—
these, O Bhārata, belong to one born with a divine nature.
Hypocrisy, arrogance, self-conceit, anger, harshness,
and ignorance— these, O Pārtha, belong to one born to the demoniacal nature.

By the word "fearless" (*abhaya*), it is understood that divinity is characterized by fearlessness and so forth, while asuric nature is characterized by hypocrisy and so forth; these are indeed one's own inherent dispositions.
"Those who hate Me in their own bodies and in the bodies of others, being envious—those hateful and cruel ones, the lowest of men, I cast into the cycles of worldly existence."
I perpetually cast those who are inauspicious into the very wombs of the Asuras.
Having entered the womb of an asura, these deluded ones, failing to reach me in birth after birth, O son of Kuntī, then go to the lowest state.
By the phrase "me as the self," it is stated that those of demonic nature (āsura-svabhāva) culminate in the attainment of blinding darkness.
Here, the creation of beings is of two kinds: divine (daiva) and demonic (āsura). That which is devoted to devotion to Viṣṇu is divine; the opposite is demonic. (Manu 3.4.123)
The supreme duty of the gods is always the performance of sacrifices and other rites,
the study of the Vedas, the knowledge of reality, and the constant remembrance of delight in the worship of Viṣṇu.
The Daityas possess strength of arm, envy, skill in battle,
proficiency in the treatises on statecraft, devotion to the worship of Śiva, and traditional learning.
Adherence to the conduct of one's caste and stage of life, Vedic study, and devotion to Acyuta,
Śiva, Sūrya, and likewise to the Goddess— this is recorded as the innate nature of humanity.
The deities are by their very nature eternal Vaiṣṇavas from time immemorial; the Daityas, on the other hand, have always been their opposites since beginningless time.
Human beings possess mixed intentions and their destinies are likewise mixed.
The phrase "of two kinds" clearly declares that the states of being gods and asuras are inherent natures (*svabhāva*),
because the word *sarga* denotes inherent nature;
the connection is thus "only of two kinds."

Even though there are a great many creations (*sarga*), the restriction [to two] is justified by the statement: "Though there be a vast multitude of creations, only two are called gods and asuras, which are superior in their fruits of good and evil, and they exist between them like fragrances.
The term *svabhāva* (intrinsic nature) is also connected here with the words "of the gods" and "of the Daityas."

"Supreme dharma" is an epithet for ritual acts such as sacrifices; it means that rituals like sacrifices take the form of supreme dharma through dedication to the Blessed One and so forth. "Devotion and remembrance of Viṣṇu and Śiva" is the implied remainder of the sentence.
"Abundance of power" (bahuśālitva) is intended here to mean the employment of physical force in an improper place;
"mastery of battle" (yuddhasatkriyā) refers to skill in combat;
and "the [system of] castes and stages of life" (varṇāśrama) indicates that [the king's role] culminates merely in the performance of those duties.
The meaning is that devotion [is directed] equally toward Acyuta and the others.
The term "beginningless" (anādi) is clear.
Precisely because it is beginningless, the phrase "by its very nature from beginningless time" is connected with the word "human beings" (mānuṣāḥ).
Those of mixed dispositions possess both correct and incorrect knowledge;
they follow mixed paths, resulting in the fruit of saṃsāra which consists of both pleasure and pain.
This same result should be understood to apply to gods and others as well.
He shows the fruit of citing the Śruti and Smṛti with the words "ityādi" (and so forth).
From such a collection of statements as this, it is understood that there is beginningless fitness.
By the word "sandarbhaiḥ" (by the textual connections), he indicates that very many statements regarding this matter are to be seen as cited elsewhere.

He states the supporting reasoning (*anugrāhakas tarkaḥ*) for the purpose of ascertaining the pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth of the aforementioned inferences, and for the purpose of refuting the interpretation of the scriptures (*āgama*) in any other sense—namely, "yadi... (if...).
If the distinction is beginningless, how is it that it is not so at present?
The "distinction" (*viśeṣa*) is an excellence (*atiśaya*) residing in its own nature, characterized as a capacity (*yogyatā*).
That distinction is the excellence that is directly perceived.
This is what is meant:
If Hiraṇyagarbha did not possess an beginningless, preeminent distinction characterized by fitness, then his present state of supreme excellence would not exist;
for this [present state] is the seed of that [excellence],
and because it is a rule that in the absence of a cause, there is an absence of the effect.
Otherwise, it would follow that everyone would possess the state of being supreme among all.
This same argument should be stated in other cases as well.

[Objection: Even if there is no beginningless distinction characterized by the fitness of Brahmā and others, the state of being supreme among all and so forth will belong to the practitioner (sādhaka) due solely to his specific unseen merit (adṛṣṭa).

And if it is argued that there is a Smṛti text to this effect, such as: "A man who is steadfast in his own duty attains the state of Viriñca after a hundred births," then the following must be said in response.
What is that specific unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), the seed of Viriñca’s supreme excellence, which arises entirely without depending on any such prior unseen merit? Or does it depend [on it]?
He refutes the first alternative with the words: "And if [it arises] from unseen merit alone..."
And it is from the unseen alone that the unseen is accepted by all the disputants.
Indeed, various substances and other factors are perceived through Śruti and Smṛti as causes for the production of the unseen (adṛṣṭa);
and the attainment of those [substances] has the unseen alone as its cause.
Therefore, all theorists except the Cārvākas accept that it is not only the fruit [of action], but rather that each subsequent unseen arises from each preceding unseen.

Therefore, since it is the cause of supreme excellence, to accept that a specific unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) arises independently of any such prior unseen merit would constitute a departure from established doctrine (*apasiddhānta*). One might argue: "Let this be the established doctrine of other disputants; however, for me, there is a dependence on specific unseen merit only for the production of the results such as supreme excellence, but not for the production of the merit itself. Or else: "That specific unseen merit which is the cause of Viriñca’s supreme excellence, although it is the effect of such an unseen merit [in another], is not itself the effect of an unseen merit. *11,178*

To the one who says, "For if the entire stream were likewise [momentary], your desired conclusion would be established," he states an over-extension (atiprasaṅga): "If it were accidental... and so forth.

If it is claimed that a particular excellence occurs spontaneously in some cases without being seen [as caused], then there would be spontaneity everywhere; thus, there would be no dependence upon the unseen (adṛṣṭa).

If, in some cases— such as when there is a cause for the excellence of Viriñca (Brahmā) or its cause— an excellence or distinction (*viśeṣa*) is held to be accidental (*ākasmika*), meaning it is accepted as being independent of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa-nirapekṣa*), that is to say,
if it is admitted that some particular excellence arises entirely without depending on such an unseen factor;
then, since there is no difference [in the reasoning], one would have to admit that even results and the like are accidental in all cases.
He explains what is to be attained: "No."
The word "everywhere" (*sarvatra*) carries over [from the previous context].
If it were not explained in this way, then since the opponent does not accept that what is unperceived by another is causeless, this undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) would be incoherent.
The intention is that the [verse] regarding "one who has fallen from his position" (*apadāka*) should also be explained in exactly the same manner.
If it is argued that even the excellence of Viriñca (Brahmā) does not depend on the unseen (adṛṣṭa), we say no;
for since the collection of visible causes belonging to a previous birth has perished, this would result in the fallacy of causelessness.
Furthermore, it must be explained from where his specific collection of visible causes also originated.
If it were signless (*nirnimitta*), there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
If it were characterized by its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāvanimitta*), then our desired conclusion is established.
By this, the claim that the Lord Viriñca possesses supreme excellence and perfection because he is satisfied by the visible activity [of creation] is also refuted.
"Because of the avoidance of the fitness for non-appropriation.
[Objection: "In that case, let the second position be accepted. To this, he replies: "If it is from the unseen force (adṛṣṭa)..."
If this distinction is not perceived, why is that beginninglessness not [the case]?
The word "becomes" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
That which is distinguished is a "distinction" (viśe�șa); the meaning is that it is an unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) to be distinguished.
The word "this" refers to the cause of Viriñca’s supreme excellence.
The beginninglessness of such a succession of unseen forces (*adṛṣṭa*), as well as the possession of beginningless fitness (*yogyatā*); that,
then, is the case.
This is what is meant:
just as the cause for Viriñca’s preeminence over all is a specific unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), so too [his state] is caused by such a specific unseen merit from a previous life.
Likewise, one must accept that [the series] is also such and also such,
because the same logic applies.

And thus, as for the objection— "Why does that very [series] serve as the basis for the beginningless stream of specific unperceived forces (*adṛṣṭa*)?"— there is no other answer than its beginningless and specific nature.

That which is called "beginningless fitness" (*anādiyogyatā*) is precisely an adventitious distinction of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*) that serves as the seed for the two adventitious factors—effort and the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*)—which are the means for attaining their respective fruits.
As it has been said:
"*The fitness known as intrinsic nature is what is called 'spontaneity' (*haṭha*)," and so forth.
Therefore, it is established that the beginningless capacity [for spiritual practice] exists in all living beings, from Brahmā down to those at the end of the Kali age.
The subsequent portion of the text is intended to support what was previously stated, namely, that "the Blessed Lord is faultless.
Now, one might object: "Not even on account of place... [B.S. 3.2.11].
This has indeed been established by such [statements] as these.
It is true;
the defectiveness that was reached through reasoning and so forth has been refuted therein.
But here, it is distinguished by the phrase "attained through perception.
If one asks why this too was not refuted in that very same place,
it is because perception does not operate with respect to the universe and so forth.
However, there is no difference whatsoever as to whether the refutation is incidental (*prāsaṅgika*) in that [previous] context or here;
for the author of the *Anubhāṣya* provides here an elaboration (*prapañca*) of the meaning previously stated,
such as the elaboration of the gradations of liberation and so forth.
Therefore, it is appropriate to elaborate upon the faultlessness of the Lord right here.
Furthermore, the determination of the essential nature of knowledge will occur in this context, and its detailed treatment is properly suited to the *Jñānapāda*.

Moreover, it has been stated that the attainment of the entirety of human goals does not occur merely through the direct perception of the Blessed One, but rather from the vision of the Lord as free from all defects.
And by this, the vision of the Blessed One as free from faults is demonstrated.
If it is asked, "Why then is this textual composition not inserted right there?", [the answer is:
because its application here consists in the detailed exposition of the natures of gods, dānavas, and humans, which makes its placement immediately following that section appropriate.
And so we shall explain later (*11,184*).
This is what is being questioned here:
it has already been established that the incarnations of the Blessed One, such as Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, are absolutely non-different from the Blessed One.
Furthermore, the mutual distinction among those persons existing at that time is perceived by direct perception;
and it has already been stated that they do not possess bodies.
Therefore, since there is no room for the distinction to reside in the body alone, [the distinction must belong to the self].
Furthermore, since independence for all [entities] is untenable,
some must be dependent;
in this way, other defects associated with differentiation should also be observed.
Because the same logic applies;
and since defects in the Vedas would be perceived by direct perception, the Blessed One would not be faultless.
In that regard, first, in order to refute the claim that difference is established by direct perception, he cites a scriptural passage, beginning with "And not... (na ca).
And for those who perceive Him, no differentiation is seen in Viṣṇu, as there is in other [beings] that possess differentiation;
the word "ca" is used in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇe*).
"Like the difference between other things" is the negative example (*vyatireka-dṛṣṭānta*).
Just as in the case of other things such as jars and so forth, a difference characterized by mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) is observed as distinct from their plurality, so it is not here.
If it were merely stated that "no difference is observed in Viṣṇu," it would be understood that even plurality is not observed; for that reason, this statement was made.
Alternatively, the construction is as follows: just as difference with respect to another counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is perceived in Viṣṇu, it is not so perceived with respect to himself.
Otherwise, one might also conclude that difference even with respect to counter-correlates such as a jar is not perceived.
Or else, it should be explained as a single compound: "in Viṣṇu, who possesses difference having another as its counter-correlate."
The purpose has already been stated. It is agreed even by the opponent that no difference is perceived nowadays between Viṣṇu and his forms such as Rāma and Kṛṣṇa.
Therefore, it was said, "even for those who see that [descent].
The genitive case is used in the sense of the instrumental;
the meaning is "even by those who see the descent."

Or rather, it is because those who perceive that [truth] do so even through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). By their very nature, living beings (*jīva*) are of three kinds, distinguished as gods, *dānavas*, and humans.
In this regard, the sense is that direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) does not, for its part, apprehend any mutual difference among the incarnations (*avatāra*).
Not only this much, but what else? To this he says: "It is indeed recognition (*pratyabhijñā*)."
...recognition itself is observed among things that possess many forms. 3.4.130cd

Among the supreme persons, in the various forms of the Blessed One, it is precisely recognition—whose object is non-difference, in the form "this is that very same one"—that is observed in the Purāṇas and other texts.
For example, there is the recognition of Jāmbavat: "This Kṛṣṇa is that very Rāma.
Thus, the sense is: how could there be any room for the cognition of difference?

Now, one might object: "Multiplicity, being untenable without difference, implies it; and thus recognition of multiple forms is simply impossible. Or, if it were possible, it would have to be an illusion. To this, he says: "And as for multiplicity... [etc.].
And plurality especially... // MDh 3.4.132ab //
The phrase "of the forms of the Blessed One" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
The meaning is that an *arthāpatti* (presumption) whose purpose is frustrated by another possible explanation does not establish difference.

Furthermore, in the case where [difference] could be explained otherwise, there would be doubt regarding difference; since even that is undesirable, he indicates an alternative explanation with the words "not by way of difference."
... nor in any way by means of distinction. Mānava 3.4.132b.
The word "is appropriate" is to be supplied in both cases.
Why?
Because there is no evidence that could provide scope for a difference between the forms of the Blessed One, and because such a difference would contradict [the established doctrine].
This is what he says with the words "in any way whatsoever" (*kathañcana*).
Thus, when supreme persons perceive the Blessed One as having a single form, and there is no cognition of another form, the knowledge of difference from that [other form] is impossible;
for it is a necessary rule that in the absence of the cognition of a counter-correlate (*pratiyogi*), there is an absence of the knowledge of difference.
It has been stated that this is because such a contradictory recognition exists even when [the identity] is present.
Nevertheless, the direct perception of people of middling capacity and others will serve as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the difference in the Blessed One’s forms.

Even though the perception of difference is impossible at the time of perceiving a single form due to the absence of the cognition of another form, it is indeed possible when that other form is present.

Furthermore, you cannot maintain that recognition (pratyabhijñā) applies even to those [atoms], for it would follow that they are of superior size; therefore, with reference to the intermediate-sized objects, he says: "And recognition... and so forth.
And those for whom there is recognition—they too have their vision stolen by that [delusion].
This is the meaning of the verse.

However, as for those people of middling capacity who lack recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) regarding the forms of the Blessed One, the construction is that they too do not perceive any difference therein.
The reason for the absence of recognition is that their vision has been stolen and destroyed by that Blessed One.
Or rather, it is by virtue of that multiplicity;

for the multiplicity perceived— strengthened by the will of the Blessed One and by their own suitability— obstructs the cognition of the non-difference that exists even when the object is being apprehended, despite its actual presence.
In this context, because of the restatement "those [beings] also have their vision stolen," it is understood that due to having their vision stolen, they lack recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).

When it is said that they do not see any difference in the form of the Blessed One, a dull-witted person might understand that they do not even see a difference from pots and other such objects; to prevent that [misunderstanding], he says: "difference" (*bheda*).
They perceive no distinction at all, nor do they see any distinction from others; Hari reveals himself to them in this way, and not otherwise.
The construction is: "and they indeed perceive the difference from others.
Now, one might ask: is the pair of entities being perceived cognized as distinct or as non-distinct?
For how can there be a cognition that is indifferent to both difference and non-difference? To this, he says: "In this way."
Thus is the statement in the *Bṛhatsaṃhitā*: ... // MAnu 3.134ab //
The word "fitness" (*yogyatā*) is to be understood as the ellipsis [for the first part].
Otherwise, by the rule beginning with *gati-buddhi-*, the designation of object (*karmasaṃjñā*) would apply, and consequently the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) would occur;
or else, the transposition of case endings (*vibhaktivyatyaya*) is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
Otherwise, he demonstrates it through both difference and non-difference:

namely, how for those who maintain the theory of non-apprehension (*akhyātivāda*), there is a cognition of the object through the power of auxiliary factors while remaining indifferent to difference and non-difference;
or as others hold, following the perception of a fragment of mother-of-pearl, there is a subsequent conceptualization (*vyāsakti*).

Likewise, what contradiction is there in this being perceived in such a way here as well through the power of the Supreme Lord? However, the perception of an inferior individual soul will have another explanation.
Thus, by one who rejects perception regarding the distinction of the form of the Lord, inference is also rejected.

Because it has already been stated that plurality is established otherwise, and by that same logic, specific forms and so forth are also established otherwise; the words "there is a statement" are to be supplied as the remainder. *11,191*
If it is argued that while a difference in the nature of the Blessed One may not be established by perception or inference,
it will nonetheless be established by scripture because the words "another" (*anya*) and so forth are heard here and there in the Purāṇas— this is not so.
Because this contradicts Vedic statements such as "There is no diversity whatsoever here," one might ask:
why does the Purāṇa not subvert the Veda? To this, he says: "No."
... nor one who follows the Purāṇas; for only one who advocates worldly perception would be capable of contradicting the Vedas. (Manu 3.4.134b–d)
The term "statement" carries over [from the previous context].
Indeed, the ancient statement regarding people's perception of difference among the forms of the Blessed One is intended solely as a restatement;
it does not concern the ultimate reality.
Because it is understood as such through direct observation and other means;
whereas the Veda possesses an intention regarding the actual state of things,
since it is determined to be so by means of inferential marks.

Therefore, that [scriptural testimony] is not capable of subverting that [perception]. But is this not contradicted by what was previously stated, namely, that there is no perception whose object is a particular form of the Blessed One?
"But now it exists"—this is not so; for if that [Veda] itself did not exist, it would be impossible for the Purāṇic statement to be a restatement of it.
Do not say this.
This is because it is possible for [the scripture] to merely restate the perception of difference produced by fallacious inferences such as "being many" and so forth.
Furthermore, it has been stated that superior and middling individuals possess no direct perception (pratyakṣa) regarding difference;
yet now, it is being admitted that such perception exists for inferior individuals.

Nor should it be said that "in that case, that very [perception] will serve as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the distinction between the forms of the Blessed One," because it is sublated by a perception whose object is the non-difference of the supreme ones;
and yet, that [perception] is not non-existent.
For it is stated in the Āgama that recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) alone is observed among those who possess manifold forms;
likewise, there is this statement of Bhīṣma:
"This very unborn one, who dwells in the heart of every embodied being whose self is imagined [as separate]..."
Having dispelled the delusion of duality, I have attained the one Sun, which appears as many according to each individual vision.
Thus [it is said].

Now, one might ask: why is it that the perception of difference (*bhedadarśana*) itself does not sublate the perception of non-difference (*abhedadarśana*)? To this, he says: "unexamined" (*aparīkṣita*).
And one who holds an unexamined view can never succeed in refuting a view that is preceded by examination. 3.135abc.
"Unexamined" means not determined to be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) through investigation. The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of drawing forward the word "not" (*na*).
That perception for which the determination of validity is preceded by investigation is "perception preceded by investigation."

Or, it refers to that perception for which the determination of validity (*prāmāṇyaniścaya*) occurs preceded by examination (*parīkṣā*). By the phrase "in some cases" (*kvāpi*), he states a restriction.
Thus, by this, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is stated: that a cognition whose validity has not been determined through examination does not subvert another cognition regarding its cause of validity.

The mention of "examination" (*parīkṣā*) is merely an illustration for the ascertainment of validity (*prāmāṇyaniścaya*), and not intended as a restrictive rule; this will become clear later. Regarding this, he provides an example: "Devadatta," etc. (*devadatta*).
... like the views of Vedadatta and others. (Manu 3.135cd)

The meaning is as follows: just as the perception of Devadatta and others, whose validity is not yet ascertained, does not sublate the perception of Yajñadatta and others, whose validity is already ascertained; so it is here.
If one asks, "What follows if such is the pervasion? [the answer is:
the perception of difference has unascertained validity, whereas the perception of non-difference has ascertained validity.
Therefore, we say that this [perception] is not a sublater of that [scriptural cognition], but rather the opposite is the case.
To the question, "Why is the perception of difference one whose validity is not yet ascertained? he says: "And not..."
And there is no ancient scriptural statement anywhere regarding the perception of that whose difference is already certain. MAnu 3.4.136a–c.
The word *ca* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*).
*Kvacitpradeśe* means "in a certain place.
The word *hi* indicates a reason (*hetau*).
First of all, for us, perception regarding the distinction between the forms of the Supreme Lord is established solely from the statements of the Purāṇas.
And as for the Purāṇic statement, it may establish that "some perceive a distinction," either as a restatement (*anuvāda*) or as an inferential mark (*liṅga*).
Therefore, the determination of its validity must be sought from that very source [the Veda].
However, there exists no scriptural statement in the Purāṇas that establishes the validity of the perception of difference.
Thus, the sense is that because of the absence of such a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there can be no determination of the validity of the perception of difference.
The ascertainment of validity occurs through two modes:
either by the ascertainment of the reality of the object, or by the examination of the cognition.
It was stated with reference to the former [mode] that "the distinction is ascertained as true."

However, according to the second interpretation, the compound is *bhedasya-darśanam* (the seeing of difference). The elision [of the case-ending] in the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhyā*) is by the rule "in the sense of abuse" (*ākrośe*).
It is described as such because it is both determined and examined, and it is that very seeing of difference.
In this regard, there is no contradiction, for [the former] is an abuse according to one's own intention, while [the latter] is certainty according to another's intention.

If the perception of difference were not understood as having established authority solely from the words of the Purāṇas, then what kind of [perception] would be understood? To this he says: "indistinct" (sammugdham).
...a confused perception is understood to occur therein. // Mānava 3.4.136cd //
The perception of difference is doubtful because of the possibility of both validity and invalidity;
this refers to the statement in the Purāṇa.
This is what is meant:
the statement from the Purāṇa merely indicates the perception of difference;
it does not, however, establish its own validity or invalidity.
Therefore, prior to the realization of the perception of non-difference, it is indeed appropriate that there be doubt regarding its validity or invalidity;
however, once the perception of non-difference has been realized, its invalidity alone is determined,
because its validity has already been ascertained from the Purāṇic statement itself.
This is because [the realization] "I have attained it" arises from hearing the sound of the word;
because it has been stated that the various inferences [such as "it resides manifoldly in every heart"] are fallacious;
and because the delusion of duality is designated as "delusion" in the phrase "with the delusion of difference shaken off."
Thus, the absence of difference among the forms of the Blessed One is established;
likewise, the absence of defects such as piercing and so forth is established, due to the lack of any means of valid cognition [to the contrary]. *11,197*
Is it not the case that direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) demonstrating its existence?
Do not say so; for [the claim] is sublated by the direct perception of great beings, which apprehends the absence of piercing and so forth.
To the question, "Why would this alone not be its sublater? he says: "Because it is precisely unexamined."
In this matter, the piercing and other rites of the Lord [the Sun] remain unexamined;
indeed, no one anywhere has ever observed an examination of them.
In this context, it refers to the interval between the presence and absence of defects such as piercing (vedha),
or else it refers to the descents of the Sovereign Lord (adhīśituḥ) here.

The connection is with the word "is seen" (*dṛśyate*). Alternatively, by the phrase "piercing and so forth," that perception is indicated. Perception accompanied by investigation is "investigative perception" (*parīkṣā-darśanam*).
Alternatively, *parīkṣā* means that which is examined;
the suffix *akāra* is applied according to the rule *gurośca halaḥ*.
It refers to both the examination and the seeing of that [object] therein.
In some cases, piercing and so forth are observed.
The point is that the perception of defects is unexamined, whereas the perception of the absence of defects is examined.
Now, one might ask: on what basis is it established that the direct perception of the Great Ones has as its object the absence of defects? To this he says: "It is indeed without defect."
Brahmā beheld him as entirely faultless and possessing every form; Rudra likewise saw him as faultless, and Purandara saw him as faultless.
"The forms of this [Viṣṇu] were seen as faultless by the best of the gods;
all others, however, are possessed of faults, while Hari alone is faultless. From this statement in the *Barku-śruti*, it follows that his vision is not defective.
*adrāk* means *adrākṣīt*;
according to the statement that "the traditional grammatical rules are not eternal," [the form] *purandaraḥ adrākṣīt* [is valid].
Even by other supreme gods,
they have been seen as possessing faults;
therefore, Hari alone is faultless.
The word "ca" (and) serves to include other scriptural passages.
Regarding this Supreme Lord, the vision of the great ones is not at all defective or grasping at faults; rather, it perceives Him as entirely faultless. *11,200*
The perception of faults is unexamined, whereas the perception of their absence is examined; why is this so? To this he says: "unpierced."
"Though unpierced, Viṣṇu appears as if pierced; though unborn, he falsely appears as if born;
and though unbound, he appears as if bound—thus does the Paiṅgi-Śruti proclaim the faultlessness of Hari. (Manusmṛti 3.4.140)
"Unpierced as if pierced":
the suffix *vati* is used with a word ending in the accusative case according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).
The word "eva" (as if) is connected with "unpierced" and so forth.
It reveals the Self.
It has been stated that this meaning is also established by implication through the preceding scriptural passage, namely the Paiṅgi-śruti.
By the statement of the result, "freedom from defect," it indicates the intended meaning.
Right here, he cites a clear scriptural passage: "By the unexamined," etc.
"By a vision that does not investigate, Hari is seen as possessing faults;
but in the vision of investigation, no fault of Hari is ever seen.
Thus says the Paiṅgi Śruti. ... MAnu 3.4.141a-e.
He says that the perception of faults is unexamined, whereas the perception of faultlessness is examined.
To the question "What follows from that?", he replies: "For [it is] a valid means of knowledge..."
...for authoritative means of knowledge have indeed been examined.

That which has been examined by means of investigation and determined to be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is alone a *pramāṇa*. That which has not been examined, however, is initially doubtful;
but when a certain contradiction arises, it is simply not a *pramāṇa* at all.
Therefore, by the observation of faultlessness through examination, the unexamined observation of faults is indeed sublated;
the reverse is not the case.
The word "hi" (for) indicates that the utility of examination for the ascertainment of validity is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
And so it will be stated [later].
On this point, some say:
"The validity of cognitions is apprehended intrinsically (*svataḥ*)."
It is not, however, dependent upon examination;
for all cognition is self-luminous and true to reality.
Therefore, since its own validity is established by itself through itself, what need is there for dependence on examination?
Others, however, say that both that cognition and its validity are apprehended by inference alone;
yet others maintain:
Knowledge and its validity are known by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) alone;
for if there were no apprehension of validity intrinsically (*svataḥ*), then it would not exist at all,
because if its [validity] depended upon investigation, it would lead to the consequence of infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
Indeed, examination (*parīkṣā*) is a specific kind of inference.
And since the determination of its validity would depend on another examination, how could there not be an infinite regress?
To this, he first avoids the consequence of infinite regress regarding the fact that the apprehension of validity depends upon examination, by saying: "No."
There would be no end to the process of investigation... // MAnu 3.4.142a //
The phrase "even if" is to be understood as "even if one accepts that the apprehension of validity depends upon investigation.
He states the reason for this: "the witness," etc.
But when it is established by witnesses, there is no doubt.
Indeed, knowledge is twofold: that which consists of a modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa-pariṇāma-rūpa*) and that which consists of the witness (*sākṣi-rūpa*).
Here, the word "but" (*tu*) serves to distinguish [the latter] from the former.
This is what is meant:
This infinite regress would occur if investigation were required in every case;
but it is not so.
For investigation is indeed required regarding a matter that is doubtful, but not regarding one that is beyond doubt.
Furthermore, doubt arises regarding objects of mental modification, such as water and the like, but not regarding pleasure and so forth, which are established by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*).
Therefore, investigation proceeds only so long as it has not yet entered into the pleasure and other states grasped by the witness; how, then, could there be an infinite regress?
This point has been explained by us in detail in the *Prakṛtyadhikaraṇa*.
To the question, "What is the reason that doubt has only the mental modification as its object and is not established by the witness-consciousness (sākṣin)? he says: "It is mental" (mānasa).
Faults may exist in a mental vision, but never in the vision of a witness.
Faults may be conceived as the causes in the form of the transformation of the mind.
The word *vai* has the sense of the word *tu*.
This is the meaning.
For doubt is of two kinds: first, that which exists from the very beginning, such as "Is this a post or a person?"
Another, however, follows upon a certainty;
for example: "This is perceived as a post—is it a post or not?"
Among these, the first is rooted in defects such as the non-perception of distinguishing features;
the second is likewise rooted in the suspicion that the first cognition was produced by a defect.
And such defects can occur only in mental perception.
Therefore, that [cognition] either arises as being of the nature of doubt, or for one who has attained certainty regarding the object, there occurs a subsequent doubt;
however, no possibility of defect exists in the perception of the witness (the self-evident).

Therefore, that [cognition] is not of the nature of doubt, nor is there doubt regarding an object already established by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*). It is clear that defects may arise in mental perception.
Why is it that [the self] cannot exist as a witness? To this he says: "Because it is very firm."
That in which there is a very firm determination is to be known as the testimony of witnesses.
"Extremely firm" means never subject to sublation. "Certainty" (*nirṇaya*) is a cognition characterized by ascertainment (*avadhāraṇa*). The particle *yatra* has the sense of *yaḥ* (that which).
This is what is meant:
defects of cognition must be postulated either by the observation of its oscillation or by the occurrence of a powerful subverting factor,
as it has been said:

"Defects [in a means of knowledge] are to be known from a stronger means of proof, and not otherwise. Furthermore, it has been established in a separate section that the testimony of witnesses consists of a definitive determination and is not sublated;
therefore, due to the absence of a [contradictory] means of proof, no defect can possibly exist therein. *11,209*

It has been stated that there is no doubt regarding an object established by the witness-consciousness; in order to make that [truth] firmly rooted in experience, he first states the object established by the witness-consciousness: "Desire," etc.
Desire, knowledge, pleasure, pain, fear, fearlessness, compassion, and so forth, are established by the witness-consciousness... [Mānava-dharmaśāstra 3.4.143a-c]
By the phrase "and so forth," effort, aversion, and the absences of these are included.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "No."
For indeed, no one there has any doubt regarding anything whatsoever. (Manu 3.143cd)
In this context, the word "kvacit" (in some cases) is to be connected [to the preceding].
By the word "hi," he states that there is never any doubt as to whether "I have happiness" or not, nor is there any doubt as to whether "this perceived happiness exists or does not exist.

It is not logical to claim that the witness-perception (*sākṣidarśana*) is indeed uncontradicted, because contradiction is observed in the case of [the appearance of] silver in a mother-of-pearl shell and similar instances.
For it is not possible for another cognition to exist there at the very moment of perception; therefore, he says: "If [it were so]... (Mānava 3.4.143ef):
"Indeed, that mental perception might be fallacious in some instances."

Any perception that is erroneous—that is, sublated—in some object such as silver in a mother-of-pearl shell and the like, is produced by instruments such as the eyes and consists solely of a transformation of the mind (manas), not of the nature of the Witness (sākṣin).
Why is this so?
Because there would be no end to the process if one were to admit that mental perception is subject to sublation.
For it has been stated that if witnesses were [to perceive things] in such a manner, it would entail the undesirable consequence of the collapse of all legal proceedings;
this is precisely what is indicated by the word "hi" (for/indeed).
Furthermore, its status as a mental perception (*mānasatva*) is possible, since the theory of misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*) has been established. *11,211*

It has been stated that for mental perception (*mānasa-darśana*), there is the possibility of defects and sublation; if so, then what kind of [perception] possesses validity? To this, he says: "The mind" (*manaḥ*).
That vision which has been examined is that wherein the validity of even the perceptions of the mind and the eye is firmly grasped by the Witness. (Manu Smṛti 3.144)
The terms "mind" (manaḥ) and "eye" (cakṣuḥ), along with the word "sound" (śabdaḥ), are indicative of the ear and the other [senses].
"Perception" (darśanam) means direct intuition (sākṣātkāraḥ).
By the word "and so forth" (ādipadena), inferential and verbal cognitions are included.
The meaning is: "of knowledge, which is a mental modification produced by the instruments of the senses, marks, and words.
The genitive case is used in the sense of selection (nirdhāraṇa).
The word "api" (even) has the sense of "even though there may be sublation due to suspected defects."

In that cognition which is well-grasped and ascertained through investigation, that is "investigated vision" (*parīkṣitadarśana*), and it is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); this is the remainder [of the definition].

Some maintain that investigation is useful only for the apprehension of the validity of perceptual and scriptural cognitions, whereas the apprehension of the validity of the cognition of the locus (*dharmijñāna*), inference, comparison, and reflective awareness (*anuvyavasāya*) does not depend upon investigation.
In order to refute that [objection] and for the sake of including all mental [perceptions], it is stated [in the verse] "among the seeing by the mind, the eye, and so forth.
Otherwise, he would have simply said, "where there is cognition," and so on.

Since the point was already complete with the mere statement "that alone is the means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*), he explains the phrase "well-grasped" (*sugṛhīta*) by way of restating what has been examined: "the perception [is well-grasped]. (11.212)

Thus, although the apprehension of the validity of cognitions such as mental perception depends upon investigation (*parīkṣā*), it has been stated that there is no infinite regress of investigations because the apprehension of the validity of the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) does not depend upon it. In this regard, what is the purpose of these two alternative hypotheses? One might raise the objection: "Why should the apprehension of the validity of perceptual and other types of cognition not also be independent of investigation—being *svataḥ* (intrinsic) in the manner described, just like the witness-consciousness? He dispels this doubt with the word "no" (*na*).
Its authority is not seen to reside merely in the vision of knowledge.
The vision of knowledge is "jñānadṛṣṭi";
[the phrase] "of that knowledge" (*tasya jñānasya*) is what is meant by this.
*11,213* This is what is being stated.
To begin with, the self-luminosity of empirical cognitions (*vṛttijñāna*) is simply untenable,
because there is no evidence for it;
for the practical functioning of cognition is adequately accounted for by its being known through the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*).
This is because the experience "I know this" is of the nature of a witness (*sākṣin*).

Furthermore, there is contradiction with such proofs as: "The cognition under dispute is not self-luminous, because it is non-self, because it is an effect, because it is impermanent, because it consists of the mind, and like pleasure and so forth.
Or, even if cognition were self-luminous, it would be so only in its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), and not with respect to its own attribute (*svadharma*), namely its validity (*prāmāṇya*).
For instance: when the Vedic sentences are heard, does the knowledge of the meaning of those sentences arise for the outsider, or not?
It cannot be the second [alternative].
Because it is impossible for an effect not to arise when its causal totality (sāmagrī) is present;
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that even for a Mīmāṃsaka, such an effect would not arise.
Furthermore, in the first case as well, does that [totality] manifest itself or not?
If the position is "no," it constitutes an abandonment of the established tenet (*apasiddhānta*).
Regarding the first [alternative], does its validity manifest or not?
Not the first.
Because that [first position] is untenable as it lacks a supporting argument;
therefore, since the validity of knowledge is not seen by the mere act of seeing it, the second [position] alone must be accepted.
And thus, since validity would be grasped by self-luminous cognition alone, how could it be so?

Furthermore, since an outsider—having been awakened by arguments such as the lack of human authorship (*apauruṣeyatva*)—also comes to accept that validity, how is it not the case that there is a dependence upon investigation?
Otherwise, there would be no disagreement whatsoever regarding the validity of Vedic knowledge, just as there is none regarding the nature of the cognition itself.
Furthermore, according to the view of one who speaks thus, errors such as the [perception of] silver in mother-of-pearl would not occur.
For an error consists precisely in the non-apprehension of the difference between this present experience and the recollection of silver.

In that case, since the manifestation of validity, as well as of the difference between the two, and of their respective natures as experience and recollection, would necessarily occur, how could there be any room for error?
For there is no distinction whatsoever between validity and [the object's] difference and so forth; thus,
the claim that both the cognition and its validity are to be inferred together is also incorrect, since [this would apply to] the cognition as well.

Because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for its being an object of measurement, and because the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding it can be accounted for otherwise; for knowledge, which perishes very rapidly, appears as "I know" through its manifestation as something present.
And because it is untenable;
and because it contradicts its immediate manifestation.
Even if knowledge were inferable, its validity is not seen to be established by the mere inference of that knowledge.
For that [cognition] must be inferred through its state of being known, through its practical activity, or through its effect;
yet, validity cannot be inferred on that basis alone,
because of the possibility of deviation.
Therefore, once cognition is apprehended merely through its state of being known (*jñātatā*), its validity (*prāmāṇya*) is to be inferred from the absence of sublation (*bādhābhāva*) and so forth;
otherwise, it would follow that even external cognitions could be inferred as valid by means of Vedic cognition.
If it is argued that even what has thus followed is set aside [as invalid], [we reply: ...
In that case, it follows that an investigation is necessarily required in order to refute objections;
and this is precisely what we shall assert.
However, the claim that "in every respect there is no need for investigation" is not acceptable.
By this, the position that [the self] is known by a witness is also refuted;
for outsiders do not perceive its validity merely through the perspective of the knowledge found in the Upaniṣads.
As for the fourth position, it is extremely weak.

[The opponent might argue: "Because the validity of that [perception] has not been seen by the Cārvākas and others merely through their observation of inferential and other types of knowledge, and because there is a lack of evidence for its classification [as a separate means of knowledge], and because there is no disagreement regarding the validity of the cognition of the subject (*dharmin*) and so forth. [To this we reply: No.
If it is argued that this view— such as the doctrine of being without an objective basis— is sublated by reasoning (*upapatti*),
then you yourself have already accepted the necessity of investigation; so enough with this prolixity.

If that is the case, then one might argue that the authority of the witness (sākṣin) should also be accepted as being grasped only through dependence on examination, just like perception and other means of knowledge, because it is improper to conceive of it in two ways; to this, he says: "by necessity" (niyamena).
"The validity [of perception] regarding pleasure and so forth is invariably within the range of the witness (*sākṣin*).
The word "is seen" (*dṛśyate*) carries over from the previous context.
That which has the witness as its range is described as such.
And being the "object-domain" (gocaratva) is intended here in the sense of being the basis (āśraya).
That which constitutes validity residing in the witness with respect to objects such as pleasure is observed to be invariably present.
This is what is meant:

If the validity of the witness-consciousness (*sākṣijñāna*) were like that of the functioning cognitions (*vṛttijñāna*), such that it were not perceived merely by its being seen, then we would postulate some additional cause;
but this is not the case.
For when a cognition of pleasure is perceived, there is never observed any non-cognition, doubt, or error regarding its validity.
Because, when a conceptualizer exists, the twofold conceptualization is not a fault.
Furthermore, if the apprehension of the validity of a witness also depended upon examination, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
One might object: "Is it not proper for one who desires the apprehension of validity to avoid this infinite regress?"
Since the infinite regress of the apprehender (grāhaka) is difficult to avoid even if there is no infinite regress of the examination (parīkṣā), he says: "Its own validity" (svaprāmāṇyam).
The witness always perceives one's own validity with complete certainty.
The connection is "as if a witness. "Because of constant certainty" means that it does not depend on investigation at all.
This is postulated on the grounds of both experience and the impossibility of otherwise accounting for it.
But if this were so, it would follow that the validity of functional cognitions (*vṛttijñāna*) is extrinsic (*parataḥ*),
since the nature of cognition itself is known by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*).

Since validity is something to be reached through investigation (*parīkṣā*), if that were so, the position that validity is intrinsic—which was maintained by the statement "not because of dissimilarity" (*na vilakṣaṇatvāt*)—would have to be abandoned; therefore, he says: "of cognition" (*jñānasya*).
For the validity of knowledge is measured by the witness who is its very perceiver.

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: because the validity (*mānatā*) of cognition—that is, its being a means of knowledge (*miti*)—is apprehended by the witness (*sākṣin*) alone, self-validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*) is indeed accepted.
Self-validity would be abandoned only if we were to say that cognition itself is what is known by the witness, but not its validity;
however, this is not the case.

Since it is accepted that, like knowledge itself, its validity is also cognizable by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*), for what purpose then is the necessity of examination (*parīkṣā*) admitted? To this he replies: "By defects," etc.
In the absence of defects, there is validity... // MAnu 3.4.147a //
The point that "ascertainment by a witness" will be explained later should also be applied here.
Thus, the two words "of validity" (*prāmāṇyasya*) and "itself" (*iti*) are to be supplied.
When the witness apprehends the cognition, he ascertains its validity as "this is valid" provided there is an absence of defects in the instrument [of knowledge].
But it is not that this [cognition] is itself a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "Of the absence of defects" (*doṣābhāvasya*).
The absence of defects is ascertained by the witness;
and in some cases, intrinsic validity (svataḥ-prāmāṇya) is indeed accepted.
The word "by means of examination" (*parīkṣayā*) is to be understood as the ellipsis.
The particle *ca* is used for emphasis.
The meaning is: "only when, due to some specific purpose, a desire to know (*jijñāsā*) has arisen, and when an opportunity for examination is obtained."
The investigation is for the purpose of ascertaining the absence of defects, not for the purpose of grasping validity;
furthermore, that [validity] is cognizable by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) just like the cognition itself.
Therefore, the meaning is that there is no abandonment of self-validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*).
It might be argued that this process would be valid if it were supported by authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), but since that is not the case, he says: "Therefore" (*ataḥ*).
Therefore, the validity of all means of knowledge would not be established [inherently];
that which is confirmed by a witness is the defining characteristic of validity. For this very reason, the validity of all cognitions is not initially established.

What indeed [is the point]? At whatever time and in whatever case validity is ascertained by a witness aided by investigation, at that very time the validity—whose own-characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) is the nature of validity itself—is established as being distinct from invalidity.
This is what is meant.

If this process— whereby a witness first apprehends validity in a general way, thinking "this is a means of valid knowledge because there is an absence of defects," and only later, when a desire to know arises, determines through investigation that it is indeed a valid means of knowledge— is not accepted, then the validity of all cognitions produced by words and other means regarding unfamiliar objects would have to be determined at the very first moment.
But this is not the case;
therefore we know that this process exists.
To facilitate the comprehension of the point already stated, he says in brief: "Not indeed," etc.
For no person ever entertains doubt regarding pleasure and the like,
nor does every person ascertain all means of valid knowledge.
Therefore, why is that which is already established in experience being denied?

Since no one entertains doubt regarding pleasure and the like, and since all people do not determine that all empirical cognitions (*vṛttijñāna*) are valid only as direct perceptions (*darśana*), therefore the validity of the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*) is apprehended by the witness itself without depending on further investigation; whereas for empirical cognitions, it depends [on such investigation]. Why, then, should this object of knowledge (*prameya*), which is established by experience, be denied?

Since it is impossible to deny the signless (*nirnimitta*), he concludes what was stated—that there would be no infinite regress in critical examination—with the words: "and because of the absence of defects, etc. (*doṣābhāvādikaṃ ca*).
And the witness perceives correctly the absence of defects and so forth.
The connection is "just like a witness.

Just as a witness, independent of any formal examination, correctly perceives both the absence of defects in himself and in the examination, as well as the validity [of the testimony], so too [is it here].
Therefore, there is no infinite regress whatsoever.
He concludes what was stated in the passage beginning with "precisely unexamined" by saying "that."
When measured by that standard, there is no fault whatsoever in Viṣṇu.
Therefore, only that which has been examined is valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
By this, it is established that there is no fault whatsoever in the Blessed One.
Consequently, the perception of faults—which is unexamined because it contradicts that [valid cognition]—is itself not a valid means of knowledge; such is the meaning.
Thus, it has been stated that an unexamined perception of faults, when sublated by an examined perception of faultlessness, is incapable of proving the Blessed One to be faulty.
Now, he indicates the logical over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) that would follow if even such [unexamined perception] were capable of proving [a point], with the words "unexamined," etc.
In what matter, indeed, would one whose vision is unexamined not be found? (3.151cd)
The point is that this [nature of being silver] indeed exists even in mother-of-pearl and the like with respect to their state as silver;
therefore, that [silver-nature] would likewise be established [in the case of the shell], since there is no distinction between them.
Thus, it has been stated that the observation of defects is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*) because it contradicts perceptual experience that has been examined.
Furthermore, this contradicts such scriptural passages as, "He is without desire, he is blameless," and so forth.
It might be argued:
"It was previously stated that because the scripture 'That thou art' (tattvamasi) and others contradict direct perception, they lack authority regarding their literal meaning."
To dispel the doubt as to how perception, which is the opposite of that [scripture], can now be declared invalid due to its contradiction with scripture, he says: "That... (tad).
Therefore, when a matter contradicts what is perceived by direct perception, even scripture lacks authority;
for in such a case, that which is born of the senses is what must be relied upon, whereas the opposite is true elsewhere.

Whenever and wherever that which is born of the senses (*akṣaja*) is the basis upon which scripture depends, then, even though scripture is stronger by its very nature, it possesses no authority regarding an object that contradicts perception. Therefore,

other than in the aforementioned relationship of the dependent and the basis, when the relationship of the dependent and the basis is reversed, the relationship of the sublated and the sublator is likewise inverted.
The meaning is that when scripture (*āgama*) is the basis upon which perception (*pratyakṣa*) depends, then perception has no authority regarding an object that contradicts scripture.
To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "In the worldly [context]. (*laukika*) //11.226//
In this worldly transaction, perception is that upon which [the other means] depend; however, in the observation of the descent [of the law], scripture is that upon which they depend.

In the worldly transaction consisting of the communication that the self and other objects established by perception possess Brahman as their essence, which is carried out through scriptures such as "That thou art," there exists here in this scripture a dependence of the scripture upon perception;
yet, regarding the perception of defects in the incarnations, Viṣṇu and others, there would be a dependence of perception and so forth upon the scripture.
This is what is meant.

Having previously stated that scripture lacks authority due to its contradiction with perception, it is not contradictory to now state that perception lacks authority due to its contradiction with scripture.
For it was not asserted that perception and scripture, in their unqualified forms, stand in a relationship of mutual sublation;
rather, the former is sublated by virtue of being dependent, while the latter is the sublator by virtue of being that upon which the former depends.
Regarding the objection, "How can there be a contradiction when that [is one way] there and another way here?",

the challenge— namely, why the scripture itself should not be invalid due to its contradiction with perception regarding the object of the fault— has already been disposed of by the very miscarriage of the fetus;
for it has been stated that scripture possesses greater force than perception because it is that upon which perception depends.
To the question of how perception depends upon scripture, he says: "By means of scripture.
For it is by means of scripture that one recognizes his status as Viṣṇu, and only then is a fault attributed here.
In this context, regarding Viṣṇu,
it is said that "it is imagined" with the intention that this is in fact merely a conceptual construction and not a valid cognition (*pramiti*).
This would be the case if the scripture were something to be depended upon (*upajīvya*).
Viṣṇu-hood ought to be known;
yet that very thing is not to be known—therefore he says: "If not."
If there were no other who was possessed of faults... || MAnu 3.154c ||

If Viṣṇu-hood were not known in [the case of] Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and others, then by perception— which apprehends defects— one would grasp that "someone other than Viṣṇu is defective," but not that "Viṣṇu is defective.
For indeed, when Devadatta-ness is not known, a cognition in the form "this Devadatta has arrived" cannot possibly arise.
Nevertheless, scripture is not that upon which [the opponent] relies;

for, having inferred Viṣṇu’s nature through characteristics such as the Śrīvatsa and Kaustubha, one might then perceive through direct perception that "Viṣṇu possesses defects. To this, he says: "The scripture... (śāstra).
For a definition is indeed established by the treatises.

The fact that characteristics such as the Śrīvatsa mark are pervaded by Viṣṇu-hood is established by scripture alone. Although, in this view, scripture is not directly the basis [for inference], nevertheless, it is unavoidable to rely upon it for grasping the pervasion (vyāpti) which serves as the root of the inference; this is the intended meaning.
[Objection: But if Viṣṇu-hood is unknown, how could there be the cognition that "someone other than Viṣṇu is possessed of defects"?
[For] if it is argued that "otherness" is as unknown as "Viṣṇu-hood," then [the opponent] says:
"In that case, it follows that [the otherness] remains unknown"—namely, "of someone" (kasyacit).
If it were merely the case that "someone might possess faults," then [the cognition] would be produced by the senses (akṣaja).

The meaning is that the intent is precisely this: that there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the non-arising of the cognition "Viṣṇu possesses defects" regarding this very object, namely, this much alone.

Now, one might object: just as "this cloth is torn," "burnt," or "soiled" is apprehended by perception itself without depending on anything else, so too will Viṣṇu be known to possess defects by perception itself without depending on scripture and the like; to this he says: "No."
For direct perception does not itself exist as a means for [proving] Viṣṇu’s possession of defects.
"By itself," meaning without depending on anything else.
This is the intended meaning:
it is logical that "cloth-ness" is directly perceived as manifested by the arrangement of its parts, and knowledge is likewise [directly perceived].
However, the state of being Viṣṇu—characterized by the perfection of all attributes, faultlessness, and being the cause of the world's origin and so forth—is not perceptible;
therefore, such knowledge is not possible, just as the knowledge that "this cloth, weighing five palas, is dirty" [is not possible regarding something imperceptible]. *11,228*
This is the collective meaning:
perception apprehending defects in Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and others must arise in one of three ways:
either "this Viṣṇu has a defect," or "this person other than Viṣṇu has a defect," or "some person here has a defect."
Because there is no other alternative,
it is not possible for the second and third [alternatives] to manifest Viṣṇu as being possessed of defects; for he does not perceive that "Viṣṇu is possessed of defects."
If it is argued that, in terms of the actual state of things (*vastuvṛtti*), this [object] is indeed Viṣṇu himself,
what follows from that? For no cognition whatsoever, even if accompanied by the actual state of things, possesses the intended qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*).
It establishes [the point],
because otherwise there would be an over-extension;
in the first case, the state of being Viṣṇu must be known in every respect.
And it has been stated in the *Śāstrayoni* Sūtra that this [Brahman] is neither known through perception nor is it inferable;

therefore, it must be understood either through scripture— as in "Viṣṇu, who dwells in the secret cave of all, appeared in Devakī, who possesses a divine form"— or through inference based on a pervasion (vyāpti) understood from scripture.
Therefore, it must be admitted in every respect that perception depends upon scripture (*āgama*).

Now, all scripture constitutes but a single statement, and that statement establishes the faultlessness of Viṣṇu, who is endowed with all attributes; thus, because of its contradiction with that [scripture], perception regarding faults is simply not a valid means of knowledge.
And for this reason as well, he says "some" in order to show that it is not an authoritative means of knowledge.
"Some perceive defects"—here too [the cognition] would not be produced by the senses.
The word "too" (*api*) implies that this applies not only to defects;
the word "and" (*ca*) serves to include inference and other means of knowledge.
One who asserts that direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of defects in the forms of the Blessed One should be questioned:

regarding the claim that certain people living at that time perceived defects in the Blessed One’s forms, what is our proof (*pramāṇa*) for this matter? Is it direct perception, inference (*anumāna*), or scripture (*āgama*)?
It cannot first of all be perception, because perception directed toward another person is impossible for others,
especially when there is a great distance in time.
Nor is there inference, due to the absence of a logical mark (liṅga).
As for scripture (āgama), it would be either the Veda or the Purāṇas and so forth;
it is not the former.
Because that [first option] is not observed,
he says "the ancient" (paurāṇam), meaning that therefore the second [option] alone must be accepted.
In this matter, the ancient saying alone [is authoritative]. // Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.4.156c //
In this case, when there exists a perception that apprehends defects in the form of the Blessed One, the remainder of the sentence is "it must be stated.
If one asks, "What follows from that? [the answer is as follows].

Does that statement from the Purāṇa, which points out those defects, consider perception as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or does it merely intend to convey the absence of a determination regarding whether it is a valid or invalid cognition, or does it regard it as invalid?
He states the fault in the first case: "That," etc.
... that very [scriptural injunction] is contradicted by this [statement]. Mānava-dharmaśāstra 3.4.156d.

A Purāṇic statement that establishes as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) a cognition apprehending faults in the forms of the Blessed One (*bhagavadrūpa*) certainly acknowledges the actual existence of those faults.
For it is not possible to both accept the validity of that which apprehends them and yet not accept them;
and since it acknowledges the existence of faults, it contradicts the very Śruti cited previously.
To the question, "What is the fault if a Purāṇic statement contradicts the Śruti?", he says: "Of the Purāṇa... [and so forth].
And the Veda is the source of livelihood for the Purāṇa... MAnu 3.4.157ab.
Indeed, a human statement must possess a root;
for we employ a statement after having brought a certain object to mind for some reason.
Otherwise, its very production would be impossible.
To the question, "Why is the Veda alone the source of the Purāṇic statement? he says: "And not... and so forth.
...and indeed no other. // Manu 3.157b //
Another [type of] treatise is that composed by a person;
the word "and" (ca) has the sense of including perception, scripture, and so forth.

To begin with, a human-authored scripture cannot be the source for that which is ancient; for if that [scripture] too were to depend upon another source, it would result in an infinite regress of blind tradition.
Nor [is it established] by perception or inference, because their objects are not within the scope of those two;
nor is it established by creative imagination (utprekṣā).
Because it would follow that [the Purāṇa] lacks authority, like the words of a deceiver.
Therefore, by the method of elimination, it is established that the Veda alone is the source upon which the Purāṇa depends.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "In case of conflict with that."
If it contradicts that [Veda], how can it be an authoritative means of knowledge with respect to it?
In the event of a contradiction with the Vedas, which are the source of livelihood,
that statement from the Purāṇa would [be invalid] if the Blessed One were possessed of faults therein.
The meaning [of the objection] is that it is inevitable that the dependent (upajīvaka) lacks authority if it contradicts that which it depends upon (upajīvya).
Now, one might argue: for the Purāṇas composed by Īśvara, their own innate knowledge (*nija-jñāna*) is the source, not the Veda;
and even for those not composed by Īśvara, the source is simply the perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the yogins.
Therefore, what fault is there even in contradicting the Veda?
It is said:
first of all, it is established beyond doubt that the Veda is indeed a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, there is no contradiction between the two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
because that would entail the consequence of [the object] being a mere conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
Therefore, when there is a contradiction with the Veda, the very basis of [the other source], such as one's own personal knowledge, is simply removed.
Nevertheless, how can it be said that the Veda alone is the source upon which the Purāṇa depends?
There is no fault here, for this is said with reference to those Purāṇas composed by non-divine authors;
for such authors lack confidence even in matters that appear to them through their own intuition.
They rely upon the Veda for the sake of reassurance, as it has been said: "The word of a teacher who has realized [the truth] for himself [is authoritative] when one is afflicted by doubt.
Alternatively, even for the determination of the authority of the Purāṇas composed by Īśvara, agreement with the Veda is required.
Otherwise, there would be the suspicion that [the Purāṇas] are rooted in mere imagination (utprekṣā). With this intention, it was stated: "The Veda alone is the source upon which the Purāṇa depends.
He refutes the second [position] with the words: "unexamined" (aparīkṣita).
And how could that which is seen without examination be considered born of the senses?

How could that which is produced by the senses (akṣaja) possibly be [invalid]? Thus, perception cannot be put forward as a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) regarding the object one desires to establish.

The point is that a critical investigator (parīkṣaka) would not be such an investigator if he were to put forward as a means of valid cognition that which has not been determined to be a means of valid cognition.
He states the refutation for the opposing case (vipakṣa): "If it were so... and so forth.
If this is so, why would an error such as [the perception of] Devadatta and others not be produced by the senses?
The meaning is: even if something has not been examined as a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), if it is presented as being direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
"An error regarding Devadatta and so forth" means: an error regarding silver and so forth in the case of Yajñadatta’s mother-of-pearl and the like.
If it is argued that [the cognition] is not a valid means of knowledge arising from the senses because it is sublated (*bādhitatva*),
then is the mere absence of sublation the cause for establishing the reality of an object?
If that were the case, it would follow that a definitive means of knowledge (*niścāyaka-pramāṇa*) is useless.
"And there is sublation of the Veda in the present case" (*11.236*).

It has been stated that because of the contradiction with the Veda—which is the basis of reliance—the two [means of knowledge], perception and the Purāṇic statement, which rely upon it, lack authority;
but that is incorrect.
If it is argued that there is no fixed rule stating that what is dependent (the *upajīvaka*) is sublated only by what it depends upon (the *upajīvya*),
for we observe that even the dependent cognition "this is silver" is sublated by the dependent cognition "this is not silver"—
then it must be explained how the relationship of the dependent and the depended-upon exists in this case.

Either it is because the negation of what has not been apprehended is impossible, such that the initial cognition "this is silver"— which consists of apprehension— is the dependent (upajīvya), while the subsequent negating cognition "this is not silver" is the dependent (upajīvaka);
or else, because a negation is impossible when the locus (dharmin) is unestablished, the initial cognition of the locus is the dependent, while the second [cognition] is the dependent.
Regarding the first, he states the meditative absorption (samādhi): "as far as one's capacity allows."
In an investigation according to one's ability, there is no fault in subverting that which is foundational;
however, there is a fault if it is not purified, for being foundational alone is not sufficient.
The ellipsis is "of that which is recognized as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) when it has undergone examination.
Regarding sublation (*bādhana*), the ellipsis is "by what [is it sublated]?"—namely, by that which depends upon it (*upajīvaka*). This is the fault [we maintain].

There would be a violation of the rule. However, there is no fault when that which is dependent is sublated by the dependent [cognition], provided that the basis of dependence has not been purified through investigation and remains undistinguished from what is non-authoritative.
Let it be that there is dependence; that is sufficient.
In the example under discussion, one first accepts the relationship of the supported and the supporter (*upajīvyopajīvaka-bhāva*).
"The state of being supported" (*upajīvyatva*) is an illustration;
it should also be understood as "the state of being a supporter" (*upajīvakatva*).
The words "of the preceding and subsequent cognitions" are to be supplied [to complete the sense].
The word *alam* is used in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*).
What is meant is this:

(Granted, let it be so: Indeed, there exists between the two cognitions—"this is silver" and "this is not silver"—the relationship of the supported and the supporter, as well as the sublation of the supported by the supporter.
Nevertheless, there is no violation of the rule that "the supporter is sublated [only] when it contradicts the supported.
For this is the true meaning of that rule:
That which is to be relied upon, having been purified through critical examination, subverts its contradictory counterpart, while it itself is not subverted by that counterpart;
however, this is not the case according to the literal text,
for in that case, there would be a contradiction of this very [text].
If we were to observe anywhere that what is to be relied upon, having been examined, is sublated by its contradictory sublater, it would not be so.
But it is not thus.
