However, the cognition "this is silver" has not been purified [of its defects].
Therefore, when that [cognition] is sublated by a subsequent dependent cognition, there is no violation of the rule;
for it does not follow that because a thing without qualifications deviates from truth, the qualified thing itself must deviate, as that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Nor should it be said that the postulation of the qualified [object] as the motivator is baseless;
for the relationship between the sublated and the sublator is observed in both ways.
Because if there were no dependence on qualifications, it would lead to a lack of systematic order (*avyavasthā*).
[Objection: But if investigation (*parīkṣā*) is accepted, that alone is sufficient;

since the uninvestigated is sublated by the investigated, and because there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in this regard, what is the use of the relationship between that which is depended upon (*upajīvya*) and that which depends (*upajīvaka*)?
It is said:
This would indeed be so if we were to accept an ultimate investigation here;
but it is not so.
However, this applies only so long as the capacity [of the means of knowledge] has not been tested;
nor is there a rule that such [untested] capacity alone constitutes a sublation,
for even that which has been tested according to its capacity is seen to be sublated.
Therefore, it is appropriate to specify [the object of] apprehension.
Nor should it be argued: "Let only ultimate investigation be what serves as the sublater; why [specify] by way of being that upon which [the cognition] depends?
For even that [ultimate investigation] is merely conventional (*sāṃvyāvahārika*).
As it has been said:
"The rule characterized by the coming together [of causes] is not the cause for its own obstruction.
But in the present case, the Veda has been examined and is that which is to be relied upon. *11,241*
Regarding the second [point], he states the rebuttal: "Even in the case of error..."
Even in error, there exists a portion that is not error... MĀnUv 3.4.160a.
The particle *hi* connects here as well to what is about to be stated.
Although this cognition "this is silver" is indeed one, it is nevertheless divided by virtue of its objective adjuncts (*viṣayopādhi*).
In that regard, while there is error with respect to the mode (*prakāra*), there is no error with respect to the essential nature (*svarūpa*) itself.
In that case, because there is never any sublation [of the cognition],
others have also said:
"All cognition is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding the substratum (*dharmin*), but it may be erroneous regarding its specific mode (*prakāra*)."

Since the admission of [the object as] a part [of cognition] itself precludes any opportunity for raising an objection regarding contradiction, he asks "What follows from that? and replies: "It is merely that" (tanmātram).
For it is by depending solely upon that [object] that the operation of a subverting cognition would occur. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 3.4.160bc)
It consists merely of a portion of the cloud;
for it is by that very [portion] that the subject (*dharmin*) is established.
The meaning of the word "for" (*hi*) is that the form of silver lacks the status of being the subject because it is that which is to be negated.
This is what is meant:

in this position, that which is the basis (upajīvya) is not sublated by that which depends upon it (upajīvaka), and that which is sublated is not the basis; therefore, this is not an example of a violation of our own rule.
At this point, the proponents of Māyā (Māyāvādins) raise an objection.
As for the claim that the non-dualistic scriptures lack authority because they contradict their own basis,
that is incorrect;
for a solution to that objection can also be easily stated.
For instance,
it must be explained how there can be a relationship of dependence between such statements as "He who is omniscient" and so forth, and [Vedic declarations] such as "That thou art";
for it has been established by the statement beginning with "It does not sublate what is already established."

It is accepted that statements such as "That thou art" (tattvamasi) negate all-encompassing omniscience and the like, as well as suffering and so forth, which are opposed to the identity [of the individual and the absolute].

Since there can be no negation without a prior apprehension, the statement "He who is omniscient" and the like must be regarded as the basis (the object of dependence), whereas "That thou art" and the like are dependent upon it.
Or rather, [it may be said that] "That thou art" and the like are the basis, while [the notion of] omniscience and so forth are what depend upon them.

Alternatively, because a negation is untenable when the locus (*dharmin*) is unestablished, the first [cognition] which establishes the locus must be depended upon, and the subsequent one is that which depends on it.

In the first case, since the initial cognition—like the cognition of silver—is itself unexamined, there is no inconsistency whatsoever in the subsequent [cognition] subverting even that which was depended upon.
In the second case, only the essential nature of Brahman is to be depended upon, just as the mere nature of the mother-of-pearl is depended upon, and not its specific attributes such as omniscience.
And thus, that which is foundational is not sublated by what follows it;
and that which is sublated, such as omniscience and the like, is not foundational—therefore, there is no contradiction whatsoever.
Here, he refutes both of these defenses with the words: "But it is not so."
... and it is not thus ... // Mānava-dharmaśāstra 3.160d //
The sense is that a resolution cannot be stated here as it can for the well-known cases of error and sublation, because of the disparity.
To the question "In what way?", he first demonstrates the disparity regarding the first position, stating: "thoroughly examined."
... when it has been thoroughly examined. // Manu 3.160d //
When the first means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has been thoroughly examined, it is not the case that "it is thus"; this is the connection [of the words].
What is meant is this:
even though the cognition "this is silver" is that which is depended upon (*upajīvya*), because it is unexamined, it is sublated by the dependent cognition "this is not silver."
For we have already stated that the principle of the supported and the supporter (*upajīvya-upajīvaka-nyāya*) has as its scope an investigation [of validity] to the extent of one's capacity;
yet the opponent objects on the basis of this very principle,
which is not appropriate.

Because [the existence of] such [entities] as "He who is omniscient" and [the existence of] "I am suffering" have been thoroughly examined; indeed, it has been established that the scriptures stating "He who is omniscient," etc., reveal reality, and that the witness-consciousness (sākṣin) is invariably non-deviant. He shows the disparity in the second position with the word "all."
For it is only by depending upon all of that that valid cognition functions.

The connection is as follows: because all such [cognitions] as "That thou art" and so forth proceed only by depending upon omniscience and the rest, it is not the case that [the Self is known through them].
This is what is meant:

just as the cognition "this is not silver" proceeds by taking the mere nature of the object present before one as its subject (*dharmin*), and not as qualified by silverness, so too the sentence "That thou art" and the like cannot proceed in that manner.

However, this is done precisely by taking as the subject (*dharmin*) the nature of Brahman qualified by omniscience and so forth, and the nature of the individual soul (*jīva*) qualified by suffering and so forth;
and thus, the contradiction with the means of apprehending the subject (*dharmigrāhakapramāṇavirodha*) remains unavoidable.
Here, the term "all" (*sarvam*) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for any one of the attributes such as omniscience.

Now, one might object: "If even sentences such as 'That thou art' were to function by depending solely upon the essential nature [of the self], what kind of fault would there be? To this, he says: "How so? (katham).

How is that Brahman to be known, characterized by omniscience and other such qualities? For if it were [known] merely as its own essential nature, it would have to be abandoned as something or other. (Manu 3.4.161)
The state of being the source of livelihood... [Mānava Dharmaśāstra 3.4.162a]
This consists of two statements.
The meaning of one of them is as follows:
if [the Self] were to subsist solely upon its own essential nature (svarūpa) while setting aside all attributes (dharma), then how could that be known which is taught in the formula "That thou art"?
This is what is meant:
for it is by restating its own nature through a word that one must say "That thou art. And there exists no word that can convey that which is devoid of all attributes (nirdharma).
Therefore, since the mere essential nature (svarūpa) does not ascend into the intellect, its cognition is indeed untenable.
We do not say that the mere essential nature is that which is depended upon;
rather, [we mean] that which is qualified by such attributes as omniscience and so forth, setting aside the specific differentiators (bhedaka).
And thus, since there would be no fault whatsoever, the following statement is addressed to the disciple:

"If that which is endowed with attributes such as reality (tattva) and so forth is what is to be relied upon, then, setting aside omniscience and the like, how can it be known that 'Brahman is that [reality] or whatever else'?
Even if this position avoids the aforementioned fault, nevertheless, the knowledge of the seeker—that "I am Brahman"—would still remain untenable.

The meaning is that since omniscience and the like constitute the defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of Brahman, if they are not included, Brahman cannot be apprehended by the intellect; furthermore, [qualities such as] "thatness" (*tattva*) and so forth are common to jars and other objects.
Having stated the sublation (*bādhaka*) involved in adopting [the definition] while excluding omniscience and the like, he states the conclusion regarding the opposite case: "etasmāt" (from this).
To the extent that it is distinguished from this [worldly conduct],
by that much alone does it possess the quality of being a source of livelihood.
Otherwise, knowledge would be impossible;
[knowledge arises] only for one who is endowed with as many qualities as there are.

One might object: "Just as the cognition 'this is not silver' proceeds by depending solely upon the thing's own nature (svarūpa), so too will this [cognition] proceed; what is the fault? To this, he says: "Of the very nature... [etc.].
... [this applies] only to one who has taken the vow, and never otherwise. Mānava 3.4.162d.
The term "being the basis of livelihood" (*upajīvyatva*) continues [from the previous context].
The meaning is that for the very reason stated regarding the lack of logical consistency (*anupapatti*), the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is also not complete.
[Objection: But surely, one who is omniscient does not need to be informed by the words "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*).
But it is simply "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*).
Nor is the aforementioned fault incurred;
for the word "That" denotes Brahman.
Words denote that which is capable of being connected [with something else], and the definition (lakṣaṇa) is capable of being connected with Brahman.
Therefore, since that [Brahman] is understood as excluded [from others] by that very word, the author, holding this intention, raises an objection: "All... etc.
But if the essential nature is said to be endowed with all characteristics, [then it is as follows].
The word "ca" (and) is used for emphasis.
If it is said that "it is expressed by the word 'tat' (that)," this should be construed by repeating the word "bhaṇyate" (is expressed).
He states the answer, which is an admission: "Let it be so."
Let it be so... (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 3.4.163c)
The meaning is: "Let that which has been stated by the opponent be so.
To the question, "How could there not be a loss of the proposition (*pratijñāhāni*) when one accepts the point asserted by the opponent? he says: "No."
... nor indeed would there be any loss ... // MAnu 3.4.163c //
For if one were to accept an object of cognition that is not intended, there would be a loss of the thesis (*pratijñāhāni*).
But by accepting this [object], there is no loss whatsoever of our own thesis.
For we state that there is a contradiction with the apprehension of the subject (*dharmī*) for the opponent; and as a rebuttal to that, the opponent has said this,
yet by this [statement], that rebuttal is not achieved.
On the contrary, the sense is that it has been further strengthened.

In response to the inquiry—whether this is accepted merely because it does not contradict the subject matter under discussion, or because it is established as being so—he says: "And one's own position... [and so forth].
...and this is our own position, clearly established. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.163d)
"Directly" (añjasā) means not merely by way of assertion;
he establishes this with the words "because."
For the meaning is in every respect already inherent even in words.
The connection is "in every respect" (*sarvaśas*).
The remainder is that this has already been established by the force of the aforementioned Sūtra.
Furthermore, even under this view, the failure of Brahman to enter into the intellect remains exactly as it was.
For words such as "that" and so forth denote, in a general sense, only that which is connected to a suitable [object],
whereas words such as "omniscient" and so forth denote it specifically;
this is because such is our experience.
And since a cognition of exclusion does not arise from that which expresses a connection in a general sense, he says "viśeṣa... with this intention.
Through the nature of both the particular and the universal, the entire essential form comes into being.
The entire nature of things, endowed with relations, is to be understood through words by way of both the particular and the universal.

While the theory of the expression of related meanings (*anvitābhidhāna*) is indeed accepted, that occurs only in a general sense from a single word and not in a specific one; thus, Brahman does not ascend to the intellect [in this manner].
And if there were a distinction, then the contradiction with the apprehension of the subject (*dharmigrahavirodha*) would remain exactly as it was; this is the meaning of the whole passage.

Some proponents of the theory of illusion (*māyāvādins*), such as the Vijñānavādins and others, accept the theory of the expression of the related (*anvitābhidhāna*); for them, this suspicion regarding non-attainment does not arise.
As for what was stated—that only that which is excluded by distinguishing properties (*vyāvartakadharma*) possesses the status of being a necessary basis (*upajīvyatva*)—that is not the case.
Because that [sublated object] is absent in subverting cognitions (*bādhakajñāna*).

Nor should it be argued that even there, it is only the excluded state (*vyāvṛttatva*) that serves as the basis of reliance (*upajīvyatva*), and not the mere intrinsic nature (*svarūpamātra*); for in the preceding erroneous cognition, the excluded state...
Because that very [object] is unestablished;
and even if it were established, error would be untenable.
For [error] depends solely upon that.
Because there is a contradiction with what has been stated thus, he says: "Insofar as it is present before one," and so forth.

In the case of an error regarding Devadatta and others, the properties such as "being present before one" exclude that form [of the object] from Caitra alone, even without [the presence of] other qualifiers.

In the case of an error regarding Devadatta and others where Caitra and others are perceived, the qualifiers— beginning with "being present before one"— which constitute the very nature of Devadatta and so forth,

differentiate him from Caitra alone even without [the cognition of] "not being present before one," because Devadatta and the rest are not known [at that time]. Therefore, the rule that subversive knowledge depends upon [a cognition] that is already differentiated is not untenable.
Nor is there an impossibility of error,
because the exclusion of the superimposed object is not admitted;
and since the word "mere" (tanmātra) excludes only that which is being superimposed, the aforementioned contradiction does not arise— this is the sense.
Surely, by this it is stated that absolute exclusion (*atyantavyāvṛtti*) is not what is required for [the definition] to be functional,
but rather mere exclusion (*vyāvṛttimātra*). That [mere exclusion] exists even in the case at hand.
If it is argued that because Brahman is also excluded by [the knowledge of] reality and so forth, it is possible for it to be the basis upon which others depend (*upajīvyatva*), we say no;
for it has already been stated that by that much alone, the knowledge "I am Brahman" cannot arise even in one who is to be enlightened.
Furthermore, he states another defect with the words "of Brahman."
Since Brahman is devoid of distinctions, what indeed could it exclude?
The connection is with the word "punaḥ" (again) regarding Brahman.

What is the agent? It excludes Brahman; [the sense is] that it excludes nothing at all. He states the fault even in the acceptance of reality and so forth, beginning with the words "yasmāt" (because).
If [it is argued that] there is proof of what is already established (siddhasādhana) with respect to any object whatsoever, then...
Since, by means of qualifiers such as "real" (*tattva*) and so forth, it is understood that [the object] is devoid of reality and the like with respect to whatever thing [is being considered],
and that it possesses the status of being a basis of reliance (*upajīvyatva*) precisely to the extent that it is excluded [from those qualifiers],
this very statement would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), as it would be a communicator of only that which is already known.
Because this meaning would have been already known through awakening (*bodhi*),
the treatise would likewise be unnecessary;
furthermore, Brahman should not be something that depends [on a treatise] for its realization, as it is already distinguished by reality and so forth.

One might argue that [the nature of Brahman] will be established by its being pure consciousness (cinmātratva) and so forth, as stated in such scriptural passages as "Brahman is consciousness and bliss" (vijñānamānandaṃ brahma) which define the characteristics of Brahman; therefore, he says: "And as for being pure consciousness... (cinmātratvaṃ ca).
And for one who maintains that there is no distinction, even the state of being pure consciousness is not to be desired.
By the word "only" (mātra), he excludes such qualities as the consciousness [of Brahman] having all things as its object;
this is also an elliptical indication of blissfulness and so forth.
The word "of Brahman" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].

Since [qualities] such as pure consciousness (cinmātratva) are not different from Brahman, they are accepted because they do not contradict its being devoid of distinctions (nirviśeṣatva); therefore, he says: "merely that" (tāvanmātra).
If that much alone were desired, why would omniscience not be [attained]? (3.4.167cd)
The point is that this [nature] also belongs to that [consciousness], because it is heard [in scripture] and because it is non-different from it.
If it is asked how there can be a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) in the case of non-difference, [the answer is:
the same applies to consciousness (*vijñāna*) and so forth as well.

And it has been stated that the method of defining the characterized (*lakṣya*) and the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) is found in the "Definition Sūtra" (*lakṣaṇasūtra*). Even though there is a commonality in their being heard (*śrutatva*), only such properties as pure consciousness (*cinmātratva*) and so forth are predicated of the subject (*dharmin*),
because they are not contradictory [to its nature].
Omniscience and so forth [cannot be the subject] because they are contradictory;

just as in the cognition "this is not silver," that which is endowed with non-contradictory properties such as being present before one can be the subject (dharmin), whereas that which is endowed with the contradictory property of being silver cannot, therefore he says: "mere consciousness" (cinmātra).
Even though [the goal] is to be accomplished through non-difference from pure consciousness...

"Non-difference with pure consciousness" (*cinmātrābheda*) means that non-difference which has pure consciousness as its object; that is what is called "to be established" (*sādhya*), meaning it is what is to be demonstrated.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: even if the non-difference with pure consciousness were accepted as the goal to be established by such statements as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), that statement would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).
To the question "How so?", he says: "It is established" (*siddham*).
... that is established for the opponent. (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 3.4.168b)
The phrase "since [it belongs] to the opponent who is to be enlightened" is the ellipsis for "that unity of consciousness.
To the question "How is it established?", he says: "one's own," etc.
Precisely because of the acceptance of non-difference from oneself... [MAnu 3.4.168c]
Because its non-difference from itself is admitted;
the word "eva" (only/just) is connected with the preceding term "siddham" (established).
To the question, "If non-difference from itself is admitted, how is non-difference from consciousness established?", he says: "cittvam" (consciousness-ness).
"...the state of being a mind, which is one's own opinion. Since it is accepted—
that is, agreed upon— as one's own [view] regarding that which is to be understood,
this is what is meant.

For one who asserts that the subject (*dharmin*) is not specified by attributes such as omniscience due to the fear of contradiction, it follows that even its nature as consciousness and bliss (*cidānanda*) should not be made the subject,
because that would entail the fallacy of making known what is already known (*jñātajñāpana*).
For there is no difference between contradiction and the making known of what is already known, both being causes for a statement not being a valid scripture (*aśāstra*).
If it is argued that the meaning of the statement is that "pure consciousness alone exists and nothing other than you exists," we say no, because such a thing does not appear [in experience].
If it is further argued that this is postulated because there is no other alternative, we say no.
Because the author of the Sūtras has already stated another meaning [in this regard]:
"It is not out of fear of contradiction that we do not attribute omniscience and so forth to the subject;
rather, [it is because] omniscience and so forth..."
It is not different from Brahman,
because that would contradict such scriptural passages as "There is no diversity here";
nor is it its own essential nature.
Because that [cognition] is dependent upon everything beginning with space,
and because everything is false,
it is impossible for such a thing to possess the nature of truth.

Intending to show that there is no inconsistency whatsoever in the view that consciousness, bliss, and so forth are the very nature of Brahman, he raises an objection with the words "sarva... (all...).
If it is argued that "omniscience [belongs to the Veda] because it depends upon everything," that is not so... // MAnu 3.4.169a-c //
The word "exists" (*vartate*) is to be supplied [to complete the sentence], meaning that omniscience exists.
The particle *iti* indicates a reason.
The word *eva* is connected with the phrase "that very thing" (*tadeva*).
The meaning is not that it is false;
he refutes this by stating, "and [it possesses] sentience."
... and the state of being conscious ... // MAnu 3.169c //
The meaning is that if one accepts the principle that "whatever depends on another is not real," then Brahman would lack the quality of consciousness (*cetanatva*).
Why? Because the suffix *lyuṭ* (which forms the word *jñatva*) has multiple meanings; taking it here as denoting the agent (*kartṛ*), he explains it as "the state of being a knower" (*jñatvam*).
... the state of being a knower ... // MAnu 3.169d //
"Cognitiveness" (cetanatva) means, first of all, the state of being a knower (jñatva).
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "No."
... nor that which is devoid of the object of knowledge. // Mānava-dharmaśāstra 3.4.169d //
The term "knowership" (jñatva) continues [from the previous context];
however, it is necessarily dependent upon an object of knowledge (jñeya).
Indeed, knowership is the state of being an agent (kartṛtva) with respect to the act of knowing.
Furthermore, the verb *jānāti* (he knows) denotes an action that requires an object;
therefore, the agency of the performer of that action, which depends upon an object, is likewise dependent.
If it is asked: "Even so, why should there not be consciousness [in the body]?"
For the Knower who is Brahman, the object of knowledge must be either itself or something else.
It is not the first case; thus he says: "itself."
And he does not consider it to be knowable by himself, especially with its specific qualities.
This is the meaning of the verse.
Why does this proponent of illusion (māyāvādī) not accept [this]? To this he says: "Because of its possessing distinctions" (saviśeṣataḥ).

Because it would entail the consequence of possessing distinctions (*saviśeṣatva*). For the relationship of agent and object, characterized by the states of "proximal" (*pratyak*) and "remote" (*parāk*), is not possible for a single thing in one and the same locus. And if it were so, it would have to be established through a distinction that serves as a substitute for difference (*bheda*).
Therefore, if one accepts that Brahman possesses both the nature of the knower and the object of knowledge, one would have to accept a distinction [within it].
Since Brahman is accepted as being without distinction, its being the object of its own knowledge is not admitted;
consequently, it must be stated that the object of knowledge is something other than itself.
And since that [consciousness] is false, how could consciousness (*cetanatva*) exist in dependence upon it?
In this same way, it must also be stated that the state of being a knower (*jñatva*) is dependent upon knowledge (*jñāna*).
Furthermore, by speaking in this manner, one cannot even say that the mere intrinsic nature (*svarūpa-mātra*) is what is relied upon.
Since even that [term] is understood to depend on something else by virtue of its own word, he says: "The word 'own' (sva) also..."
Even the word "self" is dependent upon another... MĀnuv 3.4.170c.
It depends on others and establishes an object that depends on others;
to the question "How so?", he says: "Therefore... (tasmāt).
Therefore, it is indeed exclusion (vyāvṛtti) that is declared to be the meaning of a word’s own form (svaśabdārtha). ... [Mānava-dharmaśāstra 3.4.170cd]
"From another"; the word "hi" indicates the reason;
"artha" means the cause of engagement.
Thus it has been stated by those who understand the power of words:
"its own" (*svam*) and "that form" (*tadrūpam*) constitute its "essential nature" (*svarūpam*). Furthermore, the word *rūpa* (form) is common to both itself and others.

Therefore, even though the word "own" (sva) refers to what has been attained by itself, it is understood that, according to the principle of exclusive specification (*parisaṅkhyā*), it indicates the exclusion of others.
This is true if explained in such a manner;
however, since it is not actually so, he says: "the essential nature" (*svarūpam*).
... what indeed would its own nature be, if it were not [existent]? (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.4.170)
It cannot denote its own specific form, because that would render the word "form" redundant; furthermore, that [word "form"] expresses a general state. (Manu 3.4.171)
If our intended interpretation is not accepted, then what would "intrinsic nature" (*svarūpa*) be? It would be nothing at all;
the meaning is that the word *svarūpa* would be devoid of meaning.
If it is asked how this can be so, given that the word *svarūpa* has the same meaning as the word *rūpa*, the following must be said in response.
This is stated by accepting the etymological derivation as "that which is itself and has that form.
Or, is it by assuming that this word is an indivisible whole?
Regarding the first case, he states the fault: "because of futility" (vaiyarthyāt).
Since the word "own" (sva) would be redundant in this position, [the opponent asks: "What then is this so-called 'intrinsic nature' (svarūpa)? Is it a relation?
To the question "Why is it redundant?", he says: "Because of form" (rūpa).
Because the denotation of the meaning of the word *rūpa* is already complete by that very word *rūpa* which occurs within the compound *svarūpa*,
it is not possible that the word *rūpa* does not denote the meaning of the word *rūpa*;
otherwise, even the words *utpala* and *nīlotpala* would have the same meaning.
He refutes the second [position] with the words: "And that... (tacceti).
That is the term "form" (*rūpa*);
*ca* has the sense of "because";
and "denoting generality" means that which expresses a general form.
The suffix *ṣyañ* is applied in the sense of the base itself (*svārthe*) according to the rule beginning with *cāturvarṇya*.
This is what is meant:
for the proponents of verbal testimony (*śābdāḥ*) hold that the determination of the meaning of a word is based solely on common understanding (*pratīti*).
In this context, the word "form" (*rūpa*) denotes the universal aspect,
because all [cognitions] arise from it;
whereas the word "own-form" (*svarūpa*) denotes the unique, particular aspect.
Therefore, because of that perception,
those two do not have the same referent.
As for what was stated— that Brahman would lack sentience— that is merely the restatement of what is already accepted [by the opponent].
For we do not admit that Brahman possesses sentience; since agency, characterized by the penetration of activity, is absent in that which is free from conceptual construction (nirvikalpaka),
Brahman is indeed nothing but consciousness itself.

Since the doctrines asserting sentience must be explained as having that very [non-existence] as their object, and because even sentience cannot be accepted by the opponent, he explains it with the words "of the sentient one" (cetanasya), with this intention.
For the very nature of consciousness is proclaimed to be sentience.
The "state" (bhāva) is the ground for the application of a word.
The word *sva* is used here to indicate that this state is not adventitious (*anāgantuka*).

By the phrase "for thus it is sung," he indicates the traditional rule (*smṛti*) from Pāṇini: "The suffix *lyuṭ* is applied after words denoting qualities (*guṇavacana*) and after *brāhmaṇa* and so forth, in the sense of the action (*karman*)."
And the ground for the application of the word "consciousness" (cetana) is knowledge (jñāna),
because of the Vedic root-reading "citī saṃjñāne" (to perceive).
Consequently, it is stated that Brahman is knowledge.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "Therefore... (tasmāt).
Therefore, consciousness possesses a multiplicity of specific qualities in particular.
Since consciousness is indeed knowledge, it follows that for Brahman, who is consciousness, there would result an abundance of distinctions— that is, an excessive plurality of specific qualities.
For knowledge is dependent upon the object of knowledge, the knower, and the instrument;
furthermore, attributes such as the nature of being knowledge are unavoidable.
Moreover, Brahman with attributes is not accepted by the opponent.
Furthermore, the object of knowledge and so forth are not self-existent, because that would involve a contradiction;
rather, they are false. How, then, could the cognition dependent upon them be real?
If it is asked, "Since Brahman is consciousness, how can it possess objects of knowledge and so forth? [the answer is]: Because it is consciousness, just like well-known consciousness.
Nor is it correct to say that "the nature of being knowledge" (jñānatva) is unestablished, because that would contradict [your own] admission.
He establishes the pervasion (vyāpti) with the words: "Not so."
For knowledge, devoid of both the object of knowledge and the knower, can never exist anywhere.
Regarding what was stated previously— that if Brahman were sentient, it would necessarily be endowed with both the object of knowledge and the act of knowing—

the intended restrictive rule there is "because of its being a knower, like that which is commonly accepted. In this context, he establishes the pervasion (vyāpti) of that [rule] as well by means of the verse beginning with "jñeya" (the object of knowledge).
And there is no valid means of knowledge for the claim that one who is devoid of both the object of knowledge and the knowledge itself is a "knower."
The first word "and" (*ca*) serves to conjoin [the attributes] of being devoid of the knowable and so forth, and of being knowledge;
the second, however, conjoins the two types of deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

Now, one might object: "Even though well-known knowledge is possessed of the knowable and so forth, let this knowledge which is the very nature of Brahman be devoid of them—what is the contradiction? To this, he says: "The knower, the knowable... (11.269).

If knowledge were devoid of both the knower and the knowable, then, like eating being devoid of the eater and the food, it would be mere eating; and like striking being devoid of the striker and the struck, it would be mere striking.
The connection is "only inferior.
The meaning is that it would be inferior to both the striker and the struck, since the agent is [absent].
Furthermore, if the object of the verbal root—namely, cognition—were devoid of an agent, [the same consequence would follow].

Furthermore, even if something is perceived as transitive due to the force of expectancy, if it were to become intransitive, then the aforementioned excessive logical consequence (*atiprasaṅga*) would be even greater, because there would be no distinction [between the two states].

In the case of the object of knowledge (*jñaviṣaya*) as well, one must state such an excessive logical consequence: that even an enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*) would be devoid of both the object of enjoyment (*bhojya*) and the act of enjoying (*bhojana*), and so forth.
For it is not logical that the agent of an action involving an object should be devoid of action and so forth.
Furthermore, "the knower" and "the object of knowledge" are designations for a *kāraka* (factor of action);
these two terms, "kāraka" and "producer" (*utpādaka*), are synonyms.
Furthermore, only that which is an effect (kārya) depends upon a producer;
since the knowledge called Brahman is not an effect, it does not depend upon an agent or other such factors. With this intention, he raises the objection: "Because of its eternity" (nityatvāt).
If it is argued that such [a result] would follow because of its permanence... // MĀnuv 3.4.175ab //
Eternity (*nityatva*) is an indicator (*upalak�ṣaṇa*) of being unproduced (*akāryatva*).

Even though impermanent things such as food depend upon an eater and so forth, this [Self], because it is eternal, would likewise be devoid of a knower and so on; by this, the reversal of the pervaded is suspected through the perception of what is incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*).
A producer is not merely that which brings about an effect.
If that were the case, it would follow that in expressions such as "there is a sky," the sky and so forth would lack the status of being a factor (kāraka);
rather, the agent is the locus of the verbal root's meaning, and the object is its domain, and so on.

Expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and its absence alone are the determinants of whether [an element] is connected with another or not; it is not the state of being an effect (*kāryatva*) or the state of not being an effect that determines this. For this very reason, it is logical that some verbal root-meanings are connected with objects (*karman*) and so forth, while others are not. With this intention, [the author] states an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) for one who, setting aside expectancy as the determinant, instead makes the state of being an effect and so forth the determinant: [The verse: "Even in the case of 'Bring the cow' (*gām ānaya*), there would be no connection between the cow and the act of bringing, because the cow is not an effect [of that act]. Furthermore, since the act of bringing is not an effect [of the cow], there would likewise be no connection between the cow and the act of bringing. [The commentary: In the sentence "Bring the cow," the cow is not an effect of the act of bringing; therefore, according to your view, there would be no connection between the cow and the act of bringing. Likewise, since the act of bringing is not an effect of the cow, there would similarly be no connection between the cow and the act of bringing. Consequently, the word "cow" would not denote the object of the act of bringing, and the word "bring" would not denote the action directed toward the cow. Thus, the two words would not be syntactically related (*samanvita*). Therefore, it must be admitted that expectancy and its absence are indeed the determinants of connection and non-connection. It is not the state of being an effect and so forth. Otherwise, even in the case of "The cow exists" (*gauḥ asti*), there would be no connection between the cow and existence, because the cow is not an effect of existence. Furthermore, since existence is not an effect of the cow, there would likewise be no connection between the cow and existence. Consequently, the word "cow" would not denote the locus of existence, and the word "exists" would not denote the action residing in the cow. Thus, the two words would again not be syntactically related. Therefore, it must be accepted that expectancy and its absence are the determinants of connection and non-connection. It is not the state of being an effect and so forth. Otherwise, even in the case of "The pot exists" (*ghaṭo 'sti*), there would be no connection between the pot and existence, because the pot is not an effect of existence. Furthermore, since existence is not an effect of the pot, there would likewise be no connection between the pot and existence. Consequently, the word "pot" would not denote the locus of existence, and the word "exists" would not denote the action residing in the pot. Thus, the two words would not be syntactically related. Therefore, it must be accepted that expectancy and its absence are the determinants of connection and non-connection. It is not the state of being an effect and so forth. Otherwise, even in the case of "The pot is blue" (*nīlo ghaṭaḥ*), there would be no connection between the pot and blueness, because the pot is not an effect of blueness. Furthermore, since blueness is not an effect of the pot, there would likewise be no connection between the pot and blueness. Consequently, the word "pot" would not denote the locus of blueness, and the word "blue" would not denote the quality residing in the pot. Thus, the two words would not be syntactically related. Therefore, it must be accepted that expectancy and its absence are the determinants of connection and non-connection. It is not the state of being an effect and so forth. Otherwise, even in the case of "Bring the cow" (*gām ānaya*), there would be no connection between the cow and the act of bringing, because the cow is not an effect of the act of bringing. Furthermore, since the act of bringing is not an effect of the cow, there would likewise be no connection between the cow and the act of bringing. Consequently, the word "cow" would not denote the object of the act of bringing, and the word "bring" would not denote the action directed toward the cow. Thus, the two words would not be syntactically related. Therefore, it must be accepted that expectancy and its absence are the determinants of connection and non-connection. It is not the state of being an effect and so forth. Otherwise, even in the case of "The cow exists" (*gauḥ asti*), there would be no connection between the cow and existence, because the cow is not an effect of existence. Furthermore, since existence is not an effect of the cow, there would likewise be no connection between the cow and existence. Consequently, the word "cow" would not denote the locus of existence, and the word "exists" would not denote the action residing in the cow. Thus, the two words would not be syntactically related. Therefore, it must be accepted that expectancy and its absence are the determinants of connection and non-connection. It is not the state of being an effect and so forth. Otherwise, even in the case of "The pot exists" (*ghaṭo 'sti*), there would be no connection between the pot and existence, because the pot is not an effect of existence. Furthermore, since existence is not an effect of the pot, there would likewise be no connection between the pot and existence. Consequently, the word "pot" would not denote the locus of existence, and the word "exists" would not denote the action residing in the pot. Thus, the two words would not be syntactically related. Therefore, it must be accepted that expectancy and its absence are the determinants of connection and non-connection. It is not the state of being an effect and so forth. Otherwise, even in the case of "The pot is blue" (*nīlo ghaṭaḥ*), there would be no connection between the pot and blueness, because the pot is not an effect of blueness. Furthermore, since blueness is not an effect of the pot, there would likewise be no connection between the pot and blueness. Consequently, the word "pot" would not denote the locus of blueness, and the word "blue" would not denote the quality residing in the pot. Thus, the two words would not be syntactically related. Therefore, it must be accepted that expectancy and its absence are the determinants of connection and non-connection. It is not the state of being an effect and so forth. Otherwise, even in the case of "Bring the cow" (*gām ānaya*), there would be no connection between the cow and the act of bringing, because the cow is not an effect of the act of bringing. Furthermore, since the act of bringing is not an effect of the cow, there would likewise be no connection between the cow and the act of bringing. Consequently, the word "cow" would not denote the object of the act of bringing, and the word "bring" would not denote the action directed toward the cow. Thus, the two words would not be syntactically related. Therefore, it must be accepted that expectancy and its absence are the determinants of connection and non-connection. It is not the state of being an effect and so forth. Otherwise, even in the case of "The cow exists" (*gauḥ asti*), there would be no connection between the cow and existence, because the cow is not an effect of existence. Furthermore, since existence is not an effect of the cow, there would likewise be no connection between the cow and existence. Consequently, the word "cow" would not denote the locus of existence, and the word "exists" would not denote the action residing in the cow. Thus, the two words would not be syntactically related. Therefore, it must be accepted that expectancy and its absence are the determinants of connection and non-connection. It is not the state of being an effect and so forth. Otherwise, even in the case of "The pot exists" (*ghaṭo 'sti*), there would be no connection between the pot and existence, because the pot is not an effect of existence. Furthermore, since existence is not an effect of the pot, there would likewise be no connection between the pot and existence. Consequently, the word "pot" would not denote the locus of existence, and the word "exists" would not denote the action residing in the pot. Thus, the two words would not be syntactically related. Therefore, it must be accepted that expectancy and its absence are the determinants of connection and non-connection. It is not the state of being an effect and so forth. Otherwise, even in the case of "The pot is blue" (*nīlo ghaṭaḥ*), there would be no connection between the pot and blueness, because the pot is not an effect of blueness. Furthermore, since blueness is not an effect of the pot, there would likewise be no connection between the pot and blueness. Consequently, the word "pot" would not denote the locus of blueness, and the word "blue" would not denote the quality residing in the pot. Thus, the two words would not be syntactically related. Therefore, it must be accepted that expectancy and its absence are the determinants of connection and non-connection. It is not the state
"Perpetual."
... even eternal speech would be devoid of both the expressed and the expresser. // MĀnuv 3.175bc //
If that which is not an action (akārya) were not connected with an agent, then Vedic speech, being non-action, would be devoid of both the object denoted and the speaker.

Furthermore, if that which is an action were connected with an agent, there would necessarily be a connection with an object such as the ritual act (*karman*) and so forth; this is the meaning of the particle *api*.
He states the conclusion regarding the opposite case [of the first alternative] with the words "for it is not" (*na hi*).
... for she herself is not of that same nature. (Manu 3.175d)
The connection is that "she is certainly not such.
By means of the word "ca" (and), he states the conclusion of the reversal of the second undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*).
To the question "How is she not such?", he says: "the seer" (*draṣṭā*). (*11.271*)
For there are indeed those who perceive the words of the Vedas, and the things to be expressed are directly evident.
While one should have said "speakers" (*vaktāraḥ*), the term "seers" (*draṣṭāraḥ*) was used in order not to undermine the quality of being authorless (*apauruṣeyatva*).
It has been stated that there is no inconsistency in saying "directly" (*añjasā*) when the referents actually exist.
Now, at the time of the Veda's persistence, there are indeed seers such as Vasiṣṭha and others who are the speakers, and Indra and others who are the referents.
But [this is] not the case during the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*); therefore, he says: "eternal.
"The Lord himself is indeed the eternal seer and the one to be designated. (Manu 3.4.176cd)
For there is never any speech that is devoid of a speaker, nor even one that is devoid of a subject matter.
The two occurrences of the word "ca" (and) serve to conjoin [the preceding terms] with one another;
the third has the sense of "because," and the term "vedavācaḥ" (Vedic speech) is understood to carry over [from the previous context]; the word "hi" (for/indeed) has the sense of "therefore."
Speech is the speech of the Vedas;
even in some instances of dissolution (*pralaya*),
just as the speech of the Vedas is sometimes endowed with its expressive objects and so forth, and sometimes devoid of them, so too is Brahman.

This statement is intended to dispel the hope that, while form (*rūpa*) may in conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) be associated with the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) and so forth, it will nonetheless be devoid of them from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

For, since such factors as being an effect (*kāryatva*) and the like are not probative (*aprayojaka*), rather, it is only a restricted relation caused by mutual expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) [that establishes connection].

Therefore, he concludes: "Just as eternal speech is necessarily accompanied by the knower and the object of knowledge, so too eternal cognition must be admitted to be endowed with the object of knowledge and so forth"—thus: *jñātṛjñeya* etc.
And knowledge devoid of both the knower and the known would likewise not exist.
But surely speech is not the meaning of the verbal root; rather, it is the object with respect to the meaning of the root.
How then can this serve as an example here?
It is said:

there is no fault, because the example of speech is understood merely by the fact that its state of being connected with a correlative— which is caused by expectancy— is not lost due to its eternality.
For when "speech" (*vāk*) is mentioned, there certainly arises an expectancy as to who the speaker is and what the object of speech is.
Since it is established that even phonemes possess meaning, there is no lack of common locus (*vyadhikaraṇatva*) between their eternity and their possession of an object of expression.
He says "not so" (*na hi*) to show that the very suspicion that the Knower, being eternal, might be devoid of objects of knowledge and the like, is to be refuted in this same manner.
For there exists no speaker, even if eternal, who is devoid of sentence and its denotatum;
likewise, even a knower devoid of knowledge and the object of knowledge does not exist at all.
Even the eternal speaker, the Supreme Lord, does not exist as something devoid of speech and its objects;
for that very reason, even an eternal knower does not exist as one devoid of knowledge and its objects.
Since the position is established that "power is the agent," it is logical that the eternal one is the speaker.
By this, it is stated that because there is no pervasion (vyāpti) in either case, the "perception of what is incompatible with the pervader" (vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi) is unestablished (asiddha).

It was previously asserted that for one who accepts that even an omniscient being (sārvajña)—who depends on others that are false—is himself false, it would follow as a logical consequence (prasaṅga) that he lacks sentience (cetanatva) and other such qualities.
Now, he states "moreover" (kiñca) to show that the falsity of the phenomenal world (prapañca) is itself lacking in valid authority (aprāmāṇika).
Furthermore, by what means of knowledge (*māna*) is the annihilation of everything (*sarvavilopa*) understood?
"The annihilation of everything" means the falsity of all things.
It cannot be established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), [as that would contradict its own nature].
This is because it grasps [the object] as being real;
nor can it be established by inference,
since that which is sublated by direct perception lacks validity.
Nor can it be established by scripture;
for one who seeks to demonstrate the falsity of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), that [scripture] does not exist—this is the meaning of the objection.

If it is argued, "But since there exists the scripture stating 'Not here is there any diversity whatsoever,' how can there be an absence of proof for the falsity of the entire universe?"—to this we ask: [what do you mean by this?]
In this context, he demonstrates that everything is false by considering whether or not this very sentence and its meaning are included within "everything.
Having restated the first position, he refutes it with the words: "By everything... (sarveṇa).
If that statement and its meaning are accepted along with everything else,
then there would be no denial of anything on account of its absence.
"By its absence" means by the falsity of both the sentence and its meaning;

for there would be a contradiction: if the sentence were absent, there would be no speaker to convey it, and if the falsity of the entire meaning of the sentence were absent, [the initial premise] would be undermined.
He restates and refutes the second alternative with the words: "If it is not apprehended."
If it is not perceived, then according to that same logic, there can be no denial of anything whatsoever.
In some cases, even regarding objects such as space (*ākāśa*) and so forth, denial—that is, negation—is not tenable;
this is by virtue of that same principle, namely the principle of the "sentence" (*vākya*).
This is the meaning.
It must be stated why both the sentence and its meaning are excluded from everything;
if it is argued that this is because they are untenable,
then one must explain what is untenable and why it should not be established.
If it is argued that [the example] is added, then in that case, the falsity of space and so forth would likewise not need to be demonstrated, because it is untenable.
[Objection: But surely, when an example of a statement is given, one cannot simply say, "There is no such statement as this."
One should not say that these words lack the capacity for this [meaning], or that this sentence lacks the intended purport (tātparya) regarding this.
To the question, "What is accomplished by this refutation of the alternative views? he says: "By means of reasoning... (upapatti...).
The meaning of a statement that lacks logical consistency is not understood.
Of that which is devoid [of meaning] and contradictory;
"meaning" (artha) refers to the intended purport (tātparya). This is what is being said:
We do not say that this sentence does not exist,
nor do we say that these words lack the capacity to convey meaning here;
rather, we say that this sentence has no intentionality (*tātparya*) regarding the falsity of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca-mithyātva*).
For the absence of contradiction with reason (*upapatti*) is an indicator that the intended meaning (*tātparya*) lies in what is actually perceived.
Since there is a contradiction with reason here, the author has formulated the refutation by means of an alternative analysis (*vikalpa*) in order to demonstrate this.
This might be so.

The indicators of intended meaning (*tātparya-liṅga*) are: consistency between the beginning and the conclusion (*upakramopasaṃhāra*), repetition (*abhyāsa*), novelty (*apūrvatā*), fruit (*phala*), explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), and logical justification (*upapatti*); as well as direct statement (*śruti*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), syntactical connection (*vākya*), context (*prakaraṇa*), position (*sthāna*), and name (*samākhyā*).

To the objection that even if there is a contradiction with [the evidence for] reality, one might understand from other indicators that this sentence intends to convey the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca-mithyātva*), he says: "beginning and so forth" (*upakramādi*).
For among the indicative marks such as direct action and the rest, each subsequent one is stronger than the preceding;
and among the means of proof beginning with direct audition (śruti), each preceding one is stronger than the subsequent.
Among the marks such as *upakrama* and the rest, that which is subsequent is stronger; thus, logical reasoning (*upapatti*) alone is the most powerful.
And among the group of marks beginning with direct statement (*śruti*), that which is prior is stronger.
Even in that case, it is logical reasoning itself, denoted by the word "mark" (*liṅga*), that is the strongest.

Therefore, when there is a powerful contradiction, it is not logical for other indicative marks (*liṅga*) to determine the intended meaning (*tātparya*). Why is this so? To this he says: "From the determination of the *Brahmatarka*... (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 3.4.181d).
This is because it has been thus determined in the treatise on logic known as the *Brahmatarka*.
By this, those who claim that the introduction (*upakrama*) possesses greater authority than the conclusion (*upasaṃhāra*) are refuted;
how this is so has been explained in the *Nyāyavivaraṇa*. *11,287*
For this reason as well, he states that this statement does not intend to establish the falsity of the phenomenal world: "Perception," etc.

When direct perception, logical reasoning, and many scriptural authorities are in conflict, and there is no objective reality that does not contradict the inferential mark (liṅga), [the latter prevails]. (Manu 3.4.182)
How is that very same object to be apprehended? [The answer is:
"The true sky," and so forth, is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
And because it has the nature of being a witness (*sākṣin*), it is authoritative (*balavat*).
And the proof consists in its capacity for causal efficiency and so forth;
that [proof] is powerful because it possesses pervasion and other such characteristics.
Furthermore, there are scriptural authorities such as "the universe is real" and so on.
It is stated that they are "many" in order to demonstrate their predominance;
this is an indication of their being without scope (*niravakāśatva*) and so forth.
When a particular meaning has been accepted, [it is said: "when."
In that [scripture], there is neither a referent nor a purpose in establishing any given meaning.
If it is argued that the purpose is the establishment of the non-duality of Brahman, we say no; for that very [non-duality] lacks any basis in valid cognition (*prāmāṇika*).
If it is argued that liberation is established for the self, we say no; for that [liberation] could be established even through destruction,
as it is logically consistent with those who maintain the doctrine of many souls (bahujīvavāda), just as it is with non-perception.
If it is argued that [the mention of "purpose"] is for the sake of detachment (*vairāgya*), we say no;
for that [detachment] is established by making known the fact that [sensual objects] are means to suffering.
The inclusion of the word "purpose" (*artha*) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*).
It should also be understood that there is no conformity with the [auspicious] commencement and other such factors;
not only is there an absence of conformity with the indicative marks (liṅga), but indeed, there is even opposition to them.
These two points, mentioned here and there in other texts, should be understood.
[Objection: In that case, it would follow that a statement lacking an opportunity [to apply] is not authoritative; therefore, he says: "It is established. (*upapanna*) // 11.289 //
... is not contradictory when [the child] has been born. // Mānava-dharmaśāstra 3.183b //

When the meaning of the sentence—namely, the Blessed One’s absence of internal differentiation—is not contradicted by the indications of the commencement of perception and other means of valid cognition, and is established as being consistent with them, then how could that very meaning be rejected?
Having refuted the misinterpretation of the sentence "neither here nor manifold," he states what has been established: "in its primary sense."
But when the primary meaning is available, where could such ambiguity be prohibited? (Manu 3.183cd)

Since there is no reason for restricting the scope of the negation, the primary meaning is the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*). However, if that [falsity] were non-existent, it would be impossible to negate omniscience;
for that [omniscience] is to be negated precisely because it is dependent upon false objects.
Alternatively, the phrase beginning with "yadvopapanna" constitutes a single sentence: "upapanne" means in a case that is consistent;
therefore, this refers to when the primary meaning of the sentence is actually present.
The construction is as follows: since the falsity of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) is not established by this [argument], where is omniscience being negated?
As for the connection (*saṅgati*), it should be understood through the synthesis of the connections already stated.
He concludes the point previously stated in the passage beginning with "all that depending upon it alone" with the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*).
Therefore, that which is endowed with all virtues is indeed fit for the acceptance of Brahman.
The ellipsis is that it must be accepted as the subject (*dharmin*).
Thus, the meaning of the particle "for" (*hi*) is that the contradiction with the foundational [cognition] is unavoidable for statements such as "That thou art.
This might be so.
We indeed take Brahman, as endowed with attributes such as omniscience, as the subject (*dharmin*).
However, because those [attributes] are false, there is no contradiction with the non-dual scripture (*advaitāgama*) which relies upon [Brahman].

Just as in the case of "That which is a person is a post," even though one proceeds by taking as the subject an object distinguished from others by means of the superimposed "personhood," there is no contradiction with what is relied upon; therefore, he says: "even the denial."
Denial of anything whatsoever is not justified in any way.
This is the designation "falsehood.
The word "api" (also/even) serves to conjoin it with the meaning of the preceding sentence.
By the word "all," the entire collection of qualities under discussion is expressed.

The meaning is that [the opponent's view] cannot be established in any way because there is a lack of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because it contradicts such means of knowledge as scripture (*śruti*), and because it has already been stated that since [the omniscience and other qualities] have not been previously established, they cannot be the subject of a restatement (*anuvāda*).

Now, one might object: "But surely the very sentence 'That thou art' (*tattvamasi*) and others, by establishing the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, leads to the understanding of the falsity of the entire collection of attributes such as omniscience."
If it is argued that if those qualities were real, the identity of the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman would not be logically possible,
and therefore there is no evidence for their falsity— this is not so;

for once it is established that statements such as "That thou art" (tattvamasi) have as their purport the identity of the individual soul and Brahman, the falsity of the qualities is thereby established.
Furthermore, since the establishment of one depends on the establishment of the other, there is the fault of mutual dependence (*parasparāśrayatā*).
He states another fault as well: "beginningless," etc. (*anādi* etc.).
And since it has been stated that fitness is beginningless, it must therefore be accepted in every respect.
Since the beginningless fitness of living beings has been stated and established by means of valid proofs,
for that reason it must be accepted in every respect.
This is what is meant:

When the fitness of living beings—manifesting in the forms of gods, humans, and demons, as well as their various sub-divisions—is established as beginningless, eternal, and known through valid cognition, then what can be said regarding the oneness of the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman?
Furthermore, how could one conceive of the qualities (guṇas) as being illusory (mithyā) for the sake of establishing that [oneness]?
On this very point, he states another reason: "Of the liberated ones," etc.
And the gradation among those who are liberated is not shaken by the authorities already mentioned.
"By the stated measures" means because the measures have been declared;
"it is not moved" means it cannot be rendered otherwise.
This is when even in liberation (mukti), gradation (tāratamya) is established through valid cognition.
In that case, what hope can there be for the identity of the individual soul and Brahman?
And how could statements such as "That thou art" have that as their purport, such that the assumption of the falsity of the qualities would be logical? (11.293)
He states another means of valid cognition regarding the gradations among those who are liberated: "Even among the knowers," and so forth.
Since even the wise always perform only what is auspicious,
the degree of excellence in their liberation is determined by that very same merit.
The word *eva* indicates that they also avoid evil; the word *tu* illuminates the relative distinction between performing wholesome and unwholesome deeds and their abandonment;
and the word *hi* establishes the authoritative proof for that point.
The proofs, such as "for ten kalpas" and so forth, have indeed been cited previously.
By that very [proof], he states the lack of scope for this [other] proof. It has been stated that there is a gradation in liberation due to the gradation of the means to liberation prior [to it].

But now, although liberation has been determined by knowledge, a distinction is stated based on the degree to which one has abandoned the performance of auspicious and inauspicious deeds. He states the refutation of the opposite position: "If there were no gradation in liberation... (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.4.187ab): "If there were no gradation in liberation, why would they perform auspicious deeds again? (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.4.187ab)
The word "punar" (again/furthermore) refers to that which follows knowledge (*jñānottara*).

If Brahmā and the others were not possessed of gradations [of excellence] regarding liberation, then, since liberation would be as good as already attained through knowledge alone, they would not perform auspicious deeds after the time of attaining knowledge, nor would they abandon what is inauspicious; such is the meaning.
He states the conclusion regarding the opposite case: "with difficulty," etc.
For indeed, they practice these—asceticism, knowledge, and ritual action—even with great difficulty.
Those who possess desire always fear the inauspicious, and those who are free from desire always fear the auspicious.
By the phrase "austerity, knowledge, and action," it is stated that these are auspicious.
"Knowledge" refers to hearing [the scriptures] and so forth;
"action" refers to sacrifice and so forth. The fruit of these specific qualifications—beginning with "even with difficulty"—will be understood immediately hereafter.
"And they have their desires fulfilled in the auspicious [state] forever" means that at the time of practicing one austerity or other, they desire another austerity or the like.
Therefore, the implication is that by means of various auspicious acts performed after the attainment of knowledge, they obtain a manifold perception of bliss.
This would be so, provided that auspicious acts performed after the attainment of knowledge possess fruitfulness.
But this is not the case,
because they lack the authority for those actions;
and it is well established that what is performed by one who lacks authority is fruitless.

But the performance [of duties] is possible even otherwise. For they, having previously performed auspicious acts with devotion and continuity before the arising of knowledge, have attained that state of being its very nature; thus, suspecting that they continue to perform them even after the arising of knowledge, he refutes this: "And not so," for this is not merely their own nature, because it was preceded by fear. (Manu 3.4.188cd)
This [dharma] consists of the auspicious conduct of the wise;
because it proceeds from a motivation preceded by fear— namely, that there will be transgression (*pratyavāya*) if it is not performed— and because it is practiced only with great effort,
the phrase "of the auspicious alone" means that it is undertaken through foresight by abandoning what is inauspicious.
And because of the performance of even what is auspicious with great difficulty, again and again.
By this, the fruit of the qualifiers such as "even with difficulty" (*kṛcchreṇāpi*) has been stated.
For an activity produced by its own nature (*svabhāva*) could not be of such a kind.

[Objection: But did these people not previously, at the time of performance, perform [the action] preceded by fear and only through the abandonment of what is unwholesome (*aśubha*) with great difficulty?

Therefore, anticipating the objection—"What fault is there in accepting that those who have come into existence with such a nature continue to act in that very same way even now by virtue of that very nature?"—he says: "Even such [beings]..."
If such a nature were present even in an ignorant person, it would be so for him as well.
Even that which consists of activity preceded by fear and so forth,

in the case of the practitioner of knowledge (*jñānin*), does not differ from that of the ignorant (*ajña*) regarding its performance. In this regard, one who maintains that the virtuous activity of the knowers arises solely through the force of their most ancient and primordial nature, and is not productive of a [new] fruit— [that view is being addressed].

If someone were to say in reply: "Even the virtuous activity of the ignorant is, from time immemorial, merely of a non-natural character and not productive of fruit due to the absence of any specific distinction," then what would be the response?
He raises an objection in order to release the *pratibandī* (the counter-argument): "In the case of having a fruit," etc.
If there is a means of valid cognition for its fruitfulness, then that is indeed the same for the knower.
The ellipsis [to be supplied] is that for the ignorant, action exists;
for a counter-argument (pratibandī) is applicable only when there is parity,
and such parity does not exist here.

Since there is scriptural authority for the fact that actions performed by those lacking knowledge bear fruit— such as the passage beginning, "For those endowed with wisdom [perform action born of action]"—
this [cited verse] is merely an illustration.
It should also be observed that these [beings] are qualified persons and are within the scope of ritual injunctions;
for this being so, there is no room for the postulation of an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

With the intention that, if this is the case, the postulation of an intrinsic nature is likewise untenable even with respect to those possessing knowledge (*jñānin*), he says: "In that regard" (*tatra*).

In that regard, regarding the fact that action possesses a fruit, that is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Here too, factors such as qualification (*adhikāra*) and so forth are to be understood as implied. *11,298*
To show what that authority is, he says: "Desireless" and so forth:
"Action performed without desire and preceded by knowledge is called *nivṛtta* here;
by practicing the *nivṛtta*, one attains the eternal Brahman. (Manu 3.4.190)
Here, between the two—active engagement and withdrawal—he approaches;
that is, he goes beyond with excellence. The meaning is that he becomes liberated through the accompaniment of an abundance of bliss.
To explain the meaning of this statement from the *Smṛti*, he recites another verse beginning with "By the auspicious" (*śubhena*).
For through auspicious action there is an increase in bliss, whereas through inauspicious action there is indeed a decline;
therefore, even for the wise, they must perform only what is auspicious.
There is also the existence of bliss.
Only the auspicious should be performed and the inauspicious should be abandoned;
by this, the reality of the injunction is also established.
Furthermore, there is the governing context (*adhikāra*).
In this regard, he also cites the scriptural text: "He meditates" (*upāste*).
He who worships the Self does not suffer the loss of his merit;
for from this very Self, whatever he desires, he creates that.

By this, he cites the scriptural passage: "He who worships the Self alone as his world—for him, indeed, action is never exhausted; for from this very Self, whatever he desires, that he creates. Here, "the Self" refers to the Supreme Self (paramātman).
He worships the world as the universal substratum;
the meaning is that he perceives the effect by means of the cause.
Having become liberated, that wise man creates whatever he desires—whatever action—from this very Self, through the grace of this Self.
For even one who performs many rituals, if he is ignorant, shall obtain only a finite fruit.
By the word "the ignorant" (avidvān), he cites the Śruti passage: "Even if one who does not know this performs a great meritorious deed, it is indeed exhausted for him in the end.
By this, the fruitfulness of the action of the knower is established by implication.
Furthermore, there will be application [to this later]:
"Whatever one performs through knowledge, that indeed becomes exceedingly powerful"—by the force of such statements, there is a gradation leading to liberation. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.4.193c–f)
By the phrase "yadeva" (whatever), he cites the scriptural passage: "Whatever one performs with knowledge, with faith, and with the secret doctrine (upaniṣad), that alone becomes more powerful.
Here, "vidyayā" means preceded by the direct realization of Brahman, and "upaniṣadā" refers to [the practice] appropriate for oneself.
By the force of such statements as "that which is more vigorous" and "which yields greater fruit," it is first understood that actions performed by the knower possess fruit;
from that, it follows that due to their diversity, there is an established gradation regarding their attainment of liberation—this is the meaning.
It might be argued as follows:
These statements do not establish the fruitfulness of the actions of those possessing knowledge (*jñānin*).
For, first, in the passage "He who [meditates on] the Self," there is the scriptural hearing (*śravaṇa*) that the fruits of the meditative practices (*upāsaka-karma*) are imperishable;

and furthermore, in the other case, it is possible for the words "knowledge" (*jñāna*) and "science" (*vidyā*) to mean indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*). He dispels this doubt with the words "And not... (*na ca*).
And it is not here stated that the fruit of the lay follower alone is inexhaustible.
In these statements,
the fruit of actions [is established];
likewise, it should also be understood that terms such as "knowledge" (jñāna) and so forth are not to be explained as referring to indirect knowledge (parokṣajñāna).
To the question "Why not?", he says: "For it is not so."
For indeed, without knowledge, there can never be any inexhaustibility of the fruit.
Knowledge is the direct realization of Brahman;
[it occurs] in liberation (mokṣa) and elsewhere. [It is the cause] of the fruit of actions.
This is what is meant:
it must be considered in what manner the actions performed by a lay practitioner who lacks the direct realization of Brahman result in inexhaustible fruits;
that is, do they bring about the inexhaustible liberation?
Or [is it] heaven and so forth?
Not the first, because it contradicts the Vedic scripture stating, "There is no other path. Not the second either, for the same reason.
Not the second, because it is heard that the world accumulated through merit perishes, as there are scriptural statements regarding the perishability of fruits such as heaven:
"One who does not know thus performs a great meritorious deed; yet that very deed becomes more powerful [only when known]."
Thus, there is a contradiction with the cited scripture in both positions as well.

Therefore, since the meaning of the sentence is untenable under the view that [the seeker] is ignorant, it is proper to regard the word "upāsaka" (worshipper) as merely indicating the knower (*jñānin*).
Likewise, because of the scriptural statement "he attains Brahman," it is proper to regard the word "jñāna" as signifying direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*).
For this very reason, it was stated, "by the force of the statement.
Although there are other scriptural passages here with clear meanings, such as "even though seeing this Self," and so forth,
these are nevertheless cited for the purpose of philosophical inquiry (*mīmāṃsā*).
Indeed, even in the view that [knowledge] is not the cause [of liberation], there is no inconsistency;
for actions performed by a practitioner (*upāsaka*) without intending their fruits do indeed produce knowledge, according to the scriptural statement: "One spreads forth knowledge through action."

Anticipating the objection that liberation occurs through knowledge—and thus even for those who perform actions out of ignorance, the attainment of imperishable fruit is possible by means of knowledge—the author says: "By knowledge... (jñāna...).
If it is by way of knowledge, then that does not contradict our own position.
The phrase "the inexhaustibility of the fruit of karma" continues [to apply]. This refers to that explanation provided by others;
its opposition to our own position consists in its contradiction with the gradations of liberation.
On the contrary, it is precisely in accordance with that [teaching].
Indeed, one who cannot tolerate gradations in liberation provides such an alternative interpretation, which actually establishes that very gradation in liberation.
For those desiring to know perform various kinds of actions.
Furthermore, that arising knowledge must necessarily be manifold;
otherwise, there would be the fallacy of the loss of what has been done (*kṛtavipraṇāśa*) and the acquisition of what has not been done (*akṛtābhyāgama*).
Through manifold knowledge, a manifold liberation itself must be cultivated.
"Because of the very reason stated previously.
Thus, one must certainly not provide an alternative interpretation that contradicts one's own doctrine while conforming to that of others.
Therefore, since our own interpretation is established, the subject at hand is logically consistent. *11,302*
Or rather, let there be another interpretation that is more appropriate;
consequently, these statements would fail to establish the point at hand.

Even so, since it is established by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that action subsequent to knowledge is a cause for a fruit included within liberation, one cannot abandon the gradation of liberation. Thus, he says "of that which follows knowledge" as a concessionary argument (*abhyupagamavāda*).
For even in this way, the knowledge of Jñānottara remains inexhaustible... // MAnu 3.4.195ab //
The inexhaustibility of karma—that is, its fruitfulness in leading to entry into the inexhaustible liberation—is established.
To the question "How so?", he says: "And not..."
... and not otherwise. (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 3.195b)
Because there is no other alternative; that is to say, by means of the *pramāṇa* of elimination (*pariśeṣa*).

By this, the following is also refuted: even if action subsequent to knowledge (*jñānottara-karma*) is fruitful, since there is no evidence for its fruit entering into liberation (*mokṣa*), the establishment of gradations in liberation is not proven.
He demonstrates the remainder itself with the words "pūrva" (the former).
For those virtuous deeds performed in the past, fulfillment is achieved through knowledge alone.

But for those actions already commenced, their entry into liberation occurs through experience; this applies to both those prior to and subsequent to the dawn of knowledge, for otherwise such action would not be performed.
Regarding the actions performed by one who possesses knowledge, these three possibilities arise:
that they are for the sake of knowledge, for the sake of enjoyment, or are purposeless.
Among these, it is first of all not tenable that the actions of the knower are for the sake of knowledge.
Because knowledge has already been accomplished by means of those very wholesome factors that exist prior to it;
the reason for this is that they "exist prior.
