Since the wholesome factors existing prior to knowledge have their purpose fulfilled by that very effect which is knowledge, and not by anything else.
This is because they lack any other function;
the meaning is that if they lacked the purpose of producing knowledge, they would be useless.
Furthermore, it is impossible for what arises later to be the cause of what has already arisen previously.
Nor is it for the sake of enjoyment,
because enjoyment arises solely from previously commenced prārabdha-karmas;
the reason for this is that the purpose of commenced karmas is fulfilled only through experience.
The intended meaning is as before.
The phrase "otherwise" is the reason for rejecting the charge of futility;
for if the knowledge and rituals were futile, their performance would not occur.
For those possessed of discernment do not perform an action in vain.
If it is argued that this is due to the very nature of the instrument [of action],
we reply that it would follow that the action is not preceded by intelligence.
If it is argued that [the Lord acts] for the sake of gathering the world, no;
for that purpose must also be stated.
If it is argued that it is like the case of God, no; [for the same objection applies].
Because [otherwise] there would be the undesirable consequence [of such karma persisting] even in liberation (*mukti*).

The statement regarding the result of the remainder [of karma] means that, for that reason, actions subsequent to knowledge (*jñāna*) would enter into liberation for the purpose of increasing the bliss attained in liberation.
It has been stated previously that virtuous deeds occurring before [knowledge] are for the sake of knowledge.
In that context, since it might follow that all [factors] have knowledge as their purpose, he states the distinction: "Knowledge and so forth."
All auspicious acts performed prior to the attainment of knowledge should be done without desire for their fruits, for the sake of the perfection of knowledge.

Prior to the arising of knowledge, only auspicious actions that are non-desirous (akāmya)—that is, meritorious deeds—contribute to the attainment of knowledge, but not those that are desirous (kāmya).
He states the purpose of the qualification "auspicious" by saying: "not prohibited."

...are forbidden for the obstruction of knowledge and for the sake of experience. (Mānava-dharmaśāstra 3.4.197cd) *11,305* The "obstruction of knowledge" (*jñānarodha*) consists either in the non-arising of knowledge or the suppression of that which has already arisen.
"For the sake of experience" means for the sake of suffering.
In this same way, the application (*viniyoga*) of optional rites (*kāmya*) should also be understood;
this is to be explained in the fourth [chapter].
Now, just as the qualifiers "optional" and "auspicious" are employed, so too should the qualifier "distinct from the obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*)" be employed.

Since even obligatory rites (*nitya*) and the like lack the status of being causes of knowledge—because they serve only to avoid transgression (*pratyavāya*)—the author says: "Of fitness" (*yogyatāyāḥ*).
And whatever abundance of merit arises from the power of one's fitness at the outset, that alone produces an abundance of knowledge, and not anything else. ... MAnu 3.198a-d.
Capability consists of being of the nature of Brahminhood and so forth, as well as the death of one's father and so forth;
it was performed "from the beginning," that is, prior to the arising of knowledge,
for the sake of another— namely, the mere avoidance of transgression.
Because this point has already been established in the statement, "For the sake of meditation, as there is no other purpose," no further reason is stated here.

Although it should have been said that "by the force of suitability, the auspicious [action] was performed first, and this very knowledge would bring it about," the fact that the term "abundance" (*bāhulya*) is employed in both instances is for the purpose of elaborating on what was stated: that this does not contradict our own position.
In this context, by the statement beginning with "The purpose of man [is attained] from that [knowledge], because of the word [of the Veda]," it is stated that knowledge is the means to liberation.

Furthermore, it is indicated here by the assertion that there is a gradation of knowledge resulting from the gradation of ritual action, and a gradation of liberation resulting from the gradation of knowledge.
In order to dispel the misconception that the term "knowledge" (jñāna) merely indicates simple awareness, he says: "of knowledge" (jñānasya).
Because knowledge is a constituent part of devotion, devotion is said to be knowledge.
In this treatise, wherever it is stated that knowledge is the means to liberation, there the word "knowledge" denotes or indicates devotion (*bhakti*).
Why?
Because of their connection.
Because knowledge is a constituent part of devotion;
for it has been stated that devotion is indeed the union of the knowledge of majesty and affection. Therefore, knowledge is a part—that is, a single portion—of devotion.
And thus, it is stated that [the relationship] is characterized by the relation between a part and the whole;
and the characterization of a whole by means of a part is well known in such expressions as "only a tenth part has been given. *11,311*
He states another alternative: "of knowledge itself," etc.
Devotion is said to be nothing other than a particular state of knowledge.
Whenever a specific quality of knowledge itself—characterized by its association with affection and so forth—occurs, then that aggregate is designated as *bhakti*.
This is what is meant:
knowledge and affection are the two constituent parts (*aṃśau*) of *bhakti*.
In that case, one part serves as an indicator for another part.
Thus he says: "By means of indication (lakṣaṇā), devotion itself is established.
He provides an illustration regarding the indication of one part by another part: "In the state of being beyond perception," and so forth.
Just as being indirect and being direct are two specific qualities residing in cognition.

Just as knowledge possesses two characteristics, namely being indirect (*parokṣa*) and being direct (*aparokṣa*), so too, when it is stated that "knowing Him thus" constitutes indirect knowledge as a means to liberation, its directness is implied by way of its indirectness; this is the meaning. He shows the application to the case in hand:
"The application of oil also... and so forth.
The application of unctuous substances is likewise; the distinction lies within the domain of knowledge.
It is called *snehayoga* because it is both affection (*sneha*) and a union (*yoga*), or a means (*upāya*);
or else, it is a union—that is, a connection—by means of affection. Therefore, by [one...]
And there would be a definition of one part by means of another part; this is the remainder [of the sense].
To the question, "What is the purpose of the author of the Sūtras in employing such technical usage? he says: "with this intention."
With this intention, the Śrutis generally declare that knowledge alone leads to liberation. ... MAnu 3.4.201a-c.
The scriptural passages such as "The knower of the Self crosses over sorrow" are based on two kinds of indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
This is what is meant:
indication is of two types, distinguished as conventional (*rūḍha*) and non-conventional (*arūḍha*).

In that regard, in the second [type of indication], there must be an investigation of the purpose of the speaker; however, this is not the case in the first [type], which is equivalent to direct denotation (*abhidhā*). And this is indication based on conventional usage (*rūḍhalakṣaṇā*).
Because such usage is not commonly observed in the Śrutis, one might ask: "What is the purpose of searching for [a specific meaning]?
It has been stated that the word *bhakti* denotes affection preceded by knowledge of the Greatness (*māhātmya*), and likewise, the word *jñāna* has the sense of *bhakti*.
Both of these [positions] are untenable,

because liberation is seen to arise from both devotion and knowledge; for if the word "devotion" (bhakti) were used in the sense already stated [by you], the mention of "knowledge" (jñāna) would be redundant.
(Since that [usage] is included therein), and because if the word *jñāna* had both meanings, the mention of *bhakti* would be redundant, he says: "This is that."
...so indeed this distinction is also proclaimed.
"Devotion is knowledge," as it is said somewhere... [Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.4.202a]

In some instances, this distinction—consisting of affection characterized as devotion (*bhakti*) and awakening characterized as knowledge (*jñāna*)—is also expressed by the two terms "devotion" and "knowledge. However, there is no fixed rule that the meaning must be exactly as previously stated; therefore, there is no inconsistency. This applies where devotion and knowledge... [are present].
It is said in response: since that would entail the fault of tautology, the word *bhakti* (devotion) indicates the aspect of affection by abandoning one part of its own primary meaning;

it does not, however, reside in its primary meaning alone. And the word *jñāna* (knowledge), because there is no logical inconsistency [in its primary sense], refers to its primary meaning itself and is not indicative; this is the intended sense.
Now, if liberation were impossible through mere knowledge alone without [the presence of] affection (sneha),
then one would have to resort to the word "knowledge" (jñāna) as being used figuratively (lakṣaka).
But this is not the case.
Because there is no authoritative evidence that the human goal [of liberation] is achievable through devotion alone;
because liberation is seen even for those who were hostile, such as Śiśupāla and others;
and because the claim that "those who hate are [in fact] affectionate" is a contradiction.
Therefore, since resorting to [such] a definition is untenable, he first refutes the notion that hatred is a means to liberation with the words "For not... (na hi).
"For a vision joined with hatred does not lead to the human goal, as it contradicts all the scriptures. Here,
the notion that hatred can be a means for achieving the human goal is refuted.
The term "vision" (*dṛśi*), however, was mentioned incidentally;
for the opponent has raised an objection either to refute [the notion of] affection by taking the necessity of cognition as a premise,
or for the sake of an argument *a fortiori*.
Even knowledge of greatness, when joined with hatred, is not a cause for liberation;
how much less so hatred alone?
As it has been said:
"Even inaction, if devoid of devotion to the Imperishable, does not shine, for knowledge alone is the means of purification. (*Bhagavad Gītā* 3.16).

To the question, "If hatred were accepted as a factor in the means to liberation, how would there be no contradiction with all the scriptures? he cites one such scripture: "Of the conscious being... (*cetanasyeti*).
For the conscious being, there are two things to be experienced: transmigratory existence and liberation itself.
Therein, transmigratory existence is threefold: heaven, the intermediate state, and the lower realm. (Manu 3.203)

In that regard, liberation is of two kinds: eternal happiness and likewise the other, which should be known as eternal suffering; even within the cycle of worldly existence, the means [to these] consist of optional rites and prohibited acts—this is the certainty regarding ignorance.
"Both hatred and devotion bring about liberation," according to the Paiṅgi Śruti; thus, hatred is certainly not a cause for true liberation. (Manu 3.4.205)
Of all that is born alive,
there are only two [paths]:
therein, between liberation and cyclic existence.
The middle state is human existence;
the lower states are the hells and so forth.
Eternal bliss alone should be known as liberation.
Likewise, it should be understood that there is another [type of] constant suffering within *saṃsṛti*, regarding the sphere of *saṃsṛti*; here,
"hatred" and "devotion" are connected to "the means" (*sādhana*) according to their respective fitness.
The prescriptive [text] is the means of accomplishment;
it is understood that true liberation consists in the nature of eternal bliss—this is the ellipsis. *11,317*
Since the status of being the cause of liberation for the existent is not denied, how can it be stated thus? To this he says: "The non-existent."
And it is the cause for non-liberation... // MAnu 3.4.206a //
Aversion has been stated as a cause for liberation with respect to those things whose very nature is eternal suffering;
by that, it is understood through contradiction that such [aversion] cannot be a cause for true liberation.
Now, one might object: in this scriptural passage, devotion and aversion directed toward liberation are spoken of as the causes for good and bad liberation, respectively.
But the two subjects, Viṣṇu and the material cause (prakṛti), have already been discussed.
Therefore, to address the question "What is connected with what?", he says: "In liberation... (muktāv iti).

Regarding the phrase "in liberation" (*muktau*), Keśava states: "That which is expressed by the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) 'liberation' (*mukti*) [is indicated] here in the word ending in the locative case. *11,318* In this context, within the locative-case form *muktau*, that which is expressed by the nominal stem *mukti* is intended.
If it were stated merely as "denoted by the word 'liberation' (mukti)," the application [of the term] would also occur in the case of the two types of liberation;
therefore, it is specified as "in liberation" (muktau).
To the question "by what cause? he says: "liberation" (mokṣam).
... that he grants liberation to those who are devoted to him.
From the root *muc* in the sense of "releasing," the suffix *ktin* is applied in the feminine;
however, due to the inclusion of the term "bahu-lam" (variously), this suffix occurs even in the active (*kartṛ*) sense.
Alternatively, in the word *karaṇa*, there is a metaphorical attribution of agency (*kartṛtva-upacāra*) to the instrument.
The suffix *ktin* is used here in the sense of an instrument (karaṇe), as in "that by which one is liberated is liberation.
He states the contradiction with reason that would arise if hatred were accepted as a means for liberation: "even from hatred," and so forth.
If liberation were possible even through hatred, it would constitute a contradiction of the Great Purpose.

If it is accepted that liberation is attained not only through devotion but even through hatred, then that would contradict the fact that the primary purport (*mahātātparya*) of all the Śrutis and other scriptures is precisely the excellence of the Lord’s qualities.
To the question of how this would be so, he says: "Through devotion... (*bhaktyā*).
"All the Śrutis, Purāṇas, and Āgamas declare that liberation comes from the grace of the God through devotion; such indeed are His qualities. (Manu 3.4.207c–f)
Other scriptures as well—
such as the Śruti and so forth— are well known to have liberation as their purpose and to have the attributes of the Supreme Lord as their subject matter;
in that regard, this alone is the connection.
The liberation of living beings comes from the Blessed One alone; and that [liberation] comes only from his grace;
and grace, in turn, comes through devotion alone.
Furthermore, since the Śrutis and other authorities declare that devotion belongs only to one who knows the qualities of the Lord,
how can there be no contradiction with the primary purport [of the scriptures] if liberation is accepted as resulting from hatred? *11,320*
By this, it is understood that devotion is a means to liberation; and we do not deny that. However, since [the opponent claims] that hatred is likewise [a means], he says "yadi" (if).
If liberation could result from hatred, then the entire collection of faults would have to be proclaimed.
The ellipsis here is "for the purpose of generating hatred";
however, this is not the case,
because it has already been established that [the text] merely sets forth the qualities.

The meaning is this: therefore, it is understood that the Vedas and other scriptures, being engaged in the pursuit of liberation, intend to show that liberation is achievable through devotion alone by demonstrating only virtues.

Now, one might object: there are indeed statements such as "the kings Caidya and others [attained liberation] through hatred," which establish that even hatred is a means to liberation; so how can it be said that hatred lacks the status of a means to liberation? To this, he says: "It should be remembered."

For it is with this very purpose— that the Blessed One should always be meditated upon— that he sometimes described his qualities in the Purāṇa as if out of anger, like the words of one who is enraged.
In a certain section of the Purāṇa, the connection is as follows:
with the very intention that "the Blessed One should be remembered constantly," the author of the Purāṇa speaks of liberation from hatred;
therefore, there is no contradiction with what was stated previously—this is the meaning of "hi" (for).
This is what is meant:
although an ancient statement may appear at first glance to establish that hatred is a means to liberation,
nevertheless, it does not have that as its intended meaning.
However, his intention is that the seeker of liberation must remember the Lord at all times,
as it is said: "Manu declared that an aged mother and father, a virtuous wife, and an infant son must be supported even by performing a hundred improper acts."
In this context, the intent is not that one should not perform their duties, but rather that they must be supported in every way;
so it is here as well.
"He spoke of his virtues" indicates another underlying intention.
The statement of the Blessed One, which establishes the liberation of Caidya and others despite their hatred, declares His qualities such as compassion.

Even though Caidya and others were haters due to curses and the like, the Blessed One did not take account of their temporary animosity; rather, He took into consideration only their prior devotion and granted them His grace.
The meaning of those statements is that the intent is to show His compassion, His changelessness, and His possession of true resolve.
Sentences are of two kinds: those such as "Because of enmity, the kings... and so forth, which are primarily concerned with remembrance; for these, the first [type of] movement is the primary path.
Those such as "Out of hatred, the Caidyas... and so forth, which are primarily concerned with aversion; for these, the second [type of] movement is the primary path—this is the intended meaning.
In the first explanation, he states a worldly analogy: "like the words of one who is angry.
The meaning is that just as the words of an angry person do not possess authority regarding the very meaning they express, but rather [authority] elsewhere, so it is in this case as well. *11,323*
He explains this with the words "just as."
Just as an angry father, having first rebuked his son with the command "Kill him!", speaks thus for the sake of another task, so it is said in the Purāṇas. (Manu 3.4.209)
The statement... // Manu 3.4.210a //
*Marati* is a form belonging to another verbal root (*prakṛtyantara*), as seen in the usage: "O virtuous hunter, live or die; do not live, do not die."
*Ākṣepa* means censure.
It refers to another task proclaimed by oneself;
for instance, a father enjoins something toward his son, saying, "Do this."
But he, being afraid of fatigue and the like, remains without doing anything;
then his father, becoming angry, says:
"O wretch, son of a widow, die!"

Just as that statement does not intend to enjoin the death of one's son, but rather to enjoin what is prescribed for oneself, so too, although the Purāṇic statement says "liberation occurs through recollection with hatred," it does not intend to establish hatred as the means to liberation; rather, its purpose is to establish the necessity of performing the recollection. *11,324*
Some say this is the function of the phoneme (*vyañjanāvṛtti*); others say it is the function of the intended meaning (*tātparyavṛtti*);
[and some say it is] the indication of the sentence (*vākyalakṣaṇā*).
The teachers [hold that] it is "numānam" (inference); [to the objection] "why should the meaning not be simply what is well-known?", he says: "śruti... (scriptural authority).
Because it directly contradicts the Vedas, contradicts itself,
and contradicts many traditional scriptures, [the claim that] liberation comes from hatred is not a statement of truth.
The phrase "the statement of the Purāṇas" continues [from the previous context]. The Śruti passages cited here were quoted in the preceding section.
Where the state of hatred being a means to liberation is asserted, in that very same place its opposite is also stated; thus, there is internal contradiction.

This has indeed been demonstrated by the recitation of such Bhāgavata passages as "So too was Hiraṇyakaśipu," for it does not establish liberation from hatred through the direct or primary sense (*añjasā mukhyayā vṛttyā*). (11.329)
He demonstrates the contradiction with scripture [by stating]: "Darkness" (tamaḥ).
"Through hatred they go to darkness, and likewise through devotion to liberation;

[they attain it] in Viṣṇu by the grace of Viṣṇu, and also directly through the opposite [of hatred]. Thus, even the statement regarding the six qualities serves to restrict the meaning already expressed.
The construction is as follows: by the grace of Viṣṇu alone, arising from devotion toward Viṣṇu, they attain liberation;
likewise, through hostility toward Viṣṇu, that is, through opposition which gives rise to Viṣṇu’s wrath, they immediately enter into darkness. The two particles *ca* signify conjunction.
This establishes the regulator of the stated meaning—that devotion to Viṣṇu alone is the means to liberation, and not hatred.
By the designation (*samākhyā*) of this very statement, it is proven that in the Śruti passage "of the sentient being," the word "in liberation" (*muktau*) is a synonym for Viṣṇu.
Thus, the contrary notion—that both hatred and devotion are causes of true liberation, while hatred alone is the cause of false liberation—is thereby refuted.
For this reason as well, he states that this sentence does not have the literal meaning as its primary purport: "mahātātparya... (regarding the great purport).
And if the primary purport is obstructed, how can a statement attain the status of a valid means of knowledge?

Since all scriptures that have liberation as their purpose possess a primary purport directed solely toward the qualities of the Blessed One, it is understood—by the impossibility of it being otherwise—that devotion alone is the means to liberation, and not hatred.
Therefore, because it contradicts the great purport [of the scriptures], how can a statement expressing aversion attain the status of valid authority regarding its literal meaning?
Now, one might ask: how is it that the Śruti and other authorities possess such preeminence, by virtue of which this statement is displaced from its own meaning due to contradiction with them?
It is said:
the authority of scripture (śruti) arises precisely from its being scripture,
because its own statement leaves no room for alternative interpretations.
For this very reason, it is said therein that [it is] "easily" [attained]; and because other scriptures are numerous,
it is therefore designated as "many scriptures."

In order to establish the superior authority of a statement based on its great purport (*mahātātparya*), he says "all" (*sarva*): "...for the great purport is held to consist of all matters. (Mānava Dharmaśāstra 3.4.212cd)
The meaning is that its nature consists in the fact that all treatises (*śāstra*) convey a single purpose, by virtue of not having any other purpose.
How is this obtained?
The word "purpose" (*artha*) denotes the primary object to be communicated.
It is as in the expression "of the very existent object" (*sata eva padārthasya*). That [word] ends in the singular number, and by it, its status as a signifier of that [object] is indicated.
To the question, "In what sense is this the meaning of the term 'great purport' (mahātātparya)? he says: "For [it is] denotative power... and so forth.
For the capacity to denote [meaning] is indeed the intended purport (tātparya).
That which has something else as its object to be established is "tātparya";
the state of being such is "tātparya.
Thus, the capacity for expression (vācakatva), that is, the capacity for establishing meaning (pratipādakatva), is indeed called "tātparya."
And the sense is that when it is qualified by the word "great" (mahat), this is the meaning of the term "great intention" (mahātātparya) by virtue of its fitness.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "yadarthāḥ" ("for the sake of which").
How can that purpose for which all sounds exist be abandoned when there is doubt regarding even a single word? (Manu 3.213b–d)
"Yadarthāḥ" means those whose purpose is such-and-such;
"ravāḥ" refers to the scriptures (*āgama*).

When there is doubt regarding a single word—meaning, when there is doubt concerning that which is connected to a single sentence—the sense is: having taken up a single doubtful sentence containing contradictory meanings.
This is what is meant:

all sentences, taken together, convey a single meaning without any other purpose; if a subordinate sentence is found to convey a meaning contrary to that [single] meaning, it is considered to have scope [only] because it does not contradict the meaning of the great sentence as a whole. Otherwise, it would be contradictory.
It is well established that while [the literal meaning] is set aside, its contradictory great sentence-meaning (mahāvākyārtha) is not abandoned;
for the great sentence is primary and its meaning is determined by means such as the introductory context (upakrama),
whereas the intermediate sentence is secondary and its meaning is ambiguous.
In the present context, however, the point established by all the statements taken together is that devotion alone is the means to liberation, and not hatred;
for even that which is implied by the sense is intended for that very purpose, just like the explicit subject matter itself.
The single subordinate statement (*avāntaravākya*) that teaches liberation through hatred is, as explained, subject to qualification;
therefore, it is this very [statement] that is sublated.
He concludes the refutation of hatred as a means to liberation with the words "Therefore" (*ataḥ*).
Therefore, through knowledge and devotion, the supreme goal of man shall be attained.

The meaning is that [liberation arises] precisely through knowledge of his majesty and affection for him, and not through hatred. Although it would have been sufficient to say "liberation" (*mokṣa*), by saying "the supreme human goal" (*paraḥ puruṣārthaḥ*), it is indicated that even knowledge and the like do not accrue to those who harbor hatred; for even knowledge and so forth are considered supreme human goals only in comparison to [lower] virtues such as merit (*dharma*). *11,335*

Having thus refuted the notion that hatred is a means to liberation, he now states another authoritative proof (*pramāṇa*) to refute the claim that there is no evidence for devotion (*bhakti*) being the achiever of the supreme human goal (*paramapuruṣārtha*): "Of whomsoever there is supreme devotion to the God, and as to the God, so to the Guru—for that great-souled one, these truths that have been declared indeed shine forth. (Manu Smṛti 3.4.214)
From devotion comes knowledge, from that comes further devotion, and from that, vision;
from that, liberation, and from that, devotion—she alone becomes the embodiment of bliss. (Manu Smṛti 3.4.215)
The Blessed One, pleased by devotion, would grant untroubled knowledge;
having attained his vision through that very devotion, he would grant liberation through it.
Neither by the Vedas, nor by austerity, nor by charity, nor by sacrifice can I be seen in such a form; one may attain liberation through this [knowledge].
But by means of unswerving devotion alone, O Arjuna, I who am of such a nature can be known and seen in truth, and entered into, O scorcher of the foe.
And from such statements as these, this aforementioned meaning is understood.
The meaning is that just as [one offers] what is appropriate for a god to a god, so too one offers what is appropriate for a guru to a guru.
By this, it is stated that knowledge is to be accomplished through devotion;
by the phrase "knowledge through devotion," [the attainment of] knowledge and so forth is indicated.
Knowledge arises as a certain conviction regarding the imperceptible;
from that knowledge, matured devotion (*pakvā bhakti*) comes into being;
from that, vision (*dṛṣṭi*); and from that, that devotion becomes fully matured (*paripakvā*).
Then, immediately after liberation, devotion remains;
that [devotion] would be of the very nature of bliss and not possess further fruit.
This is precisely what is expressed by the phrase "gratified by devotion."
It is said that "without agitation" occurs because devotion is absent in the absence of knowledge. By "by this very [knowledge] when it has been ripened," it is meant "when it is fully matured.
"By the Vedas" means by hearing and so forth devoid of devotion.
That for which no other object exists is "exclusive" (*ananyā*).
As it is said: "If there were such devotion toward another as there is toward Him, that would not be so;
that should be known as exclusive devotion, and it should be directed toward Viṣṇu alone."

And such is the Smṛti. However, because of the statement that "the intended connection exists," it is appropriate [to say] "I am capable" in order to know [the Self] in its true nature, according to reality.
By the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and from such statements as," he includes the previously cited passages such as "the duality of the conscious one" (*cetanasya dvayam*).
This is established by the words themselves, not merely by their meaning.
He also establishes the stated point through inference with the words "nor... (*na ca*).
"One does not obtain grace through hatred; one may obtain it through devotion.
Thus, even the principle of following what is observed is maintained in this matter:
one does not obtain the grace of the Blessed One through hatred of the Blessed One.

In this matter—that one may obtain that grace of the Blessed One through devotion to the Blessed One—it is accepted and known that there is conformity with what is seen, meaning conformity with inference based on perceptible pervasion (*pratyakṣadṛṣṭavyāptika*).
This is what is being said:
it is established, first of all, that liberation comes from the grace of the Blessed One alone.
The grace of the Blessed One cannot be accomplished through hatred of the Blessed One,
because it is the grace of the Blessed One.
Whatever is the grace of someone cannot be accomplished by hatred toward that person, just as, for example, the grace of a teacher.
Alternatively, hatred toward the Blessed One cannot be a means for attaining the Blessed One’s grace,
because it is hatred toward the Blessed One;
whatever is hatred toward something cannot be a means for attaining grace toward that thing.
Just as there is hatred toward one's teacher;

or else, the Blessed One does not feel affection for one who hates him, because he is a discerning person, like Devadatta. Or rather, one who hates the Blessed One is not an object of the Blessed One’s affection, because of that very hatred for the Blessed One.

Whoever is an object of hatred for someone is not an object of that person’s affection, as is commonly experienced; thus, when the capacity of hatred to produce serenity is refuted, its capacity to produce liberation is likewise refuted.
Similarly, the grace of the Blessed One is accomplished through devotion to the Blessed One, because it is the grace of the Blessed One.
Whatever is a grace [bestowed] by someone is achievable through devotion to that person, just as the grace of a guru [is achieved through devotion to him].
Alternatively, devotion to the Blessed One is a means for achieving the grace of the Blessed One, because it is devotion to the Blessed One;
whatever is devotion to someone is a means for achieving the grace of that person, just as devotion to a guru [is a means for achieving his grace].
Alternatively, the Blessed One shows favor toward his own devotee because he possesses the purpose of a discerning person,
just like [anyone] generally agreed upon.
Or else, one who is a devotee of the Blessed One is an object of the Blessed One’s affection because he is a devotee of the Blessed One.
Whoever is devoted to something becomes an object of affection for that thing;
as, for example, one who is devoted to his teacher.
Once it is established that devotion is a means to [attain] grace, it follows that it is indeed a means to liberation.
Now, one might object: "In the case of the Lord, who is supramundane, such an inference based on worldly analogies is not tenable;
otherwise, it would lead to the undesirable consequence of inferring fixed attributes such as atomicity [in Him].

Therefore, there is no contradiction in accepting that He, though appearing hostile, becomes gracious when He differs from the world. To dispel this doubt, he provides a scriptural statement: "He who... (yaḥ).
Those qualities of Viṣṇu which have been separately and respectfully ordained by the Veda—those alone should be accepted when they are perceived to be consistent; nothing else.
Anything else may also be accepted as belonging to Vāsudeva, according to what has been observed.
Distinctly, by way of being contrary to worldly convention;
respectfully, with focused intent;
disregarding the contradiction of what is perceived, because of its opposition to what is perceived.
Furthermore, a collection of qualities not mentioned in the Vedas and contrary to worldly experience should not be accepted at all;
rather, [only] those collections of qualities other than atomicity, magnitude, simultaneity, and so forth, which are mentioned in the Vedas [are acceptable].
The purpose of the term "qualities" (guṇāḥ) is stated as follows: "the absence of defects" (doṣābhāva).
And those absences of fault which have been declared by the Vedas—without abandoning them. And those absences of fault which have been declared by the Vedas—without abandoning them.
Moreover, even those [rules] not explicitly stated are to be understood through the power of the great purport;
thus, the speech of the *Bṛhatsaṃhitā* is indeed established as its authoritative doctrine.
The meaning is "fourfold";
the remainder is that they are both distinct from and non-distinct from the world,
existing by virtue of the power of the great purport.
The meaning is that, in every respect, there is no fault in the Blessed One, because it has been determined that this is the general purport of all the scriptures.
With this [verse], he dispels the doubt that it is improper to accept a matter not mentioned in the Vedas if it lacks authoritative basis;
the intention is that even if it is not mentioned specifically, it is established by way of general principle.
Therefore, the meaning stated therein is the authoritative final doctrine (*siddhānta*).
Alternatively, by stating that "the meaning declared in the *Bṛhatsaṃhitā* is indeed the final doctrine," he generates great respect for it.
In this way, it has been established that devotion alone is the means to liberation.
In order to dispel the notion that devotion is directed toward the Lord alone, he says: "by way of gradation."
One should certainly practice devotion toward his devotees as well, according to their relative degree of excellence... [Mānava Dharmaśāstra 3.4.223a-c]

This applies not only to Viṣṇu, but also to his devotees such as Ramā and others; this is certain in every respect, and that [devotion], when practiced, occurs precisely according to degrees of excellence.
Why is this? To this he says: "This too..."
... this too is devotion to him ... // MAnu 3.4.223c //
Since even this [devotion] performed toward his devotees is indeed devotion to the Blessed One, devotion should therefore be practiced toward them as well.
This is what is meant:
it has already been established that devotion to Viṣṇu must be performed.
And that [attainment] occurs only through devotion to His devotee, along with its constituent parts, and not otherwise.
To the question "Why is this so?", he says: "In the world... etc.
"...in accordance with the world and the Vedas.
By the word "world" (loka), inference characterized by a pervasion established in common experience is meant;
by the word "Veda," mere scripture (āgama) is meant.
He demonstrates conformity with the world, saying: "For he who... and so forth.
For he who is devoted to the principal [teacher] is necessarily seen to be devoted to his [the teacher's] dependents as well; in the opposite case, the reverse is true.
Regarding the primary [object], such as a king and so forth;
"in the opposite case" means in the absence of devotion toward him;
"the contrary" means one who lacks devotion toward the primary object.
It is invariably observed.
By this, positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) have been stated. And thus, the formal argument (prayoga) is as follows:
The subject of dispute must possess devotion to the Lord, because he partakes in the goals of human existence (puruṣārtha) through devotion to the Lord;
for whoever partakes in the goals of human existence through devotion to someone else is seen to be so, as in the case of those esteemed [devotees].

Now, it may be objected that even though Daityas and others possess devotion toward Brahmā and the like, they are observed to be devoid of devotion toward Indra and others who are themselves devotees of those [gods].
Since there would, therefore, be a deviation [of the reason], he says: "deviation."
"If there is deviation anywhere, a decline in devotion is postulated here.
(Mānava-dharmaśāstra 3.4.225ab) If deviation is alleged by another in any instance, then we postulate a decline in devotion toward that person here; that is to say, his devotion is called fruitless.
Thus, since the reason is absent in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), there is no deviation—this is the meaning.
To the question, "Why is it imagined in this way? he says: "Because of devotion," and so forth.
For this is indeed a defect of devotion: that one does not possess devotion even toward those who are devoted to Him.
That he does not show devotion even toward those devoted to Him is indeed a fault of primary devotion itself;
therefore, it is well known that primary devotion alone is corrupted and is not sufficient for the result.
It is also very well established in the Purāṇas that immortality and other such gifts are bestowed by Hiraṇyagarbha and others upon the Daityas and others only with deceit, yet they are not false.
That [the path] conforms to the Vedas will be demonstrated later.

Having established through inference that devotion to those devotees must be practiced, he now proves by inference that such devotion should be performed with varying degrees of intensity, stating: "with varying degrees of intensity."

Devotion toward them [the devotees] should truly be practiced according to their relative degree of excellence, following what is observed and in accordance with Viṣṇu’s grace; otherwise, there is fault.
Devotion performed toward those devotees of His must indeed be practiced in every way according to their relative gradation.
Why? Because it follows what is observed.
"In accordance with gradation" is itself explained by the phrase "in accordance with the grace of Viṣṇu.
This means that in whichever [person] there is greater grace of Viṣṇu, in him [the result] is greater, and so forth.
If one performs [the practice] otherwise—either by way of equanimity or by way of its opposite—it results in misfortune.
He demonstrates what was stated as "in accordance with what is seen" with the words: "one's own," etc.
Indeed, it is clearly observed even in the world that affection follows from one's own affection.
Here, by the word "self" (sva), the king and others are meant.

In accordance with their pleasure—that is, when devotion is practiced according to the way in which that person finds pleasure in someone—then, when such devotion is present, the pleasure of that king or other person is seen directly and invariably in that devotee.
This is the formal argument (prayoga) here.

The Lord is pleased with His devotees according to the degree of their devotion, because He is a conscious being, like a king. By this, another point of proof is also established, which he states as: "tāratamya... (the gradation...).
The thorough knowledge of the gradations [of merit] is also established by this very same means.

By this very argument— which establishes that liberation must be granted according to the hierarchy among the devotees of the Lord, such as Ramā, Brahmā, and others— it is proven that the previously mentioned thorough knowledge of the gradations among deities is also a means to liberation;
for indeed, it is not possible to effect liberation according to a hierarchy without first knowing that hierarchy.
The meaning of the extended application (*atideśa*) is that inference is possible in this very manner.
Regarding the point that liberation should be sought among His [the Lord's] followers in accordance with the degrees of grace from the Blessed One, he also cites scripture: "Lakṣmī... and so forth.
Lakṣmī, Viriñca, Vāṇīśa, Girijā, Indrāṅgiras,
and Sūrya and the others, in their respective order, are the objects of the Blessed One’s favor.
Devotion toward them must be practiced constantly and in due order by those seeking liberation.
Therefore, it is precisely by way of pleasing the Blessed One;
let alone the sequence [of worship], why even the mere act of devotion toward them? Because they are simply objects for pleasing the Blessed One.
And another reason is stated: "all [of them] as well."
For all these are indeed always the gurus of a man.
"Therefore, Hari is to be honored, saluted, and meditated upon on all sides"—
from this statement regarding the sixfold qualities (ṣāḍguṇya), this meaning is also determined.
Devotion to Hari leads in due order to remembrance of Him and His devotees;
from that comes praise of Hari and remembrance of Him, then praise of His devotees, and finally worship of Hari.
"Renunciation prescribed for that worship is indeed the gradual means to liberation; for by necessity, these very practices are to be constantly accomplished by all. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.4.232)
Thus is the statement regarding the commencement for the purpose of determining the means of proof.
Their status as gurus is well known by virtue of their being the initiators of knowledge.
The passage beginning with "they are to be honored" (pūjyāḥ) is an elaboration of devotion alone; [the Lord] is around Hari, not separate from him.
Furthermore, that which was stated as "in accordance with the Vedas" is also demonstrated by this.
In passages such as "devotion to them" and "remembrance of them," the word *tad* (them) refers to those belonging to Him (*tadīya*).
The phrase "in due order" is to be connected with every instance.

By "in due order," it is meant that devotion and the other qualities directed toward Hari are the primary means (*mukhya-sādhana*), whereas those directed toward His devotees are the secondary means (*amukhya-sādhana*).
The meaning is that because they are the means to liberation, they must be constantly practiced by all those seeking liberation;
this is found in the intermediate section titled "The Determination of the Means" (*sādhanavinirṇaya*). He explains this very point with the words: "one who has engaged [in practice]," and so forth.
"For when the *Pañcarātra* has begun, there is the determination of the means.
This means that within the *Pañcarātra*— which is an intermediate section [of this work]—
there exists a specific chapter titled "The Determination of the Means."
He states further inferences regarding the points already mentioned:
"Haridveṣaḥ... etc. (Verse 11.346): Hatred toward Hari does not bestow auspiciousness, because it is hatred [directed at] a virtuous being, just like [hatred directed at] one's teacher.

Devotion arises gradually and becomes the cause of Hari’s pleasure; devotion leads to what is dear to Him. Furthermore, the reasoning here is as follows: "Just as [He is] toward Himself," and so forth. (Manu Smṛti 3.4.234)
Because it is hatred toward the True One, that is, because it is hatred toward the Supreme Person (*uttamapuruṣa*).
The word "true" (*sat*) is used to exclude the possibility of deviation [from the definition] in the case of hatred directed by Vaiṣṇavas toward the Daityas and others.
[This refers to] hatred toward the Guru.

Previously, since hatred was not established as a means for attaining the grace of the Blessed One, the reason "being hatred of the Blessed One" was stated by relying on a general pervasion (*sāmānyavyāpti*); here, however, since it is not a means for attaining anything auspicious, the reason "being virtuous hatred" is stated by relying specifically on a particular pervasion (*viśeṣavyāpti*). This is a great distinction.
[The result is] devotion in due order.
The meaning is that devotion toward Ramā and others is characterized by its sequential order.
"Because devotion follows after those who are dear to Him" means because it has as its object those who are dear to Hari.
It is called "approaching what is dear to that" (*tatpriyopagā*) because it follows after and takes as its object what is dear to that [object].
Whatever devotion has as its object what is dear to something, that [devotion] arises from the cause of affection for that thing;
just as, for example, devotion toward oneself.
In this context, Devadatta is denoted by his own name (*svaśabda*).
The meaning is that, just as Devadatta’s devotion to the king beloved by the monarch is the cause of the king’s pleasure;
here, by adding a qualification to the proposition "in due order," it is established that devotion to the devotees of the Blessed One must be practiced, and that its gradations are necessary.
Alternatively, he indicates two syllogisms by this:
"Devotion to the Lord is the cause of the Lord's pleasure, because it is devotion beloved by the Lord;
the Lord is pleased only through devotion that possesses degrees of intensity directed toward Rāma and others."
"And because they possess delight toward that object precisely according to a gradation"—
this is the connection with the word "reasoning" (yuktiḥ) regarding the matter previously mentioned.
What is the use of a general pervasion?
With the intention that there is also a specific pervasion, another formal argument is stated: "By primacy," and so forth.
Devotion that follows the gradations of preeminence is supreme;
for it brings joy to Hari, just as a wife who is devoted to her own husband does.
Or thus... // Mānava-dharmaśāstra 3.236a //
Devotion toward Lakṣmī and others, which conforms to the gradations of excellence, brings pleasure to Hari;
for that devotion is supreme,
meaning it is the kind of devotion prescribed by the scriptures.
The meaning is that it is like that devotion which has Viṣṇu as its object and is accompanied by [the desire for] union with Him;
or rather, "it should be inferred in this way" is the ellipsis to be supplied.
Here too, as before, there is the establishment of two probanda either through specific similarity or by means of two separate formal arguments.
Thus ends the section concerning those who possess both marks (*ubhayaliṅga*).
Now begins the section concerning the declaration of rewards (*phalaśruti*).
// Oṃ. According to Ātreya, [the fruit belongs] to the master, because of the scriptural declaration of the fruit. Oṃ.//
It has been established in the *Puruṣārtha-adhikaraṇa* that knowledge is the cause of great fruit;

and it has been established in the *Stuti-adhikaraṇa* that ritual action belonging to the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama-karma*), as well as tranquility, self-control, and so forth, when performed after the attainment of knowledge, are causes for an excellence of bliss.

Now, regarding the doubt as to whether this fruit of knowledge, action, and so forth arises from the gods because they are the impellers (*prerakatva*), or rather from Devadatta because he is the agent (*kartṛtva*), the first sūtra sets forth the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that it belongs to the gods alone.

Having stated the established conclusion according to the view of a partial authority—namely, "The office of the officiating priest [is enjoined], for he is hired for that purpose"—the final settled conclusion is then declared: "There is an injunction for another auxiliary act; it is a third [requirement] for one who possesses that [prior qualification], like the beginning of an injunction."
In this regard, the portion of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) stating that "the fruit for the gods consists of knowledge and so forth" is indeed to be accepted;
only the restrictive emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*) is to be abandoned.
Therefore, he explains the meaning of the *pūrvapakṣa* sūtra as follows: "Knowledge... and so on.
"Because the scripture declares the fruit for the master [of the sacrifice], so says Ātreya.
... "And the fruit of knowledge, ritual action, and so forth, accrues to these [stages] in due order. (Manu 3.4.236ab)
And the fruit belongs to the gods—this is the remainder [of the sentence]. Furthermore, among these gods, it approaches them "gradually," meaning it arrives precisely by way of succession.
One proposition is that the fruit of knowledge and so forth, performed by Devadatta, belongs to the gods.
And that [sequence] occurs precisely in that order, and not by way of simultaneity or the reverse; this is the second [point].
Indicating the reason for the first [point], he establishes the second with the words "svātantrye" (in independence).
For the fruit of those who bear fruit indeed depends upon the degree of their autonomy.

The meaning is that for those who bear fruit— that is, those who partake of results— the fruit must necessarily correspond to the gradations of their autonomy, following precisely the gradations of their ownership; it cannot be equal, nor can it be the opposite.
It has been stated by you that Brahmā and the others possess fruits only according to a hierarchy, because their sovereignty likewise exists only according to a hierarchy.

By this, the reason of sovereignty (*svātantrya-hetu*) for the first proposition is indicated, which was expressed in the Sūtra by the term "Lord" (*svāmin*). Although the hierarchy regarding the attainment of the fruit was not explicitly set forth in the Sūtra, [it is implied].
Nevertheless, it has also been established that [the ownership of the fruit] is obtained by implication from the reason for ownership stated regarding the attainment of the fruit.

If, on account of independence, the fruit of knowledge and so forth performed by Devadatta were to belong to the gods, then it would follow—since there is no distinction—that the fruit of false knowledge and so forth performed by him would also belong to them; therefore, he says: "But the inauspicious...
[The verse continues: "But even in the case of the inauspicious, because of their independence and because of Hari's pleasure."
And by his command, it shall never be given to another for the sake of enjoyment.
However, the unwholesome karma of these gods does not result in any enjoyment for them anywhere.
Why?
Because even regarding unwholesome [karma], they possess independence due to Hari’s favor; for by the grace of the Blessed One, they have the power to prevent it, thinking, "May this not reach us."
By saying "let him not reach these" and "he goes elsewhere," it is indicated by the command of Hari alone that [the possession] belongs to himself;
by this, the cause for ownership is specified as being in the absence of any reason for prohibition.
As for what was stated—that [the rule] is not established because there is no distinction—that is unproven;
for he says that it is established because of the existence of specific scriptural texts, namely: "Only merit... and so forth.
"Only merit reaches him; he shall not reach the gods through sin"—such scriptural passages (śruti) are the authority for this matter [of liberation]. Manu 3.4.238a-d.
By this, he cites the Vedic scripture: "Merit alone goes to him; indeed, evil does not go to the gods.

"Him" refers to one who has entered another's body as its impeller through the meditation on the knowledge of the seven fires; such a person attains only the merit performed by that other person, not their evil.
Why?
Because he has been born as a god;
the meaning is that he does not attain [the state of] gods.
Regarding the meaning stated—that only what is auspicious occurs and not what is inauspicious—he states another establishing factor: "reasons" (*yuktayaḥ*).
...and other methods. (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.4.238d)
The others [are] distinct from the two previously mentioned;
the connection is that these are the proofs for the stated meaning.
To show what those arguments (yukti) are, he recites a scriptural statement: "Upasannā... and so forth.
For the fruit of the dharma of worship is residence in another body,
by the command of Vāsudeva and in accordance with one's prior karma.
For they constantly impel living beings toward merit and sin;
since they act without attachment or aversion, how could they incur any fault?
Merely by carrying out the command of Hari, merit is obtained by these [servants];
how then could they not attain auspiciousness through the performance of the worship of Hari?
For this reason, there is residence in another body, the impelling of merit and demerit after entering another's body,
and for the gods, the fruit of dharma produced by the worship of the Blessed One.
Therefore, how could those who incite others toward sin and the like incur any fault?
For a quality characterized by goodness (sāttvika-dharma) does not culminate in suffering;
the meaning is that it would contradict the nature of reality (tattva).
It is stated that instigating others toward sin and so forth within the city of the gods is not a cause of suffering,
because it is the fruit of sattvic dharma, just like the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).
Furthermore, those gods act solely by the command of Vāsudeva and not by their own will, strictly in accordance with the various prior karmas they have performed.
Therefore, since they constantly impel living beings toward merit and demerit without themselves possessing passion or aversion, how could they incur any fault?
The sense is that, like the king’s officers who punish thieves according to the master’s command and the nature of the offense, they are free from blame.
It is not merely that no evil accrues to the gods by impelling others toward sin and the like; rather—
However, by carrying out the command of Hari, these gods obtain merit alone, just like those who perform sacrifices such as the Jyotiṣṭoma.
Furthermore, since they are prompted by another (the Lord) for their own sake and have the intention that "this is the worship of Hari," how could the gods not attain auspiciousness?
Thus [ends] the conclusion. *11,352*
Therefore, O gods, the fruits of dharma and knowledge are swiftly attained by all living beings, from the lowest creatures up to Brahmā, in due order.
The phrase "only for those who possess knowledge of the Dharma" is to be applied here.
Although they reach [the realms] up to the world of Brahmā (āviriñca), they reach them respectively; thus, this statement of what was not previously mentioned is not a summary.
The gods obtain the fruits of knowledge and so forth that belong to others.
Regarding the inquiry as to how they belong to the realm of gods, it is said: "the gods."
For the gods alone are the distinguished controllers among the gods.
[This refers to] the gods who are inferior;
therefore, the result of their knowledge and so forth accrues to them—this is the implied meaning.
The phrase "But Brahmā" (*brahmā tu*) is an elaboration of what was stated as "up to Viriñca" (*āviriñcataḥ*).
But Brahmā is the controller of all the gods and of men;
therefore, he attains more of all virtues than anyone else.
The mention of "gods and so forth" (*devādi*) is illustrative (*upalakṣaṇa*).
"Excessively" (*adhika*) is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*).
Let it be that the gods obtain the fruit of knowledge and other qualities pertaining to others.
To the question of what the cause is for the gradations even therein, it is said: "Substance," and so forth.
The fruit is greater through ownership of property, independent cognition, and effort;
and among the gods, even that which belongs to others, the fruit of Brahmā is superior.
The statement regarding the determination of the fruit was uttered by Hari in the Bṛhattantra.

Substances refer to the sense faculties and so forth; independence with respect to them is "substance-independence. Consciousness and effort are the causes for the production of [wholesome] factors (*dharma*) and so on. The word "more" (*adhikaiḥ*) is to be understood as the ellipsis [of the comparison].
The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of including what was not explicitly mentioned.
It is "middling" because of middling independence of substance and so forth; it is "inferior" because of [only] slight [independence].
The meaning of the word "hi" (for/indeed) is that even among those gods, there is possession of unlimited independence of substance.
The phrase "determination of the fruit" (*phalanirṇaya*) is also a statement regarding a specific section [of the work].

He demonstrates the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of what was stated—that there is an excellence of fruit due to the excellence of the independence of the substance and so forth—by saying, "In the world as well."
For even in the world, an abundance of results is indeed observed through such qualities.
The meaning is that in agriculture, which is a composite activity involving such qualities as the aforementioned and additionally the independence over the material (the field) and so forth,

one observes a greater yield for whoever possesses greater independence over the field and other materials, and whoever possesses a greater degree of knowledge and effort regarding the sowing and other operations.
In this same manner, examples for the medium and small [degrees] should also be cited.
By this, what was stated—that there is a gradation of independence—is established as demonstrated.
Incidentally, he says "And thus" (*evaṃ ca*) to explain that the fruit of sin and so forth accrues to the instigating Asuras according to their respective degrees.
And thus, for those Asuras who were preceded by the Kali age, there would always be a great fruit in their unwholesome acts, such as false knowledge and the like.
The meaning is that [it refers] to "the Great" (mahat) and so forth among the great impellers.
Regarding "an inauspicious sign for inauspicious things," the word "hi" indicates the reason for its independence.
"Thus" refers to the example of the gods (*deva*). The connection is with the phrase "and of the asuras.
Regarding the matter previously stated, he provides another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) here with the verse beginning "Auspicious... (*śubha*).
The gods and the asuras shall obtain the fruits of their good and evil deeds according to their respective capacities and in due order, according to who was the instigator of each act.
"Even though they may be the instigators of sins, the gods shall not incur sin," for thus Hari spoke directly in the *Prakāśikā*. (Manu Smṛti 3.4.248)
The fruit is pure or impure according to the respective order;

"according to capacity" means "in due sequence"—this is the reasoning here. Its explanation is: "in whatever manner those various [causes] are the instigators, in that very manner [the result follows]."
The doubt and its resolution regarding the term "impellers" (*prerakāḥ*) are as before.
*11.356*. "The office of the officiating priest (*ārṭvijyam*), according to Auḍulomi, for he is hired for that purpose. *Oṃ*.

Om. There is an injunction for another auxiliary means; it is the third [kind of injunction], belonging to one who possesses that [knowledge], like the injunction regarding the beginning [of the sacrifice] and so forth. Om.

Having thus stated the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) through elaboration, he states the purport of the sūtra on the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) by means of a scriptural passage: "Even though... (*yadyapi*).
"Regarding the office of the officiating priest (*ārṭvijya*), [the sage] Auḍulomi [says] that [the seeker] is hired for that purpose.

(BS 3.4.45) "It is an injunction for another auxiliary act; according to one view, it is the third [kind of injunction], like the injunctions concerning one who possesses that [knowledge]. (BS 3.4.47)
Even so, although there is great fruit for both gods and Daityas from good and evil deeds, it shall accrue to the doer exactly as has been described.

Although it has been established in the manner just described that the fruit of action arises for both gods and demons from auspicious and inauspicious [deeds] such as knowledge and so forth, nevertheless, the fruit must indeed accrue to the agent, such as Devadatta. Furthermore, since this very point is the subject at hand in the scripture (*āgama*), the phrase "even though" (*yadyapi*) and so forth is appropriate.
This is what is meant:

it is accepted that gods and asuras experience the fruits of good and evil actions because this is established by valid cognition; however, the claim that these fruits belong to them alone is not tolerated.
But it occurs for the agent as well.

If one were to accept that the fruit belongs to the agent, there would be a contradiction with the restrictive scripture stating, "Whatever these creatures [do]," and a contradiction with the statement of Ātreya; therefore, it was said: "The great [fruit]."
The meaning is that for gods and others there is a great fruit, whereas for the agent there is little; furthermore, the intention to express a small [number] is frequently observed.
To the question "Why is the acceptance of fruit for the agent [asserted]? he says: "As has been stated."
The meaning is that this is because of the existence of Śruti and Smṛti;
these [scriptural citations] should be seen as they have been quoted in the Bhāṣya and other works.
He also states what is logical: "Therefore," etc.
Therefore, beginning with the best of men, [the results] consist of the experience of hell, the human state, heaven, and liberation. // MDh 3.4.250a-c //

The meaning is that it is only because of the existence of the fruits of good and evil for the agent that those beginning with the best of men, up to the gods and even down to the Daityas, are fit to experience [the results] starting from hell; it cannot be otherwise.
He states an exception to what was said: "But the gods... [etc.].
... but the gods [do not go] except to hell.
"But the Asuras, however, shall obtain even blinding darkness without liberation"—this is the word spoken by the Blessed One himself in the *Tattvaviveka*. (Manu 3.4.251)
They enjoy other fruits;
not only is there an absence of liberation for the asuras, but they shall even attain blinding darkness.
This is what is meant.
The best of humans attain hell, the human realm, heaven, and liberation;
the gods attain the human realm, heaven, and liberation;
and the asuras attain heaven, the human realm, hell, and the blinding darkness.
Furthermore, the hells and other such realms are not without cause,
nor is there any existence without the cause of one's own committed sins and so forth.
Therefore, it is understood that even for the agent, there is the attainment of the fruits of good and evil.
Otherwise, it would follow that hells and other realms of existence do not exist.

Nor should it be argued that although gods and asuras lack fruits resulting from their own agency, liberation and so forth are possible because of the existence of fruits caused by [another's] instigation;
for it is impossible for gods to attain human birth.
Because it is logically impossible for the Daityas to attain heaven and so forth,
and because it is in every way impossible for humans to fall into hell and so forth;
thus it was said, "beginning with the best of men."

By stating that [the performers] are the foremost among men and by mentioning various results such as hell, it is implied that "there is a word [of scripture to this effect]. Thus ends the section on the hearing of results (*phalaśruti*). *11,359*
[======= Section on Non-Confession =======] // Now begins the section on non-confession.
Oṃ. [The Lord] does not manifest [himself], because of the logical sequence. Oṃ.

Regarding the doubt as to whether the gift of knowledge should be performed through manifestation or without manifestation, [the author], because the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) here—as in the previous case—is not to be entirely rejected, states it in detail: "The gift of knowledge also... and so forth.
Because he does not manifest [the fault], [he is purified] through the sequence;
moreover, teachers who bestow knowledge shall obtain the fruit due to their distinction.
Not only the disciples, but even the teachers who bestow knowledge shall obtain the fruit of that knowledge;

and this [fruit] is especially superior to that of the disciple. Although the status of "teacher" alone would have sufficed, the inclusion of the term "bestower of knowledge" is for the purpose of making it known that [the fruit is obtained] specifically through the gift of knowledge.
The word "ca" (and) includes the Supreme Teacher and others.
To the question "Why is this so?", he says: "In liberation."
The teacher receives from the disciple eightfold the excellent merit that has been released.
Twice that amount is for his teacher; from him, it is half as much again;
beyond that, the other gods receive a thousandfold more in successive order.
"Brahmā has declared this very determination of the fruit, multiplied by a great flood [of years], himself in the treatise titled *Guruvṛtta*. (Manu Smṛti 3.4.254)
The fruit that a teacher obtains from the gift of knowledge by means of a disciple’s disciple is eightfold greater than the fruit obtained from that disciple;
and the teacher of that teacher obtains twice the fruit of that [latter] teacher,
because he is the cause of the lineage.
Beyond that, other gurus than the Supreme Guru obtain half as much fruit again, in consideration of the fruit for their own disciples;
thus, by this sequence of obtaining one and a half times [the fruit], because they set the divine command (*ājñā*) in motion, it is multiplied a thousandfold.
This phrase "by that sequence from the latter onwards" is also connected with the statement that Brahmā is multiplied by the Great Current (*mahaugha*).
The terms "thousand" and "great flood" are used for the sake of illustration, because the succession [of teachers] is not fixed.
He states that there is also reasoning for this matter established by scripture: "And that is logical."
And that is appropriate... // Mānava 3.4.254c //

It is established by reason that the fruit of the teacher’s gift of knowledge is greater than the fruit of knowledge obtained by the disciple who receives it. He indicates that reasoning with the words: "No... [Mānava Dharma Śāstra 3.4.254cd]: "...the giver of a cow would not obtain the fruit of merely a cow."
For the recipient indeed obtains the fruit equivalent to the mere cow; however, the giver of the cow does not obtain a fruit limited to the cow alone,
but rather attains a great fruit such as rebirth in heaven and so forth.
The meaning is that as it is in this case, so it is in the present instance as well. Herein is the formal argument (*prayoga*):

The giver of knowledge possesses a fruit of giving that is superior even to the fruit of the object given, because he is a giver of an object that serves as the cause for the human goal (*puruṣārtha*), just like a giver of cows.

Regarding the fact that the fruit of imparting knowledge by a teacher is even greater than the fruit of [one's own] realization of knowledge, he cites a passage from the Bhagavad Gītā as corroborative evidence: "He who... and so forth.
He who shall proclaim this supreme secret among my devotees,
having established the highest devotion toward me, will undoubtedly come to me alone.
"And there shall be no one among men who does more for me than he;
nor shall there be anyone else on earth dearer to me than he," thus said the Blessed One... [MAnu 3.4.256a-e]
The subsequent sentence, "he will request [instruction]," should be read here.

Since the giving of knowledge and the propagation of its tradition yield such great fruit, it might follow that one should give knowledge by revealing it for the sake of many people; in response to this, he states the established conclusion: "even so."
... even so ... // Mānava-dharmaśāstra 3.4.256ef //
It is true that the gift of knowledge yields great fruit in the manner described; nevertheless, it should not be performed without disclosure. Why? To this he says: "The worthy recipient" (pātra).
...a vessel is required. // MAnu 3.256f //
The phrase "by the fruit of giving" is the ellipsis.
Indeed, a gift bestowed upon a worthy recipient (pātra) is sufficient for its fruit; it is not so when given to an unworthy recipient (apātra).
On the contrary, it is indeed a cause for spiritual transgression (*pratyavāya*).
By revealing [the teaching] and bestowing knowledge even upon those who are unfit, one incurs that [transgression];
and the point is that such an act is prohibited.
Thus concludes the section on non-disclosure (*anāviṣkārādhikaraṇa*).
Now begins the section on results pertaining to this life (*aihikādhikaraṇa*) and the section on liberation as the fruit (*muktiphalādhikaraṇa*).
// Oṃ. [The fruit] belongs to this life, provided there is no obstruction; for that is seen. Oṃ.//
Oṃ. Thus, there is no restriction regarding the fruits of liberation, because that state is firmly established; because that state is firmly established, Oṃ.
He states the purport of the two sections briefly: "In this very way," and so forth.

Even in this life, [the fruit of knowledge may arise] provided there is no obstruction by what is not yet commenced, for that is observed. Thus, there is no fixed rule regarding the fruit of liberation, because that state is determined; because that state is determined, it is exactly so through non-contradiction with the very karma already set in motion.
Knowledge is said to have its fruit visible here and now, and liberation is attained even in this very life.

The purport of the first section is that knowledge is said to have its fruit perceived precisely because it is not in contradiction with *prārabdha* karma. "Having a perceived fruit" (*dṛṣṭaphalam*) means that the fruit is perceived; knowledge arises immediately after the completion of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and the other practices, provided there is no obstruction from *prārabdha* karma.
"But when that [body] exists, there is the end of that"— thus,
for the second [type of person], liberation is indeed obtained right here.
In whichever body knowledge has arisen, liberation is obtained immediately after the fall of that body, provided there is no obstruction from *prārabdha* karma.
"In the absence of darkness [it does not exist], but when that [darkness] exists, it [ends].

Thus concludes the final quarter of the third chapter in this commentary on the *Anuvyākhyāna*— the work of the venerable Pūrṇaprajña Bhagavatpāda— composed by the ascetic named Praguṇajayatīrtha as an exposition of the meanings of difficult words and sentences.
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the third chapter in the illustrious Nyāyasudhā.
